Yet local government often has a bigger effect on our daily lives.
In many countries, each city, county or district has a council.
Its members, called councilors, are elected by the residents of the area, usually every four or five years.
In some places, the council is led by a mayor, who is also elected.
Councils are responsible for many of the services that we use every day without thinking.
They collect rubbish, repair roads, look after parks and run public libraries.
They also decide where new houses, shops and schools can be built.
If a company wants to open a factory, for example, it usually needs permission from the local authority.
To pay for all this, councils receive money from the national government, and they also collect local taxes from residents and businesses.
Deciding how to spend a limited budget is one of their hardest jobs.
Should the money go to a new sports center or to care for elderly people?
Because these decisions affect them directly, residents are encouraged to take part.
Council meetings are usually open to the public, and anyone can contact their representative with a complaint or an idea.
Yet in many places, fewer than one in three people vote in local elections.
Not long ago, many people felt embarrassed about wearing second-hand clothes.
Buying used clothing was something you did only if you could not afford anything else.
Today, the situation has changed dramatically.
Second-hand fashion is one of the fastest-growing parts of the clothing industry, and it is particularly popular with young consumers.
There are several reasons for this trend.
The first is price.
A designer jacket that costs hundreds of dollars when it is brand-new may cost only a fraction of that price a year later.
The second is technology.
Apps and websites have made it easy to sell unwanted items and to find exactly what you are looking for, in your size, in minutes.
The third reason is concern for the environment.
The fashion industry produces a huge amount of waste.
Millions of tons of clothes are thrown away every year, and producing new clothes uses large amounts of water and energy.
By choosing used clothes, consumers can reduce this impact, even if only slightly.
Not everyone is happy about the change, however.
Some charity shops say that they now receive fewer good-quality items, because people prefer to sell them online.
And some critics point out that cheap second-hand clothes may simply encourage people to buy even more.
Still, for many shoppers, a good second-hand find feels better than anything new.
The first electric cars were built more than a hundred years ago, but for most of the twentieth century they were little more than a curiosity.
Petrol engines were cheaper and more powerful, and fuel was easy to find.
Today, however, electric vehicles are one of the biggest stories in the car industry.
In some countries, they already make up the majority of new cars sold.
What has changed?
The main factor is the battery.
Modern batteries can store far more energy than older ones, so a typical electric car can now travel several hundred kilometers on a single charge.
At the same time, the cost of batteries has fallen dramatically as production has increased.
Many governments have also encouraged drivers to switch by offering lower taxes or money towards a new vehicle.
Supporters point out that electric cars produce no emissions from the car itself, which means cleaner air in cities.
They are also quieter and cheaper to run, because electricity usually costs less than petrol.
However, there are still challenges.
Charging takes longer than filling a tank, and in many areas there are not enough public charging points.
Producing batteries also requires large amounts of metals, and mining them can damage the environment.
Finally, an electric car is only as clean as the electricity that powers it.
If that electricity comes from coal, the benefits are much smaller.
Everyone feels stressed from time to time: before an exam, during a job interview or when there is too much work and too little time.
But what actually happens in our bodies when we are under pressure?
Stress is the body's natural response to a threat.
When the brain senses danger, it releases hormones such as adrenaline.
Our heart beats faster, our breathing speeds up and our muscles become tense, so that we are ready to fight or to run away.
For our ancestors, who had to escape from wild animals, this reaction could save their lives.
In modern life, the threats are different, but the reaction is the same.
A little stress can actually be useful.
It helps us to focus and to perform well in a race or an exam.
The problem begins when stress continues for weeks or months.
Long-term stress can lead to headaches, sleeping problems and anxiety, and it increases the risk of depression and heart disease.
Fortunately, there are effective ways to manage it.
Regular exercise is one of the best, because it helps the body to use up those stress hormones.
Slow, deep breathing can calm the body in just a few minutes.
Talking to friends, spending time outdoors and getting enough sleep also make a real difference.
If stress becomes too much to deal with alone, it is important to ask for professional help.
The ancient Olympic Games ended more than 1,500 years ago.
For centuries, the stadium at Olympia lay buried under sand and mud.
Then, at the end of the nineteenth century, a French baron called Pierre de Coubertin had an idea.
Coubertin believed that sport could make young people healthier, give them motivation and help different nations to understand each other.
In 1894, he organized a meeting in Paris, and representatives from several countries agreed to revive the Games.
It was decided that the first modern Olympics would take place in 1896 in Athens, as a tribute to ancient Greece.
Those first Games were very different from the huge international event we know today.
Only about 240 athletes from 14 nations participated, and all of them were men.
There were no professional athletes, and some competitors were simply tourists who happened to be in Athens at the time.
Winners received a silver medal and an olive branch, not gold.
Nevertheless, the athletes were eager to win, and the Greek public was extremely proud.
The most memorable moment came in the marathon, a new race based on an ancient Greek legend.
It was won by Spyridon Louis, a Greek water carrier, and the crowd in the stadium went wild.
Women were allowed to compete for the first time four years later, in Paris.
Since then, the Games have grown into one of the largest and most impressive events on Earth, with more than 10,000 athletes from over 200 nations.
Coubertin's dream of bringing the world together through sport had come true.
Every morning, millions of people read the news, either on paper or on a screen.
But few of them think about the work that goes into each edition.
The day at a newspaper usually begins with a meeting.
The editors discuss the most important stories and decide which journalists will cover them.
Some stories are planned weeks in advance, such as elections or major sports events.
Others, like accidents or natural disasters, can happen at any moment.
A journalist's job is not simply to write.
First, they must collect information: they interview witnesses, speak to experts and read official documents.
A good journalist always checks facts with more than one source.
For a serious investigation, this process can take months.
When the article is ready, an editor reads it carefully.
They check that it is accurate and fair, cut anything unnecessary and write a headline that will attract readers.
Photographers and designers then decide how the page will look.
In the past, everything had to be finished by the evening, when the printing presses started.
Today, most news is published online first and updated throughout the day.
This means that journalists work faster than ever, but the basic rules remain the same: find the truth, check it and explain it clearly.
Every year, hundreds of thousands of young people travel abroad to work as volunteers.
They teach English in village schools, build houses, or help to protect wildlife.
Many of them describe it as the best experience of their lives.
But in recent years, some experts have started to ask whether this kind of travel really helps.
Supporters point out the benefits for everyone involved.
Volunteers learn about another culture, develop new skills and become more aware of global problems.
Local communities, in turn, receive extra help and money, since volunteers usually pay to take part.
Critics, however, argue that short trips can do more harm than good.
A volunteer who stays for two weeks may not have the skills that are really needed.
Building a school, for example, may take jobs away from local builders who need the income.
Some organizations have been criticized for running "voluntourism" programs that are more about business than about helping.
The most serious concerns involve children: visitors who come and go every few weeks can be harmful for children in orphanages.
So what should a responsible volunteer do?
Experts recommend choosing an organization carefully, staying for longer periods, and looking for projects that are run by local people.
It is also worth asking a simple question before you go: "Am I the right person for this job?"
Coral reefs cover less than one percent of the ocean floor, yet they are home to about a quarter of all marine species.
That is why scientists often call them "the rainforests of the sea."
Although corals look like colorful rocks or plants, they are actually animals.
Each coral is made of thousands of tiny creatures that build hard skeletons around themselves.
Over thousands of years, these skeletons form huge structures.
The largest of them, the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, can even be seen from space.
Corals live in a close partnership with tiny algae, which live inside them and give them both food and color.
However, this relationship is extremely sensitive to temperature.
When the water becomes too warm, the corals push the algae out and turn white.
This is known as bleaching.
If the water cools down quickly, the corals can recover, but if the heat continues, they die.
As the climate warms, bleaching events are becoming more frequent and more severe.
Reefs also suffer from pollution, fishing with explosives and damage from boats.
The loss of reefs would be a disaster not only for wildlife but also for people.
Hundreds of millions of people depend on them for food, tourism and protection from storms.
Scientists are now working to protect the reefs that remain and to grow new corals that can survive in warmer water.
The word "democracy" comes from two Greek words that mean "people" and "power."
In a democracy, power belongs to the citizens, who choose their leaders in free elections.
Today, most countries in the world hold elections of some kind, but experts say that elections alone do not make a country truly democratic.
So what else is needed?
First, voters must have a real choice between different parties and candidates, including those who oppose the government.
Second, the rules of the game are usually written in a constitution.
This document describes how the country is governed and what rights its citizens have.
In most democracies, power is divided between three parts of the state.
A parliament makes the laws, a government carries them out, and courts decide whether laws have been broken.
This division means that no single person or group can control everything.
Third, citizens need basic civil rights, such as freedom of speech and freedom of the press.
If journalists cannot criticize the president without being sent to prison, elections cannot be truly free.
Independent courts are equally important, because they protect individuals when the government acts illegally.
Finally, democracy depends on the idea of equality: every adult has one vote, whether they are rich or poor.
The majority wins, but the rights of minorities must still be respected.
The British leader Winston Churchill famously joked that democracy was the worst form of government, apart from all the others that had been tried.
It is slow, messy and full of arguments, but most people who have lived without it would not want to go back.
Every society has to decide what to do with people who break the law.
For serious crimes, the most common answer is prison.
But does locking people up actually reduce crime?
Supporters of prison give several reasons.
First, it protects the public: while a violent criminal is in jail, he or she cannot harm anyone else.
Second, the threat of punishment may stop people from committing crimes in the first place.
Third, many victims feel that justice has been done only when the guilty person is punished.
Critics, however, point to the numbers.
In many countries, a large proportion of prisoners commit another crime within a few years of their release.
Prison separates people from their families and jobs, and inside they may meet other criminals and learn new ways to break the law.
It is also extremely expensive: keeping one person in prison for a year can cost as much as a year at a top university.
Some countries have tried a different approach.
In Norway, prisons focus on education and training, and prisoners live in conditions that are as close as possible to normal life.
The country has one of the lowest rates in the world of people who reoffend.
Other alternatives include community service, where offenders do unpaid work, and restorative programs that bring criminals and their victims together to talk.
There is no simple answer, but most experts agree on one thing: if we want less crime, punishment alone is not enough.
Every minute, you breathe in and out between twelve and twenty times, usually without thinking about it.
But what happens to the air after it enters your body?
The answer is a remarkable journey that keeps every cell in your body alive.
When you breathe in, air travels down your throat and into your lungs.
Inside the lungs, it passes through smaller and smaller tubes until it reaches hundreds of millions of tiny air bags called alveoli.
Their walls are extremely thin and surrounded by blood vessels.
Here, oxygen passes from the air into the blood, while carbon dioxide, a waste gas, moves in the opposite direction and is breathed out.
The oxygen is then carried by red blood cells.
Each of these cells contains a substance called hemoglobin, which holds on to oxygen and gives blood its red color.
The heart pumps this blood through the arteries to every organ and muscle in the body.
A complete trip around the body takes only about a minute.
Why do our cells need oxygen?
They use it to turn the food we eat into energy.
Without oxygen, brain cells begin to die within about five minutes, which is why breathing problems are always a medical emergency.
When we exercise, our muscles need more energy, so we breathe faster and our heart beats harder to supply them.
Regular exercise makes the heart and lungs stronger and more efficient.
This is why fit people often have a slow heart rate when they are resting: each beat moves more blood.
Smoking, on the other hand, damages the alveoli and makes it harder for oxygen to reach the blood.
Starting university is exciting, but it can also be a shock.
Life as a freshman is very different from life at school, and many students need a few months to adjust.
One of the biggest differences is independence.
At university, nobody checks whether you have done your homework or come to class.
Professors give lectures to hundreds of students at a time, and you are expected to read and study on your own.
The academic year is usually divided into two semesters.
In each semester, you take several courses, and your final grade often depends on essays, assignments and a big examination at the end.
Deadlines are strict: if you hand in an assignment late, you may lose marks or even fail the course.
It is a good idea to use a calendar and to start big assignments early.
Money is another challenge.
Tuition fees can be very high, especially in countries like the United States, and many students take out loans.
However, there are other options.
Many universities offer scholarships to students with excellent grades or particular talents, and some give financial aid to students from poor families.
Finally, university is not only about studying.
Most campuses have dozens of clubs and societies, from sports teams to film groups and volunteer organizations.
Joining one is one of the best ways to make friends and to develop skills that employers value.
By the time they reach graduation, most students say that many of the most important things they learned did not happen in the lecture hall.
Until the eighteenth century, most people lived in the countryside and worked on farms.
Goods were made by hand, and the fastest way to travel was on a horse.
Then, in Britain, a series of inventions changed everything.
The most important of these was the steam engine.
Early steam engines were used to pump water out of coal mines.
In the 1760s and 1770s, the Scottish engineer James Watt made them far more efficient, and soon they were powering machines in factories.
Cotton cloth, which had been made slowly at home, could now be produced in huge quantities.
Towns like Manchester grew rapidly as people moved from villages to work in the new mills.
Steam also transformed transport.
In 1830, the first modern railway opened between Liverpool and Manchester, with trains pulled by steam locomotives.
Journeys that had taken days now took hours, and goods could be transported cheaply across the country.
Within a few decades, railways had spread across Europe and North America.
But this Industrial Revolution had a dark side.
Factory workers, including young children, often worked fourteen hours a day in dangerous conditions for very low wages.
Cities were crowded and dirty, diseases spread quickly, and smoke from burning coal filled the air.
It took many years of protests and new laws before working conditions improved.
Today, historians see this period as one of the most important turning points in human history.
It created the modern world, with all its benefits and all its problems.
In recent years, the news has been full of extreme weather: record-breaking heat waves, severe floods and powerful storms.
Scientists agree that climate change is making many of these events more frequent and more intense.
But how exactly does a warmer planet lead to more extreme weather?
The first link is simple: when the average temperature rises, heat waves become hotter and last longer.
A heat wave that happened once every fifty years in the past is now several times more likely.
Such heat is not just uncomfortable; it can be deadly, especially for elderly people.
The second link involves water.
Warm air can hold more moisture than cold air, about seven percent more for every degree Celsius.
When this moisture falls, it can produce much heavier rainfall than before, which increases the risk of flooding.
At the same time, heat dries out the soil faster, so regions that are already dry can suffer longer droughts.
In other words, a warmer climate can make both wet and dry extremes worse.
Warmer oceans also give more energy to tropical storms.
There is evidence that the strongest hurricanes are becoming more common, even if the total number of storms is not increasing.
Of course, not every storm or hot day can be blamed on climate change; the weather has always varied.
However, scientists can now calculate how much more likely a particular event has become.
This field, known as attribution science, helps communities to understand the risks they face and to prepare for the future.
Better forecasts, early warning systems and stronger buildings can save thousands of lives.
For many cities, tourism is a blessing and a curse at the same time.
Visitors bring money, create jobs and support local businesses, from hotels and restaurants to souvenir shops.
Across the world, travel and tourism provide around one job in ten.
But when too many people visit the same place at the same time, problems begin.
This is known as overtourism.
In Venice, fewer than 50,000 people now live in the historic center, but tens of thousands of day visitors can arrive on a single busy day.
Narrow streets become so crowded that residents can hardly walk to work.
Rents rise as apartments are turned into holiday rentals, and many local people are forced to move out.
Some destinations have decided to take action.
In 2024, Venice introduced an entry fee for day visitors on its busiest days.
Amsterdam has stopped the building of new hotels in the city.
Other places are encouraging tourists to visit in the low season or to explore less famous areas.
Not everyone agrees with these measures.
Business owners worry that fewer visitors will mean less income, and some critics say that fees turn cities into theme parks for the rich.
Finding the right balance is not easy.
As travelers, however, we can help by choosing quieter times of year, staying in hotels rather than in apartments meant for residents, and respecting the places we visit.
In the darkest months of the year, people in many parts of the world celebrate with light.
Although these festivals come from very different traditions, they share a similar message: light is stronger than darkness.
Diwali, the festival of lights, is one of the most important celebrations for Hindus, Sikhs and Jains.
It takes place in October or November and lasts for five days.
Families clean their homes, light small oil lamps called diyas and set off fireworks.
They also share sweets and visit relatives, and the atmosphere is full of warmth and affection.
For many Hindus, Diwali celebrates the victory of good over evil.
Hanukkah is a Jewish festival that lasts for eight nights, usually in December.
It remembers an ancient story in which a small amount of oil burned for eight days in the temple in Jerusalem.
Each night, families light one more candle on a special candle holder, until all eight are burning.
Children often play games and receive small gifts.
In Thailand, the festival of Loy Krathong takes place on the night of the full moon in November.
People make small floating baskets from banana leaves and flowers, put a candle inside, and let them float away on rivers and lakes.
Many believe that this carries away bad luck and shows respect to the water.
For Christians, Christmas is also a festival of light, and candles and colorful lights decorate streets and homes.
Whatever their religious meaning, these cultural celebrations bring communities together at a time of year when the nights are long and cold.
Perhaps that is why they have lasted for so many centuries.
Every day, the average person sees hundreds of advertisements.
They appear on television, on buses, in apps and on social media.
Most of the time, we hardly notice them, and many of us believe that advertising has no effect on us.
Yet companies around the world now spend more than a trillion dollars a year on it, so it must work somehow.
One of the main aims of advertising is to build a brand.
A brand is more than a name or a logo; it is the set of feelings and ideas that people connect with a product.
Think of a famous sports company: its adverts rarely talk about the quality of its shoes.
Instead, they show athletes winning, and they make us feel that we could be winners too.
Advertisers also rely on repetition.
Psychologists have found that the more often we see something, the more we tend to like it, even if we do not remember seeing it.
That is why the same slogan or tune can be repeated for years.
Another powerful tool is the celebrity.
When a famous actor or singer promotes a product, some of their popularity transfers to it.
Today, many brands also pay influencers on social media, who can seem more trustworthy than traditional stars because they look like ordinary people.
In many countries, influencers must clearly label posts that are sponsored, but not all of them do.
Understanding these techniques does not make us immune to them, but it helps.
Next time you see an advert, ask yourself: what exactly is it trying to make me feel?
Fifty years ago, the typical family in many countries looked much the same: a married couple with two or three children.
Usually, the father went out to work and the mother stayed at home.
Today, that picture is much more varied.
One of the biggest changes is the age at which people start a family.
In most rich countries, the average woman now has her first child at around thirty, several years later than in the 1970s.
People spend longer in education, they want to establish their careers first, and housing has become expensive.
Families have also become smaller, and many couples have one child or none at all.
The structure of families has changed, too.
Divorce is more common than it was, and many children grow up with a single parent or in blended families with step-parents, half-brothers and half-sisters.
More couples live together without getting married.
At the same time, people are living much longer, so it is increasingly common for four generations of one family to be alive at once.
These changes bring new challenges.
Many parents struggle to find childcare they can afford, and in households where both adults work full-time, sharing the housework can cause tension.
Meanwhile, many middle-aged adults find themselves looking after their own children and their elderly parents at the same time.
However, some things have not changed at all.
Surveys show that most people still name their family as the most important thing in their lives.
The shape of the family may be different, but its role, providing love, support and a sense of belonging, remains the same.
The universe is almost unbelievably big.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way, contains hundreds of billions of stars, and there are hundreds of billions of galaxies.
With so many stars, many scientists think it is very likely that life exists somewhere else.
But so far, we have found no proof at all.
In the past thirty years, astronomers have made a remarkable discovery: most stars have planets orbiting around them.
More than 5,000 of these distant worlds have now been confirmed.
Some are about the same size as the Earth and lie at the right distance from their star for liquid water to exist on the surface.
Since water is essential for life as we know it, these planets are the most exciting places to search.
Closer to home, scientists are exploring our own solar system.
Mars was once warm and wet, and robots are now searching its rocks for signs of ancient life.
Beneath the frozen surface of Europa, one of Jupiter's moons, there is probably a huge ocean of salty water.
Even if we only found simple bacteria there, it would be one of the greatest discoveries in history.
Other researchers are listening for signals from intelligent civilizations.
For more than sixty years, radio telescopes have searched the sky, but they have heard nothing clear.
Perhaps the distances are too great, or perhaps intelligent life is extremely rare.
For now, the question remains one of the greatest mysteries in science.
Look at the food on your plate tonight and ask yourself: where did it come from?
The rice may have been grown in Thailand, the beef raised in Brazil, and the apples picked in New Zealand.
In a modern supermarket, food from dozens of countries sits side by side.
This global food system is the result of cheap transport and advanced technology.
Refrigerated ships, trucks and planes can move fresh food across the world in days.
As a result, consumers can buy strawberries in winter and tropical fruit all year round.
For many poorer countries, exporting food to rich markets is an important source of income.
In recent years, however, people have started to worry about "food miles," the distance that food travels before it reaches us.
Transport uses fuel and produces greenhouse gases, so many shoppers assume that local food is always better for the environment.
The reality is more complicated.
Studies have found that transport is usually only a small part of the total impact of food.
The way it is produced often matters much more.
For example, tomatoes grown in heated greenhouses in a cold country can have a larger impact than tomatoes grown outdoors in Spain and brought in by truck.
Flying food by air, on the other hand, is extremely damaging, although only a small share of food travels this way.
So what should a responsible consumer do?
Experts suggest eating food that is in season, reducing waste, and eating less red meat, which has by far the largest impact of all.
Buying local can still be a good choice, especially because it supports farmers in your area.
But the distance on the label does not tell the whole story.
Every day, our bodies are attacked by viruses and bacteria.
Most of the time, we do not even notice, because the immune system defends us.
However, when a new virus enters the body for the first time, the immune system does not recognize it.
It needs several days to learn about the virus and to produce antibodies against it.
Meanwhile, the infection can spread, and the person may become seriously ill.
A vaccine trains the immune system in advance.
It contains a weak or dead form of the virus, a small harmless piece of it, or instructions that tell our cells to make that piece.
The body reacts as if it had been infected, and it remembers the enemy.
If the real virus arrives later, the immune system recognizes it immediately and destroys it before it can cause serious harm.
The idea is more than two hundred years old.
In 1796, an English doctor called Edward Jenner noticed that people who had caught cowpox, a mild disease, did not catch smallpox, which killed millions.
After a long campaign of mass vaccination, smallpox was officially declared eradicated in 1980.
Vaccines protect not only the people who receive them but also the whole community.
When enough people are vaccinated, a disease cannot spread easily, so newborn babies and people with certain illnesses, who cannot be vaccinated, are protected as well.
Most side effects, such as a sore arm or a slight fever, are mild and disappear within a day or two.
Serious reactions are extremely rare.
Today, vaccines save millions of lives every year, which makes them one of the most effective medical inventions in history.
A placebo is a fake treatment: a sugar pill or an injection of salt water with no medical ingredients at all.
Yet in experiment after experiment, a large number of patients who take one report that they feel better.
This is known as the placebo effect, and it is one of the most fascinating puzzles in medicine.
The effect is so powerful that it has changed the way new medicines are tested.
In a typical trial, one group of patients receives the real drug and another group receives a placebo.
Neither the patients nor the doctors know who is getting which.
A new medicine is only approved if it works clearly better than the fake one.
Placebos work best for symptoms that the brain helps to control, such as pain, nausea and anxiety.
They cannot cure an infection or repair a broken bone.
Scientists believe that expectation plays a key role: when we believe a treatment will help, the brain can release natural painkillers called endorphins.
The details matter, too.
In one study, people said that an expensive placebo reduced their pain more than a cheap one, although both pills were identical.
The effect also works in the opposite direction.
When patients are warned about possible side effects, some of them experience those problems even if they are only taking sugar.
This is called the nocebo effect.
Doctors cannot ethically lie to their patients, of course.
But the placebo effect shows that the way a doctor explains a treatment, and the trust between doctor and patient, can make a real difference to how we feel.
Economies do not grow at a steady rate.
Instead, they move in cycles of boom and bust, sometimes over a few years and sometimes over decades.
During a boom, businesses expand and hire more workers, so unemployment falls.
People feel confident about the future, so they spend more money on houses, cars and holidays.
This extra demand encourages businesses to invest and grow even further.
But if the economy grows too fast, prices start to rise quickly, and this inflation makes everyday life more expensive.
Sooner or later, something goes wrong.
Banks may lend too much money to people who cannot pay it back, or the price of oil may suddenly jump.
When that happens, the economy can enter a recession.
Businesses cut costs and workers lose their jobs, so consumers spend less, which causes even more businesses to struggle.
Economists call this a vicious circle.
The worst example in modern history was the Great Depression of the 1930s, when about a quarter of American workers were unemployed.
A more recent case was the financial crisis of 2008, which began when house prices in the United States fell sharply and several large banks collapsed.
To limit the damage, governments and central banks usually respond in two ways.
They lower interest rates to make borrowing cheaper, and they spend public money on projects that create jobs.
They also support people who have lost their income.
How much a government should do, and how much debt it should take on, remains one of the biggest debates in economics.
In many countries, the law protects consumers from unfair treatment.
The details vary from place to place, but the basic principles are similar.
Knowing them can save you money and a lot of stress.
First, goods must be as described.
If you order a blue wool sweater and receive a grey cotton one, you are entitled to your money back.
Second, products must be of reasonable quality and must work properly for a reasonable time.
If a product is faulty, the seller must repair it, replace it or give you a refund.
In the European Union, this legal guarantee lasts for at least two years, whatever the shop's own warranty says.
Buying online gives you extra protection.
In the EU, for example, you usually have fourteen days to return something you bought online, even if there is nothing wrong with it.
The rules are different for some items, such as food or personalized products.
A few simple habits make it easier to use your rights.
Keep your receipts, or at least a photo of them.
If a parcel arrives damaged, take pictures before you open it completely.
And remember that items bought in a sale are still covered if they are faulty.
If you need to complain, stay polite but firm.
Explain the problem clearly, say exactly what you want, and write down the name of the person you speak to.
If the shop refuses to help, a consumer organization or the relevant government office can often give you free advice.
At its height, around the year 117, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to the Middle East.
Tens of millions of people lived under Roman law, used Roman money and traveled on Roman roads.
Yet in 476, the last emperor in the West, a teenager called Romulus Augustulus, was removed by a Germanic leader named Odoacer.
How could such a powerful empire collapse?
Historians have argued about this question for centuries.
One German historian, Alexander Demandt, collected 210 different explanations that people have suggested.
Most experts today agree that there was no single cause, but a combination of problems.
The first was size.
The empire's borders were thousands of kilometers long and extremely difficult to defend.
The army needed hundreds of thousands of soldiers, and paying for them required high taxes.
The second was the economy.
To pay their bills, emperors put less and less silver into coins, so the currency lost its value and prices rose.
The third was political chaos.
In the third century, more than twenty emperors ruled in about fifty years, and many of them were murdered by their own soldiers.
Eventually, the empire was divided into an eastern half and a western half.
The weaker West suffered one invasion after another, and Rome itself was sacked by the Goths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455.
The eastern half, later called the Byzantine Empire, survived for almost another thousand years, until Constantinople fell in 1453.
A full-length animated film from a major studio can take four or five years to make and involve hundreds of artists.
Although every studio works slightly differently, the process usually follows the same basic steps.
Everything begins with the story.
Writers develop the script, and artists draw thousands of storyboards, simple sketches that show every scene like a comic.
The team watches these drawings with rough sound, and scenes that do not work are changed or removed.
Next, actors record the voices.
This usually happens before the animation itself, so that animators can match the characters' mouths and expressions to the recording.
In computer animation, artists then build digital models of the characters, the buildings and even the trees.
Each character is given a kind of digital skeleton, called a rig, so that it can move.
Animators set the most important poses, and the computer helps to calculate the movements in between.
It is slow, careful work: an animator may produce only a few seconds of film in a week.
After that, lighting artists decide where the light comes from and how shadows fall.
Then the computers render the final images.
A film shows twenty-four images, or frames, every second, so a ninety-minute film needs almost 130,000 of them, and a single frame can take hours to render.
Finally, music and sound effects are added.
The first film made entirely by computer, Toy Story, was released in 1995, and since then the technology has improved enormously.
A hundred years ago, wolves were seen as dangerous pests in the United States.
They were hunted, trapped and poisoned, and by the 1920s they had disappeared completely from Yellowstone National Park.
At the time, few people imagined the effect this would have on the park.
Without wolves to hunt them, the number of elk, a large kind of deer, grew rapidly.
The elk ate the young trees that grew along the rivers, and their huge herds could feed in the same valleys all winter without fear.
With fewer trees, the riverbanks began to wash away, and animals that depended on the trees, such as beavers and many birds, became rare.
In 1995 and 1996, scientists brought thirty-one wolves from Canada and released them in the park.
The results were remarkable.
Elk numbers fell, and the animals changed their behavior, moving more often and avoiding some open areas.
In some places, trees began to recover, beavers returned, and the rivers became healthier.
Scientists call this kind of chain reaction a trophic cascade.
However, the story is not as simple as it sounds.
Researchers still debate how much of the change was caused by wolves and how much by other factors, such as bears, hunting by humans and dry weather.
Wolves also remain controversial outside the park, because they sometimes kill farmers' cattle and sheep.
Still, Yellowstone has become a famous example of how one species can shape an entire ecosystem.
When you use a map on your phone, it seems almost magical: a small blue dot shows exactly where you are.
But your phone is actually listening to satellites that are thousands of kilometers away.
The Global Positioning System, or GPS, is a network of about thirty satellites that orbit the Earth at a height of around 20,000 kilometers.
Each one goes around the planet twice a day.
The satellites carry extremely accurate atomic clocks, and they constantly broadcast signals that say what time it is and where the satellite is.
Your phone receives these signals, which travel at the speed of light.
Because it takes a tiny amount of time for each signal to arrive, the phone can calculate its distance from each satellite.
With signals from at least four satellites, it can work out its exact position on the Earth.
A typical phone can locate you to within a few meters.
The system has to be extremely precise.
A timing error of just one millionth of a second would put your position about 300 meters away.
In fact, engineers even have to correct the clocks for Einstein's theory of relativity.
Because the satellites move fast and are far from the Earth, their clocks run slightly faster than clocks on the ground.
Without a correction, GPS would become useless within a day.
GPS belongs to the United States, but Europe, Russia and China have built their own systems, called Galileo, GLONASS and BeiDou.
Today, these networks are used for far more than finding restaurants.
They guide ships and planes, help farmers to plant crops in straight lines, and provide the exact time for banks and phone networks.
More than half of the people in the world use two or more languages in their daily lives.
For many of them, this began at birth.
They grew up with one language at home and another at school, or with parents who spoke different languages.
For a long time, many experts believed that learning two languages at once would confuse young children and delay their development.
Modern research does not support this belief.
Bilingual children generally reach the main stages of language development at the same ages as other children.
They may know fewer words in each language.
But when both languages are counted together, their vocabulary is usually just as large.
Many bilingual children mix their languages in the same sentence.
Parents sometimes worry about this, but it is completely normal, and adults do it too.
Linguists call it code-switching, and they see it as a sign of skill, not of confusion.
Some studies also suggest that bilingual people are better at switching between tasks and ignoring distractions, although the evidence is mixed.
Raising a bilingual child is not always easy.
Some families follow a "one parent, one language" rule; others speak one language at home and leave the other to school.
A common problem is that children start to refuse the home language when they notice that their friends do not speak it.
Books, films, visits to relatives and conversations with grandparents can help to keep it alive.
After all, a language is not only a tool for communication; it is also a connection to a family's history, culture and identity.
Moving into your first apartment is an exciting step, but it comes with new responsibilities.
A little preparation can save you money and stress later.
Before you sign the lease, read it carefully.
Check how long it lasts, how much the rent is, and whether bills such as water or internet are included.
Look for rules about pets, guests and decorating, and ask the landlord about anything that is unclear.
Most landlords also ask for a deposit, often equal to one or two months' rent.
You should get it back when you leave, as long as nothing has been damaged.
That is why the first day is so important.
Before you unpack, walk around and take photos of every room: marks on the walls, stains on the carpet and anything that is broken.
Send them to the landlord by email, so that you have proof of the condition of the apartment.
Next, make a realistic budget.
Besides the rent, you will probably pay for electricity, heating, internet and insurance for your belongings.
You do not need to buy everything at once.
Start with the basic equipment, such as a kettle, a few pots and plates, cleaning products and a small tool kit with a hammer, and look for second-hand furniture online.
Finally, get to know your neighbors and the rules of the building.
Find out which days the rubbish is collected and how recycling works.
Tell the landlord immediately if there are problems such as leaks or a broken heater, because small problems can quickly become big ones.
The first FIFA World Cup took place in Uruguay in 1930.
Only thirteen teams took part, and most European teams did not travel because the journey by ship took weeks.
The host nation won the final, beating Argentina four goals to two.
Since then, the tournament has been held every four years, except in 1942 and 1946, during and after the Second World War.
It has grown into one of the biggest sporting events on Earth.
More than two hundred national teams now compete in qualifying matches for a place in the finals.
The 2026 tournament, held in the United States, Canada and Mexico, was the first with forty-eight teams.
The audience is enormous.
According to FIFA, around one and a half billion people watched the 2022 final on television or online.
For many fans, supporting their national team is a matter of pride, and a single victory or defeat can affect the mood of an entire country.
The World Cup has also had its controversies.
Referees' decisions have caused many arguments, so in 2018 the tournament introduced VAR, a system that lets officials watch video replays.
Hosting the event is also extremely expensive.
Countries build new stadiums and roads, and critics point out that some stadiums are almost never used after the tournament ends.
Even so, every four years, billions of people stop to watch the same game.
More than two thousand years ago, the Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote that no one would choose to live without friends, even if they had everything else.
But he also noticed that not all friendships are the same, and he divided them into three kinds.
The first is friendship of utility.
These are people who are useful to each other, such as colleagues or business partners.
Such friendships are perfectly reasonable, but they usually end when one person is no longer useful.
The second is friendship of pleasure.
We enjoy these friends because they are fun, or because we share a hobby.
Aristotle believed that these friendships were common among young people, and that they often disappear when interests change.
The third kind is the rarest and the most valuable: friendship of virtue.
Here, two people respect each other's character, and each one wants what is good for the other, for the other person's sake.
Such friendships take a long time to develop, because mutual trust has to be built slowly.
But once they exist, they can survive long periods of absence and last a lifetime.
Modern research seems to support Aristotle's ideas.
The British scientist Robin Dunbar has suggested that most people can maintain about 150 meaningful relationships, but only around five really close friends.
And when people are asked what they value in a close friend, the same qualities appear again and again: loyalty, honesty and kindness.
A good friend keeps your secrets, is happy about your success rather than jealous, and tells you the truth even when it is uncomfortable.
At eleven o'clock on a Friday night, the emergency department of City Hospital is already busy.
Dr. Lena Ortiz has just started her twelve-hour shift, and she knows it will be a long one.
"Friday nights are always the worst," she says, as an ambulance stops outside the doors.
Patients do not wait in the order in which they arrive.
Instead, a nurse examines each one and decides how urgent the case is, a process called triage.
A man with a painful but minor injury to his finger may wait for hours, while someone who is pale and short of breath is seen immediately.
"People sometimes get angry," Lena admits, "but we have to treat the most critical patients first."
The ambulance brings a young woman who has been in a car crash.
The paramedics explain what happened while the team connects her to a monitor that shows her heart rate.
She has a deep wound on her arm and may have broken her leg.
Blood tests are sent to the laboratory, and an X-ray shows that the leg is broken in two places.
She will need surgery, so a surgeon is called and she is moved upstairs to a ward.
Not every case is so dramatic.
Occasionally, people come in with a cough or the flu, which their family doctor could easily treat.
Others simply need a prescription or someone to talk to.
But the routine can change in seconds, and the pace rarely slows down before morning.
At eight o'clock, Lena finally goes home, exhausted.
Is the job worth it?
"Absolutely," she says. "Tonight we helped about sixty people. Some of them will heal in a week, and one of them might not be alive without us."
Sam Okafor has been a firefighter for twelve years.
We asked him about the reality of the job.
What does a typical shift look like?
We work twenty-four hours at a time, and we live at the station during our shift.
When there is no emergency, we check our equipment, clean the trucks and train.
Fitness is essential, so most of us do a workout in the station gym every day.
When the alarm sounds, we have about a minute to grab our protective clothes and helmets and get on the truck.
Is it mostly fires?
Actually, no.
Fires are only a small part of what we do.
We respond to car crashes, floods and people who are stuck in lifts.
Last month, we rescued a man who had fallen through the ice on a lake.
We also visit schools to teach children about safety, because preventing a fire is always better than fighting one.
What is the most dangerous part of the job?
Smoke.
People think the flames are the biggest hazard, but most victims die from breathing smoke, not from burns.
Inside a burning building, you can barely see your own hand, so we use special cameras that detect heat.
There is also the risk that part of the building will collapse, or that gas will cause an explosion.
How do you deal with the stress?
Teamwork.
You trust your colleagues completely, and after a difficult incident, we always talk about it together.
Courage is important, but so is knowing when to ask for help.
In a democracy, winning an election is not only about having good ideas.
Candidates also need to convince millions of voters, and that requires a well-organized campaign.
A campaign usually begins with a formal announcement.
The candidate stands in front of cameras and announces that they want to become president, governor or mayor.
From that moment, their past is closely examined by journalists and by the opposition.
A single mistake, or an old comment on social media, can seriously damage their reputation.
Next, the team develops an agenda: a list of policies and proposals that will appeal to voters.
Conservative candidates might promise to cut taxes, while others might propose more public spending on health or education.
The message has to be simple enough to fit on a poster, but broad enough to attract many different groups.
Campaigns also cost a huge amount of money.
It pays for advertisements, travel and staff.
In some countries, most of it comes from private donations; in others, there are strict limits and public funding.
Critics worry that rich donors gain too much influence over politics.
As election day approaches, politicians attend rallies, give speeches and take part in televised debates.
Teams of volunteers knock on doors and encourage supporters to register to vote.
Polls show who is ahead, although they are not always accurate.
In the end, all this work comes down to one simple act: millions of people, each alone, making a choice.
Why do some people love coffee while others find it too bitter?
Why do children often refuse vegetables that adults enjoy?
The answers lie in the science of taste.
Your tongue is covered in thousands of taste buds, each containing tiny receptors.
Scientists generally agree that they detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami, a savory taste found in meat and cheese.
Contrary to a popular myth, different parts of the tongue do not detect different tastes; every area can sense all five.
However, what we call "flavor" is much more than taste.
Most of it actually comes from smell.
When you have a cold, food seems to lose its flavor because your nose is blocked.
Temperature and texture also play a role, and so does pain: the burning sensation of chili is not a taste at all but a pain signal.
The spice in ginger works in a similar way.
Our preferences are partly genetic.
Some people have a gene that makes certain bitter vegetables, such as broccoli, taste much stronger.
Studies of twins suggest that genes also explain why some people think cilantro tastes like soap.
Evolution may explain the rest.
For our ancestors, a bitter taste often meant poison, so children, who are more at risk, are naturally suspicious of it.
The good news is that tastes can change.
Research shows that children often need to try a new food ten or more times before they accept it.
So the combination of patience and repetition is probably the best advice for any parent at the dinner table.
Few sources of energy divide opinion as sharply as nuclear power.
Today, nuclear power stations generate about a tenth of the world's electricity, and in France they produce around two thirds.
As countries try to reduce carbon emissions, the debate has become more urgent than ever.
Supporters point out that nuclear reactors produce almost no greenhouse gases while they operate.
Unlike solar and wind power, they can generate electricity day and night, whatever the weather, which makes them a reliable supply.
A single power station needs relatively little land, and a small amount of uranium contains a massive amount of energy.
Statistics also show that, for each unit of electricity produced, nuclear power has caused fewer deaths than coal or oil.
Opponents, however, have serious concerns.
The first is safety.
Accidents are rare, but when they happen, the consequences can be terrible.

After the explosion at Chernobyl in Ukraine in 1986, a huge area had to be abandoned because of radiation, and after the 2011 disaster at Fukushima in Japan, more than a hundred thousand people had to leave their homes.
The second concern is waste, which remains dangerous for thousands of years and requires permanent storage deep underground.
The third is cost: building a new power station can take more than a decade and cost billions.
So who is right?
Many experts argue that the answer is not "either-or."
They believe that the fastest way to cut emissions is a combination of renewable energy and nuclear power, at least for the next few decades.
According to an old legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi.
He noticed that his goats became full of energy after eating the red berries of a certain bush.
Whether the story is true or not, historians agree that the origin of coffee lies in this part of Africa.
By the fifteenth century, people in Yemen were growing coffee and drinking it as we do today.
Religious men used it to stay awake during their night prayers, and monks helped it spread.
Merchants shipped the beans from the port of Mocha across Arabia, and soon coffeehouses appeared in cities throughout the region.
Some rulers tried to ban coffee, because they feared that people met in these places to criticize the government, but the bans never lasted long.
In the seventeenth century, coffee reached Europe.
At first it was an expensive luxury, but coffeehouses quickly became popular meeting places for writers, scientists and businessmen.
In England, they were nicknamed "penny universities."
For the price of a cup, which cost a penny, you could listen to clever conversation all day.
The rising demand had a dark side, however.
European powers built huge coffee plantations in their colonies, and much of the work was done by slaves.
Coffee, like sugar, was closely connected with the history of slavery.
Today, Brazil is by far the largest producer, and global consumption is enormous: people drink around two billion cups every day.
Every night, most of us spend about two hours dreaming, although we usually forget almost everything by the morning.
Some dreams are pleasant, some are frightening, and many are simply weird.
But why does the brain create these strange stories at all?
More than a hundred years ago, the Austrian psychoanalyst Sigmund Freud suggested that dreams reveal our hidden desires.
According to his theory, the images in a dream are symbols of wishes that we are not conscious of during the day.
His ideas were enormously influential, but modern scientists have found little evidence to prove them.
Today, there are several other explanations.
One is that dreams help us to process emotional experiences.
Brain scans show that the areas connected with emotion are highly active during dreaming, while the areas responsible for logic are much quieter.
This may explain why dreams feel so real and yet make so little sense.
Another theory says that dreams are a kind of rehearsal.
By imagining threats, such as being chased or failing an exam, the brain may prepare us to deal with danger in real life.
That might be why nightmares about being late or unprepared are so common.
There is also the possibility that dreams have no purpose at all, and that they are merely a side effect of the brain sorting memories while we sleep.
If you want to recall your dreams more often, try keeping a journal next to your bed and writing in it as soon as you wake up.
Vivid details disappear within minutes, but on paper they can last forever.
For more than a thousand years, the Silk Road connected China with the Mediterranean.
It was not a single road but a network of routes that crossed deserts, mountains and grasslands for thousands of kilometers.
The trade began around the second century BC, when the Han dynasty sent officials west to find allies and horses.
Before long, merchants were carrying precious goods in both directions.
China exported silk, porcelain and tea, while spices, glass, gold and horses traveled east.
In Rome, Chinese silk became a very desirable luxury.
Some politicians even complained that too much gold was leaving the empire to pay for it.
Few merchants traveled the whole route.
Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and caravans of camels moved slowly from one city to the next.
Cities built around oases, such as Samarkand in Central Asia, grew rich by offering markets, water and a safe place to rest.
The journey was dangerous, because travelers faced extreme heat, freezing nights and attacks by bandits.
However, the most important things that traveled along the Silk Road were not goods but ideas.
Religions such as Buddhism spread along it, and so did technologies like paper-making.
Unfortunately, diseases spread too: historians believe that the plague known as the Black Death reached Europe partly along these routes.
In this sense, the Silk Road was an early example of globalization, with all its benefits and dangers.
Sooner or later, most people need to borrow money.
You might need a loan to pay for university, to buy a car or, one day, to buy a home.
Borrowing is not necessarily a bad thing, but it is important to understand how it works before you sign an agreement.
When a bank lends you money, it charges you interest.
This is the price you pay for using someone else's money.
Interest is usually shown as an annual percentage of the amount you owe.
For example, if you borrow a thousand dollars at ten percent a year, you will owe about a hundred dollars in interest after the first year.
The longer you take to repay a loan, the more interest you pay in total.
Credit cards are a particularly expensive way to borrow.
If you pay the full amount every month, you usually pay no interest at all.
But if you only pay the minimum, the interest rate can be twenty percent or more, and the debt can grow faster than you expect.
Before they lend you money, banks want to know whether you are likely to pay it back.
In many countries, they check your credit score, a number based on your financial history.
People who have always paid their bills on time get a higher score, and they are offered lower interest rates.
Missing payments has the opposite effect.
So what is the golden rule?
Never borrow more than you can afford to repay.
Compare offers from different lenders, read the small print, and calculate the total cost, not just the monthly payment.
Every year, millions of tons of plastic end up in the ocean.
Some of it is dumped directly from ships, but most comes from the land.
It is rubbish that blows into rivers, is washed off streets by rain or is left on beaches.
Rivers then carry it out to sea.
Once plastic reaches the ocean, it can stay there for hundreds of years.
Unlike natural materials, it does not decompose; instead, sunlight and waves slowly break it into smaller and smaller pieces.
These tiny pieces, called microplastics, have now been found almost everywhere, from the deepest parts of the ocean to Arctic ice.
Ocean currents also collect floating rubbish in huge areas.
The largest, between California and Hawaii, is known as the Great Pacific Garbage Patch.
The effect on marine life is serious.
Sea turtles often mistake plastic bags for jellyfish, their favorite food.
Seabirds feed pieces of plastic to their young, and whales have been found dead with kilos of plastic in their stomachs.
Animals can also become trapped in old fishing nets, which account for a large share of the plastic in the ocean.
Scientists are still studying what microplastics do to fish, and to the people who eat them.
Cleaning up the ocean is extremely difficult, so the most effective solution is to stop plastic from getting there in the first place.
Many countries have banned single-use items such as plastic bags and straws.
Better waste collection in fast-growing cities could make a substantial difference, since a large part of ocean plastic comes from places without proper rubbish services.
And each of us can help by using less packaging and putting rubbish in the right bin.
Would you walk under a ladder or open an umbrella indoors?
Many people would not, even if they say they do not believe in bad luck.
Superstitions like these exist in every culture, and some of them are thousands of years old.
Numbers are a common source of superstition.
In many Western countries, thirteen is considered unlucky, and some buildings do not have a thirteenth floor.
In China, Japan and Korea, the number four is avoided because it sounds similar to the word for "death."
On the other hand, eight is a lucky number in China, because it sounds like the word for "wealth."
In Italy, it is seventeen that people fear.
Animals and objects have their own meanings.
In some countries, a black cat crossing your path brings bad luck, while in others it is a sign of good fortune.
Breaking a mirror is said to bring seven years of bad luck, perhaps because mirrors were once thought to hold part of a person's soul.
Many people also knock on wood after saying something positive, to protect it from bad spirits.
Why do rational people follow such beliefs?
Psychologists say that superstitions give us a feeling of control in situations that are uncertain.
This is why they are particularly common among athletes, actors and students before exams.
Some famous players wear the same socks for every match or follow exactly the same rituals before a game.
Interestingly, a few studies suggest that a lucky charm can actually improve performance slightly, simply because it makes people more confident.
So perhaps superstitions are not completely irrational after all.
In the last twenty years, computer programming has gone from a specialist skill to something that many schools teach to ten-year-olds.
Some people believe that coding is the new reading and writing, a basic skill that everyone will need.
Others are not so sure.
Supporters point out that software now runs almost every part of our lives, from banking to healthcare.
Understanding the basic concepts behind it helps people to use technology more wisely and to understand its limits.
Coding also teaches logic and problem-solving.
A program is a sequence of precise instructions, so you have to break a big problem into small steps and think about every possibility.
And there is strong demand for programmers, who are typically well paid.
Critics, however, argue that not everyone needs to become a programmer, just as not everyone needs to become an engineer.
School time is limited, and hours spent on coding are hours taken away from other subjects, such as art or history.
Moreover, artificial intelligence can now write simple code by itself.
So the most valuable skill in the future may be knowing what to ask the computer, rather than how to write the code.
Anyone who tries coding soon discovers another lesson: patience.
Programs rarely work the first time, and finding a single missing comma can take hours.
This process, called debugging, can be frustrating, but the moment when everything finally works is extremely satisfying.
Perhaps the best argument for learning to code is not a job, but the confidence that comes from creating something that works.
Energy drinks are big business.
Their advertisements show extreme sports, loud music and people who never seem to get tired, and they are particularly popular with teens and students.
But what do these drinks actually contain, and are they safe?
The main ingredient is caffeine, the same substance that is found in coffee.
A standard can contains roughly as much caffeine as a cup of coffee, but some large cans contain more than twice that amount.
Many drinks also have a very high sugar content, often more than an adult should eat in an entire day.
In general, health experts say that healthy adults can safely have up to about 400 milligrams of caffeine per day.
The recommended maximum for children and pregnant women is much lower.
In moderate amounts, caffeine can improve concentration and reaction times.
However, people who drink energy drinks frequently may experience headaches, sleeping problems, anxiety or a racing heart.
Some become dependent on them and feel terrible without their daily can.
The combination with alcohol is especially risky: because the caffeine hides the effects of alcohol, people may not realize how drunk they are.
Because of these concerns, several governments have introduced stricter regulation.
Latvia and Lithuania have banned sales to people under eighteen.
In the European Union, drinks with a high caffeine content must carry a warning on the label.
Doctors' advice is simple: if you need more energy, sleep, water and a proper meal are usually far more effective than a can with a commercial promise on it.
A trade union is an organization of workers who join together to protect their interests.
Alone, a single employee has little power to negotiate with a large company.
Together, as members of a union, they can demand better pay and conditions, and the management has to listen.
Unions first appeared during the Industrial Revolution, in an era when factory workers had almost no rights.
People worked extremely long hours in dangerous conditions, and anyone who complained could be fired immediately.
At first, unions were illegal in many countries, and their leaders were sometimes sent to prison.
Gradually, however, they won the right to exist.
Many things that we now take for granted, such as the weekend, paid holidays and safety rules, were largely the result of their campaigns.
How does a union work in practice?
Members pay a small monthly fee, and they elect representatives who speak for them.
Every year or two, these representatives negotiate an agreement with the employer about wages, working hours and other issues.
Unions also support individual members who have a conflict with their manager, for example if they believe they have been treated unfairly.
If negotiations fail, workers may decide to stop working collectively, which is known as going on strike.
In recent decades, union membership has declined in many countries, partly because traditional industries such as coal mining have almost disappeared.
However, unions remain powerful in areas like education, transport and health care.
New groups are also forming among delivery drivers and other workers in the digital economy.
When we walk through a city, we rarely think about why the streets, parks and buildings are where they are.
But in most modern cities, very little is left to chance.
Behind the scenes, city planners make decisions that affect our lives for generations.
One of their main tools is dividing the city into zones.
Residential areas are for housing, commercial areas are for shops and offices, and industrial areas are for factories.
In the past, planners kept these areas strictly separate, so that people did not have to live next to noisy, polluting factories.
Today, many prefer mixed neighborhoods, where people can live, work and shop within a short walk, which reduces traffic.
Planners are also responsible for infrastructure: roads, rail lines, water pipes and power networks.
Before a new district is built, they have to estimate how many people will live there.
They also need to know what facilities those people will need, from schools and clinics to parking and public transportation.
Building a road is only the beginning; maintenance can cost more than construction over the long term.
Big projects usually need official approval.
When a company wants to build a tower on a busy avenue, for example, it must submit a detailed proposal.
The local government then decides whether to grant a permit.
Residents can often comment on plans, and their concerns about noise, traffic or the loss of green space are taken into consideration.
Good planning is a balance between the needs of today and the needs of people who have not been born yet.
The human brain weighs only about one and a half kilos, yet it contains around 86 billion nerve cells and uses about a fifth of the body's energy.
It is not surprising that such a complex organ has produced many popular myths.
Here are five of the most common.
Myth one: we only use ten percent of our brains.
This idea appears in films again and again, but it is definitely false.
Brain scans show activity in almost every region, even during sleep, and damage to any area, however small, can have serious effects.
Myth two: people are either "left-brained" and logical or "right-brained" and creative.
The two hemispheres of the brain do specialize in different tasks, but they constantly work together, and there is no evidence that personality depends on which side is stronger.
Myth three: adults are unable to grow new brain cells.
For much of the twentieth century, scientists believed this, but research has shown that new cells can form in certain areas, such as the hippocampus, which plays a key role in memory.
The brain remains capable of change throughout our lives.
Myth four: listening to Mozart makes babies more intelligent.
This notion became extremely popular in the 1990s after a small study, but later experiments failed to find any lasting effect.
Music is wonderful for children, but it is not a shortcut to intelligence.
Myth five: a bigger brain means a cleverer person.
In fact, brain size varies considerably between healthy people, and what seems to matter more is how efficiently the different parts are connected.
The truth about the brain, in other words, is even more extraordinary than the myths.
Every year, around seven hundred million people visit zoos around the world.
For many families, a day at the zoo is a highlight of the holidays.
But more and more people are asking a difficult moral question: is it right to keep wild animals in captivity?
Supporters argue that modern zoos play an important role in conservation.
Many run breeding programs for endangered species.
Some animals that had become extinct in the wild, such as the Arabian oryx, survived only because they were bred in zoos and later returned to their natural habitat.
Zoos also fund research, rescue injured animals and teach millions of children about wildlife.
Seeing an elephant in real life, they say, can create a passion for nature that no documentary can.
Critics disagree.
They point out that even the best enclosures are tiny compared with the vast areas that animals cover in the wild.
Elephants may walk many kilometers a day, and polar bears have huge territories.
In a cage, some animals show clear signs of stress, such as walking up and down for hours.
Critics also note that most animals in zoos are not endangered at all, and that the main purpose of many zoos is entertainment, not survival.
Keeping intelligent animals for our entertainment, they say, is simply cruel.
Perhaps the answer lies somewhere in between.
Many experts believe that zoos should concentrate on species that genuinely benefit from conservation programs, give animals far more space, and work with sanctuaries and national parks.
The question is no longer simply whether zoos should exist, but what kind of zoos we are prepared to accept.
In 1839, a French artist called Louis Daguerre presented a remarkable invention in Paris: a way to capture an image of the real world permanently.
His pictures, known as daguerreotypes, were printed on thin sheets of metal and were incredibly sharp.
However, the process was slow and complicated.
In the early years, an exposure could take several minutes, so people had to sit perfectly still.
That is why they rarely smile in old portraits.
For decades, photography required expert knowledge of chemistry, heavy equipment and a darkroom.
That changed in 1888, when an American businessman, George Eastman, launched the Kodak camera.
It was small, cheap and already loaded with film.
After taking a hundred photos, customers simply sent the whole camera back to the company, which developed the pictures and returned the camera with new film.
For the first time, ordinary families could make their own photo albums.
Over the next century, photography became faster, cheaper and more colorful.
Photographers documented wars, sports and daily life, and some of their images changed public opinion about major events.
At the same time, photography became recognized as a serious art form, and galleries began to hold exhibitions of artistic photographs.
The arrival of digital cameras at the end of the twentieth century was another revolution.
Instead of film, they recorded images as millions of tiny pixels, which could be viewed instantly and deleted if they were not good.
Today, almost everyone carries a camera in their pocket, and people take well over a trillion photos every year.
Daguerre's subjects had to sit still for minutes; today, a moment can be captured, edited and shared around the world in seconds.
Around eight hundred million people live within a hundred kilometers of an active volcano.
At first, this seems surprising.
Why would anyone choose to live next to a mountain that might explode?
A volcano forms where hot liquid rock, called magma, rises from deep inside the Earth.
As pressure builds up, the magma forces its way to the surface.
During an eruption, it can flow out slowly as lava, or it can explode violently, throwing rock and ash high into the atmosphere.
One of the most famous eruptions in history took place in the year 79, when Vesuvius in Italy erupted and buried the Roman city of Pompeii under several meters of ash.
The destruction was terrible, but the ash also preserved the city almost perfectly.
Today, visitors can walk through its streets and see houses, shops and even bread that was left in an oven nearly two thousand years ago.
So why do people stay?
The main reason is agriculture.
Volcanic ash breaks down into extremely fertile soil, so the surrounding land is often ideal for farming.
In Indonesia, some of the most productive agricultural areas lie close to volcanoes.
Volcanoes also bring other benefits, such as tourism and geothermal energy, which Iceland uses to heat most of its homes.
Living near a volcano will never be completely safe, but modern science has reduced the risk considerably.
Scientists monitor active volcanoes constantly, measuring small earthquakes, gases and even tiny changes in the shape of the ground.
These signs can give a warning days or weeks before an eruption, allowing authorities to evacuate people in time.
Today, most people who marry say that they are doing it for love.
For most of history, however, marriage had much more to do with property, status and family alliances than with romance.
In many societies, parents chose their children's partners, and the bride and groom sometimes met for the first time at their own wedding.
The families of the couple negotiated the arrangement carefully, often including a dowry, a payment of money or goods from the bride's family.
A good marriage could bring land, wealth and political power.
Arranged marriages of this kind are still common in some parts of the world, although today the young people involved usually have the right to refuse.
For centuries, the law also treated husbands and wives very differently.
In many countries, a married woman could not own property in her own name or sign a contract.
Divorce was extremely difficult, especially for women.
It was only in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that these laws began to change.
Slowly, the idea of marriage as a partnership between equals became widespread.
Wedding traditions have changed, too.
In the past, most weddings were religious ceremonies held in a holy place, with a priest or another religious leader.
Today, in many countries, the majority of couples choose a civil ceremony, and some write their own vows.
Many also live together before they marry, and the average age at which people marry has risen considerably.
Yet some customs have survived for centuries: the ring, the celebration with family and friends, and the honeymoon that follows.
In detective stories, the hero often solves the crime with a brilliant guess.
In real life, the work is slower and more scientific.
It is done by forensic scientists, who analyze evidence from the scene of a crime.
Fingerprints were one of the first scientific tools used by police.
Because the pattern of lines on every finger is unique, a print left on a glass or a door can link a suspect to a crime.
Today, prints are compared automatically with millions of others in a database.
The biggest breakthrough, however, came in the 1980s with DNA analysis.
Every person's DNA, apart from that of identical twins, is different, and it can be found in blood, hair and even skin cells.
Using a tiny sample, a laboratory can identify a person with an extremely high degree of accuracy.
DNA evidence has helped to convict thousands of criminals, but it has also proved that hundreds of innocent people who had been sent to prison were not guilty.
Forensic scientists study many other kinds of evidence too.
They examine tiny traces of paint, soil or fibers from clothes, and analyze the chemistry of substances found at the scene.
They also use phone records to show where a suspect was at a particular time.
However, science is not perfect.
Samples can be contaminated, and some older methods have turned out to be less reliable than experts once claimed.
That is why, in court, a witness and a detective's investigation still matter as much as any laboratory result.
Chess is one of the oldest games still played today.
It probably began in India around 1,500 years ago, and it spread to Persia and then to Europe.
Along the way, the rules changed several times.
The queen, for example, was originally a weak piece that could only move one square, and she became the most powerful piece on the board only in the fifteenth century.
For centuries, chess was associated with kings and intellectuals.
In the nineteenth century, the first international tournaments were organized, and in 1886 the first official world champion was crowned.
Talented players became famous, and their games were studied by millions.
