In 1997, chess made headlines around the world when an IBM computer called Deep Blue defeated the world champion, Garry Kasparov.
Many people feared that the victory of the machine would destroy interest in the game.
In fact, the opposite happened.
Today, even a phone can beat the best human players, but instead of replacing them, chess engines have become training tools that help players of every level to improve.
The internet has also transformed the game.
On online platforms, millions of games are played every day between people who have never met.
Interest grew enormously in 2020, when many people were stuck at home and a popular television series, The Queen's Gambit, told the story of a young female champion.
Some top players now stream their games to huge audiences.
After fifteen centuries, the ancient game has never been more popular.
For most of the twentieth century, the standard working week was five days, from Monday to Friday.
But in recent years, a growing number of companies have experimented with something more radical: working four days a week for the same pay.
Some of the largest trials took place in Iceland between 2015 and 2019.
Thousands of public workers, from offices to hospitals, reduced their working hours without losing any income.
According to researchers, productivity and the quality of services stayed the same or even improved in most workplaces.
In Britain, a trial in 2022 involved about sixty companies, and the majority of them decided to continue with the shorter week afterwards.
Supporters say the results are not surprising.
People who have more time to rest are less likely to suffer from stress and burnout, and they take fewer days off sick.
With a clear deadline, teams also tend to cut unnecessary meetings and work more efficiently.
For employers, a four-day week can be a powerful way to attract talented staff.
However, the idea does not suit every type of job.
A factory, a school or a hospital needs people to be present at fixed times.
So a shorter week may require hiring more staff, which increases costs.
Some workers in the trials also reported that they felt under more pressure to do five days of work in four.
And critics point out that the participants were volunteers, so the results may not apply to every company.
Whether the four-day week becomes the new standard will probably depend on the kind of work people do.
Most people think that we laugh because something is funny.
But when the American psychologist Robert Provine studied people laughing in everyday conversations, he discovered something surprising.
Only a small part of the laughter followed a joke.
Most of it followed completely ordinary comments, such as "See you later" or "I know."
This suggests that laughter is mainly a social signal.
We laugh to show that we are friendly, that we agree, or that we feel comfortable with someone.
In fact, people are about thirty times more likely to laugh when they are with others than when they are alone.
Laughter is also highly contagious: when we hear someone laughing, we often start laughing ourselves, even if we do not know why.
This is why television comedies used to add recorded laughter to their shows.
Humans are not the only animals that laugh.
Apes such as chimpanzees make a breathy sound when they play or are tickled, and scientists believe that human laughter developed from this.
Even rats produce high sounds, too high for us to hear, when they are tickled.
This suggests that the roots of laughter are millions of years old and are connected with play.
Laughter also seems to be good for us.
It reduces stress, and some studies suggest that people can tolerate more pain after a good laugh, possibly because the brain releases natural painkillers.
Most importantly, laughing together strengthens the bond between people.
Comedians make us laugh at jokes, but our friends make us laugh at almost anything, and that may be what laughter is really for.
Every year, millions of people decide to become their own boss.
Some open a café, others sell handmade jewelry online, and some turn a hobby into a full-time career.
It can be an amazing experience, but it is also risky: a large number of new businesses close within five years.
So what can new entrepreneurs do to improve their chances?
The first step is research.
Before you launch anything, find out whether there are enough potential customers who are able and willing to pay for your product.
Study your competitors, too.
If the market is extremely competitive, you need a clear reason why people should choose you instead.
Next, write a business plan.
It should describe your product, your prices and your strategy for finding customers, and it should include a realistic budget.
Many people underestimate their expenses, such as rent, equipment, delivery and insurance.
Unless you have enough money to survive the first year without a profit, you may need finance from a bank, an investor or a government grant.
Location matters, especially for shops and restaurants.
Rosa Mendes, who runs a small bakery, says her previous shop failed despite excellent bread, because it was on a quiet street.
"After that failure, I moved to a busy corner near a school," she says.
"On the opening day, we sold everything by noon."
She also offers a discount to regular customers as a reward for their loyalty.
Finally, do not try to do everything alone.
Many cities offer free assistance to new businesses, from help with registration to advice on advertising.
Successful business owners usually agree that the key qualities are patience and leadership: the ability to keep going when things go wrong and to inspire the people who work with you.
In 1954, a British medical student called Roger Bannister became the first person to run a mile in under four minutes.
At the time, many people believed it was physically impossible.
Today, hundreds of athletes have done it, and the record has improved by about seventeen seconds.
Why do records keep falling?
One reason is better training.
Modern athletes are supported by experts in physics, nutrition and psychology, and every part of their performance is measured.
They know exactly what pace to run at, how much sleep they need and how to recover after a session.
The mental side matters, too: Bannister's achievement showed other runners that the "barrier" was only in their minds.
Another reason is technology.
Improvements in equipment can have an incredible effect.
In 2008 and 2009, swimmers wearing new high-tech swimsuits broke more than a hundred world records, and the suits were banned soon afterwards.
More recently, running shoes with special foam and carbon plates have helped long-distance runners to go faster.
In 2019, Eliud Kipchoge ran a marathon in under two hours, although the event did not count as an official record because of the special conditions.
A third factor is simply numbers.
More countries now take part in international sport, and more young people have access to proper coaching, so the chance of finding exceptional talent is much greater.
Will records keep falling forever?
Obviously not.
The human body has limits, and in some events, progress has already slowed down considerably.
Scientists believe that, to a large extent, the biggest improvements are behind us, and future records are likely to fall by hundredths of a second rather than by whole seconds.
Throughout history, people have traveled long distances to visit places they consider holy.
These journeys, known as pilgrimages, exist in almost every religion.
For believers, they are a way to express their faith, to ask for help or simply to feel closer to heaven.
Jerusalem is sacred to three religions: Jewish, Christian and Muslim.
Its old city, less than one square kilometer in size, contains some of the most important religious sites in the world.
For Muslims, the most important pilgrimage is the Hajj to Mecca, which every adult Muslim who is able should make at least once.
Each year, around two million people take part.
In India, millions of Hindus travel to the city of Varanasi on the river Ganges.
They believe that bathing in its waters makes the soul pure.
At dawn, the steps along the river are full of people praying, and at night, small lamps float on the water.
In Europe, one of the best-known pilgrimages is the Camino, a network of routes that lead to the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Spain.
In the Middle Ages, Christians walked there from all over the continent.
Today, hundreds of thousands of people complete the Camino every year, and many of them are not religious at all.
They walk for weeks to find silence, to think about their lives or to meet fellow travelers.
This shows that pilgrimages have a spiritual meaning that goes beyond any single religion.
Whether they travel for prayer or for personal reasons, pilgrims share the same experience.
It is a long, difficult journey that ends in a place that feels special.
For more than fifty years, robots have been exploring Mars.
Space agencies have sent orbiters that photograph the planet from above and rovers that drive across its surface.
NASA's Perseverance rover, which landed in 2021, is currently collecting rock samples that scientists hope to bring back to Earth.
The main mission is to find out whether life ever existed there.
Now some people have a bigger vision: sending humans.
Several companies and governments have announced plans to land astronauts on Mars and eventually to build permanent settlements.
Supporters argue that the potential rewards are enormous.
A human crew could do far more science than any robot, and learning to live on another planet could one day help our species to survive a disaster on Earth.
However, the challenges are extreme.
Depending on the positions of the planets, the journey takes between six and nine months.
During that time, astronauts would be exposed to dangerous radiation from space.

The Martian atmosphere is very thin and consists mainly of carbon dioxide, so nobody could breathe outside, and temperatures in the northern and southern regions can fall below minus one hundred degrees.
There is ice under the surface, but turning it into drinking water, oxygen and even fuel would require complex engineering that has never been tested.
Then there is the expense.
A human mission would probably cost hundreds of billions of dollars.
Critics ask whether that money would be better spent on problems here on Earth, such as poverty and climate change.
Supporters reply that space programs have always produced useful technologies, from better batteries to weather satellites.
Whatever happens, the first person to walk on Mars will be making history, and that person may already be alive today.
At five o'clock on a Saturday evening, the kitchen of a busy restaurant looks calm.
Vegetables have been cut, sauces are ready, and every knife is sharp.
But the head chef, Marco, knows that in an hour everything will change.
"Preparation is everything," he says. "If you are not prepared at five, you are lost at seven."
A professional kitchen works like a small army.
The head chef is in command, and a sous-chef assists him and takes over when he is away.
Each of the other cooks is responsible for one section, such as meat, fish or desserts.
When an order arrives, Marco reads it aloud, and each section starts working on its part of the dish at exactly the right moment.
All the plates for one table must be ready at the same time.
By eight o'clock, the kitchen is hot, loud and full of steam.
The cooks move quickly around each other without speaking more than necessary.
Burns and small cuts are common, and a single mistake can delay an entire table.
Before every plate leaves the kitchen, Marco checks the presentation.
"People eat with their eyes first," he explains.
The hours are long and the pay is often low, especially for young cooks.
Many experienced chefs say that they have worked sixty or seventy hours a week for years.
So why do they do it?
For most, the answer is passion.
There is great satisfaction in creating something beautiful that people enjoy, and the praise of a happy customer is a powerful reward.
For the most talented, there is also the dream of a Michelin star, one of the highest honors in the restaurant world.
Buying something online takes only a few seconds.
But as soon as you click "buy," a complex chain of events begins.
First, your order is sent via the internet to the company's servers.
The system checks your payment and finds the nearest warehouse that has the item in stock.
Large retailers have huge distribution centers, some of them as big as dozens of football fields.
Inside, thousands of products are stored on shelves up to the ceiling.
In many modern warehouses, robots do much of the work.
They carry whole shelves to human workers, who pick the right item, scan it and put it in a box.
Computer algorithms decide the size of the box and the best route for each package.
They even try to predict what customers in a particular area will buy, so that popular products are already nearby before anyone orders them.
Then comes the most expensive part of the process: the "last mile."
Your package is loaded onto a truck and then onto a delivery van, which may stop at more than a hundred homes in a single day.
Customers expect to receive their orders faster and faster, and in some cities, next-day or even same-day delivery is now normal.
This speed has a cost.
Warehouse and delivery workers often face intense pressure to meet targets, and critics have raised concerns about their working conditions.
There is also an environmental impact: millions of vans on the roads and mountains of cardboard and plastic.
About one in five items bought online is returned, and many of these returns cannot be resold, so they end up as trash.
Next time you order something, it might be worth asking whether you really need it tomorrow.
Did the moon landings really happen?
Is a secret group controlling the world?
Conspiracy theories, the belief that important events are secretly planned by powerful people, have existed for centuries.
But thanks to social media, they now spread faster than ever.
Why do so many intelligent people believe them?
Psychologists say that part of the answer lies in how our brains work.
We are very good at seeing patterns, even where none exist.
This ability once helped our ancestors to survive, but it also makes it hard for us to accept that some events are simply accidents or coincidences.
When something dramatic happens, a big explanation feels more satisfying than a small one.
Emotions play a role, too.
Research shows that people are more likely to believe conspiracy theories when they feel anxious, powerless or uncertain about the future.
A theory that blames a hidden enemy can give a feeling of control, and believers often feel that they are special because they know the "truth."
Once a person accepts a theory, it is difficult to change their mind.
Any proof against it can be seen as part of the conspiracy, and online algorithms tend to show users more of the content they already agree with.
Calling believers stupid or ridiculous rarely helps; it usually makes them trust you even less.
So what works?
Experts suggest asking calm, curious questions, such as "How do you know?" and "What evidence would change your mind?"
Teaching young people how to check sources, and how to recognize the tricks used by fake news, may be the most effective protection of all.
Last month, our teacher challenged the class to an experiment: one week without smartphones.
We could use a basic phone for calls, but no social media, no games and no messages.
Honestly, I thought it would be easy.
I was totally wrong.
On the first day, I felt weird and slightly anxious.
Every few minutes, my hand went to my pocket to check for notifications that were not there.
At the bus stop, everyone else was looking at their screens, and I did not know what to do with my eyes.
By the evening, I was bored and a little annoyed with the whole idea.
My teacher said this was a kind of withdrawal, and that it would pass.
Sure enough, things improved on the third day.
I started reading a novel on the bus, and I finished it in four days, which had not happened for years.
I also slept better, because I was not staring at a screen until midnight.
The most amazing change, though, was in my conversations.
Without a phone to hide behind, I talked to people face-to-face much more.
My friend Jess and I spent a whole lunch break talking, and I learned more about her in an hour than in a year of messages.
It was a glimpse of how friendships worked before smartphones.
Of course, there were problems, too.
I missed a party because the invitation was sent in a group chat, and finding my way to a new place without a map app was a real mess.
When the week ended, I did not get rid of my phone.
But I did delete two apps, and I now leave my phone in another room at night.
Hopefully, I will be able to keep these habits.
It is a useful tool, but for a week, I remembered what life feels like when you are not always somewhere else.
For most of human history, almost everyone was poor.
Even two hundred years ago, the great majority of people lived in what we would now call extreme poverty.
Today, according to the World Bank, the figure is below ten percent.
That still means hundreds of millions of people who do not have enough money for food, shelter and basic health care.
What caused this huge reduction?
The main factor has been economic growth, especially in Asia, where hundreds of millions of people moved from farms to jobs in factories and cities.
Better education and health care also played an essential role.
A child who goes to school and receives vaccines is far more likely to earn a good income as an adult.
However, poverty is not only about money.
Poor families often lack access to clean water, electricity and banks, and a single illness can push them back into debt.
Even in rich countries, many people struggle to pay for housing, and some become homeless.
The gap between the richest and the poorest, known as inequality, has grown in many places.
Experts have tested various solutions.
Some programs give small microloans to help people start businesses.
Others simply give cash directly to poor families, and studies suggest that most of them spend it sensibly, on food, school fees or tools for work.
In Kenya, a mobile phone money service called M-Pesa allowed millions of people to save and send money safely for the first time.
Researchers believe it has helped many households to escape poverty.
Ending poverty completely will not be easy, but the progress of the last few decades shows that it is not impossible.
For decades, parents, politicians and journalists have worried about violent video games.
In many popular games, players use weapons, fight in battles and spend hours killing enemies.
After some terrible crimes, it has been reported that the attackers had played such games, and some people concluded that the games were to blame.
But what does the evidence actually say?
Researchers have studied the question for more than thirty years, and the results are mixed.
Some laboratory experiments suggest that, immediately after playing a violent game, people may behave slightly more aggressively, for example by choosing to play a loud noise to an opponent.
However, this kind of short-term aggression is very different from real violence.
When scientists look at the bigger picture, the link becomes much weaker.
In many countries, youth violence fell during the same decades in which video games became hugely popular.
Most large studies have found no clear evidence that playing violent games makes young people commit violent crimes.
Other factors, such as mental health problems, family violence and easy access to weapons, appear to be far more important.
That does not mean that games have no effects at all.
Playing for many hours a day can cause sleep problems and leave little time for exercise, homework or friends.
On the other hand, some games may improve reaction times, problem-solving and teamwork.
Age ratings exist for a reason, and experts recommend that parents know what their children are playing and set sensible limits.
In moderation, most gamers seem to be fine.
Many people say that they are more afraid of speaking in public than of almost anything else.
Yet at school, at university and at work, giving presentations is an essential skill.
The good news is that anyone can learn it.
Start with a clear structure.
In the introduction, tell the audience what you are going to talk about and why it matters to them.
In the main part, focus on three or four key points, not ten.
Finally, give a brief conclusion that repeats your most important message.
People forget most of what they hear, so it is better to say a few things well than many things badly.
Be careful with your slides.
A common mistake is to fill them with long sentences and then read them aloud.
Visual aids should support what you say, not replace it.
A single image, a simple chart or a short phrase is usually far more effective than a page of text.
Next, think about how you speak.
When people are nervous, they often talk too fast, so try to slow your pace and pause after important points.
Look at different people in the room, rather than at your notes or the screen.
Stories and examples make a presentation memorable and help to engage the audience.
Most importantly, rehearse.
Practice your presentation several times, if possible in front of a friend, and time it carefully.
You do not need to memorize every word, but you should know your introduction and conclusion perfectly.
Feeling nervous is completely normal, and even experienced speakers feel it.
The difference is that they have learned to use that energy instead of fighting it.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built about 4,500 years ago for the pharaoh Khufu.
It contains more than two million stone blocks, and some of them weigh as much as several cars.
For centuries, people have wondered how the ancient Egyptians managed to build it without modern machines.
A popular belief, repeated in many Hollywood films, is that the pyramids were built by slaves.
However, archaeologists now think this is largely a myth.
In the 1990s, they discovered the remains of a town near the pyramids where the workers lived.
They found bakeries and the bones of cattle that had been eaten.
They also found the workers' own tombs, which were built close to the pyramid as a mark of honor.
Slaves would not have been buried with such respect.
Most experts now believe that the pyramids were built by a permanent team of skilled workers, perhaps a few thousand.
They were helped by farmers who worked for a few months each year.
During the annual flood of the river Nile, when their fields were under water, farmers were free to work on the construction.
The stone was cut with copper tools and moved on boats along the river and canals.
On land, it was pulled on wooden sledges, and the workers poured water on the sand in front of them to reduce friction.
How exactly the blocks were lifted to the top is still debated.
The most likely theory is that the workers built long ramps of mud and stone around the pyramid.
What is certain is that the project required extraordinary organization, precise mathematics and enormous effort.
The real story, in other words, is not about slaves or aliens, but about human skill.
Every weekend, thousands of children play football in parks, hoping that one day they will become professionals.
A few of them are noticed by scouts and invited to join the academy of a big club.
Some are as young as eight or nine.
Life at an academy is intensive.
Young players train several times a week with qualified coaches, who work on their technique, fitness and understanding of the game.
Goalkeepers have their own instructor, and defenders spend hours practicing how to read an attack.
The players also go to school, and the best academies take their education seriously, because they know how few will make it.
The competition is tremendous.
Every year, coaches make a selection: some players stay, and others are rejected.
Even outstanding teammates can be released suddenly if they stop improving.
At sixteen, the lucky ones receive a scholarship, and a small number of them later sign professional contracts.
It is often said that fewer than one in a hundred academy players ever play in the Premier League.
For gifted, ambitious young people, the dream of glory is powerful.
But the disappointment of being rejected can be devastating, especially for teenagers who have given up everything for the sport.
That is why many clubs now offer psychological support and help players to prepare for a different career.
The coaches say that determination and excellence matter, but so does having a plan B.
The busiest airports in the world handle more than a hundred million passengers annually.
For travelers, the experience usually takes a few hours.
They check in at the counter, go through security, perhaps do some shopping in the duty-free area, and wait at the gate.
But behind the scenes, thousands of people work day and night to make every departure possible.
Take your luggage, for example.
After you leave it at the counter, it travels through kilometers of conveyor belts under the terminal.
Machines scan every bag and read the label, then send it to the right plane.
The system has to be extremely accurate, because a single mistake can send a suitcase to the wrong continent.
Meanwhile, on the runway, ground staff carry out regular inspections to look for debris.
Even a small piece of metal can damage an engine during take-off.
Birds are another danger, and some airports even use trained falcons to scare them away.
In the kitchens, catering companies prepare thousands of meals, which are loaded aboard in special carts.
In the control tower, air traffic controllers watch the sky and give instructions to pilots.
At the busiest airports, a plane may take off or land every minute, so their job requires complete concentration.
If the weather is bad, they may have to change the plans for hundreds of flights at once.
So next time your flight is delayed, remember the countless people and machines working together to get you, and your bags, safely to your destination.
For centuries, the pub has been at the heart of British life.
The word is short for "public house," and traditionally it was a place where anyone could come in, sit by the fire and meet their neighbors.
In many villages, the pub was, and still is, the most important building after the church.
In a traditional pub, you order at the counter, called the bar, rather than waiting for a waiter.
When friends go to the pub together, they often buy drinks in "rounds": each person pays for everyone's drinks in turn.
Forgetting to buy your round is considered very bad manners.
Pubs are not only about drinking.
Most of them also serve simple, tasty food.
A classic is fish and chips, usually made with cod.
Another is the pie, filled with meat or vegetables and served with gravy.
On Sundays, many pubs offer a roast: slices of beef, lamb or pork with potatoes, vegetables and a Yorkshire pudding.
It is a real feast, and it is best to arrive with a big appetite.
Some breakfasts include bacon, eggs and beans, too.
Pubs also offer entertainment.
Many hold weekly quiz nights, where teams compete to answer questions, and some have live music, darts or a television for watching football.
However, the pub is in trouble.
Thousands have closed in recent decades because of rising costs, cheap alcohol in supermarkets and changing habits among young people.
In some villages, local residents have bought their pub together to save it, because they cannot imagine the community without it.
Every culture has its own myths: ancient stories about gods, heroes and strange beasts.
Although they come from different parts of the world, many of these tales have surprisingly similar elements.
Monsters are a good example.
In Greek mythology, the Minotaur was a terrifying creature, half man and half bull, that lived in a labyrinth on the island of Crete.
Every year, young people were sent in as food for the beast, until the hero Theseus killed it with his sword.
Stories like this may reflect real fears of the ancient world, such as wild animals or powerful enemies.
Dragons appear in the myths of both Europe and Asia, but their meaning is very different.
In many European tales, the dragon is an evil monster that breathes fire and guards gold, and a brave warrior must defeat it.
In Chinese tradition, however, the dragon is wise and kind; it brings rain for the crops and is a symbol of good luck and power.
Some myths are about the endless cycle of life and death.
The phoenix is a magical bird found in stories from Egypt and Greece.
It lives for hundreds of years, then burns and is reborn from its own ashes.
For this reason, it became a symbol of hope and eternal life.
Many myths also feature divine weapons and magical helpers.
The Norse god Thor had a hammer that always returned to his hand.
In British legend, the wizard Merlin helped King Arthur to find the sword Excalibur.
Why do these stories still attract us?
Perhaps because they deal with questions that every generation must face: how to be brave, how to fight evil and how to accept that nothing lasts forever.
Today's films and computer games are full of monsters and heroes, too, which shows that the old myths are very much alive.
If you have watched Hollywood westerns, you probably imagine the American West of the 1870s as a violent place.
In these films, cowboys ride into town, drink whiskey in noisy saloons and settle their arguments with gunfights in the street.
The reality was rather different.
Take the famous cattle towns of Kansas, such as Dodge City.
Cowboys drove huge herds of cattle there, and the animals were then sent east by railroad.
These towns were certainly rough, but historians who have studied the records found only about forty-five killings in the five most notorious towns over fifteen years.
One reason was that many towns banned people from carrying guns in the streets.
Visitors had to leave their weapons with the sheriff or at their hotel.
The most famous gunfight in history, at the O.K. Corral in Tombstone, Arizona, in 1881, lasted only about thirty seconds.
The marshal Wyatt Earp, who became a hero of countless films, was involved.
But in his own time he was a controversial figure, and some people saw him as little more than a criminal with a badge.
Cowboys themselves were also different from the Hollywood image.
Most were poorly paid young workers who spent months on the trail, sleeping outdoors and looking after cattle in heat, dust and freezing rain.
Historians estimate that about one in four cowboys was Black, and many others were Mexican.
The real West was more diverse, and less dramatic, than the films suggest.
According to the World Health Organization, about one in six people in the world lives with a significant disability.
Some are blind or deaf, some use a wheelchair, and others have disabilities that are not visible at all, such as chronic pain or mental illness.
Yet many buildings, websites and public services are still designed as if everyone could see, hear and walk perfectly.
Many disabled people argue that the main problem is not their body but the barriers in society.
A wheelchair user is not "disabled" by a ramp; they are disabled by steps.
A deaf person can enjoy a film perfectly well if it has subtitles.
From this point of view, accessibility is not a special favor but a basic right.
Technology has made a considerable difference.
Screen readers allow blind people to use computers and phones, and apps can turn speech into text instantly.
Many sign languages exist around the world, and in some countries, they are officially recognized.
Braille, a system of raised dots, has helped blind readers for almost two hundred years.
However, attitudes can be harder to change than buildings.
Disabled people still face discrimination at work, and many employers wrongly assume that they are less capable.
Awareness campaigns, accessible schools and equal employment laws all help.
After all, a world that works for disabled people works better for everyone: parents with baby buggies use ramps, too, and subtitles help anyone watching a video in a noisy café.
More than 2,200 years ago, a Greek scholar called Eratosthenes was the chief librarian in Alexandria, in Egypt.
The great library there contained a huge variety of books, and Eratosthenes studied almost everything: geography, mathematics, astronomy and poetry.
He is best known for something remarkable: he calculated the size of the Earth, without ever leaving Egypt.
Educated Greeks already believed that the Earth was a sphere, not flat.
Eratosthenes had read about Syene, a town far to the south.
There, the sun was directly overhead at noon on the longest day of the year.
At that moment, its light reached the bottom of a deep well, and objects had no shadow.
But on the same day in Alexandria, a vertical stick did have a short shadow.
Eratosthenes realized that this difference could only occur if the surface of the Earth was curved.
He measured the angle of the shadow in Alexandria and found that it was about one fiftieth of a full circle.
This meant that the distance between the two towns must be one fiftieth of the distance around the whole planet.
The distance was known from travelers and surveyors: about 5,000 stadia.
So the circumference of the Earth had to be about 250,000 stadia.
Nobody knows exactly how long a stadion was.
But according to most estimates, his result was surprisingly close to the real figure of about 40,000 kilometers.
His method, based on careful observation, simple geometry and logical thinking, is still taught in schools today.
It is a perfect demonstration that great discoveries do not always need expensive equipment, only curiosity and a clever idea.
A large symphony orchestra has between eighty and a hundred musicians.
They are divided into four main sections: strings, such as violins and cellos; woodwind, such as flutes; brass, such as trumpets and horns; and percussion, including drums.
In front of them stands the conductor, who decides how fast and how loud each part should be played.
To the audience, a concert may look effortless.
In reality, it is the result of years of preparation.
Most orchestra musicians started playing as young children and practiced for several hours a day for decades.
Even after they join an orchestra, they continue to practice at home, because each new piece must be learned perfectly before the first rehearsals.
Getting a job in a top orchestra is extremely difficult.
Hundreds of qualified musicians may apply for a single position.
Many orchestras now hold auditions behind a screen, so that the judges can hear the performer but cannot see them.
This makes the selection fairer, and researchers believe that it helped more women to be hired.
Orchestras face serious challenges today.
Audiences for classical music are getting older, and concert halls are expensive to run.
To attract new listeners, many orchestras perform film music, play in parks for free, or work with jazz musicians and popular singers.
Some also run education programs and bring young people's choirs onto the stage.
When the last note ends and the applause begins, the musicians say that all the hard work feels worth it.
What exactly is an emotion?
Psychologists define it as a strong reaction that involves both the mind and the body.
When we feel anger, for example, our heart beats faster and our muscles become tense; when we feel sadness, our energy falls and we may want to be alone.
In the 1960s, the American psychologist Paul Ekman traveled around the world showing people photographs of faces.
He found that people from very different cultures recognized the same basic emotions: happiness, sadness, fear, anger, surprise and disgust.
This suggested that some emotions are part of human nature, not just something we learn.
Emotions are useful.
Fear protects us from danger, and anger can give us the energy to fight injustice.
Gratitude and appreciation strengthen our relationships, while guilt and shame encourage us to apologize when we have hurt someone.
Even frustration can be positive if it pushes us to find a better solution.
The problem comes when emotions become overwhelming.
A moment of rage can destroy a friendship, and long periods of despair can lead to serious mental health problems.
Research shows that one simple technique can help: naming the emotion.
When people say, or even write, "I feel frustrated" or "I am terrified," the emotional part of the brain becomes less active.
Other strategies include slow breathing, meditation and talking to someone you trust.
Emotions are not good or bad in themselves.
Excitement, delight and enthusiasm make life enjoyable, and sadness is a natural response to loss.
The aim is not to stop feeling, but to understand what we feel and to choose how we act.
The United States has more tornadoes than any other country in the world, with over a thousand every year.
Many of them occur in a region of the Great Plains known as Tornado Alley, which includes parts of Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska.
Why there?
In spring, warm, wet air moves north from the Gulf of Mexico, while cold, dry air comes down from Canada.
Over the flat plains, these masses of air meet and create huge thunderstorms called supercells.
Inside them, the wind can begin to turn in a spiral.
Sometimes a narrow, rotating column of air stretches down from the cloud to the ground.
That is a tornado.
Most tornadoes are small and last only a few minutes, but the strongest ones can be devastating.
Their winds can reach more than three hundred kilometers an hour.
That is strong enough to destroy houses, throw cars through the air and fill the sky with debris.
In 2013, one such tornado hit the town of Moore, Oklahoma, destroying two schools and killing twenty-four people.
Predicting exactly where a tornado will form is still very difficult.
However, forecasters use radar to watch storms closely, and they can usually give a warning a few minutes before a tornado arrives.
When the sirens sound, people are told to go to a shelter, a basement or a small room in the middle of the house, away from windows.
Thanks to these warnings, the number of deaths has fallen considerably since the middle of the twentieth century, even though more people now live in the region.
We hear the phrase "scientists say" almost every day.
But how do scientists actually reach their conclusions, and why should we trust them?
The answer lies in a method that has developed over centuries.
It usually begins with an observation.
A scientist notices a phenomenon, such as a disease that seems to be more common in one area, and asks why it occurs.
Next, they suggest a possible explanation, called a hypothesis.
The important thing is that a hypothesis must be possible to test.
Then comes the experiment.
A good experiment is carefully designed to determine whether the hypothesis is correct.
Scientists often compare two groups that are alike in every way except one, so that they can distinguish the effect of that single factor.
They collect data in a systematic way and try to remain objective, even if they are hoping for a particular result.
Even then, a single study is rarely sufficient.
Before a study is published, other experts examine it in a process called peer review, looking for mistakes and weaknesses.
After publication, other teams try to replicate the experiment.
If they get the same results, confidence grows; if they do not, the original conclusion may be wrong.
This is why science rarely offers absolute certainty.
Instead, it talks about probability and evidence, and it is always ready to change its mind when new evidence emerges.
Some people see this as a weakness.
In fact, it is science's greatest strength: a system designed to correct its own mistakes.
Imagine that your phone falls into a lake, or your laptop is stolen.
The device can be replaced, but what about everything on it: years of photos, your school projects, important documents?
If you have not made a copy, they may be gone forever.
That is why experts recommend that you back up your files regularly.
Many people only think about it after a disaster, but by then it is usually too late.
Data can be lost in many ways: accidentally deleting a file, a broken hard drive, a virus, or ransomware.
Ransomware is a type of attack in which criminals lock your files and ask for money.
A simple and widely used strategy is the "3-2-1 rule."
Keep three copies of your important files, on two different types of storage, with one copy in a different place.
For example, you might keep the original files on your laptop, a second copy on an external disk, and a third copy online, in the cloud.
If your house is flooded, the cloud copy will survive; if the internet service closes, you still have the disk.
Most phones and computers can upload photos and documents to the cloud automatically.
It is worth checking that this setting is switched on, and that you know your password.
Remember, too, that storage devices do not last forever: an old disk or a memory card should be replaced every few years.
Finally, test your backup occasionally.
Try to restore a few files to make sure that the copy actually works.
It takes a few minutes, but one day those minutes could save your memories.
When you learn a language, you also learn a special vocabulary for talking about it.
Teachers and textbooks use these words all the time, so it is worth knowing them.
Let's start with the alphabet.
English has twenty-six letters: five vowels, a, e, i, o and u, and twenty-one consonants.
However, the spelling of English is famously irregular.
The same vowel can be pronounced in many different ways, which is why even native speakers make spelling mistakes.
Next come the parts of speech.
Nouns name things, verbs describe actions and adjectives describe nouns.
An adverb usually describes a verb: in "She sings beautifully," the word "beautifully" is an adverb.
A pronoun, such as "she" or "they," replaces a noun, and a preposition, such as "on" or "under," shows the relationship between words.
English also has two articles: the definite article "the" and the indefinite article "a" or "an."
Verbs have several forms.
The infinitive is the basic form, such as "to go," and the past participle is the form used after "have," as in "I have gone."
Modal verbs, such as "can," "must" and "should," add meaning to other verbs.
Then there are phrasal verbs, which combine a verb with a small word like "up" or "off."
They are a nightmare for learners, because "give up" has nothing to do with giving, and "put off" means to delay something.
Many words are built from smaller parts.
A prefix comes at the beginning, as in "unhappy," and a suffix at the end, as in "careless."
Knowing them can help you guess the meaning of new words, and to find an antonym, a word with the opposite meaning.
Finally, every language has idioms, expressions whose meaning cannot be guessed from the individual words, such as "it's raining cats and dogs."
And do not forget the punctuation: a sentence ends with a full stop, or with a question mark if it asks something.
The British writer George Bernard Shaw is often quoted as saying that England and America are two countries divided by a common language.
Although British and American people understand each other perfectly well, their vocabulary differs in dozens of everyday situations.
Imagine a British student visiting New York.
She walks on the sidewalk, not the pavement.
The trucks she sees would be called lorries at home, and the pullover or jumper in her bag is a sweater.
When she wants money, she looks for an ATM instead of a cashpoint.
In the evening, she orders "takeout" rather than a takeaway, and she discovers that a courgette is called a zucchini.
Buildings can be confusing, too.
In Britain, the ground floor is the one at street level, and the first floor is one level above it.
In America, the ground floor is usually called the first floor.
So if an American tells her to meet him on the first floor, she might go upstairs and wait in the wrong place.
She takes the elevator, not the lift, and throws her rubbish in a trash can, not a dustbin.
Education has different words as well.
British children go to primary school and then secondary school, while Americans talk about elementary school and high school.
At university, Americans call first-year students freshmen, and second-year students sophomores, words that are rarely used in Britain.
And a British person might say that a holiday lasts a fortnight, a word most Americans never use; they simply say "two weeks."
Which version should learners choose?
It does not really matter, as long as you are consistent and understand both.
Thanks to films, music and the internet, most British people now understand American words, and many American expressions have entered British English.
A hundred years ago, running a household was exhausting physical work.
Washing clothes by hand could take a whole day, and ironing took another.
Floors and carpets had to be cleaned with brushes.
Food had to be bought almost every day because there was no way to keep it fresh.
In most families, this work was done by women.
During the twentieth century, a series of electrical appliances transformed the home.
The washing machine reduced the laundry from a day to a few minutes of effort.
The vacuum cleaner, which people in Britain still call a "hoover," could hoover up dust from the carpets in a few minutes.
The refrigerator, and later the freezer, allowed families to store food for days or even months, so they could shop once a week.
Central heating replaced coal fires, and in hot countries, air conditioning made summer bearable.
Later came the dishwasher and the microwave.
The dishwasher meant that nobody had to wash up after dinner, and the microwave could heat a meal in minutes.
Even small inventions, such as the hairdryer, the non-stick frying pan and the remote control, made daily life a little easier.
Some historians argue that these machines had an enormous social impact.
By saving hours of work every week, they allowed many more women to take jobs outside the home.
Others point out, however, that standards of cleanliness also rose, so people did not always spend less time on housework: they simply washed their clothes more often.
Accidents can happen anywhere: in the kitchen, on the sports field or in the street.
Knowing a few simple first aid skills could help you save a life before the ambulance arrives.
The first rule is always the same: make sure the area is safe for you, then call the emergency services.
If someone is bleeding heavily, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or bandage.
Keep the pressure on until help arrives, and if possible, raise the injured part above the level of the heart.
For a small burn, hold it under cool running water for at least twenty minutes.
Do not put butter, ice or toothpaste on it, although many people believe these are good remedies.
If a person is choking and cannot breathe or speak, encourage them to cough.
If that does not work, give up to five sharp blows between their shoulders with the palm of your hand.
If the object still does not come out, you may need to use the Heimlich maneuver.
Press quickly inwards and upwards just above the stomach.
Some people are severely allergic to foods such as peanuts, or to insect stings.
If their face or throat becomes swollen and they find it hard to breathe, they need medicine immediately.
Many carry a special injection called an EpiPen, and it is worth knowing how to use one.
The most serious emergency is a heart attack that stops the heart.
If a person has collapsed and is not breathing normally, start CPR.
Push hard and fast in the center of the chest, about twice per second.
It is tiring, but it keeps blood flowing to the brain.
Many schools and workplaces offer short courses, and a few hours of training could make all the difference one day.
You do not need a large garden to grow your own food.
A few pots on a balcony or a small corner of a yard are enough to start, and gardening is one of the most relaxing hobbies there is.
Begin with easy vegetables.
Lettuce and spinach grow quickly, and you can pick the leaves a few at a time.
Courgettes and cucumbers produce so much fruit in summer that you will probably have to give some to your neighbors.
Cabbages take longer, but they survive the cold.
If you have a sunny wall, raspberries are a delightful treat: fresh, juicy and far tastier than those in the shops.
Most vegetables need at least six hours of sunlight a day, good soil and regular water.
Plant the seeds evenly, following the instructions on the packet, and do not put them too close together.
Adding compost, made from old vegetables and garden waste, will make your soil richer and reduce the amount of rubbish you throw away.
Of course, you will not be the only one who wants to eat your vegetables.
Slugs, snails and insects can destroy young plants overnight.
Instead of using chemicals, many gardeners grow flowers such as daisies nearby, which attract insects that eat the pests.
Birds help, too, and a small pond can bring in frogs, which love eating slugs.
Pick your vegetables when they are ripe, before they become too big or start to rot.
Some of your first attempts will fail, and that is normal.
But there are few pleasures greater than eating a salad that you grew yourself.
Last summer, I spent a fortnight in Kenya, and I finally went on the safari I had dreamed about since I was a child.
We stayed at a small campsite in the Maasai Mara, one of the most famous wildlife areas in Africa.
Every morning, our guide, Joseph, woke us up before sunrise, because the animals are most active in the cool early hours.
On the first morning, we drove across the plains in an open jeep.
Within minutes, we saw a group of giraffes eating leaves from the top of a tree.
A mother was standing with her calf, which was already taller than our jeep.
Later, we watched a family of elephants walking slowly towards the river.
A flock of colorful birds rose from the grass as we passed.
The highlight of the trip was the Great Migration.
Every year, more than a million wildebeest, together with hundreds of thousands of zebras, travel between the Serengeti in Tanzania and the Maasai Mara in search of fresh grass.
We watched them cross the Mara River, where crocodiles were waiting in the water.
It was the most dramatic thing I have ever seen, and also one of the hardest to watch.
Joseph taught us a lot about ecology.
He explained that every species, from the lions to the tiny insects, plays a role in the ecosystem.
He also told us that the local Maasai people had lived alongside these animals for centuries.
Tourism brings money to the region, but it also creates problems, such as too many vehicles surrounding a single lion.
"The animals were here first," he said. "We are only visitors."
When I got home, I sent Joseph a postcard to thank him.
I also started giving a small amount of money every month to a conservation project in Kenya.
It felt like the least I could do for such an unforgettable place.
Throughout history, technology has destroyed some jobs and created others.
A hundred years ago, telephone operators connected every call by hand, and lamplighters walked through the streets every evening lighting gas lamps.
Today, those jobs no longer exist.
Which jobs are disappearing now?
One example is the bank teller.
Since most people now use cash machines and online banking, many banks have closed branches and reduced their staff.
In shops, self-checkout machines are replacing cashiers, and in many countries the number of postmen and postwomen has fallen because people send emails instead of letters.
Travel agents have also become less common, since most travelers now book flights and hotels themselves.
Artificial intelligence may affect office jobs next.
Some tasks that accountants, translators and even journalists do could be done faster by computers.
However, experts say that jobs rarely disappear completely.
More often, they change: an accountant who once spent hours doing calculations may now spend more time advising clients.
Some jobs seem safe, at least for now.
It is hard to imagine a robot hairdresser or a machine that can do everything a good mechanic, butcher or babysitter does.
Jobs that require human contact, creativity or skillful hands are generally less likely to be replaced.
New jobs are appearing, too, many of which did not exist twenty years ago, such as app developer or social media manager.
The challenge for workers is to keep learning, because the most valuable skill in the future may be the ability to adapt.
We often describe people with a single word: stubborn, talkative, easygoing, cheerful.
These words describe personality traits, the ways of thinking and behaving that make each of us unique.
But are we born with them, and can they change?
Psychologists usually describe personality using five broad traits.
Some people are naturally outgoing and love company, while others, often called introverts, prefer quiet time alone.
Some are diligent and organized, while others are more careless.
Some are cautious and anxious, and others stay calm in almost any situation.
Research with twins suggests that genes explain roughly half of these differences, and the rest comes from our experiences.
The good news is that personality is not fixed.
Long-term studies show that most people become more responsible, more pleasant and less anxious as they grow older.
Important life events, such as starting a job or becoming a parent, can also shape who we are.
A shy teenager may become a confident adult, and a careless student may become a careful doctor.
Can we change our personality on purpose?
Some experiments suggest that we can, at least a little.
People who wanted to become more sociable, for example, were asked to talk to a stranger every day or to join in with group activities.
After several months, many of them reported real changes.
The key seems to be behavior: if you keep acting in a certain way, it slowly becomes part of who you are.
Personality is less like a stone and more like a river: it has a direction, but it keeps moving.
You have an important essay to write, but first you check your phone, then you tidy your desk, then you make a snack.
Suddenly, it is midnight and you have not written a word.
This is procrastination, and almost everyone does it.
Contrary to popular belief, procrastinators are usually not lazy.
Psychologists say that we put off tasks because they make us feel bad: bored, anxious or afraid of failure.
Delaying the task makes us feel better for a moment, but the stress returns later, even stronger.
So how can you buckle down and get started?
First, make the task smaller.
"Write an essay" sounds terrible, but "write the first paragraph" does not.
Many people find that once they start, it is much easier to continue.
Second, remove temptations.
Put your phone in another room, or use an app that blocks social media for a certain time.
Some students use the "Pomodoro technique": they work for twenty-five minutes, then take a five-minute break.
Third, be kind to yourself.
Research shows that students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before one exam were less likely to procrastinate before the next.
Scolding yourself only increases the bad feelings that caused the problem in the first place.
Finally, give yourself a reason to finish.
Tell a friend when you plan to hand in your work, or promise yourself a reward, such as a film or a walk, once the job is done.
Procrastination is a habit, and like all habits, it can be changed, although probably not today.
Backpacking is one of the cheapest ways to see the world.
Instead of expensive hotels and organized tours, backpackers travel with a single bag, stay in hostels and use public transport.
Here are some tips for making your money last longer.
Accommodation is usually the biggest expense.
Hostels offer beds in shared dorm rooms for a fraction of the price of a hotel, and many have a kitchen where you can cook your own meals.
In the countryside, a campsite can be even cheaper, especially if you carry your own tent.
Booking a few days in advance is usually wise in the busy season, but during quieter months you can often find a bed when you arrive.
Transport is the next thing to plan.
Buses are generally cheaper than trains, and night buses save you the cost of a bed.
In many countries, it is worth buying a rail pass that allows unlimited travel for a fortnight or a month.
Hitchhiking is still common in some places, but it carries obvious risks, so most experts advise against it.
Money itself can be expensive, too.
Before you leave, compare the exchange rates and fees charged by different banks and cards.
Avoid changing money at airports, where the rates are often poor.
Finally, remember that the best experiences are often free.
Walking through an old town, swimming at a quiet beach, climbing a mountain to watch the sunrise or chatting with other travelers at your hostel costs nothing at all.
Many backpackers say that they remember these moments long after they have forgotten the famous sights.
And do not forget to send a postcard home: your grandparents will appreciate it more than a message.
Good manners are important everywhere, but what counts as polite can vary enormously from one culture to another.
A gesture that is friendly in one country may be rude in another, so a little knowledge can save travelers from embarrassment.
Greetings are a good example.
In many Western countries, people greet each other with a firm handshake.
In Japan, bowing is more common, and the depth of the bow shows how much respect you want to show.
In Thailand, people press their palms together and bow slightly, a greeting called the wai.
Eating together has its own rules.
In China and Japan, you should never stick your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice, because this is done at funerals.
In parts of the Middle East, it is traditionally polite to eat with your right hand only.
In Korea, you should wait for the oldest person at the table to start eating before you begin.
Money can also be a source of confusion.
In the United States, tipping a waiter fifteen or twenty percent is expected, and not doing so is considered very rude.
In Japan, however, tipping is unusual and can even cause embarrassment.
Of course, these are general rules, and every person is different.
Most people are very forgiving towards visitors who make an honest mistake.
The most important thing is to show that you are trying: learn a few words of greeting, watch what local people do, and when in doubt, simply ask.
Cancer is not a single disease.
It is the name for more than a hundred different illnesses that have one thing in common: cells in the body begin to grow out of control.
Normally, our cells divide, do their job and then die in an orderly way.
In cancer, damage to a cell's genes, called mutations, causes it to keep dividing, and eventually a lump of tissue called a tumor may form.
What causes these mutations?
Some are simply bad luck, and the risk increases as we get older.
Genetics plays a role, too: certain families have an increased risk of breast cancer, for example.
However, many cases are connected with our lifestyle and environment.
Tobacco is by far the biggest single cause, responsible for most cases of lung cancer.
Too much sun can cause skin cancer, and drinking a lot of alcohol increases the risk of cancer of the liver and other organs.
The good news is that treatment has improved enormously.
Doctors can often remove a tumor in an operation, especially if it is found early.
Radiation and chemotherapy, drugs that kill fast-growing cells, can destroy cancer that has spread.
Newer treatments help the body's own immune system to recognize and attack the disease.
In many rich countries, more than half of patients now survive for at least ten years, and millions of cancer survivors live full, active lives.
Finding cancer early is one of the most important factors.
That is why many countries offer screening programs, which check healthy people for early signs of common cancers.
Experts also estimate that around forty percent of cases could be prevented by not smoking, eating well, staying active and protecting our skin from the sun.
Today, most of us cannot imagine traveling abroad without a passport.
Yet in Europe before the First World War, people could often cross borders freely without any documents at all.
Modern passports were largely introduced during and after the war, when governments wanted to control who entered and left their countries.
A passport is an official document that proves your identity and your citizenship.
Most modern passports contain a small electronic chip that stores your photo and personal details, so that border officers can check them quickly.
Some people possess two passports, because they have dual citizenship, while others, known as stateless people, have none at all.
A visa is different.
It is permission from another country to enter, and the requirements depend on where you come from and why you are traveling.
Citizens of some countries can visit most of the world without a visa, while others need one for almost every trip.
To obtain a visa, travelers may need to fill in a long application and attend an interview at an embassy.
They may also have to show a hotel reservation, a return ticket and proof that they have enough money.
Immigration is even more complicated.
People who want to live or work permanently in another country usually need a special visa.
The process can take months or years.
After a certain number of years, many can apply for citizenship.
This often requires a language test and a test of knowledge about the country's history and laws.
For most travelers, the passport is simply a small book in their pocket, but it decides where in the world they are free to go.
If you spend a day at the beach, you will notice that the sea does not stay in the same place.
In the morning, the water may reach the rocks at the top of the beach; a few hours later, it may be a long walk away.
These regular changes are called tides, and in most coastal places they happen twice a day.
The main cause is the Moon.
Its gravity pulls on the Earth, and it pulls most strongly on the side that is closest to it.
The oceans on that side rise slightly towards the Moon, creating a bulge of water.
Surprisingly, there is a second bulge on the opposite side of the Earth, because the Moon pulls less strongly on the water there.
As the Earth turns, each coast passes through both bulges.
That is why there are usually two high tides and two low tides in about twenty-five hours.
A simple diagram makes this much easier to understand than words.
The Sun has an effect, too.
When the Sun, the Moon and the Earth are in a line, their forces combine and create extra-high "spring tides."
When they are at an angle, the tides are weaker, and these are called "neap tides."
The size of the tides varies enormously from place to place.
In some parts of the Mediterranean, the difference between high and low tide is only a few centimeters.
In the Bay of Fundy in Canada, it can be more than fifteen meters, because of the shape of the shallow bay.
For fishermen, sailors and anyone who walks along the coast, knowing the times of the tides is essential.
Every year, people are trapped by the rising water because they did not check.
Every winter, in the small village of Jukkasjärvi in northern Sweden, artists build a hotel entirely from ice.
The ice comes from the nearby Torne River, which freezes solid during the long Arctic winter.
In spring, the hotel slowly melts and returns to the river, and the following year a new one is built.
The idea began in 1989 with a small igloo that was used for an art exhibition.
Some visitors asked if they could sleep in it, and the ice hotel was born.
Today, it attracts thousands of guests from all over the world, and many make a reservation months in advance.
Each room is designed by a different artist, so no two rooms are alike.
One might contain a magnificent ice sculpture of a dragon.
Another might look like a forest, with trees and delicate flowers carved from ice.
The light that shines through the walls is a stunning blue.
Even the glasses in the bar are made of ice.
Sleeping there is an unforgettable experience, but it is not for everyone.
The temperature inside the rooms is about minus five degrees, whatever the weather outside.
Guests sleep in thermal sleeping bags on beds of solid ice covered with reindeer fur.
Most people stay for only one night and spend the rest of their holiday in warm wooden cabins nearby.
During the day, visitors can go dog sledding, ride snowmobiles or visit a traditional hut where local Sami people explain their way of life.
At night, if they are lucky, they may see the northern lights dancing across the sky in waves of green and purple.
For many guests, it is the most glorious sight of their lives.
Children are a huge market.
They spend their own pocket money, and they have a strong influence on what their parents buy, from breakfast cereal to the family car.
Not surprisingly, companies spend billions trying to reach them.
But should they be allowed to?
Those who want a ban argue that young children cannot understand what an ad is.
Research suggests that until the age of about eight, many children believe that adverts simply give them information.
They do not realize that someone is trying to persuade them.
Many of the products advertised to children are also unhealthy, such as sweets, sugary drinks and fast food, and some experts connect this with rising rates of childhood obesity.
Online, the problem has become even more serious, because games and videos are full of hidden advertising and in-app purchases.
Some countries have already acted.
Sweden and Norway have banned television advertising aimed at young children, and the Canadian province of Quebec has restricted it since 1980.
Opponents of a ban, however, raise several objections.
They argue that it is the parents' responsibility, not the government's, to decide what children watch and buy.
Television channels also depend on advertising to pay for children's programs, so a ban could mean fewer good shows.
And in the age of the internet, they say, a ban on one channel is easy to avoid.
Perhaps the most practical solution is a combination: clear rules about what can be advertised to children, especially online, and lessons at school that teach young people how advertising works.
A child who understands the trick is much harder to fool.
The modern circus was born in London in 1768.
A former soldier called Philip Astley, who was a brilliant horse rider, discovered that if he rode in a circle, he could balance on the horse's back more easily.
He built a circular ring, invited audiences to watch, and soon added acrobats, clowns and music between the horse shows.
The circus had begun.
In the nineteenth century, the circus became enormously popular.
Traveling circuses moved from town to town with huge tents, and people came from miles around to see the performers.
Acrobats flew through the air on the trapeze, jugglers threw knives and balls, and athletic riders stood on galloping horses.
Many circuses also showed exotic animals, such as lions, tigers and elephants, which audiences had never seen before.
Life in the circus was hard.
Performers traveled constantly, practiced for hours every day and risked serious injuries.
For the animals, it was often worse.
They spent most of their lives in small cages and were sometimes trained using cruel methods.
In recent decades, dozens of countries have banned wild animals in circuses.
Some people thought that this would be the end of the circus.
Instead, it led to a remarkable transformation.
In 1984, a group of street performers in Quebec founded Cirque du Soleil, a circus with no animals at all.
Its shows combine acrobats, dance, music and stunning costumes, and they have been seen by hundreds of millions of people.
Today, the circus is less about danger and more about art, but the magic of watching a human leap, twist and fly through the air remains the same.
Most of us feel a little guilty about gossip.
We are told from childhood that talking about people behind their backs is not nice.
Yet studies suggest that we spend a large part of our conversations talking about other people, often more than half of the time.
Why is gossip so common?
Some scientists believe that it plays an important social role.
The British psychologist Robin Dunbar has suggested that gossip developed as a human version of grooming.
Monkeys and other primates spend hours cleaning each other's fur, which creates strong bonds within the group.
Humans live in much larger groups, so we cannot groom everyone, but we can talk.
Sharing information about others helps to build trust and friendship.
Gossip also protects groups from people who cheat.
If someone is selfish or dishonest, the news spreads quickly, and others become more careful.
In experiments, people behaved more generously when they knew that others might talk about them afterwards.
In this sense, the fear of gossip encourages good behavior.
Not all gossip is negative, either.
Researchers have found that most everyday gossip is neutral, simply news about who is getting married, who has a new job or who is moving away.
Some of it is even positive, such as praising a colleague who helped us.
Of course, gossip can also be cruel.
False rumors can destroy a person's reputation, and online, they can spread to thousands of people in minutes.
The difference, perhaps, lies in our intention: are we sharing news, or are we trying to hurt someone?
A good rule is to say nothing about a person that you would not be willing to say to their face.
We know more about the surface of the Moon than about the bottom of our own oceans.
Although oceans cover more than seventy percent of the Earth, only about a quarter of the seafloor has been mapped in detail.
The deep sea remains one of the last great areas of exploration.
The deepest place on the planet is the Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench in the Pacific Ocean.
It is nearly eleven kilometers below the surface, deeper than Mount Everest is high.
At the bottom, the pressure of the water is more than a thousand times greater than at the surface, enough to crush an ordinary submarine like a can.
Despite this, humans have been there.
In 1960, Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh made the first dive to the bottom in a special vessel called the Trieste.
They spent only twenty minutes there, and they could see very little because the vessel stirred up clouds of mud.
More than fifty years later, in 2012, the film director James Cameron went down alone.
Since then, a number of other people have made the journey.
What lives down there?
Below about a thousand meters, sunlight cannot reach, and the water is completely dark and extremely cold.
Yet it is full of life.
Many deep-sea creatures produce their own light, a phenomenon called bioluminescence, to find food or to attract a partner.
Scientists regularly discover new species, and some expeditions find dozens in a single trip.
The deep sea is also valuable for another reason: its floor contains minerals used in batteries and phones.
Some companies want to start mining them, but many scientists warn that this could destroy ecosystems that we have only just begun to understand.
For more than a century, only children have had a bad reputation.
An American psychologist at the end of the nineteenth century described being an only child as "a disease in itself."
Many people still believe that children without brothers or sisters grow up selfish, spoiled and lonely.
Is it true?
Modern research says no.
Large studies comparing only children with those who have siblings have found very few differences in personality.
Only children are not more selfish, and they are just as good at making friends.
In some studies, they even did slightly better at school, possibly because they received more attention and resources from their parents.
In many parts of the world, families are getting smaller, so only children are becoming more common.
Parents may have only one child for various reasons: they started a family later, they cannot afford more, or they simply feel that one is enough.
In some cases, parents are divorced, and the child divides their time between two homes.
Of course, growing up without siblings has both advantages and disadvantages.
Only children often have a close attachment to their parents and feel comfortable spending time alone.
On the other hand, they may miss the daily companionship of a brother or sister.
And when their parents grow old, they may have to care for them alone.
Many only children say that cousins, a nephew or niece, or close friends became like family to them.
The lesson from research is simple: what matters most is not how many children there are in a family, but how supportive and loving the family is.
Sculpture is one of the oldest forms of art.
Long before people wrote books, they carved figures from stone, bone and wood.
Over thousands of years, sculptors have used many different materials, and each one presents its own challenges.
Marble has always been a favorite of sculptors because it is beautiful and relatively easy to carve when it is freshly cut.
The most famous marble statue in the world is probably Michelangelo's David, completed in Florence in 1504.
It is more than five meters tall and was carved from a single block of stone that other artists had rejected.
With a chisel and a hammer, Michelangelo removed the stone layer by layer, and a single mistake could have ruined the whole work.
Bronze allows a completely different approach.
The artist first makes a model in clay or wax.
Then a mold is made around it, and hot liquid bronze is poured inside, a process called casting.
Because the metal is strong, bronze sculptures can have thin, delicate parts that would break in stone.
Auguste Rodin's The Thinker, a man sitting with his chin on his hand, is one of the best-known bronze works in history.
In the twentieth century, sculptors began to use industrial materials such as steel and iron, and their works became larger and larger.
The Angel of the North, a giant steel figure in the north of England, is twenty meters tall.
Its wings are wider than those of a large passenger plane.
When it was built in 1998, many local people hated it.
Today, it has become a much-loved symbol of the region.
Every second, lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about forty to fifty times.
It is one of the most powerful forces in nature.
A single flash can heat the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius, roughly five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
Lightning begins inside storm clouds.
Strong winds carry drops of water and small pieces of ice up and down.
As they hit each other, they build up an electrical charge, rather like static electricity when you rub a balloon on your hair.
When the charge becomes large enough, electricity suddenly jumps between the cloud and the ground, or between two clouds.
The heat makes the air expand so fast that it explodes with a loud bang: that is thunder.
Because light travels much faster than sound, we always see the flash before we hear the thunder.
You can use this to estimate how far away a storm is.
Count the seconds between the flash and the thunder, and divide by three to get the distance in kilometers.
There are many myths about lightning.
One is that it never strikes the same place twice.
In fact, tall buildings are hit many times every year.
Another is that the rubber tires on a car protect you.
A car is fairly safe in a storm, but that is because the electricity flows around the outer metal body and into the ground, not because of the rubber.
If you are caught outside in a thunderstorm, get inside a building or a car as quickly as possible.
Stay away from tall trees, metal poles and water, and do not wait until the rain starts: lightning can strike more than fifteen kilometers from a storm.
In the past, lightning killed many more people than it does today, largely because fewer people now work in open fields.
Last year, I started volunteering at an animal shelter every Saturday morning.
I had always wanted a dog, but my apartment is too small, so this seemed like the perfect solution.
I did not realize how much it would change me.
The shelter looks after about sixty animals at any one time, mostly dogs and cats.
Some were abandoned by their owners, some were found in the street, and others were given up because their families could no longer look after them.
On my first morning, the noise was incredible: dozens of dogs barking at once, all hoping for attention.
The work is not glamorous.
Volunteers clean cages, wash food bowls and take the dogs for walks.
We also spend time simply sitting with the more nervous animals, so that they learn to trust people again.
A vet visits twice a week to check their health, and the staff keep detailed records of each animal's personality.
My favorite was Duke, an old black dog with a grey face.
He had spent eight months at the shelter, because most visitors wanted an adorable puppy, not an elderly dog with bad hips.
But Duke was the gentlest, most faithful companion I have ever met.
Every Saturday, he waited for me by the gate, and when I left, he watched me until I disappeared.
In the spring, a retired teacher called Hannah came to the shelter.
She lived alone and wanted a calm dog to keep her company.
When she met Duke, he walked over, put his head on her knee and sighed.
She adopted him that afternoon.
I was sad to say goodbye, but also thankful.
A few weeks later, Hannah sent the shelter a photo of Duke asleep on her sofa, looking completely at home.
We pinned it on the wall, next to dozens of other happy endings.
That wall is the reason I keep coming back every Saturday.
When we watch international news, we hear about presidents, prime ministers, kings and queens.
But these titles can mean very different things in different countries.
Understanding the difference helps to explain how power works around the world.
In a republic such as the United States, the president is both the head of state and the head of the government.
He or she is elected directly by the people and leads the administration, a team of officials who run the country day to day.
If the president dies or resigns, the vice president takes over.
Britain works differently.
It is a monarchy, so the head of state is the king, but his role is mainly ceremonial.
He opens parliament, welcomes foreign leaders and represents the nation at important events, but he does not make political decisions.
Real power belongs to the prime minister, who is usually the leader of the party with the most seats in parliament.
Japan follows a similar system, with an emperor instead of a king.
Other countries combine the two models.
In Germany, there is a president, but the role is largely symbolic, and the chancellor leads the government.
In France, both the president and the prime minister have significant power, and the president is generally the more prominent of the two.
No system is perfect.
Supporters of presidential systems say that they give voters a clear choice of leader.
