Supporters of parliamentary systems argue that a prime minister who loses the support of parliament can be replaced quickly, without waiting for the next election.
What matters most, in the end, is not the title of the leader but whether the people can hold that leader publicly responsible.
The Amazon is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.
It covers an area almost as big as Australia, spread across nine countries in South America, with most of it in Brazil.
The Amazon River, which flows through the jungle, carries more water than any other river in the world.
Life in the Amazon exists in incredible abundance.
Around one in ten of all known species lives there, from jaguars and river dolphins to thousands of kinds of ants, spiders and butterflies.
Scientists discover new species every year, and many plants that grow there are used in medicines.
The forest is also home to hundreds of indigenous groups, some of whom have very little contact with the outside world.
The Amazon plays an enormous ecological role.
Its trees absorb huge amounts of carbon dioxide, which helps to slow down climate change.
They also release water into the air, creating rain that falls far away, even on farms in the south of the continent.
Unfortunately, the forest is shrinking.
Large areas have been cut down or burned to make space for cattle farms and for crops such as soy.
Scientists estimate that almost a fifth of the original forest has already been lost.
Some warn that if deforestation continues, parts of the Amazon could reach a point where they turn into dry grassland, with disastrous consequences for the climate.
There is some hope.
When governments enforce the law and support indigenous communities, deforestation falls sharply.
Preservation of the Amazon is not only a local issue; it matters to all of humanity.
A magician shows you an empty hand, closes it, and when he opens it again, there is a coin inside.
You were watching carefully, so how did he do it?
The answer usually has less to do with his hands than with your brain.
Magicians are experts in attention.
Our brains cannot notice everything at once, so they select the things that seem most important.
Magicians use this through a technique called misdirection.
They make you look at one hand while the other does the secret work.
A joke, a sudden movement or even a glance at the audience can pull your attention in the wrong direction.
When the magician looks up at a flying card, you look up, too, and you miss the coin going into his sleeve.
Magicians also exploit our expectations.
If a magician pretends to throw a ball into the air twice, many people "see" it leave his hand the third time, even though he has kept it.
Our brains predict what will happen next and fill in the gaps, and most of the time this is extremely useful.
It only becomes a weakness when someone knows how to use it against us.
Interestingly, scientists have started working with magicians to study the brain.
Their tricks provide simple experiments that show the limits of human perception.
The lesson is a little uncomfortable: we see far less of the world than we think.
But it is also rather wonderful, because a good magician reminds us how amazing the ordinary mind really is.
A biography is the story of a person's life, written by someone else.
When people write about their own lives, it is called an autobiography.
Biographies are among the most popular books in the world, from the lives of famous scientists and sports stars to those of forgotten poets.
But how is a good biography written?
The first stage is research, and it can take years.
Biographers read letters, diaries and newspapers, and they spend long hours in libraries and archives.
If the person is still alive, or died recently, they also interview family members, friends and colleagues.
Every fact must be checked, because historical records are sometimes wrong, and people's memories are often incorrect.
Next comes the writing.
A biography is not simply a list of dates.
The best biographers create a strong narrative: they choose the most important moments and show how the person changed over time.
Many start with an outline of the whole book, then write several drafts, and each revision makes the story clearer.
Biographers also face difficult moral questions.
Should they include private details that the person wanted to keep secret?
How can they write fairly about someone they admire, or someone they dislike?
A good biographer tries to be honest about a person's weaknesses as well as their achievements.
After all, the most interesting people are rarely perfect, and readers usually trust a book more when it shows the whole human being.
When the book is finished, the publisher's editors check it again before it finally reaches the shops.
Washing your hands with soap is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy.
Doctors say that it can prevent many illnesses, from stomach infections to the common cold.
But why is soap so much better than water alone?
The answer lies in chemistry.
Much of the dirt on our hands, and many germs, are held there by oil and grease.
Water and oil do not mix, so water alone simply runs over them.
Soap molecules have a special shape: one end is attracted to water, and the other end is attracted to oil.
When you rub soap on your hands, the oil-loving ends surround the dirt, while the water-loving ends face outwards.
When you rinse, the water carries the tiny packages of dirt away.
Soap does something else, too.
Many viruses are surrounded by a thin layer of fat.
Soap can break this layer apart, which destroys the virus.
That is why health experts recommend soap and water even more than hand gels, which do not work well on very dirty hands.
The way you wash matters as much as the soap.
Experts suggest washing for at least twenty seconds, about the time it takes to sing "Happy Birthday" twice.
Remember the backs of your hands, between your fingers, your thumbs and under your nails, because these are the places people most commonly forget.
Finally, dry your hands properly, because germs spread much more easily from wet skin.
It takes less than a minute, but it is one of the most effective habits you can have.
In many countries, colds and flu are much more common in winter.
Offices and schools are full of people coughing and sneezing, and doctors are busier than at any other time of year.
But it is not the cold weather itself that makes us ill.
Colds are caused by viruses, so why do they spread more easily in winter?
The first reason is that we spend more time indoors.
When it is freezing outside, people gather in warm rooms with the windows closed.
If one person has a virus, it can easily pass to everyone else through the air or on the surfaces they touch.
The second reason is the air itself.
Many viruses survive longer in cold, dry air, and central heating makes the air inside our homes even drier.
Dry air may also dry out the inside of our noses, which normally help to trap viruses before they enter the body.
A third factor may be sunlight.
Our skin produces vitamin D when it is exposed to the sun, and this vitamin seems to support the immune system.
In winter, days are short, and many people get very little sunlight, especially in northern countries.
So what can we do?
Washing our hands regularly, opening windows for a few minutes every day and staying at home when we are unwell all reduce the spread of viruses.
Sleep matters, too: people who sleep less than six hours a night are more likely to catch a cold.
And although there is no cure for the common cold, a flu vaccine each autumn can protect you from the most serious winter sickness.
In the early hours of Sunday, 2 September 1666, a fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane, in the center of London.
The baker, Thomas Farriner, and his family escaped through an upstairs window, but their servant did not.
At first, nobody was very worried.
Fires were common in the city, and the mayor, who was woken up and came to look, said that it was so small that a woman could put it out.
He was completely wrong.
The summer had been long and dry, and most houses in London were built of wood, very close together.
A strong wind carried the flames from street to street.
Warehouses near the river were full of oil, wood and other materials that burned easily, and the fire quickly grew out of control.
For four days, the fire destroyed everything in its path.
Desperate people loaded their possessions onto carts and boats, and thousands camped in the fields outside the city.
A government official called Samuel Pepys, who kept a famous diary, described the terrible scene.
He also wrote that he buried his wine and his parmesan cheese in his garden to save them.
By the time the wind dropped, more than thirteen thousand houses had been destroyed, together with about eighty churches and the old St Paul's Cathedral.
Tens of thousands of people had lost their homes.
Surprisingly, only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, although historians believe the real number was probably higher.
The disaster changed London forever.
New laws required buildings to be made of brick and stone instead of wood, and streets were made wider.
The architect Christopher Wren designed dozens of new churches and a magnificent new St Paul's Cathedral, which still stands today.
Near the place where the fire began, a tall stone column called the Monument was built to remember it.
It is sixty-one meters high, exactly the distance from its base to the site of the bakery on Pudding Lane.
Most social media platforms say that users must be at least thirteen years old.
In reality, many younger children have accounts, because it is easy to lie about your age online.
In recent years, some governments have decided to go further.
Australia, for example, passed a law requiring platforms to prevent people under sixteen from creating accounts.
Supporters of stricter limits point to worrying research.
Some studies have found that teenagers who spend many hours a day on social media are more likely to feel anxious or depressed.
Constant comparison with the perfect lives of others can damage self-confidence, and cyberbullying can follow children into their bedrooms at night.
There are also concerns about privacy, since platforms collect enormous amounts of data about their users.
Opponents of a ban, however, argue that it may do more harm than good.
For many young people, social media is an important way to interact with friends, find information and express their creativity.
Some teenagers feel isolated, for instance because of a disability or because they live in remote areas.
They may find support online that they cannot find elsewhere.
Critics also doubt that a ban can work, because clever teenagers will simply find a way around it.
Many experts believe that the answer is not only a matter of age.
They suggest better parental controls, filters that protect children from harmful content, and education that teaches young people to use social media wisely.
Platforms, too, could be required to design their apps with children's safety in mind.
They should not simply try to keep children online for as long as possible.
We all know someone who is always late.
They arrive ten minutes after the film has started, keep their friends waiting in restaurants and apologize with the same excuse every time: "The traffic was terrible!"
It is easy to think that these people are simply rude or selfish.
But psychologists say the reasons are more complicated.
One explanation is optimism.
Many people who are often late genuinely believe that everything will take less time than it does.
They remember the one morning when the drive to work took fifteen minutes, and they forget the twenty mornings when it took thirty.
Consequently, they leave home at the last minute.
Psychologists call this tendency the planning fallacy, and it affects almost everyone to some extent.
Another reason is that some people find waiting extremely uncomfortable or even stressful.
They hate arriving early and having nothing to do, so without intending to, they keep doing "just one more thing" before they leave.
One more email, one more message, one more cup of coffee, and suddenly they are late again.
Culture plays a part, too.
In some countries, arriving exactly on time for a party is considered unusual, while in others, being five minutes late for a meeting is shocking.
What counts as "late" is not the same everywhere.
If you are always late and are eager to change, experts have some practical advice.
Measure how long your regular journeys really take, and plan to arrive fifteen minutes early.
Bring a book, so that waiting does not feel like a waste of time.
And remember that being punctual is a way of showing respect: it tells people that their time matters as much as yours.
It is unlikely that you will change overnight, but small steps make a real difference.
On the Canadian flag, there is a single red leaf.
It comes from the maple tree, which is famous for producing one of the world's most delicious foods: maple syrup.
Canada produces around three quarters of the world's supply, most of it in the province of Quebec.
The process depends on the weather.
In early spring, the nights are still freezing, but the days are warmer.
This change in temperature makes the sap, a thin, sweet liquid, move up and down inside the trunk of the tree.
Farmers make a small hole in the trunk and collect the sap in buckets or through plastic tubes.
The season is short, usually just four to six weeks.
The sap does not taste like syrup at first.
It is about ninety-eight percent water, so it has to be boiled for many hours until most of the water has disappeared.
It takes about forty gallons of sap to make a single gallon of syrup.
This is why real maple syrup is expensive, and why many cheap supermarket brands are actually ordinary sugar syrup with added flavor.
Long before Europeans arrived in North America, Indigenous peoples had discovered how to collect maple sap and turn it into sugar.
Today, maple season is still an important tradition in Quebec.
Families visit "sugar shacks" in the forest, where they eat pancakes, beans and bacon covered in fresh syrup.
A popular treat is maple taffy: hot syrup poured onto clean snow, where it cools into a sticky candy that is rolled onto a stick.
Climate change is a growing concern for maple farmers, because the pattern of cold nights and warm days is becoming less predictable.
Some years the season starts earlier, and some years it is shorter.
Scientists and farmers are working together to find ways to protect this sweet and very Canadian tradition.
In 1991, two hikers in the Alps found the frozen body of a man who had died more than five thousand years ago.
Scientists called him Ötzi, and they discovered something surprising on his skin: sixty-one tattoos.
Most were simple lines, placed on his joints, and some experts think they may have been a kind of medical treatment for pain.
Tattoos, in other words, are one of the oldest forms of human art.
In many cultures, they had deep meaning.
In Polynesia, complex tattoos showed a person's family, their rank in society and their achievements.
The word "tattoo" itself comes from a Polynesian language.
In other places, however, tattoos were used to mark criminals or slaves, and this created a strong prejudice against them that lasted for centuries.
In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, tattoos in Western countries were mostly connected with sailors, soldiers and prisoners.
Many people saw them as a sign of rebellion or bad behavior.
In Japan, tattoos became associated with criminal gangs, and even today, some public baths and gyms do not allow people with tattoos to enter.
Today, attitudes have changed dramatically in many countries.
In some Western countries, roughly a third of young adults have at least one tattoo.
Tattoo artists are respected for their craft, and some of their work is shown in art galleries.
Acceptance is growing even in traditional workplaces, although some employers still prefer staff to cover their tattoos.
Before getting a tattoo, experts advise people to think carefully.
A tattoo is made by putting ink under the skin with a needle, and removing it is expensive, painful and not always completely successful.
A name or a design that seems perfect at eighteen may feel very different at forty.
When you plan a trip, choosing where to stay is one of the most important decisions.
There are many different categories of accommodation, and each one offers a very different kind of holiday.
A resort is designed so that guests never need to leave.
It usually has several restaurants, swimming pools, sports facilities and entertainment.
Many resorts are "all-inclusive," which means that food and drinks are included in the price.
Resorts are ideal for families who want to relax, although critics say that guests see very little of the real country.
Hotels range from cheap and simple to exclusive and luxurious.
In a good hotel, the staff will carry your baggage, clean your room every day and help you to reserve a table at a restaurant.
Business travelers often prefer hotels in the city center, close to meetings and public transport.
Hostels are the cheapest option, and they are especially popular with young travelers.
Guests usually sleep in shared rooms and use a shared kitchen, but many hostels also have private rooms.
The atmosphere is casual and social, and it is easy to meet people from all over the world.
In the countryside, you might stay in a small lodge, a mountain cabin or a family-run guesthouse.
These often give travelers the best impression of local life, because the owners can recommend places that are not in any guidebook.
Finally, renting an apartment can be a good choice for longer stays, although in some cities it has contributed to rising rents for local residents.
In comparison, there is no single best option.
It depends on your budget, the kind of experience you want and who you are traveling with.
The most important thing is to read the reviews carefully before you book.
If you have ever heard your grandparents say that a loaf of bread used to cost a few cents, you already understand the basic idea of inflation.
Inflation is the general rise in prices over time, which means that the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services.
Economists describe this as a fall in purchasing power.
To measure inflation, governments track the prices of a "basket" of typical purchases, from food and fuel to rent and haircuts, and publish the results as an index.
If the index rises by three percent in a year, prices overall are three percent higher than twelve months earlier.
Why do prices rise?
Sometimes the cause is on the demand side: when people and businesses want to spend more than the economy can produce, sellers can raise their prices.
At other times, the cause is on the supply side, for example when a war or a drought pushes up the cost of energy or food, and businesses pass those costs on to customers.
Expectations matter, too: if workers expect prices to rise, they demand higher wages, which can push prices up further.
A little inflation is considered healthy.
Most central banks aim to keep it at around two percent, because stable, predictable prices make it easier for businesses to plan and invest.
High inflation, however, can be extremely damaging.
It reduces the value of savings and pensions, and it hurts poorer households most, because they spend a larger share of their earnings on essentials such as food and heating.
The most common weapon against inflation is the interest rate.
When a central bank raises rates, borrowing becomes more expensive, so people take out fewer loans and mortgages, spending slows down and, eventually, prices stabilize.
The difficulty is timing.
Raise rates too slowly, and inflation may get out of control; raise them too quickly, and the economy may fall into recession.
For most of the twentieth century, cities dealt with rainwater in the same way: they tried to get rid of it as fast as possible.
Streets were covered in concrete and asphalt, and huge underground drains carried the water away to the nearest river.
As urban areas grew and storms became more intense, however, this approach began to fail.
The drains overflowed, and flooding became a regular and costly problem.
Authorities estimated that upgrading the old drains to cope with heavier storms would be extremely costly, and the damage in some districts was significantly higher every year.
A different idea has become increasingly popular: instead of fighting rain, cities should absorb it, like a sponge.
The term "sponge city" was made popular by the Chinese landscape architect Kongjian Yu, and in 2015 China launched a national program to put the concept into practice.
Sixteen pilot cities, including Wuhan, were given funding to redesign parts of their urban landscape.
The long-term target is ambitious: by 2030, eighty percent of urban areas should absorb and reuse at least seventy percent of their rainwater.
What does a sponge city look like in practice?
Many of the changes are surprisingly simple.
Car parks and pavements can be built with permeable materials that let water sink through.
Rain gardens, small areas of plants planted slightly below street level, collect runoff from roads and roofs.
Green roofs slow the water down, and restored wetlands and parks along rivers can safely hold large volumes of water during heavy storms, then release it slowly.
The stored water can later be used for irrigation, which is valuable during periods of drought.
The approach has clear benefits beyond flood control.
More green space cools cities during heat waves, improves air quality and creates habitats for wildlife.
However, sponge cities are not a complete solution.
During the most extreme storms, even well-designed systems can be overwhelmed, and converting an existing city is slow and expensive.
Most experts see them as one essential part of a broader strategy, alongside better drainage and early warning systems.
Students who stay up all night before an exam are making a well-known mistake.
Research over the past few decades has shown that sleep is not simply a break from learning; it is an essential part of the learning process itself.
Without it, much of what we learn during the day is lost.
Scientists call this process memory consolidation.
During the day, new information is stored temporarily in a small part of the brain called the hippocampus.
Its capacity is limited, a bit like the memory of a phone that fills up quickly.
Specifically, the brain seems to strengthen the memories that are most relevant to our goals and to let less important details fade.
At night, particularly during deep sleep, these memories are gradually transferred to the cortex, the outer layer of the brain, where they can be stored for the long term.
Some of the most striking evidence comes from experiments with rats.
When a rat learns its way through a maze, particular groups of neurons fire in a specific order.
Researchers detected that when the same rat sleeps, those neurons fire again in the same sequence, only much faster.
The brain appears to be replaying the day's experiences in order to strengthen them.
Scientists have also detected striking links between sleep and consciousness: during certain stages, the sleeping brain is almost as active as it is when we are awake.
Different types of memory seem to depend on different phases of sleep.

Deep sleep appears to be crucial for facts, such as vocabulary or historical dates, while REM sleep, the stage in which most dreaming occurs, may be more important for skills and for connecting ideas in creative ways.
In one well-known study, people who slept after struggling with a mathematical puzzle were far more likely to discover a hidden shortcut the next morning than those who stayed awake.
The practical lessons are clear.
Cramming all night is ineffective, because the brain has no opportunity to consolidate what it has learned.
Spreading study over several days, with a good night's sleep in between, produces significantly better results.
Even a short afternoon nap can enhance performance on memory tasks.
Adequate sleep is therefore not a luxury but a biological necessity: people who regularly sleep significantly less than seven hours perform worse on virtually every test of memory and attention.
This may also explain why infants, who learn at an astonishing speed, spend around sixteen hours a day asleep.
Sleep, in other words, is essentially where learning is completed.
Around seven thousand languages are spoken in the world today, but their future is far from secure.
According to UNESCO, roughly forty percent of them are endangered, and many are spoken by only a handful of elderly people.
Linguists estimate that, on average, a language disappears every few weeks.
Languages usually die gradually rather than suddenly.
The process often begins when speakers of a minority language come under economic or political pressure to use a dominant one.
Parents may decide that their children will have better prospects if they speak the language of schools, jobs and media.
In colonial times, some governments went further and actively punished children for using their home language at school.
Within two or three generations, the old language may survive only among grandparents.
Linguists have identified several warning signs, the most serious being that children no longer learn the language at home.
Why does this matter?
Every language represents a unique perception of the world.
Languages contain knowledge about local plants, animals and medicines, as well as songs, stories and legends that may never have been written down.
For the communities that speak them, they are also a vital part of their identity and heritage.
When a language is lost, that knowledge often disappears with it.
However, decline is not inevitable.
The most remarkable example of revival is Hebrew, which for centuries was used mainly in religious texts but became the everyday language of millions of people in Israel.
In Wales, Welsh is now taught in all schools, and in New Zealand, Māori "language nests" offer young children full immersion in the language from an early age.
Official recognition also matters: when a language appears in schools, courts and government publications, it sends a message that it is valued.
Technology helps, too: linguists record the last speakers, and indigenous communities launch initiatives such as apps, databases and interactive online courses.
Documentation alone cannot save a language, but combined with the determination of its speakers, it can give it a genuine chance of survival.
The organizers of major sporting events often insist that sport and politics should be kept separate.
History suggests that this is rarely possible.
Because the world is watching, the Olympic Games and other international competitions have repeatedly become a stage for political messages, protests and conflicts.
Governments have long understood the propaganda value of sport: hosting a major event allows a country to showcase its achievements to the world.
One of the most famous images in sporting history was taken at the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City.
After winning gold and bronze in the 200 meters, the African American sprinters Tommie Smith and John Carlos stood on the podium and each raised a fist in a black glove during the national anthem.
It was a silent protest against racism in the United States.
Both men were sent home, and for years they faced criticism and threats; today they are widely admired.
During the Cold War, the Olympics themselves became part of the rivalry between East and West.
In 1980, the United States and dozens of other countries boycotted the Moscow Games in protest against the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan.
Four years later, the Soviet Union and most of its allies stayed away from the Los Angeles Games.
Athletes who had trained for years lost their only chance to compete, and many later questioned whether the boycotts had achieved anything.
Sport has also been used as a tool for change.
Because of its policy of apartheid, the system of racial segregation that separated people by race, South Africa was excluded from the Olympics for almost thirty years.
The ban was strictly enforced in other sports as well, and South African teams were excluded from virtually every major international competition.
Many historians believe that the international sporting ban increased the pressure on the regime.
When South Africa hosted the 1995 Rugby World Cup after the end of apartheid, President Nelson Mandela wore the team's shirt at the final, a gesture that became a symbol of national unity.
These examples raise a difficult question.
Should athletes stay neutral, or do they have a responsibility to use their fame to speak out?
Some have openly criticized their own governments, regardless of the consequences for their careers.
There is no simple answer, but one thing is clear: as long as millions of people care about sport, it will never be entirely free of politics.
In 2013, a Dutch scientist called Mark Post presented a burger at a press conference in London.
It looked ordinary, but it had cost around three hundred thousand dollars to produce, because the meat had not come from a slaughtered cow.
It had been grown in a laboratory from a small sample of animal cells.
The technology behind this "cultivated meat" is relatively simple in principle.
Scientists take cells from a living animal and place them in large tanks called bioreactors, where they are fed a nutrient-rich liquid and multiply.
In theory, a single sample could produce tons of meat without raising and killing any animals at all.
Supporters argue that this could transform the food system.
Livestock farming uses a huge share of the world's agricultural land and produces a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions.
Cultivated meat could, potentially, reduce these problems while also ending much of the suffering of animals on industrial farms.
It would also be produced in sterile conditions, which might reduce the risk of diseases passing from animals to humans.
Progress has been genuine but slow.
Several start-ups have attracted significant investment, and some analysts predict that costs will fall dramatically as production grows.
In 2020, Singapore became the first country to approve the sale of cultivated chicken, and the United States followed in 2023.
However, production is still expensive and limited, and it is far from certain that it can compete with conventional meat on price.
Some experts also question the environmental benefits, because the bioreactors require large amounts of energy.
There are regulatory questions, too: which authority should assess its safety, and how should it be labeled in shops?
There is also resistance from consumers and politicians.
Surveys suggest that many people find the idea of "lab meat" unnatural, and some farmers see it as a threat to their way of life.
In 2023, Italy went as far as banning its production and sale.

Whether cultivated meat becomes an everyday food or remains an expensive curiosity will depend not only on science, but also on regulators, investors and, above all, on whether people are willing to eat it.
Answer this question as quickly as you can: a bat and a ball cost one dollar and ten cents in total.
The bat costs one dollar more than the ball.
How much does the ball cost?
Most people immediately think "ten cents," but the correct answer is five cents.
The psychologist Daniel Kahneman, who won the Nobel Prize in economics, used puzzles like this to illustrate how human thinking works.
He described two systems in the mind.
System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes faces, understands simple sentences and gives us instant reactions.
System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful: we use it to solve equations, compare complicated options or check an argument.
Most of the time, System 1 serves us well.
Life would be impossible if we had to think carefully about every decision.
But because it relies on shortcuts, it also makes predictable mistakes, which psychologists call cognitive biases.
Together with his colleague Amos Tversky, Kahneman identified dozens of them.
Their work significantly altered the way economists think about decision-making.
One is anchoring.
When people are shown a number, even a completely random one, it influences their later estimates.
This is why shops display a high "original price" next to a discount: the first number becomes the reference point.
Another is loss aversion: losing fifty dollars feels about twice as painful as winning fifty dollars feels good.
A third is confirmation bias, our tendency to notice evidence that supports what we already believe and to ignore evidence against it.
Advertisers and politicians frequently exploit these biases, sometimes deliberately.
Can we avoid these mistakes?
Kahneman himself was rather pessimistic: knowing about a bias does not make it disappear.
However, some strategies help.
For important decisions, we can slow down, consider the opposite view deliberately and ask others to check our reasoning.
Organizations can also design procedures, such as checklists, that force System 2 to become involved when it matters most.
In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mold had grown on one of his dishes of bacteria.
Around the mold, the bacteria had died.
This accidental discovery led to penicillin, the first antibiotic, which went on to save millions of lives.
Infections that had once been fatal, such as pneumonia and infected wounds, suddenly became easy to treat.
Today, this achievement is under threat.
Bacteria reproduce extremely quickly, and every time an antibiotic is used, a few of them may survive because of random genetic changes.
Those survivors multiply, and over time they create populations that the drug can no longer kill.
This process is called antibiotic resistance, and bacteria that resist several drugs are sometimes known as "superbugs."
Resistance is a natural phenomenon, but humans have made it much worse.
Antibiotics are often prescribed for colds and flu, which are caused by viruses and cannot be treated with them.
Many patients stop taking their medication as soon as they feel better, instead of finishing the full course recommended by their doctor.
In some countries, huge quantities are given to healthy farm animals to make them grow faster, and waste from factories and hospitals releases antibiotics into rivers.
The consequences are already serious.
According to one major study, drug-resistant infections directly caused more than a million deaths worldwide in 2019.
If the trend continues, routine operations, cancer treatment and even childbirth could become dangerous again.

Yet very few new antibiotics are being developed, partly because pharmaceutical companies have little financial incentive: a new antibiotic should be used as rarely as possible, so it is unlikely to be profitable.
Solving the problem will require action at every level, from better prescribing and hygiene in hospitals to international agreements on farming and new ways of funding research.
Fleming himself warned about resistance in his Nobel Prize speech in 1945.
Eighty years later, the world is finally starting to listen.
A generation ago, most workers had a single employer, a fixed contract and a regular salary.
Today, millions of people earn their living in a very different way.
They drive for ride-hailing apps, deliver food on bicycles or sell their skills online, and they are paid for each individual task, or "gig."
This is known as the gig economy.
For many people, its main attraction is flexibility.
Gig workers can often choose when and how much they work, which suits students, parents with young children and people who want to earn extra money alongside another job.
Companies benefit too, because they can respond quickly to changes in demand without the costs of permanent staff.
Consumers enjoy cheap and convenient services at the touch of a button.
Critics, however, argue that this flexibility often comes at a high price for workers.
Because most platforms treat them as self-employed rather than as employees, gig workers usually have no right to sick pay, holiday pay or a pension.
Their earnings can be unpredictable, and after costs such as fuel are taken into account, some earn less than the minimum wage.
Many are also managed by algorithms that decide which jobs they are offered and can suspend their accounts if their customer ratings fall, often without a clear explanation.
Governments and courts have started to respond.
In 2021, Britain's Supreme Court ruled that Uber drivers were "workers" entitled to the minimum wage and holiday pay, a decision that had significant consequences for the whole sector.
Other countries are considering new legislation that would create a middle category between employee and self-employed.
The challenge is to protect workers without destroying the flexibility that many of them value.
As more jobs move online, finding that balance may become one of the most important questions for the future of work.
In 2017, a painting of Christ attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, known as Salvator Mundi, was sold at auction for four hundred and fifty million dollars, the highest price ever paid for a work of art.
Two years later, a banana taped to a wall by the Italian artist Maurizio Cattelan sold for one hundred and twenty thousand dollars.
To many people, both prices seem absurd.
So what determines the value of art?
Part of the answer is rarity.
There are fewer than twenty paintings in the world that experts agree are genuine works by Leonardo, and almost all of them are in museums.
When one becomes available, wealthy collectors compete fiercely to own something that nobody else can have.
Auction houses encourage this competition, and a bidding war between two determined buyers can double the estimated price within minutes.
Provenance, the history of who has owned a work, also matters: a painting that once belonged to a king is worth more than an identical one with an unknown past.
Reputation plays a huge role, too.
The market for contemporary art is driven by a small number of influential galleries, critics and collectors.
Once they decide that an artist is important, prices can rise dramatically, and the fame of the artist becomes part of what the buyer is paying for.
Cattelan's banana was not valuable because of the fruit; the buyer received a certificate that gave them the right to display the work, replacing the banana whenever necessary.
Finally, art is an investment.
For the very rich, expensive works can be a way to store wealth, and speculation can push prices far beyond what any individual painting might seem to be worth.
Critics argue that this turns art into little more than a luxury product for the elite.
Others point out that the art market has always been shaped by money, even in Leonardo's time, when rich families paid artists to glorify them.
Whatever the price, the value of a masterpiece to the people who stand in front of it in a museum cannot really be measured in dollars.
Before 2020, working from home was a privilege enjoyed by a small minority of employees.
Then the pandemic forced millions of office workers to set up desks in their kitchens and bedrooms almost overnight.
To the surprise of many managers, much of the work carried on perfectly well.
Years later, the way we work has been permanently transformed.
For many companies, the new norm is a hybrid model, in which employees spend part of the week in the office and part at home.
Workers often value the flexibility enormously.
Avoiding a daily commute can save hours each week, as well as money, and many people find it easier to concentrate at home and to combine work with family responsibilities.
Some surveys suggest that employees would even accept a lower salary in exchange for the option to work remotely.
However, remote work has disadvantages.
Some workers feel isolated and miss the informal conversations with colleagues that can lead to new ideas.
Young employees in particular may learn less, because they have fewer opportunities to observe experienced colleagues and to receive informal feedback.
For others, the boundary between work and private life has disappeared, and they find themselves answering emails late at night.
Some companies have responded by installing surveillance software to monitor what staff do on their computers, a practice that critics see as a serious invasion of privacy.
The shift has consequences beyond individual companies.
In city centers, fewer office workers means fewer customers for cafés, shops and public transport, and many commercial buildings stand half empty.
Some cities are now converting offices into homes.
Meanwhile, some corporations have ordered their staff back to the office full-time, arguing that creativity and company culture depend on people working side by side.
The debate is far from over, but it seems unlikely that the office will ever return to exactly what it was before.
In 1950, only one city in the world had more than ten million inhabitants: New York.
Today there are more than thirty such megacities, and the largest urban area, Tokyo, is home to around thirty-seven million people.
For the first time in history, more than half of humanity lives in cities, and according to the United Nations, that share is expected to reach about two thirds by 2050.
Most of this growth is taking place in Asia and Africa.
Cities such as Delhi, Dhaka, Lagos and Kinshasa are expanding at a remarkable speed, driven by high birth rates and by migration from rural areas.
People move to cities for the same reasons they always have: jobs, education, health care and the hope of a better life for their children.
On average, city dwellers earn more than rural residents, and large urban areas generate a disproportionate share of national wealth.
However, rapid growth creates enormous challenges.
When cities grow faster than their infrastructure, roads become congested, public transport is overwhelmed and water and electricity supplies cannot keep up.
Around a billion people worldwide live in slums or informal settlements, often without clean water, proper sanitation or secure rights to their homes.
Dense populations also make cities vulnerable to heat waves, flooding and the spread of disease.
Some governments have responded with radical schemes: Indonesia, for example, is building an entirely new capital, partly because Jakarta is overcrowded and slowly sinking.
Yet dense cities can also be surprisingly efficient.
When people live close together, it is cheaper to provide them with services, and public transport, walking and cycling can replace cars.
Per person, residents of well-planned cities often use significantly less energy than people in the suburbs or the countryside.
The future of the megacity will depend largely on planning: whether governments invest in transport, housing and basic services before the people arrive, rather than after.
Football began as a working-class game played on muddy fields, but today it is a global industry worth tens of billions of dollars.
The richest clubs are run like multinational corporations, with executives, marketing departments and offices on several continents.
Where does the money come from?
The largest source of revenue for most top clubs is the sale of broadcasting rights.
Television companies and streaming services pay enormous sums to show matches, and the English Premier League alone earns several billion pounds per season from these deals.
Commercial income is the second pillar: sponsorship deals with airlines and banks, and the sale of merchandise such as shirts, scarves and video games to fans all over the world.
Ticket sales, surprisingly, make up a relatively small portion of the total.
Much of this money is spent on players.
The best players earn salaries that would have been unimaginable a generation ago, and clubs pay huge transfer fees to buy players from rivals.
Because success on the pitch brings more revenue, there is constant pressure to spend more than the club can really afford.
Many clubs make a loss year after year, and several historic clubs have faced bankruptcy after gambling on a squad they could not pay for.
Ownership has changed dramatically, too.
Many leading clubs now belong to foreign billionaires, American investment funds or, in some cases, to wealthy states such as Qatar and Saudi Arabia.
Supporters of these owners point out that their investment has built new stadiums and training facilities.
Critics argue that some states use football to improve their international image, a practice sometimes called "sportswashing," and that clubs have become assets rather than community institutions.
Fans have not always accepted these changes quietly.
In 2021, twelve of Europe's biggest clubs announced plans for a new "Super League" that would guarantee them a place every season.
Within forty-eight hours, furious protests by supporters forced most of them to withdraw.
The episode was a powerful reminder that, whatever the balance sheets say, football still belongs, at least in part, to the people who watch it.
In most democracies, a new law begins its life as a proposal called a bill.
It may be introduced by the government, by an individual member of parliament or, in some countries, even by citizens who collect enough signatures.
Before it becomes law, however, it must survive a long and often complicated process designed to ensure that it is carefully examined.
In the British parliament, for example, a bill goes through several stages, known as "readings."
Members debate its general purpose, then a committee studies it line by line and proposes amendments.

After further debate and a final vote in the House of Commons, the bill passes to the second chamber, the House of Lords, which can suggest changes and delay it but usually cannot block it permanently.
Finally, it receives the formal approval of the monarch, and it becomes an Act of Parliament.
The American system divides power differently.
Congress has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and a bill must be approved by both in exactly the same form.
In the Senate, each state elects two senators, regardless of the size of its population.
It then goes to the president, who can sign it or reject it with a veto.
Congress can override a veto, but only if two thirds of both chambers vote to do so, which rarely happens.
Because the presidency and Congress are often controlled by different parties, many bills never become law at all.
Some bills are withdrawn before the final vote, while others pass only after amendments that significantly alter their original purpose.
Throughout the process, many people try to influence the outcome.
Lobbyists representing companies, trade unions and campaign groups meet legislators to argue for their interests.
Journalists examine the details, and voters write to their representatives.
Critics argue that powerful interests have too much influence, while defenders say that lobbying is a legitimate part of democracy, as long as it is transparent.
The process can seem painfully slow.
However, the delays exist for a reason: laws affect millions of people, and a hasty decision can have serious unintended consequences.
The word "propaganda" was originally neutral.
It came from a seventeenth-century Catholic organization whose task was to spread the faith.
Today, however, it usually refers to information that is deliberately designed to influence people's opinions, often by misleading them.
Propaganda reached new heights in the twentieth century, when governments discovered the power of mass media.
During the two world wars, all sides used posters, films and radio broadcasts to encourage men to join the army and to persuade civilians to support the war effort.
Authoritarian regimes went further, controlling newspapers, banning criticism and presenting their leaders as heroes.
Some even altered photographs to remove officials who had lost the leader's favor.
Effective propaganda rarely relies on outright lies alone.
More often, it selects some facts and ignores others, repeats simple messages until they feel true, and appeals to emotions rather than reason.
Fear is particularly powerful: if people believe that their community is threatened by a dangerous enemy, they are more willing to accept extreme measures.
Another common technique is to divide the world into "us" and "them," so that criticism of the leader appears to be an attack on the nation itself.
The internet has changed propaganda in fundamental ways.
Anyone can now publish information to millions of people, and false stories often spread faster than true ones, because they tend to be more surprising and emotional.
Organized disinformation campaigns use networks of fake accounts, sometimes called bots, to make a message appear more popular than it really is.
Algorithms that show users more of what they already like can trap them in "bubbles" where they rarely encounter a different perspective.
In democracies, too, political parties employ professional advisors to shape the public's perception of their policies.
Recognizing propaganda is the first step towards resisting it.
Useful questions include: Who created this message, and why?
What information is missing?
Is it trying to make me angry or afraid?
None of us is immune, but a habit of healthy skepticism makes us much harder to manipulate.
Researchers estimate that a large proportion of what we do each day is not the result of conscious decisions but of habits.
We brush our teeth, check our phones and take the same route to work without really thinking about it.
This is extremely efficient: if we had to evaluate every small action carefully, we would be exhausted by lunchtime.
Psychologists often describe a habit as a loop with three parts.
First there is a cue, something that triggers the behavior, such as a time of day, a place or a feeling.
Then comes the routine, the behavior itself.
Finally, there is a reward, which tells the brain that the loop is worth remembering.
Over time, the brain begins to expect the reward as soon as it notices the cue, and this anticipation, partly driven by a chemical called dopamine, creates the craving that keeps the habit going.
Technology companies are well aware of this, and many apps are deliberately designed to deliver small, unpredictable rewards that keep users coming back.
Specifically, the notifications on our phones act as powerful cues that are virtually impossible to ignore.
Understanding this loop helps to explain why bad habits are so hard to break.
Addiction is an extreme example: with drugs, alcohol or gambling, the craving can become so strong that it overwhelms a person's intentions.
Many people rely on willpower alone, but research suggests that this is not an effective long-term strategy.
A more successful approach is to change the environment so that the cue disappears.
Someone who snacks in front of the television, for instance, may find it easier to stop if they do not keep snacks in the house at all.
Another is to keep the cue and the reward but replace the routine: a person who smokes when stressed might go for a short walk instead.
Building good habits follows the same logic.
Experts recommend starting with very small, consistent actions, such as doing two minutes of exercise every morning, and attaching the new behavior to an existing routine.
How long it takes varies considerably: one study found that forming a new habit took anywhere from a few weeks to almost a year, depending on the person and the behavior.
The crucial factor was not motivation, but repetition.
Persistent people who missed a day and simply continued the next were just as likely to succeed as those who never missed at all.
According to the United Nations refugee agency, more than one hundred million people around the world have been forced to leave their homes because of war, violence or persecution.
Most of them remain inside their own countries, but tens of millions have crossed an international border as refugees.
Conflicts in Syria, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Sudan, among others, have created some of the largest movements of people since the Second World War.
It is important to distinguish between different groups.
A refugee is someone who has fled their country because their life or freedom is in danger, and international law gives them the right to seek protection, known as asylum.
An economic migrant, by contrast, moves mainly to find better work or living conditions.
In practice, the line is not always clear, because poverty and violence are often closely connected.
Contrary to a common assumption, most refugees do not travel to rich countries.
The majority are hosted by neighboring countries, many of which are themselves poor.
Turkey, for instance, has hosted millions of Syrian refugees, and many live in camps or overcrowded cities where access to schools, health care and legal work is limited.
Some families spend years, or even decades, waiting to return home or to be resettled elsewhere.
The arrival of refugees can create real challenges for host countries, particularly when it happens suddenly and in large numbers.
Housing, schools and welfare systems may come under pressure, and public opinion can turn against newcomers.
However, research also shows that, given time and support, many refugees make a significant economic contribution.
They start businesses, fill labor shortages and send remittances to relatives, which support economies back home.
How societies respond to refugees is ultimately a question of values as well as economics.
Humanitarian organizations argue that countries have a moral obligation to protect people fleeing danger.
The long-term solution, however, lies in ending the conflicts that force people to leave in the first place.
In 2012, two scientists, Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier, published a paper describing a new way to edit DNA.

The technique, known as CRISPR, works like a pair of molecular scissors: it can find a specific sequence of genetic code and cut it, allowing scientists to remove, repair or replace genes with remarkable precision.
It was faster, cheaper and far easier to use than earlier methods, and in 2020 the two women received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The medical potential is enormous, particularly for inherited disorders.
Thousands of diseases are caused by a fault in a single gene, and CRISPR offers the possibility of correcting it.
In 2023, regulators in Britain and the United States approved the first treatment based on the technology, for sickle cell disease, a painful inherited blood disorder.
Doctors remove some of the patient's own blood stem cells, edit them in the laboratory and return them to the body.
For many patients, the results have been life-changing.
Making such treatments affordable will be a major challenge, since the first ones cost more than two million dollars per patient.
Researchers are also exploring ways to use gene editing against certain cancers and to develop crops that can resist drought and disease.
However, the technology also raises deep ethical questions.
Editing the cells of an adult patient affects only that person.
Editing embryos, by contrast, creates changes that could be passed on to all future generations.
In 2018, the Chinese scientist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of twin girls whose genes he had edited as embryos, supposedly to protect them against HIV.
His work was widely condemned as reckless and unethical, and he was sentenced to three years in prison.
Beyond safety, there are fears about where gene editing could lead.
If it becomes possible to choose features such as height or intelligence, rich families might buy advantages for their children, making inequality even worse.
Most scientists agree that such uses should be banned for now, while treatments for serious diseases should continue to be developed under strict supervision.
The challenge is to make sure that regulation keeps pace with the science.
After the Second World War, the United States and the Soviet Union emerged as the world's two superpowers.
They had fought on the same side against Nazi Germany, but their alliance quickly broke down.
The two countries represented opposing ideologies: American capitalism and democracy on one side, Soviet communism on the other.
For more than forty years, they competed for power and influence without ever fighting a direct war against each other.
This period became known as the Cold War.
Europe was divided in two.
In 1948, when the Soviet Union blocked all roads to West Berlin, American and British aircraft flew in food and fuel for almost a year.
In 1949, the United States and its allies formed NATO, a military alliance, and the Soviet Union later created the Warsaw Pact with the communist states of Eastern Europe.
The clearest symbol of this division was the Berlin Wall, built in 1961 to stop East Germans escaping to the West.
The competition took many forms.
Both sides built enormous arsenals of nuclear weapons, and the threat of mutual destruction made direct war virtually unthinkable.
The closest they came was the Cuban Missile Crisis in 1962, when the Soviet Union placed nuclear missiles in Cuba, less than a hundred and fifty kilometers from the American coast.
For thirteen days, the world waited, until the two leaders reached an agreement and the missiles were removed.
The rivalry also extended into space, sport and science.
The Soviet launch of Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, in 1957 shocked Americans and started the space race, which ended with the American Moon landing in 1969.
Both sides used espionage extensively, and they supported opposing forces in proxy wars in countries such as Korea, Vietnam and Afghanistan, where millions of people died.
Both sides recruited spies, and several scandals revealed how deeply each had penetrated the other's institutions.
The Cold War ended surprisingly quickly.
In the 1980s, the Soviet economy was struggling, and the reformist leader Mikhail Gorbachev introduced greater openness and economic reform.
In 1989, peaceful protests brought down communist governments across Eastern Europe, and the Berlin Wall was opened.
Two years later, the Soviet Union itself collapsed.
The collapse was so swift that virtually no experts had predicted it.
Self-driving cars are no longer science fiction.
In several cities around the world, passengers can already call a taxi with no driver, and many new cars can steer, brake and change lanes by themselves on highways.
These vehicles use cameras, radar and lasers to build a detailed picture of their surroundings, and powerful software decides how to respond.
Supporters believe that autonomous cars could save an enormous number of lives.

Around the world, more than a million people die in road accidents every year, and the vast majority of crashes are caused by human error: drivers who are tired, distracted, drunk or simply going too fast.
A computer never gets tired or checks its phone.
Manufacturers insist that their vehicles will significantly reduce accidents, although the technology still struggles in heavy snow and in situations its designers did not foresee.
However, self-driving cars raise a difficult moral question.
Imagine that a car's brakes fail and it must choose between two outcomes: continuing straight and hitting a group of pedestrians, or swerving and killing its own passenger.
This is a modern version of a famous thought experiment known as the trolley problem.
A human driver in this situation reacts instinctively, but a self-driving car must be programmed in advance, which means that someone has to decide what it should do.
Researchers at MIT explored this question with an online game called the Moral Machine, which collected around forty million decisions from people in more than two hundred countries and territories.
Most participants preferred to save more lives rather than fewer, and to save young people rather than old.
But there were striking cultural differences, and, perhaps unsurprisingly, many people said they would not want to buy a car that might sacrifice its own passenger.
In reality, such dramatic dilemmas are extremely rare.
The more immediate questions are practical ones.
If a self-driving car causes an accident, who is responsible: the owner, the manufacturer or the programmer?
Legislation in most countries has not yet caught up with the technology.
Before such cars become common, they will have to prove that they are genuinely safer than human drivers, and a few fatal crashes during testing have already led to lengthy investigations.
Until it does, the question of liability may slow down the arrival of driverless cars more than any technical problem.
Long before writing was invented, humans told stories.
Around the fire at night, people shared legends about heroes and monsters, explained where the world came from and passed on practical knowledge from one generation to the next.
Some researchers believe that storytelling is one of the features that makes our species unique.
Why are stories so powerful?
One reason is that our brains seem to be designed to remember narratives far better than lists of facts.
When we follow a story, we identify with the protagonist, experience their fears and hopes, and want to know what happens next.
Neuroscientists have found that a gripping story can make the brains of listeners work in a pattern similar to that of the storyteller, a sign of genuine connection.
Stories can also increase empathy: readers of fiction appear to be better, on average, at understanding other people's feelings.
Therapists sometimes ask patients to write about painful experiences, because turning chaos into a coherent story seems to help people cope with grief and trauma.
In the twentieth century, the American writer Joseph Campbell argued that many myths from different cultures share the same basic plot, which he called "the hero's journey."
An ordinary person is called to an adventure, faces a series of challenges, receives help from a wise mentor, overcomes a great crisis and returns home transformed.
Film makers have used this structure deliberately; George Lucas, for example, has said that Campbell's ideas influenced Star Wars.
The power of stories is not always used for good, of course.
Advertisers, politicians and propagandists all know that a moving personal story persuades people more effectively than statistics.
A single photograph of a suffering child can raise more money for charity than a report about millions of people in need.
This is why it is worth asking, whenever a story moves us, who is telling it and what they genuinely want us to believe.
Coffee is one of the most widely consumed drinks in the world, and it has been the subject of extensive scientific research.
For decades, the headlines seemed to reverse every few years.
One study suggested that coffee was bad for the heart; the next claimed it helped in the prevention of disease.
So what does the evidence actually say?
The main active substance in coffee is caffeine, which blocks a chemical in the brain called adenosine that makes us feel sleepy.
This is why coffee improves alertness, concentration and reaction times, at least in the short term.
Athletes sometimes use caffeine to enhance their performance, and it is permitted in most competitive sports.
Regular drinkers develop a tolerance, however, so they need more to get the same effect, and if they stop suddenly, they may experience withdrawal symptoms such as headaches and irritability.
Most recent large studies have reached a somewhat positive conclusion.
People who drink moderate amounts, around three or four cups a day, appear to have a slightly lower risk of several conditions, including type 2 diabetes, liver disease and some forms of cancer.
For most people, moderate drinking does not significantly increase the risk of heart disease, although it can cause a temporary rise in blood pressure.
Coffee also contains antioxidants, substances that may protect cells from damage.
Some studies have specifically assessed its effect on the brain and suggest that regular drinkers may have a slightly lower risk of Parkinson's disease.
There is a crucial limitation, though.
Most of these studies are observational: they compare coffee drinkers with non-drinkers but cannot prove that coffee itself is responsible for the difference.
Perhaps people who drink coffee also tend to be healthier in other ways, or perhaps people who feel ill stop drinking it.
This is the classic problem of correlation and causation: the fact that two things happen together does not necessarily mean that one causes the other.
Coffee is not suitable for everyone, particularly people who are sensitive to caffeine.
Pregnant women are advised to limit their intake strictly, and people who suffer from anxiety or sleeping problems may find that even small amounts make their symptoms worse.
Excessive amounts can cause anxiety, a racing pulse and trembling hands.
Caffeine stays in the body for many hours, so a cup in the late afternoon can affect sleep that night.
And a coffee full of sugar and cream is practically a dessert, a very different drink from a simple black one.
For most healthy adults, however, the evidence is essentially reassuring, and there seems to be no reason to feel guilty about the morning cup.
Between the twelfth and the fifteenth centuries, the towns of medieval Europe competed to build the tallest and most magnificent cathedrals.
These enormous buildings, many of which still dominate their cities today, were among the most ambitious engineering projects of their time.
Some took centuries to complete: work on Cologne Cathedral began in 1248, stopped for hundreds of years and was not finished until 1880.
The style most associated with these buildings is called Gothic.
Its builders wanted churches that seemed to reach towards heaven and that were filled with light, which was seen as a symbol of the divine.
This created a technical problem: tall stone walls with large windows are weak and could collapse under the weight of the roof.
Medieval engineers solved it with several clever innovations.
Pointed arches carried weight more efficiently than the round arches of earlier buildings, and ribbed vaults allowed the stone ceiling to be lighter and higher.
Most importantly, flying buttresses, stone supports built outside the walls, pushed against the walls and transferred the weight safely down to the ground.
This meant that the walls themselves could be replaced by huge windows of stained glass, which told stories from the Bible to people who could not read.
Building a cathedral required an extraordinary amount of labor and skill.
Master masons designed the structure without modern mathematics, relying on geometry, experience and simple tools.
Hundreds of workers cut and lifted stone, often using huge wooden wheels powered by men walking inside them.
Accidents were common, and many workers did not live to see the completion of the building they had worked on.
These buildings remain an important part of Europe's heritage.
When a fire destroyed the roof and spire of Notre-Dame in Paris in 2019, people around the world watched in shock, and donations for its restoration poured in.
Craftspeople using many traditional techniques rebuilt it in about five years, and the cathedral reopened in December 2024.
The medieval builders would surely have understood.
In many countries, including Britain, the United States and Australia, people accused of serious crimes have the right to a trial by jury.
A jury is a panel of ordinary citizens, usually twelve, who listen to the evidence and decide whether the defendant is guilty.
The judge, by contrast, is responsible for the legal side of the trial: explaining the law to the jurors and, if the defendant is found guilty, deciding the penalty.
The idea has a long history.
In medieval England, the jury was a group of local men who were expected to know the people involved and to investigate the facts themselves.
Over the centuries, this changed completely: today, jurors must have no prior connection to the case, and they are strictly forbidden from doing their own research.
A juror who searches for information about the case online is in breach of the rules, and the whole trial may have to start again.
During the trial, the jury hears the testimony of witnesses, who must first swear an oath to tell the truth.
Lawyers for the prosecution try to prove that the defendant committed the offense, whether it is fraud, assault or murder.
The defense, meanwhile, tries to show that there is reasonable doubt.
The jurors then discuss the case in private, sometimes for days, until they reach a verdict.
In some systems the decision must be unanimous, whereas in others a majority of ten out of twelve is considered valid.
Supporters argue that juries are essentially a protection against the power of the state.
Because the decision is made by ordinary people rather than officials, a government cannot easily use the courts to punish its critics.
Juries have sometimes refused to convict people who broke laws that the public considered unfair, regardless of the evidence.
In doing so, they showed a kind of mercy that the law itself did not allow.
Critics, however, question whether ordinary citizens can genuinely understand complex cases.
Some fraud trials last for months and involve thousands of financial documents.
Jurors may also be influenced by a defendant's appearance, by emotional testimony or by what they have read in the media before the trial.
For these reasons, many countries, including Germany and Japan, rely mainly on professional judges, sometimes sitting alongside a small number of citizens.
No system is perfect, but the jury remains one of the oldest ways of ensuring that justice is not left entirely in the hands of experts.
In some countries, one party usually wins a majority of seats in parliament and forms a government on its own.
In many others, however, no single party is strong enough, and two or more parties must agree to govern together in what is called a coalition.
Coalitions are normal in Germany, the Netherlands, Denmark and much of Europe.
There, voting systems give each party a share of seats that closely matches its share of the national vote.
The process usually begins on election night.
Once the ballots have been counted, party leaders start negotiating, sometimes openly and sometimes behind closed doors.
They must agree on a detailed program: which policies will be a priority, how the budget will be spent and who will become the minister in charge of each department.
In Germany, where the head of government is called the chancellor, these negotiations have occasionally lasted more than five months.
In Belgium, a government once took a record 541 days to form.
Supporters of coalition government argue that it produces more balanced decisions.
Because no party can simply impose its ideas, policies must be based on consensus.
A government elected by a wider range of voters is also more likely to reflect the views of the country as a whole.
Radical proposals from either side are often softened along the way.
Critics, on the other hand, point to the risk of instability.
Small parties may gain influence out of proportion to their size, since their larger partners depend on them to stay in power.
Disagreements over controversial issues, such as immigration or fiscal policy, can bring a government down, particularly when a country faces a large budget deficit and painful choices.
When a party leaves a coalition, the prime minister may be forced to resign, and a new election is called.
Coalitions also exist at other levels of government.
In federal countries such as Germany or Canada, the states and provinces have their own legislatures, and parties that cooperate in one region may be rivals in another.
Regardless of the system, one lesson seems universal: governing together requires a willingness to compromise that voters do not always appreciate, but which is essential to politics.
On the morning of 23 March 2021, a giant container ship called the Ever Given was sailing through the Suez Canal in Egypt when strong winds pushed it sideways.
Within minutes, the four-hundred-meter vessel was stuck across the canal, blocking one of the most important shipping routes in the world.
Around twelve percent of global commerce normally passes through the canal.
It connects the Red Sea with the Mediterranean and saves ships a journey of thousands of kilometers around Africa.
For six days, engineers, divers and a fleet of tugboats worked around the clock to free the ship, while its crew waited on deck.
Behind it, a queue of more than three hundred and fifty ships built up, carrying everything from oil and grain to cars, clothing and electronic components.
Experts estimated that the blockage was holding up goods worth about nine billion dollars every day.
The incident revealed how much the modern economy depends on shipping.
About ninety percent of internationally traded goods travel by sea.
The standard steel container, introduced in the 1950s, made transport so cheap that it is now practically free compared with the cost of manufacturing.
Containers can be moved from a ship to a train or a truck without being opened, and the largest ships stack more than twenty thousand of them.
This is why a phone assembled in Asia can be sold at an affordable price on the other side of the world.
However, the system has little room for error.
Most companies keep small stocks and rely on parts arriving exactly when they are needed, so a breakdown at any point in the chain can spread quickly.
Only a year earlier, the pandemic had closed factories and ports, reducing output and the availability of everything from bicycles to computer chips.
At the same time, demand for imports reached a peak.
Shipping costs rose significantly, and some exporters waited months for space on a ship.
Since then, many businesses have tried to make their supply chains more resilient, keeping larger reserves or moving production closer to home.
Egypt, for its part, has invested in an expansion of the canal to boost its capacity.
The Ever Given was eventually freed and returned to service, but it had taught the world a lesson about the hidden risks of global trade.
In 2012, Facebook paid one billion dollars for Instagram, a photo-sharing app with just thirteen employees and no profit at all.
At the time, many analysts thought the price was ridiculous.
Today, Instagram has more than two billion users and is considered one of the most successful acquisitions in corporate history.
Large companies buy smaller ones for several reasons.
The most obvious is to gain new capabilities quickly.
Developing an innovative product from scratch is slow and risky, whereas buying a start-up that has already done it provides both the technology and the skilled personnel who created it.
Apple, for example, bought the company behind Siri rather than building its own voice assistant.
Acquisitions also allow firms to enter a new market segment, to reach a rival's clients or simply to remove a competitor before it becomes a threat.
For entrepreneurs, being bought by a large company can be the ultimate reward.
Most start-ups are funded by venture capital firms, which invest money in exchange for a stake in the business.
Since the majority of these ventures fail, investors depend on the few that are sold for huge sums to make up for their losses.
However, many mergers and acquisitions disappoint.
Studies suggest that a large proportion fail to deliver the benefits promised to shareholders.
Corporate cultures often clash: a small, flexible team may struggle with the rules of a giant organization run from distant headquarters, and its most talented people frequently leave.
Buyers also tend to pay too much, especially when the outlook for a sector seems exciting and several companies compete for the same target.
Governments are increasingly concerned about the power of technology giants.

Regulators in the United States and Europe now examine proposed deals more carefully and have blocked several of them, arguing that buying up potential rivals reduces competition and, in the long term, harms consumers.
Some economists even argue that the Instagram deal itself should never have been allowed.
In the early hours of 6 June 1944, the largest seaborne invasion in history began on the coast of Normandy in northern France.
Nearly seven thousand naval vessels, from huge battleships to small landing craft, crossed the English Channel, while more than eleven thousand aircraft flew overhead.
Before dawn, heavy bombing by Allied aircraft and the guns of navy warships had tried to destroy the German defenses along the coast.
By the end of the day, around one hundred and fifty thousand Allied troops from the United States, Britain, Canada and other countries had landed on five beaches.
Planning the operation had taken more than a year.
It had been rehearsed extensively on beaches in southern England.
Its details were strictly secret, and most soldiers were told their destination only after their ships had left port.
The supreme commander, the American general Dwight Eisenhower, knew that the Germans expected an attack, but not where or when.
To deceive them, the Allies created an entire imaginary army, complete with inflatable tanks and fake radio messages, which suggested that the main attack would take place near Calais.
The deception worked so well that, even after the landings had begun, Hitler kept many of his best forces waiting in the wrong place.
The weather almost ruined everything.
The invasion had been scheduled for 5 June, but a violent storm forced Eisenhower to delay it.
His weather experts predicted a short break in the storm, and he decided to go ahead, knowing that another delay would mean waiting for weeks.
He had even prepared a short statement taking full responsibility in case the operation failed and the troops were forced to retreat.
On some beaches, the landings went more smoothly than expected.
On the beach the Americans called Omaha, however, heavy fire from German positions and rough seas turned the sand into a battlefield, and thousands of soldiers were killed or injured within hours.
Many landing craft were hit by explosives before they even reached the sand.
Despite the heavy casualties, the Allies managed to hold their positions, and in the following weeks they pushed inland.
Paris was liberated in August, and Germany finally surrendered less than a year later.
Today, the beaches of Normandy are peaceful, but the memory of that day remains strong.
Thousands of visitors come every year to see the memorials and the vast military cemeteries, where long lines of white crosses mark the graves of the soldiers who died.
Some of the soldiers buried there were never identified.
Each June, the few remaining veterans, now very old, return to remember their friends.
A stroke happens when the blood supply to part of the brain is suddenly cut off.
In most cases, the cause is a blood clot that blocks one of the arteries carrying blood to the brain; less often, a weakened blood vessel bursts.
Without oxygen, brain cells begin to die within minutes, which is why doctors say that "time is brain."
