Strokes are one of the leading causes of death and disability worldwide, and although they are more common in older people, they can happen at any age.
Recognizing the symptoms quickly makes an enormous difference.
Health campaigns in many countries teach the word FAST: Face, Arms, Speech, Time.
If one side of a person's face drops, if they cannot lift both arms, or if their speech becomes confused, it is time to call an ambulance immediately.
Other warning signs include sudden numbness, severe headaches and problems with vision.
In hospital, the first step is a brain scan, because the treatment depends on the type of stroke.
If a clot is responsible, physicians can give an injection of a powerful drug that dissolves it, but only within a few hours of the first symptoms, since a high dose becomes dangerous later.
In specialized centers, doctors can also remove the clot directly by passing a thin tube through a blood vessel from the leg all the way up to the brain.
This acute phase of treatment is a race against time.
Once the patient is stable, a long period of recovery begins.
Damage to nerve cells may cause paralysis on one side of the body, difficulty speaking or problems with memory.
Before patients are discharged, a team of therapists helps them to regain mobility and relearn everyday tasks such as walking, dressing and eating.
Speech therapy can continue for months, and many people make a remarkable recovery, because healthy parts of the brain gradually take over some of the lost functions.
Prevention, however, remains the best approach.
The main risk factors are high blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and a lack of physical activity, and experts estimate that most strokes could be avoided by controlling them.
Checking your pulse and blood pressure regularly is a simple habit that could save your life.
Imagine sending a message to a friend on another continent or watching a video stored on a server abroad.
The data almost certainly does not travel through space.
Satellites carry only a tiny fraction of international internet traffic.
Instead, around ninety-nine percent of it passes through cables lying on the seabed, some of them more than seven thousand meters below the surface.
There are now more than five hundred of these cables, with a total length of over a million kilometers.
Despite their importance, they are surprisingly thin: in the deep ocean, a typical cable is about as wide as a garden hose.
At its center are glass fibers, each thinner than a human hair, which carry data as pulses of laser light.
Every sixty kilometers or so, devices called repeaters boost the signal, which would otherwise fade over such long distances.
The most sophisticated modern cables have a transmission capacity of hundreds of terabits per second.
Laying a cable is a major engineering operation.
Specialized ships carry thousands of kilometers of cable and release it slowly as they cross the ocean, following a route that has been carefully surveyed to avoid underwater mountains.
Near the coast, where the risk of damage is greatest, the cables are protected with steel wire and buried under the seabed.
Traditionally, cables were built by groups of telephone operators, but today technology giants such as Google and Meta own or fund many of the newest ones.
Cables break surprisingly often, around two hundred times a year.
Most damage is caused by fishing boats and ship anchors, although earthquakes and underwater landslides can also cut them.
Usually, traffic is automatically sent along other routes, so users notice virtually nothing while a repair ship is on its way.

But when a volcanic eruption in 2022 cut the only cable connecting the island nation of Tonga, the country was almost completely offline for five weeks, with no backup except a few slow satellite links.
As more of our lives move online, governments increasingly regard these cables as critical infrastructure, and some worry that they could be deliberately attacked.
Protecting them, and upgrading them to meet growing demand, will be one of the quiet challenges of the coming decades.
The Arctic is one of the harshest environments on Earth.
In winter, temperatures regularly fall below minus forty degrees, and for weeks the sun does not rise at all.
In summer, by contrast, it never sets, and the frozen landscape briefly comes to life.
Fierce winds can make the air feel far colder than the thermometer suggests.
The region spans parts of eight countries, and its geographic limit is often defined as the line beyond which trees cannot grow.
These extreme seasonal changes shape everything that lives there.
Over millions of years of evolution, Arctic animals have developed remarkable ways to survive.
Polar bears have a thick layer of fat, known as blubber, under their skin, and their fur keeps heat in so effectively that they can overheat when they run.
Arctic foxes change color with the seasons, from brown in summer to white in winter, which helps them to hide from both their prey and their enemies.
Reindeer, a species of deer known as caribou in North America, travel extensive distances in huge herds, following the same routes every year in search of food.
Humans, too, have lived in this wilderness for thousands of years.
The Inuit of Greenland, Canada and Alaska traditionally survived by hunting seals and whales, using every part of the animal for food, clothing, tools and fuel.
In northern Norway and Russia, other peoples have herded reindeer for centuries, moving with the animals between winter and summer pastures.
Their knowledge of snow, ice and animal behavior, passed down over generations, is now recognized by scientists as an extremely valuable source of information.
Today, however, this way of life is under threat.
The Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average, and the sea ice that polar bears depend on for hunting is shrinking rapidly.
As the permafrost, ground that has stayed frozen for thousands of years, begins to melt, it releases the carbon stored inside it, which could make global warming even worse.
Buildings, roads and pipelines built on frozen ground are already cracking.
At the same time, melting ice is opening up a new frontier.
New shipping routes are becoming possible, and countries and companies are competing for the oil, gas and minerals beneath the ice.
For the people and animals of the Arctic, the question is whether they can adapt fast enough to a world that is changing around them.
In many countries, the traditional picture of a family, with two parents and their biological children, no longer describes how a large proportion of people actually live.
As divorce has become more common and people marry again, more and more children grow up in blended families.
These bring together a parent, a new partner and children from previous relationships.
Other families are formed through adoption or fostering, or after the death of a parent, when a widow or widower eventually finds a new partner.
The transition can be difficult for everyone.
Children may still be coping with grief or anger about their parents' separation, and they may feel that accepting a stepmother or stepfather means being disloyal to the parent who has left.
Teenagers, who are already going through a sensitive period, often find the changes hardest.
New step-siblings may have to share a bedroom, and jealousy between children who feel they are being treated differently is extremely common.
Family therapists offer several pieces of advice.
First, step-parents should not try to replace the absent parent or to impose strict discipline too early.
It is usually better to begin as a caring adult friend and to leave rules and punishments to the biological parent until trust has developed.
Second, children need time alone with their own parent, so that they do not feel the new family has taken that parent away.
Finally, adults should never ask children to choose sides or criticize the other parent in front of them.
Relationships with the wider family can also be complicated.
A child may suddenly have two sets of grandparents, a new mother-in-law may not approve of her son's choice, and holidays have to be divided between several households.
Arrangements for custody, which decide where the children live and when they see each parent, require patience and maturity from all the adults involved.
Research suggests that most children in blended families do well in the long run, particularly when the adults treat each other with respect.
Many adults who grew up in such families describe a devoted step-parent as one of the most important people in their lives.
A family, they point out, is defined not by biology but by love, time and compassion.
A two-hour film may take several years to make and involve hundreds or even thousands of people.
The process is usually divided into several phases, each with its own specialists.
Everything begins with a story.
A screenwriter turns an idea, which may be original or based on a novel, into a script, and it is common for the script to go through a dozen drafts before anyone is satisfied.
Meanwhile, a producer tries to raise the money, persuading studios or investors that the film will attract an audience.
Big-budget films in popular genres, such as superhero movies, are much easier to finance than a quiet drama with an unusual theme.
Once the money is available, the preparation starts.
The director chooses the cast, often after long auditions, and works with designers who create the sets and costumes.
Artists draw sketches of important scenes, known as storyboards, so that the whole crew understands what each shot should look like.
Locations are chosen and a detailed schedule is drawn up, because every day of shooting is extremely expensive.
If the weather changes or an actor is injured, the whole schedule may have to be rearranged.
The shooting itself may last only a few months.
Scenes are rarely filmed in the order in which they appear in the story; instead, all the scenes in one location are shot together to save time and money.
Actors therefore have to jump from the end of the story to the beginning in a single day.
Lighting a single shot can take hours, and a scene lasting one minute on screen may require an entire day's work.
The costumes, hair and make-up must look exactly the same in every shot, even when scenes are filmed weeks apart.
After shooting, the film is shaped in the editing room.
Editors select the best moments from many hours of material, while other specialists add visual effects, sound effects and the soundtrack.
Many directors say that this is where a film is really made, since the same material can produce a completely different film depending on how it is edited.
Finally, the film must find its audience.
Studios release trailers and organize publicity campaigns, and many films are showcased at festivals before they reach cinemas or streaming services.
The premiere, often held at a glamorous venue with the cast walking along a red carpet, is the final step of the publicity.
After all this effort, no one can predict whether it will succeed.
As one legendary screenwriter famously said about Hollywood, "Nobody knows anything."
For centuries, people believed that leaders were born, not made.
The ideal leader was imagined as a charming, self-confident figure, usually a man, who inspired others through the force of his personality.
Modern research paints a rather different picture.
In a famous study of companies that had gone from ordinary to exceptional performance, the business writer Jim Collins found that their leaders were not the charismatic stars he had expected.
Instead, they combined personal humility with an intense determination to succeed.
They were modest about their own achievements, gave credit to their teams when things went well and took responsibility when things went badly.
Being humble did not make them weak: many were extremely determined, even stubborn, when the long-term interests of the company were at stake.
Other studies have reached similar conclusions.

When Google analyzed what made its most successful teams different, the key factor was not how skilled or talented the members were, but whether they felt safe to take risks and admit mistakes without being embarrassed.
Leaders create this kind of environment by listening genuinely, treating people with courtesy and dignity, and admitting openly that they do not know everything.
A boss who punishes every mistake teaches employees to hide problems, which is far more dangerous in the long run.
By contrast, passionate and respected leaders who show real dedication tend to inspire the same commitment in others.
This does not mean that good leaders are simply nice.
They must be competent, make difficult decisions and sometimes say things that people do not want to hear.
The best ones are able to speak frankly while remaining respectful, and to be flexible without losing sight of their goals.
They also need self-awareness: leaders who are ignorant of their own weaknesses are likely to repeat the same mistakes.
Perhaps the most encouraging finding is that these qualities can be learned.
Leadership, according to this view, is less about personality than about behavior.
Anyone who is motivated to improve can become a better leader, whether they are running a country, a company or a school sports team.
For thousands of years, people of almost every faith have made long journeys to places they consider sacred.
These journeys, known as pilgrimages, can last a few days or several months, and the journey is often as important as the destination itself.
Some pilgrimages attract enormous crowds.

Every year, around two million Muslims travel to Mecca for the Hajj, a series of rituals that every adult Muslim is expected to perform at least once in their lifetime, if they are physically and financially able.
In India, the Kumbh Mela, held every twelve years on the banks of the Ganges, is considered the largest peaceful gathering on the planet, with tens of millions of Hindus bathing in the holy river.
Other pilgrimages are quieter and more personal.
In medieval Europe, Christians walked for months to reach the tomb of Saint James in Santiago de Compostela, in northwest Spain.
The route, called the Camino de Santiago, almost disappeared in the twentieth century, but it has since experienced an astonishing revival.
Today, more than four hundred thousand people complete it every year, and many of them are not religious at all.
In Japan, pilgrims dressed in white visit eighty-eight Buddhist temples around the island of Shikoku, a trek of more than a thousand kilometers.
Why do people choose to walk for weeks when they could travel by car or plane?
For believers, the physical effort is part of the act of worship: the tiredness, the painful feet and the simple living are a way of showing devotion and humility.
Many modern walkers say they are looking for something similar, even if they would not call it religious.
They want to escape the noise of everyday life, to think about a difficult decision or to recover from grief.
Some walk to give thanks, others to ask for mercy or forgiveness, and a few simply want to test themselves.
Walking also creates a sense of community.
Most set off before dawn to avoid the heat, and the most devoted walk the whole route in silence.
Pilgrims from different countries share meals, stories and rooms in simple hostels, and strangers help each other when someone is injured or exhausted.
Many say that the most valuable part of the journey was not reaching the destination, but the people they met on the way.
In 1789, France was one of the richest and most powerful countries in Europe, yet its government was virtually bankrupt.
Expensive wars, including French support for the American Revolution, had emptied the treasury, and a series of poor harvests had pushed up the price of bread.
Society was divided into three "estates": the clergy, the nobles and everyone else, and the first two paid very few taxes.
Desperate for money, King Louis XVI called a meeting of the Estates-General, an assembly that had not met since 1614.
Instead of approving new taxes, the representatives of the Third Estate declared themselves a National Assembly and demanded a constitution.
On 14 July, crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison, and the date is still celebrated as France's national day.
Within weeks, the new assembly had abolished the privileges of the nobility and published the Declaration of the Rights of Man, which stated that all men are born free and equal in rights.
Its ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity would inspire revolutionaries around the world.
The revolution, however, soon became more radical.
In 1792, France was declared a republic, and the following year the king was executed by guillotine.
During the period known as the Terror, thousands of people accused of being enemies of the revolution were executed, often after trials that lasted only minutes.
Eventually the revolutionaries turned on each other, and Maximilien Robespierre, the leader most associated with the Terror, faced execution himself in 1794.
Exhausted by years of chaos and war, many French people welcomed a strong leader.
In 1799, a young general named Napoleon Bonaparte seized power, and a few years later he crowned himself emperor.
Historians still debate the legacy of the revolution.
It ended the absolute power of the monarchy and spread the principle that governments exist to serve their citizens.
Yet it also showed how quickly a movement for freedom can turn into violence and, finally, dictatorship.
When a new disease begins to spread, epidemiologists act like detectives.
Their first task is identification: what is causing the illness, and how is it being passed from person to person?
Investigators interview patients, collect samples and look for a common source, such as contaminated water, food or an infected animal.
The classic example comes from London in 1854, during an outbreak of cholera in the district of Soho.
Most doctors at the time believed that the disease was spread by "bad air."
A physician called John Snow thought otherwise, and he marked every death on a map of the area.
The deaths were clustered around a single water pump on Broad Street.
When the handle of the pump was removed, the number of new cases fell, and Snow's work eventually helped to prove that cholera was carried by dirty water.
Modern investigations follow the same logic, supported by databases, genetic analysis and mobile phone data.
Scientists can now read the genetic code of a virus within days and trace how it has changed as it moves through a population.
Contact tracing, which means identifying and warning everyone an infected person has met, can stop an outbreak early.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, some countries used anonymous smartphone apps to do this automatically.
Once the source is known, health authorities can act.
They may close a restaurant, withdraw contaminated products from shops, spray insecticide to kill mosquitoes or ask infected people to go into quarantine.
If a vaccine exists, a vaccination campaign can protect the people most at risk.
Simple measures, such as washing hands and wearing masks, can also slow the spread.
Speed is crucial.
If each infected person passes a disease to two others, a single case can become thousands within a few weeks.
This is why the World Health Organization coordinates a global network of laboratories that watch for unusual illnesses.
Many experts warn that the next pandemic is a question of when, not if.
In 1889, Germany became the first country to introduce a state pension for older workers.
At the time, the retirement age was seventy, and few people lived long enough to receive the payments for more than a few years.
Today, people in rich countries typically retire in their mid-sixties and can expect to live for another twenty years or more.
This success story has created a serious financial problem.
Most state pensions are paid for by the taxes of people who are currently working.
When populations were young, there were many workers for every retired person, but as birth rates fall and people live longer, that ratio is shrinking.
In Japan, there are now fewer than two people of working age for every person over sixty-five.
The percentage of gross domestic product spent on pensions has risen steadily, placing a growing burden on the treasury.
Governments have several options, and none of them is popular.
They can raise taxes, reduce payments or increase the age at which people become eligible for a pension.
When France raised the minimum retirement age from sixty-two to sixty-four in 2023, millions of people protested in the streets.
Critics point out that a higher age is particularly unfair for manual workers, whose jobs are physically demanding and who, on average, die younger.
Another approach is to encourage people to save for themselves.
Many countries now automatically enroll employees in workplace pension schemes, with regular payments from both the worker and the employer.
Immigration can also help, since migrants are often young and ready to work.
In the short term, these measures may be painful, but economists warn that without reform, the current system simply cannot be sustained.
When Airbnb was founded in 2008, the idea seemed charming: ordinary people could earn a little extra money by renting a spare room to travelers.
Today, the platform and its competitors list millions of properties around the world.
Many of them are not spare rooms at all, but entire apartments that are rented to tourists all year round.
For visitors, short-term rentals offer a cheaper and more authentic alternative to hotels, with a kitchen, more space and the chance to live like a local.
For owners, they can be far more profitable than renting to local residents on a long-term lease.
This, according to critics, is precisely the problem.
In popular cities such as Barcelona, Lisbon and Amsterdam, whole buildings have been converted into holiday accommodation.
This reduces the supply of homes for local people and pushes up rents, sometimes dramatically.
In some historic districts, the permanent population has fallen sharply, and traditional shops have been replaced by souvenir stores and luggage lockers.
Residents complain about noise, rubbish and neighbors who change every few days.
Many cities have responded with regulation.
Some limit the number of nights a home can be rented each year, while others require owners to register and obtain a license.
New York introduced strict rules in 2023 that effectively banned most short-term rentals of entire apartments, and Barcelona has announced plans to remove all tourist apartment licenses.
The platforms argue that they help families to pay their bills and spread tourist spending beyond city centers.
The debate reflects a wider question: who is a city for, the people who live in it or the people who visit?
Corruption, the abuse of public power for private gain, takes many forms.

It may be a police officer who demands a small payment to ignore a traffic offense, a minister who gives a government contract to a friend's company, or an official who steals money from the treasury.
The World Bank has estimated that businesses and individuals pay around a trillion dollars in bribes every year.
The damage goes far beyond the money itself.
When officials are corrupt, public services suffer: roads are badly built, hospitals lack medicine, and aid intended for the poor never reaches them.
Foreign companies become reluctant to invest, and ordinary citizens lose trust in their institutions.
Where corruption is widespread, honesty can seem pointless, and a vicious circle develops.
What works against corruption?
Independent courts and a free press make it more likely that wrongdoing will be exposed and punished.
Regular audits of government spending, carried out by independent inspectors, can reveal where public money disappears.
Many countries now protect whistleblowers, employees who report illegal activity, and some allow them to do so anonymously.
Technology helps, too.
When citizens can apply for official documents online rather than in person, there are fewer opportunities to demand bribes.
The most successful campaigns, such as those in Singapore and Georgia, combined strict enforcement of the law with higher salaries for officials, so that they had less reason to accept bribes.
Corruption can never be completely eliminated, but experience shows that it can be significantly reduced when there is genuine political will.
Fire has always been part of nature.
Many forests depend on occasional fires to clear dead wood and allow new plants to grow, and some pine trees even need the heat of a fire to open their cones and release their seeds.
In recent decades, however, wildfires have become larger, hotter and more destructive.
Scientists point to several causes.
Rising temperatures and longer droughts dry out vegetation, turning it into fuel.
More people now live on the edge of forests, and most fires are started by humans, whether deliberately or through accidents such as a spark from a power line.
In some places, decades of putting out every small fire have allowed dead wood to build up, so when a fire does start, it burns fiercely.
Once a large fire has started, it can be almost impossible to control.
Strong winds carry burning embers far ahead of the flames, starting new fires on the other side of roads and rivers.
Firefighters use helicopters and planes to drop water, and they cut firebreaks, strips of land cleared of vegetation, to stop the blaze from spreading.
Sometimes all they can do is evacuate residents and wait for the weather to change.
The consequences extend far beyond the burned area.
Smoke containing toxic particles can travel thousands of kilometers and damage the health of millions of people.
When the forests of Canada burned in 2023, the sky over New York turned orange.
Burned hillsides are also vulnerable to landslides, and ash washed into rivers can pollute water supplies.
Experts increasingly argue that we must learn to live with fire rather than simply fight it.
This means removing dead wood, using carefully controlled burns in cooler seasons and building homes from materials that resist flames.
Some of these methods were practiced for centuries by indigenous peoples, whose knowledge is now being taken seriously again.
The marathon is named after a legend.
According to the story, in 490 BC a Greek messenger ran from the town of Marathon to Athens to announce a victory over the Persians, and then collapsed and died.
Historians doubt that it really happened, but when the first modern Olympic Games were held in 1896, the organizers included a long-distance race in its honor.
The distance was later fixed at 42.195 kilometers, the length of the course at the 1908 Games in London, which started at Windsor Castle.
Running a marathon is a remarkable test of endurance.
The primary challenge is energy.
The body stores a limited amount of fuel, called glycogen, in the muscles and liver, which is enough for roughly thirty kilometers of hard running.
When it runs out, runners experience what they call "hitting the wall": their legs feel heavy, their pace slows dramatically and every step becomes a struggle.
Careful training and plenty of carbohydrates before the race help to delay this moment.
Most coaches recommend building up gradually over several months, with one long run each week and plenty of rest in between.
Increasing the distance too quickly is the most common cause of injury.
Many amateur runners join a club or follow an online coaching program, and some pay a personal trainer to design a plan for them.
At the elite level, the sport has changed dramatically.

In 2019, the Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run the distance in under two hours, although the event did not count as an official record because he was helped by rotating teams of pacemakers.
New shoes with carbon plates have also helped athletes to run faster, and records have been broken repeatedly.
For most participants, however, the goal is simply to finish.
Big-city marathons attract tens of thousands of runners, many of them raising money for charity, and crowds line the streets to cheer them on.
Crossing the finish line, exhausted but thrilled, is for many people one of the greatest achievements of their lives.
You are thinking about an old friend you have not seen for years, and at that very moment your phone rings and it is them.
It feels almost magical, even slightly creepy, as if fate or destiny were involved.
Such experiences are extremely common, and many people interpret them as meaningful signs.
Mathematicians, however, point out that coincidences are far less surprising than they seem.
Consider the famous "birthday problem."
In a group of just twenty-three people, the probability that two of them share a birthday is higher than fifty percent.
Most people guess a significantly larger number, because they think about the chance that someone shares their own birthday, not the chance that any two people in the group do.
Likewise, the same principle applies to life in general.
Each of us experiences millions of events every year, so remarkable coincidences are virtually certain to happen to someone, somewhere, all the time.
What we fail to notice are the countless times we think of a friend and they do not call.
The odd events are memorable precisely because they are rare for each of us, even though they are common across a whole population.
Psychologists call the tendency to see meaningful connections between unrelated events "apophenia."
It may once have helped our ancestors to survive: someone who assumed that a noise in the grass was a predator was more likely to live than someone who ignored it.
But it also leads us to see patterns where none exist, which helps to explain the popularity of superstitions and conspiracy theories.
None of this means that coincidences cannot be delightful.
The most bizarre ones make superb stories, and there is nothing wrong with enjoying them.
The important thing is to remember that, in a world of eight billion people, strange events are exactly what we should expect.
A computer may seem mysterious, but its basic components have remained the same for decades.
At its heart is the processor, a chip that carries out instructions billions of times per second.
A modern processor contains billions of tiny switches called transistors, each only a few nanometers wide, on a piece of silicon smaller than a fingernail.
The processor works closely with memory.
Short-term memory, known as RAM, holds the programs and data that are currently in use, but it loses everything when the power is switched off.
Long-term storage keeps files permanently, and when you open an app, it is copied from storage into memory so that the processor can reach it quickly.
Input devices, such as the keyboard, microphone and touchscreen, send information to the computer, while output devices, such as the screen and speakers, present the results.
Everything a computer does ultimately comes down to numbers.
Text, images and sound are stored as binary code, long strings of ones and zeros that correspond to switches being on or off.
Hardware is only half the story.
Software, the programs that tell the hardware what to do, is written by programmers in programming languages, which are then translated into instructions that the processor can execute.
The operating system manages the whole machine, deciding which program can use the processor and memory at any moment.
Computers have become astonishingly powerful.
For decades, the number of transistors on a chip doubled roughly every two years, a trend known as Moore's Law.
The smartphone in your pocket is far more powerful than the computers that guided astronauts to the Moon.
However, engineers are now approaching the physical limits of how small transistors can be, which is one reason why researchers are exploring entirely new approaches such as quantum computing.
The average person in a rich country now buys far more clothes than twenty years ago, but keeps each item for a much shorter time.
This is the result of "fast fashion": companies copy catwalk designs and bring new styles to shops within weeks, at extremely low prices.
For consumers, cheap outfits are fun and affordable, but the true cost is paid elsewhere.
Most of these clothes are manufactured in countries such as Bangladesh, Vietnam and Cambodia, where wages are low.
In 2013, the Rana Plaza building near Dhaka, which housed several garment factories, collapsed and killed more than eleven hundred workers.
Cracks had appeared in the walls the day before, but the workers were told to return to their machines.
The disaster led to a legally binding agreement on building and fire safety, signed by many international brands.
The environmental impact is also significant.
Growing cotton requires large amounts of water and pesticides, and the dyeing of fabric releases toxic chemicals into rivers.
Synthetic fabrics such as polyester are made from oil, and every time they are washed, they shed tiny plastic fibers that end up in the sea.
Much of what people donate to charity shops cannot be sold and is exported to countries in Africa, where it often ends up in landfills.
Some brands now offer repair services and collect old clothes for recycling, and second-hand markets are growing rapidly.
Critics argue, however, that these initiatives are small compared with the scale of production.
The most sustainable garment, they say, is the one that is already in your wardrobe.
Buying fewer, better-made clothes and wearing them for longer is the simplest way to reduce the damage.
Translation is often imagined as a simple process of replacing the words of one language with the words of another.
Anyone who has tried it knows that it is far more complex.
Words rarely correspond exactly, and a literal translation can be accurate but completely unnatural, or even misleading.
Consider idioms.
An English speaker who says that it is "raining cats and dogs" does not literally mean that animals are falling from the sky.
A good translator must find an expression in the other language that carries the same meaning and the same tone.
Humor is even harder, because jokes often depend on sounds or double meanings that disappear in another language.
Cultural differences also matter: a polite request in one culture may sound rude in another, so translators must constantly decide whether to preserve the original or adapt it for their readers.
Mistakes can be expensive.

When a major international bank used the slogan "Assume nothing" in its advertising, the phrase was translated in several countries as "Do nothing," and the company had to spend millions on a new campaign.
In diplomacy, interpreters must be extremely precise, since a single word can alter the meaning of an agreement.
Simultaneous interpreters, who translate speeches while they are being given, have one of the most demanding jobs in the world.
Machine translation has improved dramatically in recent years.
Programs trained on enormous amounts of text can now produce translations that are fluent and usually accurate.
However, they still struggle with ambiguity, humor and subtle cultural references, and they sometimes make serious errors with great confidence.
For contracts, medical information and literature, human translators remain essential, at least for now.
In the early twentieth century, the last unexplored places on Earth attracted a new kind of hero: the polar explorer.
The race to reach the South Pole was one of the most dramatic stories of the age.
In 1911, two expeditions set out across Antarctica, a Norwegian team led by Roald Amundsen and a British team led by Robert Falcon Scott.
Amundsen's team relied on dogs to pull their sleds and wore fur clothing based on Inuit designs.
Scott's team used ponies and motor sledges, which soon failed in the harsh conditions, and in the end the men had to pull their own sleds.
Amundsen reached the Pole on 14 December 1911.
When Scott arrived five weeks later, he found the Norwegian flag already flying.
On the return journey, Scott and his companions died of cold and hunger, only eighteen kilometers from a supply depot.
Mountains offered a similar challenge and an equally fierce competition.
Everest, the highest peak on Earth, was first climbed in 1953 by Edmund Hillary from New Zealand and Tenzing Norgay, a Sherpa from Nepal.
At that altitude, the air contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level, and climbers risk frostbite, exhaustion and dangerous confusion.
Earlier attempts had failed, and in 1924 the British climbers George Mallory and Andrew Irvine disappeared near the summit.
Nobody knows whether they reached the top.
Today, hundreds of people climb Everest every year, helped by guides, fixed ropes and bottled oxygen.
The feat is no longer rare, and critics complain about crowds, rubbish and the risks taken by inexperienced climbers.
Yet exploration has not ceased.
Scientists are still mapping the deep ocean floor, much of which has been studied less thoroughly than the surface of Mars.
The pursuit of the unknown, it seems, is part of human nature.
Every day, thousands of diplomats around the world try to prevent conflicts, solve disputes and protect the interests of their countries.
Most of their work happens quietly, far from the television cameras.
Nearly every country has an embassy in the capital cities of its most important partners.
The head of an embassy is the ambassador, who represents their government and meets ministers, business leaders and journalists.
Embassies also help their own citizens abroad, for instance when someone loses a passport or is arrested.
Under an international agreement signed in Vienna in 1961, diplomats enjoy special protection, known as diplomatic immunity, so that they cannot easily be put under pressure by the host government.
When countries disagree, diplomats try to reach an agreement through negotiation.
Each delegation arrives with a list of priorities, and the final treaty is usually a compromise in which every side has given up something.
Negotiators pay close attention to details: a single provision in a trade agreement can be worth billions, and the precise wording of a peace deal may determine whether it lasts.
Diplomacy also takes place between many countries at once.
At the United Nations in New York, delegates from almost two hundred states debate resolutions on everything from climate change to human rights.
Cooperation is often slow, because decisions require broad agreement, but the alternative, a world without dialogue, is far more dangerous.
When talking fails, governments may use other tools, such as sanctions that restrict trade, or the exclusion of a country from international organizations.
Yet even during wars, diplomats usually keep some channels open.
Stability, after all, is rarely achieved by force alone.
Tuberculosis is one of the oldest diseases known to humanity.
Traces of it have been found in Egyptian mummies thousands of years old, and in nineteenth-century Europe it was responsible for as many as a quarter of all deaths.
Because it slowly destroyed its victims, people called it "consumption."
The disease mainly attacks the lungs, causing a persistent cough, fever, weight loss and, eventually, severe respiratory problems.
It spreads through the air when infected people cough or sneeze, which is why it thrived in crowded, poorly ventilated cities.
In 1882, the German scientist Robert Koch identified the bacterium responsible, a discovery that later earned him the Nobel Prize.
For decades, however, doctors had no effective treatment.
Wealthy patients were sent to sanatoriums in the mountains, where they rested and breathed fresh air, and X-rays were used to monitor the damage to their lungs.
The first vaccine, known as BCG, was introduced in 1921, and in the 1940s the discovery of potent new drugs finally made the disease curable.
In rich countries, tuberculosis became rare, and many people assumed that it belonged to the past.
They were wrong.
According to the World Health Organization, it still kills more than a million people every year, more than any other single infectious disease.
Most victims live in poor countries, where treatment is difficult to obtain and patients may have to take several drugs every day for six months.
When they stop early, drug-resistant forms of the disease can develop.
The battle against tuberculosis, like the battle against malaria, is therefore not only medical but also economic and political.
The tools to defeat it largely exist.
What is missing is the will to make them available to everyone.
When Maria and Tom left their office jobs in the city to run a small organic farm, their friends thought they had lost their minds.
Neither of them had grown anything more ambitious than a pot of herbs on a balcony.
The farm they bought had forty acres of land, an old barn, a small orchard of cherry and peach trees and three goats that nobody had told them about.
Spring was the busiest season.
Because organic farmers do not use chemical pesticides, weeds were a constant battle, and they spent hours every day pulling them out by hand.
They planted vegetables, sowed a field of wheat and learned, through several painful mistakes, which plants needed sun and which preferred shade.
The goats, meanwhile, escaped regularly and ate whatever they could find, including Tom's gloves.
Summer brought the first rewards.
They sold strawberries, cherries and salad at a weekly market in the nearest town, and customers were willing to pay a little more for food that had been picked that morning.
In August, they cut the grass in the top field and stored the hay in the barn for the winter.
By the autumn, the barn was full of pumpkins, apples and nuts, and the wheat had been harvested.
But when they calculated their profit for the year, they discovered that they had earned less than a third of their old salaries.
Small farms struggle to compete with large producers, and many survive only by joining a cooperative, which allows farmers to share equipment and sell their products together.
In their second year, Maria and Tom did exactly that.
They are not rich, and they work harder than ever.
Yet neither of them regrets the decision.
"In the city, I spent my days moving numbers from one spreadsheet to another," Tom says. "Here, at the end of the day, I can see what I've done."
For many young people, starting university is the biggest change of their lives so far.
After years of structured timetables and teachers who checked every piece of homework, undergraduates suddenly find themselves responsible for organizing their own time.
Teaching at university takes several forms.
In lectures, a lecturer speaks to a large audience, sometimes several hundred students, and there is little opportunity for discussion.
Seminars are smaller, and students are expected to have done the reading and to contribute their own ideas.
Attendance at lectures is often optional, but many faculties make seminars compulsory, and students who miss too many may fail the course.
Assessment also changes.
Instead of frequent tests, students usually write long essays and, in their final year, a dissertation or thesis on a subject of their choice.
They are expected to read widely, think critically and acknowledge every source they use; copying someone else's work without credit, known as plagiarism, is treated as a serious offense.
Life outside the classroom can be just as challenging.
Many first-year students live in a dorm, sharing a kitchen with strangers and learning to cook, clean and manage a budget for the first time.
Getting on with a roommate is not always easy, and loneliness is surprisingly common in the first weeks, even in a crowded building.
Joining clubs and societies is one of the best ways to make friends.
Money is another concern.
In many countries, tuition fees are high, and students borrow large sums that they will repay for decades.
Applicants are therefore wise to think carefully about their choice of course, and to consider what a diploma from a prestigious university will actually offer them.
In 2012, the American cyclist Lance Armstrong, who had won the Tour de France seven times, was stripped of all his titles.
For years, he had denied using illegal drugs, attacking journalists and former teammates who accused him.
Then, in a television interview, he finally made a full confession.
Doping, the use of banned substances to improve performance, is almost as old as competitive sport itself.
Athletes have used stimulants to fight tiredness, hormones to build muscle and techniques that increase the number of red blood cells, allowing muscles to receive more oxygen.
Some of these methods are potent, and many are hazardous: several young cyclists died of heart failure in the 1990s, and the long-term effects of hormones can be severe.
Since 1999, the World Anti-Doping Agency has coordinated the fight against drugs in sport.

Athletes must tell testers where they will be every day, so that they can be tested without warning, and samples are stored for years so that they can be analyzed again when new methods become available.
In athletics, dozens of medals have been reallocated years after the event.
The problem is not only individual.
Investigations have revealed that some doping programs were organized by coaches, doctors and even governments.
After an investigation found that Russia had run a state-supported system, the country was punished and its athletes were forced to compete under a neutral flag at several Olympic Games.
Why do athletes take the risk?
The rewards for winning are enormous, careers are short, and some believe, rightly or wrongly, that their rivals are cheating too.
Those who are caught face bans and public disgrace, while clean athletes lose medals, sponsorship and moments of glory that can never be returned.
Keeping sport clean is ultimately a question of trust: without it, no victory means anything.
Surveys suggest that around a third of adults in many Western countries believe in ghosts, and a significant number say they have seen or felt one.
Stories of the supernatural exist in virtually every culture, from haunted castles in Scotland to spirits who possess the living.
Scientists who study these experiences do not usually conclude that people are lying.
Instead, they try to understand why ordinary brains perceive extraordinary things.
One explanation is our instinct for detecting patterns.
The human brain is extremely good at recognizing faces, so good that it sometimes sees them where none exist, in clouds, in the pattern of a curtain or in the mist on a dark road.
Psychologists call this pareidolia.
In a frightening situation, when we are already alert to danger, a shadow can easily become a figure.
The body can also play tricks on us.
During sleep paralysis, a person wakes up but cannot move, and they may sense a threatening presence in the room or feel pressure on their chest.
The experience can be terrifying, and it may explain many traditional stories of night visitors.

Some researchers also believe that infrasound, low-frequency sound that humans cannot consciously hear, can produce feelings of unease and dread, and it has been measured in several buildings with a reputation for being haunted.
Culture shapes what we experience, too.
People who have grown up with vivid imagery of ghosts, through films, books and family legends, are more likely to interpret strange sounds as supernatural.
None of this proves that ghosts do not exist.
It does suggest, however, that the feeling of awe and fear in a dark, silent house tells us at least as much about our minds as about the house.
Every kitchen is, in a sense, a chemistry laboratory.
When we cook, we use heat, acids and physical force to change the structure of food, altering its texture, color and flavor.
Understanding a little of the science can make anyone a better cook.
Take the brown crust on a steak or a loaf of bread.
It is produced by the Maillard reaction, a series of chemical changes between proteins and sugars that happens above about a hundred and forty degrees.
This is why boiled meat never tastes like grilled meat: boiling water cannot get hot enough.
Sugar on its own turns brown at even higher temperatures in a process called caramelization, which gives onions their sweetness when they are cooked slowly.
Acids work in different ways.
A splash of vinegar or lemon juice can brighten the flavor of a sauce, and acids also change proteins without heat: in some dishes, raw fish is "cooked" simply by being left in lime juice.
When apples or potatoes are peeled, their surface reacts with oxygen and turns brown, which is why cooks often put them in water with a little lemon.
Some of the most useful kitchen tricks are purely physical.
Putting a lid on a pan traps steam and heats water much faster, saving energy.
Oil and water do not normally mix, but if you add egg yolk and whisk them together, you create an emulsion such as mayonnaise, in which tiny drops of oil are held in the liquid.
Chopping herbs finely releases more of their aromatic oils, while chocolate made from cocoa must be melted gently, because it burns easily.
None of this means that cooking should become a science experiment.
Grandmothers produced wonderful meals for centuries without knowing anything about proteins.
But understanding why a recipe works makes it easier to fix it when something goes wrong, and to invent new dishes of your own.
Every year, millions of people move to a new country, some in search of work or study, others fleeing war or persecution.
For every immigrant, the first months bring a mixture of excitement and confusion.
Everything that was once automatic, from buying a train ticket to making a doctor's appointment, suddenly requires effort.
Psychologists describe several stages of adjustment.
At first, newcomers often feel enthusiastic about their unfamiliar surroundings.
After a while, however, many experience "culture shock": they become tired of misunderstanding jokes, struggling with bureaucracy and never quite knowing the rules.
Loneliness and homesickness are common, particularly for people who have left their families behind.
Language is usually the greatest barrier.

Doctors, engineers and teachers who were highly respected in their own countries may find themselves cleaning offices or driving taxis, because their qualifications are not recognized or their language skills are not yet good enough.
This loss of status can be deeply painful.
Successful integration depends on both sides.
Immigrants who learn the language, make local friends and take part in community life tend to feel at home more quickly.
But host societies also play a role.
Where people are tolerant of cultural differences and employers are willing to give newcomers a chance, integration is significantly faster.
Where immigrants face hostility or exclusion, they may withdraw into their own ethnic communities.
Many people who have been through the process say that it changed them permanently.
They never feel entirely at home in either culture, but they gain the ability to see both from the outside.
It is a difficult gift, but for many, a valuable one.
What should happen to a fifteen-year-old who steals a car or joins a gang?
Most legal systems treat young offenders differently from adults, on the grounds that teenagers are less mature, more easily influenced by others and more capable of change.
Scientists have found that the parts of the brain that control impulses and assess risks are not fully developed until the mid-twenties.
In many countries, young people who commit minor offenses are not sent to court at all.
Instead, they may receive a warning or be asked to take part in a program of community work.
For more serious crimes, youth courts are usually less formal than adult ones: judges often speak directly to the young person, and the aim is to understand why the offense happened.
The evidence suggests that imprisonment is rarely effective for young people.
Teenagers who are locked up are more likely to reoffend than those who receive support in the community, partly because prison brings them into contact with more experienced criminals.
Many have also been victims themselves, of violence, neglect or abuse, and punishment alone does nothing to address these problems.
One approach that has attracted attention is restorative justice.
Offenders meet the people they have harmed, listen to how the crime affected them and agree on ways to repair the damage.
Victims often say that the experience helps them to move on, and several studies have found that it reduces reoffending.
Critics argue that this approach can seem too soft, especially after violent crimes, and that the public expects justice to include punishment.
Supporters reply that the real test of any system is not how harsh it is, but how many young people it prevents from committing crimes again.
Ask a group of newly married couples how likely they are to get divorced, and almost all of them will say that the chance is close to zero.
Yet in many countries, around four in ten marriages end in divorce.

This gap between expectation and reality is an example of what psychologists call the optimism bias: our tendency to believe that good things are more likely to happen to us than to other people, and bad things less likely.
The bias appears in almost every area of life.
Most people underestimate how long a task will take, how much a project will cost and how likely they are to become ill.
Smokers believe that they are less likely than other smokers to develop cancer, and drivers consistently rate themselves as more skilled than average.
According to the neuroscientist Tali Sharot, the brain seems to update its beliefs more readily when it receives good news than when it receives bad news.
Why would evolution produce such a trait?
One explanation is that optimism is useful.
People who expect to succeed are more likely to strive, to keep trying after failure and to take the risks that lead to greatness.
Optimistic patients often recover faster, perhaps because they follow their treatment more carefully, and they tend to suffer less from stress and depression.
But the bias has costs, too.
Governments underestimate the cost of major projects, investors ignore warning signs before a financial crash, and individuals fail to save enough for their retirement.
The solution is not to become pessimistic, which has its own dangers, but to recognize the bias and plan for it.
Wise planners add extra time and money to every estimate, and they ask a simple question: what happened last time someone tried this?
For most of history, houses were built one at a time, brick by brick, on the site where they would stand.
In many countries, they still are.
But rising construction costs, a shortage of skilled workers and the need to reduce carbon emissions are forcing the building industry to rethink how homes are made.
One solution is modular housing.
Instead of being built on site, homes are manufactured in factories as large rectangular units, rather like shipping containers, and then transported by truck and lifted into place with a crane.
A family house can be assembled in a few days, and because the work takes place indoors, it is not delayed by bad weather.
Critics once associated prefabricated homes with cheap, ugly buildings, but modern designs can be elegant, and the factories can achieve a precision that is difficult on a muddy building site.
Materials are changing, too.
Concrete and steel produce huge amounts of carbon, so architects are increasingly turning to wood, including engineered timber strong enough to support buildings of ten floors or more.
Some experimental homes use recycled plastic, straw or even compressed cardboard for walls and interior panels.
In hot countries, designers are rediscovering traditional techniques, such as thick walls, shaded terraces and courtyards, that keep buildings cool without air conditioning.
Future homes will also be designed to use far less energy.
With excellent insulation, triple-glazed windows and solar panels on the roof, some already produce more electricity than they consume.
Houses are also being designed for an ageing population, with wide doors, ramps instead of steps and kitchens that can be adapted as their owners grow older.
The home of the future, in other words, may look quite ordinary from the street.
What will change is almost everything behind its walls.
To a guest, a good hotel seems virtually effortless.
You arrive, a smiling receptionist hands you a key, and your room is spotless, with fresh towels and a comfortable bed.
Behind that simple experience, however, lies one of the most complex businesses in the service industry.
The key measure of success is occupancy: the percentage of rooms that are sold each night.
An empty room earns nothing, and its value disappears forever when the night is over, so hotels constantly adjust their prices according to demand.
The same room might cost a hundred dollars on a quiet Tuesday and four hundred during a major festival.
Most hotels also sell rooms through online booking platforms, which take a commission of fifteen to twenty-five percent on each booking.
Running a large hotel requires many departments working together.
Housekeeping staff may clean fifteen rooms in a single shift, often for low wages, while the kitchen prepares breakfast for hundreds of guests and catering for weddings and conferences.

In luxury hotels, a concierge can arrange almost anything, from theater tickets to a helicopter, and extra services such as a spa, a cocktail bar or a restaurant with a local specialty can be an important source of profit.
Above all, the industry depends on hospitality: the ability to make strangers feel welcome.
Guests forgive a small room or a slow lift much more readily than a rude receptionist.
In the age of online reviews, where a single negative comment can be read by thousands of potential customers, that ability has never been more valuable.
When the Sydney Opera House was first proposed, its builders estimated that it would cost seven million Australian dollars and take four years to complete.
It eventually cost more than a hundred million and took fourteen years.
Today it is one of the most famous buildings in the world, but its story is far from unusual.
Research by the economist Bent Flyvbjerg, who studied thousands of major projects, found that roughly nine out of ten went over budget, over time or both.
Why does this happen so consistently?
One reason is that planners systematically underestimate complexity.
At the preliminary stage, a new railway or hospital exists only as a set of drawings, and it is easy to ignore the thousands of small problems that will appear once construction begins.
Successive changes to the design, often requested by clients after work has started, add further delays.
There are also political pressures.
A project that is honestly described as expensive and slow may never be approved, so its supporters have a strong incentive to present optimistic figures.
Once construction has started and billions have been spent, it becomes almost impossible to cancel, even when costs rise dramatically.
How can such failures be avoided?
Experts recommend several approaches.
Instead of relying on their own estimates, planners should consult the records of similar projects elsewhere and adjust their forecasts accordingly.
Budgets should include a realistic contingency for unexpected problems.
And the design should be specified in detail and tested thoroughly before any building starts, because modifications are far cheaper on paper than on a construction site.
None of these measures is complicated.
What they require is the courage to be honest about uncertainty at the very beginning, when optimism is most tempting and most dangerous.
"Chocolate helps you lose weight." "Red wine is as beneficial as exercise."
Headlines like these appear every week, often based on genuine scientific studies.
Yet the interpretation of scientific results is rarely as simple as a newspaper suggests, and a few questions can help you judge whether a claim deserves to be taken seriously.
First, who was studied, and how many participants were there?

Many exciting results come from preliminary experiments on mice or cells in a laboratory, and what works in a mouse frequently fails in humans, often for biological reasons that are not yet understood.
Even in studies of people, the size of the sample matters: a study of twenty volunteers is far less reliable than one involving twenty thousand.
Second, what precisely was measured, and by whom?
A study might find that people who eat more chocolate weigh slightly less, but this does not prove that chocolate causes weight loss.
Perhaps thinner people simply feel less guilty about eating it, or perhaps the result was purely a coincidence.
Scientists try to control for such factors, but in observational studies it is broadly impossible to rule out every alternative explanation.
The most convincing evidence usually comes from randomized trials, in which participants are divided into groups by chance and some receive a placebo.
Third, how big is the effect, and is it significant?
A headline claiming that something "doubles the risk" of a disease sounds alarming, but if the original risk was one in a million, the new risk is still only two in a million.
Numerical claims without context can be deeply misleading, and journalists sometimes exaggerate them deliberately.
Finally, has the result been confirmed independently?
Good science is published in journals after peer review, in which other experts examine the methods for flaws, and important findings are repeated by independent teams.
A single study, however exciting, is rarely the final word, and a healthy skepticism is essentially the reader's best protection.
In many cities, it is now almost impossible to walk down a street without being filmed.
London has hundreds of thousands of security cameras, and in some Chinese cities there are more than one for every five residents.
Our phones record our location, our cards record what we buy, and our online searches reveal what we are thinking about.
Supporters of surveillance argue that it keeps people safe.
Cameras help the police to identify suspects, and data from phones has solved murders that would once have remained a mystery.
Facial recognition technology can now scan a crowd and identify a wanted person within seconds.
"If you have nothing to hide," they say, "you have nothing to fear."
Critics reply that this argument misunderstands the value of privacy.
Everybody has something they prefer to keep private, whether it is a medical condition, a political opinion or a relationship.
When people know that they are being watched, they tend to change their behavior, avoiding protests or controversial websites even when they have done nothing wrong.
In the wrong hands, surveillance can be used to suppress journalists, opposition politicians and minorities.
There are also practical concerns.
Facial recognition systems are sometimes inaccurate, particularly with darker skin, and innocent people have been arrested because of mistakes.
Databases can be hacked, and personal information that was collected for one purpose may later be used for another, without the owner's consent.
Most democracies try to find a balance through regulation.
Laws may restrict how long data can be kept, require a court's permission before the police access private messages, or ban certain uses of facial recognition entirely.
Whether these rules are sufficient is one of the defining questions of the digital age.
Every year, magazines and research organizations publish rankings of the world's most livable cities.
Vienna, Copenhagen and Melbourne often appear near the top.
The criteria vary considerably, but they usually include safety, health care, education, culture and the quality of the environment.
What these cities have in common, however, is less easy to measure: they are pleasant places to spend an ordinary day.
Proximity is one of the most important factors.
In a livable city, shops, schools, parks and doctors are within walking or cycling distance of most homes.
Paris has adopted the idea of the "15-minute city," in which residents should be able to reach everything they need in a quarter of an hour without a car.
Mixed neighborhoods, where homes, offices and shops sit side by side, are generally more dynamic than districts designed for a single function.
Transport is closely connected, and it is equally crucial.
Cities that prioritize cyclists and pedestrians, with safe routes, wide pavements and well-designed intersections, tend to be quieter, cleaner and healthier.
In Copenhagen, more than forty percent of journeys to work or school are made by bicycle.
Reliable public transport is equally essential, particularly for elderly people and families with children.
Green space matters, too.
Parks provide opportunities for recreation, reduce temperatures during heat waves and have measurable benefits for mental health.
Yet the most desirable cities face a growing problem: their popularity pushes up house prices, and ordinary workers can no longer afford to live there.
Vienna's solution, a long tradition of high-quality social housing, is often cited as a model.
A city is only truly livable, its supporters argue, if the people who clean its streets and teach its children can live in it too.
Between about 1650 and 1730, the Caribbean was one of the most dangerous seas in the world.
Merchant ships carrying sugar, tobacco, silver and slaves crossed the Atlantic in huge numbers, and many of them were attacked by pirates.
This period is often called the golden age of piracy.
Many pirates had previously been ordinary sailors.
Life on merchant and navy ships was brutal: wages were low, food was terrible and captains could punish sailors severely for the smallest offense.
Pirate crews, surprisingly, were often more democratic.
They elected their captains, shared their plunder according to written rules and even paid compensation to men who were injured in battle.
Some pirates became legendary.

Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard, commanded a ship with forty guns called the Queen Anne's Revenge and deliberately cultivated a terrifying image: he was said to put burning fuses in his beard before a fight.
Two women, Anne Bonny and Mary Read, dressed as men and fought alongside the pirate crew of Calico Jack, which was extraordinary at a time when women were rarely allowed on ships.
In reality, however, most pirates preferred to avoid fighting altogether: their reputation was formidable, and many ships surrendered their cargo without resistance.
The golden age ended when European governments decided that piracy was damaging trade too badly to be tolerated.
Navies hunted pirates across the Caribbean, and those who were captured were usually hanged.
Blackbeard was killed in a battle in 1718.
Today, pirates survive mainly in films and children's stories, where they appear as charming rebels rather than criminals.
The real history was far darker, but it also reveals a world in which ordinary sailors, for a brief moment, took control of their own lives.
Every year, just before the Christian period of Lent, cities around the world explode into color and music.
Carnival is celebrated in dozens of countries, but its most famous form is in Rio de Janeiro, where around two million people a day fill the streets.
The festival has ancient roots.
In Catholic countries, people traditionally gave up meat and other pleasures during the forty days of Lent, so the days before it became a time for eating, drinking and breaking the usual rules.
In Venice, people wore masks so that nobles and servants could celebrate together without anyone knowing who was who.
This idea of a world turned upside down, however briefly, remains central to the spirit of carnival.
In Rio, the highlight is the parade of the samba schools.
These are community organizations, often based in poor neighborhoods, which spend the whole year preparing a single performance.
Each school chooses a theme, writes a song and builds enormous decorated floats, while thousands of members sew costumes and rehearse their dances.
On the night of the parade, each school has little more than an hour to march through a stadium in front of judges and seventy thousand spectators.
The spectacle is breathtaking.
Carnival traditions have also traveled.

In Trinidad, carnival combines African, European and Indian influences, and London's Notting Hill Carnival, started by Caribbean immigrants in the 1960s, is now one of the largest street festivals in Europe.
For many participants, these events are more than a party.
They are a symbolic celebration of identity, freedom and community, and a reminder that joy can be a form of resistance.
Walk into any pharmacy and you will find shelves full of vitamin supplements promising stronger bones, better skin and fewer colds.
In some countries, more than half of adults take at least one every day.
But do they actually work?
Vitamins are substances that the body needs in small amounts but cannot produce by itself, or cannot produce in sufficient quantities.
A serious lack of them causes disease.
For centuries, sailors on long voyages suffered from scurvy, a painful condition caused by a lack of vitamin C, until it was discovered that citrus fruit could prevent it.
In the nineteenth century, many children in industrial cities developed rickets, which weakens the bones, because they lacked vitamin D, which the skin makes in sunlight.
For most healthy people in rich countries, however, the situation is different.
A varied diet containing fruit, vegetables, grains and some protein usually provides adequate amounts of almost everything.
Large studies have found that multivitamins do little to prevent heart disease or cancer in well-nourished adults, and the extra vitamins are often simply excreted.
The famous claim by the chemist Linus Pauling that huge doses of vitamin C could cure colds has not been supported by later research.
Some supplements can even be harmful.
Excessive amounts of vitamin A during pregnancy can damage an unborn baby, and very high doses of certain vitamins have been linked to liver problems.
Because supplements are usually regulated less strictly than medicines, their contents do not always match the label.
There are important exceptions.

Doctors recommend folic acid for women who are trying to become pregnant, vitamin D in winter for people in northern countries, and vitamin B12 for vegans, since it is found almost exclusively in animal products.
For everyone else, the most effective supplement may be a plate of vegetables.
For centuries, humans have worked hard to remove wild animals from the landscape.
Wolves, bears and eagles were hunted because they threatened livestock, and forests were cut down to make room for farms.
In Britain, the last wild wolf was killed in the eighteenth century.
Today, a growing movement argues that we should do the opposite.
Rewilding means allowing nature to recover by itself, sometimes with the help of reintroducing species that have disappeared.
Its supporters point out that ecosystems depend on complex relationships between plants and animals, and that removing a single species can have unexpected consequences.
The most famous example comes from Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where wolves were brought back in 1995 after an absence of seventy years.
Without predators, the deer population had grown so large that the animals had eaten most of the young trees along the rivers.
Once the wolves returned, the deer began to avoid open valleys, trees grew back, birds returned, and the riverbanks became more stable.
Scientists still debate how large these effects were, but the story has inspired projects around the world.
In Europe, beavers have returned to many rivers, where their dams create wetlands that store water and reduce flooding.
Eagles and owls are being released in areas where they had vanished, and some conservationists are campaigning for the return of the lynx to Scotland.
The idea is controversial.
Farmers fear for their sheep, and many rural communities feel that decisions about their land are being made by people in cities who will never have to live with the consequences.
Successful rewilding projects usually involve compensation for any losses and genuine cooperation with local people.
Nature, it seems, can revive remarkably quickly, if humans are willing to share the landscape.
When a company wants to raise money to grow, it has two main options: it can borrow from a bank, or it can sell part of itself to investors.
The second option involves issuing shares, small pieces of ownership that can be bought and sold on a stock exchange such as those in New York, London or Tokyo.
Anyone who owns shares becomes a shareholder, with a small stake in the company's future.
Investors make money in two ways.
Many companies share part of their profits with shareholders through regular payments called dividends.
More importantly, if the company does well, the price of its shares tends to rise, and investors can sell them for more than they paid.
Of course, the opposite can also happen: if the company struggles, its shares may lose most of their value.
Share prices are determined by supply and demand.
When traders expect a company to grow, they buy its shares, and the price goes up; when they are pessimistic, they sell.
News about profits, new products or the wider economy can cause prices to surge or collapse within minutes.
Newspapers often report the movement of an index, such as the Dow Jones, which measures the average performance of a group of large companies.
Markets are not always rational.
Sometimes excitement about a new technology creates a bubble, in which prices rise far above any realistic value, as happened with internet companies in the late 1990s.
When the bubble bursts, panic can spread, and a crash can wipe out the savings of millions of people.
For ordinary savers, most financial experts give the same advice.
Do not try to predict short-term movements, which even professionals rarely manage consistently.
Instead, invest regularly over many years, diversify by spreading your money across many companies, and never invest money that you might urgently need.
Historically, patient investors have been rewarded, although past performance is never a guarantee of the future.
In Japan, there is a word, karoshi, which means "death from overwork."
It describes a real phenomenon: every year, some employees die of heart attacks, strokes or suicide linked to extremely long working hours.
Although Japan is the most famous example, excessive working hours are a problem in many countries.
Why do people work so much?
For many, there is no choice: workers paid an hourly wage may need to do overtime simply to pay their rent.
For others, the pressure is cultural.
In some offices, leaving before the boss is seen as a lack of commitment, and employees compete to appear busy.
Technology has made things worse: with emails on our phones, it has become difficult to stop working at all.
The consequences can be serious.

Long-term overwork is associated with high blood pressure, depression and exhaustion, and many people eventually experience burnout: a state of complete physical and emotional tiredness in which they can no longer function effectively.
Ironically, working longer does not necessarily mean producing more.
Studies suggest that productivity falls sharply after about fifty hours a week, as tired workers make more mistakes.
Some governments and companies are experimenting with alternatives.
France gives employees a legal "right to disconnect," allowing them to ignore work emails in the evening.
Trials of a four-day week in Iceland and elsewhere found that many employees were just as productive, and considerably happier, when they worked fewer hours for the same pay.
Rest is not idleness.
Relaxation, sleep and time with family allow the brain to recover and often produce our best ideas.
As one weary manager put it after returning from her first real holiday in years: "I didn't realize how tired I was until I stopped."
Every human society has rituals.
We celebrate births and marriages, mourn the dead, mark the new year and welcome young people into adulthood with ceremonies that follow fixed patterns.
Even people who consider themselves entirely rational often have private rituals, such as wearing a lucky shirt to an interview or drinking tea in exactly the same way every morning.
Anthropologists have noticed that rituals around the world share certain features.
They are repeated, they follow rules that must not be broken, and their actions are often symbolic rather than practical.
Throwing rice at a wedding does not literally make a couple fertile, and lighting candles at a burial does not bring the dead back.
Yet the actions carry deep meaning for the people involved.
Psychologists have begun to explain why.
One function of rituals is to reduce anxiety.
When we face situations we cannot control, such as illness, exams or the death of a loved one, performing a fixed sequence of actions gives us a sense of order.
In experiments, people who performed a simple ritual before a stressful task felt calmer and even performed better.
Rituals also bind communities together.
A rite of passage, such as a graduation ceremony, publicly marks the moment when a person's status changes, and everyone present becomes a witness.
Shared mourning allows people to express grief together, which is often easier than facing it alone.
In modern societies, many traditional rituals have faded, but new ones constantly emerge.
Families invent their own holiday traditions, sports fans sing the same songs at every match, and friends gather online to mark birthdays.
Humans, it seems, need rituals, perhaps because they remind us that we belong to something larger than ourselves.
For most of history, if you wanted to communicate with someone far away, you had to write a letter, and the process was slow, unreliable and extremely expensive.
Before the invention of modern postal services, letters were carried by messengers, merchants or travelers, and they could take months to arrive, if they arrived at all.
Everything changed in the nineteenth century.
In 1840, Britain introduced the Penny Black, the world's first stamp, which allowed anyone to send a letter anywhere in the country for a single penny.
The number of letters exploded virtually overnight, and in Victorian cities the post was delivered up to twelve times a day.
People wrote to arrange meetings, to share news, to console friends and to fall in love.
For historians, this extensive correspondence is a treasure.
Letters reveal the private, often intimate thoughts of ordinary people in a way that official documents rarely do.
Soldiers' letters from the trenches of the First World War, for example, describe the reality of the fighting far more honestly than newspapers of the time, which were heavily controlled.
Some newspapers employed foreign correspondents, whose long letters home were published as reports.
