The telephone, and later email and instant messaging, gradually made letters less necessary and, eventually, virtually obsolete.

Today, many young people have never written a personal letter, and postal services around the world are handling far fewer letters than twenty years ago, although the number of parcels has grown thanks to online shopping.
Yet the letter has not entirely disappeared, and in some circles it is genuinely fashionable again.
Some people have rediscovered the thrill of writing by hand, joining clubs of penpals or sending cards to elderly relatives.
A handwritten letter takes time and thought, and that is precisely its value.
In an age of instant messages that are read in seconds and forgotten, an envelope with your name on it still says something a text cannot: someone thought you were worth the effort.
Dear Alex,
You are seventeen, and you are desperately worried about almost everything: your exams, your appearance, what other people think of you.
I am writing from twenty years in the future to offer you a few hints.
You will undoubtedly ignore most of them, but I have to try.
First, the so-called "best years of your life" are not happening now.
Being a grown-up is actually much more fun than you imagine, partly because you stop caring so much about being popular.
Self-confidence is not something you are born with; it is built slowly, through multiple small victories and a few spectacular failures.
Second, you will not get the well-paid job you dream about, at least not straight away.
Your actual first job will be in a noisy call center, and it will be tricky, tiring and occasionally hilarious.
You will learn more there about people than in any classroom.
Third, be kinder to your parents.
They are not as stupid as you think, and the conversations you avoid now are the ones you will most wish you had had.
When Dad asks you to help him in the garden, say yes.
It seems like a waste of a Saturday.
It isn't.
Fourth, learn to rest.
Ideally, you would stop checking your phone at midnight, but preferably you would also learn that doing nothing is sometimes the most thoughtful choice.
You will meet fabulous people when you stop trying so hard.
Some will be casual friends, some will be lifelong ones, and you will seldom be able to tell the difference at the beginning.
Lastly, and most sincerely: the feeling that you are invisible, that nobody really sees you, will pass.
Life does not become straightforward, but it becomes easier to handle, and you will face it with far more ease than you can imagine.
With love, and a little envy of your young knees,
Alex, aged thirty-seven
Weddings bring families together, and occasionally they also reveal how different those families are.
When Priyanka announced her engagement to Daniel, her parents were delighted, but they were also slightly worried.
Daniel's family was small and quiet, whereas Priyanka's was large, loud and Gujarati, with opinions about everything.
The two families first met properly at a dinner a month before the wedding.

Daniel's mother, soon to be Priyanka's mother-in-law, arrived with a bottle of wine and a bouquet of flowers, and Mr. Shah, soon to be Daniel's father-in-law, greeted her with a warm embrace that took her completely by surprise.
By the end of the evening, however, the two mothers were laughing together like old friends.
The celebrations lasted three days.

On the first evening, at the mehndi, the women painted the bride's hands with delicate patterns of henna, and Priyanka's future sister-in-law, Daniel's shy younger sister, was persuaded to have her hands painted too.
On the second day, there was music and dancing until midnight, and Aunt Meena, who was eighty, danced longer than anyone.
The ceremony itself took place under a decorated canopy in a garden full of spring blossom.
A trio of musicians played a gentle melody while the couple exchanged vows, and Daniel's grandmother read a verse from her favorite poem.
When the groom finally kissed the bride, both families cheered.
At the reception, Mr. Shah gave a speech that made everyone cry, and then another that made everyone laugh.
"I have not lost a daughter," he said, raising his glass. "I have gained a son-in-law who does the washing up. Darling Priyanka, you have chosen wisely."
Daniel's father, not to be outdone, promised to learn to cook curry.
The generosity of both families that weekend became a family legend, and the exquisite photographs still hang in both houses.
Joanne had been a nurse for twenty years, and she had worked the night shift on the surgical ward for most of them.
At eight o'clock every evening, she arrived for the handover, when the day staff explained the condition of each patient and any queries from their families.
Then the long night began.
In bed four was Mr. Patel, who had had a tumor removed from his stomach that morning.
He was still drowsy, and every hour Joanne checked his pulse, his blood pressure and the stitches in his wound.
In bed six was Mrs. Green, eighty-seven, who had broken her thigh bone in a fall and was in agony whenever she moved.
Joanne gave her painkillers, adjusted her pillows and held her hand until the drugs began to relieve the pain.
At two in the morning, an ambulance brought in a young man who had been injured in a motorbike accident.
He had a deep cut on his leg, which needed stitches, and a scar on his forehead from an earlier accident.
He had been unconscious for a few minutes at the scene, so the doctors sent him for an X-ray and a scan to check for injuries to his head and limbs.
Fortunately, nothing was broken.
Nights on a ward are rarely quiet.
Machines beep, patients call out, and there is always paperwork: every medicine, every test and every change must be recorded.

Nurses must respond promptly to emergencies while also finding time for small kindnesses: a cup of tea, a gentle massage of stiff shoulders, a few minutes of conversation with someone who cannot sleep.
At seven, as the sun rose, Joanne began the handover to the morning staff.
Mr. Patel was awake and asking for breakfast, Mrs. Green had finally slept, and the young man had been discharged with his leg bandaged.
It had been, Joanne said as she took off her uniform, a fairly ordinary night.
Welcome to Ashworth Hall, one of the finest country houses in the north of England.
The mansion was built in the 1680s for the first Earl of Ashworth, a distinguished soldier who had been rewarded by the king for his loyalty.
For three centuries it was home to his descendants, and it was formerly one of the richest estates in the county.
Since 1952, it has been owned by a charity and open to the public.
Your tour begins on the porch, where you can see the family's coat of arms above the door.
Inside, the Great Hall is decorated with portraits of the earls and their wives, and a set of tapestries showing the conquest of a Spanish fort.
The large rug in the center was a gift from a visiting ambassador in the eighteenth century.
The Library contains more than eight thousand books, as well as a miniature replica of the house made by one of the family's children in 1890.
In the Drawing Room, you will find the house's most famous exhibit: a decorative clock presented to the fifth earl by Queen Victoria.
The walls are covered in Italian paintings collected during the family's travels, which made them important patrons of artists at the time.
Not every part of the family's history was glorious.
The seventh earl lost most of the family fortune gambling, and he spent his last years in exile in France to escape his creditors.
Thereafter, the family struggled to pay for the upkeep of the house, and during the Second World War it was used as a hospital.

Before you leave, take a walk across the lawn to the old chapel, whose stone altar dates from the fourteenth century, and don't miss the wine cellar, which contains bottles more than a hundred years old.
The shop and café are located in the former stables.
We hope you enjoy your visit.
When you switch on a light, you probably do not think about the enormous system behind it.
Yet the electricity that reaches your home has traveled through one of the most complex machines ever built: the electrical grid.
The journey begins at a power station, which might burn gas, split atoms or use the wind and sun.
Most power stations use the same basic principle, discovered in the nineteenth century.
When a magnet spins inside a coil of copper wire, it produces an electric current.
The energy of burning fuel or moving water is used to turn huge machines called turbines, which spin the magnets.
Electricity loses energy as it travels, so before it leaves the power station, transformers increase its voltage to hundreds of thousands of volts.
It then travels across the country along thick cables made of aluminum, supported by tall steel towers.
Near towns and cities, substations reduce the voltage again, and smaller cables, often buried underground, carry it along the streets.
Inside your home, electricity flows through a circuit: it travels along one wire to each device and returns along another.
A small box, often in a hallway or cupboard, contains switches that cut the power automatically if something goes wrong.
This can happen, for example, if too many devices are plugged into a single extension lead.
Plugs and outlets differ from country to country, which is why travelers need an adapter to make their chargers compatible.
Utility companies must balance supply and demand every second.
Electricity is difficult to store.
When millions of people switch on their kettles at the same time, for example during a break in a popular football match, extra power stations must be ready to respond virtually instantly.
As more electricity comes from wind and solar power, which depend on the weather, huge batteries are increasingly being installed to keep the system stable.
Modern election campaigns are enormous operations.
In a presidential election in the United States, candidates may spend more than a billion dollars and employ thousands of staff and volunteers.
Even in smaller countries, campaigns are planned with military precision.
The process often begins long before voting day.
Parties must first choose their candidates, sometimes through internal elections called primaries, in which members vote for their preferred nominee.
Once the nomination has been decided, the party publishes a manifesto describing the policies it promises to introduce.
Campaigns then try to win the support of voters in several ways.
Candidates hold rallies, where supporters gather to cheer, wave flags and listen to patriotic speeches.
They appear on television debates, give interviews and travel constantly, shaking hands in markets and factories.
A spokesman, or spokeswoman, speaks to journalists on the candidate's behalf and responds to criticism.
Increasingly, however, the most important work happens online.
Campaigns collect huge amounts of data about voters, from their age and address to the websites they visit, and they send carefully targeted messages to different groups.
Most attention goes to so-called swing voters, who have not yet decided, because in a close contest they can determine the outcome.
Opinion polls are studied every day, and strategies change accordingly.
Critics worry that campaigns have become too partisan and too negative.
Advertisements often attack opponents rather than explain policies, and accusations of dishonesty on both sides can cause public outrage.
A scandal in the final week has sometimes forced a candidate's resignation.
Yet elections remain the moment when ordinary citizens hold power, and a campaign that forgets this rarely succeeds.
Saturday.
We arrived at the cottage late on Friday night, soaked to the skin after walking from the station in the rain, but this morning the sky was clear and the sea was a brilliant blue.
After breakfast, we followed a narrow path along a creek to the estuary, where the river meets the sea.
The area is a kind of delta, full of tall reeds, mudflats and hundreds of birds.
Through our binoculars, we watched a pair of swans gliding across the water and dozens of small birds searching the mud for worms.
Emma found a crab hiding under a rock and insisted on photographing it from every possible angle.
Sadly, the beach was also full of litter: plastic bottles, fishing nets and even a child's shoe.
We collected two bags of it before lunch.
In the afternoon, we walked to the harbor, where a small yacht club was preparing for a race.
An old man repairing his boat told us that he had sailed across the strait to France more than forty times.
He also warned us about the tides, which are extremely dangerous here, and pointed out a wind farm offshore, its white turbines just visible on the horizon.
Sunday.
Woke early and swam before breakfast, which was a terrible idea.
The water was so cold that I lost the feeling in my feet within a minute, and Emma, who was sensibly watching from the beach wrapped in a towel, laughed until she cried.
We spent the rest of the morning in a café by the harbor, drinking hot chocolate and trying to get our tan back, since summer was obviously over.
On the train home, Emma counted her photographs.
There were three hundred and twelve, and a hundred and forty of them were of the crab.
It was, we agreed, a perfect weekend.
There is an old saying in the gambling industry: "The house always wins."
It is not a boast but a mathematical fact.
Every game in a casino is designed so that, over thousands of bets, the casino earns slightly more than it pays out.
Consider roulette.
A roulette wheel has thirty-seven or thirty-eight numbered pockets, but if you bet on a single number and win, you are paid only thirty-five times your stake.
That small difference guarantees the casino a profit of between three and five percent on every bet.

Slot machines are even more profitable, and modern ones are carefully designed to keep players playing, with flashing lights, cheerful music and frequent small wins that make losses feel less painful.
Casinos also use psychology.
Most have no windows or clocks, so that visitors lose track of time.
Players use colorful chips instead of cash, which makes it easier to forget how much real money they are spending, and free drinks encourage them to stay.
The rare jackpot winner is celebrated loudly, so that everyone in the room believes that they could be next.
For most visitors, a night in a casino in Las Vegas or Macau is simply entertainment, and they set a limit on how much they are willing to lose.
For some, however, gambling becomes an addiction as powerful as drugs or alcohol.
Addicted gamblers chase their losses, borrowing money in the belief that the next bet will change their luck, and the temptation can destroy families and careers.
Many millionaires have become losers in a single night.
Governments face a difficult choice.
Casinos create jobs and generate taxes, but they also have social costs that the public must pay for.
Many countries now require casinos to fund treatment for addiction and to ban players who ask to be excluded.
The house may always win, but society does not have to lose.
Crime fiction is one of the most popular genres in the world.
Agatha Christie's novels have sold more than two billion copies, and Sherlock Holmes has appeared in more films than almost any other fictional character.
What makes these stories so addictive?
The classic detective story, often called a "whodunit," is essentially a puzzle.
A crime is committed, usually a murder, and a small group of suspects is introduced, each with a possible motive.
The detective gathers clues, and the reader is invited to solve the mystery at the same time.
The best writers play fair: every clue needed to identify the killer is present in the text, but it is hidden among red herrings, false clues designed to lead the reader in the wrong direction.
The choice of narrator is crucial.
In the Sherlock Holmes stories, the narrator is Dr. Watson, Holmes's loyal friend, who is intelligent but always a step behind.
Because we see events through his eyes, we share his confusion, and Holmes's final explanation feels like a revelation.
Christie went further in one famous novel, in which the narrator himself turned out to be the murderer, a twist that outraged some readers and delighted others.
Style matters too.
Crime writers usually prefer clear, fast-moving prose to elaborate description, and each chapter often ends with a small surprise that makes the reader turn the page.
Yet the genre is not only about puzzles.
Modern crime novels often explore serious themes, such as corruption, poverty and the failures of the justice system, using the investigation as a metaphor for society's attempt to understand itself.
Perhaps that is the real secret of their appeal: in a confusing world, they promise that the truth can be found.
When a serious crime is reported, the first hours are often the most important.
Police officers secure the scene so that nothing is moved or contaminated, and forensic specialists search it for fingerprints, fibers, blood and any other trace that the criminal may have left.
Even a single hair can now be enough to identify a suspect through DNA analysis.
Meanwhile, detectives begin to gather information.
They interview witnesses, check CCTV footage from nearby shops and roads, and examine phone records to see who was in the area.
If someone has disappeared, officers may search the backyard of their home, nearby fields and rivers, often with the help of dogs and volunteers.
The disappearance of a child triggers an immediate national alert.
Once a suspect has been identified, the police may arrest and question them.
Suspects have the right to a lawyer and the right to remain silent, and in most countries they cannot be held for more than a few days without being charged.
A confession obtained through threats or cruelty cannot be used in court.
Police officers who violate these rules can themselves face serious charges.
If there is enough evidence, the case goes to court.
The accused person may plead guilty, which usually leads to a lighter sentence, or not guilty, in which case there will be a trial.
Detectives may be asked to testify, explaining how the evidence was collected and answering questions from the defense.
Some suspects are released on bail while they wait for their trial, on condition that they stay at a fixed address.
Real investigations are rarely as quick or dramatic as those on television.
Many take months or years, and some are never solved.
The work requires patience, careful paperwork and, above all, a respect for the rights of everyone involved, including those who turn out to be innocent.
Many of the inventions that dramatically changed the world were discovered by accident.
Scientists call this serendipity: finding something valuable while looking for something else.
But as these stories show, accidents only lead to discoveries when someone is curious enough to notice them and determined enough to investigate.
In 1945, an American engineer called Percy Spencer was testing equipment for military radar when he noticed that a chocolate bar in his pocket had melted.
Instead of simply cleaning his trousers, he placed some popcorn kernels near the machine and watched them explode, utterly fascinated.
The realization that radio waves could heat food led to the advent of the microwave oven, which is now found in most kitchens in the developed world.
In 1956, another engineer, Wilson Greatbatch, was building a device to record the rhythm of the human heart.
He reached into a box for a small electronic component and, by mistake, took the wrong one.
When he installed it, the device began to produce regular electrical pulses instead of recording them.
Greatbatch recognized that he had accidentally created something that could stimulate a failing heart.
His invention, the implantable pacemaker, has since saved millions of lives.
Not every accident produces an instant success.
In 1968, a chemist at the company 3M, Spencer Silver, was trying to create a very strong glue, but he produced a weak one instead.
It stuck to surfaces but could easily be removed, which seemed worthless.
For years, nobody could think of a practical use for it, until a colleague who sang in a church choir realized that it would be perfect for bookmarks that did not fall out of his hymn book.
The result was the Post-it note, one of the most successful office products ever invented.
These stories share a common and genuinely useful lesson.
Luck plays a role in innovation, but it is never sufficient on its own.
As the scientist Louis Pasteur famously said, "Chance favors the prepared mind."
Everyone has days when they feel inexplicably grim, when small things seem irritating and the future looks full of doom.
On other days, the same problems seem trivial, and we feel capable of anything.
Moods are different from emotions: an emotion, such as anger or joy, is usually a short reaction to a specific event, whereas a mood can last for hours or days and may have no obvious cause.
Many factors influence our moods.
Sleep is one of the most important: after a bad night, people tend to be moody, weary and more sensitive to criticism.
Hunger also plays a surprising role, which is why some people become "hangry," a mixture of hungry and angry, before lunch.
Hormones, the weather and the amount of daylight we receive all have measurable effects, and in winter some people suffer from a form of depression linked to the lack of sunlight.
Our thoughts matter, too.
When we are in a bad mood, we tend to interpret neutral events negatively: a friend's short message seems cold, and a colleague's gaze seems critical.
We may even feel inadequate or worthless for no real reason.
Being unaware of this bias can lead to unnecessary arguments and childish reactions that we regret later.
Psychologists suggest several simple strategies.
Physical exercise, time outdoors and conversation with friends reliably improve mood, even when we do not feel like doing them.
Noticing a bad mood, and naming it, can also reduce its power: saying "I'm tired and irritable today" helps us avoid taking it out on others.
Most importantly, we should remember that moods pass.
If a low mood lasts for weeks and affects daily life, however, it may be a sign of depression, and it is worth talking to a doctor.
Last winter, my brother and I rented a campervan and drove from Sydney to Darwin, a journey of more than four thousand kilometers across the heart of Australia.
We had planned it as a relaxing getaway.
It turned out to be the most adventurous month of our lives.
The first days took us along the picturesque east coastline, where lush forests come down almost to the beaches.
Then we turned inland, and the landscape changed dramatically.
The outback is enormous, empty and red: for hours we saw nothing except dust, low bushes and, occasionally, a group of kangaroos that watched us with complete indifference.
The roads were straight and uneven, and the heat was so intense that the horizon seemed to blur.
Driving in the outback requires careful preparation.
Petrol stations can be three hundred kilometers apart, so we carried extra fuel, twenty liters of water and a satellite phone.
Cattle and kangaroos roam freely across the roads, especially at dawn and dusk, which is why many vehicles have huge metal bars on the front bumper.
We learned to stop driving before sunset.
The highlight of the trip was Uluru, the vast red rock in the center of the country.
It is sacred to the Aboriginal people who have lived in the area for tens of thousands of years, and visitors are asked not to climb it out of respect.
A local guide took us on a walk around its base and explained the stories connected with each cave and crack in the rock.
At sunset, the rock changed color from orange to deep purple, and the crowd of tourists fell completely silent.
The final stage took us north into the tropics, where the air became humid and the rivers were full of crocodiles.
In Kakadu National Park, a ranger warned us never to swim, however hot we felt, and showed us a sign that described exactly what had happened to the last tourist who had ignored the advice.
We did not swim.
Sean has worked as a bartender in Dublin for eighteen years.
We asked him about the job.
What does a normal night look like?
"It starts quietly: a few regulars having a pint after work, and a couple on a first date who are both too nervous to talk."
"By ten o'clock, the place is packed, the music is loud and I'm pouring drinks for two hundred people."
"On Fridays there's karaoke upstairs, which is a genuine test of patience."
What's the hardest part?
"Dealing with people who have had too much to drink. Most are harmless: they just get loud or start telling you their life story."
"But occasionally someone becomes aggressive, and then you have to stay calm and refuse to serve them."
"We're legally responsible, so I can't give another drink to someone who's obviously drunk, however much they insist."
Has the industry changed?
"Hugely. When I started, people drank beer and whiskey, and that was it."
"Now customers want craft beer from small local breweries, cocktails with fresh herbs and even bourbon from Kentucky."
"The drinks are more sophisticated, but they take much longer to make. I also see many more young people ordering soft drinks, because they care about their health more than my generation did."
What do you enjoy most?
"The people. A good bar is like a small community."
"I've seen regulars fall in love here, celebrate their weddings here and, sadly, come back after funerals."
"Sometimes a bartender is a bit like a therapist, except that we're cheaper and we're open until one in the morning."
Any advice for customers?
"Be patient when it's busy, say please, and don't wave money at me."
"I've seen you, and I'll get to you. And when I call last orders, I genuinely mean it."
In many countries, women now make up more than half of university graduates.
Yet they remain rare at the very top of business and politics: only a small percentage of the world's largest companies are led by women, and in many parliaments men still hold most of the seats.
The invisible barrier that seems to stop women rising beyond a certain level is known as the glass ceiling.
Open discrimination, such as paying women less for identical work, is now illegal in most democracies.
Researchers argue that today's obstacles are usually more subtle.

Stereotypes about leadership still influence how people are judged: a man who speaks forcefully in a meeting is often described as confident, whereas a woman who does the same may be called aggressive.
In experiments, identical CVs receive lower ratings when they carry a woman's name, even from female reviewers.
Family responsibilities also play a major role.
In most societies, women still do the majority of childcare and housework, and many reduce their working hours after having children, just at the age when careers typically accelerate.
Workplaces that reward long hours and constant availability tend to disadvantage anyone with caring responsibilities.
What can be done?
Some countries have introduced quotas requiring a minimum percentage of women on company boards, and although the policy was controversial, it rapidly increased their prominence.
Other approaches include training managers to recognize unconscious bias, offering generous parental leave to fathers as well as mothers, and making salaries transparent.
Progress has been real, if slow.
Many young women today aspire to leadership roles that their grandmothers could never have imagined, and a growing number achieve them.
The question is no longer whether women are competent to lead, which the evidence clearly shows they are, but how quickly institutions will adapt to let them.
Dictators often appear invincible.
They control the army, the police and the media, they punish critics severely and they surround themselves with loyal followers.
Yet history shows that even the most powerful regimes can collapse with astonishing speed.
Some dictators are removed by force.
A military coup, in which the army overthrows the government, has been the most common way for regimes to end, although it frequently replaces one dictator with another.
Others are defeated in wars or forced out by foreign pressure.
Many, however, fall because their own people refuse to obey them any longer.
In December 1989, the Romanian leader Nicolae Ceaușescu gave a speech to a huge crowd in the capital, expecting the usual applause.
Instead, people began to shout and whistle.
Television cameras showed the confusion on his face, and within a week the regime had collapsed amid violent unrest.
Researchers who study such events have identified a crucial moment: when the soldiers and police who are supposed to enforce repression decide not to shoot.
Once ordinary people realize that the regime's power depends on their obedience, fear can turn rapidly into courage.
Studies suggest that peaceful mass movements, involving strikes and boycotts as well as protests, have succeeded more often than violent uprisings, partly because they attract wider participation.
The downfall of a dictator is not the end of the story, however.
Building a democracy afterwards requires independent courts, a free press and a willingness to accept election results, and many revolutions have ended in new forms of tyranny.
Freedom, it seems, is easier to win than to keep.
In Britain, the word "pudding" can mean almost any dessert, and asking "What's for pudding?" at the end of a meal is a national habit.
British puddings are rarely elegant, but they are warm, generous and deeply comforting on a cold, wet evening.
The most famous is probably Christmas pudding, a heavy, dark mixture of dried fruit, nuts, spices and a little alcohol, which is traditionally prepared weeks in advance.
Before it is served, it is covered in brandy and set on fire, and the lights are switched off so that everyone can admire the blue flames.
Many families hide a coin inside, which is said to bring good luck to whoever finds it, although it is more likely to bring a trip to the dentist.
Crumble is simpler and much easier to make.
Chopped fruit, usually apples, plums or rhubarb, is placed in a dish and covered with a rough mixture of flour, butter and sugar, then baked until it is golden.
It is almost always served with custard, a sweet yellow sauce made from milk and eggs.
Some people add walnuts to the topping, and others prefer ice cream, a choice that can cause surprisingly passionate arguments.
Other classics include sticky toffee pudding, a soft sponge soaked in a rich caramel sauce.
There is also Eton mess, a chaotic combination of strawberries, cream and broken meringue.
Bakewell tart, meanwhile, is filled with jam and almond cream.
Traditional recipes used a type of animal fat called suet, which made puddings extremely heavy, although modern versions are usually lighter.
Nutritionists, understandably, do not recommend eating these every day.
But as any British grandmother will tell you, a bowl of hot crumble and custard on a rainy Sunday is not really about nutrition.
It is about comfort, memory and the feeling of home.
I am clumsy.
I walk into doors, I knock over glasses, and I once fell up a flight of stairs in front of my future mother-in-law.
My friends find this hilarious, and I have learned to laugh with them, but for years it made me feel slightly daft.
So I was delighted to discover that science has some sympathy for people like me.
Clumsiness is surprisingly complicated.

To perform even a simple action, such as picking up a cup, the brain must combine information from the eyes, the muscles and the inner ear, and then send precise instructions to dozens of muscles in the correct order.
In most people, this coordination happens automatically.
In some, it works less smoothly, and around five percent of children have a condition called dyspraxia, which makes physical coordination genuinely difficult.
Being clumsy is often linked to being distracted.
Many of my accidents happen when I am thinking about something else, which, admittedly, is most of the time.
Tiredness, stress and alcohol make everyone clumsier, and so, curiously, does being watched.
Anyone who has tried to parallel park while a group of teenagers watches knows exactly what I mean.
What I resent is the idea that clumsiness is a character flaw.
Clumsy children are often told off, mocked or chosen last for sports teams, and some grow up believing that they are incompetent at everything.
That is nonsense.
Many brilliant scientists, writers and musicians have been famously clumsy, perhaps precisely because their minds were busy elsewhere.
So, to my fellow clumsy people: be patient with yourselves.
Slow down, put your coffee in the middle of the table and wear sensible shoes.
And when you do fall over, as you certainly will, get up with dignity, take a bow and enjoy the applause.
Many of the safety rules we take for granted were written in response to catastrophe.
Behind every emergency exit sign, fire alarm and life jacket, there is often a tragedy that forced governments to act.
When the Titanic sank in 1912, more than fifteen hundred people died, partly because the ship carried lifeboats for only about half of the people on board.
This was not illegal: the regulations of the time were based on a ship's size rather than the number of passengers, which seems utterly absurd today.
Within two years, an international agreement required every ship to carry enough lifeboats for everyone.
Radio operators also had to listen for distress signals twenty-four hours a day.
A year earlier, a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York had killed a hundred and forty-six garment workers, most of them young immigrant women.
The doors had been locked by the owners to prevent theft, and many workers jumped from the windows to escape the blaze.
Public outrage led to dozens of new laws on fire escapes, sprinklers and working conditions, and it helped to strengthen the trade union movement.
Aviation offers another example.
In 1977, two passenger planes collided on a foggy runway on the island of Tenerife, killing almost six hundred people in the deadliest accident in the history of flying.
Investigators found that confusing radio messages, and a junior crew member who was reluctant to challenge the captain, had played a crucial role.
As a result, pilots now use standard phrases, and crews are trained to speak up when they see a risk, whatever their rank.
The lesson of these disasters is uncomfortable but essentially simple.
In virtually every case, the risks were known beforehand, and warnings were ignored because safety seemed expensive or unnecessary.
Needless deaths could have been prevented by preventive measures that cost far less than the tragedies themselves.
Good regulation, in other words, is often the memory of people who died, and ignoring it is dangerously irresponsible.
Jeans are probably the most successful piece of clothing in history.
Billions of pairs are sold every year, and they are worn by farmers and fashion models, presidents and teenagers, in almost every country on Earth.
Yet they began as work clothes for miners.
In the 1850s, during the California gold rush, a German immigrant called Levi Strauss opened a shop in San Francisco selling fabric and other supplies.
One of his customers, a tailor called Jacob Davis, had an idea: miners were constantly complaining that their trousers tore, so he strengthened the weak points with small copper rivets.
The two men took out a patent in 1873, and their tough blue trousers quickly became popular with miners, cowboys and railway workers.
The fabric itself had a longer history.
Denim is a strong cotton cloth, woven in a special way and dyed blue with indigo.
Its name probably comes from the French town of Nîmes: "de Nîmes" means "from Nîmes."
Because the dye fades gradually with washing, every pair of jeans slowly becomes unique.
For decades, jeans remained work clothes.
Then, in the 1950s, Hollywood changed everything.
When rebellious young film stars such as James Dean and Marlon Brando wore them on screen, jeans became a symbol of youth and rebellion, and some schools even banned them.
By the 1970s, they were everywhere, and designers began to sell luxurious versions at extremely high prices.
Today, the jeans industry is enormously lucrative, but it also has an environmental cost.
Growing the cotton for a single pair can require thousands of liters of water, and the chemicals used to create a worn, faded look can be hazardous for factory workers.
Some brands now use recycled denim and less water.
Perhaps the most sustainable choice, though, is the one the miners made: buy a tough pair and wear it for years.
Dogs have lived alongside humans for at least fifteen thousand years, longer than any other domesticated animal, and the partnership has shaped both species.
During that time, they have evolved remarkable abilities to understand us.
Recent research suggests that, in some ways, dogs read human behavior better than our closest relatives, the chimpanzees.
Consider a simple but revealing experiment involving pointing.
If you hide food under one of two cups and point at the correct one, most dogs will follow your gesture instantly, even as puppies.
Chimpanzees and wolves, by contrast, usually fail this test.
Scientists believe that this ability is at least partly innate.
For thousands of years, the dogs that paid attention to humans were the ones that received food and shelter.
Dogs are also highly sensitive to our emotions, and some can even detect illness.
Studies have shown that they can distinguish between happy and angry faces, and that they react differently to a crying person than to one who is simply talking.
When their owners look at them, levels of a hormone associated with affection rise in both the dog and the human, the same chemical process that strengthens the bond between parents and babies.
Some dogs learn an astonishing number of words.
A remarkably intelligent Border Collie called Chaser learned the names of more than a thousand toys and could fetch any of them on command.
Most pets, however, respond primarily to our tone of voice and body language rather than to the words themselves, which is why a dog may wag its tail happily when scolded in a cheerful voice.
Understanding how dogs think can make training easier, kinder and significantly more effective.
Experts recommend rewarding good behavior rather than punishing bad behavior, being consistent, and remembering that a dog pulling on its leash is usually excited rather than disobedient.
Obedience, after all, depends on trust, and dogs, perhaps more than any other animal, are eager to trust us.
What makes a song catchy?
For centuries, the answer depended primarily on talent and luck.

Today, many of the world's biggest hits are carefully designed by teams of professional songwriters and producers, who study what listeners respond to and use that knowledge with remarkable precision.
The most important element of a pop song is the hook: a short melody or phrase that gets stuck in your head after hearing it once or twice.
Hooks are usually simple, repetitive and slightly surprising, and a successful song may contain several of them.
The chorus, which is repeated several times, typically contains the main hook and the title of the song, so that listeners know what to search for.
The lyrics matter, too, although perhaps less than songwriters would like to believe.
Successful lyrics are often built around a single, universal emotion, such as falling in love or recovering from a breakup, expressed in simple words that rhyme easily.
Many listeners, research suggests, remember the melody long before they understand the words.
Streaming has changed the structure of songs.

On streaming platforms, a song counts as "played" only if a listener stays for about thirty seconds, so producers now try to grab attention immediately, often starting with the chorus rather than a long introduction.
Average song length has fallen, and some hits now last less than three minutes.
Critics complain that this approach produces songs that sound virtually identical.
Yet formulas have always existed in popular music, and every generation also produces artists who break them.
Some of the most successful songs of all time were written quickly, almost by accident, by musicians who were simply trying to express something they felt.
No formula, it seems, can completely replace that.
Twenty years ago, the high street of Hebden was dying.
The mill that had employed half the town had closed, the bank had moved away, and one shop after another had been boarded up.
Young people left for the cities as soon as they finished school, and the population grew steadily older.
Vacant buildings, uneven pavements and a run-down park gave the whole place a sad, neglected atmosphere.
The story of Hebden is not unusual.
Across many countries, small towns have suffered as industries have closed, shopping has moved online and services have been concentrated in larger centers.
What makes Hebden interesting is how its residents responded.
It began with a small group of volunteers who were utterly tired of complaining.
They raised money to buy the old grocery shop, which had closed, and turned it into a community shop run by residents.
Next, they persuaded the council to let artists use empty buildings as studios for a very low rent.
Within a few years, the high street had galleries, a bookshop, a bakery and a café with a large fireplace, where people gathered to play board games on winter evenings.
The town's picturesque surroundings, which residents had always taken for granted, began to attract visitors.
Walkers came for the pastoral landscape of hills and stone walls, and a summer festival, first organized to commemorate the town's industrial past, now attracts thousands of people.
Some families who had moved away have come back, and several young people have started businesses on the outskirts of the town.
Not everything has changed, and the recovery remains fragile.
Wages are still low, the bus service is poor, and some older residents feel that the town now belongs more to visitors than to them.
But Hebden shows that decline is not inevitable.
As Kate, one of the original volunteers, puts it: "Nobody was coming to save us, so we decided to save ourselves."
Few questions provoke such passionate disagreement at the dinner table.
The question is simple: is it moral to eat meat?
For most of history, people ate animals without thinking twice, and the question seemed virtually irrelevant.
Today, a growing number of people argue that it is morally unjustifiable, while others insist that it is natural, healthy and entirely acceptable.
The strongest argument against eating meat concerns suffering, and it is essentially a moral one.
Animals such as pigs, cows and chickens are sentient: they feel pain and fear, and many are highly intelligent.
The philosopher Peter Singer argued that if we accept that causing needless suffering is wrong, we cannot ignore the suffering of animals simply because they belong to a different species.
Most meat today comes from factory farming, where animals are kept in crowded, artificial conditions for their whole lives, which critics describe as a form of cruelty on an enormous scale.
There are environmental arguments, too, and they are increasingly persuasive and difficult to dismiss.
Livestock farming produces a significant share of greenhouse gases and uses vast amounts of land and water.
If everyone ate less meat, forests could be protected and more food could be grown for people rather than for animals.
Defenders of meat-eating reply that humans evolved as omnivores.
Meat, they point out, is an efficient source of protein and essential nutrients, particularly in poor regions where adequate alternatives are scarce.
Many farmers raise animals humanely, allowing them to live outdoors, and they argue that a good life followed by a quick death is better than no life at all.
Admittedly, this does not describe most of the meat in supermarkets.
Many people's views are, frankly, contradictory: they love their pets, feel genuinely uncomfortable about how farm animals are treated and continue to eat meat anyway.

Perhaps the most realistic solution is not a sudden conversion to vegetarianism but gradual change: eating less meat, choosing animals raised in better conditions and being honest about where our food comes from.
Conversely, those who have given up meat entirely might accept that others will take longer to reach the same conclusion.
Bridges, water pipes, railways and electricity grids rarely make headlines until something goes wrong.
When a motorway bridge collapsed in the Italian city of Genoa in 2018, killing forty-three people, investigators found that the structure had been showing signs of serious deterioration for years.
The disaster exposed a problem that affects many wealthy countries: much of their infrastructure was built decades ago and has not been adequately maintained.
In the United States, an influential association of engineers regularly publishes a report card on the nation's infrastructure, and the grades have rarely been flattering.

Thousands of bridges are classified as structurally deficient, many water systems still rely on pipes laid in the nineteenth century, and the electricity grid has struggled to cope with extreme weather.
The estimated cost of closing this so-called infrastructure gap runs into trillions of dollars.
Why does underinvestment persist when the risks are so well documented?
Part of the answer lies in political incentives.

Opening a new bridge generates positive publicity for the politicians who funded it, whereas maintenance, however essential, is invisible: nobody holds a ceremony to celebrate a pipe that did not burst.
Municipal governments, which are responsible for much of the network, often face tight budgets and taxpayers who resist higher local taxes.
Deferring repairs is tempting, because the consequences usually fall on a future administration.
There are also questions of liability and compliance.
When infrastructure is operated by private contractors, as is increasingly common, it can be unclear who is accountable if standards are not met.
Contracts may reward short-term profits rather than long-term resilience, and public oversight is often weak.

Economists broadly agree that well-designed infrastructure spending pays for itself over time, by reducing costs for businesses, creating jobs and preventing disasters that are far more expensive to repair.
The challenge is less technical than political: it requires governments to commit resources to projects whose benefits will be enjoyed by people who have not yet been born.
Every new medicine must eventually be tested on human beings, and the ethical framework governing such tests is notably complex.
Laboratory experiments and animal studies can indicate whether a drug is likely to work, but only clinical trials can establish whether it is safe and effective in people.
This creates an unavoidable ethical tension: to benefit future patients, researchers must expose current participants to risks whose nature cannot be fully known in advance.
The modern rules governing medical research were largely written in response to abuses.

After the Second World War, the trials at Nuremberg revealed that Nazi doctors had carried out horrific experiments on prisoners, and the resulting code established that voluntary consent is absolutely essential.
Yet abuses subsequently continued elsewhere.

In the notorious Tuskegee study in Alabama, which ran from 1932 to 1972, hundreds of Black men with syphilis were deliberately left untreated so that researchers could observe the disease, even after an effective cure had become widely available.
Today, most countries require that trials be approved by independent ethics committees and follow strict protocols.

Participants must give informed consent, which means that the purpose, risks and alternatives must be explained in language they can understand, and they must be free to withdraw at any time without penalty.
Particular protections apply to vulnerable groups, such as children, prisoners and people with cognitive impairments, who may be less able to protect their own interests.
Difficult questions remain, however, and they are seemingly impossible to resolve purely through rules.
Is it acceptable to give some patients a placebo when an existing treatment is already known to work?
Should pharmaceutical companies be allowed to conduct trials in poorer countries, where costs are lower but participants may have limited access to health care once the study ends?
And how should researchers handle the pressure to publish positive results, when negative findings are equally important for patients?
Transparency, including the public registration of every trial before it begins, has become one of the most important safeguards of scientific integrity.
In 1971, the economist Herbert Simon made a remarkably prescient observation: "A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention."
Half a century later, his insight describes the business model of some of the most valuable companies in history.
Social media platforms, video services and many news websites are free to use because their real customers are not their users but advertisers, who pay for access to our attention.
The logic of this model is straightforward.
The longer users stay on a platform, the more advertisements they see and the more data they generate about their preferences, which allows advertising to be targeted with increasing precision.
Companies therefore have a powerful incentive to maximize engagement, and they employ teams of engineers and behavioral scientists to do exactly that.
Critics argue that many of the resulting design features exploit well-known weaknesses in human psychology.

Notifications create a sense of urgency, infinite scroll removes natural stopping points, and algorithms learn which content provokes the strongest emotional reactions, which is frequently content that makes us angry or anxious.
The rewards are unpredictable, in the same way as those of a slot machine, which makes checking our phones a compulsive habit rather than a conscious decision.
Some former industry insiders have publicly acknowledged that these effects were anticipated and, in some cases, deliberately engineered.
The consequences extend beyond individual well-being.

If our attention is a finite resource, then its capture by a small number of platforms raises concerns about monopoly power, about the quality of public debate and about autonomy itself: the capacity to decide for ourselves what we think about.
Defenders of the industry reply that users are not passive victims, that people choose these services because they value them, and that free access to information has been enormously empowering.
Possible responses range from regulation, such as restrictions on targeted advertising for children, to alternative business models based on subscription rather than advertising.
At the individual level, simple measures, such as switching off notifications, can make a surprising difference.
The underlying question, however, is whether a system that profits from distraction can ever be fully aligned with the interests of the people it distracts.
At its height in the early twentieth century, the British Empire governed nearly a quarter of the world's population.
France, Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands and Belgium also controlled vast territories in Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Although almost all of these colonies became independent in the decades after 1945, historians increasingly argue that the legacy of colonialism continues to shape the modern world in profound ways.
One of the most visible legacies concerns borders.

At the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, European powers divided much of Africa among themselves, often drawing straight lines on maps with little regard for the ethnic, linguistic and religious communities that actually lived there.
Similar decisions were made in the Middle East after the First World War.
Some of the territorial disputes and civil conflicts of recent decades can be traced, at least in part, to these arbitrary boundaries.
The partition of British India in 1947, which created the separate states of India and Pakistan, illustrates how the end of empire could itself be catastrophic.
The new border was drawn hastily, and the resulting violence and mass migration cost up to a million lives and displaced some fifteen million people.
The aftermath still influences relations between the two countries today.
Economic legacies are more contested.
Colonial economies were typically organized to export raw materials, such as rubber, cotton and minerals, to the colonizing country, rather than to develop local industry.
Some scholars argue that this pattern of exploitation left many former colonies dependent on a narrow range of exports and vulnerable to fluctuations in global prices.
Others emphasize that post-independence policies and governance have been at least as important in determining economic outcomes.
In recent years, debates about empire have moved from academic journals into public life.
Museums face demands to return objects taken during the colonial period, and some governments have issued formal apologies or discussed reparations for historical injustices.
Such questions provoke strong emotions on all sides, but they reflect a growing recognition that the past is not entirely past.
"People in this country have had enough of experts," a British politician famously declared during a heated referendum campaign in 2016.
The remark provoked outrage among economists and scientists, but it also captured a genuine shift in public sentiment.

In many democracies, trust in professional expertise, whether that of doctors, economists, journalists or civil servants, appears to have declined, and this development has significant implications for how societies make decisions.
Several distinct explanations have been proposed.
Some point to high-profile failures that damaged the credibility of experts, such as the inability of most economists to foresee the financial crisis of 2008.
Others emphasize the internet, which has made specialist information widely accessible while also blurring the distinction between qualified knowledge and confident opinion.
The writer Tom Nichols has argued that a culture of egalitarianism has encouraged the mistaken belief that all views are equally valid, regardless of the evidence behind them.
There is, however, a more sympathetic interpretation of public skepticism.

Experts are not neutral machines; they belong to particular social groups, they sometimes have conflicts of interest, and their advice often involves value judgments disguised as technical conclusions.
When technocrats present contested political choices as the only rational option, citizens who bear the costs of those choices may reasonably feel excluded.
From this perspective, distrust is less a rejection of knowledge than a demand for accountability.
Rebuilding trust arguably requires changes on both sides, and hence a degree of humility from everyone involved.

Experts can be more transparent about uncertainty, more candid about the limits of their knowledge and more willing to explain the reasoning behind their conclusions rather than simply announcing them.
Citizens, for their part, can learn to distinguish between the inherent uncertainty of complex problems and deliberate deception.
A healthy democracy needs both expertise and skepticism: the challenge is to keep them in productive tension rather than open war.
Most people imagine memory as a kind of video recording: an accurate archive of past events that can be replayed when necessary.
This intuitive model is seemingly confirmed by our own experience, since certain memories feel extraordinarily clear.
Decades of psychological research have shown that this notion is profoundly mistaken.
Memories are not retrieved intact; they are reconstructed each time we recall them, and in the process they can be altered, distorted or even invented.
Some of the most influential evidence comes from the work of the psychologist Elizabeth Loftus.
In a classic experiment, participants watched a film of a car accident and were then asked how fast the cars had been going when they "hit" or "smashed into" each other.
Those who heard the word "smashed" estimated higher speeds, and a week later they were more likely to report having seen broken glass, although there had been none.
This phenomenon, known as the misinformation effect, demonstrates how easily information received after an event can become incorporated into our memory of it.
Subsequent studies went considerably further.
By combining genuine family stories with a fabricated one, researchers persuaded a significant proportion of adult participants that they had once been lost in a shopping center as children.
Many went on to describe the imaginary event in vivid detail, complete with emotions, and some remained convinced it had happened even after the deception was revealed.
Confidence, it turns out, is a poor indicator of accuracy, and the underlying mechanism of this distortion is still being studied.
These findings have serious implications for the justice system, notably in criminal trials, which has traditionally placed great weight on eyewitness testimony.
Research into cases in which prisoners were later exonerated by DNA evidence has found that mistaken identification by eyewitnesses played a role in the majority of them.
As a result, many police forces have changed how they conduct identity parades and interviews, avoiding leading questions that could inadvertently shape a witness's recollection.
Why would evolution produce such an unreliable system, albeit one that serves us reasonably well most of the time?
One possibility is that the purpose of memory is not solely to preserve the past accurately but to help us anticipate the future.
A flexible memory, which combines and recombines fragments of experience, allows us to imagine scenarios that have never happened, and that ability is arguably worth the occasional error.
Replacing fossil fuels with clean energy is arguably the most ambitious economic transformation ever attempted.

Coal, oil and gas still supply roughly four-fifths of the world's primary energy, and they are embedded in virtually every aspect of modern life, from heating and transport to the production of steel, cement and fertilizer.
Decarbonization therefore requires not a single technological breakthrough but the simultaneous reconstruction of entire industries.
The good news is that renewable electricity has become remarkably cheap.

Over the past decade, the cost of solar panels and wind turbines has fallen so dramatically that, in many regions, new renewable installations now generate electricity more cheaply than new coal or gas plants.
China alone now installs more solar capacity each year than the rest of the world combined.
The difficulty lies in what engineers call intermittency.
The sun does not shine at night, and the wind does not always blow, whereas demand for electricity continues regardless of the weather.

A grid dominated by renewables therefore needs ways of storing energy, such as large batteries or pumped hydroelectric reservoirs, and it needs transmission lines capable of moving power across long distances, from where it is generated to where it is used.
Building this infrastructure is slow, expensive and frequently opposed by local residents.
Some sectors are harder to decarbonize than others.

Aviation, shipping and heavy industry require concentrated energy that batteries cannot yet provide, and many governments are investing in hydrogen, which can be produced from water by electrolysis and burned without releasing carbon dioxide.
Nuclear power remains deeply divisive.

France generates most of its electricity from reactors fueled by uranium, while Germany chose to close its nuclear plants, a decision that critics argue substantially increased its dependence on coal and imported gas.
Ultimately, the pace of the transition will depend as much on politics as on technology.
Workers in coal regions fear for their jobs, consumers resent higher prices, and countries that depend on oil exports face a profound threat to their economic model.
A transition that is perceived as unfair is unlikely to survive successive elections, which is why many economists stress that its costs and benefits must be distributed equitably.
Anxiety about machines replacing human workers is nothing new.

In the early nineteenth century, English textile workers known as Luddites smashed the mechanical looms that threatened their livelihoods, and similar fears have accompanied almost every wave of technological change since.
Yet, historically, automation has tended to transform employment rather than destroy it: agricultural workers became factory workers, and factory workers eventually moved into services.
The question is whether this time is fundamentally different, and the evidence is, admittedly, inconclusive.

Earlier machines mostly replaced physical labor and routine tasks, whereas modern software, including generative artificial intelligence, can increasingly perform cognitive work: drafting documents, writing code, analyzing images and answering customers' questions.
Occupations that were once considered safe, such as translation, accounting and even parts of law and medicine, now appear vulnerable.
Economists remain divided about the likely consequences, notably for workers in the middle of the income spectrum.

Optimists argue that new tools will raise productivity and free workers from tedious tasks, allowing them to concentrate on the creative and interpersonal aspects of their jobs, and that entirely new occupations will emerge, as they have in the past.
Pessimists warn that the benefits may be concentrated among a small number of highly skilled workers and the owners of technology, while others face lower wages and less secure employment.
Research by the economist David Autor suggests that automation has already contributed to a "hollowing out" of middle-income jobs in many countries.
For organizations, the challenge is as much cultural as technical, and it is seemingly underestimated by many managers.
Introducing automation successfully requires the retention of experienced staff, whose knowledge is difficult to replace, as well as the recruitment of people with new skills.

Employees who fear for their jobs are unlikely to embrace new systems, and some companies have found that involving workers in the design of those systems produces better outcomes than imposing them from above.
At the level of society, the most frequently proposed responses involve education and social protection.
If careers are likely to involve several major transitions, then learning cannot end at the age of twenty-one, and governments may need to fund retraining throughout adult life.
Whether the displacement caused by new technology proves temporary or permanent will depend, in large part, on such choices.
In 1945, shortly after the liberation of the Netherlands, a Dutch painter called Han van Meegeren was arrested for collaboration with the enemy.
He had sold a painting by the seventeenth-century master Johannes Vermeer, a national treasure, to the Nazi leader Hermann Göring.
Facing a possible death sentence, Van Meegeren made an astonishing confession: the painting was not a Vermeer at all.
He had painted it himself.
To prove his claim, he painted another "Vermeer" in front of witnesses.
It emerged that he had deceived some of the most respected connoisseurs of the age, including experts who had declared one of his forgeries to be the finest Vermeer ever discovered.
He had used old canvases, mixed his own pigments according to seventeenth-century methods and baked the finished paintings to harden the paint and create the fine cracks typical of old works.
Ironically, the man who had fooled the Nazis became something of a national hero.
The case raises a question that continues to trouble the art world: if a forgery is so skillful that experts cannot distinguish it from the original, why should it be worth less?
From a purely aesthetic point of view, the visual experience of looking at the painting has not changed.
Yet most people feel strongly that authenticity matters.
We value a work of art not only for its appearance but for its history: the fact that a particular person made it, at a particular moment, as an expression of their vision.
A forgery, however beautiful, is essentially a lie about its own origins.
Today, museums and auction houses rely on a combination of expertise and science, and neither is sufficient on its own, hence the importance of collaboration.
Researchers analyze the chemical composition of paint, examine canvases with X-rays and use infrared light to reveal sketches beneath the surface.
Equally important is provenance, the documented history of a work's ownership, which archives, letters and old sales catalogs can help to reconstruct.
Restoration presents its own dilemmas, since removing old varnish or repairing damage inevitably involves decisions about what the artist originally intended.
The pursuit of authenticity, it seems, is never purely technical.
Over the past two decades, populist movements have substantially transformed politics in many democracies.
Populist parties have won national elections, entered coalition governments and, perhaps most significantly, pushed mainstream parties to adopt some of their positions.
Yet the term itself is notoriously difficult to define, and it is frequently used simply as an insult, which inevitably obscures its meaning.
Many political scientists describe populism not as a specific ideology but as a way of framing politics.
According to this view, populists divide society into two groups: a virtuous "people," whose will should be sovereign, and a corrupt "elite," which is accused of ignoring or betraying them.
This framework can be combined with very different policies.

Left-wing populists typically target bankers and large corporations, whereas right-wing populists often focus on immigration and national identity, but both claim to speak for ordinary citizens against a self-serving establishment.
Explanations for the rise of populism usually combine economic and cultural factors, although scholars disagree about their respective weight.
Globalization and the financial crisis of 2008 left many communities, particularly in former industrial regions, feeling that the benefits of economic growth had passed them by.
At the same time, rapid social change, including immigration and shifting attitudes towards gender and sexuality, provoked a backlash among voters who felt that their values were no longer respected.
Social media, which allows politicians to communicate directly with supporters and bypass traditional journalism, has amplified these sentiments.
The consequences for democracy are fiercely debated, and historically the record is mixed.
Some scholars argue that populism can be a corrective, forcing complacent parties to listen to neglected voters and increasing electoral participation.

Others point out that, once in power, populist leaders have sometimes weakened the institutions that limit government, such as independent courts and a free press, on the grounds that these institutions obstruct the will of the people.
Increased polarization, in which opponents are treated not as rivals but as enemies, makes the compromises on which democratic politics depends harder to achieve.
Understanding the grievances behind populism, rather than simply condemning its supporters, may be the most effective response.
For most of human history, the Arctic Ocean was regarded as a frozen wilderness of little strategic value.
Climate change is rapidly altering that perception.
As the sea ice retreats, previously inaccessible shipping routes are opening, and vast reserves of oil, gas and minerals beneath the seabed are becoming potentially exploitable.
The question of who controls the region has consequently acquired new urgency.

Unlike Antarctica, which is a continent governed by an international treaty that prohibits military activity and mineral extraction, the Arctic is largely an ocean surrounded by the territory of eight countries.
Under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, each coastal state has jurisdiction over resources within two hundred nautical miles of its coast, known as its exclusive economic zone.
A state may claim rights beyond this limit if it can demonstrate, with scientific evidence, that the seabed is a natural extension of its continental shelf.
This provision has produced overlapping claims.

Russia, Canada and Denmark, through Greenland, all argue that an underwater mountain range called the Lomonosov Ridge, which runs close to the North Pole, is connected to their respective territories.
In 2007, a Russian submarine planted a titanium flag on the seabed at the Pole, a symbolic gesture that alarmed other governments, although it had no legal significance.
Beyond legal disputes, the Arctic is becoming an arena of military competition.

Russia has reopened Soviet-era bases along its northern coast and operates the world's largest fleet of icebreakers, which it regards as essential for the Northern Sea Route, a shipping lane that can shorten the journey between Asia and Europe by thousands of kilometers.
Other Arctic states have responded by increasing their own presence in the region.

Largely absent from these debates are the region's indigenous peoples, who have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years and whose livelihoods are most directly threatened by both climate change and industrial development.
Their organizations have argued that decisions about the Arctic should not be made solely by distant capitals.
The terrain may be remote, but the choices made there will have consequences far beyond its frozen coasts.
Each of us carries trillions of microorganisms, most of them bacteria living in the digestive system.
For a long time, scientists regarded these microbes primarily as a potential source of disease, and hence as enemies to be eliminated.
Over the past two decades, however, research into what is now called the microbiome has revealed that they perform functions that are essential to our health.
Gut bacteria help us to digest food that our own enzymes cannot break down, particularly the fibers found in vegetables and whole grains.
In the process, they produce molecules that nourish the cells lining the intestine and influence how the body stores fat.
They also play a crucial role in training the immune system, teaching it to distinguish between harmful invaders and harmless substances.
Some researchers believe that the rising rates of allergies in wealthy countries may be partially explained by childhoods that are too clean to expose infants to a diverse range of microbes.
More surprisingly, the microbiome appears to communicate with the brain, via mechanisms that involve both nerves and hormones.
Gut bacteria produce chemicals that affect mood, and in experiments, mice raised without any microbes behave differently from normal mice, showing altered responses to stress.
Whether similar mechanisms operate in humans, and to what extent, remains uncertain, but the idea of a "gut–brain axis" has become one of the most active areas of medical research.
The diversity of the microbiome seems to matter, albeit in ways that are not yet fully understood.
A varied diet, rich in plants and fermented foods such as yogurt, tends to support a wider range of species, whereas diets high in processed food and sugar are associated with reduced diversity.
Antibiotics, although often life-saving, can substantially disrupt this ecosystem, and its recovery may take months.
Commercial enthusiasm has, predictably, moved faster than the science, and the claims made on packaging are rarely based on clinical trials.
Shops are full of probiotic supplements promising better digestion, stronger immunity and improved mood, yet the evidence for most of them is weak.
The microbiome differs considerably between individuals, and simply adding a few species in a capsule is unlikely to transform a complex ecosystem.
For now, the most reliable advice remains remarkably traditional: eat plenty of vegetables.
Sleep researchers have spent decades documenting what happens inside the brain at night.
Increasingly, however, their attention has turned to a broader question: what happens to a society in which large numbers of people consistently sleep too little?
Surveys in many industrialized countries suggest that between a third and a half of adults regularly get less than the seven hours that most experts recommend.
The consequences for individuals are well established and, notably, consistent across very different populations.

Chronic sleep deprivation is associated with an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease and depression, and it impairs attention and judgment to a degree that is comparable to alcohol intoxication.

Crucially, people who are sleep-deprived tend to underestimate their own impairment: after several nights of restricted sleep, they report feeling only slightly tired, even as their performance on objective tests continues to decline.
At the level of the economy, the costs are substantial, and they are borne partially by employers.

One study by the research organization RAND estimated that insufficient sleep costs some large economies more than one percent of their gross domestic product each year, through reduced productivity, absenteeism and accidents.
Several major industrial disasters have been attributed, at least in part, to errors made by exhausted workers during night shifts.
Part of the problem is structural, and hence not purely a matter of individual choice.
Each person has an internal body clock, or circadian rhythm, and people differ in their chronotype: some are naturally early risers, whereas others function best late in the evening.
Work and school schedules, however, are designed largely around the morning type.

Adolescents are particularly affected, since puberty shifts the body clock later by up to two hours, and several school districts that delayed their start times have reported improvements in attendance, mood and academic results.
Cultural attitudes play a role as well, albeit one that is harder to measure.
In many workplaces, sleeping little is regarded as a sign of dedication, and executives sometimes boast about surviving on four or five hours a night.

Researchers argue that this attitude is not only mistaken but counterproductive, and that treating sleep as a basic biological necessity, rather than an indulgence, would benefit both employees and employers.
In the 1930s, the American linguist Benjamin Lee Whorf proposed a provocative idea: the language we speak determines the way we think.

He claimed, for example, that the Hopi people of North America had a fundamentally different conception of time from speakers of European languages, because their grammar did not treat time as a series of countable units.
This hypothesis, often associated with Whorf and his teacher Edward Sapir, became known as linguistic relativity.
The strong version of the hypothesis was subsequently discredited, notably because its evidence was seemingly flawed.
Later researchers found that Whorf had misunderstood aspects of Hopi grammar.

It is also evidently possible to think about concepts for which one's language has no single word: English speakers can understand the German idea of "Schadenfreude" perfectly well without having a native term for it.
For several decades, the dominant view in linguistics, particularly in the United States, was that thought is largely universal and that languages differ only in how they express it.
More recent empirical research has revived a weaker, more subtle version of the idea, thereby reopening a debate that had seemed closed.

Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language in Australia, describe locations using cardinal directions rather than words such as "left" and "right": they might say that a cup is to the north of a plate.
As a result, they maintain a remarkable sense of orientation, knowing at all times which way they are facing, even indoors.

Similarly, experiments have consistently shown that Russian speakers, whose language has distinct words for light and dark blue, distinguish between those shades slightly faster than English speakers.
The emerging consensus is nuanced, and arguably more interesting than either extreme position.
Language does not imprison thought, and speakers of all languages share a common cognitive framework.
But habits of speech can direct attention, making certain distinctions more salient and certain patterns easier to notice.
For learners, this suggests that acquiring a new language is not merely a matter of learning new labels for familiar things, but of acquiring, to some extent, a new way of perceiving the world.
Governments, like households, often spend more than they receive in revenue, and they cover the difference by borrowing.
They do so mainly by issuing bonds, promises to repay a sum of money with interest at a specified date, which are bought by banks, pension funds and other investors.
Moderate levels of sovereign debt are normal and can be beneficial, allowing governments to invest in infrastructure or respond to emergencies.
Problems arise when investors begin to doubt that a country will be able to repay.
Such doubts can become self-fulfilling, and the underlying mechanism is straightforward.
When lenders perceive a higher risk, they demand higher interest rates, which increases the cost of borrowing and makes repayment even more difficult.

If a government can no longer meet its obligations, it may default, and the consequences can be severe: banks that hold its bonds may collapse, the currency may lose much of its value, and ordinary citizens may see their savings disappear.
Argentina has defaulted on its debts nine times since independence, most dramatically in 2001, when the crisis led to riots and the resignation of several presidents within a few weeks.
When a crisis looms, countries often turn to the International Monetary Fund, which provides emergency loans in exchange for policy reforms.
These conditions typically involve austerity: cuts in public spending, higher taxes and the sale of state assets.
The Greek debt crisis, which began in 2009, illustrated both the necessity and the costs of this approach.

In return for successive bailouts from the European Union and the IMF, Greece implemented severe spending cuts, and its economy shrank by roughly a quarter, with unemployment exceeding twenty-five percent.
Critics argue that austerity during a recession is counterproductive, since cutting spending further reduces demand and makes debts harder to repay.
Defenders reply that without reform, lenders would simply stop lending.

The debate has encouraged proposals for fairer mechanisms, such as clauses in bond contracts that allow debts to be restructured in an orderly way, thereby reducing the chaos of an uncontrolled default.
