Such mechanisms remain the exception rather than the rule, and the question of how to share the burden of unpayable debt between creditors and citizens remains politically explosive.
By 2050, the world's population is expected to approach ten billion.
Feeding all of them, while simultaneously reducing the environmental damage caused by agriculture, is arguably one of the defining challenges of the century.
Farming already occupies around half of the world's habitable land, consumes most of its fresh water and generates roughly a quarter of greenhouse gas emissions.
Pessimistic predictions about food have often been proved wrong.

In the 1960s, many experts warned of imminent mass starvation in Asia, yet the so-called Green Revolution, led by scientists such as Norman Borlaug, dramatically increased crop yields through new varieties of wheat and rice, irrigation and chemical fertilizers.
Global food production has since grown faster than population, and the proportion of people who are undernourished has fallen substantially.
These gains, however, came at an environmental price.
Intensive farming has degraded soils, polluted rivers with nitrogen and reduced biodiversity, and in some regions groundwater is being extracted far faster than it can be replaced.
Climate change adds further uncertainty, since rising temperatures and more frequent droughts are expected to reduce yields of staple crops in many tropical countries.
Researchers typically propose a combination of strategies rather than a single solution.
Yields in many parts of Africa remain far below their potential, and improved seeds, better access to credit and investment in rural infrastructure could increase them considerably.
Reducing waste is equally important, since an estimated third of all food produced is lost or discarded before it is eaten.
Dietary change, particularly lower consumption of meat in wealthy countries, would free large areas of land currently used to grow animal feed.
Food security, finally, is not only a question of production but of distribution and politics.
The world already produces enough calories to feed everyone, yet hundreds of millions of people remain hungry, largely because of poverty, conflict and unstable markets.
Ensuring that food reaches those who need it may prove as difficult as growing it in the first place.
Water is essential to life, yet delivering it safely to millions of homes is an expensive industrial operation.
Reservoirs must be built, pipes maintained, water treated and sewage removed, and all of this requires long-term investment.
Who should provide this service, and on what terms, has become one of the most contentious questions in public policy.
From the 1980s onwards, many governments privatized their water utilities, transferring them to private companies.
Advocates argued that private firms would be more efficient, attract investment that cash-strapped governments could not afford and free public budgets for other priorities.
In England and Wales, where the entire industry was privatized in 1989, investment did increase substantially in the following decades.
The results, however, have been controversial.
Critics point out that water is a natural monopoly: customers cannot choose a different supplier if they are dissatisfied, so the usual discipline of competition does not apply.
In some cases, companies have been accused of paying large dividends to shareholders while accumulating debt and failing to prevent leaks and sewage discharges into rivers.
The most dramatic backlash occurred in Cochabamba, Bolivia, in 2000, where sharp price increases after privatization provoked mass protests that forced the government to cancel the contract.
Some cities have since reversed course.
Paris brought its water services back into public ownership in 2010, a process known as remunicipalization, and reported lower prices and higher investment.
Yet public ownership is no guarantee of quality either: many publicly run systems around the world suffer from chronic underinvestment and political interference.
Singapore, often cited as a model, relies on a highly competent public agency combined with advanced technologies such as desalination and wastewater recycling.
In 2010, the United Nations formally recognized access to clean water and sanitation as a human right.
Recognizing a right, however, does not settle who should deliver it or how it should be paid for.
Perhaps the more useful question is not whether ownership should be public or private, but whether the system is transparent, adequately regulated and genuinely accountable to the people it serves.
When the modern Olympic Games were revived in 1896, they were a modest affair, organized by aristocrats who regarded amateurism as a moral ideal.

Today they are among the largest commercial events on the planet, generating billions of dollars in broadcasting rights and sponsorship, and hosting them has become an enormously expensive undertaking.
For much of the twentieth century, cities competed fiercely to host the Games, attracted by the prestige, the prospect of tourism and the opportunity to accelerate urban development.
Some succeeded spectacularly, notably Barcelona and Los Angeles.
Barcelona used the 1992 Games to regenerate its neglected seafront, transforming itself into one of Europe's most popular destinations.
Los Angeles in 1984, which relied largely on existing venues and private sponsorship, even produced a surplus.
Many other hosts were considerably less fortunate, and their experiences are historically more typical.

Montreal took three decades to repay the debts from its 1976 Games, and several of the stadiums built for Athens in 2004 and Rio de Janeiro in 2016 were subsequently abandoned, becoming so-called white elephants that are expensive to maintain and of little practical use.

Economists who have studied the Games find that cost overruns are almost universal, averaging well over a hundred percent, and that the promised long-term boost to tourism and investment frequently fails to materialize.
These findings have had consequences, both for public opinion and for the organizers themselves.
In recent years, voters in several cities have explicitly rejected Olympic bids in referendums, and the number of candidate cities has declined sharply.

In response, the International Olympic Committee has revised its approach, encouraging hosts to use temporary or existing venues and awarding the Games to cities, such as Paris and Los Angeles, that can demonstrate a credible financial plan.
The history of the modern Olympics hence reflects a broader tension between idealism and commerce, and the balance between them has shifted substantially.
The Games still offer moments of extraordinary human achievement, watched by billions, and their symbolic power remains immense.
Whether those moments justify the cost is a question each potential host must now answer for itself, with considerably more skepticism than in the past.
Few beliefs feel more fundamental than the conviction that we are the authors of our own actions.
When I decide to raise my hand, it seems obvious that I could have chosen otherwise.
Yet philosophers have questioned this intuition for centuries, and recent research in neuroscience has given the debate fresh urgency.
The traditional challenge comes from determinism, the view that every event, including every human decision, is the inevitable result of prior causes.

If the state of the universe at one moment, together with the laws of physics, fully determines its state at the next, then our choices are seemingly nothing more than links in a causal chain that began long before we were born.
On this account, the feeling of freedom is an illusion, albeit an inherently persuasive one.
In the 1980s, experiments by the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet appeared to support this conclusion.
Participants were asked to move a finger whenever they felt like it and to report the moment at which they became aware of the decision.
Brain activity associated with the movement, known as the readiness potential, began several hundred milliseconds before the conscious decision.
To many commentators, this suggested that the brain "decides" before we are aware of it, and that conscious will merely observes what has already been determined.
Subsequent research has complicated this interpretation considerably.

Critics argue that the readiness potential may reflect general preparation rather than a specific choice, and that trivial finger movements tell us little about deliberate decisions such as accepting a job or ending a relationship.
Moreover, many philosophers contend that the whole debate rests on a mistaken premise, and defend a position known as compatibilism, according to which free will is compatible with determinism.
On this view, an action is free not because it lacks causes, but because it flows from our own desires, values and reasoning rather than from external coercion.
The question is not purely academic.
Legal systems assume that people can be held accountable for their choices, and our moral practices of praise, blame and forgiveness depend on the same assumption.

Some researchers worry that widespread disbelief in free will could erode personal responsibility; others argue that recognizing how strongly behavior is shaped by circumstances could make punishment more humane and less vindictive.
Whatever the metaphysical truth, how we answer the question has profound practical consequences.
Few issues generate as much political heat, and as little shared understanding, as immigration.
Public debate is frequently dominated by anecdotes and anxieties, whereas the empirical evidence, which is extensive, receives comparatively little attention.

Moreover, the term covers groups whose circumstances differ markedly: asylum seekers fleeing persecution, for instance, raise distinct legal and moral questions from those raised by workers seeking higher wages.
For migrants themselves, the gains are usually substantial, albeit unevenly distributed.
Moving from a poor country to a rich one can multiply a worker's income several times over, even when they take jobs well below their level of qualification.

Much of this money flows back to their countries of origin in the form of remittances, which now exceed the total value of foreign aid by a wide margin and are a vital source of income for millions of families.
The effect on the host country is more contested, not least because a sudden influx of people can place visible strain on housing and schools.
A recurring concern, notably among politicians, is that immigrants reduce wages or take jobs from local workers.

Most studies, however, find that the impact on average wages is small, because immigrants do not only supply labor; they also consume goods and services, thereby creating demand and, hence, additional jobs.

Where negative effects do occur, they tend to be marginal and concentrated among low-paid workers, namely earlier immigrants and those without formal qualifications, who compete most directly with newcomers.
The fiscal picture depends heavily on who arrives and at what age.

Young, skilled migrants typically pay considerably more in taxes than they receive in public services, since their education was financed by another country and they are unlikely to need pensions or significant health care for decades.

In ageing societies facing demographic decline and shrinking workforces, such as Japan and much of Europe, immigration is increasingly regarded as a partial solution to labor shortages in sectors like health care and agriculture.
For sending countries, the story is ambiguous.
The departure of doctors, nurses and engineers, often described as a brain drain, can weaken health systems and slow development.
Yet the prospect of emigrating can also encourage people to acquire skills, not all of whom eventually leave, and returning migrants bring back capital, experience and international networks.
Economists therefore tend to argue that the key questions concern not whether migration is inherently good or bad, but how it is managed.
Over the past half a billion years, life on Earth has passed through five mass extinctions, periods in which a large proportion of all species disappeared in a geologically short time.
The most famous, sixty-six million years ago, wiped out the dinosaurs after an asteroid struck the planet.
Many biologists now believe that we are living through a sixth, and that, for the first time, its principal cause is a single species: our own.
Estimating extinction rates is notoriously difficult, since most species have never been formally described, and many disappear before scientists know they existed.
Nevertheless, the available evidence suggests that species are currently being lost at an unprecedented rate, tens or even hundreds of times higher than the natural background rate.
A major international assessment in 2019 concluded that around a million species of animals and plants are threatened with extinction, many within decades.
The most significant driver is the destruction, degradation and fragmentation of habitat.

Forests are cleared for agriculture, wetlands are drained and rivers are dammed, leaving populations of animals isolated in small patches of land where they are vulnerable to disease, inbreeding and local disasters.

Other pressures include overfishing and hunting, pollution, climate change and invasive species, such as rats and cats introduced by humans to islands whose native birds had evolved without predators and were therefore easy prey.
Why should the loss of species concern us?

Beyond the ethical argument that other forms of life have value in themselves, ecosystems and the biodiversity they contain provide services on which human societies depend, including pollination, clean water and fertile soil.
Some organisms, known as keystone species, play a disproportionate role in holding these systems together, and their removal can trigger a cascade of further losses.
Once a critical threshold has been crossed, such a collapse may be impossible to reverse.

Conservation has achieved notable successes: protected areas now cover a substantial share of the planet's land, and several species, such as some populations of whales, have recovered from the brink of extinction.
Yet these gains are small relative to the magnitude of the problem.

Halting the decline, let alone reversing its trajectory, would require changes in how land is used, how food is produced and how economic growth is measured, which is to say, changes in the way that human civilization itself operates.
Before 2020, scientists had warned for years that a severe global pandemic was not a question of whether, but of when.
Several official reviews had explicitly identified gaps in preparedness, and some governments had even rehearsed their responses in simulation exercises.
Nevertheless, when COVID-19 spread across the world, most countries were caught unprepared, and the consequences, measured in lives, livelihoods and lost education, were immense.
Experts broadly agree that the risk of future epidemics and pandemics is rising.

Most new infectious diseases are zoonotic, meaning that they originate in animals, and the expansion of agriculture into forests, the trade in wild animals and the intensive farming of livestock all increase the opportunities for viruses to cross from animals to humans.
Global travel means that a new pathogen, particularly a lethal one that spreads before symptoms appear, can reach every continent within days.
Effective preparation involves several distinct elements.
The first is surveillance: laboratories and hospitals must be able to detect unusual clusters of illness quickly and share information openly, both nationally and with the World Health Organization.

The second is the capacity to respond, including stockpiles of protective equipment, flexible manufacturing for tests and vaccines, and health systems resilient enough to cope with a sudden surge of patients without abandoning the care of chronic illness.

South Korea, which had learned painful lessons from an earlier outbreak, was able to test and trace contacts on a large scale early in the pandemic, and its initial mortality rate was substantially lower than that of many wealthier countries.
Technology offers grounds for cautious optimism.
The development of mRNA vaccines, which were designed, tested and approved within a year, demonstrated that scientific responses can now be far faster than in the past.
Genetic sequencing, meanwhile, now allows dangerous mutations to be identified within days of their appearance.
Some researchers are working on libraries of vaccine candidates for entire families of viruses, so that production could begin almost immediately after a new threat is identified.
The hardest problems, however, are political rather than technical.
Preparedness requires sustained investment in contingency plans and systems that may not be used for decades, and it offers little reward to politicians whose terms last only a few years.
It also depends on international coordination, including the fair distribution of vaccines, at precisely the moment when countries are most tempted to look after themselves.
Public inquiries have also shown how fragile public trust can be, and how quickly confusing rules on lockdowns can erode it.
Whether the lessons of COVID-19 will be remembered or forgotten remains, as yet, uncertain.
Buildings are never merely functional.
Throughout history, rulers have used architecture to communicate power, legitimacy and ideology, and the design of government buildings often reveals as much about a regime as its official speeches.
The palace of Versailles, built for the French king Louis XIV in the seventeenth century, is a classic example.

Its immense scale, its long axes and its carefully controlled gardens expressed the idea of absolute monarchy and a rigid social hierarchy, headed by a ruler whose authority extended over nature itself.

Nobles, whose position was now explicitly subordinate, were expected to live at court, where every aspect of daily life was organized around the king, and the building itself became an instrument of political control.
Twentieth-century dictatorships took this language of domination to extremes.

In Nazi Germany, the architect Albert Speer designed a new capital in which enormous halls and wide avenues would dwarf individual citizens, making them feel insignificant in comparison with the state.
Monumental architecture was intended to intimidate, and its classical columns deliberately evoked the empires of ancient Rome.
Democracies have used architecture for their own symbolic purposes.
The Capitol in Washington borrowed the forms of ancient Greek and Roman buildings to associate the young republic with classical ideals of citizenship.

In the 1950s, Brazil built an entirely new capital, Brasília, whose modernist government buildings, designed by Oscar Niemeyer, were meant to express confidence in progress and a break with the colonial past.
Some modern parliaments, such as Germany's, feature glass domes that allow citizens to look down on their representatives, a deliberate metaphor for transparency.
Power, of course, is not exercised only by states.
In many cities today, the tallest and most prominent buildings belong not to governments but to banks and technology companies, whose headquarters compete for attention on the skyline.
These towers convey prestige and permanence, and, arguably, a shift in where real influence now lies.
Critics note, however, that symbolism can be deceptive.
A transparent building does not guarantee a transparent government, and imposing facades can conceal weak institutions.
Architecture, in the end, can express ideals, but it cannot enforce them.
The meaning of a building ultimately depends on the political life that takes place inside it.
Millions of people have sent a sample of their saliva to companies that promise to reveal their ancestry and predict their risk of certain diseases.
Consumer genetic testing has become a substantial industry, and the databases it has generated contain information of extraordinary sensitivity.

Unlike a password, a genome cannot be changed if it is stolen, and it reveals information not only about the individual who provided it but also about their parents, siblings and children, none of whom consented.

The implications became dramatically clear in 2018, when police in California arrested a man suspected of being the so-called Golden State Killer, responsible for a series of murders in the 1970s and 1980s.

Investigators had uploaded DNA from a crime scene to a public genealogy website, GEDmatch, identified distant relatives of the suspect and then constructed family trees until they narrowed the search to a single person.
None of the relatives had any idea that their data had been used in this way.

Supporters of this technique, known as forensic genetic genealogy, point out that it has since solved hundreds of cases that had remained unsolved for decades, bringing a measure of justice to victims' families.
Critics argue that it effectively turns everyone into a potential genetic informant, and that the absence of clear regulation leaves too much discretion to individual investigators.
Some genealogy companies subsequently changed their policies, requiring users to opt in explicitly before their data could be searched by law enforcement.
Beyond policing, genetic data raises concerns about discrimination.
If insurers or employers could access information about a person's predisposition to disease, they might charge higher premiums or refuse to hire them.
Some countries prohibit such practices, but protections vary considerably between jurisdictions.
Moreover, even data described as anonymized can sometimes be linked back to individuals by combining it with other publicly available information.
The fundamental question is who should control the information encoded in our cells.
Individual consent, the traditional basis of data protection, seems inadequate for information that is inherently shared with relatives.
Answering it will require new legal frameworks, and perhaps a new understanding of privacy itself, as a collective rather than a purely individual right.
Criminal justice systems are designed on the assumption that it is better for a guilty person to go free than for an innocent one to be punished.
In practice, however, innocent people are convicted far more often than most citizens assume.
Since 1989, a national registry in the United States has recorded more than three thousand cases in which convicted defendants were later exonerated, many of whom had spent decades in prison.
The arrival of forensic DNA testing in the 1990s transformed the study of such cases.
For the first time, it became possible to prove with near certainty that a particular person could not have committed a particular crime.
Organizations such as the Innocence Project, founded in New York in 1992, began to reinvestigate old convictions, and the patterns that emerged were deeply troubling.
The single most common factor was eyewitness misidentification, which played a role in roughly seven out of ten of the cases overturned by DNA evidence.

Human memory is not a recording; it is reconstructed each time it is recalled, and it can be distorted by stress, by the presence of a weapon, or by the way in which police present a lineup of suspects.
Confident witnesses are especially persuasive to juries, yet confidence is a poor indication of accuracy.
Other factors are equally disturbing.
In around a quarter of DNA exonerations, the defendant had made a false confession, often after lengthy interrogation in police custody.

Unreliable forensic methods, such as the visual comparison of hair samples, were presented in court as if they were scientific, and in some cases prosecutors withheld evidence that would have helped the defense.
Defendants who could not afford an experienced attorney were particularly vulnerable.
The pressure to plead guilty adds a further dimension to the problem.
In the United States, the vast majority of criminal convictions result not from a trial but from a plea bargain, in which the defendant accepts a lesser charge in exchange for a shorter sentence.
Faced with the prospect of decades in prison if convicted at trial, even innocent people sometimes calculate that pleading guilty is the rational choice.
Reforms are gradually being introduced.
Many police forces now record interrogations and conduct lineups according to procedures designed to minimize unintentional influence.
In Britain, an independent body, the Criminal Cases Review Commission, has been investigating possible miscarriages of justice since 1997, with the power to refer cases back to the courts.
Yet no procedure can entirely eliminate human error, which is precisely why the finality of a verdict should never be confused with its infallibility.
A constitution is often described as the rulebook of a nation: it establishes the institutions of government, distributes power between them and protects the fundamental rights of citizens.
Yet no society stands still, and a document written for one generation must somehow remain relevant to the next.
How constitutions change, and how difficult it is to change them, reveals a great deal about a country's political culture.
The most visible route is formal amendment.
The Constitution of the United States, drafted in 1787, can only be amended if a proposal is approved by two-thirds of both houses of Congress and then ratified by three-quarters of the states.
This threshold is so demanding that only twenty-seven amendments have been adopted in more than two centuries, the first ten of which, known as the Bill of Rights, were added almost immediately.
Other countries have chosen different mechanisms.

In Ireland, any constitutional amendment must be approved by the people in a referendum, which has made the constitution a direct instrument of social change: since the 1990s, Irish voters have legalized divorce and same-sex marriage through such votes.

Germany's Basic Law, by contrast, contains an "eternity clause" that places certain principles, including human dignity and the federal structure of the state, beyond the reach of any amendment whatsoever.
Its authors, writing in 1949, were acutely aware of how easily democratic procedures had been exploited to destroy democracy itself in the 1930s.
Formal amendment, however, is only part of the story.
Constitutions also evolve through judicial interpretation, as courts apply general principles to circumstances their authors could never have imagined, from wiretapping to the internet.

When the Supreme Court of the United States reinterprets a clause, the practical effect can be as profound as that of a formal amendment, which is why appointments to the court have become so politically contentious.
Britain represents the most unusual case, since it has no single codified constitution at all.
Its constitutional arrangements consist of ordinary legislation, court decisions and unwritten conventions, many of which can, in principle, be changed by a simple parliamentary majority.
Supporters praise this flexibility; critics warn that it leaves fundamental rights dependent on the self-restraint of whichever government happens to hold power.
Every system, in other words, strikes its own balance between stability and adaptation.
For more than seventy years, nuclear fusion has been described as the ultimate source of clean energy, and for almost as long, it has been said to be thirty years away.
The joke reflects both the extraordinary potential of the technology and the formidable obstacles that have so far prevented it from becoming a practical reality.
Fusion is the process that powers the sun.
When the nuclei of very light elements, such as isotopes of hydrogen, are forced together, they combine to form helium and release enormous quantities of energy.

Unlike the fission reactors used in existing nuclear power stations, which split heavy atoms such as uranium, fusion produces no long-lived radioactive waste and carries no risk of a runaway chain reaction.
Its fuel, moreover, can be extracted from seawater and is virtually inexhaustible.
The difficulty lies in reproducing the conditions of a star on Earth.

Because atomic nuclei repel one another, they must collide at tremendous velocity before fusion can occur, which requires temperatures of over one hundred million degrees, several times hotter than the core of the sun.
At such temperatures, matter becomes plasma, a state in which electrons are stripped from their atoms, and no physical material could contain it.
The most widely pursued solution is the tokamak, a doughnut-shaped vacuum chamber in which powerful magnetic fields hold the plasma away from the walls.
Progress has been slow but real.
In 2022, scientists at the National Ignition Facility in California used lasers to produce, for the first time, a fusion reaction that released more energy than the lasers had delivered to the fuel.
The achievement was widely celebrated, albeit with an important qualification: the lasers themselves had consumed far more electricity than the reaction produced.
Meanwhile, ITER, an international experimental reactor under construction in the south of France, has been repeatedly delayed, and its costs have multiplied several times over.
Recent years have seen a surge of private investment, as dozens of start-up companies pursue smaller and cheaper designs, several of which promise to deliver electricity to the grid within a decade.
Sceptics note that similar pledges have been made before.

Even optimists concede that fusion is unlikely to make a significant contribution to reducing emissions before the middle of the century, which means that it cannot replace the renewable technologies already available today.
It may, nonetheless, prove decisive for the energy systems of the more distant future.
Organ transplantation is one of the great achievements of modern medicine.
Every year, surgeons around the world transplant tens of thousands of kidneys, livers, hearts and lungs, giving recipients years or even decades of life that would otherwise have been impossible.
Yet in almost every country, demand vastly exceeds supply, and thousands of patients die each year while waiting for a suitable donor.
The shortage is not simply a matter of numbers.
Most organs come from deceased donors, and only a small fraction of deaths occur in circumstances that allow organs to be used, typically in intensive care units after severe brain injury.
Organs must also be biologically compatible with the recipient, whose immune system would otherwise reject them, and even a successful transplant requires a lifetime of immunosuppressant drugs.
Living donors, who can give a kidney or part of a liver, help to close the gap, but they accept genuine surgical risks for no medical benefit of their own.
Many governments have responded by changing the rules on consent.
Under a traditional opt-in system, organs can only be taken from people who registered as donors during their lifetime.
Under an opt-out system, often called presumed consent, everyone is regarded as a potential donor unless they have explicitly registered an objection.
Wales adopted such a system in 2015, and England followed in 2020.
The evidence on whether presumed consent actually increases donation is, however, mixed.

Spain, which has had an opt-out law since 1979, has the highest rate of deceased donation in the world, but experts attribute its success less to the law itself than to a national network of specially trained transplant coordinators working in hospitals.
In practice, doctors in most opt-out countries still consult the family, and a grieving relative's refusal is usually respected.
Some economists have gone further and proposed paying donors, arguing that a regulated market would save lives.
Most ethicists reject the idea, warning that financial incentives would inevitably put pressure on the poor to sell parts of their bodies, as already happens in illegal organ markets.
The debate ultimately turns on a question that medicine alone cannot answer: whether an organ should be understood as a gift, a resource, or a commodity.
Walk into a cinema almost anywhere in the world, and there is a strong likelihood that the film on the largest screen will be a sequel, a remake or an episode in a long-running franchise.
For much of the past decade, the great majority of the highest-earning films each year belonged to one of these categories.
Hollywood, it seems, has become an industry of familiar stories.
The economic logic behind this shift is straightforward.

Major studio films now routinely cost more than two hundred million dollars to produce, with a comparable sum spent on marketing, and a single failure can wipe out a studio's profits for an entire year.
A franchise with an established audience substantially reduces that risk.
Viewers who enjoyed one episode are likely to return for the next, and the characters generate additional revenue from merchandise, video games and theme parks.
The most successful example is the Marvel superhero series, which began in 2008 and grew into dozens of interconnected films and television programs.

Its innovation was to treat each film not as a self-contained work but as a chapter in a larger narrative, rewarding loyal viewers with references to earlier episodes and encouraging them to see every new release.
Other studios rushed to imitate the model, with considerably less success.
Critics argue that the franchise era has impoverished cinema.

In 2019, the director Martin Scorsese provoked a fierce debate when he compared superhero films to theme parks rather than to cinema as he understood it, meaning an art form that confronts audiences with the unexpected.
Original films with modest budgets, the argument goes, are increasingly squeezed out of cinemas and pushed onto streaming platforms, where they compete for attention with thousands of other titles.
Defenders respond that storytelling has always depended on repetition.
Ancient myths were retold countless times, and many of the most admired works of literature were themselves adaptations of earlier material.
What matters, on this view, is not whether a story is new, but whether it is told with imagination.

There are signs, moreover, that audiences are growing tired of formula: several recent franchise releases have disappointed commercially, whereas a handful of original films have become unexpected hits.
Anyone who has played or watched sport is familiar with the idea of the "hot hand".
A basketball player who has scored several consecutive shots seems to be in a special state of form, and teammates instinctively pass the ball to them.
Players, coaches and fans overwhelmingly believe that success breeds success, and that a streak of good performances increases the likelihood of the next one.
In 1985, the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky set out to test this belief.
Analyzing thousands of shots by professional basketball players, they found no statistical evidence that a player was more likely to score after a series of hits than after a series of misses.
The streaks that seemed so meaningful were, they concluded, precisely what one would expect from random sequences.
The hot hand was a cognitive illusion, a product of the human tendency to see patterns where none exist.
The study became a classic example of how intuition can mislead us.
People systematically underestimate how often streaks occur by chance: in twenty tosses of a coin, for instance, a run of four heads or four tails in a row is more likely than not.
Paradoxically, the same misunderstanding produces the opposite error in casinos, where gamblers convince themselves that a number is "due" because it has not appeared for a while.
Economists found similar biases among investors who bought shares simply because they had risen for several days.
The story, however, took an unexpected turn.
In 2015, the economists Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo identified a subtle flaw in the original method.
When one examines what happens after streaks within a finite sequence, the expected success rate is actually slightly lower than the player's overall average, even if every shot is independent.
Once this bias was corrected, the original data appeared to show a modest hot hand after all.
The episode offers two lessons that are only apparently contradictory.
Human beings are indeed prone to seeing patterns in randomness, and our confidence in streaks is usually exaggerated.

Yet the scientists who exposed this bias were themselves vulnerable to an error in reasoning about probability, which suggests that intuitions about chance can mislead even the experts who study them.
When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, it was the only artificial object orbiting the Earth.

Today, thousands of active satellites provide communications, weather forecasts and navigation, and they share their orbits with an enormous cloud of debris: dead satellites, discarded rocket stages and millions of fragments produced by explosions and collisions.
Space agencies track more than thirty thousand objects larger than a tennis ball, and estimate that the number of smaller pieces runs into the hundreds of millions.
The danger lies in the extreme orbital velocity at which these objects travel.
In low orbit, a satellite moves at roughly twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour, so that even a fragment of paint the size of a grain of rice strikes with the force of a bullet.

The International Space Station is fitted with shielding, and it has had to change course dozens of times to avoid larger pieces of debris, while its crew occasionally shelter in their return capsules as a precaution.
Two events made the problem impossible to ignore.
In 2007, a Chinese missile test deliberately destroyed an old weather satellite, creating more than three thousand trackable fragments, many of which remain in orbit today.
Two years later, an active American communications satellite collided with a defunct Russian one, the first accidental collision between two intact satellites.
Scientists have long feared a chain reaction known as the Kessler syndrome, after the NASA scientist Donald Kessler, who described it in 1978.
If the density of objects in a particular orbit passes a critical threshold, each collision produces fragments that cause further collisions, until the orbit becomes unusable for generations.

The rapid deployment of so-called mega-constellations, in which private companies launch thousands of small satellites to provide internet coverage, has made this scenario considerably more plausible.
Solutions are both technical and political.
Engineers are testing spacecraft that could capture dead satellites with nets or robotic arms and drag them down to burn up in the atmosphere.
Regulators have begun to require operators to remove satellites from orbit within a few years of the end of their missions, replacing an earlier guideline that allowed twenty-five years.
Yet space, like the high seas, belongs to no single country, and there is no international authority with the power to enforce such rules on every nation.
The orbits around our planet are, in effect, a shared resource that can be exhausted by those who use it carelessly.
Few questions in international politics are as morally difficult as whether outside powers should use military force to stop a government from killing its own people.
The principle of sovereignty, on which the modern international order rests, holds that states should not interfere in each other's internal affairs.
Yet the atrocities of the twentieth century raised an uncomfortable question: does sovereignty protect a government that commits genocide?
The failures of the 1990s gave the debate its urgency.

In Rwanda in 1994, some eight hundred thousand people were killed in roughly a hundred days, while the international community, aware of what was happening, reduced its small force of peacekeepers rather than reinforcing it.
A year later, in Srebrenica, a town that the United Nations had declared a "safe area", around eight thousand men and boys were murdered by Bosnian Serb forces.
These events shaped the response to the next crisis.
In 1999, NATO bombed Serbia for eleven weeks to halt the persecution of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo, without the authorization of the Security Council, where Russia had threatened a veto.
Supporters described the campaign as illegal but legitimate; critics saw a dangerous precedent that powerful states might exploit to justify wars pursued for other reasons.

In 2005, the member states of the United Nations formally endorsed a doctrine known as the Responsibility to Protect, which declares that when a state fails to protect its population from mass atrocities, the international community has a duty to act, by force if necessary and with the approval of the Security Council.
The doctrine faced its most significant test in Libya in 2011.
The Security Council authorized military action to protect civilians from the forces of Muammar Gaddafi, and a NATO air campaign followed.
The operation, however, went well beyond its original mandate and contributed to the overthrow of the government, after which the country descended into years of civil war.
Russia and China, which had allowed the resolution to pass, concluded that humanitarian language had been used as a cover for regime change, and they subsequently blocked comparable action in Syria.
The dilemma remains unresolved.
Intervention risks killing civilians, destabilizing entire regions and serving the interests of the powerful, whereas inaction can mean standing by while mass murder takes place.

Perhaps the most honest conclusion is that neither sovereignty nor humanitarian principle can serve as an absolute rule, and that each case demands judgment about consequences that are, by their nature, uncertain.
Governments have counted their populations for thousands of years.

The rulers of ancient Egypt, China and Rome conducted surveys in order to raise taxes and recruit soldiers, and in 1086 William the Conqueror ordered a detailed record of land and property in England that became known as the Domesday Book.

The modern census, which aims to count every resident of a country on a single day, emerged in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and it has since become one of the most important tools of government.
The uses of census data are remarkably wide-ranging.

In the United States, the constitution requires a census every ten years in order to apportion seats in the House of Representatives between the states, so that the count directly shapes political representation.

Census figures also determine the allocation of public funding for schools, hospitals and transport, and they provide the statistical foundation for almost every other survey, since researchers rely on them to check whether their samples are representative.
Businesses use the data to decide where to open shops, and historians treat old census records as an invaluable window onto the lives of ordinary people.
Counting everyone, however, is far harder than it sounds.

Certain groups are consistently undercounted, including homeless people, young children, recent migrants and residents of remote areas, and because funding follows the numbers, the communities that most need public services may receive less than their fair share.
Questions about ethnicity, religion and language are particularly sensitive, since the categories a census uses are themselves political choices that can reinforce or challenge existing identities.
In some countries, the results of a census have been so politically explosive that governments have delayed or cancelled it altogether.
Confidentiality is essential if people are to answer honestly.

In most democracies, individual census responses are protected by law and cannot be shared with the police or tax authorities; in the United Kingdom, personal records remain closed for a hundred years.
Nevertheless, the traditional census is under pressure.
It is expensive, response rates are falling, and the results are out of date almost as soon as they are published.

Several countries, notably the Netherlands and much of Scandinavia, have already replaced it with continuously updated administrative registers, which are cheaper and more timely but, critics point out, require the state to hold far more information about its citizens.
Many of the most valuable companies in the world began as small start-ups financed by a particular kind of investor: the venture capitalist.
Unlike a bank, which lends money and expects to be repaid with interest, a venture capital fund provides money in exchange for a stake in the company, known as equity.
If the company fails, the investment is lost; if it succeeds spectacularly, the fund's share may be worth hundreds of times what it paid.
This structure shapes the underlying logic of the entire industry.

Most start-ups fail, often because they never find a viable business model, and many of the rest produce only modest returns, so a fund's performance typically depends on a handful of extraordinary successes within its portfolio.

Investors therefore look for companies that could, at least in theory, grow to an enormous size, and they are relatively uninterested in businesses that promise steady but limited profits, however sound they may be.
Hence the industry's obsession with rapid growth, which it tends to value far more than immediate profit.
In 2013, the investor Aileen Lee coined the term "unicorn" for a private start-up valued at more than a billion dollars, precisely because such companies were then so rare.
Funding usually arrives in stages.
Founders may begin with savings, loans from family or small sums from wealthy individuals, before raising successively larger rounds from venture funds as the company grows.
At each round, the company's valuation is negotiated, and the founders' share of ownership is gradually reduced.
Investors eventually expect to recover their money when the company is bought by a larger firm, sometimes becoming one of its subsidiaries, or when its shares are listed on a stock exchange.
Supporters credit venture capital with financing much of the innovation of the past half-century, from personal computers to online services and new medicines.
Critics, however, identify several distortions.
In boom years, speculative enthusiasm can push valuations far beyond anything justified by a company's revenue, as happened during the internet bubble of the late 1990s.
The pressure to grow rapidly can encourage companies to lose money for years in order to capture a market, thereby driving out competitors who have to make a profit.
The industry is also strikingly concentrated: a large share of funding goes to a few regions, notably Silicon Valley, whilst only a tiny fraction goes to companies founded by women.
If the allocation of investment depends on who the investors happen to know, then some valuable innovations may never be funded at all.
Almost everything we buy has spent weeks in transit before reaching us, yet the vast system that moves it remains largely invisible.

Logistics, the business of storing goods and moving them from where they are made to where they are needed, accounts for a substantial share of the world economy, and its efficiency is one of the main reasons why so many goods are now so cheap.
Between the factory and the shop, goods typically pass through ports, wholesale distributors and regional warehouses, each of which adds cost and delay.
The most important innovation in the history of the industry was remarkably simple: a steel box of standard size.
Before the 1950s, maritime cargo was loaded onto ships piece by piece, a slow and labor-intensive process that could keep a vessel in port for longer than it spent at sea.
In 1956, the American entrepreneur Malcolm McLean sent a converted tanker from Newark to Houston carrying fifty-eight containers that could be lifted directly from trucks onto the ship.
Within a few decades, containerization had reduced the cost of loading cargo dramatically, making it economical to manufacture goods on one continent and sell them on another.
A second revolution took place inside factories.
In the decades after the Second World War, the Japanese carmaker Toyota developed a system in which parts arrived from suppliers only shortly before they were needed on the assembly line.
This just-in-time approach reduced the need for expensive warehouses full of inventory, and it was subsequently imitated by manufacturers and retailers throughout the world.
Efficiency, however, inevitably comes at a price.
A system without spare stock has little capacity to absorb shocks, and the pandemic of 2020 revealed just how fragile global supply chains had become.

When factories closed and demand shifted suddenly, shortages spread from one industry to the next, containers piled up in the wrong ports, shipping carriers cancelled voyages, and freight rates multiplied several times over.
Many companies have since reconsidered their strategies, holding larger reserves, building more robust networks of suppliers and moving some production closer to home.
Today, the most expensive part of the journey is often the last few kilometers, from the local depot to the customer's door.
The growth of online shopping has created demand for rapid delivery to individual homes, which is far less efficient than transporting goods in bulk to shops.

Retailers have responded with highly automated warehouses, where sensors track every item and robots bring shelves to human workers, and with software that calculates the optimal route for every delivery van.
The cheapness of convenience, it turns out, depends on an extraordinary amount of hidden labor and machinery.
"A lie can travel halfway around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes."
The saying is frequently attributed to Mark Twain, although there is no reliable evidence that he ever said it, which neatly illustrates its point.
In 2018, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology published one of the largest studies of how information spreads online.

Analyzing around a hundred and twenty-six thousand stories shared on social media over more than a decade, they found that false stories were considerably more likely to go viral than true ones, and that they reached large audiences roughly six times faster.
Strikingly, the difference was driven not by automated accounts but by human users.
Why should falsehood have this advantage?
The researchers suggested that false stories tend to be more novel than true ones, and that novelty attracts attention and makes the person who shares it appear well informed.
False stories also provoked stronger emotional reactions, particularly surprise and disgust.
Recommendation algorithms, which are designed to maximize engagement, can amplify these tendencies, since content that provokes outrage is precisely the content that keeps users scrolling.
In the confused hours after a disaster, speculation rushes to fill the vacuum left by the absence of reliable information.
Journalists and fact-checkers have developed sophisticated methods of verification.

When dramatic footage appears during a crisis, they examine shadows, street signs and weather records to establish where and when it was filmed, and they search for earlier versions of the same images, which frequently turn out to come from a different event altogether.
Some of these are deliberate hoaxes, but many more are genuine images that have simply been stripped of their context.

Yet corrections rarely receive as much coverage as the original claims, and people who have already accepted a false story often resist evidence that contradicts it, especially when the story confirms their political views or the correction comes from a source whose credibility they doubt.
The rise of synthetic media has raised the stakes further.
Artificial intelligence can now generate convincing images, voices and videos of events that never happened, and such deepfakes are becoming cheaper and easier to produce.
In several recent elections, recordings allegedly showing candidates making offensive remarks circulated widely before anyone could establish whether they were real.
Paradoxically, the greatest danger may not be that people believe false content, but that they stop believing anything at all, dismissing authentic evidence as fake whenever it is inconvenient.
A healthy information environment depends not only on better technology, but, arguably, on a public that values accuracy over excitement.
There are novels that we admire and novels that seem to understand us.
George Eliot's Middlemarch, first published in eight parts between 1871 and 1872, belongs firmly to the second category.
Rereading it more than a century and a half after its appearance, one is struck less by its portrait of a vanished society than by how contemporary its characters feel.
Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, set the book in a fictional provincial town around 1830, amid growing demands for political reform.

Its heroine, Dorothea Brooke, is an intelligent and idealistic young woman who longs to do something significant with her life, but whose society offers her intellect almost no outlet beyond marriage.

She marries Edward Casaubon, an elderly scholar, in the naive belief that assisting his great work will give her life purpose, only to discover that the work is hopeless and the man incapable of affection.
In parallel, the novel follows Tertius Lydgate, an ambitious doctor who arrives in the town determined to reform medicine.
His marriage to the charming but self-absorbed Rosamond Vincy gradually drains him of both money and idealism.
What distinguishes Eliot's treatment of these marital disasters is her refusal to reduce anyone to a villain.
Even Casaubon, the most obvious candidate, is presented with remarkable empathy: a frightened man, painfully aware that his life's work has failed, and unable to admit it even to himself.
The narrator is integral to the novel's appeal.
Eliot constantly steps back from the action to reflect on the underlying motives of her characters, and she does so with a mixture of irony and tenderness that rarely becomes sentimental.
Some modern readers find these reflections tedious, and it must be admitted that the book, at over eight hundred pages, demands considerable stamina.
The reward, however, is an unusually intimate sense of how people deceive themselves, and of how seemingly small decisions can shape an entire life.
Virginia Woolf famously described Middlemarch as one of the few English novels written for grown-up people, and the verdict still holds.
It is a novel about disappointment that is never itself disappointing.

Its closing pages offer a quiet consolation: that the good in the world depends not only on famous deeds, but on the countless unrecorded acts of ordinary people who live faithfully and are soon forgotten.
Ingrid Solberg is a glaciologist who has spent more than twenty summers studying the ice of Norway, the Alps and Antarctica.
We spoke to her shortly after her return from a gruelling field season on a rapidly shrinking glacier.
What first drew you to glaciers?
"Honestly, the silence, although that turned out to be an illusion."
"A glacier is constantly cracking, groaning and dripping; once you learn to listen, it is surprisingly vocal."
"What kept me there, though, was the realization that the ice is an archive."
"Snow that fell thousands of years ago is compressed into distinct layers, and each layer preserves a record of the climate at the moment it fell."
"Dust, volcanic ash and fine sediment trapped in the ice tell us about ancient eruptions and droughts."
How do you read that archive?
"We drill ice cores, long cylinders of ice extracted from deep inside a glacier or ice sheet."
"Tiny bubbles in the ice contain samples of ancient air, so we can measure directly how much carbon dioxide the atmosphere contained in the distant past."
"The oldest continuous cores from Antarctica cover roughly eight hundred thousand years, and they show that today's concentrations are unprecedented in that entire period."
What have you seen change during your career?
"The glacier where I did my doctoral fieldwork has retreated by almost a kilometer, and its surface has dropped so much that the huts we used are now stranded high above the ice."
"The duration of the melting season has increased by several weeks, and as the surface drops into warmer air, the retreat gains momentum."
"In the Alps, some small glaciers have disappeared entirely, and ski resorts now cover the ice with reflective sheets in summer to slow the melting, with marginal success."
"It is a strangely touching sight, like wrapping a patient in a blanket."
Why should people who live far from glaciers care?
"Because glaciers are the water towers of the world."
"Hundreds of millions of people, notably in the countries around the Himalayas, depend on rivers fed by meltwater during the dry season."
"In the short term, faster melting means more water and a higher likelihood of floods; in the long term, once the ice has gone, it means far less."
"And the melting of the great ice sheets inevitably raises sea levels everywhere."
Do you still find the work hopeful?
"I find it clarifying."
"The ice has no political stance; it does not negotiate or exaggerate, it simply responds to the temperature."
"That is precisely why its testimony is so valuable, and why I think we should listen to it."
Ada Lovelace is now celebrated as one of the pioneers of computing, a remarkable reputation for a woman who died in 1852, almost a century before the first electronic computers were built.
Her fame rests predominantly on a single document, and the story of how she came to write it reveals a great deal about the intellectual world of Victorian Britain.
She was born in 1815, the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron.
He left the family when she was a few weeks old and never saw her again.

Her mother, determined that Ada should not inherit what she regarded as her father's dangerous imagination, insisted on a rigorous education in mathematics and science, an unusual upbringing for an aristocratic girl at the time.
The strategy was only partially successful: Ada became a gifted mathematician, but she never lost her taste for imaginative speculation, which she later described as "poetical science".
At seventeen, she met Charles Babbage, an eccentric inventor who had designed mechanical calculating machines of extraordinary complexity.
His most ambitious project, the Analytical Engine, was never built, so its existence remained purely theoretical.
On paper, however, it contained many of the essential features of a modern computer, including a memory, a processing unit and the ability to follow instructions supplied on punched cards.
The two became close friends and correspondents, and Babbage admired her analytical ability enormously.
In 1843, Lovelace translated an article about the Analytical Engine by the Italian engineer Luigi Menabrea.
She added a series of notes that ended up nearly three times as long as the original.

One of them set out, in careful mathematical notation, how the machine could calculate a complex sequence known as the Bernoulli numbers, and it is often described as the first published computer program.
Historians still debate how much of this work was hers and how much was Babbage's, but there is no dispute about the originality of her wider vision.
Whilst Babbage saw a powerful calculator, Lovelace saw a machine that could manipulate any symbols according to rules, not merely numbers.
She speculated that such an engine might one day compose elaborate pieces of music, an insight that anticipated the digital age by more than a century.
She also explicitly insisted, however, that the machine could originate nothing by itself and could only do what it was instructed to do.
That claim remains, arguably, at the centre of debates about artificial intelligence today.
She died of cancer at the age of thirty-six, and her notes were largely forgotten until the pioneers of modern computing rediscovered them in the twentieth century.
In many countries, students are receiving better grades than ever before.

At some universities in the United States, the most common grade awarded is now the highest one available, and in Britain the proportion of students graduating with a first-class degree more than doubled in the decade after 2010.
Unless students have become dramatically more capable in a single generation, which seems implausible, grades have inevitably lost some of their meaning.
A degree is, after all, a credential, and its value depends on what it tells people who have never met the student.
The causes of this trend are both economic and cultural.
Where students pay high tuition fees, they increasingly regard themselves as customers, and institutions compete to attract them partly by promising good outcomes.
University rankings frequently reward high rates of top grades, which creates an obvious institutional incentive to award more of them.
In many systems, moreover, teaching staff are assessed partly through student evaluations, and there is evidence that students rate generous examiners more favourably.
Some of the rise may reflect genuine improvement.
Teaching methods have changed, assessment criteria are more transparent and rigorous, and students now have access to resources that earlier generations could only have dreamed of.
It is also arguably fairer to assess students against fixed standards rather than against each other, even if that means many of them reach the top category.
The costs, however, are considerable, and they are not evenly distributed.

When a high proportion of candidates receive the same top grade, grades cease to distinguish between excellent and merely competent work, and employers and selective universities turn to other criteria.

Those criteria, such as work experience, internships and the reputation of a student's institution, tend to favour applicants from wealthier families, who possess the contacts and resources to acquire them.
Grade inflation may therefore, paradoxically, undermine the very meritocracy it appears to celebrate.
Solutions are not straightforward, and each has distinct drawbacks.
Some institutions have introduced limits on the proportion of top grades that can be awarded, but such quotas can penalize strong students who happen to belong to an exceptionally able cohort.
Others report additional statistical information alongside each grade, such as the student's position within their class, which allows readers to interpret the result in context.
Ultimately, however, the credibility of grades depends on a willingness among teachers and institutions to disappoint students when their work deserves it.
My dearest Lina,
Your mother tells me that you have been asked to write a school project about your family's history, and that you would like me to contribute.
I am delighted, although I warn you that a grandmother asked to reminisce is a dangerous thing: once I start, I may never stop.
I was born in Hanoi, the youngest of six siblings, in a house so small that four of us shared a single bed.
My parents worked from dawn until late at night, whilst my eldest sister effectively raised me.
Our possessions were minimal, but I do not remember feeling poor, perhaps because everyone around us lived in the same way.
What I remember instead is noise, laughter, and the sense that the house belonged to all of us equally.
When I was twenty-four, your grandfather Minh and I moved to Manchester, where he had been offered a place to study engineering.
There were only a handful of Vietnamese families in the city then, and we felt like pioneers, albeit not very brave ones.
Most of our neighbours were kind, although a few were openly hostile.
I will not pretend that it was easy.
The winters seemed endless, and my English was poor.

Your grandfather's scholarship made no provision for spouses, and the qualifications I had earned at home were not recognized as equivalent to British ones, so for several years I cleaned offices at night.
It was a blow to my self-esteem that I felt for a long time, and I have never forgotten the dignity of the women who worked alongside me.
They became an integral part of my life, and they taught me more about empathy and humility than any university could have done.
Your generation will face difficulties of its own, and some of them, notably the cost of housing, will be harder than mine.
You will have more choices than I ever had, which is a blessing, but choice inevitably brings its own anxieties.
People sometimes praise my resilience, but migration is really a long process of adaptation, and I suspect that growing up is much the same.
When your parents divorced and there were difficult months over custody, I watched you cope with a composure far beyond your years, and I was immensely proud of you.
If there is one thing I would like you to include in your project, it is this.
Every family history is a history of sacrifice, most of it invisible.
My sister, arguably the cleverest of us all, gave up her own education so that I could continue mine, and I have never been able to repay her.
You do not owe us anything, my darling, but I hope you will remember that you stand on the shoulders of people who loved you before you were born.
I am enclosing the silver bracelet my mother gave me on my wedding day, the only heirloom our family possesses, and I would like you to have it.
With all my love, Grandma
Disagreement is an unavoidable and, at its best, valuable part of working and living with other people.
Disagreement is not inherently a sign of dysfunction: teams that never argue tend to make worse decisions, since flawed ideas go unchallenged.
Yet most of us have been involved in disagreements that became hostile, left everyone feeling defensive and resolved nothing whatsoever.
The following principles, drawn from research on negotiation and conflict, can help make disagreement more constructive.
First, make sure you understand the other person's stance before you respond to it.
A useful technique is to summarize their view in your own words, notably its strongest points, and ask whether you have understood it correctly.
This not only prevents misunderstandings but also signals respect, which makes the other person more willing to listen in return.

Philosophers sometimes recommend going further and constructing the strongest possible version of an opposing argument, sometimes called a "steelman", rather than attacking a weak caricature of it, known as a "straw man".
Second, separate the problem from the person.

Criticize ideas, proposals and decisions, never character or motives, and avoid sweeping statements such as "you always" or "you never", which invite the other person to defend their entire identity rather than a specific point.
Describing the effect of an action on you, as in "I was worried when the report arrived late", is far less likely to provoke a defensive reaction than an accusation.
Third, look for common ground before focusing on differences.
People who disagree about methods frequently share the same underlying goals, and acknowledging this explicitly can transform a contest into a joint search for a solution.
It also helps to distinguish between disagreements of fact, which can often be settled by empirical evidence, and disagreements of value, which may require compromise.
Finally, be willing to change your mind, and say so explicitly when you do.
Conceding a point is widely perceived as a sign of weakness, but in practice it tends to increase your credibility, demonstrate your integrity and encourage others to show similar humility.
If emotions are running high and hostility is growing, it is perfectly legitimate to suggest a pause and return to the discussion later.
The aim of a good disagreement, after all, is not victory but a better understanding, and ideally a better decision, than either side could have reached alone.
A few years ago, I spent eleven days visiting seven European cities, and I remember almost nothing about any of them.
My itinerary had been optimized for efficiency: early trains, famous sights, a photograph at each one and a hurried dinner before collapsing into another anonymous hotel.
I returned home exhausted, with hundreds of pictures and a vague sense that I had been everywhere and nowhere.
I have subsequently become a convert to what is sometimes called slow travel.

The principle is simple: visit fewer places, stay longer in each, travel between them overland whenever possible, and treat the time spent in transit as part of the journey rather than an obstacle to it.

Rather than attempting to see everything, the slow traveller rents a room in an ordinary neighbourhood, shops at the local market and returns to the same café until the owner begins to recognize them.
The aim is not to collect destinations but to experience, however partially, what it might feel like to live somewhere else.
What it offers is a degree of immersion that no guided tour can provide.
Critics will object that this is a luxury available solely to people with generous holidays or flexible jobs, and they have a point.
Yet the underlying idea can be adapted to almost any budget or schedule.
A long weekend spent exploring a single town in depth may prove more memorable than a week spent racing between seemingly identical capitals, and it is arguably more relaxing.
There are also compelling ethical arguments for travelling more slowly.
Aviation accounts for a growing share of global emissions, and a single long-haul flight can produce more carbon dioxide than some people generate in an entire year.
Mass tourism, moreover, has placed an unsustainable burden on cities, notably Venice and Barcelona, where residents complain that their neighbourhoods have been transformed into theme parks.
Visitors who stay longer tend to spread their spending more widely, supporting small, locally owned businesses rather than international chains.
I do not want to romanticize the approach.
Slow travel can be tedious, and there is something faintly absurd about affluent tourists pretending to be locals for a fortnight.
Authentic experience cannot be purchased, and a neighbourhood does not become more genuine simply because a visitor has chosen to stay in it.
But the alternative, which treats the world as a checklist to be completed as quickly as possible, seems to me far worse.
The best journeys I have made were the ones in which, for a few days, I stopped being a tourist at all.
On a summer night, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the adjacent countryside.

This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, has been recognized for more than two centuries, but it has acquired new significance as climate change increases the frequency and intensity of heatwaves.
Heat already kills more people than any other type of extreme weather in many wealthy countries, and the mortality risk is concentrated in cities.
Several mechanisms combine to produce the effect.

Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb solar energy during the day and release it slowly at night, which is why the difference between city and countryside is often greatest after sunset.
Tall buildings trap heat between them and reduce ventilation, while the absence of vegetation deprives cities of the cooling that plants provide through evaporation.
Cars, air conditioners and industry add further heat, and air conditioning, ironically, warms the streets outside in order to cool the rooms inside.
The consequences are not evenly distributed.

Poorer neighbourhoods typically have fewer trees, denser housing and fewer homes with air conditioning, so their residents face greater exposure to high temperatures and have fewer means of escaping them.
Elderly people living alone are especially vulnerable, since the body's capacity to regulate its temperature declines with age.
During the European heatwave of 2003, tens of thousands of excess deaths were recorded, predominantly among elderly residents of city apartments.
Fortunately, the heat island is one of the few climate problems that municipal authorities can address largely on their own.
Planting trees is among the most effective interventions, since a mature canopy can lower the temperature of the street beneath it considerably.
The Colombian city of Medellín transformed dozens of roads and waterways into green corridors, reportedly reducing local temperatures by around two degrees.
Paris has been converting concrete school playgrounds into shaded gardens that are opened to neighbouring residents during heatwaves.
Other solutions are strikingly simple.
Painting roofs white, or covering them with vegetation, can reduce the temperature of the building beneath and of the air around it.
Where space is scarce, vertical gardens can even be grown on the walls of buildings.
Lighter materials for pavements, fountains in public squares and designs that allow wind to circulate between buildings all play a part.
Adapting cities to extreme heat will inevitably be costly, but the alternative, as the death tolls of recent summers suggest, is considerably worse.
Long before refrigerators, human beings discovered that certain foods could be preserved by allowing microbes to transform them.
Cabbage became sauerkraut or kimchi, milk became yogurt and cheese, and grain became bread and beer.

Almost every culinary tradition in the world relies on fermentation in some form, and in recent years these ancient techniques have enjoyed a remarkable revival in restaurants, supermarkets and home kitchens.
The underlying process is remarkably varied.
In the fermentation of vegetables, bacteria convert natural sugars into lactic acid, which lowers the pH of the food and prevents the growth of the organisms that cause it to rot.
In bread and beer, yeast converts sugars into carbon dioxide and alcohol, which is what makes dough rise and gives beer its bubbles.
The acidic environment and the by-products of fermentation also create the distinctive sour, sharp and savoury flavours that people in many cultures prize.
Much of the recent enthusiasm, however, concerns health rather than flavour.
Scientists have become increasingly interested in the microbiome, the trillions of microbes that live in the human gut and appear to influence everything from digestion to the immune system.

In a small study at Stanford University in 2021, volunteers who ate several servings of fermented food a day for ten weeks showed a greater diversity of gut microbes and lower levels of inflammation than those who increased their intake of fibre instead.
Such findings, albeit promising, should be interpreted with caution.
Many commercial products labelled as fermented have been pasteurized or filtered, a process that kills the living microbes they once contained.
Some drinks marketed as healthy contain substantial amounts of sugar, and the evidence that particular foods produce lasting benefits for people who are already healthy remains limited.
Home fermentation also carries small risks, which rigorous hygiene and reliable recipes largely eliminate.
Whatever the scientific verdict, the appeal of fermentation is not purely nutritional.

For many enthusiasts, it offers a way of reconnecting with the practices of their grandparents, and a small act of resistance against an industrial food system that values convenience and uniformity above all else.
There is also a particular satisfaction in collaborating with invisible organisms, and in producing something that is, in a very literal sense, alive.
In October 1347, a fleet of trading ships arrived in the Sicilian port of Messina, carrying sailors who were dying of a terrifying disease.
Within four years, the plague that came to be known as the Black Death had spread across the whole of Europe, killing between a third and a half of its population.
It remains the deadliest pandemic in recorded human history, and its consequences reshaped European society for centuries.
The disease was caused by a bacterium carried by fleas that lived on rats, although historians now believe that it also spread directly between people.
Contemporary observers, of course, knew nothing of this mechanism.
Doctors attributed the plague to poisoned air or to the alignment of the planets, while many religious leaders interpreted it as divine punishment for human sin.

In their fear, some communities searched for scapegoats, and Jewish communities across Europe were accused of poisoning wells and subjected to horrific persecution; in Strasbourg in 1349, hundreds of Jews were burned to death.
The economic aftermath was, in some respects, surprising.
With so many people dead, there was an acute shortage of labour, and the peasants who survived found themselves in an unusually strong bargaining position.
Wages rose sharply, and landowners who could no longer find workers were forced to offer better terms or watch their fields return to wilderness.
In England, the government responded with the Statute of Labourers of 1351, which attempted to fix wages at their levels before the plague and to prevent workers from moving in search of better pay.
The attempt to turn back the clock generated deep resentment.
In 1381, provoked by a series of new taxes, thousands of peasants marched on London in the Peasants' Revolt, the largest rebellion in medieval English history.

The rebellion was brutally suppressed, but the old system in which peasants were bound to the land of their lords continued to decline, and many historians regard the Black Death as a turning point in the gradual transition from the medieval to the modern economy.
The plague left its mark on culture as well.
Art of the period became preoccupied with death, depicting skeletons dancing with kings and peasants alike, a reminder that no one could escape it.
Some scholars argue that the loss of faith in traditional authorities, both medical and religious, helped to prepare the ground for the intellectual upheavals of later centuries.
Most moral traditions condemn lying, and yet almost everyone lies, frequently and seemingly without guilt.
Empirical studies in which participants keep a diary of their conversations suggest that the average person tells at least one lie a day, most of them small and apparently harmless.
We tactfully praise a meal we did not enjoy, claim to be busy when we simply want to be alone, and assure a nervous friend that their presentation went well.
Hence the familiar distinction between malicious lies and so-called white lies, which most people regard as harmless.
The question is whether such deception is merely forgivable or whether it can actually be right.
The most uncompromising answer was given by the German philosopher Immanuel Kant.
Kant argued that lying is inherently wrong, because it treats other people as objects to be manipulated rather than as rational beings whose autonomy deserves respect.
In a notorious example, he maintained that if a murderer came to your door asking where your friend was hiding, you would still not be permitted to lie to him.
