Few readers have found this conclusion acceptable, and even sympathetic scholars tend to treat it as an embarrassment, albeit an instructive one.
The opposite approach judges lies solely by their consequences.
If a lie prevents harm, protects someone's feelings or produces more happiness than the truth, then, on this view, it may be not only permissible but obligatory.
The weakness of this approach is that it inevitably underestimates the hidden costs of deception.

Each lie, however well intended, slightly erodes the trust on which relationships and institutions depend, and people who discover that they have been deceived, even for their own good, frequently feel humiliated rather than grateful.
A doctor, a politician or a journalist who is caught lying may lose their credibility permanently, and experience the discovery as a betrayal of their profession.
Medicine offers a revealing illustration.
In the middle of the twentieth century, many doctors routinely withheld a diagnosis of cancer from their patients, believing that the truth would destroy their hope.

Within a few decades, that paternalistic attitude had largely disappeared, and full disclosure is now regarded as a basic obligation, partly because patients cannot make meaningful decisions about their treatment without accurate information.

Doctors still exercise discretion, however, about how and when to deliver bad news, which suggests that honesty and tact are not necessarily in conflict, and that integrity involves more than simply stating facts.
Perhaps the most defensible stance lies between the extremes.

Truthfulness deserves a strong presumption in its favour, so that anyone who lies should be able to justify doing so, ideally in terms that the person deceived would accept if they knew the full circumstances.
Lying to the murderer at the door passes this test easily; lying to a colleague to avoid an awkward but candid conversation almost certainly does not.
At a quarter to six in the morning, Marta Ruiz climbs the stairs of the control tower, collects her headset and sits down in front of a radar screen crowded with small green symbols.
Each symbol represents an aircraft, and for the duration of her session she will be responsible for guiding dozens of them safely through her sector of the sky.
Before taking over, she spends several minutes with the controller she is replacing, who briefs her on the weather, the traffic and any unusual situations.
The fundamental principle of her work is separation.
Aircraft must be kept a minimum distance apart, both horizontally and vertically, and controllers achieve this by instructing pilots to change their speed, altitude or direction.
No aircraft may take off, land or enter a new section of airspace without clearance, and every instruction must be read back by the pilot to confirm that it has been correctly understood.
Strict protocols govern every exchange between the tower and the cockpit.

Communication follows a precise and highly standardized vocabulary, and English is, notably, used for international flights throughout the world, which is why controllers and pilots must demonstrate a certified level of proficiency in the language.
Much of the work consists of anticipating problems before they arise.
Marta constantly calculates where each aircraft will be in five or ten minutes, looking for conflicts between their paths long before they become dangerous.
On a busy morning, she may be speaking to fifteen pilots at once, adjusting a sequence of arrivals to achieve the optimal spacing of around two minutes between them.
When a thunderstorm forces aircraft to deviate from their planned routes, the entire sequence has to be rebuilt in a matter of seconds.
Automatic detection systems warn her if two aircraft come too close, but her aim is never to hear them.
The mental demands of the job are immense, and its rules reflect a clear understanding of human limitations.
Controllers are required to take mandatory breaks, typically after no more than two hours at the screen, because concentration deteriorates rapidly with fatigue.
Every incident, however minor, is reported and analysed, not in order to punish individuals but to identify underlying weaknesses in the system.
When Marta finishes her shift in the early afternoon, she describes the feeling as a kind of pleasant exhaustion.
"Nobody notices when we do our job well," she says, "and that is exactly how it should be."
In September 1941, German and Finnish forces completed the encirclement of Leningrad, the Soviet Union's second-largest city, and began one of the longest and most destructive sieges in history.
Rather than attempting to capture the city street by street, which would have been costly in both time and casualties, the German command decided to starve it into submission.
The blockade, one of the most brutal episodes of the entire war, lasted almost nine hundred days.
The first winter was the most terrible.

Food stocks had been destroyed by bombing in the early weeks, and by November the daily bread ration for many civilians had fallen to about a hundred and twenty-five grams, much of it made with sawdust and other inedible additives.
Temperatures fell to minus thirty degrees, the water pipes froze and electricity failed across most of the city.
People burned furniture and books to keep warm, and many died quietly in their apartments or collapsed in the streets on their way to collect their rations.
The only route into the city ran across Lake Ladoga to the east.
In summer, supplies were brought across by boat; in winter, once the ice was thick enough, lorries drove across the frozen lake along what became known as the Road of Life.
The journey was immensely dangerous, since the ice could crack under heavy loads and the road was within range of German artillery.
Nevertheless, it allowed hundreds of thousands of people, predominantly children, the elderly and the sick, to be evacuated.
Cultural life continued, seemingly in spite of everything, and it acquired an extraordinary symbolic significance.

In August 1942, the city's surviving musicians, many of them so weak from hunger that they could barely hold their instruments, performed Dmitri Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony, which he had begun writing in Leningrad during the first months of the siege.
The performance was broadcast by loudspeakers across the city and towards the German lines, as a deliberate statement that Leningrad had not been defeated.
The siege was finally broken in January 1944.

Estimates of the number of civilians who died vary considerably, but most historians believe that it was around eight hundred thousand, the majority from starvation, a toll greater than the combined civilian losses of Britain and the United States in the entire war.
The city, renamed Saint Petersburg in 1991, still commemorates the anniversary of its liberation every year, and the experience of the siege remains an integral part of its identity.
For much of the twentieth century, many sociologists were confident that religion would gradually disappear as societies became wealthier, better educated and more scientifically sophisticated.
This theory, known as secularization, seemed to be confirmed by events in Western Europe, where church attendance fell dramatically in the decades after the Second World War.
In several European countries today, fewer than one in ten people attends a religious service in a typical month.
Yet the global picture is far more complicated.

Religious affiliation is growing, not shrinking, as a proportion of the world's population, largely because religious families tend to have more children and because the fastest-growing populations are in regions where faith remains strong.

Christianity is expanding rapidly across sub-Saharan Africa, where Pentecostal congregations attract millions of new members, and Islam is projected to grow faster than any other major religion over the coming decades.
Even in wealthy countries, the story is not uniform: the United States remains considerably more religious than most of Europe, notably in its southern states.
Sociologists have therefore refined their theories.

Some argue that what is declining is not belief itself but traditional institutions: many people who describe themselves as having no religion still pray, believe in some form of higher power or consider themselves "spiritual but not religious".
Others point out that religion has always provided more than doctrine.

Congregations offer community, support in times of crisis and a shared framework of meaning, and where these functions are provided by other institutions, such as the welfare state, religious observance tends to weaken.
Theological disagreements have also reshaped religious life.

Within many traditions, orthodox and liberal groups have drifted apart over questions such as the role of women, sexuality and the interpretation of scripture, and some denominations have split entirely.
Paradoxically, the most conservative congregations are often the ones that are growing, perhaps because they demand more of their members and offer, in return, a stronger sense of belonging.
The question of whether religion is declining, then, has no single answer.
In some places and among some groups, it clearly is; elsewhere, it is flourishing; and almost everywhere, it is changing.
What seems increasingly implausible is the confident prediction of the last century that modern societies would inevitably leave faith behind.
When prices rise rapidly, most people expect the government to do something about it.

In most wealthy countries, however, the responsibility for controlling inflation lies not with elected politicians but with the central bank, an institution that is usually independent of the government and whose mandate is to keep prices stable.
Many central banks, including the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, explicitly aim for inflation of around two per cent a year.
Governments, meanwhile, retain control of fiscal policy, namely taxation and public spending, and when the two arms of policy pull in opposite directions, the results can be chaotic.

Whilst the details differ between countries, their principal instrument is the interest rate at which commercial banks can borrow from the central bank, which in turn influences the rates that households and businesses pay on loans and mortgages.
When the central bank raises its rate, borrowing becomes more expensive and saving becomes more attractive.
People spend less, companies postpone investment, and the reduced demand for goods and services, notably in the housing market, inevitably slows the rise in prices.

The process, however, operates with a considerable delay, whose duration is typically between one and two years, which means that central banks must act on the basis of forecasts rather than current conditions.
This makes monetary policy a delicate balancing act.
If rates rise too slowly, inflation may become entrenched, as workers demand higher wages to compensate for rising prices and companies raise prices to cover higher wages.
If they rise too quickly, the economy may fall into recession, with rising unemployment and the failure of many businesses that were perfectly viable when borrowing was cheap.

In the early 1980s, the chairman of the United States Federal Reserve, Paul Volcker, raised interest rates to almost twenty per cent and defeated inflation, albeit at the cost of a deep and painful recession; inflation subsequently remained low for decades.
Expectations play a crucial role.

If people believe that inflation will remain high, they behave in ways that make it so, which is why central banks devote so much effort to communicating their intentions and protecting their credibility.
A central bank that is seen to be under political pressure may find that its announcements lack credibility.
Rumours about forthcoming decisions can trigger intense speculation in financial markets.
After the financial crisis of 2008, central banks faced the opposite problem.

With interest rates already close to zero, they could not provide further stimulus by cutting rates, so they began buying enormous quantities of government bonds, a policy known as quantitative easing, in order to inject liquidity into the financial system.
Critics argue that the policy inflated the prices of assets such as shares and houses, benefiting those who already owned them and thereby widening inequality.
The debate illustrates a broader point: decisions taken by unelected officials about interest rates can have profound consequences for millions of people who never voted for them.
Every computer you have ever used, from a pocket calculator to the most powerful supercomputer, works in fundamentally the same way.
Information is stored in binary form, as bits that can each be either zero or one, and the processor manipulates these bits according to precise instructions, billions of times a second.
Quantum computers are based on an entirely different principle, one that exploits the strange behaviour of matter at the smallest scales.
In quantum mechanics, a particle such as an electron can exist in a combination of states at once, a property known as superposition.

A quantum bit, or qubit, can therefore represent zero and one simultaneously, and when qubits are linked through a phenomenon called entanglement, the number of states they can represent together grows exponentially.
In theory, a machine with a few hundred reliable qubits could solve certain problems that would take a conventional computer longer than the age of the universe.
The practical difficulties, however, are immense.
Qubits are extraordinarily fragile: the slightest vibration, change in temperature or stray magnetic field can destroy their delicate quantum state, a problem known as decoherence.
Most current machines must therefore be cooled to temperatures colder than outer space, and even then they make frequent errors.
Correcting those errors requires many additional qubits, which means that a genuinely useful quantum computer may need millions of them, far more than any laboratory has yet managed to build.
Despite these obstacles, governments and technology companies are investing billions in what is often described as a race, with the United States and China notably prominent.

The potential applications include the design of new medicines and materials, since quantum computers could simulate molecular behaviour with unprecedented accuracy, as well as problems in logistics and finance.
The most discussed consequence, however, concerns security.

Much of the encryption that protects online banking, private messages and government secrets relies on mathematical problems that conventional computers cannot solve in any reasonable time, but that a sufficiently powerful quantum computer could solve quickly.

Security agencies have warned that hostile states may already be collecting encrypted data in order to decrypt it in the future, and researchers are racing to develop new forms of encryption that even quantum machines could not break.
Whether practical quantum computers are five years away or fifty remains, for now, a matter of speculation.
The penalty kick is one of the purest contests in sport.
A single player shoots from eleven metres, and a single goalkeeper tries to stop the ball, which can travel at more than a hundred kilometres per hour and reaches the goal in less than half a second.
Since that is too little time for the goalkeeper to see where the ball is going and then react, the contest inevitably becomes a guessing game, and both players must, in effect, decide in advance.
Even a goalkeeper with exceptional reflexes cannot rely solely on reaction.
This makes the penalty a perfect subject for economists who study strategic decision-making.
According to game theory, the optimal strategy for both sides is to be unpredictable.
If a player always shoots to the same side, a well-prepared goalkeeper will eventually anticipate it; if a goalkeeper always dives to the same side, a well-prepared player will exploit it.
Right-footed players, for instance, predominantly shoot to their natural side, whilst goalkeepers who know this can gain a small but significant advantage.
Remarkably, rigorous statistical studies of thousands of professional penalties suggest that players and goalkeepers behave very much as the theory predicts.
They randomize their choices in roughly the proportions that maximize their chances of success.
One anomaly concerns the middle of the goal.
Goalkeepers dive to one side in the overwhelming majority of penalties, even though shots aimed at the centre are saved relatively rarely.

Psychologists have suggested that this reflects a phenomenon known as action bias: a goalkeeper who stays still and concedes a goal appears to have done nothing, whereas one who dives the wrong way at least appears to have tried.
The fear of looking foolish, seemingly, can outweigh the rational calculation of probability, and intuition is not always a reliable guide.
Psychological pressure has a measurable effect too, and its intensity increases with the stakes.
Adrenaline, which improves performance in many physical tasks, may impair the fine control needed for an accurate shot.

In major tournaments, penalties taken to avoid immediate defeat are converted noticeably less often than those that could win a match, which suggests that the fear of failure is more disruptive than the hope of success.
Players who hurry, shooting within a second or two of the referee's whistle, also tend to miss more often.
Perhaps they are trying to escape an unbearable moment rather than concentrating on the task.
Conversely, players whose teams have already scored in a shoot-out appear to benefit from a kind of psychological momentum, notably in the later rounds.

Some elite teams have taken these empirical findings seriously, and it is now common for goalkeepers to carry notes about their opponents' preferences, sometimes written on their water bottles, and the rules explicitly restrict the tricks that goalkeepers may use to distract the taker.
Yet the penalty retains an irreducible element of chance, and that, arguably, is precisely why audiences find it so compelling.
No amount of statistical analysis can remove the immense loneliness of the player walking towards the ball, or the possibility that everything will be decided by a single moment of nerve.
Diabetes is one of the most common chronic diseases in the world, affecting more than five hundred million adults, and its prevalence has roughly quadrupled since 1980.
It occurs when the body cannot regulate the level of glucose, a sugar that provides energy to its cells, and it is largely preventable in its most common form.
Nevertheless, it remains widely misunderstood.
The key to understanding the disease is a hormone called insulin, which is produced by the pancreas and allows cells to absorb glucose from the blood.
In type 1 diabetes, which usually begins in childhood, the immune system mistakenly destroys the cells that produce insulin, and patients must inject it for the rest of their lives.
In type 2 diabetes, which accounts for around ninety per cent of cases, the body still produces insulin, but its cells gradually become resistant to it, so that glucose accumulates in the blood.
Over time, high levels of blood sugar damage blood vessels and nerves throughout the body.
Diabetes is a leading cause of blindness, kidney failure, heart attacks and strokes, and in severe cases poor circulation in the feet can lead to amputation.
What makes type 2 diabetes particularly dangerous is that it can develop silently for years; many people are diagnosed only after complications have already begun.
The risk factors are well established.
Genetic predisposition plays a role, as does age, but the dramatic rise in cases worldwide is predominantly associated with obesity, inactivity and diets high in sugar and processed food.
The disease is increasingly common in low- and middle-income countries, where urbanization has transformed traditional diets and ways of life within a single generation.
Encouragingly, type 2 diabetes can often be prevented or delayed, and in some cases even reversed.

Large clinical trials have shown that modest weight loss and regular physical activity can reduce the risk among high-risk individuals by more than half, an effect considerably greater than that of any medication.

Some public health experts argue, however, that individual advice is insufficient, and that governments should also regulate the marketing of sugary food and drink, since the environment in which people make their choices shapes those choices profoundly.
Most prisoners are eventually released from custody, and what happens to them afterwards is one of the most revealing tests of a criminal justice system.
In many countries, a large proportion of those released are convicted of another offence within a few years, and in some the figure exceeds half.
Each case of reoffending represents new victims, further costs and, arguably, a failure of the system that was supposed to change the offender's behaviour.
The obstacles facing former prisoners are considerable.
Many leave prison with no home, no savings and no job, and a criminal record makes employment immensely difficult to find.
Employers are frequently reluctant to hire anyone with a conviction, and former prisoners are particularly vulnerable in the first weeks after release, notably to homelessness and debt.

Relationships with families have often broken down, and some prisoners, particularly those who served long sentences, find it hard to cope with ordinary tasks such as opening a bank account or using public transport.
Those who were juvenile offenders when they entered the system may have spent their entire adult lives inside it.
Most systems attempt to manage this transition through probation or parole.

Prisoners released early on parole remain under supervision, must report regularly to an officer and can be returned to prison if they break the conditions of their release, for instance by missing appointments or failing a drug test.
Supporters argue that supervision protects the public and gives offenders structure.
Critics point out that heavy caseloads leave officers little time for anything beyond checking compliance, and that minor violations can send people back to prison without any new crime.
Some countries have taken a different approach.

Norway, whose prisons are often cited as among the most humane in the world, organizes its system around rehabilitation and the principle that life inside should resemble life outside as closely as possible, so that release is a gradual step rather than a sudden shock.
Prisoners study, work and cook for themselves, and in the final stage of their sentences many live in open prisons from which they commute to ordinary jobs.
Norway's reoffending rate is among the lowest recorded anywhere, although comparisons between countries are notoriously difficult, since they define and measure reoffending in different ways.
Employment appears to be the single most important factor.

Empirical studies consistently find that former prisoners who obtain stable work are substantially less likely to reoffend, which has led some governments to offer incentives to employers who hire them and to limit the circumstances in which old convictions must be disclosed.
Such policies are inevitably controversial, since they can be portrayed as rewarding criminals.
Yet the alternative is a cycle in which the same individuals pass repeatedly through prison, at enormous cost to themselves, their victims and the public.
When Charles Darwin visited the Galápagos Islands in 1835, he noticed that the finches on different islands had beaks of different shapes, each suited to the food available on that particular island.

The observation subsequently contributed to his theory of evolution by natural selection, and ever since, islands have been regarded as natural laboratories in which evolutionary processes can be observed with unusual clarity.
The reason is isolation.
When a small number of animals or plants reach a remote island, perhaps carried by storms or floating on vegetation, they are cut off from the populations on the mainland.
Their offspring adapt to local conditions, which are often very different from those on the mainland, and over many generations they may evolve into entirely new species.
Because island populations are small, chance inevitably plays a larger role than it does elsewhere, and unusual traits can spread rapidly.
Some of the most striking consequences concern size.
On many islands, large mammals tend to become smaller over time, a phenomenon known as island dwarfism, presumably because limited food favours animals that need less of it.
Small animals, by contrast, often grow larger, since the absence of predators removes the advantage of being small and easy to hide.
The Indonesian island of Flores was once home to dwarf elephants and giant rats, and to a small species of human, only about a metre tall, whose remains were discovered in 2003.
The same isolation that produces such diversity also makes island species exceptionally vulnerable.
Having evolved without predators, many island birds lost the ability to fly and the instinct to flee, and when humans arrived with rats, cats and pigs, they had no defence.
The dodo of Mauritius, a large flightless pigeon, was extinct within a century of the first European landing.
Islands cover a small fraction of the Earth's land surface, yet they account for a disproportionate share of recorded extinctions, particularly among birds.
Conservationists have responded with some notable successes.
On hundreds of islands, invasive rats and other predators have been eliminated, allowing seabirds and native plants to recover within a few years.
Such projects are expensive and require rigorous planning, since a single surviving pregnant rat can undo the entire effort.
But they demonstrate that the damage caused by human arrival is not always irreversible, and that the laboratories Darwin admired can, with care, be restored.
By the early 2000s, the vinyl record appeared to be finished.
Compact discs had replaced it in the 1990s, digital downloads were replacing compact discs, and the few factories that still pressed records were closing one after another.
Today, remarkably, sales of vinyl have risen for more than fifteen consecutive years, and in some countries they now generate more revenue than CDs.
The revival is puzzling at first sight.
Streaming services offer almost every recording ever made, instantly and for a modest monthly subscription, whereas a single new vinyl album can cost as much as three months of streaming.
Records are fragile, heavy and inconvenient, and they must be turned over every twenty minutes or so.
Audio engineers continue to debate whether the analog sound of vinyl is genuinely superior, and many listeners admit that they cannot tell the difference.
The explanation seems to lie less in the acoustics than in the experience.
Buyers describe the pleasure of owning a physical object, with large artwork and printed lyrics, in an age when most music exists only as data.

Playing a record also demands attention: it is difficult to skip tracks or listen while doing something else, so the listener is encouraged to hear an album from beginning to end, in the order its creators intended.
In a world of endless choice, some people seemingly welcome a format that asks them to choose less.
Interestingly, the revival has not been driven predominantly by older listeners nostalgic for their youth.

Surveys suggest that a substantial share of buyers are under thirty, and that many of them also use streaming services, treating records less as a replacement than as a supplement: they stream to discover music and buy vinyl to keep the albums they love.
Some buyers, remarkably, do not own a record player at all, and purchase albums as decorative objects or as a way of supporting artists directly.
Record shops that had closed a decade earlier have reopened, selling new releases alongside vintage compilations.
That support matters, because streaming pays musicians very little per play, and for many independent artists the sale of physical formats has become a vital source of income.

The revival has created problems of its own, however: the few remaining factories cannot keep up with demand, waiting times for pressing have grown to many months, and the petroleum-based plastic from which records are made sits uneasily with growing environmental concerns.
Even so, the story of vinyl is a reminder that technological progress does not always move in one direction, and that people value objects for reasons that efficiency alone cannot explain.
In most democracies, voting is a right that citizens may choose to exercise or ignore.
In a minority of countries, however, including Australia, Belgium and Brazil, it is also a legal obligation, and citizens who fail to vote without a valid excuse can be fined.
As turnout has fallen in many established democracies, the idea of compulsory voting has attracted renewed interest, and it raises fundamental questions about the nature of democratic participation.
The case in favour rests largely on the problem of unequal participation.
Where voting is voluntary, turnout tends to be highest among older, wealthier and better-educated citizens, and lowest among the young and the poor.
Since politicians naturally pay most attention to those who vote, the interests of non-voters may be systematically neglected, which can reinforce inequality.

In Australia, where voting has been compulsory since 1924, turnout regularly exceeds ninety per cent, and supporters argue that parties are therefore obliged to appeal to the whole electorate rather than mobilizing their most loyal supporters.
Opponents raise objections of principle, notably concerning individual liberty.
Freedom, they argue, includes the freedom not to participate, and a citizen who does not vote may be making a deliberate political statement, namely that none of the candidates deserves support.
Forcing people to vote who have no interest in politics, moreover, may simply produce random or poorly informed choices, which hardly improves the quality of democratic decisions.
Supporters have responses to both arguments.

In most systems with compulsory voting, what is legally required is attendance rather than a valid vote: citizens may spoil their ballot or leave it blank, so the freedom to reject every candidate is preserved.
The penalties are also modest, typically a small fine, and there is some evidence that the obligation gradually changes attitudes, so that voting becomes a social norm rather than a burden.
Whether compulsory voting would work elsewhere is uncertain.

It is most readily accepted in countries with a strong tradition of civic duty and efficient, trusted electoral administration, and it might provoke hostility where citizens already distrust the state.
But the debate itself is valuable, since it forces democracies to ask whether low turnout is a sign of contentment, of apathy or of a deeper alienation that no law can cure.

In October 1517, a German monk and professor of theology named Martin Luther wrote ninety-five arguments against the sale of indulgences, documents that the Catholic Church sold to reduce the punishment of sins after death.
Similar criticisms had been made before, and their authors had usually been persecuted or silenced.

Luther's arguments, however, spread across Germany within weeks and across Europe within months, and they started a movement that permanently divided Western Christianity and challenged the doctrine of papal authority.
The crucial difference was a technology that had not existed a century earlier.
Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg had developed a printing press with movable metal type in the German city of Mainz.
Before then, books had been copied by hand, a slow and expensive process that kept them predominantly in the hands of the Church and the wealthy.
By 1500, presses were operating in more than two hundred cities, and millions of books had been printed.
Luther grasped the potential of the new medium more quickly than his opponents.

Instead of writing long theological treatises in Latin, which only scholars could read, he produced short, vivid pamphlets in German, an early and remarkably effective form of propaganda, often illustrated with woodcuts that explicitly mocked the Pope and the clergy.
These cheap publications could be printed quickly, carried by travelling merchants and read aloud in taverns to people who could not read themselves.
In the decade after 1517, Luther's writings accounted for roughly a third of all books printed in German, which made him, arguably, the first best-selling author in history.
The Church responded with its own publications, but its efforts at censorship proved largely ineffective.
Printers were numerous, scattered across many small states and motivated by profit, and banning a book inevitably made people more eager to read it.

Luther's translation of the Bible into German, published in full in 1534, allowed ordinary believers to read scripture for themselves, and it contributed both to rising literacy and to the standardization of the German language.
Historians caution against giving the printing press all the credit for the Protestant Reformation.

Political rivalries between German princes and the Pope, resentment of the Church's wealth and genuine theological disagreement all played essential roles, and many earlier reform movements had failed for reasons that had nothing to do with technology.
Nevertheless, the parallel with our own time is difficult to ignore.

Then, as now, a new information technology allowed ideas to spread faster than authorities could control them, with consequences that were liberating, destabilizing and, in the religious wars that followed, catastrophically violent.
In 2017, the French club Paris Saint-Germain paid Barcelona two hundred and twenty-two million euros for the Brazilian forward Neymar, more than double the previous world record for a transfer fee.
The deal shocked many fans, but it was the logical conclusion of a trend that had been accelerating for decades.
Unlike American sports franchises, which operate in closed leagues with strict controls on spending, European clubs compete in an open market with few restrictions.
The market for professional footballers has become one of the most unusual in the global economy, with prices that bear little obvious relationship to anything outside the game.
The explanation begins with television.

Since the 1990s, the value of broadcasting rights has multiplied many times over, and English clubs in the Premier League now share several billion pounds a year from domestic and international television deals.
Add sponsorship, merchandise and ticket sales, and the leading clubs have revenues equivalent to those of large companies, notably in England.
Since success on the pitch generates further revenue, clubs compete fiercely for the small number of players who can make a decisive difference, and the price of exceptional talent inevitably rises.
Hence the extraordinary prices, which make some purchases essentially speculative.
A transfer fee is essentially compensation paid to a club for releasing a player before his contract has expired.
Its valuation therefore depends not only on the player's ability but on the length of his remaining contract, his age, his potential resale value and the financial desperation of the clubs involved.
Agents, who represent players and frequently receive a percentage of each deal, have become powerful intermediaries.
Critics argue that their incentives encourage a high turnover of players, which is rarely good for either the players or their teams.
Economists who have rigorously studied the market find that spending on wages predicts league position remarkably well, whereas spending on transfer fees is a much weaker predictor of success.
The implication is that many clubs overpay for famous names whilst undervaluing players whose contributions are less visible.

A handful of clubs have exploited this inefficiency, using statistical analysis to identify undervalued players, buying them cheaply and subsequently selling them at a substantial profit, and managing their squads almost like an investment portfolio.
The market's critics raise wider concerns.
The enormous sums concentrated in a few wealthy leagues make it increasingly difficult for smaller clubs to compete.
Several clubs have been driven into bankruptcy by spending money they did not have in pursuit of promotion.

Football's governing bodies have introduced rules limiting how much clubs may lose, but compliance has been inconsistent, and the richest owners have found ingenious ways around them, arguably undermining the entire system.
For supporters, the transfer market has become a source of both excitement and unease.
Every summer brings the hope of a new star, and the growing suspicion that the game they love is increasingly governed by money rather than merit.
Gravity is the most familiar force in nature and, in some respects, the most mysterious.

It keeps our feet on the ground, holds the Moon in orbit around the Earth and shapes the structure of the entire universe, yet it is extraordinarily weak compared with the other fundamental forces: a small magnet can lift a paper clip against the gravitational pull of the whole planet.
In the seventeenth century, Isaac Newton described gravity as a force of attraction between any two objects, proportional to their masses and decreasing with the square of the distance between them.
His theory was astonishingly successful.
It explained the motion of the planets, the tides and the trajectory of a falling apple with the same set of equations.
It even allowed astronomers to predict the existence of an unknown planet from tiny irregularities in the orbit of another.
Newton himself, however, was uneasy about one aspect of it: he could not explain how one object could pull another across empty space without anything connecting them.
Albert Einstein's answer, published in 1915 as the general theory of relativity, was radically different.
Gravity, he proposed, is not a force at all but a curvature of space and time, or spacetime, caused by mass and energy.
A planet orbits the sun not because it is being pulled but because it is following the straightest possible path through a curved geometry.

The theory explained a small anomaly in the orbit of Mercury that Newton's equations could not, and it predicted that light passing close to the sun would be bent, a prediction confirmed during a solar eclipse in 1919.
Some of the theory's predictions seemed so extreme that even Einstein doubted them.

It implied that a sufficiently dense concentration of mass would curve spacetime so severely that nothing, not even light, could escape, which is precisely what astronomers now believe black holes to be.
It also predicted that violent events, such as the collision of two black holes, would send ripples through spacetime itself.
In 2015, almost exactly a century later, detectors in the United States recorded such gravitational waves for the first time, produced by a collision more than a billion years ago.
Yet gravity remains incompletely understood.

General relativity describes the universe on large scales with extraordinary precision, while quantum mechanics describes the behaviour of particles with equal precision, and the two theories are, at a deep level, incompatible.
Reconciling them, in a so-called quantum theory of gravity, is arguably the greatest unsolved problem in physics, and it may require ideas as radical as those that Einstein introduced a century ago.
In most wealthy countries, it is illegal to dismiss a woman because she is pregnant.
Yet surveys consistently find that many women experience disadvantage at work during pregnancy or after returning from maternity leave.
They may be passed over for promotion, have their responsibilities reduced or be encouraged, more or less subtly, to leave.

The gap between legal protection and everyday experience is one of the most persistent and seemingly intractable problems in employment policy, not least because such discrimination is rarely explicit.
Economists have documented, with considerable statistical care, what is sometimes called the motherhood penalty.

Before they have children, men and women with similar qualifications earn broadly similar amounts; after the birth of a first child, women's earnings typically fall sharply and never fully recover, whilst men's are largely unaffected.

Even in countries with generous parental leave, the pattern is remarkably consistent, which suggests that it reflects deep assumptions about who is responsible for caring for children rather than purely economic factors.
Part of the explanation lies in working patterns.
Many mothers move to part-time work or choose less demanding roles in order to accommodate the needs of a baby or toddler, and careers in many professions still reward long and unpredictable hours.
But empirical studies also reveal discrimination that cannot be explained by such choices.

In experiments where employers were sent identical job applications that differed only in whether the candidate was described as a parent, mothers were rated as less committed and offered lower salaries, whereas fathers were, if anything, treated more favourably.
Policies designed to address the problem have inevitably had mixed results.

Long periods of maternity leave protect mothers' jobs, but if only women take them, they can reinforce the assumption that childcare is a female responsibility and discourage employers from hiring young women at all.

Several countries, notably Sweden, have therefore reserved a portion of parental leave explicitly for fathers, on a use-it-or-lose-it basis, and the proportion of fathers taking extended leave has risen substantially as a result.
Some demographers link the motherhood penalty to falling fertility, since women who expect their careers to suffer may postpone or forgo having children.
The broader lesson is that legal protection alone cannot change deeply held norms.
Flexible working, affordable childcare and a more equal division of parental responsibilities all appear to matter, and none of them is achieved simply by passing a law.
As long as the arrival of a child is regarded as a career problem for women and a private matter for men, the motherhood penalty is likely to persist.
The great museums of Europe and North America contain millions of objects from every part of the world, and many of them were acquired in circumstances that would now be regarded as unacceptable.
Some were purchased legally; others were taken during wars or colonial expeditions, sometimes by brutal force, or excavated from archaeological sites without permission.

In recent years, demands for the return of such objects to their countries of origin have grown considerably louder, and the question of who owns the past has become one of the most contentious in the cultural world.
The debate has intensified amid wider discussions of colonial history, and it raises difficult questions of sovereignty and legitimacy.
The Benin Bronzes offer a particularly stark example.

In 1897, a British military expedition attacked the kingdom of Benin, in what is now Nigeria, burned its capital and removed thousands of sculptures and plaques, many of which were subsequently sold to museums and private collectors across Europe.

For decades, requests for their return were explicitly refused, but attitudes have shifted, and several institutions, notably in Germany, have now transferred ownership of their collections to Nigeria.
The arguments for restitution are both moral and practical.
Objects taken by force, supporters argue, never legitimately belonged to those who took them, and keeping them perpetuates the injustice of their removal.

Such objects are also integral to the identity of the communities that created them, whose descendants may have to travel thousands of kilometres, and obtain visas they are often refused, simply to see their own heritage.
Museums have traditionally offered several counter-arguments.
Great collections, they argue, allow visitors to compare cultures side by side and to understand human history as a shared inheritance rather than a set of separate national stories.
Some have also claimed that objects are safer in their care, although this argument has become increasingly implausible as museums in the countries of origin have developed their own expertise.
Critics also point to the immense imbalance between the collections of former colonial powers, predominantly in Europe, and those of the countries whose heritage they hold.
Arguably the most famous dispute concerns the marble sculptures removed from the Parthenon in Athens by Lord Elgin in the early nineteenth century.
Displayed in the British Museum ever since, they have been the subject of controversy for more than two centuries.
There are no simple principles that settle every case.

Objects bought legally from willing sellers raise different questions from those taken as the spoils of war, and it is not always clear which modern state, community or family has the strongest claim to an ancient object.
But the direction of the debate is unmistakable.
Increasingly, museums are being asked not only what they own but how they came to own it, and they are discovering that the answer to the second question can change the answer to the first.
People who join cults are frequently assumed to be weak, gullible or unusually naive.
Empirical research on the subject suggests a different picture.
Many former members were intelligent, educated and idealistic.

Most joined not because they were searching for a strange belief system but because they were lonely, grieving or going through a period of transition, such as moving to a new city or starting university.
In such moments, anyone can be vulnerable to a group that offers warmth, purpose and certainty.
Recruitment typically begins with kindness rather than doctrine.

New recruits are welcomed with overwhelming attention and affection, a technique sometimes called love bombing, and they are introduced to the group's beliefs gradually, so that each step seems small and reasonable.

By the time the more extreme demands appear, such as donating one's savings or cutting off contact with family, the recruit has already invested a great deal of time, emotion and identity in the group.
Leaving at that point means admitting that one has been deceived, which is psychologically immensely costly.
Once inside, members are subjected to forms of manipulation that psychologists describe as coercive control.

Their time is filled with activities, leaving little opportunity for reflection; their contact with outsiders is restricted; and doubts are treated as evidence of personal weakness or disloyalty rather than as reasonable questions.

Most such groups are organized as a rigid hierarchy, and a charismatic leader, often claiming special knowledge or a unique relationship with a higher power, becomes the only legitimate source of truth.
Gradually, members learn to distrust their own perceptions, their sense of self becomes fragile and their personal autonomy disappears, which makes leaving even harder to contemplate.
Many cults are relatively harmless, albeit eccentric, and some eventually dissolve or evolve into ordinary religious movements.
The most dangerous, however, have been responsible for financial exploitation, sexual abuse and, in a small number of notorious cases, mass deaths.

Because the line between an intense community and a coercive group can be difficult to draw, experts tend to focus on behaviour rather than belief: the key questions concern whether members are free to leave, to disagree and to maintain relationships outside the group.
For families, the most useful advice is often counter-intuitive.
Confronting a relative angrily or demanding that they choose between the group and their family usually strengthens the group's hold, since it confirms the leader's warnings about hostile outsiders.

Maintaining contact, asking gentle questions and making clear that the door is always open appear to be far more effective, and many former members subsequently say that it was precisely such patient contact that eventually made it possible for them to leave.
Twenty years ago, the word "podcast" barely existed.

Today, there are several million podcasts in existence, covering every conceivable subject from ancient history to knitting, and hundreds of millions of people around the world listen to them every week.
Their rise is one of the most remarkable developments in modern media, and it has revived a form of storytelling that many assumed had been made obsolete by television.
Part of the appeal is convenience.
Unlike radio, podcasts can be heard whenever the listener chooses, and unlike video, they can be enjoyed while doing something else, such as commuting, cooking or exercising.
But convenience alone does not explain the extraordinary loyalty of many listeners, who subscribe to the same programmes for years and describe the hosts, whom they have never met, almost as friends.
Researchers attribute this loyalty to the peculiar intimacy of the human voice.
Podcasts are typically heard through headphones, directly in the listener's ears, and their informal, conversational style creates a sense of being included in a private conversation.
Psychologists describe the relationships that result as parasocial: one-sided attachments that nevertheless feel genuine to the listener.
The economics of podcasting are equally distinctive.

The technical barriers to entry are minimal: a microphone, a laptop and an internet connection are enough to start, which has allowed thousands of independent creators to find audiences in niches that no broadcaster would consider viable.
At the same time, the industry has become increasingly concentrated, as large companies pay enormous sums for exclusive rights to the most popular programmes.
Most podcasts earn little or nothing, whilst a handful generate millions from advertising, often read by the hosts themselves in the same friendly voice they use for everything else.
That intimacy, critics warn, carries risks.

Listeners who trust a host as they would a friend may be less inclined to question what they hear, and podcasts, unlike newspapers or broadcasters, are rarely subject to editorial standards or fact-checking.

Some of the most popular programmes have spread misleading claims about health and politics to audiences of millions, prompting a debate about whether platforms should bear responsibility for what they distribute.
The podcast, in short, has revived the oldest form of human communication, a voice telling a story, together with its oldest dangers.
In April 1815, Mount Tambora, a volcano on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, exploded in the most powerful eruption in recorded history.
The explosions were heard more than two thousand kilometres away, and the mountain lost roughly a third of its elevation.
Tens of thousands of people on the surrounding islands died, killed immediately by the eruption or subsequently by the famine that followed the destruction of their crops.
The consequences, however, extended far beyond Indonesia.

The eruption injected immense quantities of sulphur gas high into the atmosphere, where it formed a fine layer of volcanic particles that spread around the globe and reflected a small fraction of sunlight back into space.
The effect on global temperatures was modest, perhaps half a degree, but it was enough to disrupt atmospheric circulation and weather patterns across the Northern Hemisphere.
The following year, 1816, became known in Europe and North America as the year without a summer.
In New England, snow fell in June, and frosts in July and August destroyed crops across the region.
In Europe, persistent precipitation and cold caused harvests to fail from Ireland to Switzerland, food prices inevitably soared and there were riots in several countries.
Historians estimate that the resulting famine and disease killed tens of thousands of people in Europe alone, predominantly among the poor.
The hardship also prompted mass migration, including a wave of families leaving New England for the west.
Nobody at the time understood the underlying cause.

News travelled slowly from the Pacific, and it was not until the twentieth century that scientists established the connection between the eruption and the strange weather, using empirical evidence from ice cores and tree rings.
Some contemporaries attributed the cold to sunspots; others saw it as divine punishment.
The gloomy summer left an unexpected cultural legacy.

Confined indoors by constant storms at a villa beside Lake Geneva, a group of young English writers held a competition to see who could write the most frightening story, and eighteen-year-old Mary Shelley began the novel that became Frankenstein.

Today, Tambora serves as a reminder of a more serious lesson, with profound implications: that a single natural event on the other side of the world can, through the interconnected systems of climate and trade, disrupt the lives of millions.

Scientists estimate that an eruption of similar magnitude occurs once or twice in a thousand years, and that the next one would be felt in a world far more densely populated, far more dependent on global food supplies and therefore far more vulnerable.
Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily expensive.

The process can take more than a decade, and most of the candidate drugs that pharmaceutical companies investigate fail at some stage, either because they do not work or because they turn out to be unsafe.
Industry estimates of the average cost of bringing a single successful drug to market run into billions of dollars, although critics argue that these figures are inflated.
The patent system is designed to make such investment worthwhile.
A patent grants the inventor of a new medicine the exclusive right to sell it, usually for twenty years from the date of the application, during which no competitor may produce a copy.
The company can therefore charge prices far above the cost of manufacturing, and the resulting profits, in theory, finance the research that produces the next generation of drugs.
Once the patent expires, other manufacturers may produce generic versions, and prices typically fall dramatically, sometimes by more than ninety per cent.
The system's defenders argue that it has been immensely productive.

Without the prospect of a temporary monopoly, they point out, private investors would have little incentive to fund risky research, and many of the medicines that have transformed treatment for cancer, heart disease and infections would never have been developed.
Critics, however, identify serious problems.

High prices place life-saving medicines beyond the reach of millions of patients, particularly in poorer countries, and even wealthy health systems increasingly struggle to afford the newest treatments.

The system also distorts research priorities: companies naturally focus on diseases that affect people who can pay, so that conditions predominantly affecting the poor, such as many tropical infections, receive comparatively little investment.
Some companies, moreover, have been accused of making minor changes to existing drugs in order to extend their patents, a practice that delays the arrival of cheaper generics.
The conflict became acute during the HIV epidemic around the turn of the century.
Effective antiretroviral drugs were available, but at prices that made them unaffordable in Africa, where the disease was killing millions.

When manufacturers in India began producing generic versions at a fraction of the cost, and South Africa passed a law allowing their import, dozens of pharmaceutical companies took the South African government to court, before withdrawing the case amid international outrage.

Several alternatives have been proposed, including prizes for companies that develop medicines for neglected diseases, public funding for research in exchange for affordable prices, and voluntary agreements that allow cheaper production for poorer countries.
None has replaced the patent system, which remains, for all its flaws, the principal mechanism through which new medicines are financed.
The underlying dilemma is unlikely to disappear: society wants companies to invent new treatments, and it also wants everyone who needs them to be able to afford them.
Between the Malay Peninsula and the Indonesian island of Sumatra lies a narrow stretch of water about nine hundred kilometres long.
Roughly a quarter of all the goods traded by sea are in transit through it at some point.
The Strait of Malacca connects the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea, and it is the shortest maritime route between the oil fields of the Middle East and the factories of East Asia.
Every year, tens of thousands of ships pass through it, including a large proportion of the tankers, predominantly carrying crude oil, that supply China, Japan and South Korea.
The strait has been of immense importance for more than a thousand years.
Its position between two monsoon systems meant that merchant ships sailing between India and China often had to wait there for the winds to change.
Powerful trading ports inevitably grew up along the adjacent shores.
In the fifteenth century, the sultanate of Malacca controlled much of this trade, and its wealth attracted European powers, beginning with the Portuguese, who captured the city in 1511.
Singapore, founded as a British trading post in 1819 at the southern entrance to the strait, subsequently became one of the busiest ports in the world.
Today, the strait is what strategists call a chokepoint: a narrow passage whose closure would disrupt the global economy.
At its narrowest point, near Singapore, the navigable channel is less than three kilometres wide, and a single accident involving a large tanker could block it for days.
Alternative routes exist, through other straits further east, but they would add days to each voyage and billions of dollars to shipping costs, notably for Japan.

China, which depends heavily on imported oil, has invested in pipelines and ports in neighbouring countries, partly to reduce what its leaders have described as the country's vulnerability to a blockade.
Piracy was once a serious problem in the strait, with dozens of attacks on ships every year in the early 2000s.

Close coordination between the navies of Malaysia, Indonesia and Singapore, including joint patrols, together with the sharing of intelligence, have since reduced it considerably, although small-scale robberies still occur.
Environmental concerns are growing too, since the immense volume of traffic produces considerable pollution.
A major oil spill in such a busy and ecologically sensitive area would be catastrophic for fisheries and coastal communities.
The narrow strip of water that made Malacca rich six centuries ago remains, in other words, one of the most strategically important places on Earth.
Autism is a lifelong developmental condition that affects how people perceive the world and interact with others.
It is described as a spectrum because it varies enormously from one person to another.
Some autistic people need substantial support in their daily lives, while others live independently, work in demanding professions and may not be diagnosed until adulthood, if at all.
The characteristics of autism fall broadly into two groups.
The first concerns social communication.
Autistic people may find it difficult to interpret facial expressions, tone of voice or unspoken social rules, and they may prefer direct, literal language to hints and irony.
The second concerns patterns of behaviour and perception.
Many have intense, focused interests, a strong preference for routine and unusual sensory experiences, so that ordinary noises, lights or textures may feel overwhelming.
The number of people diagnosed with autism has risen sharply in recent decades, which has led to widespread speculation about an "epidemic".
Most researchers attribute the increase predominantly to changes in diagnosis rather than to a genuine rise in prevalence.
The definition of autism has broadened considerably, and awareness among doctors and teachers has improved.
Groups who were previously overlooked, notably girls and women, whose autism often presents differently, are increasingly being identified.
The claim that vaccines cause autism, which originated in a fraudulent study published in 1998 and later withdrawn, has been thoroughly disproved by large studies involving millions of children.
In recent years, many autistic people have challenged the idea that autism is simply a disorder to be cured.

The concept of neurodiversity holds that differences in how brains work are a natural part of human variation, comparable to differences in personality, and that many of the difficulties autistic people face arise from a world designed for other people.

Advocates point to the distinctive strengths often associated with autism, such as attention to detail, honesty and the ability to concentrate intensely, while acknowledging that for some people the condition brings serious challenges.
In practical terms, relatively simple adjustments can make a considerable difference.
Quiet spaces in schools and workplaces, clear written instructions, advance warning of changes and interview processes that do not depend on small talk have all been shown to help.

Unemployment among autistic adults nevertheless remains strikingly high, which suggests that the greatest obstacles are often not the characteristics of autism itself but the reluctance of institutions to accommodate them.
In August 1973, at a party in the recreation room of an apartment building on Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, a young DJ who called himself Kool Herc tried something new.
He had noticed that dancers became most excited during the short instrumental passages of funk records, known as breaks.
In those passages, the singing stopped and only the drums continued.
Using two turntables and two copies of the same vinyl record, he began to play the break on one, then the other, extending a few seconds of rhythm into several minutes.
Many historians subsequently came to regard that evening as the moment hip-hop was born.
The music emerged from a neighbourhood in crisis.
In the 1970s, the South Bronx was among the poorest areas in the United States, marked by deprivation and the collapse of municipal services.
A new motorway had divided its communities, landlords were abandoning buildings, and fires, many of them started deliberately, destroyed thousands of homes.
Public funding for music education had been cut, and many young people had no access to instruments.
What they did have were records, speakers and an extraordinary capacity for invention.
From these limited materials, a whole culture developed with remarkable momentum.
DJs competed to find the most obscure records with the best breaks; dancers invented the acrobatic style that became known as breakdancing.
Graffiti artists covered trains and walls with elaborate painted letters, and MCs, originally hired to encourage the crowd, began to speak in rhyme over the music.

Their rhymes, which became known as rapping, described life in the neighbourhood with humour, boasting and, increasingly, anger at poverty, police violence and inequality, notably in songs that were explicitly political.
For several years, hip-hop existed almost entirely at live parties, and the music industry, seemingly hostile to anything it had not invented itself, ignored it.
That changed in 1979, when a group called the Sugarhill Gang released a record that became a surprise commercial success, and within a decade rappers were selling millions of albums.

The technology of sampling, which allowed producers to take fragments of existing recordings and combine them into new tracks, transformed the sound of the music, allowed producers to remix older songs and subsequently provoked a series of legal disputes about copyright.
Today, hip-hop is arguably the most influential popular music in the world, and it has shaped fashion, language and advertising far beyond the neighbourhood where it began.

Its commercial success has not been without controversy: critics have accused parts of the industry of glorifying violence and materialism, and some of the genre's pioneers have complained that the music they created has been commercialized beyond recognition.

Yet the story of hip-hop remains a striking testament to the creativity of young people with very few resources, and to the capacity of a marginalized community to invent something that the whole world would eventually imitate.
When protest movements spread across several countries in the early 2010s, social media was widely credited with making them possible.
Activists could organize demonstrations within hours, share footage that governments wanted to suppress and reach millions of sympathizers without relying on newspapers or television.
Some commentators predicted that digital technology would inevitably and permanently shift power from states to citizens.
A decade later, the picture looks considerably more complicated.

Digital tools have undeniably lowered the cost of participation: signing an online petition, sharing a post or joining a boycott requires almost no effort, and campaigns that once took years to build can now attract global attention within days.
But critics argue that the ease of online participation is precisely its weakness.
The term "slacktivism" describes the tendency to support a cause through gestures that make people feel involved without requiring any real commitment or risk.
The sociologist Zeynep Tufekci has offered a more nuanced analysis.
Movements that grow rapidly online, she argues, often skip the slow, tedious work of building organizations: holding meetings, resolving disagreements, developing leaders and agreeing on demands.
As a result, they can mobilize enormous crowds but struggle to negotiate, to adapt their tactics or to survive the moment when public attention moves elsewhere.
Earlier movements, which had to organize without such tools, were slower to grow but frequently more resilient.
Governments have also learned to use the same technology.
Authoritarian states monitor online activity to identify activists, flood social media with propaganda and occasionally shut down the internet entirely during periods of unrest.
The same platforms that allow a protest to be organized also create a detailed record of who took part in it.
None of this means that digital activism is ineffective.

Online campaigns have exposed injustices, raised money for disaster relief and forced companies to change their policies, and for marginalized groups they can provide visibility that traditional media long denied them.

The most successful movements, however, tend to combine online advocacy with the patient work of offline organizing, using the internet to attract attention and traditional methods to turn that attention into lasting change.
In little more than a decade, the smartphone has transformed childhood in wealthy countries.
Most children now receive their first phone before they reach secondary school, and many adolescents spend several hours a day on social media, games and video platforms.
Over the same period, rates of anxiety and depression among teenagers have risen in several countries, and a vigorous debate has developed about whether the two trends are connected.
Those who believe that smartphones are responsible point to the timing.
The rise in mental health problems among young people accelerated around 2012, roughly when smartphones with front-facing cameras became widespread and social media moved onto mobile devices.

They argue that constant comparison with carefully edited images of other people's lives damages self-esteem, particularly among girls, and that notifications designed to capture attention disrupt sleep, concentration and face-to-face friendships.
Other researchers are considerably more skeptical of the empirical evidence.

They point out that most of the evidence is correlational: it shows that heavy users of social media tend to be less happy, but not whether social media causes unhappiness or unhappy teenagers simply spend more time online.
In several large studies, the statistical association between screen time and wellbeing turned out to be very small, comparable in size to the association between wellbeing and eating potatoes.
These researchers warn against a moral panic of the kind that previously greeted novels, radio, television and video games.
Faced with uncertain evidence, policymakers have nevertheless begun to act.
Several countries, notably France, have banned phones in schools, arguing that even if the effects on mental health are disputed, the effects on concentration in lessons are not.
Some parents have made collective agreements not to give their children smartphones until a certain age, so that no child is excluded for being the only one without a phone.
Perhaps the most defensible position combines caution with humility.

The evidence may not justify the claim that smartphones have destroyed a generation, but it does suggest that the quality of children's online experiences matters more than the quantity, and that devices designed to maximize engagement are not neutral tools.
Children, after all, did not design these technologies; adults did, and it is adults who bear the responsibility for deciding how, and when, children should use them.

In 2015, a consortium of some two hundred and seventy researchers published the results of an ambitious project: they had attempted to repeat a hundred studies previously published in leading psychology journals.
Fewer than half of the replications produced results consistent with the originals, and even where effects reappeared, they were typically about half as large as first reported.

The findings, which came to be known as the replication crisis, prompted a profound and often uncomfortable reassessment of scholarly practice, not only in psychology but in medicine, economics and several other fields.
Outright fabrication of data turned out to be rare.
The more pervasive problem lay in a set of practices that were widespread, largely tolerated and, taken individually, ostensibly innocent.

Researchers might collect data until a result reached statistical significance and then stop, test many variables and selectively report only those that produced a striking effect, or formulate their hypothesis only after seeing the data, while presenting it as if it had been predicted in advance.
Critics call this last habit hypothesizing after the results are known.
Each of these choices increases the probability of a spurious result, or false positive, and in combination they can make almost any hypothesis appear to be confirmed.
Studies that relied on correlation rather than randomized experiments were especially vulnerable, since a correlation, however striking, need not reflect any causal relationship.
The underlying cause was a system of incentives that rewarded novelty over rigour, and the discrepancy between the two was rarely discussed.

Journals preferred surprising, positive findings, careers depended on publication in those journals, and studies that failed to find an effect were seldom published at all, so that the scholarly record came to overstate systematically the strength of the evidence.

The episode that did much to trigger public skepticism was the publication, in a respected journal, of a series of experiments by the psychologist Daryl Bem that purported to show that people could anticipate future events.
The methodology was entirely conventional; that, precisely, was the problem.
The response has been remarkably constructive.

Many researchers now preregister their studies, publicly recording their hypothesis, sample size and planned analysis before collecting any data, so that subsequent deviation from the plan is visible.
Some journals have adopted formats in which studies are accepted on the basis of their design, before the results are known, thereby removing the incentive to produce dramatic findings.
Large, collaborative replications across many laboratories have become routine, and data are increasingly shared openly, so that others can validate or challenge an analysis.
It would be a mistake to conclude that psychology, or science more generally, is unreliable.

The crisis was identified by scientists themselves, using the methods of science, and the reforms it provoked are, in a sense, a demonstration of the self-correcting capacity that distinguishes scientific inquiry from other ways of knowing.

But it offers a salutary warning about the gap between the ideal and the practice of research, and about the ease with which intelligent, honest people can deceive themselves when their careers depend on finding what they hope to find.
In a footnote to The Open Society and Its Enemies, published in 1945, the philosopher Karl Popper formulated what he called the paradox of tolerance.
Unlimited tolerance, he argued, must lead to the disappearance of tolerance, since a society that tolerates even those who would destroy it will eventually be destroyed by them.

Written in the aftermath of a war in which intolerant movements had exploited democratic freedoms in order to abolish them and install totalitarian rule, the observation carried an obvious and painful force.
Popper's conclusion is often quoted, but less often read with care.

He did not suggest that intolerant opinions should be suppressed as a matter of course; on the contrary, he insisted that as long as they could be countered by rational argument and kept in check by public opinion, suppression would be unwise.

The right to suppress arose, in his view, only when intolerant movements refused to engage in argument at all, forbade their followers to listen to reason and resorted to violence in place of persuasion.
The distinction is between intolerant ideas, which a confident society can afford to answer, and intolerant action, which it cannot afford to permit.
In practice, drawing that line is far from straightforward.

Contemporary debates about hate speech, misinformation, the regulation of online platforms and the proscription of extremist parties all turn on the question of when rhetoric becomes a form of action, and reasonable people disagree profoundly about the answer.
Some argue that speech which dehumanizes a group of people is inherently a precursor to violence, and that its propagation should therefore be restricted before the harm occurs.

Others, following John Stuart Mill, contend that the suppression of opinion is almost always futile and frequently counterproductive, since it deprives society of the opportunity to refute error and lends martyrdom to those it silences.
A further difficulty is that the concept of intolerance can itself be deployed strategically.

Movements across the political spectrum have learned to present their opponents as the intolerant ones, whose exclusion is therefore justified, and a principle intended as a narrow safeguard of last resort can easily become a pretext for silencing ordinary, if contentious, dissent.
In deeply divisive times, the temptation to treat every opponent as an enemy of the open society is considerable.
What Popper's paradox ultimately offers is not a rule but a discipline.
It reminds pluralistic societies that tolerance is not the same as indifference, and that its survival may occasionally require difficult choices.

But it also implies that such choices should be rare, reluctant and justified by genuine threats rather than by discomfort, since a society that suppresses too readily has already begun to abandon the principle it claims to defend.
When the financial crisis of 2008 turned into a recession, policymakers across the developed world initially responded in the manner recommended by John Maynard Keynes.
They cut taxes, increased spending and allowed their deficits to grow, in the hope of sustaining demand while private spending collapsed.
Within two years, however, the prevailing mood had changed.

Alarmed by rising public debt and by the crisis in Greece, which could no longer borrow at affordable rates, many governments embarked on programmes of austerity, cutting discretionary public spending and raising taxes in an attempt to restore the confidence of financial markets.
The theoretical justification rested on a contested proposition: that reducing deficits would, by reassuring investors and lowering interest rates, stimulate rather than depress economic activity.
Critics countered that the size of the fiscal multiplier, the amount by which a reduction in government spending shrinks the economy, is not constant.
It is particularly large, they argued, when interest rates are already close to zero and the private sector is reluctant to spend.

In 2013, economists at the International Monetary Fund, which had supported many austerity programmes, published an unusually candid analysis acknowledging that it had systematically underestimated the damage such policies would cause.
The consequences were most severe in the countries subjected to the most stringent conditions.
Greece, whose successive bailouts were conditional on dramatic cuts, experienced a downturn comparable in scale to the Great Depression.
Its economy shrank by roughly a quarter, and unemployment exceeded a quarter of the workforce, reaching more than half among the young.
State property was sold off in a hurried programme of privatization, and repeated cuts to pensions left many pensioners in a precarious position.
Because the economy shrank faster than the debt, the ratio of debt to national income actually rose, which rather undermined the rationale for the policy in the first place.
The political aftermath has proved at least as significant as the economic one.

Austerity was frequently presented as a technical necessity, beyond the reach of democratic choice, and its costs fell disproportionately on those most dependent on public services, while the bankers widely blamed for the crisis appeared to escape relatively lightly.

Several studies have linked the resulting discontent to the subsequent rise of populist parties in Europe, as voters turned against incumbent governments and the established parties that had implemented the cuts.
None of this settles the underlying question, which is genuinely difficult.
Governments cannot borrow indefinitely, and there are circumstances in which a loss of market confidence leaves them with few alternatives.

The more modest lesson of the austerity decade is that the timing of fiscal consolidation matters enormously, that its distribution matters just as much, and that economic policies presented as unavoidable tend, sooner or later, to provoke a political reckoning.
Reading is, in evolutionary terms, an astonishingly recent invention.
Writing systems appeared little more than five thousand years ago, and for most of that period only a small minority of people could read.
