Natural selection, therefore, cannot have produced a region of the brain dedicated to the task.
How, then, does a child's brain acquire so complex a skill in a few years?
The neuroscientist Stanislas Dehaene has proposed an influential answer, which he calls neuronal recycling: reading colonizes circuits that evolved for other purposes and repurposes them.
Brain imaging reveals that, in literate adults, written words activate a small area on the underside of the left hemisphere that in illiterate people responds predominantly to faces and objects.

As a child learns to read, this region becomes specialized for the recognition of letters and their combinations, in effect competing with, and partially displacing, the face recognition that previously occupied it.

From there, the visual encoding of a word is connected to the brain's existing networks for spoken language, so that written symbols come to evoke sounds and, through them, the semantic knowledge stored elsewhere in the brain.

The whole process relies on a cognitive system of remarkable speed: a proficient reader identifies a familiar word and completes the retrieval of its meaning in a fraction of a second, apparently without effort.
This account has practical implications for teaching.

Children arrive at school having absorbed since infancy thousands of spoken words and much of the grammatical structure of their language; what they lack is a way of connecting print to this existing knowledge.
The ability to hear the separate sounds within words, known as phonological awareness, is a prerequisite for making that connection.
Because reading depends on linking letters to the sounds of speech, methods that teach these correspondences explicitly and systematically are consistently more effective for beginners.
Such methods, known as phonics, outperform approaches that encourage children to recognize whole words by their shape or to guess them from context.

The evidence for this conclusion, drawn from longitudinal studies and randomized trials, is among the most robust in educational research, although the debate between rival approaches has been conducted, at times, with an intensity more suggestive of dogma than of science.
The same framework illuminates dyslexia, a persistent and often congenital difficulty in learning to read that affects a substantial minority of children regardless of intelligence.

In most cases, the underlying problem appears to lie not in vision but in the ability to discern the individual sounds of speech, which makes the connection between letters and sounds unusually difficult to establish.

Intensive intervention during the formative early years of schooling, focusing on the links between letters and sounds, can substantially improve outcomes, which is why early screening, to ascertain which children are at risk, is increasingly recommended.
Perhaps the most striking implication of this research is how profoundly literacy reshapes the brain itself.

Adults who learn to read late in life show many of the same changes as children, which demonstrates that the adult brain retains considerable plasticity and that literacy can transform cognition at any age.

But the intrinsic difficulty of the task also explains why so many children struggle, and why, in a society that assumes universal literacy, the failure to teach reading well is not merely an educational shortcoming but a profound injustice.
Earthquakes do not, on the whole, kill people; buildings do.
The overwhelming majority of deaths in a major earthquake are caused by the collapse of structures, which is why two earthquakes of comparable magnitude can produce radically different casualties.

In 2010, an earthquake near Port-au-Prince in Haiti killed well over a hundred thousand people; a few weeks later, an earthquake in Chile that released several hundred times more energy killed fewer than a thousand.
The difference lay predominantly in the quality of construction and in the enforcement of building codes.
Many of the buildings that collapsed in Port-au-Prince were built of unreinforced masonry or of concrete slabs containing too little steel.
Understanding why buildings fail requires an appreciation of the forces involved.
Seismic waves shake the ground horizontally and vertically, and a building responds by swaying, its upper floors lagging behind the movement of its foundations.

Every structure has a natural frequency at which it tends to vibrate, and if this coincides with the frequency of the ground motion, the amplitude of the oscillations can grow dramatically, a phenomenon known as resonance.

Local geology and topography also matter: soft, waterlogged soils can amplify shaking considerably and may even lose their strength altogether, behaving temporarily like a liquid and causing buildings to tilt or sink.
The central principle of earthquake engineering is not rigidity but controlled flexibility.
A structure of excessive stiffness may crack suddenly under stress, whereas one designed to bend can absorb and dissipate the kinetic energy of the shaking without catastrophic failure.

Reinforced concrete must therefore contain carefully arranged steel bars that lend it a degree of elasticity, allowing it to deform without disintegrating, and the connections between beams and columns, which are particularly vulnerable, require meticulous detailing.

More sophisticated techniques include base isolation, in which a building rests on flexible bearings that decouple it from the ground, and large dampers that counteract swaying; the skyscraper Taipei 101 contains a spherical steel mass weighing more than six hundred tonnes suspended near its top for precisely this purpose.
The technical knowledge to build safely is, for the most part, well established; the obstacles are economic and political.
Stringent building codes raise construction costs, and in poor countries with rapidly growing cities, much construction is informal and escapes regulation entirely.

Even in wealthy countries, retrofitting older buildings is expensive and disruptive, and because major earthquakes are rare in any particular place and their timing is not foreseeable, the precaution tends to be postponed until a calamity makes it too late.

Japan offers the most instructive counterexample: successive disasters have produced some of the strictest codes in the world and a remarkable culture of preparedness, and the devastation caused by each earthquake has been used, systematically, to improve the next generation of buildings.
For more than a thousand years after the collapse of the Western Roman Empire, a Christian, Greek-speaking state that called itself Roman ruled from the city of Constantinople.

Western historians later named it the Byzantine Empire, and for centuries the adjective carried connotations of decadence and needless complexity, as though the empire had been little more than an elaborate epilogue to the classical world.
Posterity, in short, was unkind, and only recent scholarship has substantially revised that verdict.
Byzantium's longevity was itself an extraordinary achievement.

Constantinople, a bastion protected by massive land walls and by its position on a peninsula between two seas, withstood repeated sieges by Persians, Arabs, Bulgarians and Russians, and for much of the medieval period it was the largest and wealthiest city in Europe.

The empire preserved a sophisticated bureaucracy, a system of law codified under the emperor Justinian that later shaped legal traditions across Europe, and a cosmopolitan culture in which merchants, scholars and diplomats from three continents mingled.
The Hagia Sophia, completed in 537, remained the largest church in the world for almost a thousand years, and its gilded mosaics still astonish visitors today.
In a devout society, religion was central to Byzantine identity and, frequently, to its internal strife.
Theological disputes about the nature of Christ, which may seem arcane to modern observers, divided the population, provoked riots and shaped imperial policy.
What one emperor defended as true doctrine, his successor might condemn as heresy.

During the eighth and ninth centuries, a movement known as iconoclasm led emperors to prohibit religious images, which its supporters regarded as idolatry, and the destruction that followed deprived later generations of much of the empire's early art.
Relations with the papal authorities in Rome deteriorated steadily, and in 1054 the Eastern and Western churches formally separated.
The most devastating blow came not from Muslim armies but from fellow Christians.
In 1204, the soldiers of the Fourth Crusade, diverted from their original objective by Venetian commercial interests and a disputed claim to the throne, captured and plundered Constantinople.
The empire was eventually restored, but in a diminished form, and it never recovered its former strength before the Ottomans finally captured the city in 1453.
The crusaders carried off relics and treasures, among them four bronze horses that can still be seen in Venice.
Yet Byzantium did not simply disappear.

Greek scholars who fled westward carried classical manuscripts, many preserved for centuries in monastic libraries, that contributed to the Italian Renaissance, and the Orthodox Church, which the empire had nurtured and whose senior patriarch still resides in Istanbul, spread its liturgy, its art and its alphabet across Eastern Europe.
Russian rulers subsequently claimed Moscow as the "Third Rome", the legitimate heir of Constantinople, and the Ottoman sultans who conquered the city adopted many of its administrative practices.

The empire that Western historians once dismissed as a byword for decay proves, on closer inspection, to have been one of the great civilizations of history, and one whose influence persists, often unrecognized, in the religious and political cultures of much of the modern world.

In 1958, the British sociologist Michael Young published a satirical novel entitled The Rise of the Meritocracy, in which he imagined a future Britain where social position was determined entirely by intelligence and effort.
Young intended the word he coined as a warning, yet within a generation it had become an aspiration, embraced by politicians of every persuasion as the epitome of a fair society.
Few principles seem less contentious: what could be more equitable than rewarding people according to merit rather than birth?
The difficulty, as Young foresaw, is that merit is not distributed independently of privilege.
Affluent parents can purchase tutoring, coaching and admission to schools that confer lasting advantages, and the children of graduates are markedly more likely to become graduates themselves.
At dozens of selective American colleges, more students come from the richest one per cent of families than from the poorest sixty per cent.
A system that claims to reward talent thus tends, over time, to entrench the very inequalities it was supposed to dismantle.
The philosopher Michael Sandel has argued that meritocracy damages not only equality but also the moral outlook of winners and losers alike.
Those who succeed are encouraged to believe that their success is wholly their own achievement, and therefore rightful, which breeds a certain contempt for those who have not.

Those who fail, conversely, are told that their position reflects their own shortcomings, a verdict more humiliating than the frank injustice of an aristocratic order, in which nobody pretended that the poor deserved their poverty.
Sandel links the resulting resentment to the populist revolts of recent years, in which voters without degrees turned against a governing class that seemed to regard them with condescension.
The legal scholar Daniel Markovits adds a further twist: meritocracy, he contends, harms even its apparent beneficiaries.
Elite professionals work exhausting hours to justify their status, and their children endure a relentless competition that begins in infancy and consumes the whole of adolescence.
The prize is real, but the price is a life organized around the pursuit of credentials rather than intrinsic interests.
None of this implies that positions should be allocated arbitrarily, or that competence is irrelevant; nobody wishes to be operated on by a surgeon chosen at random.

Rather, critics propose that societies should moderate the rewards attached to success, broaden the routes to a dignified life beyond the university, and cultivate a certain humility about the role of luck.

Sandel has even suggested that the most oversubscribed universities should choose among qualified applicants by lottery, precisely to puncture the illusion that the winners have earned every advantage.
Merit may be indispensable, but a society that worships it risks mistaking good fortune for virtue.
Almost every digital service now asks for our consent before collecting our data, and almost nobody reads what they are consenting to.

Privacy policies are notoriously long and opaque, written in impenetrable legal jargon, and one widely cited estimate suggested that reading every policy an ordinary internet user encounters would take several weeks a year.
The ritual of clicking "I agree" has become so habitual that it is difficult to regard it as a meaningful choice at all.
The model of notice and consent rests on a presumption borrowed from contract law: that individuals are the best judges of their own interests and can weigh the costs and benefits of disclosure.
But the conditions that make consent meaningful in other contexts are largely absent here.

Consent is valid, philosophers argue, only when it is informed, voluntary and specific, whereas data collection is typically invisible, bundled with services that are difficult to refuse, and put to uses that were not foreseeable when the box was ticked.
In effect, users routinely waive rights they barely know they possess.
The deeper difficulty is that the harms of data collection are frequently collective rather than individual.

Through aggregation, information that is innocuous in isolation can reveal a great deal, and data disclosed by one person can expose others who never consented: a relative's genetic test, for example, implicates the whole family.
Even metadata, the record of whom one contacted and when, can map a person's relationships without disclosing the content of a single message.

Anonymity offers less protection than is commonly supposed, since researchers have repeatedly shown that supposedly anonymous records can be traced back to identifiable individuals by combining a handful of details.
The practice is insidious precisely because it is invisible.
European regulators have attempted to strengthen consent rather than abandon it.

The General Data Protection Regulation, which took effect in 2018, requires consent to be freely given, specific and unambiguous, and it prohibits companies from making access to a service conditional on unnecessary data collection.

Yet its most conspicuous consequence for ordinary users has been a proliferation of cookie banners, many designed with manipulative techniques that make refusal more laborious than acceptance, while companies adept at exploiting loopholes continue their intrusive tracking.
Enforcement, moreover, has been patchy.
For this reason, a growing number of scholars argue that the burden should shift from individuals to institutions.

Rather than asking people to police their own privacy, the law could simply forbid certain practices outright, regardless of consent, just as it forbids the sale of unsafe food even to willing customers.
It could also restrict the dissemination of especially sensitive categories of information, such as health records, and penalize data gathered surreptitiously.
Consent would retain a role, but a more modest one, confined to choices that individuals are genuinely equipped to make.
The question is not whether people should control their data, but whether a click can bear the moral weight that we have placed upon it.
When we begin a novel, we tend to extend a certain trust to the voice that tells it.

Much fiction depends on verisimilitude, the impression that the events described could really have occurred, and we assume, unless given reason to think otherwise, that the gaps in the account are gaps in knowledge rather than deliberate omissions.

The critic Wayne Booth, writing in 1961, called a narrator unreliable when the narrator's values and perceptions diverge from those implied by the work as a whole, so that the reader comes to understand more than the teller does.
The device is as old as storytelling, but modern fiction has exploited it with particular sophistication.
Unreliability takes several distinct forms.

Some narrators are deliberately deceptive: in Agatha Christie's The Murder of Roger Ackroyd, published in 1926, the doctor who narrates the investigation turns out to be the murderer, having omitted his own crucial actions without ever stating anything strictly false.
The novel provoked outrage among readers who felt that the rules of the genre had been violated, and it remains a textbook case of narration that is technically accurate yet profoundly misleading.

Other narrators are unreliable because they are naive or disturbed; the narrator of Poe's "The Tell-Tale Heart" insists on his sanity with an idiosyncratic precision that progressively demonstrates its absence.
The most subtle cases involve self-deception.

Stevens, the butler who narrates Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, recounts his decades of service to an aristocrat who sympathized with the Nazis, and his account is punctuated by reflections on dignity that reveal, implicitly, how much he has chosen not to see.
His restraint is so complete that the emotional catastrophe of the novel, a love he never acknowledged, is conveyed almost entirely through what he leaves out.
The reader's task is to reconstruct the story that lies beneath the story, attending to textual clues that the narrator cannot control.
Nabokov's Lolita presents the most troubling variation.
Its narrator, Humbert Humbert, is an articulate predator whose eloquence is itself an instrument of manipulation, and whose allusions to poetry and myth lend his crimes a spurious glamour.
The novel's notoriety derives partly from the discomfort of being seduced, sentence by sentence, by a voice one ought to find abhorrent.
Readers who fail to resist his rhetoric risk becoming complicit in his self-justification, which is precisely the moral test the novel sets.
Why should unreliability hold such fascination?
One answer is that it dramatizes something true of all narration: every account of events is partial, shaped by the interests, blind spots and preconceptions of the person telling it.
By making this partiality visible, the unreliable narrator trains readers in a skepticism that extends well beyond fiction, to memoirs, political speeches and the stories we tell about ourselves.
It is, in a sense, a lesson in the ethics of listening.
The pharmaceutical company Purdue Pharma launched OxyContin, a slow-release form of the opioid oxycodone, in 1996, with one of the most aggressive marketing campaigns in the history of medicine.

Sales representatives assured doctors that the risk of addiction among patients treated for pain was minimal, citing as evidence a brief letter published in a medical journal in 1980 that had never been intended to support such a conclusion.

Within a few years, prescriptions had multiplied, and the drug had become notorious in the mining communities of Appalachia, where manual labour, chronic injury and economic decline created a vast market for pain relief.
In the language of epidemiology, the ensuing crisis arrived in three waves.

The first was driven by prescription painkillers, and the second, from around 2010, by heroin, as a crackdown on overprescribing pushed people who were already dependent towards cheaper illicit drugs.
The third, from around 2013, was driven by fentanyl, a synthetic opioid of such potency that a quantity the size of a few grains of salt can prove fatal.

Because fentanyl is cheap to manufacture and easy to smuggle, it has increasingly been mixed into other drugs and pressed into counterfeit pills, often without the knowledge of the people who take them.
In 2021 alone, more than a hundred thousand Americans died of drug overdoses, the majority of them involving opioids.
The epidemic cannot be blamed on a single company, but the role of the manufacturers has been the subject of protracted litigation.

Purdue pleaded guilty to federal charges of misleading the public in 2007 and again in 2020, and members of the Sackler family, who owned the company, agreed to contribute billions of dollars towards a settlement, although its terms were contested in the courts for years.
Distributors and pharmacy chains, which shipped enormous quantities of pills to small towns without raising the alarm, have also paid substantial sums.
Critics argue that regulators were negligent, and that the close ties between the Food and Drug Administration and the industry compromised their judgement.
The response has been hampered by the stigma attached to addiction.
For decades, dependence was treated primarily as a moral failing and a matter for the police, and the incarceration of users did little to reduce either consumption or deaths.

Medical evidence, by contrast, strongly supports a regimen of substitute medication such as methadone or buprenorphine, which reduces cravings and markedly lowers the risk of death, yet in many areas such treatment remains inaccessible, subject to stringent rules or simply unaffordable.
Naloxone, a drug that can reverse an overdose within minutes, has become more widely available, and its distribution to police officers, teachers and families has saved countless lives.
The opioid epidemic is, in one sense, a story of corporate malpractice and regulatory failure.
But its geography points to deeper causes: the communities most afflicted are often those that have suffered prolonged economic decline, the loss of stable employment and the erosion of social ties.
The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton have grouped overdoses with suicides and alcohol-related illnesses as "deaths of despair".
Tackling the supply of drugs is necessary, but without addressing the conditions that make them so appealing, it is unlikely to be sufficient.
During the late Middle Ages, the Church sold indulgences, certificates that promised to reduce the punishment that sinners would otherwise suffer after death.
The trade became so lucrative, and so open to abuse, that in 1517 it provoked the famous protest of Martin Luther and, ultimately, the Reformation.
Critics of carbon offsets have not been slow to draw the comparison.

An offset allows a company or an individual to compensate for its own emissions by paying for an equivalent reduction elsewhere, such as the protection of a forest or the replacement of smoky stoves in poor households, and the resulting credits are traded in a burgeoning market worth billions of dollars a year.
The principle is not absurd.

Carbon dioxide mixes rapidly in the atmosphere, so a tonne avoided in Indonesia has the same effect on the climate as a tonne avoided in London, and reductions are often far cheaper in some places than in others.
In theory, offsets channel money towards the cheapest available cuts, including the protection of forests whose stewardship might otherwise be unaffordable for the communities that depend on them.
For emissions that are genuinely difficult to eliminate, such as those from long-haul aviation or cement production, some form of compensation may be unavoidable.
The practice, however, is rife with difficulties.

The first is additionality: an offset is meaningful only if the reduction would not have happened anyway, yet it is intrinsically difficult to prove what would have occurred in a hypothetical world without the payment.
Projects that protect forests which were never actually threatened generate spurious credits, and developers have strong incentives to overstate the danger.

The second is permanence: carbon stored in trees returns to the atmosphere if the forest burns, and in 2021 wildfires in the western United States consumed forests that had already been used to generate offsets.
The third is leakage: protecting one forest may simply displace logging to another.

An investigation published in 2023 concluded that most of the rainforest credits approved by the largest certification body were unlikely to represent genuine reductions, a finding the organization vigorously disputed, and the market remains opaque, dominated by intermediaries whose fees absorb much of the money.
Beyond these technical problems lies a moral objection.

By allowing the affluent to continue polluting with a clear conscience, offsets may delay the structural changes that the climate crisis requires, and they can lend credibility to corporate pledges of neutrality that are, on closer inspection, largely cosmetic.
Just as indulgences were said to encourage sin by making absolution purchasable, offsets may encourage emissions by making them appear costless, turning carbon into one more tradable commodity.
There is also a question of justice when projects in poor countries restrict the land use of marginalized communities in order to compensate for the consumption of wealthy ones.
Defenders of offsets acknowledge many of these failings but argue that the remedy is reform rather than abolition.

They propose more stringent verification, a shift from avoided emissions to the physical removal of carbon from the air, and a change in the claims that buyers may make, so that companies describe their purchases as contributions to climate finance rather than as proof of neutrality.
Most climate scientists agree on a hierarchy: emissions should first be reduced as far as possible, and offsets reserved for the residual emissions that cannot yet be eliminated.
Used in this way, offsets may play a modest role; used as a substitute for reduction, they risk becoming, like the indulgences of old, a way of purchasing peace of mind rather than salvation.
For most of the history of art, painters did not attempt to represent space as it appears to a single observer, nor did they prize verisimilitude in the modern sense.
Egyptian artists depicted each part of the body from its most characteristic angle, and medieval painters sized figures according to their spiritual importance rather than their position.
Even the illusionistic frescoes of ancient Rome, though often convincing in their spatial effects, lacked a single consistent system.

The technique that we now take for granted, linear perspective, in which parallel lines converge towards a vanishing point and objects diminish in size with distance, was devised in Florence in the early fifteenth century.
According to his early biographer, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated the method, some time around 1415, with an ingenious experiment.
He painted a small panel depicting the Baptistery of Florence and drilled a hole through its centre.
Viewers stood in the doorway of the cathedral opposite, looked through the hole from the back of the panel and saw the painting reflected in a mirror held at arm's length.
When the mirror was lowered, the real building appeared in exactly the same place, and the correspondence between image and reality was so precise that observers could hardly discern any difference.
To heighten the effect, he covered the sky of the panel with burnished silver, so that it reflected the actual clouds drifting overhead.
The method was set down in 1435 by the humanist Leon Battista Alberti, whose seminal treatise On Painting described a picture as an open window through which the viewer looks at the world.

Alberti explained how to construct a grid of lines, perpendicular to the surface of the picture, converging on a central point at the height of the viewer's eye, so that figures and buildings could be placed within a coherent, measurable space.
The method spread rapidly, and within a generation it had become a prerequisite of ambitious painting.
Masaccio's fresco of the Holy Trinity, painted around 1427 in the church of Santa Maria Novella, shows the effect at its most arresting.
A painted vault with perfectly symmetrical panels appears to recede into the flat wall, so convincingly that early viewers are said to have believed a chapel had been cut into the masonry.
Perspective was more than a technical trick.
It embodied a new conception of the relationship between the individual and the world, in which space was homogeneous, infinite and governed by geometry.
This space was organized around the gaze of a human observer, with every object, from the foreground to the horizon, assigned its exact place.

In 1927, the art historian Erwin Panofsky argued that perspective was therefore not a neutral discovery about vision but a symbolic form, a cultural convention that expressed the rational, anthropocentric outlook of the Renaissance.
The system rests, after all, on a paradoxical abstraction: it assumes a viewer with a single motionless eye, whereas real human vision uses two eyes that are constantly moving.
Other artistic traditions made different choices, and not out of ignorance.

Chinese landscape painters often employed a shifting viewpoint that allows the eye to travel through a scroll, as though walking through the mountains, rather than freezing the scene from one position.
Japanese printmakers, for their part, used oblique projections in which parallel lines never meet at all.
In Europe itself, the dominance of perspective lasted roughly four and a half centuries before the Cubists dismantled it, breaking objects into multiple simultaneous viewpoints.

Yet it has survived in another form, reproduced mechanically by the camera: every photograph and every video game constructs its image according to the principles that Brunelleschi demonstrated with a mirror in a Florentine doorway.
Autonomous weapons, systems that can select and attack targets without further intervention by a human operator, are no longer confined to science fiction.

Defensive systems that automatically shoot down incoming missiles and projectiles have existed for decades, and advances in artificial intelligence have made it possible to extend such autonomy to drones, vehicles and ships.
A United Nations report on the conflict in Libya suggested in 2021 that a drone may have attacked retreating fighters without any direct human command, possibly the first such incident on record.
Proponents advance several arguments in their favour.

Machines do not panic, seek revenge or act out of hatred, and some engineers contend that, properly designed, they could adhere to the laws of war more consistently than exhausted and frightened soldiers.

Speed is another attraction: in a battle fought between swarms of drones, the latency introduced by waiting for a human decision could prove fatal, and a state that refused to automate might find itself at a decisive disadvantage.
From this perspective, autonomy is simply the latest stage in a long history of military innovation, analogous to the introduction of the rifle or the aircraft.
Critics raise objections of three kinds.

The first is technical: identifying a legitimate target requires judgement about context and intention that current systems lack, since a farmer carrying a rifle and an insurgent carrying a rifle may look identical to a camera, and an erroneous classification cannot be undone.

The second concerns accountability: if a machine commits what would, in a human, be a war crime, it is unclear whether responsibility lies with the commander who deployed it, the programmer who wrote its software or the company that sold it, and this diffusion of blame may leave victims without recourse.

The third is moral: many argue that the decision to take a human life should never be delegated to an algorithm, since doing so treats the person killed as an object to be processed rather than a human being whose death demands justification.
There is also a strategic danger.
Because autonomous systems can be relatively cheap, their proliferation could place formidable firepower in the hands of small states, paramilitary groups and terrorists.
Interactions between rival systems operating at machine speed could escalate a minor incident into a full conflict before any human had time to intervene.
Stability between rivals depends on the ability to signal intentions and to pause, both of which become harder when decisions are compressed into milliseconds.
Since 2014, diplomats have discussed the issue within a United Nations framework, but progress has been slow.

Dozens of states and many human rights organizations support a binding treaty that would prohibit systems operating without meaningful human control, while several major military powers prefer voluntary guidelines, arguing that a ban could not be verified and would merely hinder responsible states.
A few governments have announced unilateral restrictions on their own forces, but these commitments are easily reversed.
The history of arms control offers some encouragement: chemical weapons were outlawed after their use in the First World War, and blinding lasers were banned before they were ever deployed.
Whether the same can be achieved for autonomous weapons, whose underlying technology is ubiquitous in civilian life, is far less certain.
According to a puzzle recounted by the Greek writer Plutarch, the Athenians preserved the ship of the hero Theseus as a venerable relic.
As each plank rotted, it was replaced, until no original timber remained.
Was it still the same ship?
And if someone had gathered the discarded planks and reassembled them, which of the two vessels would have the better claim to be the original?
The puzzle seems like an idle curiosity until one notices that human beings are in an analogous position.
Most of the cells in our bodies are replaced many times over a lifetime, and our beliefs, tastes and memories change almost beyond recognition between infancy and old age.

The philosopher John Locke, writing in the late seventeenth century, posited that personal identity consists not in the continuity of a body or a soul but in the continuity of consciousness, and above all of memory.
Locke deliberately avoided metaphysical speculation about the soul: I am the same person as the child who broke a window forty years ago, on his view, because I can remember doing so from the inside.
The theory has considerable intuitive appeal, since it explains why, in hypothetical stories in which two people exchange bodies, we tend to say that each person goes wherever their memories go.
But it faces an obvious objection: we forget most of our past, and it would be an absurdity to conclude that a person who suffers total amnesia has thereby ceased to exist.
The Scottish philosopher Thomas Reid offered an ingenious counterexample.
Imagine a brave officer who, as a boy, was beaten for stealing apples, and who, as an elderly general, remembers his heroism as a young officer but has forgotten the beating entirely.
By Locke's criterion, the general is the officer and the officer is the boy, yet the general is not the boy.
This violates the logical axiom that if A is identical to B and B to C, then A must be identical to C.

Later philosophers sought to reconcile the theory with this objection by replacing direct memory with overlapping chains of psychological connection, so that identity could persist through sequential stages even where no single memory spans the whole.

The most radical contribution came from Derek Parfit, one of the most eminent moral philosophers of his generation, who asked his readers to contemplate a hypothetical teleporter that scans a person's body, destroys it and constructs an exact replica on Mars.
Is the traveller transported, or killed and replaced by a stranger who merely believes himself to be the original?
Such thought experiments were designed to unravel our most confident intuitions.

Parfit then imagined a malfunction in which the original survives alongside the replica, and argued that since both would be psychologically continuous with the person who stepped into the machine, the question of which one was really him may be intrinsically empty.

His paradoxical conclusion was that personal identity is not what matters: what we should care about is the continuity of our memories, intentions and character, whether or not that continuity preserves a single, indivisible self.
Parfit found this conclusion liberating rather than troubling.
Once he ceased to regard his existence as a deep further fact, he wrote, he felt less imprisoned by his own life and less troubled by the morbid thought of his death.
He also noted the resemblance between his view and the Buddhist doctrine that the self is an illusion.
Many philosophers remain unconvinced, insisting on our embodiment: we are, fundamentally, living organisms, and our identity is a matter of biology rather than psychology.
The debate is unresolved, but it matters beyond the seminar room, since much of our moral and legal thinking presupposes a stable self.
We punish people for crimes committed decades ago, hold them to promises made in youth, and argue about the moral status of embryos and of patients with dementia.
Imagine a pasture open to all the herders of a village.
Each herder receives the full benefit of adding one more animal to the common land, since the profit accrues to him alone, while the cost of the resulting overgrazing is shared among everyone.
Rational individuals, each pursuing their own interest, will therefore keep adding animals until the pasture is destroyed, even though all of them would have been better off with restraint.
The biologist Garrett Hardin set out this parable in a celebrated essay published in 1968, concluding that freedom in a commons brings ruin to all.
The logic applies wherever a resource is valuable, finite and difficult to fence off.
Fisheries are the classic case: each fleet has an incentive to catch as much as possible before its rivals do, and as scarcity increases the race only intensifies.

The cod stocks of the Grand Banks off Newfoundland, once among the richest fishing grounds on Earth, collapsed so completely in the early 1990s that the Canadian government imposed a moratorium that put tens of thousands of people out of work.

Groundwater, forests and the atmosphere itself, into which every nation releases carbon while bearing only a fraction of the consequences, display the same structure, which economists describe as a negative externality.
Hardin saw only two remedies.

The commons could be privatized, so that each owner bore the full cost of misuse, or it could be regulated by the state, which would impose enforceable limits through what he called mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon.

Both remedies have been widely applied, and both have their merits: tradable fishing quotas, for example, have helped some stocks to recover by allotting each boat a fixed share of the permitted catch.

But privatization can exclude the poorest users, who may depend on common resources for their subsistence, and distant governments frequently lack the local knowledge that effective regulation requires.
The political scientist Elinor Ostrom, who in 2009 became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in economics, challenged the assumption that there were only two options.

Studying communities from Swiss alpine meadows to Japanese forests and Spanish irrigation systems, she documented numerous cases in which users had managed shared resources for centuries, without either privatization or central control.
In the Swiss village of Törbel, for instance, a rule dating from 1517 forbade any villager to send more cows to the summer pastures than he could feed through the winter.

Ostrom identified the conditions that such arrangements tend to share: clearly defined boundaries, rules devised by the users themselves, monitoring by people answerable to the community, graduated penalties for those who break the rules, and cheap ways of resolving disputes, a form of stewardship that was neither private nor public.
Her work showed that Hardin's model rested on a stark individualism, and that he had conflated two different situations.
What he described was not a commons in the historical sense, a resource governed by a community with its own customs, but an open-access resource that nobody governs at all.

The tragedy, in other words, is not inevitable: it arises when trust, communication and reciprocal obligations break down, or when a resource is so vast, like the oceans or the atmosphere, that the cohesion of a small community cannot be reproduced.
That, perhaps, is the most sobering lesson for a world whose most pressing problems concern precisely such global commons.
As recently as 1870, European powers controlled roughly a tenth of the African continent, most of it in coastal enclaves and mercantile outposts.
By 1914, they controlled almost all of it: only Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.
The speed and scale of this colonization, which contemporaries called the scramble for Africa, have few parallels in history, and its consequences continue to shape the politics of the continent.
Historians have long debated its causes.

Economic explanations emphasize the demand of industrializing Europe for commodities such as rubber, palm oil and minerals, and for new markets, although many colonies ultimately proved less profitable than their advocates had promised.

Political explanations stress the rivalry among the European powers, for whom annexing territory became a matter of prestige, and the fear that any region left unclaimed would be seized by a competitor.

Ideology supplied a pretext: imperialism was presented as a civilizing mission, and missionaries and campaigners against the slave trade, whose aims were ostensibly humanitarian, lent the enterprise an air of moral purpose.

Technology made it feasible: quinine reduced deaths from malaria among Europeans, steamships carried them up the rivers into the interior, and the machine gun gave small colonial forces overwhelming firepower.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885, convened by the German chancellor Otto von Bismarck, is often said to have divided Africa among the Europeans.

In fact, it did something more modest but equally revealing: it established rules by which claims to African territory would be recognized, requiring that a power demonstrate effective occupation before others were obliged to respect its claim.
Not a single African was present.

The borders that emerged over the following decades were negotiated in European capitals, often drawn arbitrarily along lines of latitude and longitude, and they frequently divided peoples who shared a language and culture while enclosing rivals within a single territory.
Colonial rule was imposed and maintained by coercion, and in some places its brutality was extreme.

In the Congo, which King Leopold II of Belgium governed as his personal possession from 1885 to 1908, a system of forced labour for the extraction of rubber relied on heinous methods, including hostage-taking, mutilation and murder, and millions of people are thought to have died from violence, starvation and disease.

In German South West Africa, now Namibia, the suppression of a Herero and Nama uprising between 1904 and 1908 left survivors in camps where many died in abject conditions, and it is now widely regarded as the first genocide of the twentieth century, a description the German government formally accepted in 2021.
Where European colonists settled in large numbers, as in Kenya and southern Africa, the seizure of land left grievances that endured long after independence.
Such episodes were not aberrations but the logical extremes of a system founded on the premise that African lives and labour could be commandeered for European purposes.
African resistance was persistent and sometimes successful.

At the battle of Adwa in 1896, the Ethiopian army inflicted a decisive defeat on an Italian invasion force, preserving the country's independence and inspiring defiant anti-colonial movements across the continent.

When the colonies won independence, mostly in the 1950s and 1960s, the new states inherited the colonial borders, and in 1964 the Organisation of African Unity resolved to respect them, reasoning that any attempt to redraw them would unleash endless conflict.

The decision preserved a fragile stability, but it also fixed frontiers that bore little relation to the societies they enclosed, a legacy of colonialism whose effects, from secession movements to disputes over resources, are still felt.

For much of the twentieth century, even small American towns supported a daily or weekly newspaper that reported on council meetings, court cases, school boards and local businesses, news that may seem parochial but on which local democracy depends.
Since 2005, the United States has lost more than a third of its newspapers, and the number of journalists working for them has fallen by roughly two thirds.

Researchers now speak of news deserts: communities, home to millions of people, with no reliable source of local news at all, and in rural areas where the population is sparse, entire counties have no newspaper.
The collapse was not primarily caused by a decline in readers' interest, but by the disintegration of a business model.
Local newspapers had depended on advertising, particularly classified advertisements for jobs, homes and cars, which migrated rapidly to free websites in the early years of the internet.

Advertisers then shifted their spending to search engines and social media platforms, which could target consumers with a precision that no newspaper could match, and which now absorb a disproportionate share of all advertising revenue.

Many surviving papers were acquired by investment funds and media conglomerates that treated them as declining assets, and a steady attrition of newsroom staff preserved profitability while the titles withered.
The consequences for democratic accountability have been measurable.
One study found that when a local newspaper closed, the cost of borrowing for the local government subsequently rose, apparently because lenders regarded its finances as less closely watched.

Other research has linked closures to lower turnout in local elections, to fewer candidates standing for office, and to higher rates of corruption, since officials who know that no reporter will attend their meetings face less pressure to behave well.

Journalists have traditionally cultivated informants within local institutions, obtained documents through public records requests and sat through the tedious hearings at which consequential decisions are made, and no algorithm performs these functions.
The decline of local news has also altered political behaviour.

As readers turn instead to national outlets, which cover politics as a contest between two parties, local elections become nationalized, and voters increasingly choose local officials according to their national party rather than their record on potholes, schools and planning.
Scholars have found that split-ticket voting, in which voters support candidates from different parties for different offices, declines after local papers close, a sign of growing polarization.

Meanwhile, the vacuum is often filled by partisan websites designed to resemble local newspapers, whose dissemination of thinly disguised propaganda and misinformation is difficult for readers to detect.
No single remedy has emerged.
Nonprofit newsrooms, funded by philanthropic foundations and readers' donations, have multiplied, although they remain concentrated in affluent cities and precarious in their finances.

Some governments have begun to subsidize local journalism directly or through tax credits, and in Britain the public broadcaster funds reporters placed in local news organizations to cover councils and courts.
Critics warn that public money may compromise journalistic independence, but proponents reply that the alternative, a democracy in which nobody is watching, is considerably worse.
Few debates in contemporary culture generate as much heat, or as little agreement, as the one over cultural appropriation.

The term refers to the adoption of elements of one culture, such as its clothing, music, symbols or rituals, by members of another, and it is used most pointedly when the borrowing culture is dominant and the source culture has been marginalized.
Critics regard such borrowing as a form of exploitation, while defenders see it as the ordinary process by which cultures have always evolved.
In multicultural societies, where the boundaries between communities are constantly negotiated, the question has become especially contentious.
The history of popular music offers a vivid illustration.

The Black singer Big Mama Thornton had a hit with "Hound Dog" in 1953, for which she received a tiny share of the royalties; three years later, Elvis Presley's version sold millions and helped make him the most famous entertainer in the world.
For many critics, the episode typifies a recurrent pattern in an industry segregated by race, in which Black musicians created styles that white performers emulated and profited from.
The objection is not to the music being shared, but to the unequal distribution of recognition and remuneration.
A second concern involves objects of religious or ceremonial significance.

Feathered headdresses, which in several Native American nations are earned through acts of courage and worn only by particular individuals, became a fashionable accessory at music festivals, prompting several festivals, after an outcry from Native American groups, to ban them.
To wear one as a costume, critics argue, is comparable to wearing a military medal one has not earned: it turns something that others hold sacred into an object of mockery.

In 2015, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston invited visitors to try on a copy of a kimono in front of Claude Monet's painting La Japonaise, and the protests that followed, which accused the museum of treating Japanese culture as an exotic costume, led it to modify the event.
Defenders of cultural exchange raise several objections.

All cultures are hybrids, formed by centuries of trade, migration and conquest, and many of the achievements we most admire, from jazz to the cuisines of the world, are products of precisely the kind of diffusion and synthesis that the critique of appropriation seems to condemn.
Pablo Picasso's encounter with African sculpture transformed Western art; few would now wish that it had never happened.

There is also a philosophical difficulty: the concept presupposes that cultures are homogeneous entities with clear boundaries and recognized spokespeople, whereas in reality they are internally diverse and contested, and nobody has the authority to grant or refuse permission on behalf of millions.

Demands for authenticity can also trap minorities in static images of themselves, and some writers worry that the argument, taken to its extreme, would confine artists to their own backgrounds and encourage a parochial and insular conception of identity.
A more productive approach may be to ask not whether borrowing occurs, since it always has, but how it occurs.

Borrowing that acknowledges its sources, that involves genuine engagement rather than superficial imitation, that shares its rewards with the communities from which it draws, and that respects what is considered sacred is generally regarded as appreciation rather than appropriation.
Such distinctions will not settle every case, and reasonable people will continue to disagree about particular examples.
But they shift the debate from the question of ownership, which is intractable, to questions of acknowledgement, reciprocal benefit and power, which can at least be discussed.

Everything that astronomers have ever seen through their telescopes, every star, planet, cloud of interstellar gas and luminous galaxy, appears to account for only a small fraction of the matter in the universe.
The rest, which neither emits nor absorbs light, is known as dark matter, and although its gravitational effects are detectable almost everywhere, no experiment has yet ascertained what it is.
It is one of the strangest puzzles in modern science: the dominant form of matter in the cosmos has never been directly observed.

The first hint came in 1933, when the Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured the speeds of galaxies within a distant cluster and found that they were moving far too fast to be held together by the gravity of their visible stars.
Zwicky posited the existence of an invisible dark matter, but his conjecture was largely ignored for four decades.
During the 1970s, the American astronomer Vera Rubin, working with Kent Ford, found a similar discrepancy within individual galaxies.
Stars at the periphery were orbiting just as fast as those near the centre, whereas, if most of the mass were concentrated in the visible core, they should have moved much more slowly.
The simplest explanation was that each galaxy was embedded in a vast, roughly spherical halo of unseen matter.
Since then, the evidence has accumulated from several independent directions.

Because mass produces a curvature of space itself, massive objects bend the paths of light passing near them, a phenomenon predicted by Einstein and known as gravitational lensing, and the degree of bending around clusters of galaxies implies far more mass than can be seen.

In one celebrated case, two clusters that collided left their hot gas, which contains most of their ordinary matter, in the middle, while the bulk of the mass, mapped by lensing, passed straight through, exactly as dark matter would be expected to behave.

Measurements of the faint radiation left over from the early universe suggest that, to a first approximation, ordinary matter makes up only about five per cent of its total content, dark matter roughly twenty-seven per cent, and an even more mysterious dark energy the remainder.
What could dark matter be?
For decades, the favoured hypothesis was a new kind of heavy particle that interacts with ordinary matter only through gravity and the weakest of other forces.

Physicists have built extraordinarily sensitive detectors, shielded from cosmic rays in deep mines, in the hope of catching the rare collision of such a particle with an atomic nucleus, and particle colliders have searched for signs of it as well.
So far, none has been found, and the parameters within which the favoured candidates could still exist have narrowed considerably.
Other candidates, from extremely light particles to black holes formed in the first moments of the universe, remain under investigation.
A minority of physicists draw a more radical conclusion: perhaps there is no dark matter at all, and the laws of gravity themselves require modification at very low accelerations.

This approach, first proposed in 1983, reproduces the rotation of galaxies with remarkable economy, but it struggles to account for the behaviour of colliding clusters and the pattern of radiation from the early universe.
The dispute illustrates a recurrent dilemma in science: when observations deviate from theory, one may either posit an unseen entity or revise the theory, and history offers examples of both.

Neptune was discovered in 1846 because astronomers inferred its existence from irregularities in the orbit of Uranus, but the odd orbit of Mercury was explained not by a hypothetical planet called Vulcan, as some expected, but by the new theory of gravity that Einstein published in 1915.
Whether dark matter proves to be a Neptune or a Vulcan remains, for now, an open question.
Shortly before Christmas in 1954, a small group of devout believers gathered in a suburban house in the American Midwest to await the end of the world.

Their leader had received what she believed were messages from a distant planet announcing that a great flood would destroy the continent, and that the faithful would be rescued by a flying saucer at midnight.
Among the group, unknown to its members, were several social psychologists who had infiltrated it in order to observe what would happen when the prophecy proved unfounded.

Midnight came and went, and no saucer arrived, yet instead of abandoning their beliefs, the most committed members began, for the first time, to seek publicity and to recruit new followers with remarkable zeal, as if converts could supply the affirmation that events had denied.
One of the observers, Leon Festinger, developed from such episodes a theory that has become one of the most influential in social psychology.

When people hold two cognitions that are psychologically inconsistent, such as "I am a sensible person" and "I have given up everything for a prophecy that proved false", they experience an unpleasant tension, which he called cognitive dissonance, and the tension is commensurate with the importance of the beliefs at stake.

Since the facts cannot be changed, the easiest way to restore consistency is often to find a more palatable interpretation of them, and the believers duly concluded, with a certain audacity, that their devotion had saved the world from destruction.
Paradoxically, the greater the sacrifice a belief has required, the more tenaciously it tends to be defended.
Festinger and his colleague James Carlsmith tested the theory in a famous experiment in 1959.
Students spent an hour performing tedious, repetitive tasks, such as turning pegs on a board, and were then asked to tell the next participant that the tasks had been enjoyable.
Some were paid one dollar for telling this lie and others twenty dollars, a considerable sum at the time.
Afterwards, those who had been paid only a dollar rated the tasks as markedly more enjoyable than those who had received twenty.

The explanation, according to Festinger, was that twenty dollars provided a sufficient reason for lying, whereas one dollar did not, so the poorly paid students resolved the discrepancy between their words and their experience by changing their opinion of the task.
Later research extended the theory in several directions.
People who endure an unpleasant initiation to join a group tend to value the group more highly than those admitted without effort, as if to vindicate the price they have paid.
After making a difficult choice between two attractive options, people typically inflate the merits of the option they chose and disparage the one they rejected.

Smokers who cannot quit find reasons to regard the evidence about the dangers of smoking as erroneous or exaggerated, and staunch partisans who support a politician through a scandal often become more, not less, loyal, since admitting error would imply that their earlier judgement was flawed.
The theory also illuminates the aversion of the powerful to apologizing: to acknowledge a serious mistake is to accept a cognition, "I did harm", that contradicts a cherished self-image.
Not every finding has survived intact.

Some psychologists have argued that people are less troubled by inconsistency than the theory assumes, and that many dissonance effects can be explained more simply: people infer their attitudes from their own behaviour, much as they would infer the attitudes of others.
Several classic experiments have also proved difficult to replicate, and the size of the effects may have been overstated.
Nevertheless, the core insight remains widely accepted, and it carries an uncomfortable implication.

The capacity for self-justification is not a failing peculiar to fanatics but an ordinary feature of human cognition, and the people most confident of their own rationality may be those least equipped to notice it at work.
Between the 1960s and the 1990s, the political scientist Robert Putnam observed, more Americans went bowling than ever before, but fewer of them did so in organized leagues.
The image of the solitary bowler became the emblem of a much larger argument, which he set out in his book Bowling Alone, published in 2000.
The dense network of clubs, associations and informal gatherings that had once knit American communities together, he argued, was unravelling.
Membership of parent-teacher associations, trade unions, fraternal societies and religious congregations had suffered a steady attrition.
People also entertained friends at home, attended public meetings and signed petitions less often than their parents had.

Putnam's central concept was social capital: the networks of relationships, together with the norms of reciprocal obligation and trust they sustain, that enable people to cooperate for mutual benefit.

Like physical and human capital, he argued, social capital is productive, creating conditions conducive to cooperation: communities rich in it tend to have safer streets, healthier residents, better schools and more responsive government.

His earlier study of Italian regional governments had found that the regions of the north, with long traditions of civic association, were governed markedly better than those of the south, even when they received the same powers and resources.

Putnam distinguished between bonding capital, which strengthens ties within a homogeneous group, and bridging capital, which connects people across social divides, and he suggested that the latter is rarer and more valuable to a pluralistic democracy.
Putnam identified several causes of the decline, and he attempted to estimate their relative weight.

Suburban sprawl and longer commutes played a part, as did the pressures of work and the entry of women into the labour force, which removed much of the unpaid effort on which voluntary associations had depended.
Television was a more significant culprit: each additional hour spent watching it correlated with less involvement in almost every form of civic activity.
But the largest factor was generational.

An unusually civic-minded generation, shaped by the Depression and the Second World War, was gradually replaced by children and grandchildren who, for reasons that are still debated, joined less, trusted less and voted less.
The thesis provoked a vigorous debate.

Some critics argued that Putnam had mistaken the transformation of civic life for its disappearance: people had not succumbed to apathy but were associating in new forms, through informal networks, campaign groups and, later, online communities that his measures failed to capture.

Others pointed out that many of the associations whose decline he lamented had been exclusionary, segregated by race and gender, and that nostalgia for a lost golden age of community risked idealizing a society that had been anything but egalitarian.
His later research suggesting that ethnic diversity is associated, at least in the short term, with lower levels of trust among neighbours proved especially contentious.
Putnam himself insisted that the challenge was to build new, more inclusive forms of solidarity rather than to reduce diversity.
Whatever the precise causes, the question Putnam raised has only grown more pressing.

Measures of loneliness, of distrust in institutions and of weakening social cohesion have risen in many wealthy societies, and the online platforms that promised to connect people have often fostered insular communities of the like-minded rather than bridges between them.

In a more recent book, Putnam described twentieth-century America as moving from individualism to community and back again, and argued that the earlier upswing had been deliberately built by reformers.
If social capital was constructed once, he suggested, it can be constructed again, but only by people willing to show up.
Imagine two drivers who, on the same evening, drink the same amount, climb into their cars and drive home equally carelessly.
One arrives home without incident; the other, through no additional fault of her own, hits a child who runs into the road.

Most of us would judge the second driver far more harshly, and the law in most countries would impose a far more punitive sentence, yet the only difference between the two lies in circumstances that neither controlled, a matter of pure happenstance.

The philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, writing in 1976, called this phenomenon moral luck, and it poses a serious challenge to some of our most cherished assumptions about responsibility.
According to a principle that seems almost axiomatic, people should be judged only for what is within their control.
Immanuel Kant expressed it memorably when he wrote that a good will would shine like a jewel, valuable intrinsically, even if, through some misfortune, it accomplished nothing at all.
If this principle is correct, the two drivers deserve identical reproach, and to punish the unlucky one more severely is to distribute blame arbitrarily, however natural the instinct may be.
Yet the principle, taken seriously, threatens to dissolve moral judgement altogether, since almost everything we do depends on factors we did not choose.
Nagel distinguished several kinds of luck.
Resultant luck concerns the way our actions turn out, as in the case of the drivers.

Circumstantial luck concerns the situations we happen to face: under the Nazis, many ordinary Germans became perpetrators or accomplices of heinous crimes that, had their parents emigrated a few years earlier, they would never have had the opportunity to commit.
Constitutive luck concerns the kind of person we are, our temperament, inclinations and capacities, which are shaped by genes and upbringing long before we are able to reflect on them.
If we subtract everything attributable to luck of these kinds, very little seems to remain of the agent who is supposed to be responsible.
Williams offered a more provocative example, loosely based on the painter Paul Gauguin, who abandoned his family in order to devote himself to art in the South Pacific.
Whether his decision was justified, Williams suggested, may depend on something he could not know when he made it: whether he would succeed in becoming a great painter.
If he failed, he would be left with no vindication for the harm he had caused, and if he succeeded, the achievement might, in some sense, justify it after the event.
The suggestion that success can confer justification in retrospect struck many readers as troubling, but it captures something familiar: we do judge ambitious gambles by their outcomes.

Williams also observed that a lorry driver who, through no fault of his own, runs over a child will feel remorseful in a way that a mere spectator would not, and will find little solace in being told that he was not to blame.
Philosophers have responded in three broad ways.

Some insist, with Kant, that luck is morally irrelevant, so that the careless driver who arrives safely is exactly as blameworthy as the one who kills; the law's unequal treatment then becomes a practical concession, perhaps justified by its deterrent effect or by the demand of victims' families for retribution commensurate with the harm done.
Others accept moral luck as an ineliminable feature of the moral life, and argue that the demand for a purely luck-free morality reflects an illusion of complete self-control.

A third group distinguishes between blame, which should track only what agents control, and other moral responses, such as regret and the obligation to make amends, which may legitimately extend to outcomes.

None of these positions is entirely comfortable, which may be the most instructive lesson of the debate: our concept of responsibility combines paradoxical intuitions that no theory has yet fully reconciled.
An Italian proverb, traduttore, traditore, puns on the similarity between the words for translator and traitor.
The joke expresses a suspicion as old as translation itself: that anyone who carries a text from one language into another must betray it in some respect.
Words that denote the same object may connote quite different things, and grammatical features such as gender or degrees of politeness often have no exact counterparts elsewhere.

Every translator must therefore choose, sentence by sentence, which aspects of the original to preserve and which to sacrifice, and the history of translation is, in large part, a history of arguments about how those choices should be made.
The most enduring of these arguments concerns literal fidelity.
Cicero, and later Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into the Latin vernacular of his day, declared that they rendered not word for word but sense for sense.
A verbatim translation, they believed, would be clumsy and often unintelligible.

Yet Jerome made an exception for scripture, where, he said, even the order of the words is a mystery, and throughout the Middle Ages the sacred status of certain texts encouraged a literalism that sometimes produced barely grammatical prose.
In the twentieth century, the linguist Eugene Nida, who worked on Bible translation, set out an influential distinction in a treatise on the subject.
Formal equivalence mirrors the structure of the original, whereas dynamic equivalence aims to produce on modern readers the effect that the original produced on its first audience.
The opposite temptation is to sacrifice semantic precision to elegance.

Translations of classical authors produced in seventeenth-century France, smooth, polished and freely adapted to contemporary taste, became known as les belles infidèles, the beautiful unfaithful ones.
The phrase implies that beauty and fidelity are incompatible in translations as in women, an assumption that has not aged well.

In 1813, the German theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher framed the dilemma in terms that remain influential: the translator either leaves the author in peace and moves the reader towards him, or leaves the reader in peace and moves the author towards the reader.
The first approach produces translations that feel foreign, preserving the idiosyncratic syntax and cultural references of the original.
The second produces translations that read as if they had been written in the reader's own language, at the cost of assimilating the foreign text to local expectations.
Poetry presents the dilemma in its most acute form, since meaning in verse is inseparable from sound, rhythm and the lyrical qualities of the original.

When Vladimir Nabokov translated Alexander Pushkin's verse novel Eugene Onegin, he abandoned rhyme and metre altogether in favour of a strictly literal rendering, accompanied by a commentary of more than a thousand pages explaining every allusion, archaic word and colloquial nuance.
He argued that a rhymed translation inevitably distorts the sense, particularly since Russian, with its long polysyllabic words and flexible word order, rhymes far more easily than English.
Readers who wanted the music, he suggested, should learn Russian.

His critics, including his former friend Edmund Wilson, responded that the result was accurate but unreadable, and the ensuing quarrel became one of the most celebrated literary disputes of the century.
Machine translation has transformed the practical side of the profession, and for many purposes, from technical manuals to tourist menus, it now produces serviceable results.
Its limitations become apparent where meaning depends on tone, irony, idiomatic expression or cultural allusion, precisely the dimensions that literary translators spend most of their time weighing.

Every translation is, at best, an approximation, and no translator can fully reconcile fidelity and fluency, because the difficulty arises not from ignorance of vocabulary but from the irreducible difference between languages and the cultures they embody.
A good translation does not eliminate that difference; it negotiates it, and the negotiation is itself a form of interpretation.
The Nile has shaped the civilization of Egypt for more than five thousand years, and the country still depends on it for almost all of its fresh water.

Yet the great majority of the water that reaches Egypt does not originate there: it falls as seasonal rain on the highlands of Ethiopia, more than two thousand kilometres upstream, and flows down the Blue Nile to join the White Nile at Khartoum.

The topography of the basin makes the downstream states uniquely vulnerable, and when Ethiopia began building a vast hydroelectric dam on the Blue Nile in 2011, it touched the most sensitive nerve in the region's geography.
For Ethiopia, the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, as it is officially called, represents a national aspiration.
When construction began, more than half of the country's population lacked access to electricity.
The dam, designed to be the largest in Africa, promised to more than double the nation's generating capacity and to earn revenue from exports of power to its neighbours.

Because foreign lenders were reluctant to finance it amid the dispute, much of the cost was raised at home, through bonds bought by citizens and contributions deducted from the salaries of civil servants.
This made the project a potent symbol of self-reliance and a remedy for long-standing grievances.

Ethiopian officials also point out that colonial-era agreements, including a treaty of 1959 between Egypt and Sudan that allocated almost the entire flow of the river between them, were concluded without Ethiopia's participation and cannot bind it.
For Egypt, the dam represents an existential threat.

With a population of more than a hundred million, an arid climate and a rapidly growing demand for water, the country fears that any shortfall in the flow, particularly during the years in which the reservoir is being filled, could devastate the agrarian heartland of the Nile delta, where millions of smallholders farm for their subsistence.
Egyptian leaders have invoked historic rights to the river, and at moments of tension their rhetoric has been belligerent.
Occasional hints that military action could not be ruled out have threatened to escalate the dispute, although they have alternated with more conciliatory gestures.

Sudan, positioned between the two, has wavered: it stands to benefit from more regular flows and cheaper electricity, but it worries about the safety of its own dams if the operation of the structure upstream is not coordinated.
The legal principles that might resolve the dispute pull in different directions.

International water law affirms both the right of every state to an equitable and reasonable share of a shared river and the obligation not to cause significant harm to others, but it offers little guidance on how to reconcile the two when they conflict.
Years of protracted negotiations, mediated first by the United States and later by the African Union, have produced agreement on general principles but not on the questions that matter most.
These include how quickly the reservoir may be filled, how much water must be released during a prolonged drought, and whether the rules should be legally binding.
Egypt wanted any agreement to stipulate minimum releases, while Ethiopia resisted limits on the operation of its own dam.
In 2020, Ethiopia began filling the reservoir without a comprehensive agreement, a unilateral step that Egypt condemned.
The dam began generating electricity two years later.
The dispute is a striking example of a problem that climate change is likely to make more common.

Hundreds of river basins cross national borders, and many of them are contentious, since upstream states are building dams to meet surging demand for energy and irrigation while downstream states depend on a flow they cannot control.

Engineers note that, if operated cooperatively, the dam could benefit all three countries, since storing water in the cool Ethiopian highlands loses far less to evaporation than storing it in desert reservoirs further downstream.
In the posturing of all three governments, however, domestic politics has often taken precedence over technical compromise.

The obstacle is not hydrology but trust: an arrangement that would be mutually advantageous requires each party to believe that the others will honour it in a drought, when the temptation to act unilaterally will be greatest.
Some of the most admired companies of 1960s America were also the most incoherent.

ITT, originally a telephone company, acquired hundreds of businesses under its chief executive Harold Geneen, among them a chain of hotels, a car rental firm, an insurer and the bakery that made Wonder Bread.
Such conglomerates, which assembled disparate businesses under a single corporate roof, were celebrated as the triumph of professional management.
A skilled executive, it was believed, could run a bakery and an insurer with equal success.
Several arguments supported the model.
Diversification promised to smooth profits, since a downturn in one industry might be offset by growth in another.
Headquarters could allocate capital among its divisions more efficiently than outside investors, who knew less about them, and could exploit synergies by sharing expertise and distribution networks.
There were less flattering motives too.
In the United States, antitrust law made it difficult for large firms to buy competitors or suppliers, so ambitious managers expanded into unrelated fields instead.
Accounting conventions also rewarded acquisitions, because buying a company with a low share price relative to its earnings could make the buyer's own profits per share appear to grow.
By the 1970s, the flaws of the model had become apparent.
Shareholders did not need a conglomerate to diversify their risk, since they could do so far more cheaply by holding a range of shares.
The complexity of sprawling corporations also made them opaque to investors and difficult to manage, and markets began to value many conglomerates at less than the sum of their parts.
During the 1980s, financiers seized the opportunity: through leveraged buyouts, they acquired undervalued conglomerates with borrowed money, broke them up and sold the pieces at a profit.
Management theorists, meanwhile, urged companies to divest peripheral activities and concentrate on their core competences.
General Electric seemed to prove the exception.
Under Jack Welch, who ran it from 1981 to 2001, the company made jet engines, medical scanners and light bulbs, broadcast television programmes and operated a vast financial arm.
By the end of his tenure it was the most valuable company in the world.
Its fortunes reversed after the financial crisis of 2008, which exposed the risks concealed within its financial division.
Successive chief executives sold off much of the empire, and between 2023 and 2024 the company split into three separately listed businesses devoted to aviation, healthcare and energy.
Conglomerates have nevertheless flourished elsewhere.
In South Korea, family-controlled groups known as chaebol, such as Samsung and Hyundai, dominate the economy, and in India the Tata group makes products ranging from salt to software.
Economists explain their persistence by the weakness of institutions in developing economies.
Where capital markets are shallow, contracts are hard to enforce and skilled managers are scarce, a trusted group can provide finance, talent and reputation from within.
Critics counter that such groups can become too powerful, deterring new entrants and fostering cronyism between tycoons and politicians.
