The history of the conglomerate suggests that no corporate structure is intrinsically superior, and that its merits depend on the institutions that surround it.
Pain seems the most straightforward of sensations.
Touch a hot stove and it hurts; the harm is in the hand, and the hurt, we assume, is a direct measurement of it.

This was essentially the view of René Descartes, who in the seventeenth century compared the body to a machine in which fire tugging at the skin of the foot pulls a cord, a conduit that rings a bell in the brain.
The model has an appealing simplicity, but a century of research into the physiological basis of pain has shown that it is profoundly misleading.
Some of the earliest evidence came from the battlefield.
During the Second World War, the American anaesthetist Henry Beecher observed that many soldiers with appalling wounds reported little pain and declined morphine.
Civilians with comparable surgical wounds, by contrast, asked for relief far more often.
Beecher concluded that the meaning of an injury shapes the experience of it: for the soldier, a wound meant escape from the front and survival, while for the civilian it meant disruption and anxiety.
The intensity of pain, in other words, is not proportional to the extent of anatomical damage.
In 1965, the psychologist Ronald Melzack and the physiologist Patrick Wall proposed an influential explanation of such observations.
Signals from damaged tissue, they argued, pass through a kind of gate in the spinal cord, which can be opened or closed by other signals travelling from the body and down from the brain.
Rubbing a bruised elbow inhibits the transmission of pain signals, which is why the instinct to do so brings relief, and emotion and cognition can dampen or amplify the signal from above.

The details of the theory have been revised, but its central insight, the brain's constant modulation of incoming signals, has endured: pain is not simply received by the brain but actively constructed by it.
The most dramatic demonstration of this is phantom limb pain.
Most people who lose an arm or a leg continue to feel sensations in the missing limb, and many experience persistent, sometimes excruciating pain in a part of the body that no longer exists.
Some patients obtain relief when a mirror creates the illusion that the missing limb has returned, which suggests to neurologists that the pain arises from the brain's map of the body.
Chronic pain, from persistent backache to recurrent migraine, presents a subtler version of the same phenomenon.

In many patients, pain continues for months or years after the original injury has healed, because the nervous system itself has become sensitized, amplifying ordinary signals and generating pain without any ongoing damage.
Around one adult in five is thought to live with chronic pain, which makes it one of the leading causes of disability in the world.
These findings have profound implications for treatment.

Drugs that are effective for acute pain, such as opioids, frequently fail in chronic cases, and prolonged use can even increase sensitivity to pain, a paradoxical effect of which doctors are increasingly aware.
Instead, many specialists now recommend a holistic regimen combining gradual physical activity, psychological therapy and education about how pain works.
Such treatment can help patients to restore the calibration of an overprotective alarm system.
None of this means that chronic pain is imaginary; on the contrary, it is as real as any other experience the brain produces.

The rare people born with a congenital inability to feel pain, who often suffer fractures and burns without noticing and whose lifespan is frequently shortened, remind us why the alarm evolved in the first place.
Every year, more than two million people visit the former Nazi concentration and extermination camp at Auschwitz, in southern Poland.

Hundreds of thousands tour the eerie, abandoned city of Pripyat near Chernobyl, the site of the worst nuclear accident in history, and crowds gather at the memorial where the World Trade Center once stood.
In 1996, two scholars coined the term dark tourism to describe travel to places associated with death, disaster and atrocity.
The phenomenon has since become a significant industry, raising questions that are as much ethical as commercial.
The attraction is not new.
Within days of the Battle of Waterloo in 1815, sightseers were walking among the carnage and wreckage, and some collected teeth and buttons as souvenirs.
Victorian Parisians queued to view unidentified corpses displayed behind glass at the city morgue, and public executions drew enormous crowds until well into the nineteenth century.
What is new is the scale of the phenomenon, driven by cheap travel and social media, and the professionalization of the sites themselves, which now employ curators, guides and marketing departments.
Defenders of such tourism argue that it performs an indispensable moral function.
Standing in a gas chamber, hearing recorded eyewitness testimony or seeing the rows of shoes taken from victims conveys the reality of atrocity in a way that no textbook can.
Survivors of genocide have often been among the strongest advocates of such visits, precisely so that posterity cannot claim ignorance.

Commemoration, on this view, is an obligation owed to the dead, and bearing witness, even at a distance of generations, is a way of resisting the collective amnesia that allows history to repeat itself.
Tourism can also bring income to communities that have been devastated by disaster, and fund the preservation of remnants that might otherwise decay.
Critics worry that the line between remembrance and spectacle is easily crossed.

Visitors photographing themselves smiling at the entrance to Auschwitz, or posing in protective suits among the derelict buildings of Chernobyl, suggest that for some the experience offers a morbid thrill, a form of gratification rather than moral reflection.
The proliferation of gift shops, themed tours and dramatized reconstructions raises the concern that suffering is being turned into a commodity, packaged for consumption and stripped of its meaning.
There is also a subtler risk: that visitors leave with a sense of having discharged their moral duty, their curiosity satisfied, without any lasting change in understanding.
Much depends on how sites are managed and how visitors conduct themselves.
Many memorials have developed codes of etiquette, discouraging frivolous behaviour and designing exhibitions that place individual stories, rather than sensational horrors, at the centre.
Some sites, such as Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was imprisoned, present themselves as places of reconciliation as well as memory.
The motives of visitors are rarely pure, and a mixture of curiosity, empathy and even prurient fascination may be inescapable.
But the alternative, allowing such places to fall into oblivion, would arguably be worse, since what is not seen is more easily forgotten.
Jeremy Bentham, writing in 1789, began his most famous work with a bold declaration: nature has placed humanity under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.
From this premise he derived a principle of startling simplicity: the right action is the one that produces the greatest happiness for the greatest number.

Moral questions could therefore be settled by calculating the pleasures and pains that each option would cause, weighing their intensity, duration and certainty, and adding them up without regard to whose they were.
This doctrine, later called utilitarianism, has been among the most influential and most contested ideas in the history of ethics.
Utilitarianism began as a reforming creed.
Because it counted everyone's happiness equally, it was radically egalitarian, and Bentham used it to attack practices defended only by tradition.
He campaigned for the reform of a brutal penal code and argued for the extension of suffrage, and in an essay unpublished in his lifetime he defended the legalization of homosexuality.
He even extended moral concern beyond humanity: the question, he wrote, is not whether animals can reason or talk, but whether they can suffer.
His disciple John Stuart Mill tried to rescue the theory from the charge that it reduced human life to the pursuit of crude sensation.
Some pleasures, Mill argued, are intrinsically superior to others, so that it is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.

Critics replied that this distinction smuggled in values that pleasure alone could not justify, since it presupposes a standard, other than the quantity of happiness, by which pleasures can be ranked.
The most serious objections concern justice.
Imagine a surgeon with five patients who will die without organ transplants, and one healthy visitor whose organs would save them all.
A simple utilitarian calculation seems to recommend killing the visitor, a conclusion that almost everyone finds abhorrent.

The philosopher John Rawls argued in 1971 that utilitarianism fails to take seriously the separateness of persons, treating happiness as an aggregate whose maximization may require the sacrifice of some individuals for the benefit of others.
Its callous indifference to rights, critics say, treats society as though it were a single person balancing present pains against future pleasures.
Others object that the theory is excessively demanding: if every pound spent on luxuries could instead relieve suffering elsewhere, then almost every comfortable life is morally deplorable.
Utilitarians have responded by refining their theory.
Rule utilitarians argue that we should follow the rules whose general observance produces the most happiness, and a rule forbidding surgeons to kill their visitors plainly passes that test.

Others accept the demanding conclusion: the philosopher Peter Singer has argued since 1972 that affluent people are obliged to give much of their income to relieve poverty, an argument that inspired the effective altruism movement.
That movement has directed billions of dollars towards charities chosen for their measurable impact.
It suffered a severe blow in 2022, however, when a cryptocurrency exchange whose founder had publicly embraced its principles collapsed amid allegations of fraud.
The episode revived an old worry: that a doctrine which justifies means by their ends can be invoked to rationalize almost anything.
On a Friday in May 2017, staff at hospitals across England found that their computers had been locked, and messages on their screens demanded payment in Bitcoin in exchange for restoring their files.
The malicious software, known as WannaCry, spread within hours to more than two hundred thousand computers in some hundred and fifty countries.
In England alone, thousands of appointments and operations were cancelled, leaving a backlog that took weeks to clear, and ambulances were diverted from affected hospitals.
The American and British governments later blamed hackers working for North Korea, although attribution in cyberspace is notoriously difficult.
WannaCry was an example of ransomware, a form of cybercrime that has become one of the most lucrative on the internet.
The attackers infiltrate a network, often through a deceptive email or an unpatched flaw in widely used software.
They then encrypt its files so that they cannot be opened without a key that only the attackers possess.
Increasingly, they also steal sensitive data and threaten to publish it, a tactic known as double extortion, which ensures that even a victim with good backups has reason to pay.
Payment is typically demanded in cryptocurrency, which offers a degree of anonymity and can be moved across borders almost instantaneously.
What was once the work of isolated criminals has become an industry of considerable sophistication.
Developers now lease their software to affiliates, who carry out attacks in exchange for a share of the proceeds, and some criminal groups even operate help desks to assist their victims in paying.
Many of the most prolific groups are based in countries without extradition agreements with their victims' governments, which allows the perpetrators to operate with near impunity.
The flaw exploited by WannaCry had itself been discovered by an American intelligence agency, which kept it secret for its own use until the tool was stolen and leaked.
The episode fuelled a fierce debate about whether governments should disclose such weaknesses to the companies that could fix them.
The consequences of an attack can extend far beyond the victim.

In 2021, a crippling attack on the company that operates the largest fuel pipeline in the United States forced it to shut down for several days, prompting panic buying and shortages across the east coast.
The company paid a ransom of more than four million dollars, about half of which investigators later recovered by tracing the cryptocurrency.

The episode demonstrated that critical infrastructure, from power grids to water treatment plants, depends on computer systems designed with little thought for security, and that a single outage can cascade through an interconnected economy.
Whether victims should pay remains contentious.
Paying may be the quickest way to restore essential services, but it funds the criminals, encourages further attacks and offers no guarantee that stolen data will be deleted.
Some governments have proposed banning payments by public bodies, while critics warn that a ban could simply push payments underground or leave hospitals unable to function.

Specialists agree that prevention is far cheaper than cure: offline backups, prompt installation of security updates, stronger authentication and the separation of networks can greatly reduce the damage.
Yet many organizations still regard cybersecurity as a technical afterthought rather than a strategic priority, and until that changes, criminals will continue to find hapless targets.
When we think of fungi, we usually picture mushrooms, but a mushroom is to a fungus roughly what an apple is to an apple tree: a temporary structure for the dispersal of spores.

The main body of most fungi is a mycelium, a vast, interconnected mesh of microscopic threads that spreads through soil, wood or living tissue, competing with microbial rivals for nutrients as it grows.
Because it is hidden, this network is easy to overlook, yet fungi are among the most consequential organisms on Earth.
Their genealogy places them closer to animals than to plants, and they form a kingdom of their own, of which only a small fraction of the estimated species have been described.
Fungal networks can reach astonishing dimensions.

A single honey fungus in a forest in Oregon extends over nearly ten square kilometres and may be several thousand years old, which makes it a candidate for the largest living organism in the world by area, though not by biomass.
Its only conspicuous parts, clusters of mushrooms that appear each autumn at the base of the trees it slowly kills, give little indication of the labyrinth of threads beneath the surface.
Other species form dense mats through which water and nutrients travel as though through a system of pipes.
The most important role of fungi may be their partnership with plants.
The roots of the great majority of land plants are intertwined with fungi that supply water and minerals such as phosphorus in exchange for sugars that the plants produce through photosynthesis.

This reciprocal arrangement is ancient: fossils suggest that when plants first colonized the barren, primeval continents more than four hundred million years ago, fungi served as their roots before roots had evolved.

Some researchers have gone further, arguing that fungal networks connect neighbouring trees and allow them to exchange carbon and chemical signals, a so-called wood wide web through which older trees nurture seedlings.
The idea has captured the public imagination, but recent reviews have concluded that the evidence for such transfers in natural forests is weaker than popular accounts suggest.
Fungi are also the great recyclers of the living world, converting the residue of dead organisms into the inorganic nutrients on which plants depend.

Certain species are among the few organisms capable of breaking down lignin, the tough substance that gives wood its strength, and without them fallen trees would accumulate for centuries, locking away nutrients that other organisms need.

They have given humanity bread, beer and cheese through fermentation, and in 1928 a mould contaminating a laboratory dish led Alexander Fleming to the discovery of penicillin, the first widely used antibiotic.
Psychedelic compounds produced by some mushrooms are currently being tested as treatments for depression.
Not all of their effects are benign.

Parasitic fungi cause devastating blights in crops, and a fungus spread by the international trade in amphibians has contributed to the decline of hundreds of species of frogs and salamanders, many of them endemic to a single region.
It has driven dozens of species to extinction, making it one of the most destructive contagions ever recorded in wildlife.
Warmer temperatures may also allow fungal pathogens that currently cannot survive in the human body to adapt, a possibility that researchers in microbiology regard with growing concern.
The hidden kingdom, in other words, sustains much of life on Earth and threatens parts of it, and we understand remarkably little about either role.
The idea sounds, at first hearing, like a utopian fantasy: the state would pay every citizen a regular sum of money, enough to live on, with no conditions attached.
The affluent and the poor, the employed and the unemployed, would receive the same amount, and nobody would have to prove that they were looking for work.
Yet the proposal for a universal basic income has a long pedigree, and it has attracted egalitarian thinkers on the left as well as champions of the free market on the right.

Thomas Paine proposed a version of it in 1797, and in the 1960s the economist Milton Friedman advocated a related scheme, a negative income tax, under which people earning below a threshold would receive payments rather than pay tax.
Advocates advance several arguments.
Existing welfare systems are often complex and intrusive, and the bureaucrats who administer them must constantly police eligibility.
They also create perverse incentives: when benefits are withdrawn as earnings rise, a claimant who takes a low-paid job may be scarcely better off, a phenomenon known as the poverty trap.
A universal payment, which is never withdrawn, would eliminate this trap and the stigma attached to claiming.
It would also streamline a bewildering array of benefits into a single payment.

It would also recognize the value of work that earns no remuneration, such as caring for children or elderly relatives, and give workers greater bargaining power, since nobody would be forced by destitution to accept menial drudgery on any terms.
Some proponents argue that such a floor will become indispensable if machines automate large numbers of jobs.
The evidence from experiments is suggestive rather than conclusive.
Finland gave two thousand unemployed people a monthly payment of five hundred and sixty euros for two years, a sum that was not taxable and carried no obligation to seek work.
Recipients reported less stress and better health, while their employment rose only slightly.
In Stockton, California, a small programme that paid residents five hundred dollars a month found that recipients, many of whom held precarious jobs, spent the money mainly on food and bills.
Full-time employment among them rose faster than in a comparison group, contrary to the fear that free money would discourage work.
Alaska has paid every resident an annual payout from its oil revenues since 1982, apparently without reducing overall employment.
But these schemes were temporary, targeted or modest, and people who know a payment will end in two years may behave differently from those who expect it for life.
The most obvious objection is cost.

Paying every adult in a large economy an income sufficient to live on would require sums so sizable that they would far exceed the budgets of existing welfare programmes and necessitate substantial increases in taxation.
If the payment were set lower to make it affordable, it might be too meager to replace targeted benefits for people with disabilities or high housing costs, some of whom could end up worse off.

Economists also warn that where housing is scarce, landlords might capture much of the payment through higher rents, an inflationary effect that would erode its value and effectively subsidize property owners.

There is, finally, a moral objection: to pay people regardless of whether they contribute violates, for many, the principle that those who are able to work should do so in return for the support of the community.
The debate often turns less on economics than on competing visions of society.

Supporters see a basic income as a simple and transparent form of redistribution and an instrument of freedom, giving each individual the security to pursue education, care or creative work rather than mere subsistence.
Opponents see it as an expensive abandonment of the ideal of the self-reliant breadwinner, for whom work is a source of dignity as well as income.

Between these positions lies a range of intermediate options, from more generous child benefits to guaranteed payments for particular groups, which may prove more politically feasible than a full universal scheme.
When the original Pennsylvania Station in New York was demolished in 1963, many New Yorkers watched with disbelief.
The edifice, completed in 1910, had been modelled on the baths of ancient Rome, with a waiting room of monumental grandeur.

Its replacement was a cramped underground concourse beneath an office tower and an arena, and one architectural historian remarked that travellers had once entered the city like a god and now scuttled in like a rat.

The outrage led directly to the creation of a commission with powers to protect historic buildings, and in 1978 the Supreme Court upheld the city's right to prevent the owners of Grand Central Terminal from building a tower above it.
The case for preservation rests on several foundations.
Old buildings embody the craftsmanship, aspirations and memories of previous generations, and they give cities a distinctive character that homogeneous modern development rarely achieves.
Streets lined with venerable houses and ornate facades attract residents, tourists and investment, and visitors prize the authenticity of places that have evolved over centuries.
Their loss is irreversible: a demolished building cannot be recovered.

There is also an environmental argument, since the manufacture of new materials and the process of construction release large amounts of carbon, so that adapting an existing building is frequently greener than replacing it.
Critics of preservation argue that it has become excessively rigid.
In many prosperous cities, extensive historic districts restrict what can be built, worsening the scarcity of housing and contributing to prices that exclude all but the affluent.

Preservation rules can freeze a neighbourhood at an arbitrary moment in its history, sometimes out of nostalgia rather than architectural judgement, protecting buildings of modest merit while preventing the dense, lively development that cities need.
The practice of retaining a historic facade while demolishing everything behind it, which critics mock as architectural taxidermy, preserves the appearance of the past while destroying its substance.
Cities have always been remade.
In the middle of the nineteenth century, Baron Haussmann demolished much of medieval Paris to build broad boulevards, parks and sewers, displacing tens of thousands of poor residents.
The city that tourists now admire as timeless was, in its day, a brutal act of modernization.

Conversely, the historic centre of Warsaw, which German forces deliberately razed in 1944, was painstakingly reconstructed after the war, partly on the basis of eighteenth-century paintings, and is now a World Heritage Site.
Many cities that eagerly demolished their past for modernist towers and urban motorways in the 1960s later came to regret it.

These examples complicate any simple opposition between old and new: the admired Paris was once a demolition site, and the old town of Warsaw is younger than many of the buildings that preservationists elsewhere defend.
A growing number of architects advocate adaptive reuse as a way of reconciling the two imperatives.
London's Tate Modern occupies a former power station, and New York's High Line has transformed a derelict elevated railway into one of the city's most popular parks.
Such projects suggest that the real choice is not between freezing the city and erasing it, but between thoughtless destruction and a more discriminating form of change.
That form of change treats the existing fabric of the city as a resource rather than an obstacle.
Few ideas in popular psychology are as widely known, or as simplistic, as the five stages of grief: denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.
They were introduced in 1969 by the psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in her book On Death and Dying.
They have since been applied not only to bereavement but to divorce, redundancy and even the defeat of a sports team.

Hospitals, counsellors and films have presented them as a roadmap through loss, and many grieving people have worried that they are grieving incorrectly because their experience does not follow the sequence, a worry that compounds their heartbreak.
The origins of the model are rarely remembered.

Kübler-Ross developed it from interviews with patients who were themselves dying, not with people mourning the death of someone else, and she offered it as a description of common reactions rather than a prescriptive sequence.
Later in life she insisted that grief is nonlinear, and that few people pass through all the stages in order.
Her work had real merits: it helped to bring death out of the silence that surrounded it in mid-century medicine, and it encouraged doctors to listen to dying patients.
But its simplicity made it easy to misapply, and it hardened into a kind of dogma that the evidence never justified.
When researchers began to study bereaved people systematically, they found a far more varied picture.

The psychologist George Bonanno, following hundreds of widows and widowers over several years, concluded that the most common response to loss is not a prolonged passage through stages but resilience.
Most people experience intense sorrow, yet continue to function, and their distress gradually subsides within months.
A minority suffer grief that is clinically significant, sometimes for years, while some people actually feel relief after a death that ends a long period of caring for a sick relative.

A study of bereaved adults at Yale found that acceptance, supposedly the final stage, was the most commonly reported response from the first weeks, while the dominant painful emotion was not anger or denial but yearning, a bittersweet longing for the person who had died.
Grief for an estranged parent can be especially complicated, mingling loss with regret for a reconciliation that will now never happen.
Research has also challenged older assumptions about what healthy grief looks like.

Following Sigmund Freud, who distinguished normal mourning from pathological melancholy, many therapists believed that mourners had to detach themselves emotionally from the dead so that they could form new attachments.

More recent scholars argue that it is normal, and often a source of solace, to maintain a continuing bond with the deceased: talking to them, keeping their possessions, or consulting them in imagination at moments of decision.

Many cultures institutionalize such bonds through laments and rituals of commemoration, from the festivals at which Mexican families welcome the spirits of their dead to the annual visits to ancestral graves that are common across East Asia.
In cultures that prize stoicism, by contrast, mourners may feel pressure to recover quickly and to grieve in private.
Grief, on this view, is less a problem to be solved than an adaptation to a changed relationship.

In 2022, the American Psychiatric Association added prolonged grief disorder to its diagnostic manual, defining it as intense yearning or preoccupation with the dead person that persists for at least a year and impairs daily life.
Supporters argue that recognizing the condition will help the minority who suffer severely to obtain treatment, including specialized psychotherapy, which can be effective.
Critics fear that it risks turning a universal human experience into a pathology, and they note that distinguishing grief from depressive illness is not always straightforward.
Perhaps the most useful lesson of the research is a humble one: there is no single correct way to grieve, and the forms that grief takes are as idiosyncratic as the relationships it mourns.

Over the coming two decades, the generation born after the Second World War is expected to pass on an unprecedented quantity of wealth to its children, in the United States alone a sum estimated in the tens of trillions of dollars.
Much of it is held in houses, whose value has risen far faster than wages, so that for many younger adults an inheritance has become the most plausible route to owning a home.
The consequences will be felt not only in national economies but within families, where the division of an estate can reveal, and sometimes create, deep rifts.
Economists have long worried that inheritance undermines the principle that rewards should reflect effort.

The economist Thomas Piketty has shown that in nineteenth-century France, inherited wealth accounted for a large share of national income, before two world wars and the redistribution that followed diminished it.
He argues that it is now regaining its former importance.

In a society where inheritance matters more than earnings, the lottery of birth determines life chances, which sits uneasily with egalitarian ideals, and a hereditary elite can perpetuate itself indefinitely.

Even the industrialist Andrew Carnegie, one of the richest men of his era, declared that the man who dies rich dies disgraced, and believed that large bequests corrupted their beneficiaries, fostering indolence rather than enterprise.
Yet taxes on inheritance are among the most contentious of all levies, even among people who will never pay them.
In Britain, fewer than one estate in twenty is large enough to be taxable, but opinion polls consistently find majorities in favour of abolishing the tax.
Part of the explanation is emotional: the desire to provide for one's children is among the deepest human impulses, and a tax that falls at the moment of death strikes many as an intrusion on grief.

Part is practical: the wealthiest families can often reduce their liability through trusts, gifts and loopholes, so the burden falls disproportionately on the moderately affluent, whose wealth is concentrated in a single house.
Legal traditions differ sharply in how much freedom they allow.

English law permits people to leave their property to whomever they choose, subject to limited claims by dependants, whereas French law, following the Napoleonic Code, reserves a fixed share for each child, a rule originally intended to break up aristocratic estates.
Under either system, the division of an estate can become a stage on which familial grievances are replayed.

A sibling who spent years caring for a frail parent may feel entitled to a share commensurate with that sacrifice, while one who lived far away may regard anything other than an equal division as a verdict on the parent's love.
In families dominated by a powerful patriarch, a will can be a final instrument of control, and children estranged from a parent may discover that they have been left nothing at all.
Disputes over wills, once rare, have become markedly more common in several countries, and lawyers report that the most bitter are rarely about the money alone.
Mediators report that some families, confronted with the task of dividing an estate, find in it an occasion for reconciliation rather than conflict.
The investor Warren Buffett has said that he intended to leave his children enough to do anything, but not so much that they could do nothing.
His formula captures the ambivalence that surrounds inheritance: the wish to protect those we love, and the suspicion that unearned wealth can erode ambition as easily as it relieves hardship.
How societies and families resolve that tension will shape not only the distribution of wealth in the coming decades but the relationships between generations.
Apologizing seems the simplest of social acts, yet it is remarkably easy to do badly.
Politicians and corporations have developed an ingenious repertoire of euphemisms that resemble apologies while avoiding their substance.
"I am sorry if anyone was offended" regrets the reaction rather than the offence, and implicitly shifts responsibility onto the offended.

"Mistakes were made", a phrase used by more than one American president, deploys the passive voice to acknowledge an error without identifying anyone who made it, a construction so blatantly evasive that it has become proverbial.
The very ubiquity of such formulas attests to how much a genuine apology costs.
Researchers who have analysed apologies identify several elements that make them effective.
An apology must acknowledge the specific wrong, accept responsibility for it unequivocally, convey remorse that is palpable rather than formulaic, and, where possible, offer to repair the damage.
Explanations can help, but only if they do not slide into excuses or self-vindication; the moment an apology includes the word "but", it tends to lose its force.
Even a heartfelt apology can fail if it omits the essentials.
In one experimental study, participants rated acceptance of responsibility and an offer of repair as the most important components, while a request for forgiveness mattered least.
An apology is, in effect, a voluntary surrender of status: by admitting fault, the apologizer confers moral authority on the injured party, which is precisely why the powerful find it so difficult.
Public apologies by states for historical injustices have become increasingly common since the late twentieth century.

In 1970, the West German chancellor Willy Brandt, visiting the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto uprising, unexpectedly fell to his knees, a gesture whose spontaneity many Poles and Jews found more eloquent than any speech.

In 2008, the Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd apologized in parliament to the Stolen Generations, the Aboriginal children forcibly removed from their families under policies that lasted for much of the twentieth century.
It was a gesture of reconciliation that many had awaited for decades.
Such apologies cannot undo the past, but they can affirm a shared account of what happened, and they matter most to those whose grievances were previously denied.
An apology that arrives too late, however, may leave its recipients more indignant than consoled.
Their value depends heavily on consistency: an apology followed by officials who disparage its victims or deny the original wrong can do more harm than none at all.
The law has long discouraged apologies, since an admission of fault can be used against the apologizer in court.

In medicine, this created a culture in which doctors who made errors were advised by malpractice lawyers to say nothing, compounding the distress of patients who wanted above all an honest explanation.

Many American states have since passed laws that prevent expressions of sympathy from being used as proof of liability, and some hospitals have adopted programmes of full disclosure, in which errors are admitted promptly and compensation offered.
One university health system reported that after adopting such a programme, the number of lawsuits it faced and the cost of settling them fell substantially.
The difficulty of apologizing well reflects a tension between two human needs: to protect our reputation and to repair our relationships.
A good apology sacrifices the first for the second.

That is why apologies extracted under pressure, delivered in carefully vetted language or laced with innuendo about the victim's own conduct so often fail: they reveal that the speaker's priority remains his or her own image.
Nor does an abject display of self-reproach help, since it redirects attention to the feelings of the apologizer.
A simple, specific and unconditional apology, offered without calculation or posturing, can be one of the most magnanimous acts of which people are capable.
In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted with enormous force, injecting millions of tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere.

The gas formed tiny droplets of sulphuric acid that reflected a fraction of incoming sunlight back into space, and over the following year the average temperature of the planet fell by around half a degree.

Ever since, a small number of scientists have asked whether humanity might deliberately reproduce this effect to counteract global warming, by spraying reflective particles into the stratosphere from aircraft.
The proposal, known as solar geoengineering, has an audacity that makes it one of the most promising and most alarming ideas in climate policy.
Its appeal is easy to understand.

Despite decades of negotiations, the world continues to emit greenhouse gases at close to record levels and temperatures continue to rise inexorably, and even if emissions ceased tomorrow, the residual warming already locked in would continue to cause harm for decades.
Models suggest that a relatively modest injection of particles could offset a significant share of that warming, quickly and at a cost measured in billions rather than trillions of dollars a year.

For vulnerable countries, from arid regions facing calamitous heatwaves to low-lying islands threatened by rising seas, some argue that it would be irresponsible not to study an option that might reduce suffering in the decades before emissions fall.
The risks, however, are formidable, and some may be irreversible.
Dimming the sun would not remove carbon dioxide from the air, so the oceans would continue to acidify, and the cooling would last only as long as the spraying continued.

If it stopped abruptly, because of war, economic collapse or political change, the suppressed warming could return within a few years, far faster than ecosystems or societies could adapt, a scenario known as termination shock.
Starting would therefore bind posterity to an intervention that could not safely be abandoned.

Every intervention in so complex a system risks unintended consequences, and altering the balance of sunlight could make rainfall more erratic and disturb the monsoon on which billions of people depend for their food.
Many critics add that the mere prospect of a technological fix could weaken the resolve to cut emissions, an effect sometimes described as moral hazard.
Perhaps the deepest problem is political.

Because solar geoengineering would be relatively cheap, a single country, or even a wealthy maverick, could in principle deploy it unilaterally, altering the climate of the entire planet without the consent of anyone else.

A nation suffering a devastating drought might blame a neighbour's meddling with the climate, whether or not the connection was real, and disputes over the planetary thermostat could become a source of belligerent tension.
These fears are not hypothetical: in 2022, a start-up company conducted a renegade experiment, releasing balloons carrying sulphur dioxide into the sky over Mexico without permission.
The Mexican government responded by announcing a ban on such experiments.
Scientists disagree about whether even research should proceed.
Some argue that the technology is too dangerous to develop at all and have called for an international agreement not to use it, warning that research creates momentum towards deployment.

Others, including an influential committee of American scientists, have recommended a cautious programme of research, subject to strict accountability and public oversight, so that the world understands the risks before a desperate government acts without that knowledge.
The principle of precaution, in other words, cuts both ways.

A planned balloon experiment by Harvard researchers in Sweden was cancelled after objections from the Indigenous Saami Council, illustrating how contested even a small test can be and how many stakeholders expect a voice.

What is clear is that solar geoengineering, if it is ever used, will require institutions of global governance, capable of equitable decisions, that do not yet exist, and that it can at best buy time, not substitute for the reduction of emissions.
Few images are as instantly recognizable as that of a Scotsman in a kilt, woven in the tartan of his clan, an outfit that ostensibly embodies centuries of Highland tradition.
Yet much of this tradition is surprisingly recent.
The short kilt, historians have argued, was devised in the eighteenth century, possibly by an English industrialist who found the traditional belted plaid impractical for his workers.

The elaborate genealogy of distinctive tartans for each clan was largely a creation of the nineteenth century, and a lavishly illustrated book of clan tartans published in 1842, which claimed to reproduce an ancient manuscript, was later exposed as a fabrication.
Such examples inspired a celebrated collection of essays, The Invention of Tradition, edited by the historians Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger and published in 1983.
Hobsbawm defined invented traditions as practices that seek to instil certain values by repetition and that imply, often spuriously, continuity with a venerable past.

He argued that they proliferate during periods of rapid social change, when older customs have been disrupted by industrialization and migration, and when new states need to foster national cohesion among citizens who have little else in common.
The authority of an invented tradition derives precisely from the belief that it is not invented at all, so its artifice must remain invisible.
Monarchies proved especially adept at this kind of invention.
Many of the ceremonies, jubilees and commemorations that surround the British crown, and that visitors assume to be medieval, were elaborated in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
This was precisely when the monarch's political power was declining, and ceremonial grandeur offered a substitute.

The investiture of the Prince of Wales at Caernarfon Castle in 1911, conducted with archaic costumes and pageantry that suggested great antiquity, was in fact devised for the occasion, partly by the politician David Lloyd George.
Earlier coronations had often been shambolic affairs, and only as the monarchy became a national symbol rather than a source of power were its rituals polished to perfection.
The phenomenon is by no means confined to Britain.
The Olympic torch relay, which seems to link the modern games to ancient Greece, was introduced for the Berlin games of 1936, emulating an imagined classical ritual.

The white wedding dress became fashionable in the West after Queen Victoria wore one in 1840, and the Christmas tree was popularized in Britain in the same decade, partly through images of the royal family gathered around one.

National costumes, folk dances and patriotic songs throughout Europe were codified by nineteenth-century nationalists, who drew selectively on rural customs to construct an image of the nation's authentic character, often more homogeneous than the reality.
Critics of the concept point out that all traditions were invented at some point, so the distinction between genuine and invented ones is less clear than it appears.

A custom does not become meaningless merely because its origins are recent or its history embellished, and the tartan is no less cherished by modern Scots for having been systematized by Victorian manufacturers.
Traditions are malleable: they are continually reinterpreted by those who practise them, and their authenticity lies less in their pedigree than in the significance they hold for a community.
Many satisfy a nostalgia for a stable past that never quite existed.
Hobsbawm's insight was not that invented traditions are fraudulent, but that the past is a resource that the present constantly reshapes for its own purposes.
When Herman Melville's sixth novel appeared in the autumn of 1851, first in London as The Whale and a month later in New York as Moby-Dick, few readers knew what to make of it.
The British edition had been published without its epilogue, so reviewers were baffled that a narrator could recount a shipwreck in which, apparently, everyone had drowned.
The book sold about three thousand copies in Melville's lifetime, and when he died in 1891, working as a customs inspector in New York, he had long since sunk into obscurity.

Posterity has been kinder: a hundred and seventy-five years later, it is routinely named among the greatest novels ever written, a canonical text whose reputation can deter the very readers it deserves.
The plot can be summarized in a sentence.

Captain Ahab, who lost a leg to the ferocity of a white sperm whale, sails the whaling ship Pequod around the world in pursuit of the animal, determined to avenge himself, and his tenacious obsession destroys the ship and every member of its crew except the narrator, Ishmael.
Melville drew on the true story of the Essex, a whaling ship sunk by a whale in the Pacific in 1820, and on his own experience as a young mariner aboard a whaler.

But the plot occupies only a fraction of the book, which is by turns an adventure, a metaphysical meditation, a tragedy on a Shakespearean scale, an encyclopedia of whaling and a comic novel of considerable eccentricity.
First-time readers are often startled by the digressions.

Whole chapters are devoted to the classification of whales, the anatomy of the whale's head, the uses of its blubber and the processing of its carcass, and some chapters are written in the form of a play, with stage directions.
These passages can seem ponderous, yet they serve a purpose: by piling up facts about the whale, Melville demonstrates how little the facts reveal.
The creature remains, at the end, as inscrutable as it was at the beginning, a labyrinth of meanings that no reader can fully fathom.
The famous chapter on the whiteness of the whale, which meditates on why a colour associated with purity can also inspire terror, is among the most unsettling essays in American literature.
The novel also rewards reading as a portrait of a society.

The crew of the Pequod, drawn from every continent, forms a floating microcosm of a multicultural nation, and the tender friendship between Ishmael and the harpooner Queequeg, a Pacific islander, defies the racial prejudices of its time.

The whaling industry itself, which hunted animals across the globe to extract the oil that lit American homes and greased its factories, anticipates with uncanny precision the fossil fuel industries that succeeded it.

Ahab has become an archetype of the obsessive leader, and his willingness to sacrifice his crew to his private vengeance has been read as an allegory of demagoguery, of imperialism and of the modern pursuit of mastery over nature.
None of this makes Moby-Dick an easy book, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise.
Its prose ranges from biblical grandeur and lyrical rapture to bawdy humour, sometimes on the same page, and its ambition occasionally outruns its control.
But its difficulty is inseparable from its greatness: Melville set out to write a book as vast and as unknowable as the ocean, and he very nearly succeeded.
For readers willing to surrender to its currents, the voyage remains, a hundred and seventy-five years on, one of the most exhilarating that literature can offer.
Of all the questions science has attempted to answer, few are as fundamental, or as stubbornly unresolved, as how life began.

The Earth formed about four and a half billion years ago, and for its first few hundred million years the embryonic planet endured an intense bombardment by asteroids and comets that would probably have sterilized its surface.

Yet the oldest widely accepted traces of life, microbial mats preserved in ancient rock strata, date from about three and a half billion years ago, and some geologists claim to have found evidence that is older still.

On a geological timescale, life appeared almost as soon as conditions allowed, which raises the question of whether its emergence was a stochastic accident or an almost inevitable consequence of chemistry.
Charles Darwin, in a private letter written in 1871, speculated about a warm little pond containing the right chemicals, in which a protein compound might form and undergo further changes.
Eighty years later, the chemist Stanley Miller tested a version of this conjecture.

He passed electric sparks, intended to mimic lightning, through a sealed mixture of water, methane, ammonia and hydrogen, gases then thought to resemble the primeval atmosphere, which held no free oxygen because photosynthesis had not yet begun.

Within days the mixture contained amino acids, the building blocks of proteins, which showed that some of the molecules of life can be synthesized from inorganic ingredients without any biological intervention.
But the experiment also exposed the magnitude of the task: a mixture of amino acids is no more a living cell than a pile of bricks is a cathedral.
The deepest difficulty is a paradox at the heart of biology.
In modern cells, DNA stores the instructions for making proteins, but proteins are required to copy DNA, so that neither could have arisen first without the other.
A widely favoured solution is the hypothesis of an RNA world.

RNA, a close chemical relative of DNA, can carry genetic information, and in the 1980s researchers discovered that some RNA molecules can also perform catalytic functions previously thought to be the preserve of proteins.
If an RNA molecule arose that could copy itself, however imperfectly, natural selection could begin to operate, favouring variants that replicated faster or more accurately.
The nascent machinery of biology might then have emerged from chemistry by a process of successive iteration.
Where this happened is equally contested.

One influential proposal places the origin of life at hydrothermal vents on the ocean floor, where warm, alkaline fluids seep through porous rock whose mineral lattice is riddled with tiny compartments.
These natural chambers could have concentrated molecules and supplied a steady source of chemical energy, much as membranes do in living cells.

A rival school favours hot springs on land, where repeated cycles of wetting and drying could have encouraged small molecules to link into longer chains, something that is difficult in the open ocean.
Each scenario explains some features of early life and struggles with others, and experiments designed to reproduce them in the laboratory have so far yielded only partial results.
Some scientists have proposed that life, or at least its ingredients, arrived from space.

Meteorites and samples returned from asteroids have been found to contain amino acids and other organic compounds, and organic molecules have also been detected in interstellar clouds, which confirms that such substances form naturally in the cosmos.
But the idea that life itself originated elsewhere merely relocates the question.

Part of the difficulty is that there is no sharp line between chemistry and biology: any definition of life, whether it emphasizes reproduction, metabolism or the capacity to evolve, seems to admit borderline cases.
The transition was probably gradual, passing through incipient forms that would scarcely have been recognizable as living, which may explain why their origin has proved so elusive.
Until recently, the deliberate hastening of death by doctors was illegal almost everywhere, and it remains one of the most contentious questions in medical ethics.
Today, a growing number of jurisdictions permit some form of assisted dying.
In the Netherlands and Belgium, doctors may end the lives of patients who request it and whose suffering is judged unbearable and without prospect of improvement.
In Oregon and several other American states, terminally ill adults with a prognosis of six months or less may obtain a lethal prescription to take themselves.

Canada, which legalized medical assistance in dying in 2016, has since extended it to people whose deaths are not reasonably foreseeable, and in 2025 Britain's House of Commons voted for a bill to legalize the practice for the terminally ill after a deeply polarized debate.
The case for legalization rests above all on autonomy.

If competent adults are entitled to make decisions about their own bodies, including the refusal of life-sustaining treatment, it seems arbitrary to deny them the right to decide the timing and manner of their death when they are afflicted by an incurable illness.

Proponents also appeal to compassion: even the best palliative care cannot relieve every form of suffering, and for some patients a swift and merciful death is preferable to a prolonged decline that they regard as a violation of their dignity.

Where assisted dying is prohibited, the determined find other means: some travel abroad at great expense, while others end their lives alone and violently, sometimes earlier than they would have chosen, because they fear losing the capacity to act.
Opponents raise objections of several kinds.

Some hold that human life has an intrinsic value that no individual may legitimately destroy, so that deliberately ending it is never morally permissible, a view shared by many religious traditions but also defended on secular grounds.
Others accept the principle of autonomy but doubt that the choice can be truly free in practice, fearing subtle forms of coercion.

Elderly, disabled or impoverished patients may feel an unspoken pressure to spare their families the burden of caring for them, and in Oregon a substantial proportion of those who request assistance cite the fear of being a burden as one of their reasons.
A patient who is clinically depressed may request death for reasons that treatment could address.

Disability rights campaigners, speaking for groups that are often marginalized, warn that a law which treats a life of dependence as a reason for death sends a message about whose lives are worth living.
A further concern is that eligibility, once established, tends to expand.

Belgium extended euthanasia to minors in 2014, and in the Netherlands, where it now accounts for roughly one death in twenty, cases involving dementia and psychiatric illness have become increasingly common.

Critics cite Canada's expansion beyond terminal illness, and a planned extension to people whose sole condition is mental illness, as evidence that incremental steps lead inexorably to practices that the original legislation was designed to exclude.

Supporters reply that such extensions reflect deliberate democratic choices, and that safeguards, such as independent assessment by two doctors and the waiting periods that most laws stipulate, have generally worked as intended.
Unlike most medical decisions, the choice is irrevocable, which is why the quality of those safeguards matters so much.
The debate also concerns the identity of medicine itself.
The Hippocratic tradition forbade doctors to give a deadly drug even if asked, and many physicians feel that participating in death would betray the trust on which their profession depends.
Others note that doctors already administer high doses of morphine that may hasten death, and regard the distinction as one without a difference.
Most jurisdictions therefore allow doctors to refuse on grounds of conscience.

Whatever one's view, the controversy has had one beneficial effect: it has drawn attention to the uneven provision of palliative care, which remains inaccessible to many who need it, and without which no choice about the end of life can be genuinely free.
Trainee flight attendants at a major American airline in the early 1980s were taught to smile not merely with their faces but, as their instructors put it, as if they really meant it.

They were encouraged to imagine the cabin as their own living room and passengers as guests, and to reinterpret the rudeness of a belligerent customer as the understandable anxiety of a frightened child.

The sociologist Arlie Russell Hochschild, who observed their training, coined a term for what they were being asked to do: emotional labour, the management of one's feelings to create a publicly observable display, sold for a wage.
Her book The Managed Heart, published in 1983, has since become a classic of the sociology of work.
Hochschild's insight was that the display of emotion had become a commodity.

In an economy increasingly dominated by services, many workers are paid not only for what they do but for how they appear to feel while doing it: the waiter's warmth, the nurse's calm, the call-centre operator's courteous patience.
Employers stipulate these displays in training manuals and scripts, monitor them through customer surveys and mystery shoppers, and treat any lapse in demeanor as a failure of performance.
Friendliness has become obligatory, and staff are trained to appease complaints with apologies they may not feel.

The obligation can run in either direction: bill collectors, whom Hochschild also studied, were expected to adopt an abrasive manner calculated to intimidate debtors, suppressing any sympathy they felt.
Hochschild distinguished between two strategies.
In surface acting, the worker feigns an emotion that she does not feel, smiling while seething inwardly.
In deep acting, she tries to summon the required feeling itself, for instance by imagining reasons to sympathize with an obnoxious or patronizing passenger.
Both involve effort, but research since then has found that surface acting is more strongly associated with emotional exhaustion, burnout and depressive symptoms.
Perhaps the persistent gap between what one displays and what one feels, the daily artifice of the job, is itself a source of strain.

Deep acting may be healthier, but Hochschild feared that it carried a subtler cost: workers who routinely manufacture feelings for their employer may become estranged from their own emotions, uncertain which of them are authentic.
Emotional labour is unevenly distributed.

Women are disproportionately employed in occupations that demand it, from nursing and teaching to hospitality, and they are also expected, in many workplaces, to perform unacknowledged emotional work, such as soothing colleagues or smoothing over conflicts.
Because such skills are intangible and often regarded as natural rather than acquired, they tend to be undervalued, and the jobs that require them are frequently poorly paid.

The meager remuneration of care workers, whose emotional attentiveness is central to the quality of their work, is a case in point, and high rates of staff attrition in care homes are one consequence.
Technology has intensified the monitoring of emotional performance.

Drivers and delivery workers are rated by customers after every trip, call centres use software that analyses the tone of employees' voices, and a single disgruntled review can affect a worker's income, encouraging a submissive eagerness to please.
At the same time, the concept has expanded well beyond its original meaning, and it is now used to describe everything from planning family birthdays to the effort of remaining polite online.
Hochschild herself has warned that such stretching may blunt its critical edge.
Her original point remains pertinent: when feelings are bought and sold, it is worth asking who controls them, and at what cost to the person who has to perform them.
Jonathan Swift's A Modest Proposal, a short pamphlet published in 1729, offered a solution to the poverty of Ireland: the children of the poor should be sold as food for the tables of the rich.
The tone of the pamphlet is one of reasonable, even humane, calculation, complete with estimates of costs, and its horror emerges precisely from the gap between that tone and its monstrous content.

It remains perhaps the most celebrated work of satire in English, and it illustrates the central technique of the form: to expose an injustice by exaggerating the logic of those who tolerate it until that logic becomes grotesque.
Satire is as old as literature.

The Roman poet Juvenal declared that, in the face of the vices of his city, it was difficult not to write it, and critics have long distinguished his bitter, indignant manner from the gentler ridicule of his predecessor Horace.
In every era, satirists have played a subversive role, targeting the powerful, the pompous and the hypocritical.
In every era, too, the powerful have tried to silence them, through censorship, prosecution for libel and defamation, or simple violence.

Charlie Chaplin's film The Great Dictator, released in 1940, mocked Hitler at a time when many governments were still reluctant to offend him, while in the Soviet Union political jokes circulated by word of mouth, and telling the wrong one could lead to imprisonment.
Why should the powerful fear laughter?
One answer is that authority depends on a certain solemnity, an aura that ridicule punctures.
A leader who is feared can survive being hated, but it is much harder to survive being made to look farcical, and satire can unite people who dare not protest openly in a kind of defiant complicity.

This is why totalitarian and authoritarian governments are often more tolerant of criticism framed as argument than of mockery, and why an innocent comparison between a leader and a cartoon bear can be censored.

Satire also serves an informational purpose: studies of American comedy news programmes have found that their audiences are often as well informed about current affairs as viewers of conventional news.
Yet the political effectiveness of satire is disputed.

In 1961, the comedian Peter Cook opened a satirical nightclub in London, which he said would be modelled on the Berlin cabarets of the 1930s that had done so much to prevent the rise of Hitler, a joke that captured the impotence of the form.

Some critics argue that satire functions as a safety valve, allowing audiences to discharge their anger in laughter rather than action, and that it can breed a knowing cynicism and political apathy in which nothing seems worth changing.
There is also the problem of misunderstanding: irony depends on an audience that recognizes it, and satirical articles have repeatedly been reported as genuine news by readers who missed the joke.

The stakes of satire were brutally demonstrated in January 2015, when gunmen murdered twelve people at the Paris offices of the magazine Charlie Hebdo, which had published cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad.

The attack provoked worldwide solidarity with the principle of free expression, but also a contentious debate about whether satire that offends religious minorities, and that some regard as blasphemy, is punching down rather than up.
Satirists themselves have generally insisted that no subject should be exempt from ridicule, while acknowledging that the choice of target reveals the values of the satirist.
The most enduring satire, like that of Swift, tends to aim its derision at those who hold power, and it is that direction, rather than the laughter itself, that gives it moral force.
On the morning of 16 October 1962, President John F. Kennedy was shown photographs taken by an American spy plane over Cuba.
They revealed that the Soviet Union was building clandestine launch sites for missiles capable of carrying nuclear warheads to Washington and most other cities in the United States.
For the next thirteen days, the two superpowers came closer to the brink of nuclear war than at any other moment in history.
The crisis remains the most intensively studied episode of the Cold War.
Why had the Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev attempted so perilous a gambit?
He wished to protect the revolutionary government of Fidel Castro, which the United States had tried to overthrow at the Bay of Pigs the previous year, and to redress a strategic imbalance.
American missiles in Turkey could strike the Soviet Union within minutes, while the Soviets possessed few weapons that could reach America.
Kennedy nevertheless regarded the deployment as an intolerable provocation.
His military advisers, some of them openly belligerent, overwhelmingly favoured an air strike against the sites, followed perhaps by an invasion, arguing that anything less would appease the Soviets.

Kennedy, wary of starting a war that might escalate beyond control, chose instead a naval blockade, which he described, in a careful euphemism, as a quarantine, since a blockade in international law is an act of war.
On 22 October, Kennedy announced the discovery in a televised address and demanded the removal of the missiles in what amounted to an ultimatum.
He warned that any nuclear attack from Cuba would be met with a full retaliatory response against the Soviet Union.
Two days later, as the quarantine took effect, Soviet ships approaching the line of American vessels slowed and turned back.
The secretary of state, Dean Rusk, remarked that the two sides had been eyeball to eyeball and the other fellow had just blinked.

But the crisis was not over, and the risk of escalation grew: work on the missile sites continued, and each side struggled to interpret the intentions of the other through a fog of rhetoric, posturing and delayed communication.
The most dangerous day was 27 October.
An American spy plane was shot down over Cuba and its pilot fatally wounded.
In the Caribbean, American warships dropped practice depth charges to force a Soviet submarine to surface, unaware that it carried a torpedo with a nuclear warhead.

According to later accounts, the exhausted captain of the submarine, believing that war might already have begun, considered firing it, and was dissuaded only because a senior officer on board, Vasili Arkhipov, refused to give his consent.

Meanwhile, Khrushchev sent two contradictory letters: the first, conciliatory in tone, offered to withdraw the missiles in exchange for a promise not to invade Cuba, while the second added a demand that the United States remove its own missiles from Turkey.
Kennedy's advisers decided to respond publicly to the first letter and to ignore the second.
His brother Robert privately told the Soviet ambassador that the missiles in Turkey would be withdrawn within months, a reciprocal concession, provided that the arrangement remained secret.
On 28 October, Khrushchev announced that the Soviet sites would be dismantled.

The secrecy of the concession allowed Kennedy to appear victorious, and it contributed to the perception in Moscow that Khrushchev had been humiliated, one of the reasons he was ousted two years later.
The crisis led to the installation of a direct telephone line between the two capitals and to a treaty restricting nuclear tests.
Decades later, it emerged that Soviet forces in Cuba had also possessed short-range nuclear weapons, unknown to the Americans, which they might have used against an invasion.
The revelation led the former American defence secretary Robert McNamara to conclude that the world had avoided annihilation partly through sheer happenstance.
In hindsight, the crisis revealed how quickly a deterrent can become a trigger for war, and how much depends on the judgement of a few exhausted individuals.
By many measures, the pace of technological progress ought to be accelerating exponentially.

There are more scientists and engineers alive today than at any previous point in history, research budgets have grown enormously, and cheap computation allows them to analyse data and share findings instantaneously.
Yet productivity growth in wealthy economies has been sluggish for decades, and a growing body of evidence suggests that, in many fields, each new advance requires ever greater effort.
The question of whether ideas are getting harder to find has become one of the most consequential debates in economics.
The most cited evidence comes from a seminal study published in 2020 by four economists at American and British universities.

They examined the semiconductor industry, where the number of transistors on a chip has doubled roughly every two years for half a century, and found that sustaining that rate now requires about eighteen times as many researchers as it did in the early 1970s.

Similar patterns appeared in agriculture and medicine, and across the economy as a whole, the authors calculated, research effort must double roughly every thirteen years merely to keep growth constant.
Another study found that scientific papers and patents have become progressively less likely to overturn existing knowledge and more likely to make incremental refinements to it.
Several explanations have been proposed.

The most intuitive is that the easiest discoveries were made first: once electricity, antibiotics and the internal combustion engine had been invented, the remaining opportunities were inevitably harder to exploit.

The economist Robert Gordon has argued that the inventions of the century after 1870, which brought running water, electric light and the car into ordinary homes, transformed daily life far more than the digital technologies that followed.
Since then, he suggests, much of domestic life has remained comparatively stagnant: a kitchen of today would be perfectly recognizable to someone from the 1960s.

A second explanation is what one economist has called the burden of knowledge: as the frontier of each field recedes, researchers must spend longer mastering what is already known, and the growing specialization of knowledge forces them to work in large teams, making interdisciplinary leaps harder.

A third points to institutions: funding agencies averse to risk that favour safe, incremental proposals, regulations that make experimentation costly, and incumbent firms that guard proprietary knowledge rather than share it.
Skeptics caution against drawing pessimistic conclusions.
Conventional statistics may underestimate the value of digital goods, many of which are free, and the economic impact of a technology depends on its diffusion, which can take decades.
Electricity, for example, transformed factories only when they were redesigned around it.

Recent years have also produced breakthroughs that appeared almost overnight, from vaccines developed within a year of a new pandemic to the burgeoning field of artificial intelligence, and the cost of solar power has fallen by roughly nine tenths within a decade.
Perhaps, the optimists suggest, the productivity of research is not declining but merely shifting to new domains, where its rewards are not yet measurable.
Whatever the diagnosis, the stakes are high, since sustained improvements in living standards depend in the long run on the discovery of new ideas.
If ideas are indeed getting harder to find, merely maintaining progress will require devoting a growing share of society's resources to research, and spending those resources more effectively.

Proposals range from funding talented individuals rather than specific projects, which gives researchers the freedom to pursue risky ideas that may take decades to come to fruition, to allocating some grants by lottery, which would reduce the bias towards conservative proposals.
Others urge governments to nurture nascent fields before their value becomes obvious.

The investor Peter Thiel once complained that humanity had wanted flying cars and got instead a hundred and forty characters, and whether his pessimism is warranted will depend partly on how willing societies are to tolerate the failures that ambitious research entails.
Imagine being able to reach almost everything you need, your work, your children's school, a doctor, shops and a park, within a quarter of an hour on foot or by bicycle.

That is the premise of the fifteen-minute city, a concept proposed in 2016 by the urbanist Carlos Moreno and adopted with particular enthusiasm by Anne Hidalgo, the mayor of Paris, who made it the centrepiece of her campaign for re-election in 2020.
To its admirers, it offers a practical utopia of short journeys and lively streets.
The idea spread rapidly, and cities from Melbourne to Milan have since adopted versions of it in their plans.
The concept is less novel than its branding suggests.
Before the car, most cities were necessarily compact, and neighbourhoods combined homes, workshops and markets within walking distance.

In the twentieth century, planners separated these functions through zoning, creating homogeneous districts for housing, industry and commerce, and many people came to depend on long commutes along congested arterial roads towards centralized business districts.
The critic Jane Jacobs argued in 1961 that the resulting monotony was destroying urban life, and that vibrant streets depend on a dense mixture of uses that brings people outside at all hours.
The fifteen-minute city revives her insight, presenting decentralized, localized services as a remedy for congestion, pollution and the sedentary habits associated with dependence on the car.
Its advocates insist that it is not a nostalgic retreat into the past but a practical response to climate change.
Paris has pursued the idea with unusual determination.
It has closed a riverside expressway to cars, created hundreds of kilometres of cycle lanes, reduced parking and opened school playgrounds to local residents outside school hours.
In so doing, the city has given precedence to pedestrians and cyclists over drivers.
Supporters point to cleaner air and the transformation of streets once dominated by traffic into places where people linger.
Barcelona's superblocks, in which clusters of streets are closed to through traffic and handed over to pedestrians, pursue a similar goal.
The concept has nevertheless attracted criticism from several directions.
Some urbanists argue that it suits dense, affluent city centres but offers little to sprawling suburbs and rural areas at the periphery, where services are sparse and distances great.

Others warn that improving the amenities of a neighbourhood raises property values and rents, displacing the very residents whose lives it was meant to improve, a process known as gentrification whose costs fall disproportionately on marginalized groups.

There is also the question of work: most jobs cannot be relocated to every neighbourhood, and a city in which people rarely travel beyond their own district could become insular, parochial and socially segregated.
Ensuring that the benefits are equitable, critics argue, requires investing first in the poorest districts.
The most unexpected opposition came in 2023, when the concept became the subject of conspiracy theories.
In Oxford, a plan to restrict traffic on certain roads at certain times was misrepresented online as a scheme to confine residents to their neighbourhoods under a kind of permanent curfew.
Protesters claimed that fifteen-minute cities were a pretext for surveillance and control.

The claims were baseless, a textbook case of misinformation, but they tapped into genuine resentment among drivers who felt that their needs were being disregarded, and several politicians echoed them.

The episode illustrated how an innocuous planning idea can become a symbol in wider cultural conflicts, and it suggested that the success of such schemes depends as much on persuasion and consultation as on design.

For roughly two centuries, from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth, it was customary for young men of the British upper classes to complete their education and refinement with a long journey across the continent of Europe.

The Grand Tour, as it came to be known, typically took the traveller through France and over the Alps to Italy, where Rome, Florence, Venice and Naples were the principal destinations, and it could last anything from a few months to several years.

Accompanied by a tutor and servants, the young traveller was expected to acquire languages, manners, a cosmopolitan polish and a first-hand acquaintance with the venerable monuments of antiquity that he had studied at school.
The journey was undertaken for the edification of the young, but also for the prestige of their families.
The journey itself was arduous.
Travellers crossed the Alps by carriage where roads allowed and were otherwise carried over the passes in chairs by porters, and bandits, disease and dishonest innkeepers were constant hazards.

Yet the discomforts were part of the experience, and the sight of the mountains, once regarded merely as an obstacle, came to be prized for its sublime grandeur, contributing to a new aesthetic sensibility that would culminate in Romanticism.

In Italy, the tourists visited ruins and galleries, attended the opera and sat for portraits, and the excavations at Herculaneum and Pompeii, begun in the eighteenth century, added a thrilling sense of discovery.
The Grand Tour was also a vast exercise in shopping.

Painters such as Canaletto in Venice produced views of the city specifically for British buyers, and in Rome, Pompeo Batoni specialized in portraits of young Englishmen posed among classical statues and ruins.
Aspiring connoisseurs sought to emulate the collections of Italian princes, shipping home crates of sculptures, paintings and antiquities, some genuine and many of dubious provenance.

The influence on British taste was profound: architects who had absorbed the sophistication of Roman design shaped the neoclassical style, and many of the treasures that tourists brought home now form the core of museum collections.
The tour did not escape criticism.

The economist Adam Smith complained in 1776 that young men returned from it more conceited and more dissipated than when they left, having learned a smattering of foreign languages and wasted their time in frivolous indulgence.
Satirists mocked the returning tourists for their affectation of foreign fashions and manners, and parents worried, with reason, about the gambling and seduction to which their sons were exposed.

A few women also travelled, often as members of families or as widows, and some of their letters and journals offer more perceptive observations of the social milieu they encountered than the conventional accounts of their male counterparts.
The wars that followed the French Revolution interrupted the Grand Tour, and after 1815 the railway and the steamship transformed travel.

In 1841, Thomas Cook organized his first excursion, a train journey for temperance campaigners, and within a few decades his company was taking affluent middle-class tourists across the continent in weeks rather than years.
The Grand Tour had been an aristocratic rite of passage, and it became the archetype of travel as self-improvement; its successors made foreign travel accessible to hundreds of thousands.
