Many features of modern tourism, from the guidebook to the souvenir and the obligatory visit to famous sights, can be traced to it, and so can the snobbery with which seasoned travellers have always regarded newcomers.
For most of human history, sugar was a rare luxury.
Honey and fruit supplied the only concentrated sweetness available to most people, and when refined cane sugar reached medieval Europe it was sold by apothecaries as a costly spice and medicine.
Its transformation into an everyday commodity was bound up with one of the greatest crimes of the modern era.

The plantations of the Caribbean and Brazil that supplied Europe's growing appetite, and enriched its mercantile empires, were worked by enslaved Africans, and a large proportion of the millions transported across the Atlantic ended their lives cutting cane.
By the twentieth century, sugar had become one of the cheapest sources of calories in the world and a ubiquitous indulgence.
Its cheapness owed much to politics.

Governments in Europe and the United States have long protected their own producers with tariffs, quotas and subsidies, while food manufacturers discovered that sugar could make almost any processed product more palatable, from bread to sauces.
As evidence emerged in the 1960s linking diet to heart disease, the industry surreptitiously intervened in the science.

Documents discovered decades later revealed that a sugar industry group had paid researchers at Harvard, in an arrangement that remained clandestine for half a century, to write an influential review that played down the role of sugar and emphasized the dangers of dietary fat.
For a generation, public health advice concentrated on reducing fat, and manufacturers replaced it in many low-fat products with sugar.
The evidence against excessive sugar consumption is now substantial.
High intakes, particularly in sweetened drinks, are associated with weight gain, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay.

Although correlation alone cannot prove a causal link, controlled trials support the connection with weight gain, and because calorific drinks do not produce the same sense of fullness as solid food, they are especially easy to overconsume.
For some people, consumption can become almost compulsive.

The World Health Organization recommends that free sugars, those added to food or naturally present in honey and juices, should provide less than a tenth of daily energy intake, and ideally less than a twentieth.
Many people in wealthy countries consume far more, often without realizing it, since sugar is an insidious additive even in savoury foods that do not taste particularly sweet.
In response, dozens of countries have introduced taxes on sugary drinks.

Mexico, which has some of the highest rates of obesity and diabetes in the world, imposed an excise of one peso per litre in 2014, and purchases of taxed drinks fell in the following years, most sharply among poorer households.
Britain adopted a different design in 2018, taxing drinks according to their sugar content, so that only the sweetest were taxable at the highest rate.
This gave manufacturers an incentive to reformulate their products, and many cut sugar before the tax took effect, so that the quantity sold in soft drinks fell substantially.

Critics describe such measures as paternalistic and regressive, since they fall disproportionately on the poor, who spend a larger share of their income on food, whereas the affluent barely notice the extra cost.
Supporters reply that the poor also suffer disproportionately from the diseases the taxes aim to prevent.
The politics of sugar illustrates a broader tension in public health.

Individual choices about what to eat are shaped by prices, marketing and the composition of foods that consumers rarely examine, and by an evolved craving for the instant gratification of sweetness, reinforced by a palate trained from childhood to expect it.
The modern food system is extraordinarily good at exploiting that craving.
Whether governments should intervene in those choices, and how far, is a question about the proper limits of the state as much as about nutrition.
Among mammals, human females are unusual in a way that has long puzzled evolutionary biologists.
Women's fertility ends around the age of fifty, yet many live for decades afterwards, even in societies without modern medicine.

Very few other animals stop reproducing so long before the end of their lifespan: apart from humans, the phenomenon has been documented only in a handful of species of toothed whales, including killer whales.
From the perspective of natural selection, which favours traits that increase the number of an individual's descendants, a long life without reproduction seems paradoxical.

One influential answer emerged from anthropological fieldwork among the Hadza, a community in Tanzania who still live largely by hunting and gathering, and for whom foraging is a matter of subsistence.

During the 1980s and 1990s, the anthropologist Kristen Hawkes and her colleagues observed that older women were among the most productive foragers in the group, spending long hours digging up tubers, and that much of the food they gathered went to their grandchildren.
When a mother had a new baby, the help of a grandmother allowed her older children, now past infancy, to be fed, which in turn allowed mothers to have children at shorter intervals.

Hawkes hypothesized that this assistance might explain the evolution of human longevity: women who lived long after their own reproductive years, and helped to feed their daughters' children, would have left more descendants than those who did not.
Evidence for this grandmother hypothesis has come from unexpected sources.

Researchers who analysed archival church records that trace the genealogy of families in Finland and Canada over the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries found that women gained roughly two additional grandchildren for every decade they survived beyond the age of fifty.
The benefit was markedly smaller when the grandmother lived far away from her children, which suggests that it depended on her practical assistance rather than on some other factor.

Among killer whales, older females lead their groups to feeding grounds, especially in years of scarcity when salmon are hard to find, and adult sons are far more likely to die in the year after their mother's death.
The hypothesis is not without rivals.
Some researchers argue that menopause evolved partly to prevent generational conflict.

In many ancestral societies, as in many patriarchal ones today, young women moved into their husbands' families, and a grandmother who continued to reproduce would compete with her daughters-in-law for scarce resources, while her own late-born children would be less likely to survive.
Others suggest that the explanation lies in the risks of childbirth, which increase with age, making it more advantageous for older women to invest in the offspring they already have.
These accounts are not mutually exclusive, and the debate illustrates how conjecture about the distant past must be tested against sparse evidence.
Whatever its evolutionary origins, the role of grandmothers remains conspicuous.

In many countries, grandparents provide a large share of informal childcare, allowing parents, and particularly mothers, to remain in paid work, a form of familial support on which many economies silently depend.
In China, where hundreds of millions of rural people have migrated to cities for work, millions of children are raised mainly by grandparents in their home villages.

Demographers warn that as families become smaller and more dispersed, and as people become parents later in life, this ancient safety net may weaken, just as ageing populations make it more necessary than ever.
If we want to know what it might be like to encounter an intelligent alien, some biologists suggest, we should look not to the stars but to the sea.

The last common ancestor of humans and octopuses, a simple worm-like creature, lived some six hundred million years ago, which means that the intelligence of the octopus evolved entirely independently of our own.
It is one of the most striking examples in evolution of two lineages, separated by an immense gulf of time, whose paths converge on complex minds by utterly different routes.
To human observers, the result remains almost inscrutable.
The nervous system of the octopus is organized in a way that has no parallel among vertebrates.

A common octopus has around five hundred million neurons, comparable to the number in the brain of a dog, but roughly two thirds of them are located not in its head but at the periphery of its body, in its eight arms.

Each arm is adept at tasting and touching what it explores through the suction of hundreds of suckers, and it appears capable of a degree of autonomous action, continuing to reach and grasp even when severed from the body.
This decentralized architecture suggests a kind of cognition very different from ours, in which the central brain issues general instructions and the arms work out many of the details for themselves.
The abilities that result are remarkable.
Octopuses in laboratories have learned to solve puzzles, open jars from the inside with remarkable agility and find their way through mazes.
Captive individuals are notorious for escaping from their tanks, squeezing their boneless, malleable bodies through any gap larger than their beak.
In the wild, some carry coconut shells across the sea floor to use as portable shelters, a behaviour that many researchers regard as tool use.

Keepers report that octopuses can recognize individual humans and treat them differently, sometimes squirting water at people they seem to dislike, and each animal appears to possess an idiosyncratic temperament.
Perhaps their most astonishing skill is camouflage.

Using millions of cells in the skin that contain pigment and can be expanded or contracted, an octopus can change its colour, pattern and even texture in a fraction of a second, matching the colour and contours of the rocks, corals or weeds around it with uncanny precision.

Paradoxically, most octopuses appear to be colour-blind, possessing only one type of light-sensitive cell in their eyes, and scientists are still investigating how they achieve such accurate matching.
One possibility is that their skin itself can detect light.
Some species go further, mimicking the shapes and movements of venomous animals such as sea snakes to deter predatory fish.
For all their sophistication, octopuses are defined by the brevity of their lives.

Most species have a lifespan of only a year or two, and they are solitary, so that almost nothing can be passed on from one generation to the next: each individual must learn about the world from scratch.
Females typically stop eating while they guard their eggs and die soon after the young hatch.
The growing evidence of their intelligence has had practical consequences: in 2022 Britain formally recognized octopuses and other cephalopods as sentient beings in its animal welfare law.
Proposals to farm them on an industrial scale have provoked fierce opposition, and some American states have moved to prohibit the practice.

The steel magnate Andrew Carnegie argued in an essay of 1889 that the rich had a duty to distribute their fortunes during their lifetimes for the public good, rather than leave them to heirs who might squander them.
He practised what he preached, financing more than two thousand public libraries across the English-speaking world, a munificence that few contemporaries could match.

A century later, philanthropy on a comparable scale has returned: the foundation established by Bill and Melinda Gates has spent tens of billions of dollars on global health, and more than two hundred billionaires have signed a pledge to give away the majority of their wealth.
The achievements of large-scale philanthropy are real.

Foundations financed the research behind the high-yielding crops of the Green Revolution, which dramatically increased food production in Asia and Latin America, and they have been central to the campaign that has reduced cases of polio by more than ninety-nine per cent since 1988.
The beneficiaries of such programmes number in the hundreds of millions.

Because they are free from electoral cycles and the pressure to produce quick results, foundations can take risks and pursue long-term goals that governments and markets neglect, funding unfashionable research or unpopular causes.
In a pluralistic society, their defenders argue, the diversity of private initiatives is itself a public good.
Critics, however, see a problem of democratic legitimacy.
A foundation is subject to no electoral accountability, and its priorities reflect the preferences, sometimes idiosyncratic and sometimes parochial, of the individuals who endowed it.

When a single donor can reshape the education system of a city, or determine which diseases receive the most research funding, power over public affairs shifts from citizens to the wealthy, turning plutocrats into unelected policymakers, however benevolent their intentions.

One philanthropic programme in the United States spent heavily on breaking up large high schools into smaller ones, before its sponsors concluded that the results had been disappointing and changed course.
The students who had been the subjects of the experiment had no say in it.
There is also a financial objection.
In many countries, donations to charity are tax-deductible, which means that the public effectively subsidizes philanthropy by forgoing revenue that it would otherwise have collected.
The spending remains entirely discretionary, while taxpayers who never consented bear part of the cost, and because the richest donors give the most, the benefit accrues disproportionately to them.

Critics add that a culture which celebrates the magnanimity of billionaires distracts attention from the question of how their fortunes were made, and from policies, such as higher taxes or stronger labour laws, that might reduce the need for charity in the first place.
If society wants redistribution, on this view, it should achieve it through taxation rather than charity.
Philanthropy can also function as a form of reputation management, burnishing the image of donors whose businesses have caused harm.
Few critics propose abolishing philanthropy altogether.

More modest reforms include requiring greater transparency from foundations, whose finances are often opaque, limiting the tax advantages they receive, and obliging them to spend their endowments within a fixed period rather than existing in perpetuity.
Some donors have moved in this direction voluntarily: in 2025, the Gates Foundation announced that it would spend almost all of its assets over the following two decades and then close.
The underlying question is not whether generosity is admirable, but whether a democracy should allow so much of its public agenda to be set by those who happen to be rich.
The popular history of invention is a gallery of solitary geniuses.
Thomas Edison invents the light bulb, Alexander Graham Bell the telephone, Isaac Newton calculus, and each triumph is attributed to the singular brilliance of one exceptional mind.
The story is appealing, and it flatters a culture of individualism, but it misrepresents how most discoveries are actually made.
Historians of science have repeatedly found that major innovations emerge not from isolated individuals but from networks of people working on similar problems at the same time.
The most telling evidence is the frequency of simultaneous discovery.

Newton and the German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz developed calculus independently in the late seventeenth century, and the bitter dispute over which of them deserved precedence, fuelled by accusations of plagiarism, divided European mathematics for generations.
Newton used his eminence as president of the Royal Society to steer an official inquiry in his own favour.

Charles Darwin was prompted to publish his theory of evolution by natural selection only after receiving, in 1858, a manuscript from Alfred Russel Wallace, who had arrived at essentially the same idea while working in what is now Indonesia.
Bell and a rival inventor, Elisha Gray, submitted documents concerning the telephone to the American patent office on the same day in 1876.
A study published in 1922 listed nearly a hundred and fifty such cases, and the sociologist Robert Merton later argued in a seminal essay that multiple discovery is not the exception but the rule.
Why should discoveries so often occur concurrently?
The answer is that each invention depends on prerequisites: existing knowledge, available materials, suitable tools and a demand that makes the effort worthwhile.
Invention usually proceeds by incremental steps, each building on the last.

The electric light bulb could not have been invented before the development of reliable generators and vacuum pumps, and once those existed, attempts followed almost inexorably: more than twenty inventors produced incandescent lamps before Edison.
In England, Joseph Swan demonstrated a working bulb at almost the same time, and the two men eventually merged their British interests rather than fight over patents.
Which of several competing inventors wins the credit is often a matter of happenstance.
The writer Steven Johnson has described this situation as the adjacent possible: at any given moment, the ideas within reach are determined by what has already been achieved.
Even the inventors celebrated as lone geniuses rarely worked alone.

The laboratory of Edison at Menlo Park employed dozens of machinists, chemists and assistants, and his genius lay as much in organizing collective effort through endless iteration as in technical prowess.
Scientific credit has always been unevenly distributed, and those at the margins of institutions, such as women, junior researchers and technicians, have frequently been consigned to obscurity.
The Nobel Prizes, which may be shared among no more than three laureates, reinforce the impression of individual achievement even when a discovery required the work of thousands.
The detection of gravitational waves, for instance, was announced in 2016 by a collaboration of more than a thousand scientists.
The myth of the lone genius is not harmless.

It encourages policies that reward a few celebrated individuals rather than the institutions, communities and infrastructure that make discovery possible, and it may discourage talented people who do not recognize themselves in the heroic archetype.

It also shapes the law: patent systems grant exclusive rights to whoever files first, even when others were on the verge of the same idea, a winner-takes-all arrangement that suits the mythology better than the history.
Posterity tends to remember only the name on the patent.
Recognizing that invention is cumulative and collaborative does not diminish the achievements of individuals, but it places them where they belong, within a vast and largely anonymous enterprise.

A series of devastating droughts struck the Sahel, the semi-arid belt that stretches across Africa south of the Sahara, during the 1970s and early 1980s, and many thousands of people died, along with millions of the livestock on which their subsistence depended.
Alarming reports described the desert as advancing southwards like an army of sand dunes, swallowing farmland at the rate of several kilometres a year.
The image of a moving desert shaped international policy for decades, and it inspired ambitious schemes to halt the Sahara with walls of trees.
The reality proved more complicated.
When satellite measurements became available, they showed that vegetation in the Sahel fluctuates markedly with rainfall in a cyclical pattern, retreating in dry years and recovering in wet ones.
Much of the region has in fact become greener since the rains partly returned in the 1990s.
Scientists now regard the image of an advancing front as simplistic, and the speed of its supposed advance as greatly overstated.
What occurs instead is a patchy process of localized degradation, in which soils lose their fertility and vegetation in some places while neighbouring areas remain productive.

The United Nations defines desertification as land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from both climatic variations and human activities, and such areas, which cover about two fifths of the land surface of the Earth, are home to roughly two billion people.
The human causes are well understood.

Where populations grow rapidly, vegetation is sparse and alternatives are scarce, pastures are overgrazed, trees are cut for firewood, and fields are cultivated without the fallow periods that once allowed them to recover.
Stripped of vegetation, the soil is exposed to wind and heavy rain, which erode the fertile topsoil that took centuries to form.
Poorly managed irrigation causes a different problem: as water evaporates, it leaves salts behind, and over the years the accumulation of salt can turn fertile land into a wasteland.
Climate change adds further pressure, making rainfall more erratic and droughts more intense in many drylands.
Rich countries are not immune.

During the 1930s, farmers on the Great Plains of the United States, having ploughed up millions of acres of native grassland to grow wheat in a burst of agrarian optimism, were struck by a prolonged drought.
The exposed soil was carried away in enormous dust storms that darkened skies as far away as the Atlantic coast.

Hundreds of thousands of people abandoned their farms in what became known as the Dust Bowl, one of the worst ecological calamities in American history, an exodus immortalized in John Steinbeck's novel The Grapes of Wrath.
The disaster led the government to establish a service devoted to soil conservation, which taught farmers to plant windbreaks, rotate crops and plough along the contours of the land.
Large-scale tree-planting schemes have had mixed results.

China has planted billions of trees along the edges of its northern deserts since 1978, but many have died because the species chosen were unsuited to the dry climate, and in some places they have depleted scarce groundwater.
Some of the most striking successes have come from below.

In Niger, farmers who began in the 1980s to protect and prune the stumps of native trees sprouting in their fields, rather than clearing them, have helped to regenerate tree cover on several million hectares, improving soils and crop yields at almost no cost.

The lesson, many researchers argue, is that reversing land degradation depends less on grand engineering than on giving the people who live on the land the security and incentives to manage it well, a form of stewardship that has often worked where schemes imposed from above have failed.
Universities are among the oldest institutions in the world, older than most nations, and yet there is surprisingly little agreement about what they are for.
Some see them as engines of economic growth, training the skilled workers and generating the research on which modern economies depend.
Others regard them as communities devoted to the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake, whose value cannot be reduced to the remuneration of their graduates.

As participation has expanded, driven by a proliferation of new institutions, from a small elite to a large proportion of each generation in many wealthy countries, and as students have come to bear more of the cost, the question has acquired a new urgency.
The modern research university owes much to the reforms associated with Wilhelm von Humboldt, who helped to found the University of Berlin in 1810.
Humboldt insisted on the unity of teaching and research and on academic freedom, the principle that scholars should pursue scholarly inquiry wherever it leads, free from political interference.

A few decades later, the English theologian John Henry Newman argued in a seminal series of lectures that the purpose of a university was to cultivate the intellect, and that knowledge was intrinsically valuable rather than a means to profit.
By the 1960s, the American educator Clark Kerr was describing a very different institution, a sprawling multiversity serving a multitude of stakeholders, from government agencies to industry.
Today the economic justification dominates public debate.
Graduates in most countries earn considerably more, on average, than people without degrees, and holders of a doctorate or other postgraduate degree earn more still.
Governments justify spending on higher education by pointing to its contribution to productivity and innovation, yet economists disagree about why the premium exists.

One view holds that universities impart valuable skills; another, known as signalling, holds that much of the premium reflects the fact that a degree certifies qualities, such as intelligence, aptitude and perseverance, that students already possessed.
If the second view is largely correct, then expanding access may produce an escalating competition for credentials rather than a more proficient workforce.
The question of cost has become especially contentious.
In the United States, student debt now exceeds one and a half trillion dollars, and in some institutions high rates of attrition leave many students with debt but no degree.

In countries where tuition is free, the burden falls on taxpayers, including those who never attended university, which some critics regard as a subsidy from the less affluent to the more affluent, since students from wealthier families are disproportionately represented.
Defenders of public funding reply that the benefits of an educated population, from better public health to more informed democratic participation, extend well beyond the graduates themselves.
Perhaps the most persistent tension is between vocational and liberal conceptions of education.

Governments increasingly encourage students to choose subjects whose qualifications are readily marketable, and some institutions have reduced or closed departments of languages, history and philosophy.

Critics denounce this approach as philistine, warning that a purely utilitarian university would neglect precisely the capacities that a changing economy and a fragile democracy most need: the ability to think critically, to weigh evidence and to understand cultures other than one's own.

The most convincing answer to the question of what universities are for may be that they serve several purposes at once, and that their value lies partly in holding those purposes in balance, resisting the pressure to reduce education to any single measure.

A typical American supermarket stocks tens of thousands of different products, and a shopper looking for a jar of jam, a pair of jeans or a mobile phone contract may face a bewildering plethora of almost identical options.

Conventional economics assumes that such abundance is unambiguously good: more options mean a greater chance of finding exactly what matches one's idiosyncratic preferences, and anyone who prefers fewer can simply ignore the rest.
Paradoxically, many people find the proliferation of choice less liberating than exhausting.
A famous experiment appeared to explain why.
In 2000, two psychologists set up a tasting stall in a Californian supermarket, displaying on some days twenty-four varieties of jam and on others only six.

The larger display attracted more shoppers, but only a small fraction of those who stopped at it bought a jar, perhaps because they could not discern any meaningful difference, whereas nearly a third of those who saw the smaller selection made a purchase.

The psychologist Barry Schwartz popularized the finding in a book arguing that an excess of choice can produce paralysis, anxiety, regret and endless rumination, a phenomenon he called the paradox of choice and attributed to the cognitive costs of comparison.
Schwartz drew on a distinction made by the economist Herbert Simon between two strategies.

Maximizers seek the best possible option and feel compelled to conduct an exhaustive search before deciding, whereas satisficers settle for the first option that meets their standards, without ruminating on the alternatives.

In one study of graduates looking for jobs, maximizers found positions with higher starting salaries than satisficers, yet they were less satisfied with the result and more prone to anxiety and depressive moods.

The more options there are, the more a maximizer has to investigate, and the more likely it becomes that some unchosen alternative will seem, in retrospect, to have been better, leaving the chooser remorseful.
Subsequent research has qualified these conclusions considerably, and the original effect may have been overstated.

Attempts to replicate the jam experiment have produced mixed results, and a review that combined the findings of dozens of studies found that, on average, the effect of large assortments on satisfaction and purchasing was close to zero.

Choice overload appears to occur only under conditions conducive to it: when the options are difficult to compare, when people do not already know what they prefer, and when the decision must be made quickly.
For people whose predilections are already settled, a large assortment is an advantage rather than a burden.
The debate has practical implications for the design of public policy.
When employees must actively choose to join a pension scheme, many never do so, out of an aversion to complex paperwork and a tendency to postpone.
When they are enrolled automatically, with the option of leaving, participation rises dramatically.

Such defaults, sometimes called nudges, preserve freedom of choice while acknowledging the limits of human attention, although critics worry that they give governments and companies a subtle power to steer behaviour.
In affluent societies, where material needs are largely met, the burden of trivial choice may be one of the less obvious costs of abundance.

Perhaps the most useful conclusion is not that choice is bad, but that its value depends on circumstances: freedom to choose matters most for decisions that express who we are, and least for the countless frivolous ones that merely consume our time.
On a freezing December morning in 1849, a group of young men were led into a square in St Petersburg, dressed in white shirts, and told that they were to be shot.
Among them was Fyodor Dostoevsky, a twenty-eight-year-old writer whose first novel had been hailed as a work of genius by an eminent critic a few years earlier.
The prisoners had been convicted of belonging to a circle that discussed forbidden ideas and read subversive texts critical of the Tsar.
The first three were tied to posts and the soldiers raised their rifles; then, at the last moment, a messenger arrived with news that the Tsar had spared their lives.
The reprieve had been contrived all along, a piece of calculated cruelty intended to teach the young men a lesson.
Dostoevsky was sent instead to a prison camp in Siberia, where he spent four years performing arduous labour in fetters, followed by several more as a soldier in a remote garrison.
The only book he was permitted to read was a copy of the New Testament, given to him on his way into exile.
He shared his barracks with murderers and thieves, and his incarceration, which he later described in a fictionalized memoir, transformed his view of human nature.
He came to believe that even the most brutal criminals possessed an inner life of great complexity, and he abandoned the radical ideas of his youth for a devout, even fervent, Orthodox Christianity.
He also suffered increasingly from epilepsy, whose seizures he described as moments of euphoria followed by devastating exhaustion and melancholy.
The years after his return were marked by misfortune.
His first wife and his beloved brother died within months of each other, and the magazine they had run together suffered a calamitous collapse, leaving him at the mercy of his creditors.
On journeys to Germany, he developed a compulsive addiction to roulette, losing money he had borrowed and pawning his clothes to play again.

In 1866, facing a contract that would have given a ruthless publisher the rights to all his works if he failed to deliver a new novel by a fixed date, he dictated The Gambler to a young stenographer, Anna Snitkina, in less than a month, a feat of remarkable tenacity.
She became his second wife, and her shrewd management of his finances and publications gave him, for the first time, a degree of stability.
Over the following fifteen years he was astonishingly prolific.
Out of this turmoil came the novels on which his reputation rests.
Crime and Punishment, published the same year as The Gambler, follows a destitute student who murders a pawnbroker to prove that an extraordinary man may transgress moral law.
He then disintegrates under the weight of his guilt, pursued less by the police than by his own remorseful conscience.
The Idiot imagines a perfectly good man adrift in a corrupt society, and Demons dissects the nihilism and zeal of revolutionary conspirators.

His final novel, The Brothers Karamazov, completed a few months before his death in 1881, is a vast metaphysical drama of faith and doubt in which the murder of a father becomes an inquiry into freedom, suffering and responsibility.

Its most famous chapter, in which one brother narrates a parable of Christ returning to Spain during the Inquisition, has been read as one of the most powerful arguments against religious authority ever written, bordering on heresy for so devout an author, although Dostoevsky intended the novel as a whole to answer it.
Dostoevsky's characters argue with themselves with the same ferocity as with one another, and critics have described his novels as polyphonic, giving every antagonist the strongest possible case.
Friedrich Nietzsche called him the only psychologist from whom he had anything to learn, and the existentialists of the twentieth century regarded him as a precursor.
His life, marked by a mock execution, imprisonment, illness, addiction and grief, can seem as extreme as his fiction, and posterity has sometimes found the two hard to disentangle.

Yet what makes his work endure is not melodrama but a visceral understanding, earned at great cost, of how people rationalize their cruelty, crave both retribution and forgiveness, and search, often desperately, for meaning.
The jury of the official Paris exhibition of 1863 rejected so many paintings that the Emperor Napoleon III allowed the rejected works to be shown in a separate exhibition.
Crowds came to jeer, and one picture in particular, Édouard Manet's image of a naked woman picnicking with two clothed men, became an object of public mockery and outrage.

Eleven years later, a group of painters organized their own exhibition, and a critic, in a review dripping with derision, mocked a hazy view of a harbour by Claude Monet entitled Impression, Sunrise, and gave them the name by which they are still known: the Impressionists.
The pattern had been set: for the next century, the most important art would repeatedly arrive as an affront.
Why did artists abandon, one after another, the canonical conventions that had governed European painting since the Renaissance?
One common explanation points to photography, invented in the 1830s, which relieved painters of the obligation to record appearances with verisimilitude.
Freed from that duty, painters could explore what the camera could not capture: light, sensation, emotion and the act of painting itself.
Another emphasizes the upheavals of modern life, the growth of cities, the speed of trains and later the carnage of the First World War, which seemed to demand new forms of expression.
A third stresses the logic of artistic competition: once innovation became the measure of seriousness, each generation had to outdo the audacity of the last.
The rupture accelerated in the early twentieth century.
In 1907, Pablo Picasso painted a group of women whose faces resembled African masks and whose bodies were broken into angular planes, a work that baffled even his closest friends.
Over the following years, he and Georges Braque developed Cubism, depicting objects from several viewpoints at once.

By the 1910s, painters such as Wassily Kandinsky and Kazimir Malevich had abandoned representation altogether, and in 1915 Malevich exhibited a black square on a white ground, which he presented as the zero point of painting.
During the 1920s, surrealism turned instead to the imagery of dreams.
The most radical challenge came from Marcel Duchamp.
In 1917, he submitted to an exhibition in New York a porcelain urinal, signed with a false name and entitled Fountain.
The organizers, who had promised to show any work whose artist paid the fee, refused to display it, regarding it as a scandalous prank, and the original was lost.
Fountain was, in effect, the antithesis of everything the academies had taught.

Yet by the end of the century, a poll of hundreds of art experts named it the most influential work of modern art, because it posed a question that has haunted art ever since: if an ordinary object can become art simply because an artist chooses it, what, if anything, distinguishes art from everything else?
Modern art was never merely an aesthetic dispute.

In 1937, the Nazi regime organized an exhibition of so-called degenerate art in Munich, displaying works by Kandinsky, Paul Klee and others alongside mocking slogans, and it attracted more than two million visitors, far more than an accompanying exhibition of approved art.
Totalitarian governments of the left and right alike distrusted art that could not be easily understood or controlled, and many modernist artists were forced into exile.
Posterity has since overturned the verdicts of their persecutors.
Today, the works once derided by philistines as provocations hang in national museums and sell for enormous sums, and the scandal of the new has itself become a convention.
Whether this represents the vindication of modernism or its domestication is a question on which critics still disagree.
Milton Friedman published an article in the New York Times Magazine in 1970 with a deliberately provocative title: the social responsibility of business, he declared, is to increase its profits.

Executives, Friedman argued, are employees of the shareholders who own the company, and when they spend its money on social causes, whether reducing pollution beyond what the law requires or hiring the unemployed, they are in effect imposing a tax on the owners without their consent.
If society wants such goals pursued, elected governments should pursue them, and the fiduciary duty of managers is to maximize profitability within the rules of the game.
The argument became the foundation of what came to be called the doctrine of shareholder value.

Economists added a theory of incentives: because managers might pursue their own interests, such as empire-building or a comfortable life, at the expense of shareholders, their remuneration should be tied to the share price of the company.
From the 1980s onwards, executive pay increasingly took the form of shares and options, and companies returned vast sums to investors through dividends and the repurchase of their own shares.

The doctrine flourished amid a broader enthusiasm for deregulation and privatization, and its supporters credit it with a period of restructuring that made many sluggish corporations leaner and more profitable.
Critics argue that the doctrine has had damaging consequences.

By focusing managers on the share price, it encourages short-term thinking: in one survey, a majority of senior financial officers said they would sacrifice projects that created long-term value in order to meet quarterly earnings targets.
It may also encourage companies to cut investment, wages and research, or to outsource jobs, in order to finance buybacks that raise the share price and, with it, executive pay.

Even Jack Welch, the former chief executive of General Electric and one of the most celebrated practitioners of the doctrine, remarked after retiring that shareholder value was, on the face of it, the dumbest idea in the world.

There is, moreover, a philosophical objection: shareholders are not the only people who invest in a company, since employees invest their careers, suppliers their relationships and communities their infrastructure.
Alternatives have long existed.

In Germany, the law requires large companies to give employees half the seats on their supervisory boards, and the arrangement is often credited with a more egalitarian corporate culture, while German firms have not obviously suffered for it.

In 2019, nearly two hundred chief executives of large American corporations signed a statement redefining the purpose of a company as serving all its stakeholders, including customers, employees, suppliers and communities, rather than shareholders alone.
Investors, too, have increasingly claimed to weigh environmental and social factors in their decisions.
Skeptics doubt that such declarations amount to more than rhetoric and posturing.
A manager who is accountable to everyone, they argue, is effectively accountable to no one, since any decision can be justified by appeal to one group or another.
Amorphous commitments to social purpose may simply give executives greater discretionary power with less accountability.
Some studies have found that companies which signed the 2019 statement did not behave noticeably differently afterwards.
Meanwhile, a political backlash in the United States has portrayed sustainable investing as ideological, and several states have restricted its use by public pension funds.
The question of whose interests a corporation should serve therefore remains unresolved, and its answer depends less on economic theory than on the rules that societies choose to write.

Nearly a century ago, the economist John Maynard Keynes predicted that by the early twenty-first century, technological progress would allow people in wealthy countries to work as little as fifteen hours a week, a utopia of leisure that has failed to arrive.
Productivity has indeed grown roughly as he expected, yet working hours have fallen far less.

The anthropologist David Graeber offered a provocative explanation in an essay published in 2013: rather than using technology to reduce work, he argued, societies have invented vast numbers of jobs that are essentially superfluous.
The essay spread rapidly online, and Graeber later expanded it into a book whose title is too vulgar to repeat in polite company.
Graeber defined a pointless job as one so completely unnecessary that even the person doing it cannot justify its existence, although they may feel obliged to pretend otherwise.
He distinguished several types.
Flunkies exist to make their superiors feel important, while goons are needed only because rivals employ goons of their own, as in much corporate lobbying.
Box-tickers produce procedural paperwork allowing organizations to claim they are doing something they are not, and taskmasters supervise people who need no supervision.
A survey in Britain in 2015 found that more than a third of workers did not believe their job made a meaningful contribution to the world, which Graeber regarded as confirmation of his conjecture.
What troubled Graeber most was a moral paradox.

Many of the jobs whose value is most obvious, such as nursing, teaching and caring for the elderly, involve exhausting drudgery and often menial tasks, are poorly paid and are increasingly subject to the control of bureaucrats.
Jobs that their holders regard as futile, meanwhile, are often comfortably rewarded.

Paradoxically, the more obviously useful a job is, the less it tends to pay, and Graeber suggested that envious colleagues sometimes resent those who do useful work, as though the gratification of meaningful work were itself a form of payment.

He attributed the proliferation of pointless jobs not to market forces, which ought to eliminate waste, but to a kind of managerial feudal order, in which status within large organizations depends on the number of subordinates one commands.
Critics have challenged both the evidence and the theory.
Much of Graeber's evidence consisted of anecdotes sent to him by readers.

Researchers analysing a large European survey of working conditions found that only about one worker in twenty regarded their job as rarely or never useful, far fewer than his figures implied, and they found little to substantiate the claim that such jobs were multiplying.
Moreover, those who felt this way were not concentrated in the administrative and financial occupations he had singled out, but were scattered across many kinds of work.
The researchers concluded that the feeling of uselessness was associated less with the nature of a job than with poor management, a lack of autonomy and a toxic workplace culture.
Economists add that many roles which seem pointless from the inside, such as regulatory compliance or coordination between departments, serve functions that individual workers may not see.
Even if Graeber overstated his case, his essay touched a nerve.

Its popularity suggests that many people feel estranged from the purpose of their work, and that the gap between what work demands of them and what they believe it ought to mean is a source of considerable distress, apathy and cynicism.

The questions he raised, whether economies are organized to meet human needs or merely to keep people occupied, and whether pay is ever commensurate with social value, remain worth asking, particularly as machines automate more of what humans once did.
It is difficult to imagine a modern city without restaurants, yet the institution is surprisingly young.
Until the second half of the eighteenth century, a traveller in Paris who wanted a meal outside a private home had limited options.

There was the inn, which served whatever the host had cooked at a single table at fixed hours, with little regard for the palate of the guest; there was the tavern, offering wine and simple food; and there was the caterer, who sold cooked dishes to take away.
The idea of an establishment where strangers could sit at separate tables, choose from a menu of priced dishes and eat whenever they wished did not yet exist.
The first restaurants were not, in fact, places to eat heartily.
The word originally referred to a restorative broth, and the establishments that opened in Paris in the 1760s presented themselves as places for people of delicate health to recover their strength.

One of the earliest and most entrepreneurial proprietors, a man named Mathurin Roze de Chantoiseau, advertised his premises as a kind of health resort where a refined clientele could consume light, nourishing soups in elegant surroundings.
Because they offered restoratives rather than meals, such establishments were able to evade the rules of the powerful guilds, which acted as monopolists over the sale of cooked food.
The historian Rebecca Spang has shown that many later stories about the origins of the restaurant, including the claim that it was invented by a chef who had served the nobility, are largely myths.
The restaurant nevertheless flourished in the decades around the French Revolution.

As the guilds lost their privileges and the capital filled with deputies and officials from the provinces who needed somewhere to dine, the city witnessed a proliferation of restaurants, whose number grew from a handful to several hundred.

Some chefs who had worked in aristocratic households did open establishments of their own, bringing the elaborate cuisine of the aristocracy to anyone who could pay, and new customers sought to emulate its refinement.
The restaurant thus became, in a modest way, an egalitarian institution: a merchant with money in his pocket could eat the same dishes as a duke.
The restaurant also created a new kind of social experience.
Diners sat among strangers yet in a sense apart from them, each party at its own table, enjoying a curious combination of anonymity and conspicuous display.

The printed menu, with its list of dishes and their prices, allowed customers to exercise individual choice and to indulge idiosyncratic tastes, and it encouraged new forms of etiquette and a new vocabulary of taste.

In 1803, the writer Alexandre Grimod de la Reynière began publishing an annual guide to the gastronomic pleasures of Paris, and the restaurant critic, an arbiter of reputations who could make or break an establishment, was born.
From Paris, the institution spread across Europe with the burgeoning middle classes and eventually reached every corner of the world.

By the end of the nineteenth century, grand hotels with opulent dining rooms employed chefs such as Auguste Escoffier, who organized kitchens into disciplined brigades with a strict hierarchy of specialized cooks, a system that is still widely used.

In 1900, a French tyre company began publishing a guide intended to encourage motorists to drive further, and its system of awarding stars to restaurants became the most coveted distinction in the profession.
The restaurant, which began as a place to restore the health of the frail, has become one of the principal theatres of cosmopolitan urban life.

My dear Tom, when you telephoned on Sunday, you apologized three times for having only ten minutes to talk, and you mentioned, as though it were an achievement, that you had not taken a full day off since the spring.
I did not say so at the time, but it worried me, and I have been ruminating on it ever since.

You have always worked diligently, and I admire that, but somewhere along the way you seem to have concluded that rest is something to be earned, rationed and slightly ashamed of, and that indolence is a vice.
I want to try, at the risk of sounding like an interfering old woman, and without, I hope, any tone of reproach, to persuade you otherwise.
The philosopher Bertrand Russell published an essay entitled In Praise of Idleness in 1932, in which he argued that a great deal of harm is done by the belief that work is inherently virtuous.

He pointed out that much of the world's work is drudgery, that modern technology could allow everyone to do far less of it, and that the leisure thus gained, if it were fairly shared, might be devoted to curiosity, friendship and the arts rather than to exhaustion.
He blamed a puritanical morality, inherited from an age when the labour of the many supported the leisure of the few, for our inability to enjoy the freedom that machines had made possible.
I thought of him when you described your hectic weekends.
The idea is much older than Russell.
Seneca, whose stoicism you once mocked as a teenager, wrote that life is long enough if we know how to use it, and that most of us squander it on a compulsive busyness that leaves nothing behind.
Pascal observed that many of our troubles come from our inability to endure an hour of solitude in a quiet room.
I have come to believe they were right, and not only for philosophers.

The hours I spent as a young mother, staring out of the kitchen window while you slept, were not wasted, and I remember them now with a wistful fondness and a little melancholy: they were my solace, the only moments in the day when I could hear myself think.
There is even some evidence that idleness is useful.

Psychologists have found that when the mind is allowed to wander, it continues to work on problems beneath the surface, and that people who return to a task after a period of rest often solve it more readily than those who persevere without a break.
The apparent inefficiency of a wandering mind is an illusion, and rest is not superfluous to thought but part of it.
Many of the best ideas I ever had at work arrived in the bath or on a walk, never at my desk.

I mention this not because I think you should rest in order to be more productive, since that would turn even leisure into one more task to be performed relentlessly, but because I suspect you believe that every idle hour is a loss, and it is not.
So here is my request, which you are free to ignore.
Take one day a week on which you do nothing that anyone could call useful.
Walk without a destination, read something frivolous that will not advance your career, or simply sit in the garden and watch the light change.
You will feel guilty at first, and the first few idle Sundays may feel less like recuperation than lassitude; that is the old morality speaking, and it will grow quieter with practice.
This is a heartfelt plea, not a rebuke, and the years are more ephemeral than they seem.
I would rather you lived a slower life with room in it for the people you love, and for yourself, than a successful one that you are too tired to notice.
With all my love, Mum.
Tomorrow is Mom's birthday.
Ruby is nine, and her brother Finn is seven.
"Let's make a cake for Mom," Ruby says.
"But we can't cook," says Finn.
"Dad can help us," says Ruby.
That evening, they talk to Dad in the garden.
Dad loves the idea.
"On Saturday morning, Mom goes to the supermarket with Grandma," he says.
"She comes home at twelve. We have three hours."
Finn jumps up and down.
"A secret cake!" he says.
On Saturday, Mom leaves at nine o'clock.
Ruby, Finn and Dad run into the kitchen.
Ruby reads the recipe from a book.
Dad puts eggs, milk and butter in a big bowl.
"Finn, can you add the sugar?" Dad asks.
Finn takes a white box from the shelf and adds two big cups.
The cake goes into the oven, and the kitchen smells good.
But there is flour on the floor, on the table and on Finn's face!
At eleven o'clock, the cake is ready.
It looks beautiful.
Finn tries a small piece.
His face changes.
"It is terrible!" he says. "It is not sweet at all!"
Dad looks at the white box.
"Oh no. This is not sugar. This is salt!"
Finn is sad, and Ruby is worried.
"Mom is coming home in one hour," Ruby says. "What can we do?"
Dad thinks for a moment.
"We have fruit, and we have ice cream," he says. "Let's make something new."
They work fast.
Ruby cuts bananas and oranges.
Finn washes the apples and the grapes.
Dad puts ice cream in a big glass bowl, and they put the fruit on top.
Then they put three candles in it.
Finally, they clean the kitchen together.
At twelve o'clock, the door opens.
"Happy birthday, Mom!" the children shout.
Mom looks at the fruit and the candles, and she smiles.
"Thank you! It is beautiful. Did you make it?"
"Yes," says Finn. "And there is no salt in it!"
Mom does not understand, but everyone laughs.
On Friday evening, the Parker family is very busy.
Tomorrow they are going to have a picnic by the river.
Mom makes sandwiches, and Dad puts water and juice in a bag.
Ella, who is eight, finds her ball and her kite.
Her little brother Toby is only five.
He puts his toy trucks in his bag.
"I can't wait!" Toby says.
Before bed, Ella looks at the weather on Dad's phone.
There is a picture of a sun.
"It's going to be sunny!" she says.
Everyone goes to bed happy.
On Saturday morning, Ella wakes up early.
She hears a strange noise on the window.
She opens the curtains.
The sky is dark and gray, and it is raining hard.
"No!" she says. "The phone was wrong!"
Toby comes into the room in his pajamas.
He looks out of the window, and he starts to cry.
"No picnic?" he says.
Dad looks at the rain.
"I'm sorry," he says. "We can't go to the river today."
The children are very sad.
Then Mom has an idea.
"Who says we need a river for a picnic?" she asks.
She moves the table and the chairs to the wall.
Then she puts a big green blanket on the living room floor.
"This is our grass," she says.
Dad brings the sandwiches, and Ella brings the juice.
Toby puts his trucks around the blanket.
They eat, play games and listen to music.
Dad tells funny stories, and Toby laughs and laughs.
In the afternoon, the rain stops.
Ella looks out of the window, and she calls everyone.
"Look!" she says.
There is a big rainbow over the river.
"Next time," Toby says, "let's have our picnic under the rainbow!"
Amir is eight years old.
Every Saturday, he goes to the town library with his mom.
His mom borrows books with her card.
But today is special.
Today, Amir is going to get his own library card.
The librarian, Ms. Ortiz, smiles at him.
"Write your name here, please," she says.
Amir writes his name very carefully.
Ms. Ortiz gives him a small blue card with his name on it.
"Now you can borrow books," she says.
Amir runs to the children's room.
He finds books about space, books about dinosaurs and books about the sea.
Soon he has twelve books in his arms.
They are very heavy.
He puts them on the desk in front of Ms. Ortiz.
"I want these, please," he says.
Ms. Ortiz laughs.
"That is a lot of books! I'm sorry, but you can borrow five books at one time."
"Only five?" says Amir.
His face is sad.
"You can bring them back in two weeks, and then you can take five more," she says.
Choosing is hard.
Amir looks at every book again.
Finally, he takes two books about space, one about dinosaurs, one about the sea and one funny book for his little sister, Layla.
Layla is only four, and she cannot read yet.
So every night, Amir reads to her in bed.
He reads the funny book first, and Layla laughs.
Then he reads about space.
"Is the moon far away?" Layla asks.
"Very far," says Amir. "But one day, I want to go there."
After two weeks, Amir takes the books back to the library.
They are clean, and he is not late.
Ms. Ortiz looks at the books and at Amir.
"Did you read all of them?" she asks.
"Yes," says Amir. "And I read them to my sister, too."
Ms. Ortiz gives him a small gold star for his card.
"You are a real reader," she says.
In Mrs. Kerr's classroom, there is a fishbowl on the window shelf.
In the fishbowl, there is a little orange goldfish called Bubbles.
The children love Bubbles.
Every morning, one student feeds him.
On the last Friday before the holiday, Mrs. Kerr asks a question.
"The school is closed for two weeks. Who can take Bubbles home?"
Many hands go up.
Noah's hand goes up first.
"Can I take him, please?" he asks.
"Yes, you can, Noah," says Mrs. Kerr.
She gives him a small box of fish food.
"Feed him two times a day. Not too much!"
Noah's mom drives Noah and Bubbles home.
Noah puts the fishbowl on the kitchen table.
Then he hears a small sound behind him.
It is Tiger, the family cat.
Tiger sits on a chair and looks at the fishbowl.
His eyes are very big.
"No, Tiger!" says Noah.
"Bubbles is not your dinner!"
Noah moves the fishbowl to the top of a tall shelf.
But that night, he hears a noise in the kitchen.
He runs down in his pajamas.
Tiger is on the shelf, next to the fishbowl!
Bubbles swims fast around the bowl.
Noah takes Tiger down from the shelf.
"You are a bad cat," he says, but he is not angry for long.
He takes the fishbowl to his bedroom, and he closes the door.
For two weeks, Bubbles lives on Noah's desk.
Noah feeds him two times a day.
He cleans the water on Saturday.
He also reads books to Bubbles before bed.
Tiger sits outside the door every night, and he is not happy.
After the holiday, Noah takes Bubbles back to school.
"How was your holiday with Bubbles?" asks Mrs. Kerr.
"Good," says Noah. "But next time, can Tiger come to school, too?"
Everyone laughs.
Grandpa Joe is seventy years old today.
All the family comes to his house for a birthday lunch.
After the cake, his granddaughter Zoe gives him a small box.
Grandpa opens it.
There is a new phone inside.
"A phone?" Grandpa says. "But I have a phone."
He takes out his old phone.
It is very small, and it has a lot of buttons.
"This phone is different, Grandpa," says Zoe.
"You can take photos with it, and you can see us when you call."
Grandpa looks at the new phone for a long time.
"OK," he says. "But you have to teach me."
On Saturday, Zoe comes to Grandpa's house for a lesson.
"First, touch the camera here," she says.
"Then look at the screen and press the big white circle."
Grandpa takes a photo of his cat, Bella.
"Good!" says Zoe. "Now you can send it to the family."
That night, the family's phones do not stop.
Grandpa sends twenty photos!
There is a photo of Bella, a photo of the floor and a photo of Grandpa's shoes.
There is also a very dark photo of the inside of his pocket.
Zoe's mom laughs so hard that she cries.
Zoe writes a message: "Grandpa, one photo is OK!"
Grandpa practices every day.
He learns to write messages and to find music.
Then he learns to make video calls.
On Sunday evening, everyone in the family is at home.
Suddenly, all their phones ring at the same time.
It is Grandpa!
His face is on every screen.
"Hello, everyone!" he says. "Can you see me?"
"Yes, Grandpa!" they all say.
Zoe's aunt in Canada is in the call, too.
Grandpa smiles a big smile.
"This phone is wonderful," he says. "Now I can see you every day."
Then his cat walks in front of the camera.
"And you can see Bella, too!"
Kate is seventeen, and she has her first job.
This summer, she is going to work at a small café called The Blue Cup.
The owner is Mr. Lopez, a friendly man with a big smile.
On Monday morning, Kate arrives at seven o'clock.
She wears a black apron with a blue cup on it.
Mr. Lopez shows her the coffee machine, the cups and the cakes.
"This is lemon cake, and this is chocolate cake," he says.
"Write every order on paper. It helps."
But Kate thinks, "I can remember. It is easy."
At eight o'clock, the café is full of people.
Everyone wants coffee, and everyone is in a hurry.
A man asks for a coffee with milk and a lemon cake.
Kate gives him a tea and a piece of chocolate cake.
"This is wrong!" the man says. "I don't have time for this!"
He is very angry, and he leaves.
Kate's face is hot.
Then she gives a woman a cold coffee, not a hot one.
She drops two cups on the floor.
She wants to go home.
At ten o'clock, an old lady comes to the counter.
Her name is Mrs. Evans, and she comes to the café every day.
She looks at Kate's red face.
"Is it your first day, dear?" she asks.
"Yes," says Kate. "And it is a terrible day."
"Everyone has a first day," Mrs. Evans says. "Take your time. I am not in a hurry."
Kate smiles for the first time that day.
She takes a pen and some paper.
From now on, she writes every order down.
The afternoon is better.
She makes no mistakes.
At five o'clock, the angry man comes back.
"I'm sorry about this morning," he says. "I was late for work."
"That's OK," says Kate. "A coffee with milk and a lemon cake?"
The man laughs. "Yes, please. You remember!"
"I write everything down now," Kate says.
Alice is eleven, and she lives in New York.
One day, her English teacher has an idea for the class.
"You are going to write to students in Japan," she says.
Alice's pen pal is a boy called Hiro.
He lives in Osaka.
Hiro's first email is short.
"Hello, Alice. My name is Hiro. I am eleven. I like soccer and cats. I have a little sister. My English is not good. Sorry!"
Alice smiles.
She writes back about her family, her school and her dog.
"Your English is good!" she writes.
Every week, Alice and Hiro write to each other.
Hiro writes about Japanese food, his school and the big festivals in Osaka.
He sends photos of his cat, Mochi.
Alice sends photos of the snow in New York and of her dog in a red coat.
Hiro's English gets better and better.
Alice learns some Japanese words, too.
She can say "arigato," and it means "thank you."
Then, in May, Hiro writes very exciting news.
"My family is coming to New York in July! Can we meet?"
Alice reads the email three times.
Then she runs to her mom.
"Mom! Hiro is coming!"
In July, Alice and her mom go to the airport.
Alice has a sign with big letters: "WELCOME, HIRO!"
She is excited, but she is a little shy, too.
"What if we have nothing to say?" she asks her mom.
"You wrote fifty emails," says her mom. "You have a lot to say."
A lot of people come out of the doors.
Then Alice sees a boy with a soccer ball in his hand.
He sees her sign and waves.
"Alice?" he says.
"Hiro!" says Alice.
For a moment, they are both quiet.
Then they both start to talk at the same time, and they laugh.
Hiro's mother, Mrs. Tanaka, smiles at Alice's mom.
"They are not pen pals now," she says. "They are friends."
Omar is eleven, and he loves machines.
In two weeks, there is a science fair at his school.
Every student has to make something new.
"Let's make a robot," Omar says to his friend Lin.
"A robot? But robots are expensive!" says Lin.
"Not this robot," says Omar with a smile.
Omar's family has a lot of old boxes in the garage.
The two friends start to work.
They use a big box for the body and a small box for the head.
They make arms and legs from paper tubes.
Lin paints two big eyes and a funny mouth.
After a week, the robot looks great.
But there is one problem.
It does not move.
It just stands in the garage.
"A robot has to move," says Omar.
He is not happy.
Two days before the science fair, Omar's dad, Mr. Hassan, comes into the garage.
"What are you doing?" he asks.
"We are making a robot, but it doesn't move," says Lin.
Mr. Hassan thinks.
Then he goes into the house.
He comes back with Omar's old toy car.
"This car has a small motor," he says. "Maybe your robot can use it."
Omar and Lin take the motor and the wheels from the car.
They put them under the robot.
Omar pushes the button.
The robot moves!
It goes across the garage, and its head turns left and right.
Lin and Omar jump and shout.
On the day of the science fair, the hall is full.
Some students have computers and big machines.
Omar and Lin have a box robot.
When the judges come, Omar pushes the button, and the robot moves across the table.
Everyone laughs, and the judges write something on their paper.
At the end of the day, the judges give the prizes.
Omar and Lin do not win first prize.
But they get a prize for "Best Idea."
"Our robot was cheap, but it was a great idea," says Lin.
"And it moves," says Omar.
The summer vacation starts today.
Mei is nine, and she loves to climb trees.
There is a big old tree in the park near her house.
Mei climbs very high.
From the top, she can see the river and the school.
"Mei! Be careful!" her mother calls from a park chair.
"I'm OK, Mom!" Mei says.
Then her foot moves on a wet part of the tree.
She falls to the ground.
Her arm hurts very much, and she cries.
Her mother drives her to the hospital.
They wait for an hour.
Then a doctor calls, "Mei Chen?"
The doctor's name is Dr. Adams.
She has a kind face and a quiet voice.
"Hello, Mei. What happened?" she asks.
"I fell from a tree," Mei says. "My arm hurts."
Dr. Adams looks at the arm carefully.
"Does it hurt here?" she asks.
"Yes!" says Mei.
They take an x-ray.
On the x-ray, Mei can see the bones in her arm, and one bone is broken.
"You need a cast for six weeks," says Dr. Adams.
"Six weeks?" says Mei. "But it is summer! I can't swim!"
The cast is white and heavy.
Mei is sad in the car.
"A summer with no swimming and no trees," she says.
Her mother holds her hand.
"I have an idea," she says.
At home, Mom gives Mei some colored pens.
Mei's friends come to visit her.
They write their names on the cast, and they draw pictures.
There is a sun, a cat, a flower and a funny face.
Soon the white cast has many colors.
After six weeks, Dr. Adams takes the cast off.
Mei's arm is OK again.
"Can I keep the cast?" she asks.
Dr. Adams laughs. "Of course. It is a work of art!"
On a cold, rainy night, Oscar and his mom are in the living room.
Oscar is reading, and his mom is watching TV.
Suddenly, they hear a noise at the door.
It is not a knock.
It is a small, sad sound.
Mom opens the door.
There is a little dog on the step.
It is brown and white, and it is very wet.
It has a red collar, but there is no name on it.
"Oh, poor dog!" says Oscar. "Can it come in, Mom?"
Mom thinks for a second.
"OK, just for tonight," she says.
Oscar dries the dog with an old towel.
He gives it some water and a little chicken.
The dog eats everything, and then it sleeps near the warm window.
"I'm going to call you Rainy," Oscar says quietly.
In the morning, Rainy is waiting for Oscar at the kitchen door.
Oscar is very happy.
"Can we keep him, Mom?" he asks.
"He has a collar, Oscar," says Mom.
"That means he has a family. Maybe they are looking for him right now."
Oscar is quiet.
He knows his mom is right.
So they make posters.
Oscar takes a photo of Rainy, and Mom writes, "Is this your dog? Please call us."
They put the posters on the trees and in the shop windows on their street.
Then they wait.
In the afternoon, the phone rings.
It is an old lady called Mrs. Hill.
One hour later, she is at the door.
When the dog sees her, he runs to her and jumps up and down.
"Biscuit!" she says, and she starts to cry.
"Thank you, thank you. I looked for him all night."
Oscar is happy for Mrs. Hill, but he is sad, too.
Mrs. Hill looks at his face.
"Biscuit likes you," she says.
"I am old, and my legs are not strong. Can you help me? Can you walk him every Saturday?"
Oscar looks at his mom, and she smiles.
"Yes!" he says. "Every Saturday!"
Biscuit barks.
Maybe he says yes, too.
Sophie is eleven, and she loves soccer.
She is the goalkeeper for her school team, the Green Lions.
On Saturday, the Green Lions have their biggest game of the year.
It is the final, and they are going to play the Blue Stars.
The Blue Stars are very good.
They have a tall boy who can kick the ball very hard.
On Friday night, Sophie cannot sleep.
She thinks about the game and about the tall boy.
"What if I make a mistake?" she asks her mom.
"Everyone makes mistakes," her mom says. "Just try your best."
The game starts at ten o'clock.
Many parents and students are there.
After five minutes, the tall boy gets the ball.
He kicks it hard.
Sophie jumps, and the ball touches her hands.
But it goes between them and into the goal.
Now it is 1–0 to the Blue Stars.
Sophie looks at the ground.
Her face is red, and she wants to cry.
At half time, she sits alone.
Her friend Amara sits with her.
"Don't worry, Sophie," Amara says. "It was a very hard kick. We need you. You can do it!"
Coach Ray comes, too.
"Forget the goal," he says. "Watch the ball, not the boy."
In the second half, the Green Lions play better.
Amara gets the ball and runs fast.
She kicks it into the goal.
Now it is 1–1!
Everyone shouts and jumps.
One minute before the end, a Green Lions player pushes the tall boy.
It is a penalty for the Blue Stars.
The tall boy puts the ball on the spot.
Sophie stands in the goal.
Her legs are shaking.
"Watch the ball," she says quietly.
The boy kicks.
Sophie watches the ball, and she jumps to the left.
She catches it!
The game ends 1–1, and the two teams share the cup.
Coach Ray smiles at Sophie.
"You had a bad start, but you did not stop," he says. "That is a real goalkeeper."
This summer is very hot.
Every day, the sun is strong, and there are no clouds.
The news on TV says, "Tomorrow is going to be the hottest day of the year."
Jada is twelve.
She is at home with her dad, and they are drinking cold juice.
Their house has an air conditioner, so it is cool inside.
Then Jada thinks of her grandma.
"Dad, Grandma Rose's apartment doesn't have an air conditioner," she says.
Her dad stops drinking.
"You're right," he says. "Let's call her."
Grandma Rose is seventy-eight.
She lives alone on the top floor of an old building.
She takes a long time to answer the phone.
"Hello? Oh, it's you. I'm OK… I'm just a little tired," she says.
But her voice is very quiet.
Jada and her dad drive to Grandma's building.
Inside the apartment, it is very hot.
The windows are closed, and Grandma is sitting on the sofa in a thick sweater.
Her face is red.
"Grandma! You should not wear that sweater today!" says Jada.
"And you should drink some water," says her dad.
"I'm not thirsty," says Grandma.
"Old people often do not feel thirsty," says Dad. "But you need water."
Jada gives her grandma a big glass of cold water.
Dad opens the windows on the other side of the apartment, away from the sun.
He puts a wet towel on Grandma's neck.
After ten minutes, her face is not so red.
"You shouldn't stay here today," says Dad.
"The library is open, and it has air conditioning. Let's go there."
Grandma laughs a little.
"The library? I'm seventy-eight!"
"They have newspapers and magazines, Grandma," says Jada. "And I can read with you."
They spend the afternoon at the cool library.
Grandma reads the newspaper, and Jada reads a book next to her.
In the evening, Dad buys Grandma two new fans.
"Call us every day this week," he says.
"I will," says Grandma.
"And I will drink my water."
On Monday morning, there is a new student in Class 3A.
Her name is Nora, and she is from Brazil.
"Please say hello to Nora," says the teacher, Mr. Ross.
"Hello, Nora!" the class says.
Nora says hello very quietly.
She does not speak much English yet.
Emily sits near the window.
She looks at the new girl.
Nora looks sad and a little afraid.
At lunch, Nora sits alone at a big table.
She eats her sandwich and does not look at anyone.
Emily thinks, "I want to talk to her. But how?"
The next day, Emily sits with Nora at lunch.
"Hi, I am Emily," she says with a smile.
Nora smiles, too, but she does not say anything.
Then Emily sees Nora's notebook.
There are beautiful pictures in it: birds, flowers and a big yellow cat.
"Wow! Did you draw these?" Emily asks.
Nora understands, and she says, "Yes."
Emily takes a pencil and draws a dog.
It is not very good, and Nora laughs.
Nora points at the cat in her notebook.
"Gato," she says.
"Gato? Is that 'cat' in Portuguese?" asks Emily.
"Yes! Cat," says Nora.
Now they both laugh.
Every day at lunch, Emily and Nora draw together.
Emily teaches Nora English words, and Nora teaches Emily Portuguese words.
After a month, Nora can say a lot in English.
One day, Mr. Ross has an idea.
"Our class is going to paint a big picture for the school hall," he says.
"Nora, can you help us? You are a great artist."
Nora is surprised, but she says, "Yes, I can!"
The picture is beautiful.
There are birds, flowers, a big yellow cat and a funny dog in it.
"Your dog is still not very good," Nora tells Emily.
"I know," Emily says. "But it is our dog."
On a rainy Sunday, Ivy is at her grandpa's house.
She is bored.
"Can I look in your big desk, Grandpa?" she asks.
"Yes, you can," says Grandpa Walter.
In the desk, Ivy finds an old black and white photo.
In the photo, there is a street with small shops and old cars.
There is a cinema with a big sign, and there are a lot of people.
A young man in a hat is standing in front of the cinema.
He is smiling.
"Grandpa, who is this?" Ivy asks.
Grandpa puts on his glasses.
"That is me!" he says. "I was twenty years old."
"You?" Ivy laughs. "You were young!"
Grandpa sits down, and he looks at the photo for a long time.
"This was Park Street, sixty years ago," he says.
"There was no supermarket then. There were small shops. I knew all the owners."
"And the cinema?" asks Ivy.
"The Star Cinema. I went there every Saturday. It was the best place in town."
He smiles.
"I met your grandma there. She was in the next seat."
Ivy's eyes are big.
"Is the cinema still there?" she asks.
"I don't know," says Grandpa. "I don't go to Park Street very often now."
"Let's go and see!" says Ivy.
The rain stops, and they take the bus to Park Street.
Everything is different.
The small shops are not there.
There is a big supermarket, a bank and a phone shop.
Grandpa is quiet.
Then Ivy sees an old building at the end of the street.
It has a big sign.
"Grandpa, look!" she says.
The sign says "STAR."
The building is not a cinema now.
It is a café.
But the old sign is still there.
They go in and sit by the window.
Grandpa has a coffee, and Ivy has a hot chocolate.
"Grandma and I sat here, in the dark, and we watched movies," Grandpa says.
Ivy takes a photo of Grandpa by the window.
"Now you have a new photo at the Star," she says.
Daniel is ten, and he is a very shy boy.
At school, he does not talk much.
But at home, in his bedroom, he sings.
He sings songs from the radio and from old movies.
One evening, his big sister Grace stops at his door.
She listens.
Daniel's voice is clear and beautiful.
Grace opens the door.
"Daniel! You can sing! You can really sing!"
Daniel's face goes red.
"Please don't tell anyone," he says.
The next week, there is a poster in the school hall.
"Singing Contest: Friday, May 20. Everyone can take part!"
Grace shows the poster to Daniel.
"No," says Daniel. "I can't sing in front of people."
"You can," says Grace. "I can help you."
Every evening, Daniel sings for Grace in the living room.
Then he sings for Grace and their parents.
Then he sings for Grace, their parents and their grandma.
Every time, it is a little easier.
Finally, he puts his name on the contest list.
On Friday, the hall is full of students and parents.
Daniel is number seven.
When he walks onto the stage, his legs are shaking.
He looks at all the people, and his mouth is very dry.
The music starts, but he cannot sing.
Nothing comes out.
Then he sees Grace in the front row.
She smiles and shows him her hands, like in the living room.
Daniel closes his eyes.
He thinks about the living room, and he starts to sing.
His voice fills the hall.
When he finishes, everyone stands up and claps.
Daniel does not win first prize.
He wins second prize.
But his music teacher, Mrs. Cole, comes to him after the contest.
"Daniel, can you sing in our school concert in December?" she asks.
Daniel looks at Grace.
"Yes," he says. "I can."
Hana wakes up, and her room is very bright.
She looks out of the window.
Everything is white: the street, the cars and the trees.
There is a lot of snow!
Her little brother Kenji runs into the room.
"Hana! Listen to the radio!"
A man on the radio says, "There is no school today because of the snow."
"No school!" the children shout, and they dance around the room.
After breakfast, they put on their coats, hats and gloves.
They go out into the garden.
They make a big snowman with a carrot for a nose.
Then they throw snowballs at each other and laugh.
Across the street, there is a small old house.
Mr. Grant lives there alone.
He is eighty-five, and he walks with a stick.
Hana sees his face at the window.
He does not look happy.
There is a lot of snow in front of his door, and he cannot open it.
"Kenji, look at Mr. Grant," says Hana.
"He can't go out. He can't go to the shop!"
Kenji stops playing.
"Let's help him," he says.
The children get Dad's big shovel from the garage.
They cross the street and knock on Mr. Grant's window.
"Hello, Mr. Grant! Can we help you?" asks Hana.
Mr. Grant smiles. "Oh, thank you. Yes, please!"
It is hard work.
Hana moves the snow, and Kenji helps with his small red shovel.
After an hour, the door can open.
"Do you need anything from the shop?" Kenji asks.
"Some milk and some bread, please," says Mr. Grant, and he gives them some money.
When they come back, Mr. Grant has hot chocolate for them.
They sit in his warm kitchen.
He tells them about the snow when he was a boy, seventy years ago.
"The snow was up to the windows!" he says.
At the end of the day, Hana and Kenji are tired and cold.
But it is their best snow day ever.
Poppy is six years old.
One morning at breakfast, she puts her hand on her mouth.
"Mom! My tooth is moving!" she says.
Her mom looks.
One of Poppy's small front teeth is wobbly.
"That's great, Poppy!" says Mom. "Your first wobbly tooth! A big new tooth is coming."
But Poppy is not happy.
"Is it going to hurt?" she asks.
"No, not much," says Mom.
Poppy does not believe her.
All day, she does not eat apples or bread.
She only eats soup and yogurt.
