That evening, her big brother Theo sits on her bed.
He is ten, and he has a big smile with some new teeth.
"Are you scared, Poppy?" he asks.
"Yes," says Poppy. "I don't want my tooth to go."
"Do you know about the tooth fairy?" Theo asks.
Poppy shakes her head.
"When a tooth comes out, you put it under your pillow," says Theo.
"At night, the tooth fairy comes. She takes the tooth, and she leaves a gift."
"A gift?" says Poppy.
"Yes. When I was six, she gave me a coin and a little letter," says Theo.
Poppy thinks about this for a long time.
The next day, Poppy is brave.
At lunch, she takes a big red apple.
Mom and Theo watch her.
She eats a big piece, and then she stops.
There is something small and white in the apple.
It is her tooth!
"It came out!" she says. "And it didn't hurt!"
Everyone laughs, and Poppy smiles a big smile with a hole in it.
That night, she puts the tooth under her pillow with a letter.
The letter says, "Dear Tooth Fairy, this is my first tooth. Please be careful with it."
In the morning, there is a coin and a very small letter under the pillow.
"Thank you, Poppy. You are very brave," it says.
Poppy looks at Theo.
Theo is looking out of the window, and he is smiling.
It is Saturday morning.
Leo is ten years old, and today is a big day for him.
He wants to visit his friend Max, and he wants to go alone.
"Can I take the bus, Mom?" Leo asks.
His mother thinks for a moment.
"OK," she says. "Take the number 5 bus and get off at the park. Max's house is near the park."
She gives him some money and her old phone.
"Call me when you get there."
Leo walks to the bus stop.
He is excited, and he is a little afraid, too.
A big red bus comes.
Leo gets on quickly and sits by the window.
He does not look at the number on the front of the bus.
It is not the number 5.
It is the number 3.
The bus goes through the city.
Leo looks out of the window and waits for the park.
He sees shops, a church and a big hotel.
Then he sees a factory and green fields.
There is no park.
"Oh no," Leo thinks. "This is the wrong bus!"
His face is hot, and his hands are cold.
At the next stop, Leo gets off.
There is a woman at the stop with a big bag of apples.
"Excuse me," Leo says. "Where is this? I want to go to the park in the city."
The woman smiles.
"You are far from the city now. This is the road to the airport."
"The airport?" Leo says. "Oh no!"
"Don't worry," she says. "Wait here for the number 5. It goes back to the city, and it stops at the park."
Leo waits at the stop, and he calls his mother.
"Mom, I am OK, but I took the wrong bus."
His mother is quiet for a second.
Then she asks, "Where are you now?"
"Near the airport. But a lady helped me. The number 5 is coming soon."
"Good," says his mother. "I am proud of you. You asked for help, and that is smart."
The number 5 bus comes, and this time Leo looks at the number two times.
Forty minutes later, he is at Max's door.
"You are late!" Max says. "Where were you?"
"At the airport," Leo says.
Max laughs. "The airport? Are you going on a trip?"
"Not today," Leo says, and he laughs too.
Marco is twelve.
His family has a small pizza shop on Hill Street.
After school, Marco often helps his father, Mr. Rossi.
He washes the dishes and cleans the tables.
One Friday afternoon, the phone rings.
It is Ms. Lane, a teacher from the school near the river.
"Hello! Can I order twenty pizzas for our school party?" she asks.
Mr. Rossi is very surprised.
"Twenty? Yes, of course! When do you need them?"
"At six o'clock this evening, please."
Mr. Rossi writes it down.
Then he looks at the clock.
It is three o'clock.
Mr. Rossi starts to work fast.
He makes the first five pizzas.
Then he picks up a big bag of flour, and he stops.
"Ow! My back!" he says.
He sits down on a chair.
His face is white, and he cannot stand up.
"Dad! Are you OK?" asks Marco.
"My back hurts," says Mr. Rossi. "I can't make fifteen more pizzas."
Marco thinks for a moment.
"I can make them, Dad," he says. "You can tell me what to do."
Mr. Rossi looks at his son.
"OK," he says. "Let's try."
Mr. Rossi sits on his chair, and Marco works.
"Put the tomato on the pizza. Not too much!" says his father.
"Now the cheese. Now the chicken. Good!"
Marco's sister Nico comes home from school, and she helps, too.
She puts the pizzas in boxes.
They count them: sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen… twenty!
At five forty, the pizzas are ready.
Marco's uncle drives them to the school.
At six o'clock, Ms. Lane calls again.
"The pizzas are here, and they are delicious!" she says. "The children love them. Thank you!"
Mr. Rossi smiles at Marco and Nico.
"Thank you, my two young cooks," he says.
"Next week, you can be the boss!"
In spring, Class 2B has a new project.
Behind the school, there is a small garden, and it is for them.
Their teacher, Ms. Stone, gives every student a little tomato plant.
Every morning, the children water the plants.
Ava draws pictures of them in her notebook.
Lucas measures them with a ruler.
"Mine is ten centimeters!" he says one day.
In June, there are small green tomatoes on the plants.
A week later, some of them are red.
"Next Monday, we can pick them and make a salad," says Ms. Stone.
The children are very excited.
On Monday morning, Ava runs to the garden first.
Then she stops.
The red tomatoes are not there.
Some green ones are on the ground, and some leaves have holes in them.
"Oh no!" she says. "What happened?"
The other children come.
Some of them are angry, and some of them are sad.
"Who ate our tomatoes?" asks Lucas.
"I know! It was the big boys from Class 5A!"
"Wait," says Ms. Stone. "We don't know that. Look carefully first."
The children look.
Near the plants, there are very small footprints in the dirt.
"These are not the big boys' feet," says Ava.
That afternoon, the class sits quietly behind the classroom window.
They watch the garden.
After twenty minutes, something moves under the plants.
It is a little brown rabbit!
It eats a tomato, and its nose moves up and down.
The children laugh, and the rabbit runs away.
"We can't be angry with a rabbit," says Lucas.
So the class has a new plan.
They put a small fence around the tomatoes.
Then they plant some carrots outside the fence.
"These carrots are for our rabbit," says Ava.
In July, the class makes a big tomato salad, and the rabbit has its carrots.
Chloe's dad, Tom, was forty-five years old, and he worked in an office.
He sat at a desk all day, and he was a little overweight.
One evening at dinner, he made an announcement.
"I'm going to run a marathon," he said.
Chloe almost dropped her fork.
"Dad, you've never run more than five kilometers," she said. "A marathon is forty-two!"
"I know," said her dad. "That's why it's a challenge."
The marathon was in six months.
Tom bought new running shoes and made a training plan.
He also changed his diet.
No more burgers and no more cola.
Instead, he ate a lot of fruit, vegetables and pasta.
The first weeks were very hard.
After three kilometers, Tom's legs hurt, and he could hardly breathe.
But he did not give up.
He ran early every morning before work, and on Sundays he ran for two hours.
Slowly, his body got stronger.
He lost eight kilos, and he felt more energetic at work.
Sometimes Chloe ran with him on her bike.
She carried a water bottle and a watch to check his speed.
"You're getting faster, Dad," she said one day.
Her dad smiled, but he was too tired to answer.
On the day of the marathon, the city streets were full of runners and people cheering.
Chloe and her mother waited near the finish line.
They followed Tom's progress on an app on their phones.
For the first twenty-five kilometers, everything went well.
Then, at kilometer thirty, his dot on the map stopped moving.
Five minutes passed.
Then ten.
Chloe was worried.
Finally, her phone rang.
"I've injured my ankle," said her dad. "I think I have to stop."
Chloe jumped on her bike and rode to kilometer thirty.
Her dad was sitting on a bench with his head in his hands.
"Six months of training," he said sadly. "And I can't finish."
Chloe sat next to him.
"Can you walk?" she asked.
"Slowly," he said.
"Then let's walk," said Chloe. "Nobody said you have to run."
They walked the last twelve kilometers together.
It took almost three hours.
When they reached the finish line, most people had gone home.
But a woman called Mrs. Harris was still there with the last medals.
She put one around Tom's neck.
"You finished," she said. "That's what matters."
Tom gave the medal to Chloe.
"This is half yours," he said.
Every summer, the whole family met at Grandma Rosa's house by the sea.
There were cousins, uncles, aunts and a lot of noise.
And there was always Grandma's famous plum cake.
Nobody knew the recipe.
"It's a secret," Grandma always said, and she laughed.
Last winter, Grandma died.
In July, the family decided to meet at her house one more time.
Elena, who was fifteen, looked at the empty kitchen.
"It won't be the same without her plum cake," she said sadly.
Her little brother Mateo agreed.
"Let's try to make it," he said. "How difficult can it be?"
They searched the kitchen for the recipe.
They looked in every drawer and every cupboard.
They found old letters, photos and lots of spoons, but no recipe.
So they asked the family.
Their mother, Sofia, remembered that Grandma always used a lot of butter.
Uncle Paulo said that the cake smelled of cinnamon.
Aunt Lucia remembered that Grandma put the plums on top, not inside.
And their cousin said, "She always added something from a little blue bottle."
The first cake was too dry.
The second cake was burned at the bottom, because they forgot to check the oven.
The third cake tasted good, but it was not Grandma's cake.
Something was missing.
That evening, Elena found the little blue bottle in the back of a cupboard.
It was lemon juice.
On the bottle there was a small label in Grandma's writing: "Three spoons. With love."
Elena's eyes filled with tears.
The next morning, Elena and Mateo tried again.
First, they mixed the butter and the sugar until it was soft and pale.
After that, they added eggs, flour, cinnamon and three spoons of lemon juice.
They poured the mix into a pan and put the plums on top.
Finally, they baked it for forty minutes and watched the oven the whole time.
At lunch, they brought the cake to the table.
The family went quiet.
Their mother took a piece and closed her eyes.
"That's it," she said softly. "That's Grandma's cake."
Elena wrote the recipe in a new notebook.
At the bottom, she added: "With love."
Now it is not a secret anymore.
It is a tradition.
It was the day before the holidays, and the train was full.
Theo was nineteen, and he was going home for the first time since September.
He had a big black case next to him. Inside it was his cello.
Theo studied music at a college in the city.
He played beautifully when he was alone, but in front of people, he became so nervous that his hands shook.
Last week, he failed an important audition because of his nerves.
Outside, it was snowing heavily.
Suddenly, the train stopped in the middle of a white field.
"There is snow on the line," said the driver. "We'll be here for about three hours. We're very sorry."
Everyone in the carriage groaned, and some people looked worried.
An old lady was sitting opposite Theo.
She had white hair, a red scarf and very bright eyes.
"Terrible weather, isn't it?" she said with a smile.
Theo was shy, but three hours was a long time, so he answered.
Her name was Ada, and she was on her way to visit her grandchildren.
She asked Theo about the big case.
He told her about his college, his cello and the audition.
"I love the music," he said, "but I don't think I can play for an audience."
Ada listened carefully and did not say anything for a moment.
"Can I tell you something?" she said at last.
"I played the cello for fifty years."
Theo looked at her again, and suddenly he knew her face.
She was Ada Lind, one of the most famous cellists in the world.
He had a poster of her in his room when he was twelve.
"Before every concert, my hands shook, too," said Ada.
"For fifty years. Nerves are not a problem. They show that you care."
Then she pointed at the case.
"These people are cold and bored. Why don't you play for them?"
Theo's heart was beating fast, but he opened the case.
At first, his hands shook, and the first notes were not good.
Then he looked at Ada, and she nodded.
He closed his eyes and played the music he loved.
Slowly, the carriage became quiet.
People stopped looking at their phones.
A little girl stood on her seat to see better.
When he finished, everybody clapped, and a man at the back shouted, "More!"
Theo played for two more hours, until the train started to move again and continued its journey.
At the station, Ada gave him a card with her phone number.
"Call me before your next audition," she said.
In the spring, Theo tried again, and this time he passed.
His hands still shook a little, but now he felt confident, and he knew that was OK.
The Paper Planes were a school band with four members.
Zara played the guitar, Kai played the violin, Leo played the drums, and Marcus was the singer.
Marcus had a great voice, and he loved to be in front of an audience.
Leo was the opposite.
He was quiet and shy, and he always sat at the back behind his drums.
But he wrote most of the band's songs in his notebook at night.
In May, the band had exciting news.
They were invited to play at the town's summer festival, in front of more than a thousand people.
It was their biggest concert ever.
They practiced every day after school until their fingers hurt.
Two days before the festival, Zara's phone rang.
It was Marcus, and his voice sounded terrible.
"I'm ill," he said slowly. "I can't sing. I can hardly speak."
The doctor had told him to rest his voice for a week.
The band met in Zara's garage.
"We have to cancel," said Kai sadly.
"No," said Zara. "Somebody else can sing."
"Who? I can't sing, and you can't sing," said Kai.
They both looked at Leo.
"Me? No way," said Leo.
"But you know every word," said Zara. "You wrote the songs!"
"Writing is different from singing," said Leo. "I'll be terrible."
"Just try one song," said Kai. "Only for us. Nobody else is here."
Leo looked at the floor for a long time.
Then he picked up the microphone.
At first, his voice was very soft.
Then he closed his eyes and sang the chorus.
His voice was not like Marcus's voice.
It was lower and gentler, and it was full of feeling.
When he finished, nobody said anything.
Then Zara started to clap.
"You're singing on Saturday," she said.
On Saturday, the festival was crowded and noisy.
Leo's hands were shaking as he walked onto the stage.
A friend of Kai's played the drums, and Leo stood at the front for the first time.
He looked at the audience, and his mouth went dry.
Then he saw Marcus in the first row.
Marcus could not speak, but he gave Leo a big smile and two thumbs up.
The music began, and Leo started to sing.
After the first song, the crowd cheered.
After the last song, they cheered even louder.
When Marcus was well again, the band had a new plan.
Now The Paper Planes have two singers.
And Leo still writes the songs.
Diego was seventeen, and he loved bikes more than anything.
This summer, his uncle Ray gave him a job in his small bike repair shop.
The shop was on a busy street near the university, and many students came there.
Uncle Ray was an expert.
He could repair anything: a broken chain, a flat tire, a bent wheel.
For the first two weeks, Diego only watched and cleaned the tools.
Then his uncle let him do small jobs.
Diego learned quickly, and he felt very proud.
"You have good hands," said his uncle. "But remember: be careful and check everything twice."
One Friday afternoon, Uncle Ray had to go to the bank.
"You're in charge," he told Diego. "I'll be back in an hour."
It was the busiest hour of the week.
Five customers came in, and they all wanted their bikes quickly.
A man called Mr. Grant brought an old red bike.
"The brakes don't work well," he said. "Can you fix them? I need the bike to go to work tomorrow."
Diego adjusted the brakes in ten minutes.
Another customer was waiting, so he did not test the bike.
Mr. Grant paid the bill and rode away.
On Monday morning, Mr. Grant came back.
His face was red, and his arm was covered with a bandage.
"I'm afraid there's a big problem," he said to Uncle Ray.
"Your assistant fixed my brakes on Friday. On Saturday, they didn't work at all, and I fell off my bike at a traffic light."
Diego felt terrible.
His uncle looked at the bike.
One brake was loose.
It was a simple mistake, but it was dangerous.
Diego stood up.
"It was my fault," he said. "I didn't check it twice. I'm really sorry, Mr. Grant."
Mr. Grant was quiet for a moment.
He had expected the boy to make excuses.
"Well," he said, "at least you're honest."
Uncle Ray repaired the brakes, and this time Diego watched every step.
Then Diego tested the bike three times on the street.
They did not ask Mr. Grant to pay, and Uncle Ray gave him a new helmet as a gift.
After that day, Diego never rushed a job again.
Before every bike left the shop, he checked it twice and rode it once.
At the end of the summer, Mr. Grant came back with his daughter's bike.
"I want Diego to repair this one," he said.
Diego smiled.
It was the best compliment of his summer.
For his fourteenth birthday, Dev got the best present of his life: a blue mountain bike.
He rode it everywhere, to school, to the park and to his friends' houses.
On the first day, he put a small lion sticker under the seat.
He always locked the bike, of course.
One Saturday, he rode to the bookshop on Castle Street to buy a comic.
He locked the bike outside and went in.
He was inside for only ten minutes.
When he came out, the bike was gone.
The lock was lying on the ground, cut in two.
Dev ran home, and his mother drove him to the police station.
A police officer called Officer Ruiz wrote down his description of the bike.
She asked him a lot of questions.
Where was he? What was he doing? Was anyone standing near the bike?
Dev remembered a man in a grey hoodie who was waiting across the street.
Officer Ruiz was honest with him.
"We'll do our best," she said, "but many stolen bikes are never found."
Dev went home and did not eat his dinner.
A week later, Dev's cousin Asha was looking at a website where people sell old things.
Then she saw an advertisement: "Blue mountain bike. Almost new. Only 80 dollars."
She sent the link to Dev at once.
Dev looked at the photos very carefully.
In the third photo, he saw something small under the seat.
It was a lion sticker.
"That's my bike!" he shouted, and he called Officer Ruiz.
Officer Ruiz had a plan.
Asha wrote to the seller and said that she wanted to buy the bike.
They agreed to meet in a supermarket car park the next afternoon.
When the seller arrived with the bike, two police officers were waiting for him.
He tried to run away, but he did not get far.
In his van, the police found six more stolen bikes.
That evening, Dev got his bike back.
"Thanks to your sticker, six other people will get their bikes back, too," said Officer Ruiz.
The next day, Dev bought a new lock, the strongest one in the shop.
And he put lion stickers on all his things.
Mason was eleven, and he had never been camping.
His dad had a plan for the summer holiday: two nights in a tent near Pine Lake.
"No phones, no TV, just nature," Dad said.
Mason was not sure it was a good idea.
They packed the car with a tent, two sleeping bags, a small cooker, food and a map.
Dad also packed an old compass.
"My father gave it to me when I was your age," he said proudly.
The forest was beautiful.
Tall trees stood around the lake, and the air smelled of pine.
They hiked for two hours to find a good place for their tent.
Mason saw a deer between the trees and a lot of strange insects.
Putting up the tent was more difficult than Dad expected.
The instructions were missing, and the tent fell down twice.
Mason laughed so much that he had to sit down.
Finally, the tent was up.
They cooked sausages on the small cooker and ate them by the lake.
The sunset was fantastic, and Mason had to admit that camping was fun.
In the middle of the night, a loud noise woke Mason up.
It was thunder.
Rain was falling heavily on the tent, and the wind was shaking it.
Then Mason felt something cold.
Water was coming into the tent!
His sleeping bag was wet.
"Dad! Wake up!" he shouted.
His dad turned on his torch.
"We have to go to the car," he said. "It's too dangerous here."
But in the dark and the rain, they could not see the path.
Dad took out the old compass.
"The car is to the south," he said. "Follow me."
The path was dark and slippery.
Branches hit their faces, and once Mason fell into a bush.
Dad held his hand and checked the compass again and again.
Mason was frightened, but he did not say anything.
He did not want his dad to worry.
It took them forty minutes to reach the car.
They were wet and cold, and their shoes were full of mud.
They sat in the car and waited for the storm to finish.
Dad turned on the heating and gave Mason a dry sweater from his bag.
Dad looked at Mason.
"I'm sorry," he said. "This was a terrible idea."
"No, it wasn't," said Mason. "Your compass saved us."
Dad was quiet for a moment.
Then he told Mason about his own first camping trip with Grandpa, forty years ago.
"It rained then, too," he said, and they both laughed.
In the morning, the sun came out, and the forest was quiet and fresh.
They walked back to the lake.
The tent was on the ground, and their food was everywhere.
But the lake was shining in the sunlight, and a family of ducks was swimming near the shore.
"Dad," said Mason, "can we come back next summer?"
His dad smiled.
"Only if we buy a better tent," he said.
On Sunday, Mrs. Brooks baked two dozen chocolate cookies.
She put them in a glass jar on the kitchen counter.
"These are for the school party on Friday," she said. "Don't touch them!"
On Monday morning, there were twenty cookies in the jar.
On Tuesday morning, there were sixteen.
Mrs. Brooks was annoyed.
"Somebody is eating the cookies at night," she said at breakfast.
Everyone said, "It wasn't me!"
Ivy, who was ten, loved mystery books.
"I'll find the thief," she said. "I'm going to be a detective."
Her big brother Sam laughed at her.
"Good luck, detective," he said.
Ivy took a notebook and made a list of suspects.
First, there was Sam.
He was fourteen, and he was always hungry.
Second, there was Dad.
He was on a diet, and he said he missed sweets very much.
Third, there was Grandpa, who often woke up at night.
And finally, there was Pepper, the family dog.
Ivy looked for clues.
Near the jar, she found some crumbs.
On the floor, there were small brown marks.
"The thief must be tall," she wrote in her notebook. "The jar is high. It can't be Pepper."
On Wednesday night, Ivy did not sleep.
She hid behind the sofa with a torch and waited.
At midnight, she heard footsteps on the stairs.
Someone was coming into the kitchen!
It was Dad.
He opened the fridge, took a glass of milk and looked at the cookie jar for a long time.
Then he sighed, closed the fridge and went back upstairs.
He didn't take a cookie!
"So it wasn't Dad," Ivy thought.
Then she fell asleep behind the sofa.
In the morning, there were only ten cookies in the jar.
Ivy was angry with herself.
Then she noticed something.
There was a chair next to the counter, and on the chair there were small brown paw prints.
That night, Ivy watched again, and this time she stayed awake.
At two o'clock, Pepper came into the kitchen.
He jumped onto the chair, then onto the counter, and he opened the jar with his nose!
Ivy turned on the light.
Pepper looked at her with a cookie in his mouth.
At breakfast, Ivy told the family everything.
Sam stopped laughing.
"Not bad, detective," he said.
Mrs. Brooks moved the jar to the top of the fridge.
And on Friday, Ivy's class had ten cookies and a funny story.
Mia wanted a digital camera more than anything.
She loved taking photos, but her old phone took terrible pictures.
The camera she wanted cost four hundred dollars, and she had only sixty.
"Get a job," said her brother.
"I'm fifteen," said Mia. "Who will give me a job?"
Then she had an idea.
Many people on her street had dogs, but they were busy at work all day.
Mia made a small advertisement and put it in every mailbox: "Dog walker. Ten dollars a walk. Reliable and friendly!"
Her first client was Mrs. Kowalski, an old lady who lived at number twelve.
Her dog, Biscuit, was big, brown and very lazy.
Mrs. Kowalski gave Mia a list of rules.
Biscuit went out twice a day, at eight and at five.
He never ate chocolate, and he was afraid of cats.
Mia walked Biscuit every afternoon after school.
He was slow, but he was sweet, and soon they were best friends.
Other neighbors saw them and called Mia, too.
After a month, she had four regular dogs and a calendar full of walks.
One Friday, Mia had a problem.
She had a test the next day, so she decided to walk all four dogs at the same time.
It was not a good idea.
In the park, a small black cat jumped out of a bush.
Pepper, a young dog, ran after it, and the other dogs pulled in three different directions.
When Mia looked round, Biscuit was gone.
She looked everywhere for an hour.
She looked in the bushes, by the lake and behind the café.
It was getting dark, and she felt worse and worse.
How could she tell Mrs. Kowalski?
At last, Mia walked to number twelve with the other three dogs.
She was ready to say sorry.
But there, on the doorstep, was Biscuit, fast asleep.
He was afraid of the cat, so he had simply walked home.
Mia told Mrs. Kowalski the whole story anyway.
The old lady laughed.
"Thank you for being honest," she said. "But next time, only two dogs at a time!"
Three months later, Mia bought her camera.
Her first photo was of Biscuit, of course, asleep on the doorstep.
Harper Carter was sixteen, and her family lived in a small town in Ohio.
This spring, her school had an exchange program with a school in Lyon, France.
A French student called Lucas was going to stay with her family for three weeks.
Later, Harper would stay with his family in France.
Harper was excited, but also a little nervous.
"What if he doesn't like us?" she asked her mom.
"Just be yourself," her mom said.
When Lucas arrived at the airport, he gave Harper a kiss on each cheek.
Harper's face went red.
"In France, this is how we say hello," Lucas explained with a smile.
"Here, we usually just say hi," said Harper, and they both laughed.
In the first week, Lucas noticed many differences.
The Carters had dinner at six o'clock.
"In my family, we eat at eight or even later," said Lucas.
The portions were much bigger, and everyone drank water or soda with dinner.
In France, lunch was the most important meal, and it often lasted more than an hour.
The school was different, too.
It was bigger than his school in Lyon, and it had a huge sports center and a stadium.
Students chose many of their subjects, and there were clubs for everything, from chess to cooking.
"Your school is more fun than mine," Lucas said.
"But our bread is better!"
One evening, Harper's grandmother came to dinner.
Lucas wanted to be polite, so he brought her flowers.
He chose yellow chrysanthemums, because they were beautiful and cheap.
But when Harper saw them, her eyes opened wide.
"Those are fine here," she whispered. "But aren't chrysanthemums for funerals in France?"
Lucas laughed.
"You're right! In France, my grandmother would be shocked," he said.
"But I checked on the internet. Here, they're just flowers."
Harper's grandmother loved them.
She put them in the middle of the table.
"Customs are funny things," she said. "The same flower can mean happiness in one country and sadness in another."
The three weeks went very fast.
Lucas learned to play baseball, and he cooked a French dinner for the family.
Harper learned some French words and how to make a real crêpe.
At the airport, it was time to say goodbye.
This time, Harper gave Lucas a kiss on each cheek.
"See? I'm learning," she said.
"See you in Lyon in June!" said Lucas.
"I'll bring the bread," said Harper. "Just kidding!"
Ana was on the bus home from school when her phone made a sound.
It was a text message from a number she did not know.
"Congratulations! You are the winner of our weekly prize: a new smartphone! Click the link to receive your prize today."
Ana's heart jumped.
Her phone was old, and the screen was broken.
She had wanted a new one for months, but her parents said it was too expensive.
"This must be my lucky day," she thought.
But the message said she had to click before six o'clock.
It was already five thirty.
At home, Ana sat on her bed and looked at the message again.
She clicked the link.
A colorful website appeared with a photo of the phone.
"To receive your prize, enter your name, address and bank card details. We need a small fee of two dollars for delivery."
Two dollars was nothing for a new phone.
Ana took her mother's bank card from the kitchen drawer.
She started to type the number.
At that moment, her brother Leo came into the room.
He was nineteen and studied computer science at the university.
"What are you doing with Mom's card?" he asked.
Ana showed him the phone.
Leo read the message, and his face changed.
"Stop! Don't type anything," he said. "This is a scam."
"How do you know?" asked Ana.
"Look at the website address," said Leo.
"It's strange, and there are mistakes in the English. Real companies don't send prizes to people who never entered a competition."
He explained that the thieves wanted the card number, not the two dollars.
"With these details, they can take all the money from Mom's account," he said.
Ana felt cold.
She had almost done something terrible.
Leo helped her to close the website and delete the message.
Then they told their mother everything.
Ana was worried that her mother would be angry.
But Mrs. Diaz only hugged her.
"I'm glad you didn't finish," she said. "These people are very clever. Many adults believe them, too."
Mrs. Diaz called her bank, Maple Bank, to tell them about the message.
The bank said it was a common trick, and they thanked her.
That weekend, Ana made a poster for her school: "Too good to be true? Then it probably isn't true."
Her teacher put it on the wall of every classroom.
And in December, Ana's parents bought her a new phone from a real shop.
Owen was fourteen, and he was very good at science.
His little sister Maya was nine.
She had to make a project for her school science fair on Monday.
She wanted to build a model of a volcano that could really erupt.
"Can you help me, Owen?" she asked on Wednesday.
"Of course," said Owen. "We'll build it together on Saturday afternoon. I promise."
Maya was so happy that she hugged him.
For the rest of the week, she talked about nothing else.
She collected everything they needed: paper, glue, paint, an empty bottle, vinegar and baking soda.
On Saturday morning, Owen's best friend Jake called.
"I've got the new game," he said. "Come over!"
Owen forgot all about his promise.
He went to Jake's house, and they played all day.
He did not look at his phone.
When he came home at seven o'clock, the house was quiet.
Maya was sitting at the kitchen table with all her materials.
She had waited for him all afternoon.
Her eyes were red.
"You promised," she said quietly.
Then she went to her room and closed the door.
Owen felt terrible.
He sat on the stairs for a long time.
Their mother came and sat next to him.
"Everyone makes mistakes," she said. "But a real apology is not only words. What are you going to do?"
Owen knocked on Maya's door.
"I'm really sorry," he said. "It was my fault. I forgot, and that's not OK."
Maya did not answer.
"Can I make it up to you?" said Owen. "We can build the volcano tomorrow. The whole day. No phone, no games."
After a minute, the door opened a little.
"Promise?" said Maya.
"Promise," said Owen, and he gave her his phone. "You can keep it until Monday."
On Sunday, they worked from breakfast until dinner.
They made the mountain from paper and glue, and they painted it brown and green.
Owen explained the science: when vinegar and baking soda mix, they make a gas, and the gas pushes the liquid out.
Maya wrote everything in her notebook.
On Monday, Maya's volcano erupted in front of the whole class.
Red foam poured down the mountain, and everyone cheered.
She won second prize.
That evening, she gave Owen his phone back and a small card.
On it she had written: "Thank you for keeping your second promise."
Noor's class visited the city art gallery on a rainy Thursday.
Most of her classmates were bored.
They looked at their phones and waited for lunch.
But Noor loved paintings.
She wanted to be a painter one day.
Their guide, Mr. Wells, took them to a room with old landscapes.
"This painting is almost three hundred years old," he said.
It showed a quiet valley with a river, some cows and a small castle on a hill.
The frame was gold and very heavy.
Noor looked at the painting very carefully.
In the sky above the castle, she noticed something strange.
Under the blue paint, there was a shape, like the outline of a face.
She could see an eye and part of a nose.
"Excuse me," she said to the guide. "Is there a face in the sky?"
Some of her classmates laughed.
Mr. Wells came closer and looked for a long time.
"I've worked here for twenty years," he said slowly, "and I've never noticed that."
He took a photo with his phone and wrote down Noor's name.
Two weeks later, the school received a letter from the gallery.
Noor was invited to come back with her parents.
In a room behind the exhibition, a restorer called Dr. Kovac was waiting for them.
She showed them a large black and white image on a screen.
"This is an x-ray of the painting," she explained.
"It shows the layers of paint under the landscape."
On the screen, there was a portrait of a young woman.
She was wearing a simple dress, and she was holding a letter.
"The painter used the same canvas twice," said Dr. Kovac.
"Paint and canvas were expensive. Maybe he did not like his first painting, or maybe he could not sell it."
Over the centuries, the top layer became thinner, and the face started to appear.
Nobody knew who the young woman was.
But the gallery was very excited about the discovery.
They decided to put the x-ray next to the landscape in a new exhibition called "The Hidden Portrait."
On the wall, there was a small sign: "Discovered by Noor Ahmed, age 13."
On the opening night, her classmates came to see it.
Nobody was looking at their phones this time.
"How did you see it?" asked her friend Ivan.
Noor smiled.
"I just looked," she said. "Really looked."
The library at Oakfield School was very old.
It had dark wooden shelves, tall windows and thousands of dusty books.
Some of the books were more than a hundred years old.
In October, a strange rumor spread around the school.
People said there was a ghost in the library.
After the last lesson, when the room was empty, you could hear noises: soft steps, a scream and books falling from the shelves.
Some students were so frightened that they stopped going there.
Zoe did not believe in ghosts.
She loved mystery novels, and she wanted to solve the mystery.
Her friend Arjun was not so sure.
"I'm not scared of ghosts," he said, "but I'm scared of the dark."
On Friday, they asked the librarian, Mrs. Hale, if they could stay late to finish a project.
She agreed, but she looked worried.
"I'll be in the office until six," she said. "Please don't go into the old room at the back."
At five o'clock, the sun went down, and the library became very quiet.
Arjun turned on his phone's light.
Then they heard it: a soft step, then another.
It came from the old room at the back.
A book fell on the floor with a loud bang.
Arjun grabbed Zoe's arm.
"Let's go home," he whispered.
But Zoe was already walking toward the door.
Her heart was beating fast.
She opened the door slowly.
The room was full of boxes and broken chairs.
A window at the top was open, and cold air came in.
Then, from the top of a bookshelf, two big yellow eyes looked down at them.
Arjun screamed.
The eyes screamed too.
Then something white flew across the room, over their heads and out of the window.
Zoe started to laugh.
"It's an owl!" she said. "A barn owl! It lives in here!"
Mrs. Hale came running from her office.
When she heard the story, she laughed, too.
"So that's our ghost," she said.
The owl came in through the broken window at night to look for mice.
Its wings knocked the books off the shelves, and its scream sounded like a person.
The school repaired the window, but it did not want to make the owl homeless.
So the students built a wooden owl house and put it on the roof of the library.
Zoe wrote a story about the adventure for the school magazine.
She called it "The Library Ghost."
And Arjun?
He is still scared of the dark, but now he loves owls.
Ines had a small flower shop called Petals on the corner of Market Street.
She had worked there for thirty years.
Everyone in the area knew her, and she knew everybody's favorite flowers.
But last spring, a big supermarket opened on the same street.
It sold flowers, too, and they were much cheaper.
Slowly, Ines's customers stopped coming.
Some days, only two or three people came into the shop.
At the end of the month, she could hardly pay the rent.
Her granddaughter Lena was nineteen and studied business at the university.
One Saturday, she came to help in the shop, and she saw the empty room.
"Grandma, why didn't you tell me?" she asked.
Ines shrugged.
"I didn't want you to worry. Maybe it's time to close."
"No," said Lena. "You can't compete with the supermarket on price. But you can offer something they can't."
"Like what?" asked Ines.
"Your knowledge," said Lena. "You know everything about flowers. The supermarket doesn't."
They sat down with two cups of tea and a notebook.
Lena had lots of ideas.
"How about a weekend workshop? You could teach people to make their own bouquets."
"What if we deliver flowers by bike? Old people in the area can't always come to the shop."
"And we could open an account on social media and post photos of your flowers every day."
Ines laughed.
"Social media? At my age?"
"I'll do that part," said Lena.
They started the next week.
Lena took beautiful photographs of the shop and wrote short stories about each flower.
People loved them.
Soon, the shop had two thousand followers.
The first workshop was on a Saturday morning.
Twelve people came, and they paid twenty dollars each.
Ines showed them how to choose flowers, how to cut the stems and how to make a bouquet that lasts.
She was nervous at first, but she soon relaxed.
She told stories, made jokes and answered hundreds of questions.
Six months later, Petals was busier than ever.
The workshops were full every weekend, and a student delivered flowers by bike every afternoon.
Even some people from the supermarket came to buy their flowers from Ines.
One evening, Ines counted the money in the till.
For the first time in a year, there was enough to pay the rent and more.
She looked at her granddaughter, who was writing a new post on her phone.
"You should be a business teacher," she said.
"No," said Lena. "I learned everything from you. I just used different tools."
Rana was very excited when she got on the plane.
She was flying to Lisbon for her cousin Nadia's wedding.
It was her first journey abroad alone.
In her suitcase, she had a special present: the wedding dress that her grandmother had made for Nadia.
Her grandmother was too old to travel, so Rana had to take it.
"Be careful with it," her grandmother had said. "It is our family's gift."
The flight was long, and there was a delay in Paris.
Rana had to change planes, and she almost missed her second flight.
She ran through the airport and arrived at the gate just in time.
When she finally sat down, she was hot and tired, but happy.
In Lisbon, Rana waited for her luggage with the other passengers.
Bags and suitcases came out one by one.
People took their things and left.
After thirty minutes, the belt was empty, and Rana was the only person there.
Her suitcase was missing.
She felt sick.
The wedding was in two days, and the dress was in that suitcase!
She went to the lost luggage office.
A man called Pedro was working at the desk.
"I'm sorry," he said. "Sometimes bags stay in Paris when passengers change planes. Can you describe your suitcase?"
"It's large and green, with a black handle and four wheels," said Rana. "There's a red label with my name on it."
Pedro typed everything into his computer and gave her a form with a number on it.
"We will call you as soon as we find it," he promised.
Nadia met Rana outside the airport and gave her a big hug.
When she heard the news, she tried to smile.
"Don't worry. The airline will find it," she said.
But Rana could see that she was worried, too.
The next day, there was no call.
Rana checked her phone every five minutes.
In the evening, she phoned the airport, but they had no information.
She could not sleep that night.
She thought about her grandmother, who had worked on the dress for six months.
On the morning of the wedding, Rana's phone finally rang.
It was Pedro.
"Good news! Your suitcase arrived on the first flight from Paris. A driver can bring it to your hotel in one hour."
Rana almost cried with happiness.
At ten o'clock, a driver knocked on the door with a large green suitcase.
Rana opened it with shaking hands.
The dress was there, perfect and white.
That afternoon, Nadia wore it at her wedding, and everyone said she looked beautiful.
Rana took a photo and sent it to her grandmother.
The reply came a minute later: "It traveled further than I ever did!"
The school science fair was in six weeks, and Priya and Kofi still needed an idea.
Kofi wanted to build a robot, but they did not have enough money.
Then Priya read an article about plants.
Some people claim that plants grow faster when they listen to music.
"Is that true?" asked Kofi.
"I don't know," said Priya. "Let's find out."
They bought six small bean plants of the same size.
Two plants would listen to classical music, two would listen to rap, and two would have no music at all.
Kofi was sure that the rap plants would win.
"Rap has more energy," he said.
Priya thought that classical music was better for plants, but she did not say anything.
Their science teacher, Mr. Reed, looked at their plan.
"It's a good idea," he said, "but is it a fair test?"
He explained that everything except the music had to be the same.
The plants needed the same light, the same water and the same temperature.
"If one room is warmer than the others, you won't know what made the difference," he said.
So they changed their plan.
They put each pair of plants in a separate box with a lamp and a small speaker.
Every day after school, they gave each plant exactly half a glass of water.
Every Friday, they checked how tall the plants were and wrote the numbers in a notebook.
In the fourth week, something went wrong.
Kofi's little brother, Bruno, went into the garage to play.
He thought the plants in the quiet box looked lonely and thirsty.
So he gave them a big glass of orange juice.
The next morning, the two plants looked terrible.
Their leaves were yellow, and one of them was nearly dead.
Kofi was really angry.
"Now we can't finish the experiment!" he shouted.
Priya thought for a moment.
"We can't use those two plants," she said, "but we can be honest about what happened."
So they wrote everything down in their notebook.
At the end of six weeks, they looked at their numbers.
The classical music plants were twenty-four centimeters tall, and the rap plants were twenty-three.
"That's almost the same," said Kofi. "So music doesn't help?"
"Maybe not," said Priya. "Or maybe our test was too small."
At the science fair, other students had more exciting projects, like rockets and robots.
But the judges liked Priya and Kofi's work.
They liked the fair test, the careful notes and the honest description of the orange juice problem.
Priya and Kofi won second prize.
"Science isn't about getting the answer you want," said Mr. Reed. "It's about finding the truth."
Bruno was very proud. "I helped!" he told everyone.
Tariq was fifteen, and he loved his life.
He had great friends, he played in the school football team, and his best friend Sami lived next door.
Then, one evening in March, his mother made an announcement.
"I've got a new job," she said. "It's a great opportunity. But it's in Northgate."
Northgate was eight hundred kilometers away.
Tariq could not believe it.
"So we have to move? I have to change schools?" he said.
"I'm sorry," said his mother. "I know it's hard."
Tariq went to his room and shut the door.
He did not speak to his mother for two days.
The next three months went very fast.
They packed everything in boxes.
Tariq's football team gave him a shirt with all their names on it.
On his last night, he and Sami sat on the wall between their gardens, like they did when they were small.
"We can still play video games together online," said Sami.
"It won't be the same," said Tariq.
Neither of them said anything for a long time.
Northgate was a big, grey city by the sea.
It rained almost every day.
Their new apartment was on the tenth floor, and Tariq's room was smaller than his old one.
From the window, he could see the harbor and hundreds of other buildings.
He did not know a single person.
The first weeks at his new school were lonely.
The students were polite, but they already had their friends.
At lunch, Tariq sat alone and messaged Sami.
"I miss home," he wrote.
"I'm worried that I'll never make friends here."
Sami replied: "Join a team. That's how you met me, remember?"
The next day, Tariq found a notice about football training after school.
He was nervous, but he went.
He wore the shirt with his old team's names on it.
A tall girl called Lena looked at it.
"Nice shirt. Are you any good?" she asked.
"Watch," said Tariq, and he smiled for the first time in weeks.
He scored two goals that afternoon.
After training, Lena and three other players invited him to get pizza.
They talked and laughed for two hours.
That night, Tariq called his mother from the pizza place.
"I'll be home late," he said. "I'm with my team."
His mother put down the phone and smiled.
Northgate was still grey, but it did not feel so cold anymore.
It was a cold evening in January, and Jamal was doing his homework in his family's apartment on the sixth floor.
His little sister Nina was watching cartoons.
Suddenly, the lights went out.
The TV went black, and the heating stopped.
Outside the window, the whole street was dark.
It was a power cut.
Their parents were at work until ten o'clock.
Jamal found a torch in a kitchen drawer.
Nina was frightened of the dark, so she held his hand.
"Don't worry," said Jamal. "The power will come back soon."
But he was not sure.
Then they heard a noise in the hall.
Someone was knocking on metal and calling for help.
The sound was coming from the elevator.
"Hello? Is anybody there? I'm stuck!"
It was the voice of an old woman.
Jamal ran to the elevator door.
"Hello! My name's Jamal. I live on this floor. Are you OK?"
"I'm Mrs. Weiss, from the eighth floor," said the voice. "I'm fine, but it's very dark in here, and I'm scared."
Jamal called the emergency number on his phone.
They said an engineer would come, but it could take two hours because the power cut was very big.
Jamal stayed by the elevator and talked to Mrs. Weiss.
Nina brought a blanket and some biscuits, and they pushed the biscuits through a small gap in the door.
Soon, other doors opened.
Mr. Sato from apartment 6B brought candles.
A student called Hannah brought hot tea in a flask.
People sat in the hall with their candles and talked.
They had lived in the same building for years, but most of them had never spoken to each other.
Mr. Sato told funny stories about his job as a chef.
Hannah played the guitar.
Even Mrs. Weiss laughed inside the elevator.
At half past nine, the engineer arrived and opened the elevator.
Mrs. Weiss came out slowly, holding the blanket.
"Thank you, all of you," she said.
"I've lived here for thirty years, and tonight I met my neighbors for the first time."
A few minutes later, the power came back.
The lights came on, and everyone cheered.
When Jamal's parents came home, they found a party in the hall.
Now, on the first Saturday of every month, the neighbors have dinner together.
They call it "Power Cut Night," even when the lights are on.
Priya loved radio.
Every morning, she listened to a news program while she had breakfast.
One day, she had an idea.
"Our school should have its own radio station," she told her friend Ben.
Ben was good with computers and audio equipment.
"That's a brilliant idea," he said. "We can do a show at lunchtime."
They asked the principal, Mr. Okafor, for permission.
He agreed, and he gave them an old room next to the library.
They called their station "Radio Hill."
For two weeks, they prepared everything.
Ben set up two microphones, a laptop and some speakers in the dining hall.
Priya wrote a script with news, music and an interview with the school's football captain.
On Monday at twelve thirty, the first show began.
"Good afternoon, and welcome to Radio Hill!" said Priya.
Her voice was shaking.
In the dining hall, three hundred students stopped talking and looked at the speakers.
At first, everything went well.
Priya read the school news, and Ben played a popular song.
Then it was time for the interview.
But the football captain was not there.
He had forgotten!
Priya looked at Ben in panic.
There were ten minutes of empty time.
Ben had an idea.
He wrote something on a piece of paper and showed it to Priya: "Ask the audience."
Priya took a deep breath.
"We have a question for you today," she said into the microphone.
"What do you think about the school lunches? Come to the radio room and tell us your opinion!"
For a moment, nothing happened.
Then the door opened, and a girl came in.
"In my opinion, the pizza is great, but the soup is awful," she said.
Everyone in the dining hall laughed.
Soon there was a line of students outside the door.
Some agreed, and some disagreed.
One boy said, "I think the soup is fine. You just need more salt."
The discussion was so lively that the show finished ten minutes late.
The next day, the school cook came to the radio room.
Priya was worried that she was angry.
But the cook smiled.
"I listened to your show," she said. "Thank you for the opinions. I'm going to change the soup."
Now "Your Opinion" is the most popular part of Radio Hill.
Every Monday, students discuss a new topic, from homework to the school uniform.
And the football captain finally did his interview.
He was the first guest to arrive early.
On Monday morning, everyone at Ashford School was talking about the same photo.
It showed a large grey fin in the river, near the old dam.
Under the photo, someone had written: "SHARK IN THE RIVER! Keep your children at home!"
By lunchtime, thousands of people had shared it.
Some parents said that their children could not walk by the river anymore.
Yara and Felix wrote for the school newspaper.
"This is the biggest story of the year," said Felix. "Let's put it on the front page!"
"Wait," said Yara. "First, we need to check if it's true."
Yara had a list of questions from their media class.
Who took the photo? Where and when? Did anyone else see the shark?
They tried to find the person who posted it first, but the account had no name and no other photos.
"That's strange," said Yara.
Then Felix looked at the photo more closely.
"Look at the trees," he said. "They're all green, but it's November."
Apparently, the photo was not from this week at all.
Next, they called Dr. Moss, a scientist who studied the river.
She laughed when she heard the story.
"Our river is far too cold for sharks," she said. "And most sharks need salty water."
"So what's in the photo?" asked Felix.
"I think someone added the fin with a computer," said Dr. Moss.
That evening, Yara searched for the picture online.
She found it on a website from three years ago.
It was an April Fool's joke from another country, and the river in it was not even their river!
Felix was disappointed. "So there's no story," he said.
"There is a story," said Yara. "It's just not the one we expected."
They wrote an article called "The Shark That Never Was."
It explained how the fake photo spread so fast and how readers could check the news for themselves.
The article was on the front page of the school newspaper.
The next day, the town's real newspaper wrote about it, too.
And down by the river, children were playing again.
Kenji was twenty-five, and it was his first time in Europe.
In his bag, he had an old photo of his grandfather.
In the photo, his grandfather was young and smiling, and he was standing next to a stone statue of a sleeping lion.
On the back, someone had written: "Porta Nova, 1968."
Kenji's grandfather died last year.
Kenji wanted to find the lion and take a photo in the same place.
But he only had one afternoon in Porta Nova, because his train to Rome left at six.
To make things worse, his phone battery was dead.
He had a paper map from his hotel, but it looked very old.
First, Kenji asked a barber who was standing outside his shop.
"The Sleeping Lion? Go straight on, turn left at the roundabout, and it's opposite the bookshop," said the barber.
Kenji followed the directions carefully.
But opposite the bookshop there was no lion, only a petrol station.
Next, he asked a police officer.
"Hmm, I think it's somewhere near the new mosque," she said. "Take the second street on the right-hand side."
Kenji walked and walked.
He found the mosque, a playground and three cafés, but no lion.
It was four o'clock, and his feet hurt.
Kenji sat down on a bench, tired and disappointed.
A girl on a skateboard stopped in front of him.
"Are you lost?" she asked in English.
Her name was Bea, and she was about sixteen.
Kenji showed her the photo and told her the story.
Bea looked at the photo for a long time.
"I know this lion," she said. "But it isn't in the street anymore."
She explained that ten years ago the city moved it into the museum, because the rain was damaging the stone.
"The museum closes at five," she added. "Come on! It's not far."
They ran through the old streets, and Bea rode her skateboard next to him.
They arrived at five to five.
The man at the door wanted to close, but Bea explained everything, and he let them in.
And there it was: the sleeping lion, in the middle of a quiet white room.
It looked exactly like the lion in the photo.
Kenji stood where his grandfather had stood fifty-eight years before.
Bea took his picture with her phone.
Kenji felt like crying, but he was smiling, too.
He caught his train with one minute to spare.
Bea sent him the photo that evening, and they still write to each other.
"Next time," she wrote, "I'll show you the rest of the city, with a better map."
Nana Joy's seventieth birthday was in three weeks.
Every year, she cooked for everyone else's birthdays, but she never had a party for herself.
"This year, let's have a surprise party for her," said Hannah.
Her brother Luis loved the idea.
"We'll invite all her friends," he said. "And we'll make a cake!"
They made a list.
Hannah would organize the guests and the food.
Luis would buy balloons and make a big sign that said "Happy 70th, Nana!"
Their parents would take Nana out to the cinema on the day.
The most important rule was simple: Nana must not know anything.
Keeping a secret from Nana was not easy.
She lived with them, and she noticed everything.
One afternoon, she found forty balloons under Luis's bed.
"They're for a school project," Luis said quickly.
"Forty balloons?" said Nana. "What kind of project is that?"
Another day, she picked up the phone and heard Hannah's friend say, "Is the party still on Saturday?"
Hannah took the phone and hurried upstairs.
"It's Sofia's party," she said later.
Nana just smiled.
On Saturday, their parents took Nana to the cinema at three o'clock.
The moment the car left, Hannah and Luis started work.
They put up the balloons and the sign.
They made sandwiches, and they tried to bake a chocolate cake.
Unfortunately, the cake came out of the oven flat and black.
"Oh no," said Luis. "What are we going to do now?"
At five, twenty guests arrived and hid in the living room.
Hannah turned off the lights.
Everyone waited in silence.
They heard the car, then footsteps, then a key in the door.
The lights came on. "SURPRISE!" everybody shouted.
Nana stood at the door with a big box in her hands.
She did not look surprised at all.
"Thank you, my darlings," she said. "I brought the cake."
Inside the box was a beautiful cake from the bakery.
Hannah's mouth fell open. "You knew? Since when?"
"Since the forty balloons," said Nana.
"But I didn't want to spoil your fun, so I pretended."
Everybody laughed, and Luis hid the black cake in the kitchen.
It was the best party the family had ever had, and Nana danced until midnight.
Nora Bell had a small bakery in the village of Little Brook.
She baked bread every morning, and she made beautiful cakes for birthdays and weddings.
One Monday, the phone rang while she was taking bread out of the oven.
It was Martin Hughes, a farmer who lived in the hills.
The line was very bad, and his voice kept disappearing.
"My daughter Emily is getting married on Saturday," he said.
"It's a small, romantic wedding. We need a cake for thirty people, and we can pay about three hundred…"
Then the line went dead.
Nora only heard two words clearly: "cake" and "three hundred."
She tried to call him back, but there was no answer.
A cake for three hundred people! It was the biggest order of her life.
Nora called her sister and two friends, and they worked day and night.
They used forty kilos of flour, two hundred eggs and thirty jars of strawberry jam.
The kitchen was so full of cakes that there was no room to walk.
They had to keep some of them in the neighbors' refrigerator.
On Friday evening, the cake was finally ready.
It had seven levels, and it was as tall as Nora.
She felt tired, but she was very proud.
On Saturday morning, Nora and her sister drove the cake to the farm very slowly.
When they arrived, Martin came out to meet them.
He looked at the enormous cake, and his face went white.
"What's this?" he asked.
"Your cake for three hundred people," said Nora.
"Three hundred? No! I said thirty people and three hundred dollars!"
Nora wanted to cry.
For a moment, nobody said anything.
Then Emily came out of the house in her wedding dress.
She looked at the cake and started to laugh.
"It's the most beautiful cake I've ever seen," she said. "Dad, let's invite the whole village!"
And that is what they did.
Martin called everyone he knew, and that afternoon three hundred people came to the farm.
They ate cake, danced in the field and sang until late at night.
Everybody agreed that it was the best wedding in the history of Little Brook.
Martin paid for the whole cake, and he even gave Nora a big tip.
But since that day, Nora has had a new rule: big orders by email only!
Every year in October, the students at Hillside School chose a class president.
This year, everybody thought that Marcus would win.
He was funny, he was good at sport, and everybody knew him.
His posters were everywhere, and his promises were big.
"If I win, there will be no homework on Fridays!"
"If I win, we'll have pizza for lunch every week!"
Nadia sat at the back of the class and listened.
She was quiet, and she did not have many friends.
"He can't do any of those things," she said to her friend Ellis.
"The teachers decide about homework, not the class president."
"Then why don't you try?" said Ellis.
Nadia laughed, but that night she could not stop thinking about it.
The next morning, Nadia's name was on the list.
Some students were surprised. "Nadia? Who's Nadia?"
Nadia did not make posters.
Instead, she asked every student in the class one question: "What is the biggest problem at our school?"
The answers surprised her.
Many students said that the library was too noisy for studying.
Others said that half of the lockers were broken.
And three new students said that they felt lonely, because nobody talked to them.
Nadia wrote everything down.
She realized that these were real problems with real solutions.
On election day, each person had to give a speech.
Marcus went first.
He told jokes, and everybody laughed and clapped.
Then it was Nadia's turn.
Her legs were shaking.
"I can't promise pizza," she began, "and I can't promise no homework."
"But I asked all of you about our school, and I listened."
She talked about the library, the lockers and the new students.
"If you vote for me, I'll ask the head teacher for a quiet room in the library," she said.
"I'll ask the school to fix the lockers, and I'll start a lunch club for new students."
When she finished, the room was quiet for a moment, and then people started to clap.
The next day, the teacher read the results.
Marcus had fourteen votes. Nadia had sixteen.
Nadia could not believe it.
Marcus walked over and shook her hand. "Well done," he said. "Your ideas were better than mine."
"Then help me," said Nadia. "Everybody listens to you."
By the end of the year, the library had a quiet room, and most of the lockers worked again.
The lunch club had twenty members.
And once a month, the club had a pizza lunch, thanks to Marcus.
Ben Mora was not a high mountain, but it was famous for its views.
On a clear day, you could see the sea from the summit, sixty kilometers away.
Nadia, Felix and Tom had planned the walk for weeks.
They were university friends who loved the outdoors, but only Nadia had any real experience in the mountains.
The weather forecast was good: sunny in the morning, with a small chance of fog later.
Nadia insisted that everyone should bring warm clothes, a map, a compass, a torch and plenty of water.
Felix laughed at her.
"It's a six-hour walk, not an expedition," he said. "My phone has a map."
But he packed a jacket anyway, just to keep her quiet.
They started at eight o'clock in bright sunshine.
The path climbed steeply through a forest and then along a rocky ridge.
It was hard work, but the views were spectacular, and by noon they had reached the summit.
They ate their sandwiches, took dozens of photos and enjoyed the silence.
While they were resting, Nadia noticed a grey wall of cloud in the valley below.
It was moving towards them surprisingly fast.
"We should go down now," she said.
Felix wanted to wait for one more photo, but she was already packing her bag.
Within fifteen minutes, the fog had covered the whole mountain.
They could barely see ten meters in front of them, and the temperature dropped sharply.
The path, which had been so obvious in the sunshine, seemed to disappear among the rocks.
Felix checked his phone.
There was no signal, and the battery was almost dead because of the cold.
Nadia took out her map and compass.
"The path goes south-east from here," she said calmly. "We just need to follow the compass and take it slowly."
They had been walking for about an hour when Tom slipped on a wet rock.
He fell awkwardly and cried out in pain.
His ankle was already swelling, and when he tried to stand, he could not put any weight on it.
He was pale and shaking.
Felix looked at Nadia.
For the first time that day, he looked frightened.
"What do we do?" he whispered.
Nadia knew that they could not carry Tom down the steep path in the fog.
It was too dangerous, and it would soon be dark.
The most important thing was to keep him warm.
Wet and injured people could develop hypothermia very quickly, even in summer.
They helped Tom to a place behind a large rock, where there was some protection from the wind.
They put all their spare clothes on him and sat close on either side of him.
Felix, who had laughed at Nadia's heavy bag that morning, was now very grateful for it.
Nadia walked a few meters up the slope, where she found a weak phone signal, and called the emergency number.
She gave their position from the map as precisely as she could.
Then the signal disappeared.
She did not know whether the rescue team had understood her.
Every ten minutes, she blew her whistle three times, the international signal for help.
Hours passed.
It grew dark and colder, and Tom stopped talking.
Felix held his hand and told him stupid jokes to keep him awake.
Just before eleven, they heard a whistle in the distance, then voices.
A moment later, two lights appeared in the fog.
The mountain rescue team had found them.
The leader, a grey-haired man called Grant, checked Tom quickly and wrapped him in a special blanket.
"You did everything right," he told Nadia.
"Your position was accurate, you stayed together, and you kept him warm. That's what saves lives."
It took four more hours to carry Tom down the mountain on a stretcher.
Tom's ankle was broken, and he spent two nights in hospital, but he made a full recovery.
A month later, the three friends went back to Ben Mora on a perfectly clear day.
This time, Felix carried the heaviest bag.
Inside it, among the warm clothes and the torch, there was a map, a compass and a whistle.
Richard was fifty-two and the director of a large insurance company.
He worked twelve hours a day, answered emails at midnight and ate most of his meals at his desk.
He had not taken a holiday for three years.
"I'll rest when I retire," he always said.
One Monday morning, in the middle of a meeting, he suddenly felt dizzy and fell to the floor.
He woke up in hospital.
It was not a heart attack, but his doctor, Dr. Osei, was very serious.
His blood pressure was dangerously high, he was overweight, and his tests showed signs of exhaustion.
"If you continue like this," she said, "the next time will be much worse."
Dr. Osei gave him medicine for his blood pressure.
Then she wrote something else on a piece of paper and handed it to him.
It said: "Gardening. Twice a week. At least two hours."
Richard laughed.
"Gardening? I don't have time for gardening."
"Then make time," she said. "Or I can write your prescription for a different kind of garden: the one in the cemetery."
She explained that many doctors now prescribed activities such as gardening, walking groups and volunteering.
Research showed that spending time outdoors, doing gentle exercise and meeting people could reduce stress and improve both physical and mental health.
She gave him the address of a community garden where local people rented small pieces of land, called allotments, to grow vegetables.
Richard's allotment was a disaster.
It was covered in weeds, the soil was hard and full of stones, and he had no idea what to do.
On his first Saturday, he spent an hour pulling up weeds and then sat on an upturned bucket, exhausted and bored.
The woman on the next allotment was watching him.
She was about seventy, very small and very determined, and her allotment was full of beans, tomatoes, pumpkins and flowers.
"You're doing it wrong," she said.
Her name was Mrs. Patel, and she had been growing vegetables there for thirty years.
Over the following weeks, Mrs. Patel taught him everything.
She showed him how to dig properly without hurting his back, when to plant each vegetable, and how to make compost from kitchen waste.
She was a strict teacher.
When he checked his phone, she took it away and put it in her shed.
"The emails will still be there in two hours," she said. "The weeds won't wait."
Slowly, things began to change.
Richard found that he looked forward to Saturday mornings.
The physical work made him tired in a good way, and he slept better than he had for years.
He started walking to work, and he stopped eating at his desk.
He even began to leave the office at six.
His colleagues noticed that he was calmer and more patient.
"You've changed," his assistant told him. "You actually listen now."
When he went back to Dr. Osei three months later, his blood pressure had fallen, and he had lost eight kilos.
She smiled.
"The prescription is working," she said.
In September, Richard harvested his first vegetables: a basket of beans, some tomatoes and three enormous pumpkins.
He was prouder of them than of anything he had achieved at work.
He gave one pumpkin to Mrs. Patel, who examined it carefully and said, "Not bad. For a beginner."
That winter, Mrs. Patel became ill and could not work on her allotment for several months.
Richard looked after it for her, as well as his own.
Every week, he took her fresh vegetables and news of the garden, and he stayed for a cup of tea.
When she was well again, she found that her flowers had been perfectly cared for.
"You've learned," she said.
"I had a good teacher," Richard replied. "And a very good doctor."
Leo was twenty-three, and he hated speaking in public.
At university, he had once walked out of a presentation because his hands were shaking so badly.
He had never managed to overcome his fear.
So when his older brother Daniel asked him to be his best man, his first feeling was not joy but panic.
"You know what that means, don't you?" said Daniel, smiling.
"You'll have to give a speech at the wedding. Two hundred guests."
Leo swallowed.
He wanted to say no, but Daniel had always been there for him, and he could not refuse.
"Of course," he said. "I'd be honored."
The wedding was in three weeks.
Leo spent every evening trying to write the speech, and the process was extremely stressful.
He read advice online, watched videos of famous best man speeches and wrote pages of jokes.
He was not satisfied with any of them, and most were terrible.
Some were funny but would embarrass Daniel in front of Sophie's family.
In the end, he wrote a speech that was clever and safe, full of quotations from famous writers.
He practiced it in front of the mirror every night until he knew every word by heart.
He was still terrified, but at least he was prepared.
A week before the wedding, Leo visited his grandfather, Karl, who was eighty-nine and lived in a small house by the river.
He read the speech aloud, and his grandfather listened with his eyes closed.
When Leo finished, there was a long silence.
"It's very good," said Karl at last. "But it isn't you."
Leo felt disappointed.
"What do you mean?"
"All these famous writers," said his grandfather. "They don't know Daniel. You do."
"Tell them one true story about your brother. Just one. That's all a good speech needs."
On the morning of the wedding, disaster struck.
Leo could not find the paper with his speech.
He searched his jacket, his car and the hotel room, but it had disappeared.
He had learned the speech by heart, but his mind was completely empty.
He could not remember a single quotation.
The ceremony was beautiful, and Sophie looked gorgeous in her white dress.
But Leo hardly noticed.
At the reception, he sat at the top table, unable to eat, while the minutes went by.
Then the music stopped, and someone handed him a microphone.
Two hundred faces turned towards him.
Leo stood up.
His hands were shaking.
He looked at his grandfather, who was sitting at a table near the front, and Karl gave him a nod of encouragement.
"Good evening, everyone," Leo began. "I'm Leo, Daniel's younger brother. I had a speech, but I've lost it, so I'm going to tell you a story instead."
People laughed, and he felt a little better.
He told them about the winter when he was nine and had been bullied at school.
Every day, three older boys waited for him at the gate.
He had told nobody, but somehow Daniel found out.
The next morning, Daniel, who was only thirteen, walked him to school, stood at the gate and said nothing at all.
He did the same thing every morning for a month.
The boys never came back.
"Daniel has never told anyone about this," Leo said.
"But that's who he is. He is generous, he protects the people he loves, and he doesn't need to make a speech about it."
He turned to Sophie.
"Sophie, you've married the best person I know. Everyone, please raise your glasses to Daniel and Sophie."
The room exploded with applause.
Daniel's eyes were wet, and he hugged his brother for a long time.
Later that night, Leo found his speech.
It was in his grandfather's pocket.
Karl just winked.
Oakdale School did not have many clubs.
It was a small school in a poor part of the city, and there was never enough money for extra activities.
But every day at lunchtime, the caretaker, Mr. Obi, sat in a corner of the library with an old chessboard, playing against himself.
Aisha was twelve and very shy.
She had moved to the city from Nigeria a year earlier, and she still felt a sense of isolation and found it difficult to make friends.
She often spent lunchtime in the library, and one day she stopped to watch Mr. Obi.
After a while, he looked up.
"Do you know how to play?" he asked.
She shook her head.
"Would you like to learn?"
Mr. Obi turned out to be an excellent teacher.
Before he became a caretaker, he explained, he had been a mathematics teacher in Lagos, and he had played chess for his university.
He taught Aisha how each piece moved, then the basic strategies, and then he made her think.
"Don't just look at your next move," he said. "Ask yourself what your opponent wants."
Aisha lost every game for the first two months.
Then, slowly, she started to improve.
She practiced online at home in the evenings and borrowed chess books from the library.
She began to see patterns on the board that she had never noticed before.
In the spring, she beat Mr. Obi for the first time.
He shook her hand very seriously, and then he laughed so loudly that the librarian told him to be quiet.
Other students noticed.
First one boy, Samuel, asked if he could participate, and then four more.
By the summer, the lunchtime chess club had fifteen members.
Mr. Obi used his own money to buy three more chessboards from a second-hand shop.
The head teacher, who had never paid much attention to the caretaker, came to watch one day and was amazed.
Students who usually got into trouble were sitting silently, thinking hard.
Aisha changed, too.
Chess gave her confidence and a new motivation.
She made friends in the club, she began to speak more in lessons, and her marks in maths improved considerably.
"Chess teaches you that every mistake is a lesson," Mr. Obi told her. "You only lose if you don't learn."
The following year, Mr. Obi entered the club in the national schools' chess tournament.
The other teams came from famous private schools, with professional coaches and matching jackets.
The Oakdale team had borrowed T-shirts and a caretaker.
Nevertheless, Mr. Obi told them to ignore the jackets and concentrate on the board.
Some of the other players laughed when they arrived.
They stopped laughing after the first round.
Samuel won his game, and so did Aisha.
Round after round, the small team from Oakdale kept winning.
It was an impressive result: they finished in third place out of forty schools, and Aisha won every one of her seven games.
At the prize ceremony, Aisha was named the best young player of the tournament.
When she walked up to receive her medal, she looked for Mr. Obi in the crowd.
He was standing at the back, clapping harder than anyone.
The story appeared in the local newspaper, and a generous businessman who read it gave the school money for a proper chess club.
Mr. Obi still works as the caretaker, but three afternoons a week, he is also the official chess coach.
He has a badge that says so, and he wears it every day.
For eleven years, Petra had worked as a security guard at the City Museum.
Her shift started at ten at night and finished at six in the morning.
Most people would have found the job boring, but Petra loved it.
During the day, the rooms were full of noisy tourists, but at night she had the paintings all to herself.
Her favorite was "The Girl with the Blue Umbrella," painted by Anna Weber in 1911.
It showed a young woman walking through the rain in a crowded city street.
It was the most valuable painting in the museum, and Petra had looked at it every night for more than a decade.
She knew every detail: the red flower on the girl's hat, the dog in the corner, and a tiny crack in the paint just above the umbrella, shaped like the letter Y.
In March, the painting was taken away for two weeks for restoration.
The work was done by Viktor Albrecht, a famous restorer who had worked for museums all over Europe.
When the painting came back, the director held a small ceremony to celebrate its return.
Everyone agreed that the colors looked brighter than ever.
That night, Petra stood in front of the painting as usual.
At first, she could not explain what was bothering her.
Then she saw it.
The crack above the umbrella was gone.
She moved closer and used her torch.
There was no Y, no crack at all, only smooth, perfect paint.
Of course, a restorer might repair a crack.
But the more she looked, the more differences she noticed.
The red flower was slightly larger.
The dog's tail was pointing in a different direction.
Petra felt cold.
She was almost certain that she was looking at a copy.
The next morning, Petra told the director.
He listened politely, but she could see that he did not take her seriously.
"Mr. Albrecht is one of the most respected experts in the world," he said.
"He removed the old damage. That's his job. Perhaps you are tired after your shift."
Petra went home angry, but she did not give up.
She found an old guidebook that she had bought years ago.
On page forty-two, there was a large photo of the painting.
With a magnifying glass, she could see the dog's tail clearly, and it pointed to the left.
In the painting now hanging in the museum, it pointed to the right.
This time, she went directly to the police.
Inspector Hollis was a quiet man with tired eyes, but he listened to Petra for an hour without interrupting.
Then he compared the photo in her book with the painting on the wall.
"You may be right," he said.
The museum agreed to let a scientist examine the painting.
The analysis took three days.
It showed that one of the white paints contained a chemical that was not produced until the 1950s.
Anna Weber had died in 1938.
The painting was definitely a forgery.
The police searched Albrecht's studio outside the city.
Behind a false wall, they found the real "Girl with the Blue Umbrella," wrapped in cloth and ready to be sold to a private collector abroad.
They also found four other copies of famous paintings, and evidence that he had done the same thing before.
Albrecht was arrested at the airport the same evening.
A month later, the real painting returned to the museum.
This time, the director invited Petra to the ceremony, and he made a short speech.
He admitted that he had not believed her at first, and he thanked her in front of everyone.
Journalists wanted to interview her, and the newspapers called her "the guard with the golden eyes."
Petra did not enjoy the attention very much.
That night, when the visitors had gone, she walked through the silent rooms as usual and stopped in front of her favorite painting.
She switched on her torch.
There, just above the umbrella, was the tiny crack in the shape of a Y.
She smiled.
"Welcome home," she whispered.
To his parents, Arun was a quiet, hardworking student who wanted to become a doctor.
They had moved from India before he was born, and they had worked extremely hard to give him opportunities they had never had.
His father drove a taxi at night, and his mother worked in a pharmacy.
Every evening, they asked him the same question: "Have you done your homework?"
But Arun had a secret.
Three evenings a week, when he told his parents he was studying at the library, he was actually at a youth center in Brixton, dancing.
