He had discovered breakdancing two years earlier, when he saw a group of dancers in the street, and it had changed his life.
When he danced, he forgot about exams, grades and everyone's expectations.
He felt completely free.
His crew was led by Kai, a former champion who taught young people for free.
Kai thought that Arun was the most gifted dancer he had seen in years.
"There's a national competition in March," he told him one night.
"The winners get a place at a famous dance academy. You could win it, Arun."
Arun trained harder than ever.
He practiced new moves in his bedroom with the door locked and watched videos of great dancers on his phone under the blanket.
His marks at school began to fall.
His younger sister Meera noticed that he was always tired and that his shoes were worn out.
She guessed the truth, but she promised not to tell.
The competition was on the same Saturday as an important chemistry exam that his parents had paid for, a special test for students hoping to study medicine.
Arun could not do both.
He told his parents that the exam started early and that he would be home late.
It was the biggest lie he had ever told.
At the competition, Arun danced better than he had ever danced before.
The audience cheered, and the judges gave him the highest score of the day.
He won first prize.
But when he came out of the hall, holding the trophy, his father was waiting outside in his taxi.
The exam center had phoned home to ask why Arun had not arrived.
The drive home was silent.
At home, his mother was crying in the kitchen.
"We work day and night for you," his father said, struggling to control his temper.
"And you lie to us so that you can dance in the street?"
For the first time in his life, Arun did not stay quiet.
He told them everything: how dancing made him feel, how hard he had worked, and how Kai believed in him.
"I'm sorry I lied," he said. "But I'm not sorry I danced. I don't want to be a doctor. I've never wanted to be a doctor."
His father walked out of the room without a word.
For three days, nobody in the house spoke about it, and the silence was stressful for everyone.
Then, one evening, Meera sat down next to her father with her phone.
"You should see this," she said.
It was a video of Arun's performance at the competition, which had been watched fifty thousand times.
Mr. Rao watched it once, then again.
He saw the concentration on his son's face, the incredible control of every movement, and the crowd standing up to cheer.
He had never seen Arun look so happy.
When he looked up, his eyes were wet.
The next day, he drove Arun to the youth center and asked to speak to Kai.
They talked for an hour about the academy, about scholarships and about the possibility of combining dance with school.
For the first time, Arun felt hopeful about the future.
On the way home, Mr. Rao was quiet for a long time.
Then he said, "When I was your age, I wanted to be a singer. My father said no."
He smiled sadly.
"I don't want you to spend your life driving a taxi and wondering what might have happened."
Lucy had wanted to work in a hotel since she was a child.
So when the Harbor View Hotel offered her a job as a receptionist, she was delighted.
On her first morning, her manager, Gordon, showed her the computer system, explained how to check guests in and out, and gave her a smart blue uniform.
"Smile, stay calm, and never argue with a guest," he told her.
"And if there's a problem, call me."
At two o'clock, Gordon left for a meeting in another city.
He would be back the next morning.
Lucy was alone at the front desk for the first time.
For a few hours, everything went well.
At six o'clock, a woman in an elegant grey coat arrived.
"Good evening," she said. "I have a reservation under the name Fenwick. The suite with the sea view."
Lucy checked the computer and gave her the key.
Twenty minutes later, a tall man with a suitcase came to the desk.
"Hale," he said. "I booked the sea view suite for three nights."
Lucy looked at the screen, and her heart sank.
Because of a computer error, the same suite had been booked twice.
And Mrs. Fenwick was already inside it.
Lucy tried to call Gordon, but his phone was switched off.
Mr. Hale was waiting, and he did not look like a patient man.
Then she noticed something in the reservation notes.
Next to Mr. Hale's name, Gordon had written: "Important! Hotel critic. Writes for a famous travel magazine."
Lucy took a deep breath.
She remembered Gordon's advice: smile, stay calm.
But she also knew that a calm smile would not be enough.
"Mr. Hale, I'm very sorry," she said. "I'm afraid there's been a mistake with our booking system, and the suite is not available tonight."
She explained the situation honestly, without blaming anyone.
Mr. Hale's face became very serious.
"This is unacceptable," he said. "I booked this room two months ago."
Lucy did not argue.
"You're absolutely right," she said. "Let me see what I can do."
She checked every room in the hotel.
There was one room free on the top floor, which was normally kept for the owner's family.
It was smaller than the suite, but it had a private balcony with a view of the whole harbor.
Lucy made a decision without asking anyone.
She offered Mr. Hale the top-floor room for free for the first night, and dinner in the hotel restaurant as an apology.
She promised that the suite would be ready for him the next day, and she would personally make sure of it.
She also offered to carry his suitcase herself.
Mr. Hale looked at her for a long moment.
Then he nodded.
"All right," he said. "Let's see this balcony."
That night, Lucy could hardly sleep.
She was sure that she would lose her job.
When Gordon returned the next morning, Lucy told him everything.
He was quiet while she spoke.
Then he said, "You gave away the owner's room and a free dinner, on your first day, without asking me?"
Lucy nodded miserably.
Gordon started to laugh.
"That's exactly what I would have done," he said.
Two months later, Mr. Hale's review appeared in the magazine.
He wrote that the Harbor View Hotel was comfortable but not perfect: there had been a problem with his booking.

"However," he continued, "the way the young receptionist dealt with the problem was the best service I have experienced in any hotel this year. Mistakes happen everywhere. What matters is what happens next."
The owner framed the article and hung it behind the front desk.
Edith Kerr had lived on the second floor of Rowan Court for forty-one years.
She knew every sound in the building: the pipes that knocked in winter, the lift that complained every time it stopped, and the cat on the third floor that cried for its breakfast at six.
She was eighty, a retired piano teacher, and she liked peace and quiet.
In September, a young man moved into the apartment above hers.
His name was Jay, and on the first day he carried up a lot of boxes and a very large drum kit.
Edith watched from her window and felt a little nervous.
The first evening, the drumming started at nine o'clock.
It was loud, fast and continuous, and it shook the lamp on Edith's ceiling.
It stopped at eleven.
The next evening, the same thing happened, and the next.
Edith tried to be patient.
She put cotton in her ears, turned up the radio and went to bed later.
Nothing helped.
After two weeks, she was exhausted, and her doctor noticed that her blood pressure had risen.
"You need to talk to him," her daughter said on the phone.
"Or complain to the building manager."
Edith did not like arguments.
So she wrote a polite note and pushed it under Jay's door.
"Dear neighbor, I would appreciate it if you could play less often in the evenings. I am elderly and I need my sleep. Thank you. Edith Kerr, flat 2B."
The drumming stopped for two nights.
Then it started again.
Finally, Edith filed an official complaint with the building manager, who arranged a meeting in the lobby.
Jay arrived looking embarrassed.
He was younger than she had expected, perhaps twenty, and very polite.
"I'm really sorry, Mrs. Kerr," he said. "I had no idea the noise was so bad downstairs."
He explained that he was a music student, and in three months he had an audition for a place in a professional orchestra.
He had to practice four hours a day, and during the day he worked in a café to pay the rent.
"The evening is the only time I have," he said.
Edith looked at him for a moment.
"An orchestra?" she said. "Which piece are you preparing?"
When he told her, her face changed.
It was a piece she had once taught to her own students.
They talked for an hour.
By the end, they had made an unusual agreement.
Jay would practice on a special electronic drum kit with headphones in the evenings, which the music school agreed to lend him.
He would only use his real drums on Saturday afternoons, when Edith visited her daughter.
And twice a week, he would come downstairs to Edith's apartment, where she would help him with the difficult rhythms in his audition piece on her old piano.
For the next three months, the building was quieter than it had been for years.
But on Tuesday and Friday evenings, the other residents heard something new: the sound of a piano and drums playing together, followed by laughter.
In December, Jay passed his audition.
The first person he told was Edith.
A few months later, he invited her to his first concert with the orchestra, and he booked her a seat in the front row.
After the concert, a journalist asked him who had inspired him most.
"My neighbor," Jay said, and pointed to a small old lady in the front row.
"She complained about my drumming. Then she taught me how to do it properly."
The four members of the marketing team at Bright Ideas Ltd did not like each other very much.
Nora, the team leader, was organized but bossy.
Ben was loud and full of ideas, but he never finished anything.
Kit was very quiet, and nobody knew much about her.
Raj was brilliant with numbers but hated working with other people.
After a disastrous project, their manager, Mr. Slate, decided that they needed some team-building.
He booked them a session in an escape room.
"You'll be locked in a room for sixty minutes," he explained. "The only way out is to solve the puzzles together. If you work as a team, you'll escape."
Nobody was enthusiastic.
The room was designed to look like a scientist's laboratory from the 1950s.
There were shelves of old bottles, a desk full of papers, a huge map on the wall and a heavy metal door with a padlock that needed a four-digit code.
A screen on the wall showed a clock counting down from sixty minutes.
When the door closed behind them, the lights went dim, and a recorded voice said: "The professor has disappeared. Find his secret formula before time runs out."
For the first ten minutes, it was chaos.
Nora tried to give everyone instructions.
Ben ran around the room opening every drawer.
Raj sat in a corner and tried to solve a number puzzle alone.
Kit said nothing at all.
They found nothing useful, and the clock kept moving.
With forty-five minutes left, Nora stopped and took a deep breath.
"This isn't working," she said. "Let's split up. Ben, you search the shelves. Raj, you take the desk. Kit, what do you want to do?"
Kit looked surprised that anyone had asked her.
"The map," she said quietly. "I think there's something on the map."
It worked.
Ben found a key hidden inside a bottle, which opened a drawer in the desk.
Inside the drawer, Raj found a sheet of numbers that looked meaningless, but within minutes he realized that it was a simple code.
"Every number is a letter," he explained, and for once he sounded excited.
The code spelled a sentence: "Look where the professor was born."
Everyone turned to the map.
It was covered in tiny cities, rivers and mountains.
But where had the professor been born?
Ben searched the papers on the desk and found an old passport.
The place of birth was written in faded ink, and nobody could read it.
Nobody except Kit.
She held the passport under the desk lamp, turned it slowly, and read the name of a small town.
Then she found it on the map in seconds.
Next to the town, someone had drawn four very small numbers.
"How did you do that?" Ben asked.
"I used to help my grandfather restore old maps," Kit said, shrugging. "You learn to see small things."
With only thirty seconds left, Nora put the numbers into the padlock.
Nothing happened.
Everyone groaned.
Then Raj shouted, "Backwards! Everything in the professor's code was backwards!"
Nora tried again, in reverse order.
The lock clicked open with three seconds to spare, and the four of them fell out of the door, laughing and cheering like children.
On Monday, Mr. Slate noticed something different about the marketing team.
Nora asked for other people's opinions before making decisions.
Ben finished his reports, because Raj was checking the numbers.
And in the team meeting, when they were stuck on a problem, everyone turned to the quiet woman in the corner.
"Kit," Nora said, "what do you see?"
Two days before their final history exam, Leah's best friend, Priya, sent her a message late at night.
It was a photo of a piece of paper with a list of questions.
Under it, Priya had written: "Don't tell anyone!!! It's the real exam!"
Leah stared at her screen.
She recognized the school's logo at the top of the page.
The next morning, she asked Priya where it had come from.
Priya explained that a boy in another class had taken a photo of it on a teacher's desk, and now it was being shared in a secret group.
"Half the year has it," she said. "It would be stupid not to use it."
Leah had studied hard for weeks.
History was her best subject, and she needed a high grade to get into the university course she wanted.
If half the students had the questions, their marks would be much higher than hers, and the results would be completely unfair.
But there was a bigger problem.
If she told a teacher, Priya would probably be in serious trouble.
She might even be excluded from the exam.
And everyone would know that Leah had reported her best friend.
That evening, Leah did not open the photo, but she could not stop thinking about it.
The uncertainty made her feel sick.
She went to visit her grandmother, Nana Ruth, who had been a headteacher for thirty years and always gave wise guidance.
She did not mention any names, but she explained the situation.
Nana Ruth listened carefully.
"This isn't really about the exam," she said. "It's about what kind of person you want to be."
She did not tell Leah what to do.
Instead, she asked questions.
What would happen if nobody said anything?
Was there a way to stop the cheating without destroying her friendship and her loyalty to Priya?
And had she shown Priya the same honesty that she expected from others?
Leah realized that she had not.
She had been so worried about what might happen that she had not even told her friend that she thought it was wrong.
The next day, Leah asked Priya to meet her in the park after school.
It was the most challenging conversation of her life.
She told Priya that she had not looked at the questions, and that she thought using them was cheating.
Priya immediately became defensive.
"Everyone's doing it," she said. "You're just jealous because you studied for nothing."
Leah did not argue, and she tried hard to keep her temper.
She said that she was going to tell Mr. Grant, their history teacher, that the exam had been leaked, but that she would not give him any names.
"I don't want you to get in trouble," she said. "But I can't pretend I don't know. It isn't fair to the people who haven't seen it."
Priya walked away without saying goodbye.
That evening, Leah sent an email to Mr. Grant.
She explained that a photo of the exam was being shared, acknowledged that she should have told him sooner, and apologized.
The next morning, the school announced that the exam had been postponed for a week and that a new paper would be written.
Consequently, many students were furious, but nobody was punished, because nobody knew exactly who had seen the photo.
For three days, Priya did not speak to Leah, and Leah felt terribly lonely.
Then, on the fourth day, she appeared at Leah's door with two cups of hot chocolate and her history notes.
"I'm sorry," she said. "You were right. And now I actually have to study. Will you help me?"
They studied together every evening that week, and Priya found a new motivation.
Fortunately, they both passed with good grades, and neither of them has forgotten the lesson.
For three years, Tomás had saved every penny he could.
He worked in a supermarket on weekdays and delivered pizzas at weekends, and he rarely went out with his friends.
His goal was simple: to buy a car.
The bus to his college took an hour each way, and he was tired of standing in the rain.
By the summer, he had four thousand dollars.
It was not a fortune, but it was enough for a good second-hand car.
He spent every evening looking at advertisements online, comparing prices, ages and mileage.
Then he saw it: a small red car, only five years old, with low mileage, for three thousand eight hundred dollars.
The photos looked fantastic.
He called the seller, a man called Mr. Crane, who invited him to see it the next day.
Mr. Crane was friendly and talkative.
He explained that the car had belonged to his mother, who had only driven it to the shops.
It was clean and shiny, and the engine sounded quiet.
"Lots of people are interested," he said. "If you want it, I need a decision today."
Tomás almost said yes immediately.
But something made him hesitate.
He asked if he could come back the next morning with a friend.
Mr. Crane looked annoyed, but he agreed.
The friend was Bex, who had been at school with Tomás and now worked as a mechanic in her uncle's garage.
She arrived with a toolbox and a flashlight, and she spent forty minutes examining the car.
She looked underneath it, checked the oil, and listened carefully to the engine.
"It isn't a bad car," she told Tomás quietly.
"But it hasn't only been driven to the shops. The tires are worn, the brakes will need replacing soon, and there's rust underneath. And look at this."
She pointed to a small scratch near the back light, where the paint was a slightly different color.
"It's been in an accident and repainted."
Tomás felt disappointed, but Bex was calm.
"It's still worth buying," she said, "but not for that price. The repairs will cost about seven hundred dollars. Offer him less."
She gave him some advice: be polite, explain your reasons, and be ready to walk away.
Tomás had never negotiated anything in his life.
His heart was beating fast when he spoke to Mr. Crane.
He explained what Bex had found, and he offered three thousand dollars.
Mr. Crane laughed.
"Three thousand? That's ridiculous. The car is perfect."
Tomás took a deep breath.
"It needs new brakes and tires, and it's been in an accident," he said. "Three thousand is a fair price. If you don't agree, I understand."
He started to walk away.
"Wait," said Mr. Crane. "Three thousand four hundred."
In the end, they agreed on three thousand two hundred.
Bex's uncle replaced the brakes and tires the following week, and he charged Tomás only for the parts.
With the money he had saved, Tomás bought insurance and a full tank of petrol.
The first place he drove was to Bex's garage, to thank her.
"I owe you," he said.
"You do," she laughed. "You can drive me to the cinema on Saturday."
He did, and the next Saturday, too.
Four years later, they still drive to the cinema every Saturday, but now they are married, and the little red car has a baby seat in the back.
The apartment on Carver Street had four bedrooms, one small kitchen and one bathroom.
In September, four students who had never met moved in.
Hana was from Japan and studied medicine.
Tomasz was from Poland and studied computer science.
Jade was from London and studied fashion, and Kwame, from Ghana, was a music student who played the trumpet.
On the first evening, they sat in the kitchen and ate pizza together.
Everyone was polite and friendly.
"This is going to be a great year," said Jade, and the others agreed.
They did not know each other's habits yet.
Hana got up at six every morning to study.
Tomasz played online games until three in the morning.
Jade loved cooking enormous meals for her friends.
And Kwame had to practice the trumpet for two hours a day.
By October, the kitchen was a battlefield.
After Jade's dinners, piles of dirty plates stayed in the sink for days.
Somebody kept drinking other people's milk.
Tomasz shouted at his computer in the middle of the night, and Kwame's trumpet practice shook the thin walls every afternoon.
Nobody wanted to start an argument, so they started writing notes instead.
"Whoever took my milk, please replace it," said the first one, on the fridge door.
"Some people need to sleep at night!!!" said the next.
Soon the fridge was covered with angry messages, and the flatmates avoided each other in the hall.
Jade started eating in her room.
Tomasz waited until the kitchen was empty before he made coffee.
Hana bought a small fridge for her bedroom, which cost more than she could really afford.
Kwame, who hated conflict, simply stayed at the music department until late every evening.
The friendly atmosphere of the first evening had completely disappeared.
In November, Hana had her most important exam of the year.
The night before, she went to bed early, but at midnight she was woken up by loud music.
Jade was having a birthday party in the living room, and Tomasz was shouting at his game.
Hana lay awake until four.
The next day, she came home pale and exhausted.
She was sure she had failed.
In the kitchen, she found a mountain of dishes and no milk.
She had spent the whole morning answering questions about the human heart, and her own heart was still beating too fast.
Something inside her broke.
For the first time, the quiet girl who never complained began to shout.
"Does anybody in this flat ever wash a plate?" she cried. "I had the most important exam of my life today, and I slept for three hours!"
"It was my birthday!" said Jade. "I told everyone about the party last week."
"You wrote it on a note," said Tomasz. "Nobody reads the notes anymore. There are too many of them."
Within minutes, all four flatmates were in the kitchen, and everyone was blaming everyone else.
It was Kwame who finally raised his hands.
"Stop," he said calmly. "We're not enemies. We just have different lives. Let's have a proper meeting, tonight, with tea and no shouting."
At eight o'clock, they sat around the kitchen table.
It was awkward at first, but slowly they began to listen to each other.
"I'm sorry about the dishes," said Jade. "I'm always rushing to class, and I tell myself I'll do them later. Then I forget."
"I'm sorry about the party, too," she added, looking at Hana. "I didn't know about your exam."
Tomasz apologized for the noise; he had not realized how thin the walls were.
And Tomasz also confessed that he was the milk thief.
Everyone laughed, and the tension disappeared.
By ten o'clock, they had a plan.
They made a cleaning rota and put it on the fridge instead of the angry notes.
They agreed on quiet hours after eleven on weeknights.
Tomasz would wear headphones, and Kwame arranged to practice in a room at the university.
They would buy milk, bread and coffee together from a shared fund.
The plan did not solve everything, but it worked surprisingly well.
Every Sunday, one of them cooked a meal from their own country, and the others did the washing-up.
Hana taught them to make sushi, and Kwame's spicy jollof rice became famous in the building.
They also discovered things about each other that the notes had hidden.
Tomasz, who seemed to care only about games, was building a free app to help refugees learn the local language.
Jade designed costumes for a children's theater at weekends.
And Kwame, it turned out, sent half of his part-time salary to his younger sisters in Accra.
A few weeks later, Hana received her exam result.
To her amazement, she had passed with a good grade.
That evening, the others surprised her with a cake, and Kwame played a very quiet version of "Happy Birthday" on his trumpet, even though it was not her birthday.
In June, the landlord, Mr. Pollard, asked if they wanted to stay for another year.
They looked at each other and immediately knew the answer; they did not even need to discuss it.
"Same time next year?" asked Mr. Pollard.
"Same time next year," they answered together, and Kwame promised to keep the trumpet quiet.
Four strangers had become something close to a family, and the flat was full of warmth.
It had been raining in Millford for three days without a break.
The river, which usually flowed quietly past the old houses on Mill Lane, was brown, fast and much higher than normal.
On the radio, the local authority issued a flood warning, but most residents were not worried.
The river had not flooded the town for more than fifty years.
Twelve-year-old Mateo lived at number four with his mother, Lina, who worked night shifts at the hospital.
Next door, at number six, lived Mr. Jonas, an old man with a grey beard who never smiled and often shouted at children who kicked their football against his fence.
Everyone on the street avoided him.
Mateo was a little scared of him.
At ten o'clock that night, while his mother was at work, Mateo woke up because his feet were wet.
Water was coming under the front door and spreading across the floor.
He looked out of the window and felt his heart stop.
The street had become a river.
Cars were floating, and the water was rising quickly.
He tried to call his mother, but there was no signal.
The electricity went off, and the house was suddenly dark.
Mateo grabbed his phone, a torch and the family photo album and ran upstairs.
He was terrified.
Then he heard a voice outside.
"Is anybody there? Mateo!"
It was Mr. Jonas, standing in water up to his waist, holding a rope and a lamp.
"Come to the window," he called. "Don't come down. The water is too strong."
He threw one end of the rope up to the window and told Mateo to tie it around the heavy bed.
Then, slowly and carefully, he helped the boy climb down to a small boat that he had pulled from his garage.
"My father was a fisherman," he said. "I've had this boat for forty years. I never thought I'd use it on Mill Lane."
Mateo thought that they would go to safety immediately.
Instead, Mr. Jonas turned the boat towards the other houses.
"Mrs. Hayes at number twelve can't walk well," he said. "And there's a family with a baby at number nine. We have to check."
For the next three hours, they moved from house to house in the dark.
Mateo held the torch and shouted names, and Mr. Jonas rowed.
They helped Mrs. Hayes out of her upstairs window and carried the baby's family to the church on the hill, which was being used as an emergency shelter.
By two in the morning, the boat had carried eleven people to safety.
Mr. Jonas's hands were bleeding from the rope, but he refused to stop until every house on the street had been checked.
When Lina finally reached the church at dawn, she found her son asleep next to an old man with a grey beard.
She hugged Mateo for a long time.
Then she turned to Mr. Jonas, and she did not know what to say.
"Thank you" did not seem like enough.
The water went down after two days, but the damage was enormous.
Floors, furniture and walls were destroyed, and it took months to repair the houses.
But something else had changed on Mill Lane.
The neighbors, who had hardly spoken to each other before, now worked together every weekend, cleaning, painting and sharing tools and meals.
Mr. Jonas repaired more doors than anyone.
He still did not smile very often.
But the next summer, when Mateo's football flew over his fence, he threw it back.
And after a moment, he asked if he could play, too.
Leila and her younger brother Sami had always dreamed of running their own restaurant.
Their grandmother, whom they called Teta, had taught them to cook when they were children, and her recipes were famous in the family.
But a restaurant was far too expensive, so they decided to start with something smaller: a food truck.
They used all their savings to buy an old delivery van and convert it into a kitchen.
It took four months of hard work.
Sami, who was good with tools, installed the equipment, and Leila designed the menu and the logo.
They painted the truck bright orange and called it "Teta's Kitchen."
In May, they parked it on Harbor Street, near a busy office area, and opened for business.
On the first day, they sold forty lunches.
They were exhausted but extremely happy.
The problems began in the second week.
Customers started to post reviews on a popular website.
Some were kind, but many were negative.
"Great smell, but I waited thirty minutes for a sandwich," wrote one person.
"The falafel was dry," wrote another. "And too expensive for the size."
Sami was furious.
"These people don't know anything about food," he said, reading the reviews on his phone.
"Our recipes are perfect. They're Teta's recipes!"
Leila was not so sure.
She had noticed that some customers left half of their food.
By June, sales had fallen by half.
Some days, they sold fewer than fifteen lunches, and they had to throw away food at the end of the day.
After paying for fuel, ingredients and the parking permit, there was almost nothing left.
Leila began to wonder whether they had made a terrible mistake.
One Saturday, Teta came to see the truck for the first time.
She was eighty-one, and she walked slowly with a stick, but her eyes missed nothing.
She sat on a folding chair, ate a falafel sandwich and said nothing for a long time.
"Well?" asked Sami.
"It's good," said Teta. "But it isn't my falafel."
She explained that they were cooking everything in the morning and keeping it warm for hours, so it became dry.
"I always fried mine at the last moment. Fresh from the oil. That's the secret."
She also pointed out that their menu was too long.
"You have twelve dishes and two people," she said. "Of course the customers wait. Choose four things and make them perfectly."
Sami opened his mouth to argue, then closed it again.
He knew she was right.
That night, Leila and Sami sat in the truck and read every review again, but this time they tried to learn from them instead of being angry.
They made a list of the most common complaints: slow service, dry food, small portions, and high prices.
They reduced the menu to four dishes.
They bought a second fryer so that they could cook everything fresh while customers waited, and they prepared the vegetables in advance to save time.
They also made the sandwiches bigger and lowered the price slightly.
The changes cost money they did not really have.
Their cousin Rashid lent them some, and they promised to pay him back by the end of the year.
"This is our last chance," Leila said.
At first, nothing seemed to happen.
Then, slowly, the reviews began to change.
"Best falafel in the city, and ready in five minutes," wrote someone in July.
A local food blogger visited and posted a video, which was watched by thousands of people.
Soon there was a queue outside the orange truck every lunchtime.
Sami even replied politely to a new negative review.
"Thank you for your feedback," he wrote. "You're right about the sauce. We've changed it. Please come back and tell us what you think."
The customer came back and changed his review to five stars.
In December, Leila and Sami paid Rashid back, with a large box of falafel as interest.
They were already talking about a second truck, and they were eager to start.
When they told Teta, she just smiled.
"Good," she said. "But remember: fresh from the oil."
Clara had always dreamed of becoming a journalist, so when the Riverside Gazette offered her a summer internship, she accepted immediately.
The reality was far less exciting than she had imagined.
For the first week, she answered phones, made coffee and checked the spelling in other people's articles.
The editor, Mr. Donovan, was a tall man with grey hair who rarely smiled.
On Friday, Clara asked him when she could write something of her own.
He looked at her over his glasses.
"Everyone starts at the bottom of the ladder," he said.
"Find me a real story, and I'll give you a page."
After that, Clara spent every evening walking around the town with a notebook.
She read old newspapers, listened to conversations on the bus and talked to shopkeepers.
But nothing she found seemed important enough for Mr. Donovan.
One hot afternoon, she stopped at the Green Leaf Café, the most popular café in town.
A large sign above the door said: "100% organic. 100% local."
The owner, Felipe, was an old friend of her aunt Rita, and he always gave Clara a free cookie.
While she was waiting for her coffee, she noticed a delivery van behind the café.
The boxes that the driver was unloading had the name of a huge wholesale supermarket on them, a company two hundred kilometers away.
Curious, Clara took a photo.
Over the next two weeks, she went back several times.
Every Tuesday, the same van arrived.
The labels on the boxes described ordinary vegetables and eggs, not organic ones.
She also called the two farms that were named on the café's menu.
One had closed three years earlier.
The other had not sold anything to the Green Leaf for a long time.
When Clara showed her notes to Mr. Donovan, he looked interested for the first time.
"That's a real story," he said.
"People pay extra because they believe the food is organic. If it isn't, they have a right to know."
Then he raised a finger.
"But before we publish a word, Felipe must have the chance to respond. That's the rule."
That evening, Clara had dinner with her aunt and told her everything.
Rita put down her fork.
"Felipe has worked so hard for that café," she said quietly.
"His wife has been ill for two years. If you write this, you could ruin him."
Clara could not sleep that night.
She liked Felipe, and she did not want to hurt anyone.
But she kept thinking about a young mother she had seen at the café, paying almost double for "organic" food for her baby.
The next morning, Clara went to the café with her notebook and her phone.
Her hands were shaking.
She showed Felipe the photos and asked him directly whether his food was really organic.
At first, he denied everything.
Then he sat down heavily and put his head in his hands.
He explained that when his wife became ill, his costs had risen sharply.
The local farms were too expensive, so he had started buying cheaper food "just for a few months."
He had been too ashamed to change the sign.
"I told myself it was only temporary," he said. "Then it became normal."
He asked her not to publish the story.
Clara said that she could not promise that, but that she would include his side of the story.
Clara's article appeared on page three the following week.
It was fair: it explained what she had discovered, but it also included Felipe's explanation and his apology.
The same day, Felipe took down his old sign.
The new one said: "Good food. Honest prices."
Some customers stopped coming, but many others appreciated his honesty.
A young farmer read the article and offered to sell him organic vegetables at a lower price.
A month later, Rita called her niece.
"I was wrong," she said. "You did the right thing, and you did it kindly."
At the end of the summer, Mr. Donovan offered Clara a part-time job.
"You found a story," he said, and for once he smiled.
"And you remembered that there is a person behind every story. That's what makes a good journalist."
Ravi had sent out forty-three applications in three months.
Most companies never replied, and the others sent polite messages that began with the words "Unfortunately, on this occasion…"
He was starting to lose hope.
He had a degree in business, but no experience, and every job seemed to require at least two years of it.
Then, on a rainy Monday, an email arrived from Brightway, a company that made solar panels.
They wanted to interview him for a position as a customer service team leader.
The interview was on Friday at nine o'clock.
Ravi spent the whole week preparing.
He read everything about the company, practiced his answers in front of the mirror and asked his grandmother, whom everyone called Nani, to act as the interviewer.
Nani took the job seriously.
"Why should we hire you, young man?" she asked, looking at him over her glasses.
Ravi laughed, but he could not think of a good answer.
On Friday, Ravi woke up at six, full of nervous energy.
He put on his only suit and his best tie.
While he was drinking his coffee, his little brother ran into the kitchen and knocked the cup out of his hand.
A brown stain spread across his white shirt.
He changed into a blue shirt that did not match the tie and ran to the bus stop.
Ten minutes later, the bus broke down on the main road.
The driver apologized and said that another bus would arrive "shortly."
It did not.
Ravi started to walk, then to run.
It began to rain.
At twenty past nine, he arrived at Brightway, wet, out of breath and late.
The receptionist looked at him with sympathy and gave him a towel.
"Ms. Carter is waiting for you," she said.
Ms. Carter was a calm woman in her fifties.
Ravi apologized for being late and explained what had happened, briefly and without making excuses.
To his surprise, she smiled.
"Well," she said, "this job is all about dealing with problems. It sounds like you've had some practice this morning."
The interview lasted an hour.
She asked him to describe a time when he had dealt with an angry person.
Ravi told her about the two summers he had worked in his uncle's shop, and about a customer who had shouted at him for ten minutes because a delivery was late.
He had listened, apologized, found the parcel and delivered it himself that evening.
The customer later became one of the shop's most loyal clients.
Then Ms. Carter asked the question he had feared all week.
"What is your greatest weakness?"
Ravi had prepared a clever answer, but he suddenly decided not to use it.
"Honestly? I've never managed a team," he said.
"I know that's the main part of this job. But I learn fast, and I'm not afraid to ask for help."
The next week was the longest of Ravi's life.
He checked his email every few minutes.
He was sure that the coffee, the rain and his honest answer had destroyed his chances.
"You did your best," Nani told him. "Whatever happens, you should be proud of that."
On Thursday, his phone rang.
It was Ms. Carter.
She explained that there had been more than two hundred applicants, and that some of them had much more experience than him.
Ravi's heart sank.
"But you were the only one who didn't pretend to be perfect," she continued.
"And you arrived soaking wet, calm and polite. That told me more than any CV."
Ravi started his new job two weeks later.
His team was made up of six people, most of them older than him, and for the first few days he felt like an impostor.
But he remembered what he had promised in the interview.
He asked questions, listened carefully and admitted when he did not know something.
Slowly, his colleagues began to trust him.
On Friday evening, he went to his grandmother's house with a box of her favorite sweets.
"So," said Nani, "why did they hire you, young man?"
This time, Ravi knew the answer.
"Because I told the truth," he said. "And because I didn't give up in the rain."
Linh had studied English for eight years, and she was good at grammar.
She could write excellent essays and she usually got top marks in tests.
But in September, she was going to study in Glasgow, and she was terrified.
Whenever she watched videos of real conversations, people spoke so fast and used so many strange expressions that she understood almost nothing.
One day, she saw a poster in a café in Hanoi: "Language exchange! Practice English, help someone learn Vietnamese. Every Thursday at 7 p.m."
Linh felt nervous, but she was also eager to improve, so she went.
Her partner was Callum, a tall young man from Scotland who taught at an international school.
He had lived in Vietnam for a year and was learning Vietnamese.
They agreed to speak English for half an hour and Vietnamese for half an hour.
The first conversation was a disaster.
Callum had a strong Scottish accent, and he spoke quickly.
When he said, "I'm knackered, it's been a wee bit of a nightmare at work," Linh just stared at him.
Then it was her turn to laugh, because Callum tried to order a coffee in Vietnamese and accidentally asked for a "chicken" instead.
Vietnamese tones, he explained, were the hardest thing he had ever tried to learn.
Over the following weeks, Linh learned to ask questions without feeling embarrassed.
"Sorry, what does 'knackered' mean?"
"Could you say that more slowly?"
"Is that a formal word, or can I use it with friends?"
Callum was patient and generous with his time, and he always gave her examples.
She discovered that textbooks had not taught her how people really talk in everyday interaction.
Nobody said "I am very tired"; they said "I'm exhausted" or "I'm shattered."
People did not say "Goodbye"; they said "See you" or "Take care."
And English was full of idioms that made no sense at all: "It's a piece of cake" meant that something was easy, and "break a leg" meant "good luck."
Linh taught Callum things, too.
She explained why Vietnamese people ask "Have you eaten yet?" as a greeting, and how the words for "you" and "I" change depending on the age of the person you are speaking to.
Callum found this fascinating.
"In English, we just say 'you' to everybody," he said. "Your language tells you exactly who you are to each other."
They both made plenty of mistakes.
One evening, Linh wanted to say that she was excited about her trip, but she said that she was "exciting."
Callum smiled and explained the difference: "You're excited. The trip is exciting."
Another time, Callum told a Vietnamese colleague that he was "very full," meaning he had eaten a lot, but his pronunciation made it sound like something much ruder.
They laughed about it for weeks.
Linh realized that making mistakes was not something to be ashamed of.
It was simply part of learning.
Every mistake she made with Callum was one she would not make in Glasgow.
By August, Linh could follow Callum even when he spoke fast, and she had started to use some Scottish words herself, which made him laugh.
Her confidence had grown, and so had her motivation.
On their last evening, Callum gave her a small notebook.
Inside, he had written fifty Scottish expressions, with their meanings and an example for each one.
It was a lovely farewell gift.
Linh gave him a notebook, too, with fifty Vietnamese phrases, and a warning about the word for "full."
Two weeks later, on her first day in Glasgow, a bus driver said something to her very fast.
A year earlier, she would have panicked.
Now she smiled and said, "Sorry, could you say that again, a wee bit more slowly?"
The driver laughed, and Linh felt very satisfied.
"Where did you learn that?"
"From a friend," she said.
Owen had not been to Elm Street for fifteen years when the lawyer's letter arrived.
His uncle Ian had died, and he had left Owen his bookshop, Bramble Books.
Owen remembered it from his childhood: a narrow shop full of dusty shelves, the smell of old paper, and his uncle reading poetry aloud to anyone who would listen.
Owen was thirty-two and worked in an office in the city.
He had no time for a bookshop, and he did not need one.
When he visited, he found that the business was in a terrible state.
The shop had lost money for six years in a row.
The roof leaked, the windows were dirty, and there were piles of unpaid bills behind the counter.
An estate agent told him that the building was worth a lot of money.
"A coffee chain would pay well for this location," he said.
Owen decided to sell.
On his last day in the shop, a woman came in and stopped when she saw him.
"Owen? It's me, Maya. From the summer holidays!"
They had played together in the shop as children, building castles from old books while Ian pretended not to notice.
Maya was now a primary school teacher, and she lived around the corner.
When Owen told her about his plan, her face fell.
"You can't," she said. "This is the last bookshop in the whole town. Where will the kids go?"
"People buy books online now," Owen replied. "It's cheaper. The shop can't compete."
"Maybe it can't sell books like a website," said Maya. "But it could do things that a website can't."
Over coffee, Maya explained her idea.
The shop could become a meeting place for the neighborhood.
There could be story hours for small children, a book club, poetry evenings and a corner where students could study after school.
Local people could volunteer to help, and the town's writers could give talks.
Mrs. Liu, who owned the bakery next door, might even sell cakes there.
Owen was not convinced.
"And who is going to pay for the roof?" he asked.
Maya had an answer for that, too.
They could ask the community for help, and offer membership to people who wanted to support the shop.
"Give it six months," she said. "If it doesn't work, sell it. I won't say a word."
Owen looked around at his uncle's shelves.
Then, to his own surprise, he agreed.
The first weeks were exhausting.
Owen worked in the city during the day and painted shelves in the evening.
Maya organized volunteers, and within a month, twenty neighbors were helping to clean, repair and sort the books.
A local builder fixed the roof at cost price.
Mrs. Liu brought cakes every Saturday.
When the shop reopened, a hundred people came to the first poetry evening.
The children's story hour was so popular that they had to add a second one.
More than three hundred people became members, and many of them bought their books in the shop instead of online, even though it cost a little more.
"We're not just buying a book," one woman told Owen. "We're buying a place to be together."
In the spring, while he was cleaning his uncle's old desk, Owen found an envelope with his name on it.
Inside was a short letter, written a few months before Ian died.
"Dear Owen," it said. "I know the shop is not worth much money."
"Sell it if you need to. But first, sit in it for an hour and remember the boy who built castles from books."
At the end of the six months, the shop was not rich, but for the first time in years, it was not losing money.
Owen left his office job and became the full-time manager of Bramble Books.
He framed his uncle's letter and hung it above the counter.
And on Saturday mornings, he can often be found reading poetry aloud to anyone who will listen.
Skarra was a small island with one village, one shop and about two hundred sheep.
In summer, a ferry came from the mainland twice a day.
Most tourists spent a few hours walking along the cliffs and then left on the six o'clock boat.
Lucía, a photographer from Spain, had come to photograph the famous colors of the sunset over the western cliffs.
A magazine had promised to pay well for the right picture.
Jonah was a backpacker from Australia who had arrived on the same morning ferry.
They had talked briefly on the boat, then gone in different directions.
At half past five, they met again at the top of the cliffs.
The light was changing, and the sky was turning gold.
"Just five more minutes," Lucía said, and she kept taking photos.
Jonah checked his watch, then looked at the view and forgot about it.
When they finally ran down to the harbor, the ferry was already a small white shape on the horizon.
There was no hotel on Skarra, only a small guesthouse.
The owner shook her head.
"Sorry, dears. Every room is taken. There's a wedding tomorrow."
The next ferry was at nine the following morning.
Outside, the wind was getting stronger, and dark clouds were coming in from the sea.
Jonah had a small tent in his backpack, but it was not designed for a storm.
Lucía had nothing except her cameras and a light jacket.
They looked at each other, not sure whether to laugh or panic.
"We could sleep in the bus shelter," Jonah suggested.
"There are no buses on this island," said Lucía. "There isn't even a bus shelter."
At that moment, an old woman in a yellow raincoat stopped her bicycle beside them.
"You two missed the ferry, didn't you?" she said. "Everybody does, once. Follow me."
Her name was Mrs. MacLeod, and she lived in the old lighthouse at the end of the island.
Her husband had been the lighthouse keeper for forty years, until the light became automatic.
He had died five years ago, but she had refused to leave.
By the time they arrived, the storm had begun.
Rain beat against the windows, and waves crashed against the rocks below.
Mrs. MacLeod made a pot of tea and a huge plate of cheese sandwiches, and they sat by the fire.
She told them stories about the island: about ships that had sunk on the rocks, and about the night her husband had rescued eleven fishermen.
Jonah explained that he had left a job he hated in Sydney and had been traveling for eight months.
He did not know what he wanted to do next, and that frightened him.
Lucía said that she was worried, too.
She had been a photographer for ten years, but magazines paid less and less, and she was thinking of giving up.
Mrs. MacLeod listened quietly.
"My husband used to say that the storm always looks worse from inside," she said. "In the morning, you can see what it really was."
Lucía woke before dawn.
The storm had passed, and the air was completely still.
She climbed the narrow stairs to the top of the lighthouse and gasped.
The sea was silver, the sky was pink, and a group of dolphins was jumping through the waves.
She took photo after photo.
When she came down, Jonah was helping Mrs. MacLeod to repair a window that the storm had broken.
He was surprisingly good with tools.
"I used to love building things," he said, almost to himself. "I forgot about that."
At nine, they stood at the harbor with Mrs. MacLeod.
Lucía tried to give her some money, but she refused.
"Send me a photo," she said. "That's enough."
Two months later, Lucía's photograph of the dolphins at dawn appeared on the cover of a famous travel magazine.
It brought her more work than she had had in years.
She sent a large print to the lighthouse, and another one to Jonah, who had gone home to Australia to train as a carpenter.
On the back of both, she wrote the same words: "The storm always looks worse from inside."
It was almost midnight when the twins, Max and Ella, got on the last train home after a concert.
The carriage was almost empty.
The only other passenger was a small old woman sitting by the door, holding a handbag tightly and looking around nervously.
Every time the train stopped, she stood up, looked at the station name and sat down again.
"I think she's lost," Ella whispered.
Max, who was always more confident, walked over.
"Excuse me," he said. "Are you OK? Can we help you?"
The woman looked at him with worried eyes and said something that neither of them understood.
Then she said one word in English: "Hotel."
It was clear that she spoke almost no English.
Max took out his phone to use a translation app, but his battery was dead.
Ella's phone had no signal in the tunnel.
They would have to manage without technology.
Ella sat down next to the woman and spoke slowly and clearly, using simple words and pointing.
"You. Hotel. Name?"
The woman shook her head.
She did not remember, or she did not understand.
Then she opened her handbag and took out a small card.
It was a key card from a hotel, but the name had been printed in tiny letters, and half of it had worn off.
They could only read "Gr…" and "Plaza."
"Where are you from?" Max asked, pointing at her and then at the world.
The woman understood.
"Korea," she said. "Seoul."
She pointed to herself and said "Kim."
Then she made a big circle with her arms and said "people," and held up ten fingers, then ten again.
"A group," said Ella. "She's with a tour group of about twenty people. She must have lost them."
Mrs. Kim nodded as if she had understood the tone, if not the words.
She mimed eating and then pointed back in the direction they had come from.
They guessed that the group had had dinner somewhere in the city center, and that Mrs. Kim had got on the wrong train.
At the next station, the train came out of the tunnel, and Ella's phone found a signal.
She searched for hotels in the city with "Plaza" in their name.
There were four, but only one began with "Gr": the Grand Plaza, near Riverside Station.
She showed Mrs. Kim a photo of the building.
The old woman's face lit up, and she said something very fast in Korean that was obviously "Yes!"
The problem was that Riverside Station was in the opposite direction, and it was the last train.
Max and Ella looked at each other.
They could not leave her alone in the middle of the night.
They got off with her at the next stop and called a taxi.
Using the translation app on Ella's phone, which was now working, they explained to Mrs. Kim what they were doing.
She held Ella's hand during the whole journey.
When they arrived at the Grand Plaza, twenty worried Korean tourists were standing outside with the hotel manager and a police officer.
When they saw Mrs. Kim, they cheered.
Her daughter, who spoke good English, ran over and hugged her mother, crying.
The group had been searching for two hours.
Mrs. Kim's daughter insisted on paying for the twins' taxi home.
Before they left, Mrs. Kim took a small silk bag from her handbag and gave it to Ella.
Inside was a jade bracelet.
Her daughter translated her words: "In Korea, we say that a stranger who helps you at night is not a stranger."
Six months later, a letter arrived from Seoul with photos of Mrs. Kim's garden and an invitation.
The twins are saving money for the trip.
And Ella has started learning Korean, just in case.
Dr. Omar Haddad had finished medical school only three months earlier.
Tonight was his first night shift alone on the medical ward at St. Anne's Hospital.
There were thirty-two patients on the ward and only three nurses.
The senior doctor, Dr. Peters, was at home, and Omar could call him only in an emergency.
The most experienced nurse was Grace, a small woman in her sixties who had worked at the hospital for almost forty years.
She gave him a cup of strong tea and a list of patients.
"Don't worry, Doctor," she said. "Most nights are quiet. And if they're not, we'll deal with it together."
Omar tried to smile, but his hands were shaking slightly.
The night was not quiet.
At midnight, a man with a chest infection developed a high fever.
At one o'clock, a young woman who had been admitted with stomach pain became dizzy and fainted in the bathroom.
At two, an elderly man became confused and tried to leave the ward in his pajamas.
Omar ran from bed to bed.
He examined patients, ordered blood tests and wrote prescriptions.
Every decision felt enormous.
What if he made a mistake?
Twice, he picked up the phone to call Dr. Peters, and twice, Grace gently asked him a few questions that helped him to find the answer himself.
At half past three, Grace came to find him.
"Could you look at Mrs. Doyle in bed twelve?" she asked.
"She says she just feels a bit tired, but something isn't right."
Mrs. Doyle was eighty-four and had been admitted with a minor infection.
Her heart rate, blood pressure and temperature were all normal.
She was polite and apologized for waking the doctor.
"I'm fine, dear," she said. "Just tired. You should go and help someone who's really ill."
Omar was exhausted, and there were other patients waiting.
He was about to write "no problems" in her notes when Grace spoke quietly.
"She did the crossword with me every evening this week," she said. "Tonight she couldn't find the words. And look at her hand."
Omar looked more carefully.
Mrs. Doyle was holding her cup with her left hand, and her right hand lay strangely still on the blanket.
When he asked her to squeeze his fingers, her right hand was noticeably weaker.
When he asked her to smile, one side of her mouth did not move properly.
Suddenly, Omar was wide awake.
These were signs of a stroke.
With a stroke, time is critical.
Every minute without treatment, millions of brain cells die.
Omar called Dr. Peters immediately, and this time he did not hesitate.
Within twenty minutes, Mrs. Doyle had a CT scan.
It showed a blood clot in her brain, and she was given medicine to break it up.
For the rest of the night, Omar checked on her every half hour.
By morning, her hand was already a little stronger, and she was able to say his name.
When Dr. Peters arrived at eight, he read the notes and nodded.
"You acted quickly," he said. "Well done."
"It wasn't me," Omar said. "It was Grace. She noticed before anyone else."
At the end of his shift, Omar found Grace in the staff room, putting on her coat.
"How did you know?" he asked. "All her numbers were normal."
Grace thought for a moment.
"Machines measure numbers," she said. "Nurses know people. Mrs. Doyle is the kind of woman who never complains, so when she says she feels tired, you listen."
Three weeks later, Mrs. Doyle left the hospital.
She could walk with a stick, and she was doing the crossword again, although she said it took her longer.
Before she left, she gave Omar a card.
Inside, in shaky handwriting, she had written: "Thank you for listening."
Omar kept it in his pocket for the rest of his career.
Every student in Sofia's class had to make a short documentary about the history of their town.
Sofia, Hugo and Amira chose Hartley Mill, the huge brick factory by the river.
It had been closed for thirty years, and its windows were broken.
In a few months, it would be demolished to make space for new apartments.
At first, their research was disappointing.
The library had a few old photos and a short booklet written in the 1970s, full of dates and numbers.
The mill had opened in 1862, it had employed up to two thousand workers, and it had produced cotton cloth.
It was accurate, but it was boring.
"There are no people in this story," Amira complained.
Then Sofia had an idea.
Her grandfather, Luca, had worked at the mill for twenty-five years.
Grandpa Luca was eighty-four and lived in a small house near the river.
When the three students arrived with their camera, he laughed.
"Nobody has asked me about the mill for thirty years," he said. "Sit down. I'll make some tea."
He talked for two hours.
He had started work at fifteen, sweeping the floors.
Later, he operated the huge looms that wove the cotton.
The noise was so loud that the workers could not hear each other, so they learned to read lips and communicate with their hands.
"We used to have whole conversations without saying a word," he said, and he showed them some of the signs.
The work was hard and sometimes dangerous.
But he also remembered the good times: the brass band, the football team, and the summer trip to the seaside, when the whole factory closed for a week and everyone went together by train.
"It wasn't just a job," he said. "It was a community."
Then he told them something that was not in any book.
In 1972, the owners had wanted to cut the wages of the women who worked at the mill, who were already paid less than the men for the same work.
The women went on strike.
Their leader was a young weaver called Mrs. Walsh.
"At first, most of the men didn't support them," Grandpa Luca admitted.
"Some of us laughed. I'm ashamed of that now."
But after two weeks, the men joined them, and the whole factory stopped.
After a month, the owners gave in.
The women's wages were not cut, and a few years later they received equal pay.
The students were amazed.
They searched old newspapers in the library and found two short articles about the strike, with a photo of Mrs. Walsh standing on a box and speaking to a crowd.
Amira discovered that Mrs. Walsh's daughter still lived in the town, and she agreed to be interviewed, too.
Their documentary was only fifteen minutes long, but it was full of faces, voices and stories.
It showed Grandpa Luca making the old hand signs, and Mrs. Walsh's daughter holding her mother's photo.
When they showed it at school, the room was silent at the end, and then everyone applauded.
The film was shown at the town hall, and then on local television.
Hundreds of former workers and their families contacted the students with their own memories.
The mill was still demolished, but the builders agreed to keep one wall of the old factory and put a plaque on it.
It tells the story of the strike of 1972, and it names Mrs. Walsh.
On the day it was unveiled, Grandpa Luca stood in front of it for a long time.
Then he turned to Sofia and made one of the old hand signs.
She did not need a translation.
It meant "thank you."
Irene was seventy-one, and since her husband had died two years earlier, the evenings had been very quiet.
Her granddaughter Zara had taught her to use a tablet so that they could chat, and Irene had joined a group for people who loved gardening.
That was where she met David.
He said he was an engineer from Norway who was working on an oil platform in the North Sea.
He was a widower, too, and his photos showed a handsome man in his sixties with kind eyes.
He wrote long, beautiful messages about his late wife, his garden and the loneliness of life at sea.
Soon they were messaging every day.
Irene felt happier than she had for years.
She told Zara about him, blushing like a teenager.
Zara was pleased for her grandmother, but something made her uneasy.
"Have you ever talked to him on video?" she asked.
Irene shook her head.
"The internet on the platform is too weak, he says."
After two months, David had a problem.
His bank card had stopped working, he explained, and he needed to pay for a new part for the platform's equipment.
It was only temporary.
Could Irene lend him eight hundred pounds?
He would pay it back as soon as he returned to land.
Irene sent the money that afternoon.
A week later, David needed money again, this time for a doctor.
Then for a ticket home.
Each message was full of love and apologies, and each request was a little bigger than the last.
By the end of the month, Irene had sent him more than three thousand pounds.
When Irene mentioned the money, Zara felt sick.
She had read about romance scams: criminals who create fake profiles, spend months building trust with lonely people, and then invent emergencies to ask for money.
But she knew her grandmother would be hurt and embarrassed if she simply said, "He's a liar."
So she asked questions instead.
Why could an engineer earn a good salary but not pay for his own ticket?
Why did the company not help him?
Why had he never once appeared on video?
Irene had an answer for everything, but her voice became less certain each time.
That evening, Zara did a reverse image search with one of David's photos.
It took less than a minute.
The photo belonged to a doctor in America who had no idea that his pictures were being used.
The same face appeared on dozens of fake profiles, with different names and different stories.
The next day, Zara went to her grandmother's house and showed her the results.
Irene looked at the screen for a long time.
Then she began to cry, not because of the money, but because of the loneliness that had made her believe.
"I feel so foolish," she said.
Zara held her hand.
"You're not foolish, Grandma. These people are professionals. They do this to thousands of people."
They reported the scam to the police and to Irene's bank.
The bank managed to stop the last payment, although the rest of the money was gone.
Irene blocked David, and when he sent a message from a new account, she did not reply.
But the story did not end there.
A few weeks later, Irene gave a talk at her local library about what had happened to her.
Forty people came, and afterwards, three of them admitted that they were being targeted in the same way.
Irene started a small group where older people could learn about online safety and, just as importantly, meet each other face-to-face.
"The best protection against loneliness," she told them, "is real friends."
Nia and Oscar had been friends since their first week at university.
Nia studied computer science, and Oscar studied economics, but they had the same dream: to start their own company.
In their final year, they came up with an idea.
Every evening, supermarkets throw away huge amounts of food that is still perfectly good, simply because it will be out of date the next day.
Their app, called FreshLeft, would show shoppers which items were available at a discount in nearby shops, so that they could buy them before closing time.
The shops would reduce waste and earn some money, customers would save money, and less food would end up in the bin.
For six months, they worked on FreshLeft every evening and every weekend.
Nia wrote the software, and Oscar visited shops to persuade the managers to take part.
Most of them said no, but a few agreed to try.
By the spring, twelve shops in their city were using the app, and more than two thousand people had downloaded it.
The results were encouraging.
In the shops that used FreshLeft, food waste fell by about a third.
But they had a problem: they were almost out of money.
To grow, they needed investors.
They were invited to present their idea to a group of investors, led by a woman called Ms. Varga, who had helped many famous startups.
They would have ten minutes.
If the pitch went well, FreshLeft could expand to the whole country.
The night before, they had their first serious argument.
Oscar wanted to make the numbers look bigger.
"Everyone exaggerates in these meetings," he said. "Let's say we have five thousand users, not two. And let's say we'll be in a hundred shops by the end of the year."
Nia refused.
"If we lie now, we'll have to keep lying," she said. "And they'll find out. These people check everything."
Oscar was furious.
"Do you want this to work or not?" he shouted, and he left the apartment.
Nia did not sleep that night.
The next morning, Oscar arrived at the meeting five minutes before it started.
They did not speak.
When they walked into the room, Nia saw that he was holding their original presentation, with the real numbers.
Oscar spoke first.
He explained the problem of food waste, and Nia demonstrated the app.
Then they showed their results: twelve shops, two thousand users, and a thirty percent reduction in waste.
"These numbers are small," Oscar admitted. "But they're real, and they're growing every week."
Ms. Varga asked difficult questions for twenty minutes.
How would they compete with bigger companies?
What would happen if supermarkets built their own apps?
Nia and Oscar did not know every answer, and they said so.
A week later, Ms. Varga called them.
She was willing to invest, but she wanted them to work with an experienced adviser.
"Most people who pitch to me exaggerate," she said. "You two didn't. That's rare, and it's why I trust you."
After the call, Oscar was quiet for a moment.
"I'm sorry about that night," he said. "I was scared. I thought the truth wasn't enough."
"It was enough," said Nia. "It was just small."
Two years later, FreshLeft was used in more than a thousand shops.
The number was real.
In September, the head teacher of Northfield School made an unusual announcement.
The school had been chosen for a national pilot program.
For one term, every student in year ten would have an AI tutor on their laptop, which would help them with maths, science and English.
The tutor, called Max, would give each student exercises at exactly the right level, check their work instantly and explain their mistakes.
The students were excited.
Some teachers were less enthusiastic.
Ms. Park, who had taught English for twenty years, listened with her arms crossed.
"So what will we do?" she asked at the staff meeting. "Just sit and watch?"
At first, Max was a huge success.
It never got tired or impatient, and it was available at any time of day or night.
Ella, who had always struggled with maths, found that she could finally ask "stupid" questions without feeling embarrassed.
Her marks improved for the first time in years.
But her friend Diego soon discovered a problem.
If he asked Max the right way, it would simply give him the answers.
Within a week, half the class knew the trick.
Homework that used to take an hour now took five minutes, and the average score went up dramatically.
The company that made Max was delighted with the results.
It published a press release that described Northfield as "the school of the future."
Ella felt uncomfortable.
She used Max properly, to understand her mistakes, and she knew how much work that took.
When she saw Diego finish a whole week of homework during one lunch break, she wondered whether her friends were learning anything at all.
Ms. Park was suspicious.
In November, she gave the class a surprise test: an essay written by hand, in the classroom, with no laptops.
The topic was simple: "Describe a person who changed your life."
The results were a disaster.
Many students who had received top marks from Max for weeks could barely write a paragraph.
Their sentences were short and confused, and some of them just stared at the paper.
Diego handed in a page with three lines on it.
The next day, Ms. Park returned the essays without any marks.
Instead, she wrote a single question on the board: "Who has been doing your thinking?"
The room was silent.
Then Priya raised her hand.
"Max was doing it," she said quietly. "At least, for some of us."
Ms. Park nodded.
"Thank you for being honest," she said. "Now let's talk about what we do next."
Ms. Park did not ban Max.
Instead, she organized a class debate: "Should AI tutors replace teachers?"
Ella and Priya argued that AI was patient, cheap and available to everyone, even students whose parents could not afford private lessons.
Diego, surprisingly, argued against it.
"Max did my homework," he admitted, "but it didn't care whether I learned anything. A teacher notices when you're pretending."
The discussion lasted two lessons.
By the end, most of the class agreed on a compromise.
Max was useful for practice and for explaining mistakes, but it should not give answers, and important work should be discussed with a human teacher.
Ms. Park wrote their ideas in a letter to the head teacher.
In January, the school sent its report to the government.
It included the students' letter and the results of Ms. Park's test.
The company changed Max so that it asked students questions instead of simply giving answers.
The pilot continued, but with teachers in charge.
In June, Ms. Park gave the class another handwritten essay.
This time, Diego wrote four pages about his grandfather, who had taught him to fish.
It was not perfect, but every word was his own.
At the bottom of the last page, Ms. Park wrote in red ink: "Now I can hear you."
On Monday evening, the news reported that nurses at St. Mark's Hospital would go on strike the following week.
They wanted higher wages and more staff.
Hospital managers said there was no money.
The government said it was "disappointed" and urged both sides to keep talking.
For Jonah, who was sixteen, it was just another news story.
But at the dinner table, he realized that it was going to be much more than that.
His mother, Clare, was a nurse at St. Mark's.
His father, Dave, drove a bus, and his route passed right in front of the hospital.
"So you're really going to do it?" Dave asked.
"Yes," said Clare. "We voted last week. Ninety percent of us said yes."
Dave shook his head.
"What about the patients? What about the people waiting for operations?"
Clare put down her fork.
She explained that emergency care would continue during the strike, and that nurses would still work in intensive care and the emergency department.
"We're not doing this because we want to," she said. "We're doing it because patients are already in danger."
"There aren't enough of us. Last night I had fourteen patients on my own. Nobody can look after fourteen people properly."
Dave was quiet for a moment.
Then he said, "Everyone is tired. I work long hours, too. But I can't just stop driving when I'm unhappy."
"Maybe you should," said Clare, and the argument began.
Jonah hated it when his parents argued.
Over the next few days, the atmosphere at home became tense.
At school, the strike was a hot topic, too.
Some of his friends said the nurses were heroes.
Others repeated what their parents had said: that the strike was selfish and dangerous.
Jonah did not know what he thought.
His grandmother, Rose, had been a nurse for forty years.
One afternoon, he went to visit her and asked her opinion.
She thought carefully before she answered.
"There were strikes in my time, too," she said. "I never went on one. I felt that my duty was to my patients."
She paused.
"But I also watched many good nurses leave the job because they were exhausted. Sometimes I wonder whether I was wrong."
On the first day of the strike, Dave's bus stopped in front of the hospital as usual.
Outside the gates, about two hundred nurses were standing in the cold, holding signs.
One of them said: "Tired nurses make mistakes. Safe staffing saves lives."
Dave saw Clare in the crowd.
She looked tired and cold, but determined.
An old man got on the bus with a walking stick.
He had just visited his wife in the hospital.
As he sat down, he looked out of the window at the nurses and said to Dave, "They looked after my wife like she was their own mother. Whatever they want, they deserve it."
At the end of his shift, Dave did something unexpected.
He bought twenty cups of coffee from the café across the road and carried them to the picket line.
When Clare saw him, she did not say anything at first.
Then she laughed and took a cup.
"Does this mean you agree with me?" she asked.
"It means I understand you better," he said. "I'm still not sure a strike is the right answer. But I'm sure you're not doing it for yourselves."
The strike lasted four days.
In the end, the hospital agreed to hire more nurses and to increase pay a little, although not as much as the union had asked for.
At dinner that evening, the family talked about it calmly, and Jonah realized something.
His parents had not really changed their opinions.
But they had listened to each other, and that seemed more important.
In 2001, the students at Brookfield School had buried a time capsule under the tree in the playground.
It was a metal box containing letters, photos and objects that showed what life was like at the time.
A small sign next to the tree said: "Do not open until 2026."
Nadia had been one of those students.
She had been ten years old, and she remembered writing her letter very carefully in her best handwriting.
Now, twenty-five years later, she was a teacher at Brookfield herself, and she had been asked to organize the opening ceremony.
On a sunny morning in June, the whole school gathered in the playground.
Dozens of former students had come back, some with their own children.
Two teenagers dug up the box, which was dirty and a little rusty but still closed.
When Nadia opened it, everyone moved closer.
Inside, wrapped in plastic, there were dozens of envelopes and some strange objects.
There was a CD of pop music, a newspaper from 2001, a small toy robot and a mobile phone that was about as thick as a brick.
The children in the audience laughed at the phone.
"Where's the screen?" one of them asked.
The most interesting part was the letters.
Each student had been asked to write about their life and to make predictions about the world in 2026.
Nadia read some of them aloud, and the audience laughed and clapped.
Some predictions had been surprisingly accurate.
One boy had written that "everybody will carry a small computer in their pocket."
Another student had predicted that people would watch films on the internet instead of buying them.
Others were completely wrong.
Several students had been certain that cars would fly by now, and one girl had predicted that school would be cancelled forever and replaced by robots.
"Not yet," said Nadia, and the teachers laughed loudest of all.
Nadia found her own letter and read it quietly.
She had wanted to become a vet, to live in a big city and to have a horse.
None of it had happened.
But at the end, she had written: "I hope I am happy and I hope I am kind."
She smiled.
She thought she probably was.
At the bottom of the box, there was one more envelope, older and thicker than the others.
It said: "From Mr. Holt, class teacher. To the teacher who opens this box."
Mr. Holt had been Nadia's teacher when she was ten.
He was the reason she had become a teacher.
He had been patient, funny and endlessly curious, and he had died a few years earlier.
Her hands shook slightly as she opened the letter.
"Dear teacher," it began. "I don't know who you are, but I imagine you are tired. Teaching is hard work."
"Some days, you will feel that nothing you do makes a difference."
"But somewhere in your class, there is a child who will remember one thing you said for the rest of their life."
"You will probably never know which child, or which words. That is the strange magic of this job."
Nadia could not read the rest aloud.
Another teacher had to finish it for her.
Afterwards, several former students came to tell her their own memories of Mr. Holt.
Each of them remembered something different he had said.
That afternoon, Nadia's class began preparing a new time capsule, to be opened in 2051.
Her students wrote letters and made predictions.
One boy, Toby, wrote that people would live on Mars.
Nadia also wrote a letter, addressed "To the teacher who opens this box."
She did not tell anyone what she wrote, but she put it at the very bottom, just like Mr. Holt.
After her grandfather's funeral, Mia helped her mother to clear out his house.
Grandpa Joe had lived there for sixty years, and the attic was full of boxes: old photos, letters, tools and newspapers that he had never thrown away.
It was dusty, slow work, and every object brought back a memory.
In a small wooden box at the bottom of a cupboard, Mia found an envelope.
It was addressed to "Frank Mitchell, Toronto, Canada," and it had a stamp on it, but it had never been posted.
The date on the back was 1985.
"Frank?" Mia asked her mother. "Who's Frank?"
Her mother looked surprised.
"Your grandfather's younger brother. They had a terrible argument when I was a child, and Frank moved to Canada. They never spoke again."
"What was the argument about?"
"I never really knew. Something about the family business. Your grandfather refused to talk about it."
Mia opened the envelope carefully.
Inside was a single page in her grandfather's neat handwriting.
"Dear Frank," it began. "I have started this letter many times, and each time I have thrown it away."
"I was wrong about the shop, and I was wrong to say what I said."
"I was angry and proud, and I have regretted it every day since you left."
"I miss my brother. If you can forgive me, please write back."
Mia read it twice, and then she started to cry.
Her grandfather had written the letter and put a stamp on it, but he had never found the courage to send it.
For forty years, it had waited in a box, and now it was too late.
Or was it?
That night, Mia could not sleep.
Frank would be very old now, if he was still alive, but it was possible.
She searched online for Frank Mitchell in Toronto.
There were dozens of people with that name.
Then she remembered that her grandfather's family had owned a bakery, and she searched for "Mitchell bakery Toronto."
The first result was a small family bakery that had opened in 1986.
On its website, there was a photo of the founder: an old man with a white beard who looked remarkably like her grandfather.
Under the photo, it said: "Frank Mitchell, still baking at 86."
Mia called the bakery the next evening.
