A woman answered, and after a long explanation, she went to find her father.
The man who came to the phone had a slow, deep voice.
When Mia explained who she was, there was a long silence.
"Joe's granddaughter," he said finally.
"Is he…?"
Mia told him gently that her grandfather had died a month earlier.
Then she read him the letter.
When she finished, she could hear that he was crying.
"I wrote to him, too," Frank said. "Three times. But I never sent them. I was too proud. We were both such fools."
He paused.
"I wish I had picked up the phone just once. Just once."
In the summer, Mia and her mother flew to Toronto.
They met Frank, his daughter and his grandchildren, relatives they had never known existed.
Frank showed them the bakery and gave them bread made from the same recipe his mother had used seventy years earlier.
Before they left, Frank gave Mia the three letters he had written to his brother.
"Put them with his," he said. "They belong together."
Now the four letters are kept in the same small wooden box, and Mia has made herself a promise.
She never lets an argument with someone she loves last longer than a day.
Chloe was nineteen and had just finished school when she decided to spend three months as a volunteer in a village in the Andes, high in the mountains of Peru.
She had paid an organization to arrange everything, and she would teach English at the village school.
She arrived full of enthusiasm.
Her suitcase was full of colorful books, games and posters, and her notebook was full of plans.
She would change the way English was taught, organize a sports day and perhaps even raise money for a new school library.
The village was beautiful but poor.
Most families grew potatoes and kept llamas, and the nearest town, Cusco, was four hours away by bus.
The altitude gave Chloe headaches for the first week, and at night it was freezing.
The school had one teacher, Rosa Quispe, who had taught there for twenty-two years.
She taught thirty children of different ages in a single room, in two languages: Spanish and Quechua, the language most families spoke at home.
Rosa welcomed Chloe politely, but she did not seem very excited about her ideas.
When Chloe suggested moving the desks into groups and playing loud games, Rosa just said, "Let's see."
Chloe was disappointed.
She thought Rosa was old-fashioned.
In her second week, Chloe decided to do something special.
She took photos of every child and put them on a big poster on the classroom wall, with the words "Our Wonderful Class" in English.
She also posted some of the photos online so that her friends at home could see her work.
The next morning, three parents came to the school.
They were upset.
Nobody had asked them for permission to photograph their children, and one father was particularly angry that his daughter's picture was on the internet.
Chloe did not understand everything they said, because they were speaking Quechua, but she understood their faces.
She felt terrible.
That evening, Rosa invited Chloe to her house for dinner.
Chloe expected to be criticized, but Rosa was kind.
She explained that many families in the village had had bad experiences with visitors.
Tourists often took photos of the children as if they were part of the scenery, and then disappeared.
"Every year, a new volunteer comes with new ideas," Rosa said, "and every year, they leave after three months. The children get attached, and then they lose another friend."
Chloe was silent for a long time.
Then she asked a question that she should have asked on the first day.
"What do you actually need?"
Rosa smiled for the first time.
"Somebody to help the older children who are behind in reading," she said. "Quietly. Every day."
Chloe apologized to the parents, with Rosa translating, and she deleted the photos.
For the rest of her stay, she did exactly what Rosa had asked.
Every afternoon, she sat with four older children and read with them, slowly and patiently, in Spanish.
She also learned some Quechua, and the children laughed at her terrible pronunciation.
It was not the dramatic change she had imagined.
But by the end of the three months, one boy, Mateo, who had hardly been able to read, finished his first book.
He read the last page aloud to the whole class, and everyone clapped.
When Chloe went home, she did not post any photos.
Instead, she wrote a long email to the organization, suggesting that volunteers should stay longer, learn the local language and ask teachers what they need before they arrive.
Two years later, she went back to the village for a whole year.
This time, she brought no posters.
The invitation arrived by email on a Monday morning: "Westbrook High, twenty-year reunion. Saturday, June 14th."
Grace read it twice and closed it.
She was thirty-eight, a successful architect with two children and a busy life.
She had not been back to her hometown for years, and she was not sure she wanted to go.
The reason was Liam.
At school, they had been inseparable.
They sat together in every lesson, spent every weekend at each other's houses and planned to go to the same university.
Then, in their final year, something happened.
Grace had been chosen for a scholarship that Liam had wanted desperately.
A few days later, she heard from another student that Liam had called her a liar and a cheat behind her back.
She never spoke to him again.
In the end, her friend Rania persuaded her to go.
The school hall looked smaller than she remembered.
Old classmates hugged, laughed and showed each other photos of their children.
Everyone seemed to have fond memories of their school days.
Some had changed completely; others looked exactly the same, only with grey hair.
Their old history teacher, Mr. Ellis, gave a short speech that made everyone laugh.
Then Grace saw him.
Liam was standing near the door, holding a glass of lemonade and looking as nervous as she felt.
For a moment, neither of them moved.
Then he walked over.
"Hi, Grace," he said. "It's been a long time."
They went outside and sat on the steps where they used to eat lunch.
At first, they talked about safe things: jobs, children, the town.
Liam was a teacher now, and he had a daughter who was eleven.
Then, suddenly, he said, "I've wanted to ask you something for twenty years. Why did you stop talking to me?"
Grace was shocked.
"You know why," she said. "You told people I was a liar. That I cheated to get the scholarship."
Liam stared at her.
"I never said that," he said quietly.
"I was jealous, yes. I was angry with myself for a week. But I never said anything bad about you. Who told you that?"
When Grace told him the name, Liam closed his eyes.
It was a boy who had also applied for the scholarship, and who had been known for spreading rumors.
"He told me you'd said I wasn't good enough," Liam said. "I thought that was why you were avoiding me."
For a long time, neither of them spoke.
Twenty years of friendship had been lost because of a lie that neither of them had checked.
"I wish I had just asked you," Grace said finally, acknowledging her mistake.
"Me too," said Liam. "I was too proud."
They sat on the steps until the reunion was over and the caretaker came to lock the doors.
They talked about everything that had happened in two decades: university, jobs, marriages, the deaths of parents, the births of children.
It felt strange and wonderful at the same time, like finding a book you loved as a child and discovering that it still made you laugh.
The old affection was still there.
Grace and Liam now live three hundred kilometers apart, but they speak every week.
Last summer, their families spent a holiday together by the sea, and their children became friends immediately.
When people ask Grace what she learned from the whole story, she always gives the same answer.
"If someone tells you that your friend has hurt you," she says, "ask your friend first."
At six o'clock on Friday evening, the university's engineering hall was packed with two hundred students for the annual hackathon.
The rules were simple.
Each team would have exactly forty-eight hours to design and build a piece of software that solved a real problem, and on Sunday evening they would present their work to a panel of judges.
This year's challenge came from Mrs. Okonkwo, the director of Hillside Food Bank.
She explained that local supermarkets threw away tons of perfectly good food every week, often because it was close to its sell-by date.
The shops were happy to donate it, but they usually called at the last minute, and the food bank rarely had volunteers available to collect it in time.
"Every week, food that could feed a hundred families ends up in the bin," she said. "Help us fix that."
Anjali, a third-year computer science student, had put together a team of four.
Leo was the most talented programmer she knew, although he was also the loudest, and he tended to dominate every discussion.
Farah was a design student who could make any screen look elegant.
The fourth member, Jun, was a first-year student whom nobody knew well.
He had signed up alone, and the organizers had placed him with them at random.
They spent the first two hours brainstorming.
Leo was keen on an ambitious idea: an app that used artificial intelligence to predict which shops would have surplus food, with live maps, notifications and a points system to reward volunteers.
He had already started drawing the interface on the whiteboard.
Twice, Jun began to say something, and twice Leo spoke over him without noticing.
The third time, Anjali raised her hand.
"Sorry, Leo. Can we just hear what Jun wants to say?"
Leo looked surprised, then slightly embarrassed.
Jun cleared his throat.
"My grandmother volunteers at a food bank," he said quietly. "Most of the volunteers are over seventy. They don't use apps. But they all have mobile phones, and they all read text messages."
Jun's idea was almost embarrassingly simple, but it was far more sensible for people who were not comfortable with technology.
When a shop had food to donate, a staff member would fill in a short online form.
The system would then send a text message to the nearest available volunteers, and the first person to reply "YES" would get the job.
Everyone else would receive a second message saying that the collection had been taken.
Leo was not convinced at first.
"It's hardly revolutionary," he complained. "The judges want to see something exciting."
"The judges aren't going to use it," Anjali replied. "Mrs. Okonkwo's volunteers are."
In the end, they agreed on a compromise: Jun's text system at the center, with Leo's map as an extra feature for the food bank staff.
By three o'clock on Sunday morning, the prototype was almost ready.
Farah was asleep under a table, Anjali was on her fifth coffee, and Leo was testing the database.
Then his screen went black.
The server they had been using had crashed, and when it restarted, twelve hours of work had disappeared.
Leo put his head in his hands and swore. It was a nightmare.
Jun, who had been working silently and independently in the corner, looked up.
"I made a backup every hour," he said. "Just in case. We've lost about forty minutes."
For a moment, nobody spoke.
Then Leo stood up, walked across the room and shook Jun's hand very seriously.
"You," he said, "are a genius."
On Sunday evening, twenty-four teams presented their projects.
Many of them were technically brilliant.
One team had built a robot that sorted food by its expiry date, and another had designed a virtual reality game about hunger.
When it was their turn, Anjali asked Jun to explain the idea, since it was essentially his.
He was visibly nervous, but his explanation was clear and precise.
Then, instead of a video, they gave a live demonstration.
Anjali filled in the form as if she were a supermarket manager, and a moment later, Mrs. Okonkwo's phone, which they had borrowed that morning, buzzed in her hand.
She read the message aloud, typed "YES," and the audience applauded.
They did not win, which was a slight disappointment.
First prize went to the robot, which the judges described as "the most innovative project in the history of the competition."
But the team came second, and after the ceremony, Mrs. Okonkwo came to find them.
"The robot is wonderful," she said. "But I can't afford a robot. I can afford text messages. Could I start using your system next week?"
Six months later, Hillside Food Bank was collecting almost twice as much food as before, and three other food banks in the region had asked to use the system.
The four students still met every few weeks to maintain and upgrade it.
At one of these meetings, Leo admitted that he had learned more from the hackathon than from any course.
"Mostly," he said, looking at Jun, "that the best idea in the room doesn't always come from the loudest person."
Jun smiled, but he did not say anything.
He did not need to.
Zoe Mitchell had been working in the marketing department of Brightwell, a company that made kitchen equipment, for three years.
She was talented, ambitious and occasionally a little too quick to say what she thought.
In January, the company appointed a new head of marketing, Trevor Holt, who had previously worked in finance.
Trevor was a decent, hard-working man, but he was not a natural communicator, and his first weeks had been awkward.
On his first Friday, Trevor gave a presentation to the whole department about his plans for the year.
It lasted seventy minutes and contained eighty-four slides, most of them full of tables of numbers.
Several people fell asleep, and one colleague was practically snoring.
Trevor did not seem to notice, and at one point he referred to the company's best-selling product by the wrong name.
After the presentation, Trevor sent an email to all four hundred employees in the company, thanking them for their attention and attaching his slides.
Zoe read it at her desk and, still irritated, decided to forward it to her friend Amira in the design team with a comment.
"Honestly," she wrote, "that was the most boring hour of my life. Does he even know what we sell? Eighty-four slides! I nearly died."
She pressed "send" and went to make a coffee.
When she came back, her screen was full of new messages.
Some colleagues had sent laughing faces.
Others had written, "Zoe, did you mean to send this to everyone?"
Her stomach turned to ice.
It was, she would later admit, the most humiliating moment of her career.
Instead of pressing "forward," she had pressed "reply all."
Her comment had gone to the entire company, including the chief executive and, of course, Trevor Holt himself.
Zoe tried to recall the message, but it was too late: virtually everyone had already opened it.
She considered pretending that her account had been hacked.
She considered going home sick and never coming back.
For ten minutes, she sat frozen, reading the email again and again, as if the words might change.
Her phone buzzed constantly with messages from colleagues, some sympathetic and some openly delighted by the scandal.
Then she remembered something her first manager had told her years earlier.
"Everyone makes mistakes," Kate had said. "What people remember is how you deal with them."
Zoe took a deep breath, stood up and walked to Trevor's office.
The door was open.
He was sitting at his desk, staring at his screen.
"Mr. Holt," she said, "I'd like to apologize for my email. It was rude and unprofessional, and it was meant to be private, but that's no excuse. I should never have written it."
"It was a genuine mistake, but the words were mine, and I take responsibility for them," she added.
Trevor looked at her for a long time.
She could not tell whether he was angry or hurt.
"Thank you for coming to tell me in person," he said at last. "Most people would have hidden."
Then, to her surprise, he smiled slightly.
"The worst part is that you're partly right," he said. "I spent twenty years in finance. I know numbers, but I've never been good at presenting. Eighty-four slides was a mistake."
He paused.
"And I did get the product name wrong, didn't I?"
Zoe nodded, embarrassed.
"Then perhaps you could help me," Trevor said. "I have to present to the board next month. I'd like it to be a lot shorter."
Zoe did not escape completely.

The human resources department gave her a formal warning, and she had to attend a short course on professional communication, which she found both embarrassing and, to her annoyance, genuinely useful.
For weeks, colleagues she hardly knew joked about slides whenever she passed them in the corridor.
Some of the jokes were hilarious, and slowly she learned to laugh at herself.
But she also kept her promise to Trevor.
Together, they reduced his board presentation to twelve slides, with more pictures, fewer numbers and a short story about a customer at the beginning.
It was a success, the board was genuinely impressed, and afterwards the chief executive asked Trevor who had helped him.
A year later, when a senior position became available in the team, Trevor recommended Zoe for it.
"You made a stupid mistake," he told her, "and then you handled it better than most senior managers I've known. That tells me more about you than a perfect email ever could."
Zoe still checks every email twice before she presses "send."
She has also become a little more humble about her own opinions, and a lot more careful about where she shares them.
Helen Marsh hated flying, and she hated delays even more.
She was a management consultant who spent half her life in airports, and she had a reputation, among colleagues and airline staff alike, for being extremely demanding.
On a Thursday in February, she boarded Flight 214 from Dublin to Boston with a laptop full of slides for a presentation the following morning.
The contract she hoped to win was worth two million dollars.
Two hours into the flight, the captain made an announcement.
A passenger had become seriously ill, and the plane would make an emergency landing at the nearest available airport.
Forty minutes later, they touched down in a snowstorm at Egilsstaðir, a small town in eastern Iceland with a population of about two and a half thousand people.
An ambulance was waiting on the runway.
The sick passenger, an elderly man, was taken to hospital, and everyone on board applauded when they heard later that he would recover.
Then came the bad news.
During the landing, engineers had detected a technical fault in one of the plane's systems, and a replacement part would have to be flown in from Reykjavik.
Because of the storm, it could not arrive until the next afternoon.
Two hundred passengers were stranded in a town with one small hotel, which was already full.
Helen marched straight to the airline's desk in the tiny terminal, where a young woman called Ingrid was trying to calm a crowd of exhausted travelers.
"This is completely unacceptable," Helen said. "I have a meeting in Boston at nine o'clock tomorrow morning. What exactly are you going to do about it?"
Ingrid apologized for the inconvenience and explained, patiently, that the airline would provide meal vouchers and accommodation.
"Accommodation where?" Helen demanded. "You've just told us the hotel is full."
Ingrid hesitated.
The honest answer was that she did not yet know.
But while Helen had been complaining, something remarkable had been happening in the town.
Word had spread on local radio and social media, and residents had begun arriving at the airport in cars and four-wheel drives, offering spare beds, sofas and floors.
The school opened its gym, and a woman from the bakery arrived with two hundred cinnamon rolls.
Helen was assigned to a farmer called Björn and his eighty-year-old mother, Gudrun.
She was horrified.
She had not slept in a stranger's house since she was a child, and the farmhouse was forty minutes away along a road that had virtually disappeared under the snow.
She spent the journey composing, in her head, a furious letter to the airline's chief executive.
Gudrun spoke almost no English, but she did not need to.
She took Helen's wet coat, sat her down beside a wood stove and put a bowl of lamb soup in front of her.
Björn phoned his cousin, who knew someone at the hospital, to find out how the sick passenger was doing.
Then he lent Helen his own bedroom and slept on the sofa.
When she tried to pay him, he looked genuinely offended.
"You are a guest," he said simply.
At midnight, Helen was still awake, answering emails and trying to rearrange her meeting by video call.
Björn knocked on the door.
"Come outside," he said. "Quickly. Put on your coat."
She almost refused.
The storm had passed, and the sky was completely clear.
Above the white fields, enormous curtains of green light were moving slowly across the stars, twisting and folding as if they were alive.
Helen had seen photographs of the northern lights, but nothing had prepared her for the real thing.
She stood in the snow for an hour, her laptop forgotten, while Gudrun watched from the doorway, wrapped in a blanket, and smiled.
The replacement part arrived the next afternoon, and Flight 214 finally landed in Boston twenty-six hours late.
Helen's clients had agreed to postpone the meeting, and to her surprise, the presentation went better than she could have hoped.
She began by telling them about the night in Egilsstaðir.
She won the contract.
Back home, she wrote two letters.

The first was a formal complaint to the airline, pointing out, quite reasonably, that passengers had been given almost no information for four hours and that the compensation offered did not meet the legal requirements.
The airline later accepted her points and paid every passenger in full.
The second letter was to the people of Egilsstaðir, and it was published in the local newspaper.
"I arrived in your town as a very angry woman," she wrote. "I left as a grateful one. Thank you for reminding me that the most important things in life are never on the schedule."
In the autumn of 1991, the Harcourt Emerald disappeared from a locked cabinet in Harcourt Hall, a grand manor house in the Welsh countryside.
The stone had belonged to the Harcourt family for two hundred years, and it was insured for two million pounds.
There was no sign of a break-in.
Only three people had been in the house that night: the elderly Lady Harcourt, her nephew Julian, and the housekeeper, Nesta Lloyd, who had worked for the family for thirty years.
Suspicion fell almost immediately on Nesta.
She had a key to the cabinet, she had financial problems after her husband's death, and she had been seen near the library late that evening.
The police searched her cottage twice and questioned her for hours.
They never found the emerald, and she was never charged, but in a small village, that did not matter.
People stopped speaking to her in the shop, and she lost her job.
The young detective who had worked on the case was called Gwen Parry.
She had never believed that Nesta was guilty, but her senior officers had ignored her doubts, and the case was eventually closed.
Thirty years later, Gwen was retired and living alone with two cats, but the Harcourt case still bothered her.
She kept a copy of the file in a box under her bed.
Then, one spring morning, a young man called Theo Bright knocked on her door.
He produced a popular podcast about unsolved crimes, and he wanted to make a series about the missing emerald.
Gwen was suspicious at first.
"Why this case?" she asked him. "There are hundreds of unsolved crimes."
"Because my grandmother grew up in Llanfair," Theo said. "She always said the wrong person was blamed."
She had seen too many journalists who were more interested in drama than in truth.
But when Theo told her that Nesta Lloyd was still alive, aged ninety-one, and that she had agreed to be interviewed, Gwen fetched her coat.
Nesta lived in a care home near the coast.
"I've waited a long time for someone to ask me properly," she said when they arrived.
She was frail, but her memory was sharp, and she told them the same story she had told the police in 1991.
That night, she said, she had gone to the library to close the windows before a storm.
The cabinet had been locked.
On her way back, she had smelled cigarette smoke in the corridor, which had surprised her, because Lady Harcourt had banned smoking in the house.
Gwen checked the old file that evening.
In 1991, a cigarette end had been found beneath the library window and kept as evidence, but nobody had considered it important.
Julian Harcourt, the nephew, had told the police that he did not smoke.
Nobody had checked whether that was true.
Theo tracked down Dennis Ward, a gardener who had worked at Harcourt Hall in the nineties.
The old man laughed when they asked him about Julian.
"Didn't smoke? He smoked like a chimney," he said. "He used to hide behind the greenhouse so his aunt wouldn't see. And he was always short of money. Gambling, people said."
Gwen contacted her former colleagues, and after months of persuasion, the police agreed to reopen the case.
The cigarette end, which had been stored in a plastic bag for three decades, was sent for DNA analysis, a technique that had barely existed in 1991.
The result matched Julian Harcourt, who was now seventy and living in a villa in the south of France.
"Thirty years," Gwen said quietly when Theo read her the email. "Thirty years, and the answer was sitting in a plastic bag."
When detectives confronted him with the evidence, Julian finally confessed.
He had owed a fortune to a gambling club, and he had taken the emerald from the cabinet using his aunt's key, which he had copied weeks earlier.
He had sold it secretly to a dealer in Amsterdam, and he had allowed the housekeeper to be blamed.
Because of the time that had passed, he could no longer be prosecuted for the theft, but he could be sued, and the story made headlines around the world.
Gwen drove to the care home herself to tell Nesta the news.
The old woman listened in silence, and then she began to cry.
"For thirty years, people looked at me as if I were a thief," she said. "My own sister believed it. Thank you for not giving up."
The following month, the village held a small ceremony in Nesta's honor, and dozens of people who had once ignored her came to apologize.
She died peacefully that winter, with her name finally cleared.
For twenty-five years, Café Moreno had stood on the corner of Station Road, serving strong coffee, homemade cakes and conversation.
Rosa and Luis Moreno knew virtually all of their customers by name, and many of them had been coming every morning for decades.
It was not a fashionable place, but it was warm, and it was theirs.
In January, a large sign appeared in the window of the empty bank opposite: "Brew and Co. Opening soon."
Brew and Co. was an international chain with more than three thousand branches.
When it opened in March, with free coffee for a week, bright lights and a queue down the street, Luis stood at his window and watched in silence.
By the end of April, Café Moreno's income had fallen by almost a third.
Their daughter, Elena, had just finished a business degree.
One Sunday evening, she sat her parents down at the kitchen table with a laptop and a pot of coffee.
"Let's look at this properly," she said. "No emotions. Just the options."
Luis muttered that it was impossible to discuss the café without emotions, but he sat down anyway.
The first option was to compete on price.
They could reduce the cost of a coffee, introduce loyalty cards and offer discounts to students.
But Elena's calculations showed that their profit margins were already tiny, and that a price war against a company with thousands of branches was one they would almost certainly lose.
The second option was more surprising.
A week earlier, a representative of Brew and Co. had visited the café and offered to buy the lease.
The sum was generous: enough for Rosa and Luis to retire comfortably, with a decent income for life.
"On the plus side, you'd be financially secure for the rest of your lives," Elena said carefully. "The main drawback is obvious. Café Moreno would disappear."
Rosa's eyes filled with tears, and for a while nobody spoke.
The third option was the one Elena preferred, although it was also the riskiest.
Instead of trying to be a cheaper version of Brew and Co., Café Moreno should become something the chain could never be.
"They have efficiency," she said. "We have personality. They sell coffee. We sell a place where people know you."
She proposed a series of innovative changes.
Luis, who had worked on a coffee farm in Colombia as a young man, would start roasting their own beans in a small machine at the back.
Rosa's famous cakes, which had always been available only in the morning, would be sold all day.
And in the evenings, when the café was usually closed, they would host events: a book club, language exchanges and an open-mic night for local musicians.
Luis was skeptical.
"Weighing it up, it's a lot of work for two people in their sixties," he said.
"Having said that," Rosa replied, looking at him, "what would you do if we retired? Watch television?"
Luis laughed for the first time in weeks.
They agreed to try for one year, and to reconsider the offer if it failed.
The first months were exhausting and financially risky.
Luis burned three batches of beans before he got the roasting right, and the first book club attracted only four people, one of whom fell asleep.
But slowly, word spread.
Elena handled the publicity, and her campaign on social media was modest but remarkably effective.

A local food blogger wrote about the "best coffee in the city, roasted by a man who talks to his machine," and the open-mic nights became so popular that people had to stand outside and listen through the windows.
The café also became something its owners had not planned: a refuge for people who were lonely.
Mrs. Harris, a widow who lived alone above the chemist's, came every afternoon to play chess with Mr. Okoro, a retired engineer.
Students did their homework at the big table by the window, and nobody asked them to leave when their coffee was finished.
By the following spring, Café Moreno's income was significantly higher than it had been before Brew and Co. arrived.
The chain was still busy across the road, serving commuters who wanted a quick coffee on their way to the station, and Elena realized that the two businesses were not really competing at all.
They were selling different things.
One evening, the manager of Brew and Co. came over for the open-mic night, sat at the back and ordered one of Rosa's cakes.
"Don't tell my boss," he said to Luis with a grin, "but your coffee is better than ours."
Luis poured him a second cup, on the house.
Hollins Park was an ordinary state school on the edge of the city, and nobody expected its debating team to go very far.
The club had been started two years earlier by Mr. Petrov, a history teacher who believed that every student should learn to argue well.
"Not louder," he liked to say. "Better."
This year's team had three members.
Chloe Dunn was confident and quick, a natural performer who could make an audience laugh within seconds.
Isaac Mensah was calm and logical, and he always had the right statistics.
The third member, Tanvir Hossain, was the most brilliant thinker Mr. Petrov had ever taught, and also the shyest.
In his first debate, he had been so nervous that he had forgotten his entire speech and sat down after thirty seconds.
To everyone's surprise, including their own, Hollins Park won the regional competition and then the national semi-final.
In the final, they would face St. Aldric's, a famous private school whose team had won the championship four times in six years.
The debate would take place in a historic hall in Oxford, in front of an audience of five hundred people and a panel of three judges.
A week before the final, the organizers announced the motion: "This house believes that social media does more harm than good to young people."
Hollins Park would oppose it.
In other words, they had to argue that social media was, on balance, beneficial.
Tanvir was horrified.
He had deleted all his social media accounts a year earlier, after being bullied online, and he genuinely believed that the motion was true.
"I can't argue for something I don't believe," he told Mr. Petrov.
Mr. Petrov nodded sympathetically.

"That's precisely why debating is valuable," he said. "If you can understand the strongest version of the other side, you'll understand your own opinion much better. You don't have to agree with it. You just have to take it seriously."
For the next week, Tanvir researched the other side thoroughly.

He read studies about teenagers who had found support online when they felt isolated, about young activists who had organized campaigns, and about disabled students who used social media to make friends.
He also talked to his younger cousin, who had come out as gay online long before she dared to tell her family.
Slowly, his view became more complicated.
He still believed that social media could be cruel, but he could no longer pretend that it was only cruel.
The hall in Oxford was even grander than they had imagined, with wooden panels, portraits of famous former students and a ceiling decorated in gold.
The St. Aldric's team arrived in matching blazers and shook hands politely, with the relaxed confidence of people who had done this many times before.
Their first speaker was superb.
She described rising rates of anxiety among teenagers, the pressure to look perfect and the addictive design of the apps, and the audience applauded loudly.
Chloe replied with energy and humor, and Isaac with statistics, but by the halfway point, the judges' faces suggested that St. Aldric's were ahead.
Tanvir was the last speaker.
When he stood up, his hands were shaking so badly that he had to put his notes on the table.
Then he did something that nobody had expected.
He told the audience that a year earlier, he would have agreed with every word the other team had said.
He described being bullied, and deleting his accounts, and feeling relieved.
"But then I asked myself a question," he said, and his voice grew steadier.

"Firstly, who was I protecting? Myself, yes. But what about my cousin, who found the courage to be herself online before she could do it at home? Secondly, what about the disabled student who can't easily leave her house, for whom social media is not a distraction but a lifeline? The problem isn't the technology. The problem is how it's designed and how we use it. To sum up: you don't solve a problem by pretending that everyone has the same experience as you."
When he sat down, there was a moment of complete silence.
Then the hall filled with applause, and some members of the St. Aldric's team were clapping too.
The judges took twenty minutes to decide.
Hollins Park won by two votes to one, and Tanvir was named the best speaker of the tournament.
Afterwards, Mr. Petrov found him outside, sitting on the steps and looking slightly stunned.
"So," the teacher asked, "do you believe it now?"
Tanvir thought about it seriously.
"I believe it's more complicated than I thought," he said.
Mr. Petrov smiled. "That," he said, "is the best answer anyone has ever given me."
Tomás Oliveira had never seen snow before he landed in Ontario in the last week of August.
Of course, there was no snow in August, but his new host mother, Linda Pemberton, assured him that it would come.
"By January, you'll be sick of it," she laughed, as she drove him from the airport to their home in a quiet town surrounded by lakes and pine forests.
The Pembertons were friendly and welcoming.
Rob, the father, was a quiet engineer who was keen on fishing.
Their daughter Ellie, who was nine, asked Tomás about a hundred questions in the first hour, most of them about snakes in the jungle.
"I'm from São Paulo," Tomás explained patiently. "It's a city of twelve million people. The only snakes I've ever seen were in the zoo."
Their son Kyle, who was sixteen, said hello, shook his hand and instantly went back to his room.
In the first weeks, Tomás was thrilled by everything, and life in a new country seemed genuinely thrilling.
Tomás joined the school soccer team, tried maple syrup on bacon and learned that Canadians apologize even when you step on their feet.
But as the autumn went on, small differences began to accumulate.
The family ate dinner at half past five, which Tomás considered practically the middle of the afternoon.
At home in Brazil, dinner was at nine, and it was loud and chaotic: everyone talked at the same time, and nobody left the table for hours.
Here, the meal was over in twenty minutes, and Kyle usually ate with his phone next to his plate.
Tomás felt that he was always being ignored, and it bothered him more than he admitted.
The Pembertons, meanwhile, had their own frustrations, although they were far too polite to mention them openly.
Tomás took twenty-minute showers every morning, so there was never any hot water left for anyone else.
He left his dirty dishes in the sink, his laundry on the stairs and his wet towels on the bedroom floor.
And because of the time difference, he called his mother at eleven every night, speaking Portuguese so loudly that Ellie could not sleep.
The explosion came in November, on a grey Sunday afternoon.
Linda found the kitchen in a mess after Tomás had made himself a snack, and she finally lost her patience.
"You're always leaving things everywhere," she said sharply. "This isn't a hotel, Tomás."
Tomás, who had been feeling lonely and homesick for weeks, reacted badly.
"And this isn't a family!" he shouted. "Nobody here even talks to me!"
He ran upstairs and slammed the door.
Lying on his bed, he wrote a long message to the exchange organization asking to be moved to a different family.
He did not send it.
Instead, he stared at the ceiling and wondered whether coming to Canada had been a terrible mistake.
Downstairs, he could hear Linda and Rob talking in low voices.
That evening, Rob knocked on his door.
"We'd like to have a family meeting," he said. "All five of us. No phones."
Tomás nearly refused, but something in Rob's calm, decent voice made him follow him downstairs.
The meeting was awkward at first, and for a while nobody was keen to speak.
Then Linda apologized for losing her temper, and Tomás apologized for shouting, and suddenly everyone was talking frankly for the first time.
Tomás explained that in Brazil, silence at dinner usually means that someone is angry, so he had assumed they did not like him.
Linda explained that in their family, nobody ever complained directly, so petty problems grew into big ones.
Even Ellie contributed: she wanted to be allowed to stay up late on Fridays, like Tomás.
They agreed on some simple rules.
Showers would last ten minutes.
Tomás would call his mother before ten, from the living room.
Dinner would move to half past six, and phones would stay in a basket by the door.
At the end, Kyle, who had hardly spoken, looked up.
"I didn't mean to ignore you," he said, embarrassed. "I'm just not great at talking to new people. Do you want to come to hockey practice on Tuesday?"
Tomás was a terrible hockey player, and his first attempts on the ice were hilarious.
He spent most of that winter falling over on the ice while Kyle laughed at him, and he loved every minute of it.
In return, he taught the family to cook feijoada, a Brazilian stew of black beans and meat, and on Saturday nights the dinner table became almost as loud as his mother's.
When the snow finally came, it was deeper than anything he had imagined, and Ellie made him build a snowman every weekend until March.
In June, the whole family drove him to the airport.
Ellie cried, Linda cried, and Rob pretended that he had something in his eye.
Kyle gave him a hockey shirt with "OLIVEIRA" printed on the back.
"You're still terrible," he said, hugging him. "Come back and practice."
On the plane, Tomás realized that, ironically, the argument in November had been the best thing that happened all year.
It had taught him that living with other people is not about avoiding problems, but about being brave enough to discuss them openly.
Soraya Karimi had been a medical interpreter at the city hospital for three years.
She had arrived in Britain from Kabul at the age of twelve, speaking no English at all, and she still remembered how it felt to sit in a doctor's office unable to understand a word.
Now she spent her days translating between Dari and English for patients who were often frightened, confused and far from home.
On a busy Monday afternoon, she was called to the cardiology department.
The patient was Mrs. Ahmadi, a seventy-eight-year-old widow who had been brought in by her son, Jamal, after complaining of pains in her chest.
The doctor, Dr. Hughes, was a senior cardiologist with a reputation for being brilliant but impatient.
He had twelve other patients waiting, and his schedule was extremely demanding.
Dr. Hughes began asking questions rapidly, and Soraya translated each one.
When did the pain start?
Was it sharp or dull?
Did it spread to her arm or jaw?
Mrs. Ahmadi answered slowly, and at one point she put her hand on her chest and said a phrase that, translated literally, meant "My heart is tight."
Soraya hesitated, because the phrase was genuinely unclear.
In Dari, as in many languages, the expression can describe physical pain, but it is also commonly used to mean sadness or worry.
A good interpreter must not add or remove anything, but she must also make sure that the meaning is precise.
"Doctor, she said 'my heart is tight,'" Soraya explained. "In Dari, that can mean pain, but it can also mean she feels sad or anxious. Could I ask her to clarify?"
Dr. Hughes looked up from his notes for the first time.
"Yes. Please do."
It turned out that Mrs. Ahmadi meant both.
She had felt a heavy, squeezing pain when she climbed stairs, but she was also deeply worried because her husband had died of a heart attack at the same age.
The distinction changed the direction of the whole consultation.
Dr. Hughes slowed down, sat on the edge of the bed and explained each test carefully.
The tests showed that two of the arteries supplying Mrs. Ahmadi's heart were seriously blocked.
She would need an operation.
Before Dr. Hughes could tell her, however, her son Jamal took Soraya aside in the corridor.
"Please don't translate everything," he said quietly.
"In our family, we don't tell old people bad news. It will frighten her, and fear is bad for the heart. Just tell her she needs a small procedure."
Soraya understood precisely why he was asking.
In many Afghan families, protecting elderly relatives from painful truths is considered an act of love and respect.
Her own grandmother had never been told the name of the illness that killed her.
But Soraya was also bound by a professional code.
Interpreters must translate accurately and completely, and they must not take sides.
Moreover, in British law, a patient has the right to understand her treatment and to give her own consent to an operation.
If Soraya lied, even kindly, she would be taking that right away.
"I'm sorry," she told Jamal gently. "I can't change what the doctor says. But I can ask him to speak to all of you together, and to be as careful as possible."
Dr. Hughes agreed to her suggestion.
That evening, he met Mrs. Ahmadi, Jamal and Jamal's wife in a quiet room, with Soraya beside him.

Before giving any information, he asked Mrs. Ahmadi a question that Soraya had suggested: "How much would you like to know about your illness, and would you like your son to make some of the decisions with you?"
The old woman looked at her son, and then at the doctor.
"I buried my husband because nobody told us the truth in time," she said. "Tell me everything. Then I will decide with my son."
Soraya translated every word, and she saw Jamal lower his head.
Dr. Hughes explained the operation, the risks and the likely benefits in simple language, pausing after each sentence so that Soraya could translate accurately.
Mrs. Ahmadi listened with great dignity, asked three sensible questions and signed the consent form herself.
The operation was a success, and her recovery was remarkably swift.
A week later, when Soraya visited the ward, Mrs. Ahmadi was sitting up in bed, complaining loudly about the hospital food.
She took Soraya's hand and held it for a long time.
"You gave me my own voice," she said.
Jamal thanked her too, a little awkwardly but sincerely, with genuine warmth.
"I was trying to protect her," he admitted. "I didn't realize she wanted to protect herself."
Dr. Hughes changed something, too.
He began booking interpreters for longer appointments, and he started asking every patient, in whatever language they spoke, how much they wanted to know.
"Your job isn't just translating words," he told Soraya one day. "It's making sure people are genuinely heard."
When Iris Campbell died at the age of ninety-one, she left almost everything to her three grandchildren, equally.

There was not much money, but there was the lake house: a small wooden cottage on the shore of a Scottish loch, surrounded by pine trees, with a dock, an old canoe and a view that had not changed in a hundred years.
The three of them had spent every childhood summer there.
Those summers had been the happiest of their lives: swimming in freezing water, picking berries and listening to Iris's bizarre stories about the ghosts of the loch.
The lawyer read the will in his elegant office in Edinburgh.
Afterwards, the three siblings went for a coffee, and within ten minutes a fierce argument had begun.
Claire, the eldest, was a lawyer herself in London, with two teenage children and a demanding job.
She thought the only sensible solution was to sell the house and divide the money.
"None of us can look after it," she said. "The roof leaks, the kitchen is from the nineteen-seventies, and it's five hours from where I live."
Ben, the middle child, was a talented musician who had always struggled financially.
He was forty and still renting a small flat, and his share of the sale would allow him, for the first time, to buy a home.
He agreed with Claire, although he looked uncomfortable saying so.
Hana, the youngest, was utterly horrified.
She was twenty-nine, worked from home as a graphic designer and had visited Iris at the lake every month for the last five years of her life, often staying for weeks.
"Gran wanted the house to stay in the family," she said. "She told me so, many times."
"Then why didn't she write that in the will?" Claire replied sharply.
Nobody had an answer.
Beneath the argument about the house lay older resentments.
Claire had always felt that she was expected to be the mature one, responsible for everyone.
Ben felt that his sisters had never taken his career seriously.
And Hana suspected that the others thought she had spent time with Iris to secure the house for herself, an idea that hurt her more than she could say.
In the end, they agreed to spend one weekend at the house together before making any decision.
It was the first time all three of them had been there at the same time for almost twenty years.
The cottage smelled of wood smoke and old books, exactly as it always had, and for the first evening they were polite and careful with each other, like strangers.
On Saturday morning, Ben found the old canoe under the house and dragged it down to the water.
To everyone's surprise, it still floated.
The three of them paddled out into the middle of the loch, as they had done as children, and when Claire lost her balance and nearly fell in, they laughed until they could hardly breathe.
For an hour, nobody mentioned the will, and it felt genuinely like the old days.
That evening, while looking for candles in a drawer, Hana found an envelope addressed to all three of them in their grandmother's handwriting.
Inside was a short letter.

"I haven't told you what to do with the house," Iris had written, "because it isn't my decision any more. It's yours. But I hope you'll decide together. The house was never really the point. You were."
Hana read it aloud, her voice shaking, and when she finished, Ben quietly wiped his eyes.
Claire read it twice, as if she were checking a contract, and then put it down and said nothing for a long time.
It was so typical of Iris: gentle, witty and completely impossible to argue with.
They talked until two in the morning, with a mixture of tears and laughter.
For the first time, they spoke frankly to each other: about money, about the past, about the things they had never said.
Claire admitted that she was exhausted and could not take on another responsibility.
Ben admitted that he was ashamed of needing the money.
Hana admitted that she had been lonely since Iris died, and that the house was the only place where she still felt close to her.
By Sunday afternoon, they had reached a compromise.
An independent valuation would decide the price of the house.
Hana would move there permanently and buy her siblings' shares gradually, paying in monthly installments over ten years, partly with money from renting two rooms to visitors in summer.
Ben's share would be paid first, so that he could buy his flat.
And every August, whatever happened, all three families would spend a week at the lake together.
It was not the solution any of them had wanted at the beginning, but it was a decent one.
But as they locked the door on Sunday evening, Claire looked back at the cottage, the dark water and the canoe lying upside down on the dock.
"Gran knew exactly what she was doing, didn't she?" she said.
Hana smiled and gently took her sister's hand.
"She always did."
The boat dropped Maya Chen on the small stone jetty of Inishglas on a grey Monday morning in October.
The island was barely a kilometer long, a rocky ridge with a white lighthouse at one end and nothing at the other except sheep and wind.
Maya was twenty-six and had been working in journalism in Dublin for only three years.
Her editor had sent her to write about the end of an era.
On Sunday, the Inishglas light would become fully automated, and Declan Moran, the last lighthouse keeper in Ireland, would leave the island for good.
Declan was waiting for her at the top of the path.
He was sixty-four, with a white beard and hands like old rope.
"You'll want tea," he said, taking her bag.
"And I suppose you'll want stories. Everybody does. But I warn you, most of this job is polishing brass and writing down the weather."
For the first two days, Maya followed Declan everywhere.
She discovered that he had been right: the job was essentially a routine.
Every evening at sunset, he climbed the hundred and twelve steps of the spiral staircase to switch on the light.
Every morning at dawn, he switched it off again and polished the enormous glass lens until it shone.
Every three hours, day and night, he recorded the wind speed, the visibility and the state of the sea in a thick logbook.
"Why does it matter now?" Maya asked. "Ships have satellite navigation."
"Most of them do," Declan said. "But machines fail, and the sea doesn't care about technology. When everything else breaks down, a fisherman can still see a light."
He paused.
"Besides, the light has never been switched off by accident in a hundred and forty years. I'd like to keep it that way until Sunday."
On the third evening, a storm arrived from the Atlantic, and the whole tower shook in the wind.
Sitting by the stove, Declan finally began to talk.
In the winter of 1987, he said, he had been working on Inishglas for only two years.
One night, during a storm much worse than this one, the electricity failed completely, and the backup generator refused to start.

"I had been trying to repair it for an hour," Declan said, "when I heard the radio. A fishing boat called the Sea Rose had lost her engine and was drifting towards the rocks. Six men on board. And they were looking for my light."
He had lit an old paraffin lamp, carried it to the top of the tower and turned the heavy lens by hand, so that the beam kept sweeping across the water.
He did it for nine hours, until his arms were shaking and the sky began to grow light.
The crew of the Sea Rose used the beam to steer away from the rocks until a lifeboat reached them at dawn.
"Did anyone thank you?" Maya asked quietly.
Declan smiled.
"The captain's wife knitted me a jumper. I wore it until it fell apart."
Later that week, Maya asked him whether he had ever been lonely.
For a long time, he did not answer.
Then he took a photograph from a drawer and handed it to her.
It showed a young woman with dark curly hair, laughing on the jetty.
"Brigid," he said. "My wife. She lived here with me for thirty years."
Brigid had been a teacher on the mainland before she married him, and on Inishglas she had taught herself to paint.
Her paintings of the sea still hung on every wall of the cottage.
She had died six years earlier, after a short illness, and since then Declan had kept the light alone.
"People think the worst thing about this place is the storms," he said. "It isn't. It's the silence after them."
On Sunday evening, two engineers arrived by boat to complete the automation.
They installed sensors, a solar panel and a small computer that would switch the light on and off without human help.
It took them less than an hour.
Declan watched in silence, his hands in his pockets and his face utterly still.
At sunset, he asked if he could climb the stairs one last time.
Maya went with him.
At the top, the new system switched the light on by itself, and the great beam swept out across the sea as darkness fell, exactly as it had done for a hundred and forty years.
Declan wrote one final entry in the logbook: "Wind northwest, moderate. Visibility good. Light working. Keeper leaving."
Then he closed the book and put it under his arm.
Maya's article was published the following weekend and read by thousands of people.
Among the letters the newspaper received was one from a man called Paddy, who had been the youngest crew member on the Sea Rose in 1987.
"I have three children and five grandchildren," he wrote. "None of them would exist without that light. Please tell Mr. Moran that I still think of him every time there is a storm."
Dr. Nadia Aziz had spent twenty years recording endangered languages, but she had never worked anywhere as remote as the Karavan valley.
To reach it, she took two flights, a bus, a jeep and finally a donkey, which carried her recording equipment up a narrow path above a river.
The valley was home to about three hundred people, most of whom spoke the national language.
Only two of them still spoke Varesh, the language their ancestors had used for at least a thousand years.
Its grammar was virtually unknown to outsiders, and no dictionary of it had ever been published.
Both speakers were eighty-four years old.
Arvo was a retired shepherd who lived at the top of the village, and Selim, his cousin, was a former blacksmith who lived at the bottom.
Nadia's plan was essentially simple: she would record them talking to each other, so that future generations could hear how the language sounded in natural conversation.
There was only one problem.
Arvo and Selim had not spoken to each other for forty years.
Nobody in the village could agree on the cause of the quarrel.
Some said it had been about a piece of land; others said it had started at a wedding, when Selim had made a joke about Arvo's singing.
Whatever the reason, both men were extremely stubborn, and their feud had become a legendary part of village life.
When Nadia visited Arvo, he told her proudly that he spoke the "real" Varesh, whereas Selim spoke a lazy version.
When she visited Selim, he told her precisely the opposite.
So Nadia recorded them separately.
Over three months, Arvo taught her the names of forty kinds of grass, most of which had no translation in any other language.
Selim sang her the songs that blacksmiths had once sung while they worked, and taught her dozens of proverbs.
One of them, roughly translated, meant: "A hammer that is too proud breaks its own handle."
Nadia wondered whether Selim understood the irony.
The recordings were valuable, but they had a crucial limitation.
Although each man spoke fluently, some parts of the language only appeared in conversation: jokes, arguments, the way people greeted each other or interrupted.
Without two speakers talking, those things would be lost forever.
It was Leyla, Arvo's granddaughter, who suggested a remarkably sensible solution.
She was sixteen and had begun to regret that she had never learned her grandfather's language.
"They won't talk to each other," she said. "But they might both talk to me. If they have to teach me, they'll have to agree on the words."
The first lesson took place in the village school, on neutral ground, with Leyla sitting between the two old men.
At first, they spoke only to her, and they refused even to look at each other.
But when Arvo taught her a word for "snow that falls in spring," Selim could not resist correcting his pronunciation.
Arvo replied furiously, in Varesh, that Selim had been pronouncing it wrong since 1953.
Nadia, sitting quietly in the corner with her recorder running, was utterly astonished and could hardly breathe.
It was the first conversation in Varesh that anyone had heard in forty years.
Over the following weeks, the arguments gradually became discussions, and the discussions became stories full of wit and humor.
Despite their differences, the two cousins discovered that they remembered the same childhood: the same games, the same teachers and the same terrible winter of 1947.
One afternoon, Selim finally apologized for the joke at the wedding.
Arvo said that he had forgotten about it years ago, which everyone knew was untrue, and then he laughed for the first time in front of his cousin since they were young men.
Nadia left the valley the following spring with more than two hundred hours of recordings, including a grammar, a dictionary of four thousand words and dozens of songs.
It was, she wrote in her report, the most extensive record of any language in the region.
Leyla had learned enough to hold a simple conversation, and she had started teaching basic words to the younger children at the school.
Her enthusiasm was infectious, and several teenagers joined her classes.
Arvo died peacefully two years later, and Selim died the following winter, surrounded by his grandchildren.
Varesh is no longer anyone's first language, and it may never be again.

But in the village school, children still sing the blacksmiths' songs, and every spring, when the late snow falls, somebody always says the word that Arvo and Selim argued about, and argues about how to pronounce it.
Edith Blake had written forty-one crime novels, and every one of them had been a bestseller.
When she died in March at the age of eighty-four, newspapers around the world published long obituaries, and her fans left flowers outside her cottage.
A week before her death, she had phoned her publisher, Harrow and Finch, with extraordinary news.
She had finished one final novel, called The Glass Orchard.
Edith had never trusted computers.
She typed everything on the same old typewriter she had bought in 1968, and she never made copies.
"If a book is good enough, it will survive," she liked to say.
So when a courier delivered a thick brown parcel to the office on a Friday afternoon, everyone knew that it contained the only copy in existence.
Oliver Grant, the senior editor who had worked with Edith for thirty years, signed for it personally.
He opened the parcel, checked that the pages were all there and locked it in the metal cabinet in his office.
"Nobody touches it until Monday," he announced.
"I'll start reading it first thing in the morning."
On Monday morning, Clara Mendes, the youngest editor on the team, arrived early and heard shouting from Oliver's office.
The cabinet door was open, and the manuscript had vanished.
Nothing else was missing: not the laptops, not the petty cash, not even the expensive bottle of whisky that Oliver kept for special occasions.
The director of the company, Ngozi Achebe, called the police, but the officer who came seemed rather unimpressed.
"There's no sign of a break-in," he said, examining the lock.
"Whoever opened this had a key. Are you sure it isn't just in the wrong place?"
Oliver was furious, but the officer promised only to "look into it."
After he had gone, Ms. Achebe closed the door and turned to Clara.
"You've read every one of Edith's books," she said quietly.
"You know how a mystery works. Find out what happened, and please be discreet. If the press hears about this, it will be a disaster."
Clara began with the facts.
Only two people had keys to the cabinet: Oliver himself and Dev, the security manager.
However, everyone on the floor knew that Oliver kept a spare key in his top drawer, because he was always losing the other one.
To make matters worse, the security cameras had been switched off for maintenance over the weekend.
The security log was more helpful.
It showed that Martin Hale, the head of marketing, had come into the building on Saturday morning.
Martin admitted it instantly.
"I forgot my laptop," he said, looking slightly embarrassed.
"I was there for ten minutes. Ask Dev."
Dev confirmed his story: Martin had not even gone near Oliver's office.
Then there was Julian, Edith's nephew, who had inherited everything, including the rights to her books.
He had visited the office on Friday afternoon to discuss the contract, and he had made no secret of his opinion that Harrow and Finch paid too little.
In the recycling bin, Clara found a printed email confirming a meeting between Julian and a rival publisher.
It looked suspicious, but when she called him, Julian laughed.
"Of course I met them. It's called negotiating," he said. "But why would I steal my own aunt's book? Without that manuscript, I have nothing to sell."
By Wednesday, Clara had a list of suspects but no answer.
Oliver, meanwhile, was behaving strangely.
He barely left his office, he snapped at anyone who mentioned the manuscript, and he looked as if he had not slept for days.
Clara assumed that he was genuinely heartbroken.
That afternoon, the team held a meeting to decide what to tell Edith's fans.
Someone suggested announcing that the book would be delayed.
"We can't lie to them," Oliver said.
"Edith's readers are loyal. They'd forgive us anything except that. And honestly, after that ending, with the gardener turning out to be the killer, they deserve the truth."
The room went silent.
Oliver's face turned red.
Nobody else had read a single page of The Glass Orchard, and according to his own story, neither had he.
Clara said nothing, but after the meeting she walked past his coat, which was hanging by the door.
A train ticket was sticking out of the pocket.
It was dated Sunday evening.
She found him alone in his office, staring at the empty cabinet.
"You took it home on Friday, didn't you?" she said gently.
"You couldn't wait until Monday."
For a long moment, Oliver said nothing.
Then he covered his face with his hands.
"I read it all weekend at my sister's house," he admitted.
"It's her best book, Clara. And on the train home, I fell asleep. When I woke up at my station, I grabbed my coat and ran. I didn't realize that I'd left the bag until I was on the platform."
He had been too ashamed to tell anyone, so on Monday he had opened the cabinet himself and pretended to be shocked.
"Thirty years in this business," he said miserably, "and I've lost the most valuable book I've ever held."
Clara picked up the phone and called the railway's lost property office.
The man who answered put her on hold for what felt like an hour.
When he came back, he sounded amused.
"A brown leather bag with a typed manuscript inside? Yes, it's here. A passenger handed it in on Sunday night."
He paused. "She left a note, actually. It says, 'Sorry, I read the first three chapters. Please publish it soon. I need to know how it ends.'"
The Glass Orchard was published that autumn and became the fastest-selling book in the company's history.
Oliver told the whole story in the introduction, which readers found both honest and hilarious.
And on the first page, just below Edith's name, there was a new dedication: "To the stranger on the train, who couldn't wait either."
Monte Negro had not erupted for fifty-two years.
Most people in Las Brisas, the village at its foot, had never seen lava, and many of them regarded the volcano as a friendly giant rather than a threat.
Its slopes were covered in vineyards, and the wine from the black volcanic soil was famous across the island.
Dr. Marisol Vega, a volcanologist at the island's monitoring station, was less relaxed.
In September, her sensors began recording small earthquakes beneath the mountain, most of them too weak for anyone to feel.
At first there were ten a day.
Within three weeks, there were more than two hundred, and they were becoming shallower.
The ground above the volcano had risen by eight centimeters, which could mean only one thing: magma was moving upwards.
Marisol drove to Las Brisas to meet the mayor, a cheerful man called Ruiz who had known her since she was a child.
She did not waste time, and she spoke frankly.
"I'm afraid I have bad news," she said. "We believe an eruption is likely within the next few weeks. We can't predict exactly when or where, but the village is in the most dangerous zone."
The mayor's smile disappeared.
He asked the questions that everyone would ask: How certain was she? Could it be a false alarm? What would happen to people's homes, their animals and their harvest?
Marisol answered as honestly and precisely as she could.
Volcanoes were unpredictable, she admitted, and it was possible that the magma would stop moving and nothing would happen.
"But if we wait for certainty," she said, "we may wait until it's too late."
The regional authorities ordered an evacuation of Las Brisas on the first of October.
Most of the eight hundred residents left within two days, taking what they could carry: photographs, documents, pets and, in some cases, entire kitchens.
The school became a storage center, and families from neighboring towns offered spare rooms.
But Don Aurelio, an eighty-seven-year-old farmer, refused to leave.
His family had grown grapes on the same slope for five generations, and he had stayed during the last eruption, in 1973, when he was a young man.
"The mountain knows me," he told the police officers who came to his door. "It won't touch my house."
Marisol went to see him herself.
She sat in his kitchen, drank the strong coffee he insisted on making and listened to his stories about 1973.
Then she showed him the data on her laptop: the earthquakes, the rising ground, the gas measurements.

"I know how hard this is," she said gently. "But this is not the same as 1973. The magma is much closer to the surface, and it's right under your vineyard. I'm not asking you to leave forever. I'm asking you to leave for now, so that you can come back."
The old man looked out of the window at his vines for a long time, his face stern and utterly still.
Then he stood up slowly and fetched his coat.
"My granddaughter Carmen has a sofa," he said. "It's very uncomfortable."
It was the closest thing to agreement she was going to get.
Eleven days later, at four in the afternoon, the side of Monte Negro split open with a sound like thunder.
A column of ash and smoke rose three kilometers into the sky, and two rivers of lava began to flow slowly down the slope towards the empty village.
Over the next six weeks, the lava destroyed the church, the school and more than two hundred houses.
The residents watched on television as their homes disappeared one by one.
It was devastating, but nobody was killed or seriously injured.
Don Aurelio's farmhouse was one of the last buildings to be buried.
His granddaughter said that he did not speak for three days.
When the eruption finally ended in December, the island government promised compensation and began planning a new village on safer ground.
Scientists from around the world came to study the new landscape, and Marisol's monitoring data was used to improve warning systems at other volcanoes.
The following spring, Marisol received an invitation to a small ceremony on the edge of the lava field.
Don Aurelio was there, leaning on a stick, next to a patch of land that had been saved.
He had planted six young vines in it.
"In five years there will be wine again," he told her. "And the first bottle is yours. You were right, and I was a stubborn old fool."
Marisol laughed and shook his hand.
"A stubborn old fool who is still alive," she said. "That's all I wanted."
Arjun Mehta had written about trains for fifteen years, and he still believed that a night train was the most romantic way to travel.
On a snowy evening in December, he boarded the sleeper from Vienna to Venice and found compartment six, which he would share with two strangers.
The first was Mrs. Ilse Weber, an elegant woman of about eighty with silver hair and a large black handbag, which she placed carefully on the bunk beside her.
She was going to Venice, she explained, to visit her sister for Christmas, as she had done every year for half a century.
The second was a young man called Felix, with long hair, a torn jacket and a guitar case covered in stickers.
He said very little, put on his headphones and fell asleep almost instantly.
Mrs. Weber looked at him suspiciously.
"Young people today," she whispered to Arjun, and he smiled politely without answering.
At ten o'clock, the conductor collected their tickets and passports, and the lights in the compartment were dimmed.
Outside, the snowy mountains of the Alps slid past in the darkness.
Arjun woke at two in the morning to the sound of a woman crying.
Mrs. Weber was standing in the corridor in her dressing gown, talking to the conductor.
Her handbag had disappeared.
Inside it were her purse, her glasses, her medication and, most importantly, a gold necklace that had belonged to her mother, which she was bringing as a gift for her sister.
"It was the boy," she said, pointing at the empty bunk.
Felix was not in the compartment.
Several passengers had come out of their compartments to see what was happening, and within minutes, the whole carriage seemed to agree with her.
A businessman from the next compartment, Mr. Lorenz, said he had seen "a long-haired type" walking towards the back of the train.
The conductor promised to call the police, who would board the train at Villach.
Arjun said nothing, but something about the story bothered him.
He had spent enough time on night trains to know how easily people jumped to conclusions.
Felix's guitar case was still on the luggage rack, and so were his backpack and his coat.
If he had stolen the bag, why would he leave all his own belongings behind?
A few minutes later, Felix appeared at the end of the corridor, carrying a cup of tea from the dining car.
He stopped when he saw the crowd outside his compartment, and his face turned pale when Mrs. Weber began shouting at him in German.
"I couldn't sleep," he said, confused. "I went to get some tea. I didn't take anything."
Mr. Lorenz laughed unpleasantly.
"That's what they all say."
Arjun asked Mrs. Weber, gently, when she had last seen her bag.
She had taken it to the bathroom at the end of the carriage just after midnight, she said, and then she had come straight back to bed.
Or had she?
She frowned.
She was no longer entirely sure that she had brought it back.
Arjun and the conductor walked to the bathroom together.
It was empty.

But in the compartment opposite, whose door was slightly open, an elderly man was snoring loudly, and beside him on the bunk was a large black handbag, almost identical to the one Mrs. Weber had described.
When the conductor woke him, the old man was utterly embarrassed.
He had found the bag in the bathroom, assumed it was his wife's, and brought it back without looking inside.
His wife's bag, which was a slightly different shade of black, was under her pillow.
Mrs. Weber opened her bag with trembling hands.
Everything was there, including the necklace.
Then she turned to Felix, who was standing awkwardly in the corridor with his tea.
For a long moment, she did not seem to know what to say.
"I am very sorry," she said at last, in careful English. "I judged you by your hair. That was wrong of me."
Felix shrugged and smiled.
"It happens a lot," he said.
Mr. Lorenz had already disappeared back into his compartment.
Nobody slept much for the rest of the night.
Instead, Felix took out his guitar and played quietly, and Mrs. Weber, to everyone's astonishment, sang along to an old Austrian folk song in a surprisingly strong voice.
When the train arrived in Venice the next morning, she insisted on introducing Felix to her sister on the platform.
In the article he wrote about the journey, Arjun described it as the most bizarre night he had ever spent on a train, and the one that had taught him the most.
Hannah Kowalski had worked in the finance department of Redwood Construction for six years, and she had a reputation for noticing things that other people missed.
Her colleagues joked that she could find a missing penny in a spreadsheet of a million rows.
So when she was asked to prepare the accounts for the annual audit, she went through every payment carefully.
One name kept appearing: Northfield Supplies.
Over two years, Redwood had paid it almost nine hundred thousand pounds for building materials.
The invoices looked perfectly normal, but when Hannah checked the delivery records, she could not find a single delivery from Northfield on any of the company's sites.
Out of curiosity, she searched for the supplier's address online.
It was a small flat above a hairdresser's in another city.
That evening, she found one more detail that made her feel sick.
According to public records, the sole director of Northfield Supplies was a man called Martin Price.
Graham Price, Redwood's finance director, had a brother-in-law with exactly the same name.
The next morning, Hannah took her findings to her manager, Derek Shaw.
She expected him to be shocked.
Instead, he closed the door and lowered his voice.
"I'd leave this alone if I were you, Hannah," he said.
"Graham has been here for twenty years. There's probably a perfectly innocent explanation."
"Then why can't I find any deliveries?"
Derek sighed.
"Look, you've got a mortgage and two kids. The company is struggling, and there are rumors about redundancies. Do you really want to be the person who accused the finance director of fraud?"
It was not exactly a threat, but it was close enough.
Hannah went home and did not sleep.
She kept imagining the consequences: losing her job, being unable to find another one, her children's faces.
At three in the morning, she got up and made a cup of tea.
Somewhere around four, she realized that she could not pretend she had not seen the numbers.
Her conscience simply would not allow it.
Hannah's old university friend, Sofia Reyes, was an employment lawyer.
They met in a café far from the office, and Sofia listened without interrupting.
"First of all, you're legally protected," she said when Hannah had finished.
"Whistleblowers who report fraud in good faith can't be fired for it. But you need evidence, not suspicions, and you mustn't take anything you're not entitled to see."
Over the following two weeks, Hannah worked methodically.
She made copies of the invoices, the payment records and the missing delivery reports, all of which she had access to as part of her normal job.
She wrote down dates and times in a notebook that she kept at home.
Then, following Sofia's advice, she called the regulator's confidential hotline and submitted everything anonymously.
For a month, nothing happened.
Then, one Tuesday morning, three investigators arrived at Redwood's headquarters and asked to see the finance director.
The office went silent as Graham Price was led into a meeting room.
Through the glass wall, Hannah could see him shaking his head and waving his hands.
At first, Graham denied everything.
He claimed that Northfield was a genuine supplier and insisted that the missing delivery records were simply an administrative error.
But the lead investigator, a quiet, patient woman called Ms. Adebayo, had already traced the payments.
The money had gone from Northfield's account directly into a property that Graham and his brother-in-law had bought in Spain.
After two days of questioning, Graham admitted the fraud and resigned.
Nobody officially knew who had reported him, but offices are full of rumors.
Some colleagues stopped talking when Hannah walked into the kitchen.
Derek avoided her completely.
One day she found a note on her desk that said only, "Traitor."
The weeks that followed were the loneliest of Hannah's working life.
But slowly, the atmosphere changed.
When the full story appeared in the newspapers, people realized that the stolen money could have saved the jobs that the company had cut the previous year.
An older engineer, whom Hannah barely knew, stopped at her desk one morning.
"My son was one of those redundancies," he said quietly. "Thank you."
The new finance director introduced stricter controls, and Derek was moved to another department.
A few months later, Hannah left Redwood to become the head of audit at a large children's charity.
At her interview, the chairwoman asked her why she wanted the job.
"Because people give money to charities believing it will reach the children," Hannah said. "Someone has to make sure it does."
She still keeps the note that said "Traitor" in her desk drawer.
When young accountants ask her for advice, she sometimes shows it to them.
"Doing the right thing isn't always popular," she tells them.
"But the numbers don't lie, and neither should we."
The email arrived at 7:45 on a Tuesday morning, while Amara was still in her pajamas.
"Dear Ms. Osei," it began, "we are delighted to offer you the position of junior software engineer at Brightline."
She read it three times, then screamed so loudly that her flatmate came running out of the bathroom.
Brightline was one of the most exciting young companies in the city, and after six months of applications, rejections and interviews, Amara had finally been chosen.
The salary was thirty-eight thousand pounds a year, more than she had ever earned.
She was ready to reply immediately and accept, but first she called Professor Lin, her former university tutor, to share the news.
He congratulated her warmly.
Then he asked a question that she had not expected.
"Are you going to negotiate?"
Amara laughed nervously.
"Negotiate? Professor, they've just offered me my dream job. What if they change their minds?"
"They won't," he said. "Companies expect candidates to negotiate. The worst they can say is no. But do your research first."
That evening, Amara opened her laptop and started investigating.
She read salary surveys, compared job advertisements and sent messages to three former classmates who worked in similar roles.
The picture that emerged was clear.
For a junior engineer with her qualifications in that city, the typical range was between forty-two and forty-six thousand.
Brightline's offer was significantly below the market rate.
She also discovered some statistics that made her uncomfortable.
Several studies had found that women were less likely than men to negotiate their first salary, and that the gap, once created, tended to grow throughout their careers.
A few thousand pounds now could mean tens of thousands over twenty years.
Amara wrote a short script and practiced it in front of the mirror.
