Imogen played Hedda as a cruel, powerful woman who enjoyed controlling other people; Tess had always seen her as an inherently frightened one, trapped in a marriage she despised and terrified of an ordinary, tedious life.
"Then play that," Felix said. "I'd rather see an authentic mistake than a perfect copy."
Her portrayal changed almost immediately, becoming less polished but far more vulnerable.
The other actors, who had been politely patient until then, began to watch her with genuine curiosity.
The first twenty minutes passed in a kind of trance, whilst her heart hammered against her ribs.
Tess was acutely aware of the heat of the lights, the rustle of eight hundred programmes and the faint smell of dust, and yet she seemed to be watching herself from somewhere high above the stage.
Then, in the middle of a scene with her husband, Tesman, her mind went completely blank.
The silence lasted perhaps three seconds, although it felt like an hour.

The actor playing Tesman, a veteran of forty years, simply repeated his previous line with a slightly puzzled expression, as if his wife had not heard him, and the words came back to her as suddenly as they had disappeared.
Nobody in the audience seemingly noticed.
Several people subsequently told her that the pause had been the most chilling moment of the evening.

At the end of the first act, as the lights faded, the actor playing Tesman squeezed her hand in the darkness and whispered that she was doing beautifully, which was either the kindest lie anyone had ever told her or not a lie at all.
In her dressing room during the interval, Tess sat in front of the mirror and was quietly sick into a wastepaper basket.
Then her phone buzzed with a message from Imogen, who was watching a live broadcast of the performance at home.
"Your Hedda is terrified," it said. "Mine is cruel. Yours is better. Don't you dare change anything in the second half."
Tess read it three times, and then she laughed, which was not something she had expected to do that evening.
Her fatigue vanished, replaced by an exhilarating sense of freedom.
Otis appeared at the door with a glass of water and a five-minute warning.
"To be candid," he said, "I've worked on this production for three months, and tonight is the first time I've felt sorry for her."
She did not need to ask whom he meant.
She drank the water, looked at her reflection for a long moment and saw, for the first time, not Imogen's Hedda but her own.
The second half passed more quickly than the first.
When the final scene ended and the lights went down, there was a profound silence, so long that Tess wondered, for one terrible moment, whether the audience had hated it.
Then the applause began, and it went on for so long that the cast had to come back for four curtain calls.
Felix, who rarely praised anyone explicitly, stood at the back of the stalls throughout, applauding with the rest of the audience.
The reviews the next morning were predominantly about her.

One critic, notably the most severe in London, described her performance as a revelation; another, less generous, complained that her Hedda was too sympathetic, which Tess secretly regarded as the highest possible praise.
Imogen returned to the role a week later, as everyone had always known she inevitably would, and Tess went back to the rehearsal room with the other understudies.
Her debut as a leading actress had lasted a single night, but it had been enough, arguably, to show her what kind of actor she wanted to be.
But something had changed.

Within a month, Felix offered her the leading role in his next production, and Imogen, who turned out to be as generous in person as she was frightening on stage, sent her a bottle of champagne with a card that said simply: "Never copy anyone again."
Tess kept the card long after the champagne had gone, propped against the mirror of every dressing room she was ever given.
At thirty-four, Olivia Marsh was a senior associate at Grant & Whitfield, one of the largest law firms in London, and she had not slept for more than six hours in a row for three years.

Her work consisted predominantly of litigation between large companies, disputes worth hundreds of millions of pounds in which, as far as she could tell, nobody was ever entirely right or entirely wrong.
She was good at it, well paid for it and, increasingly, unable to remember why she had wanted to do it.
Her tenure at the firm had been marked by rapid promotion and, more recently, by a fatigue that no holiday seemed able to cure.
The moment of clarity came on a Tuesday evening in the office, when she realized that she had read the same paragraph of a contract eleven times without understanding a word of it.
Her doctor used the word burnout and recommended a month of rest.

Olivia, who had never done anything by halves, resigned instead, sold her car and booked a one-way ticket to Portugal, where an old university friend, Luca Bellini, ran a small family vineyard in the Douro valley.
The work at the vineyard was physically gruelling in a way she had never experienced.

The vines grew on steep terraces cut into the hillside, and during the harvest she spent ten hours a day bent over them with a pair of scissors, cutting bunches of grapes and carrying them in baskets down paths too narrow for machines.
Her hands blistered, her back ached, and at night she slept for nine hours without dreaming.
Luca's business was far more fragile than she had assumed.
His family had farmed the same terraces for five generations, and their reliance on a single crop made them acutely vulnerable to bad weather and bad luck.
A single hailstorm could destroy a year's crop, the price of grapes was set by large wine companies, and a new regulation on water use threatened to make the family's traditional methods illegal.
One evening, Luca showed her the official letter, forty pages of dense Portuguese legal language, and admitted that he had no idea what most of it meant.
Olivia's Portuguese was poor, but her understanding of how regulations worked was excellent.
With a dictionary and a great deal of patience, she worked out that the new statute contained several provisions for small producers, none of which the ministry had mentioned in its letter.
Luca was exempt from the most expensive requirements, provided he applied before the end of the year.
Within a month, word had spread, and Olivia found herself helping a dozen neighbouring families fill in forms at Luca's kitchen table, paid in wine, olive oil and an alarming quantity of cake.
She returned to London the following autumn with a clear sense of what she wanted, and an equally clear sense of the obstacle in her way.
The job she wanted was head of legal at the Clearwater Trust, a charity that helped rural communities defend their rights to land and water.
It paid less than half her former salary, and the other candidates had spent their entire careers in the nonprofit sector.
Staff turnover at the trust was remarkably low, which meant that vacancies were rare and fiercely contested.
She had spent a year picking grapes.
Friends who worked in recruitment warned her that employers were suspicious of gaps in a CV, particularly in law, where long hours were regarded as a sign of commitment.
Several suggested that she describe the year as "a consultancy project in Portugal", which was technically accurate and deliberately misleading.
Olivia decided that she would rather tell the truth and lose the job than begin it with a lie.
The interview was conducted by Ruth Okeke, the trust's director, a former human rights lawyer with a reputation for asking candid questions and listening carefully to the answers.
Her first question went straight to the gap.
"You left one of the most prestigious firms in London to pick grapes," she said. "Why should I believe you won't leave us too?"
Olivia had rehearsed a polished answer, and she abandoned it, since it now seemed to her inherently dishonest.
She explained that she had burned out, that she had not left to find herself but because she could no longer function, and that the year had taught her more about the law than the previous five.
In London, she had represented companies that could afford to hire her; in the Douro, she had seen what happened to people who could not.
"I didn't leave the law," she said. "I left the wrong side of it."
The answer was unusually candid for a job interview, and from the long silence that followed, Olivia sensed that it had been either a serious mistake or exactly the right thing to say.

Ruth wrote something in her notebook, then asked about the regulation in Portugal: how Olivia had found the provisions for small producers, how she had explained them to families who distrusted lawyers, and what she would have done differently.
They talked for an hour longer than the interview had been scheduled to last.
Ruth subsequently called, two days later, to offer her the job.
Afterwards, she admitted that Olivia had not been the most experienced candidate, and that two members of the panel had been worried about the gap in her CV.
"But you were the only one who had actually sat at a kitchen table explaining a statute to a farmer," she said. "And you were the only one who told me the truth about why you'd stopped."
Olivia started in January.
Her salary was modest, her office was a converted storeroom, and her working hours, she discovered, were inevitably almost as long as they had been at Grant & Whitfield.
Her predecessor, who had retired after twenty years, had left her an impressive portfolio of cases and a filing system of astonishing chaos.

The difference was that she slept well, and on the shelf above her desk, beside the legal handbooks, she kept a bottle of Luca's wine, unopened, with a label that read: "For the next time you forget why."
The last plane of the summer left Halvorsen Station on a clear February afternoon, and fourteen people stood on the ice to watch it disappear.
For the next eight months, until the sun returned and the runway could be used again, they would be entirely isolated from the rest of the world.
No aircraft could reach them in the Antarctic winter, and in a genuine emergency the nearest help was more than a thousand kilometres away.
At that latitude, the sun would disappear completely in May and not rise again until August.
Kristin Lund had spent three previous winters at the station, but this was her first as its leader.
She was responsible for the scientific programme, the machinery that kept them warm, and above all for the safety and morale of thirteen people living in acute confinement.

Previous winters had taught her that the greatest dangers were often psychological rather than physical: fatigue, boredom and the slow build-up of resentment between people who could not avoid each other.
Her predecessor had given her a single piece of advice before he left: "Most of the job is boring. The part that isn't boring is the part that matters."
The storm arrived in late May, in the permanent darkness of midwinter, with a speed that surprised even the meteorologist.
Within an hour, the wind was gusting at over a hundred kilometres per hour, and snow was being driven horizontally across the ice with such density that visibility fell to less than a metre.
Station rules were explicit: in such conditions, nobody went outside except in an emergency, and then only in pairs, clipped to the guide ropes that connected the buildings.
At a quarter past nine that evening, Kristin discovered that Ollie Brennan was missing.
Ollie was twenty-four, the youngest person on the station, a cheerful electronics technician who treated every problem as a puzzle.
The automatic weather mast four hundred metres from the main building had stopped transmitting, and he had seemingly decided to fix it before the data gap grew too long.
He had signed out correctly, taken a radio and clipped onto the rope, but, crucially, he had gone alone, and he had not answered his radio for forty minutes.
Kristin called the senior members of the team into the kitchen, the warmest room in the station.
Dev Malhotra, the station's engineer, was adamant that they should go out immediately.
"If he's injured, every minute counts," he said. "Give me two people and I'll follow the rope to the mast."
Inês Carvalho, the doctor, was more cautious, and her reasoning was coolly clinical.
"In this wind, a search team is vulnerable too," she said. "If someone falls and loses the rope, we'll have two casualties instead of one."
She explained that hypothermia could kill a person lying still in such conditions within a couple of hours, but that a person who was sheltered and dressed properly might survive until morning.
Everyone looked at Kristin.
She was acutely aware that whatever she decided, she would have to live with it for the rest of her life.
If she waited and Ollie died, she would never forgive herself; if she sent a team and someone else was lost, she would have broken the very rules she had been appointed to enforce.
She thought, absurdly, of her predecessor's advice about the part of the job that was not boring.
"We go," she said, "but we go according to the contingency plan, and nobody improvises."
Three people would follow the rope, each clipped on separately, with a fourth waiting at the door holding a second rope as a lifeline.
They would report by radio every fifty metres, and if they had not reached the mast within thirty minutes, they would turn back, whatever they had found.
Kristin would lead the team herself.
"You can't," said Dev. "If something happens to you, who runs the station?"
"You do," she said. "That's why you're staying."
Outside, the storm was beyond anything she had imagined.
The noise was immense, a continuous roar that made speech impossible, and the snow found its way through every gap in her clothing.
She could not see her own hands, let alone the others; the only reality was the rope, frozen and stiff, sliding through her gloves.
Every fifty metres she shouted into the radio, and every time Dev's calm voice answered, counting the minutes with reassuring precision.
She knew that disorientation was the real enemy: people who had let go of a rope in a whiteout had been known to walk in circles until they collapsed, sometimes within a few metres of safety.
At three hundred and sixty metres, her boot struck something soft.
Ollie was lying curled against the wall of the small instrument hut beside the mast, sheltered from the worst of the wind, still clipped to the rope.
He was shivering violently, which Inês had told her was a good sign, and when she shone her torch into his face, he grinned.
"Radio battery died," he shouted into her ear. "Cold. Stayed put. Like the manual says."
Ollie subsequently spent two days in the station's small medical room, recovering from mild hypothermia and a certain amount of embarrassment.
The subsequent review concluded that he had made one serious error, going out alone, and several good decisions, notably staying on the rope and seeking shelter rather than trying to walk back blind.
Kristin's own conduct was also scrutinized, as protocol required, and the report found that she had acted appropriately, albeit at considerable personal risk.

Kristin introduced two new mandatory rules: every radio would carry a spare battery kept warm inside the user's clothing, and nobody, however experienced, would ever go outside alone during a storm warning.
On the twenty-first of June, the longest night of the year, the station celebrated midwinter with the traditional dinner.
Ollie, fully recovered, stood up to make a speech and raised his glass to "the most boring leader in Antarctica, who follows every rule, and who walked into a hurricane to find me".
Everyone laughed, and Kristin laughed with them, although she was so profoundly moved that she found it difficult to speak.
Later, alone in her office, she wrote in her logbook that the decision had not felt like courage.
It had felt like arithmetic performed in fear: a set of risks weighed against each other, with no correct answer, only a less terrible one.
Perhaps, she thought, that was what leadership was: not the absence of fear, but the willingness to decide while afraid, and to take responsibility for the consequences.
Outside, the wind had dropped, and for the first time in weeks the sky was clear, full of stars and the slow green curtains of the southern lights.

Hugh Farrant had been climbing in the Himalaya for thirty-five years, and in that time he had acquired a reputation for two things: an uncanny sense of when to turn back, and a manner of speaking so understated that newcomers often failed to notice when he was alarmed.
He had once described a collapsing ice wall as "rather untidy" and a broken ankle, his own, as "a bit of a nuisance".
Among climbers, his understatement was proverbial.
His clients adored him, and his demeanor at moments of crisis, so calm as to seem nonchalant, had become part of the legend that filled his expeditions every year.
This year's team was small.
Pemba Sherpa, the sirdar, adept at reading both weather and people, had climbed with Hugh for two decades and had stood on the summits of eleven of the highest mountains on Earth.
Dr. Ines Carvalho, a Portuguese physician who specialized in the effects of altitude, had joined as the expedition doctor.

And Josh Kellerman, twenty-four, from Colorado, was attempting his first Himalayan peak, a seven-thousand-metre mountain called Chomo Tari, with the kind of tenacity that only people who have never failed at anything possess.
The first three weeks went well.
The team established its camps in stages, climbing high during the day and descending to sleep, so that their bodies could adapt to the thinning air.
The work was arduous and repetitive, but Josh was strong and cheerful, and he treated every setback as an opportunity to prove his determination, dismissing any mention of peril with a grin.
Hugh liked him, although he occasionally watched the young man with the wistful expression of someone remembering his own youth.

By the end of the third week they reached Camp Four, a precarious ledge of snow and rock at almost six thousand eight hundred metres, from which the summit was a long day's climb along a narrow ridge.
The forecast promised two days of calm weather, and they went to bed at six in the evening, planning to leave at midnight.
Josh lay awake in his sleeping bag, too excited to sleep, listening to the silence.
It was an eerie silence, so complete that he could hear his own heart.
They left at midnight, as planned, their headtorches forming a thin line of light on the ridge.
For five hours the climbing was cold but straightforward.

Then, shortly after dawn, as menacing clouds gathered in the west, the wind arrived, rising within minutes to a gale of a ferocity that none of the forecasts had predicted, driving ice crystals into their faces and forcing them to crouch against the slope.
Hugh crawled across to Josh and shouted into his ear.
"It's getting a bit breezy," he said. "I think we might want to have a little chat about our plans."
Josh, who could see the summit less than two hundred metres above them, took this to mean that Hugh was not particularly worried.
"We're so close," he shouted back. "Another two hours and we're there."
Hugh nodded thoughtfully, as if the idea had some merit.
"We could," he said. "Although it would be a bit of a shame to lose a few toes over it."
Josh laughed, assuming it was a joke.
It was Pemba who finally explained.
While Hugh made his way along the rope to speak to Ines, the sirdar put a heavy hand on Josh's shoulder and leaned close.
"Every phrase is a euphemism," he said. "When Hugh says a bit breezy, he means this is very dangerous. When he says a shame to lose toes, he means he thinks you will lose them."
He paused, then added, with a faint smile that the wind almost erased: "I have climbed with him for twenty years. I speak Hugh very well."
Ines, meanwhile, had examined the others and was not happy with what she had found.

Josh had stopped shivering, which was not a good sign, and his speech was becoming slightly slurred, one of the first symptoms of hypothermia, whose onset is insidious precisely because its victims stop feeling cold.
The fingers of his left hand, when she removed his glove, were white and hard.
"Frostbite," she told Hugh. "Early stage. If we go down now, he keeps them."
Hugh considered this for perhaps two seconds.
"Right," he said. "I think we'll call it a day."
Josh argued, but not for long; even in his confused state he could see that further argument was futile.
He was beginning to understand that the calm voice was not an absence of fear but a discipline, a practised stoicism, a way of keeping panic at bay so that decisions could be made clearly.
The descent took nine hours, the wind battered them relentlessly, and it was the hardest thing he had ever done.

Twice he slipped, and twice the rope that joined him to Pemba held; once the wind was so strong that they had to lie flat on the ridge and wait, and Josh, exhausted, felt a strange lassitude creeping over him, a desire simply to close his eyes.
Ines slapped his cheek, not gently, and kept talking to him until he answered.
They reached Camp Three after dark, and by the following evening they were safely at base camp, where a helicopter took Josh to a hospital in Kathmandu.
He kept all his fingers and all his toes.
Two days later, the weather cleared, and another team reached the summit without difficulty, which Josh found almost unbearable to read about.
In hindsight, he would come to see the retreat as the best decision of the whole expedition.
Hugh visited him in hospital and sat on the edge of the bed, turning his hat in his hands.
"Bit of a setback," he said, "but the mountain will still be there next year."
Josh had been rehearsing an angry speech about how close they had been, but he found that he no longer wanted to deliver it.
"Pemba says you speak a language of your own," he said instead. "What does a bit of a setback actually mean?"
Hugh smiled. "It means I was more frightened on that ridge than I have been for twenty years," he said. "And that I'd very much like to climb with you again."
It was, Josh realized, the most heartfelt compliment he had ever received.
Neil Hardcastle had flown to Osaka convinced that the deal was as good as signed.

Hallwood Furniture, the family firm in Sheffield where he was sales director, made handcrafted oak tables and chairs of impeccable quality, and for two years he had been trying to persuade Aozora, a prestigious chain of Japanese department stores, to sell them.

A contract would be the most lucrative in the company's history, and Neil had already told the board to expect good news. It would also secure the jobs of forty craftsmen, which gave the negotiations a precarious urgency.

He was a brisk, cheerful man whose approach was more entrepreneurial than diplomatic and who prided himself on plain speaking, and he regarded the elaborate etiquette of international business as an obstacle to be got through as quickly as possible.
With him was Yuki Tanabe, a junior colleague who had grown up in Kyoto and Nottingham and who spoke both languages with native fluency.
She had been brought along to interpret, although Mr. Kenji Mori, the senior buyer at Aozora, spoke good English, and Neil treated her presence as largely a courtesy.
Yuki suspected, from the tone of the correspondence, that things were less certain than Neil believed, but she was twenty-six, and it did not seem her place to say so.
The first meeting took place in a quiet room on the top floor of Aozora's headquarters.

Mr. Mori and his colleague, Ms. Sato, received Neil's business card with both hands, studied it with care and placed it on the table in front of them, and Neil, who had stuffed theirs into his pocket, did not notice Yuki wince.
He then launched into his presentation with his customary energy, and at the end he asked, beaming, "So, shall we cut to the chase and talk numbers?"
There was a long silence, which Neil interpreted as agreement, a presumption that Yuki knew to be erroneous.
Ms. Sato's expression was inscrutable, and Mr. Mori's eventual reply was meticulously worded.
"Your tables are very beautiful," Mr. Mori said at last. "We will consider your proposal carefully. It may be a little difficult."
Neil left the building in high spirits.
"Did you hear him?" he said to Yuki in the taxi. "Very beautiful. Consider carefully. That's as good as a yes."
Yuki took a deep breath.
"I think we might be talking at cross purposes," she said. "In that context, 'it may be a little difficult' is usually a polite way of saying no."
Neil was incredulous, then indignant.
"Then why not just say no?" he demanded. "It would save everyone a lot of time."

Yuki explained, as tactfully as she could, that in many Japanese business settings a direct refusal was considered abrasive, since it caused embarrassment to both sides, and that disagreement was often expressed implicitly, through hesitation, euphemism and what was left unsaid.
The anthropologist Edward Hall had described such cultures as high-context: much of the meaning of a message lay not in its words but in the relationship and the situation.
Neil's own culture, by contrast, prized explicitness, and the two styles could produce misunderstandings in which each side found the other either rude or evasive.
"And the silence?" Neil asked.
"Silence isn't agreement," Yuki said. "It's time to think. When you asked to cut to the chase, I think Mr. Mori heard that you were impatient, and possibly that you didn't respect the process."
Neil, she added, had broken several of the tacit rules of the room without realizing it.
She added that "cut to the chase" was an idiomatic, colloquial phrase that even fluent speakers of English as a second language might not understand literally.
Neil was quiet for the rest of the journey.
That evening, at Yuki's suggestion, they did something Neil had never done in twenty years of selling: they asked for a second meeting, not to press for an answer, but to understand the objection.
Yuki wrote the request in Japanese, in the most courteous register she could manage, and Mr. Mori agreed to see them over dinner.
In the relaxed setting of a small restaurant, and with Yuki gently steering the conversation, the real problem emerged.
Mr. Mori, far more talkative than in the office, recounted his own early humiliations in London, where colleagues had mistaken his reserve for a disdainful coldness.
Business in Japan, Yuki had explained to Neil beforehand, rested on reciprocal trust built slowly over time.
It was not the price at all.
Aozora's customers expected furniture to last for decades, and the stores guaranteed repairs for as long as a customer owned a piece.
Oak, Mr. Mori explained, behaved unpredictably in the humid summers of Osaka, and a British supplier twelve thousand kilometres away could not guarantee to repair a joint that had loosened.

He had tried, in the first meeting, to signal this concern tacitly, by praising the beauty of the tables and saying nothing about their practicality, and he had assumed that Neil understood, never suspecting the discrepancy between what he had said and what Neil had heard.
The contract that was eventually signed, eight months later, looked very different from the one Neil had imagined.

The contract stipulated that Hallwood would train two craftsmen in Osaka to carry out repairs, and to modify the construction of its joints for humid climates, a change that Neil's father, who had founded the firm, called the most useful thing a customer had ever told them.
The first order was smaller than Neil had hoped, but the profitability of the account grew every year.
On the flight home after the signing, Neil asked Yuki whether she would lead the Japanese account in future.
"You were right, and I was an idiot," he said, with an uncharacteristically self-deprecating smile. "Is there a polite Japanese way of saying that?"
Yuki smiled. "There are several," she said. "But they would all take a great deal longer."
Clara Oyelaran had bought two seats on the morning flight from Vienna to Toronto: one for herself, and one for her cello.

The instrument, a venerable cello made in Italy in 1780, had been lent to her by a foundation that supported young musicians, after a competition at which the judges had described her as a virtuoso, and it was worth considerably more than her flat.
She had flown with it dozens of times, strapped into its seat beside her, and she had a recital in Toronto the following evening that she had been preparing for a year.
At the gate, a supervisor named Mr. Brandt informed her that the cello could not travel in the cabin.
A new policy, he said, restricted the size of objects occupying passenger seats, and the rule allowed no exceptions.
Clara showed him the booking, the airline's own written confirmation that the seat had been purchased for a musical instrument, and the published policy, which stipulated nothing of the kind.
Mr. Brandt was courteous, sympathetic and utterly intransigent.
She could check the cello into the hold, or she could miss the flight.
It was, Clara thought, an arbitrary and unilateral decision, but there was no time to argue.
She checked it in, wrapped in every jumper she had, with a label that said "fragile" in four languages.

In Toronto, the case came out on the baggage belt with a crack across its lid, and when she opened it in the airport, her hands shaking, she found that the neck of the cello had been forced out of its joint and a long fracture ran down its front.
She cancelled the recital that evening, afraid that the damage might be irreversible.

It was, she said later, the worst moment of her professional life, not because of the money, but because she felt she had failed to protect something that had survived for two hundred and forty years before she was born.
The repair, estimated by a specialist luthier in Vienna named Herr Engel, would cost more than thirty thousand euros and take four months.
Clara submitted a claim to Transalpine Airways with photographs, the booking confirmation and the luthier's report.
The reply, which arrived three weeks later, was perfunctory.

It expressed regret for her inconvenience, stated that the airline's liability for checked baggage was limited by international convention to a sum of roughly fifteen hundred euros, and suggested that the damage might have been caused by turbulence, an event of force majeure for which the company could not be held responsible.
Clara was not a combative person, and her first reaction was a kind of numb despair.

But she possessed a quiet tenacity, and she noticed that the letter did not mention the seat she had bought or the airline's contractual obligations, and that the explanation about turbulence was not a finding but a conjecture.
Her agent, who had dealt with airlines before, gave her a piece of advice.
"Don't shout," he said. "Escalate. Politely, in writing, one level at a time, and keep a record of everything."
She did exactly that.

She meticulously wrote a chronology of the events, with times, names and the exact words Mr. Brandt had used, recorded verbatim, and she sent it to the airline's complaints department, asking specifically for the policy under which her purchased seat had been refused.

When the department replied with a slightly longer version of the same letter, she asked, courteously, for her complaint to be escalated to a manager, and when the manager did not reply at all, she wrote to the airline's chief executive.
Each reply came from a different bureaucrat, but her tone never changed: she was precise, unemotional and entirely unwilling to go away.

She also discovered, with the help of a lawyer who specialized in aviation, that the airline had no recourse to the limit on liability if the damage resulted from its own deliberate decision, and that forcing a passenger to check in an instrument for which a seat had been purchased was arguably such a decision.
She also learned that the "new policy" Mr. Brandt had cited did not exist in any document the airline could produce.
She lodged a formal complaint with the national aviation ombudsman, attaching the entire correspondence, and waited.
Two weeks later, her telephone rang.
The caller introduced herself as Delphine Arnaud, from the office of the chief executive, and she began with an apology that was, for the first time, specific.
Her tone was conciliatory, and she acknowledged that Clara's seat should have been honoured, that no such policy existed, and that the earlier replies had been inadequate.

The airline would pay for the full repair, offer reimbursement for the cancelled recital and cover the foundation's insurance costs, and it had already issued new guidance to its staff on the carriage of musical instruments.
Clara listened, thanked her and then asked one more question.
"Would you have called me if I hadn't written to the ombudsman?"
There was a pause.
"Honestly," said Delphine, "I'm not sure. But I'm glad you did. We've learned something from this."
The cello came back from Vienna five months later.
Herr Engel had repaired it with such skill that the fracture was invisible, although he warned her that its voice had changed slightly, becoming a little darker in the lower register.
Clara thought it sounded, if anything, more beautiful, and she felt a kind of vindication in knowing that it would outlast them all and pass to posterity.
She played the postponed recital in Toronto the following spring, and she flew there with the cello strapped into the seat beside her.
At the gate in Vienna, a young supervisor looked at her boarding passes, smiled and said, "We've had a memo about you."
At half-time in the final of the county cup, Harlow Vale were losing three–nil, and the score flattered them.
Their opponents, Chelmsford City, were a formidable side, with a striker named Hannah Blythe whose pace and agility had torn the Harlow defence apart for forty-five minutes.
The first goal had come from a mistake, the second from a deflection, and the third from a move of such tactical sophistication that even the Harlow supporters had applauded it, a little ruefully.
Harlow were underdogs in any case: an amateur club whose players were nurses, teachers, students and shop assistants who trained two evenings a week under floodlights on a council pitch.
An ignominious defeat seemed inevitable.
The players walked off the pitch in silence and sat down in the cramped dressing room without looking at one another.
Their coach, Siobhan Kearney, a former international from Galway, had a reputation for ferocity at half-time.
Her speeches were famous in the local league, and some players still told the story of the evening she had kicked a bucket of water across the room.
The team were braced for another such performance.
But Siobhan did not shout.
She stood by the door for almost a minute, looking at each of them in turn, and what she saw told her that shouting would be worse than useless.
Poppy Adair, the nineteen-year-old goalkeeper whose fumble had allowed the first goal, was crying silently into a towel.
Two of the defenders were quarrelling in low, bitter voices about whose fault the second goal had been.
The rest of the team sat with the forlorn, exhausted lassitude of people who have already accepted defeat.
Jade Okoro, the captain, whose tenacity had carried the team through the season, tried to rally them.
"Come on," she said. "We've come back from worse."
It was not true, and everyone knew it, and her voice cracked on the last word.
Siobhan put a hand on her shoulder.
"Sit down, Jade," she said quietly. "You've done enough talking for one day. Let me have a go."
"I won't pretend this is easy," Siobhan began. "It isn't. They're better than us today, and they may be better than us in the second half as well."
Several players looked up, surprised; it was not the rhetoric they had expected.

"But I'm not interested in the score," she went on. "Nobody in this room can change the first half. What I want to know is whether we can win the second one. Three–nil down, a second half we win is still a second half we win."
She turned to Poppy, who was still hiding her face.
"Poppy, you dropped a ball. Every goalkeeper who ever lived has dropped a ball. I'm not going to rebuke you for it, and nobody else in this room is either."
She looked hard at the two defenders, who stopped quarrelling.
"Blame is a luxury for teams that are winning," she said. "We can't afford it."
Then she became entirely practical.
Chelmsford, she pointed out, were playing with a complacency that came from their lead: their defenders were holding the ball too long, confident that nobody would challenge them.

Harlow would switch to a more aggressive formation, press them high up the pitch and pursue them relentlessly, because a team that thinks it has already won is at its most vulnerable and most likely to succumb to pressure.
She gave each player a single, simple task, and made each of them repeat it back to her.
"Nobody is responsible for the result," she said. "Every one of you is responsible for your one job. If we all do our job, the result will take care of itself."
Finally, she reminded them who they were.

"Half of you worked a night shift this week," she said. "Kayla sat an exam on Thursday. Jade, you came straight here from the hospital. Those girls in the other dressing room are good footballers. You are good footballers who also hold this town together. Go and show them what that looks like."
Whatever Chelmsford had expected, it was not what happened next.
Harlow came out with a defiant energy that seemed to take their opponents by surprise, pressing and harrying them into mistakes.
On the hour, Kayla Moss intercepted a careless pass and scored, and ten minutes later Jade rose above two defenders to head in a corner.
The Harlow supporters, who had been sitting in glum silence, were suddenly on their feet in a wave of euphoria.
Chelmsford, rattled, began to argue among themselves, and their cohesion, so impressive in the first half, disintegrated.
With five minutes left, Hannah Blythe broke clear and shot from close range, and Poppy, the goalkeeper who had wept at half-time, flung herself to her left and tipped the ball round the post.
In the third minute of stoppage time, Kayla's shot struck the crossbar and bounced away.
Then the referee blew the final whistle.
Harlow Vale had lost, three–two.
For a few seconds nobody on the Harlow side moved.
It was a peculiar kind of heartbreak, sharper than a heavy defeat would have been, because victory had come so close.
But the crowd, including many of the Chelmsford supporters, stood and applauded them as they left the pitch, and the Chelmsford coach sought Siobhan out to shake her hand.
"I don't know what you said to them at half-time," she said, "but I'd like to borrow it."
For Siobhan, the evening was bittersweet.
In the dressing room, Siobhan found Poppy sitting alone, staring at her gloves.
"You made the best save of the match," she told her. "Remember that one, not the other."
The following season, Harlow Vale reached the final again, against the same opponents, and won it by a single goal.
It was a sweet vindication, but when the players were asked afterwards about the best moment in the club's history, most of them chose a second half that they had won and a match that they had lost.

At two o'clock in the morning, Celia Moreau found Anselm Frei alone in the surgeons' office on the fourth floor, with a sheet of paper in front of him and a cup of coffee that had long since gone cold.
She did not need to read the paper to know what it was.
Twelve hours earlier, a twenty-six-year-old patient named Daniel Asante had died on the operating table during an emergency repair of his aorta, the main artery carrying blood from the heart.
Anselm had led the operation, and Celia, as the anaesthetist, had been at his side throughout.
The complication that killed Daniel had developed with terrifying speed.

The wall of the artery had torn in a place where, according to every scan, it should have been strong, and within minutes the bleeding had become uncontrollable, spreading inexorably despite everything the team could do.

Anselm had fought for two hours with extraordinary tenacity, trying every technique he knew, and when he finally stepped back from the table, Celia had seen in the face of this usually stoical man something she had never seen in twenty years of working with him: not grief, exactly, but a kind of disbelief.
He had then gone to tell Daniel's mother, who had been waiting in the corridor with her two younger children.
"I've written my resignation," he said, without looking up, his voice full of reproach directed entirely at himself.

Anselm was fifty-five, and he was one of the most respected cardiac surgeons in the country, known for his technical prowess and for a perfectionism that his registrars both admired and feared; they sometimes joked that he believed himself infallible.
He had lost patients before, as every surgeon in his field inevitably did, but he had never lost one so young in circumstances he could not explain, and he had never felt so remorseful.
"If I missed something," he said, "I shouldn't be operating. And if I didn't miss anything, then I don't understand my own job any more."
Celia sat down opposite him.
She knew him well enough to recognize that arguing would be futile, and that telling him it was not his fault, which she believed, would sound like the kind of patronizing reassurance he despised.

She also knew that exhaustion and shock were distorting his judgement, and that a decision made at two in the morning after a death, which would be irrevocable once announced, was the opposite of the careful, evidence-based reasoning on which his career had been built.
"I'm not going to tell you what to do," she said. "But before you do anything drastic, will you let me ask you a few questions?"
He shrugged, which she took as consent.
She asked him first whether he still regarded surgery as a vocation, and he said, without hesitation, that he did.
She asked him what he would say to a registrar who came to him in the same situation, having lost a patient after doing everything correctly.
He was silent for a long time.
"I would tell them to wait for the review," he said eventually. "I would tell them that surgeons who are never uncertain are dangerous, and that the ones who care this much are the ones we need."
"Then why is it different for you?" Celia asked.
He did not answer.
She asked him how many patients were on his list for the following month, and he told her: thirty-one, several of them with conditions that few other surgeons in the region could treat.
She asked whether he would want those patients to be operated on by someone who had resigned in a moment of remorse, or by someone who had taken the time to understand what had happened.
"You're manipulating me," he said, but there was the faintest trace of a smile in his voice.
"Yes," she said. "But only a little. Sleep on it, Anselm. The letter will still be there in the morning, and so will I."
He went home, although he later admitted that he had not slept, and he did not submit the letter.
A week later, the hospital held its regular retrospective meeting to review deaths and complications, a process designed not to assign blame but to learn.

The post-mortem had revealed an anatomical abnormality: Daniel had a rare congenital weakness in the wall of his aorta, a condition so unusual that it appeared on none of the scans and had been described only a handful of times in the medical literature.
The reviewers concluded that the tear had not been foreseeable, and that no surgeon could reasonably have saved him.
Anselm listened to the findings without visible emotion.
Afterwards, he told Celia that the conclusion brought him less solace than he had expected.
"It wasn't my fault," he said. "But he's still dead. I think I wanted it to be my fault, because then I could have done something about it."
Celia understood exactly what he meant. In hindsight, she thought, he had needed a reason more than he had needed forgiveness.
The hardest thing about their profession, she had come to believe, was not the possibility of error but the certainty that some losses could not be prevented at all.
Anselm took three weeks of leave to recuperate, which he spent walking in the mountains near Zurich, where he had grown up, and when he returned, he operated again.
He also did something he had never done before: he wrote to Daniel's mother, explaining in plain language what the review had found, and asked whether she would like to meet him.

She did, and they talked for an hour, and at the end she thanked him for not pretending that he knew more than he did. It was, he thought, a magnanimous thing to say to the man who had operated on her son.
A year later, Celia found a single sheet of paper in her pigeonhole.
It was the letter of resignation, unsigned, with a note clipped to it in Anselm's precise handwriting.
"You were right to make me wait," it said. "I've kept this to remind me that the worst decisions are the ones that feel most urgent. Thank you for the questions."
The flood of 2019 had reached the second step of the war memorial in the market square of Harwick, and the town had not forgotten it.
Hundreds of homes in the Old Quay, the low-lying district between the harbour and the estuary, had been evacuated, and some families had not returned for a year.
The council's response had been ambitious: a concrete barrier more than two kilometres long, with steel gates that could close across the mouth of the river whenever a storm surge threatened.
At the time, the plan had seemed a triumph of civic resolve, and nobody had dwelt on its sizable cost.
Five years later, the barrier had still not been built, and the latest estimate had just arrived on the desk of Sandra Blake, the leader of the council.

Rising prices for steel and concrete had almost doubled the cost, leaving a shortfall of sixty million pounds that the government showed no sign of covering, and the council faced a dilemma with no palatable solution.
The engineers also warned that, as sea levels rose inexorably, the barrier would have to close more and more often, and that within fifty years it might be obsolete, a costly burden for posterity.
Sandra read the report twice and then did something she had been resisting for months: she telephoned an engineer in Rotterdam.
Joost van Dijk had spent thirty years managing water in a country where much of the land lies below the level of the sea.
He arrived in Harwick on a grey morning in March, walked the length of the proposed barrier in borrowed boots and spent an afternoon studying old maps in the town library.

The maps revealed the true topography of the district and what the town had forgotten: that the Old Quay had once been salt marshes, which absorbed the tides and released them slowly, and that the district had been built only after the marshes were drained in the nineteenth century.
"Your town is standing in the place where the water used to rest," he told Sandra that evening. "The water remembers, even if the people don't."
He was not, he insisted, against barriers; his own country depended on them.

But the Dutch had learned, after centuries of building ever higher embankments, that walls alone were a precarious strategy, since every wall eventually met a flood higher than itself, and the higher the wall, the more calamitous its failure.

Their newer approach, which they called room for the river, sought an equilibrium between land and water rather than a permanent victory over it, giving floodwater somewhere harmless to go: parks and squares designed to flood, farmland that could be sacrificed temporarily, and buildings raised above the likely level of the water.
The public meeting was held in the town hall, and it was not friendly.
Derek Whitfield, a populist councillor with a gift for slogans who had built his career on opposing Sandra, accused her of abandoning the Old Quay to save money.
"We were promised a wall," he said, to loud applause. "Now we're being told to learn to swim."

His rhetoric was effective because it tapped a genuine grievance: the people of the Old Quay had suffered most in 2019, and they felt, not unreasonably, that the rest of the town had forgotten them. The debate had become so polarized that nuance seemed impossible.
Joost listened to an hour of angry speeches before he was invited to speak.
He did not defend the plan, or attack the barrier, and he spoke with a disarming simplicity.

"For five years, this town has been asking one question," he said. "How do we keep the water out? It is a good question, but it has become a very expensive one. I would like to suggest a different question. Where can the water go without hurting anybody?"
There was a pause, and then someone at the back laughed, but it was not a hostile laugh.
The first person to take the question seriously was Gwen Pugh, who ran a café on the quay and had lost almost everything in the flood.
She invited Joost for coffee the next morning and asked him to explain, in plain English, what room for the river would mean for her street. She was, she warned him, a natural skeptic.

He drew on a napkin: the empty car park behind the café, lowered by a metre and planted with grass, would become a square where children played in summer and where, perhaps once in ten years, the sea would be allowed to sit for a day before draining away.
The houses along the quay could be protected with lower walls, and the most vulnerable could have their ground floors adapted so that a flood became an inconvenience rather than a calamity.
"You're asking us to live with the water," Gwen said slowly.
"I'm asking you to stop pretending that you don't," Joost replied.
She looked out at the harbour, where the tide was coming in over the mud, and was quiet for a long time.
"My grandmother used to say the quay was borrowed from the sea," she said finally. "I always thought it was just a saying."

The final plan, agreed by the council after six months of contentious debate and consultation with every stakeholder, was neither the wall that Derek had demanded nor the pure vision that Joost had sketched.

The barrier was shortened and lowered, which halved its cost, and the money saved was allocated to a network of flood parks, raised walkways and the restoration of a small area of salt marsh at the edge of the estuary, which soon sheltered a burgeoning population of birds.
Gwen's car park became the first of the flood squares.
Derek voted against the plan with characteristic belligerence, then attended the opening of the square and was photographed eating an ice cream in it.
Two winters later, a storm bringing torrential rain drove the North Sea higher than it had been since 2019.
The shortened barrier closed; the square behind the café filled with grey water; and the houses of the Old Quay stayed dry.
The next morning, when the water had drained away, Gwen opened the café as usual and put a sign in the window.
"Borrowed from the sea," it read. "Returned on time."
For Sandra, the night brought a quiet vindication; she had spent it in the control room watching the gauges, and she went home at dawn without making a speech.

For eleven summers, the excavation on the island of Westray, at the northern edge of Orkney, had produced a steady, unspectacular harvest: stone walls, broken pottery, the bones of cattle and sheep, and the remnants of hearths where people had cooked their meals four and a half thousand years ago.

Dr. Elspeth Rowan, who directed the dig, had built her reputation on the argument that this Neolithic settlement had been largely self-sufficient and insular, a small, homogeneous farming community at the edge of the known world, and she had defended this view against skeptics for two decades.
She was a painstaking scholar, and her careful publications had made the site one of the best documented of its period in Europe.
On a windy afternoon in July, Mateo Quispe, a doctoral student from Lima, was cleaning the floor of a small stone chamber when his trowel struck something that was not stone.
Within an hour, he had exposed the curve of a human skull.
Burials were rare on the site, and Elspeth, summoned from the finds tent, knelt beside the trench for a long time before she said anything.
"Nobody touches anything else today," she said finally. "We do this properly or not at all."
It took nine days to excavate the grave, working with brushes and dental tools, meticulously recording each fragment of bone in its exact position.
The skeletal remains were those of a woman in her thirties, lying on her side with her knees drawn up, and in her arms were the fragile bones of an infant.
Beside her head lay a stone ball, carved with a spiral pattern of extraordinary precision, and at her feet someone had placed the skull of a young cow.
Callum Drever, a local farmer who had volunteered on the dig for nine summers, stood at the edge of the trench with his cap in his hands.
"She was somebody," he said quietly. "You don't bury a nobody like that." The grave was plainly an act of commemoration by a community that had valued her.
The ceremonial care of the burial was striking, but it was not, in itself, incompatible with Elspeth's account of the site.
What was incompatible came six months later, when the laboratory results arrived.
The osteologist, Dr. Sunita Rao, had analysed the chemical isotopes preserved in the woman's teeth.
Because the enamel of a tooth forms in childhood and records the chemistry of the water and food a person consumed, it can reveal where she spent her early years.
The woman in the grave had not grown up on Orkney.
Her isotopic signature was incongruous with the local geology and matched, most closely, regions hundreds of kilometres to the south, possibly on the European mainland.
The genomic evidence, analysed separately, suggested that her ancestry, too, was not typical of the island's other inhabitants, and hinted at migratory routes that nobody had suspected.
The results were not conclusive about where exactly she had come from, but they were conclusive about where she had not. Elspeth read the report three times.

For twenty years she had argued that the settlement was isolated, and here, in the most elaborate burial ever found there, was a woman who had travelled a great distance to reach it, and who had been honoured when she died.
It was not the kind of discovery that could be explained away.
She felt, she admitted to Mateo, a mixture of excitement and something very close to embarrassment.
The team spent a long evening in the cottage they rented, arguing about what it might mean.
Mateo hypothesized that she might have come as a bride, forging an alliance between distant communities, a practice well documented in other societies.
Sunita posited that it was conceivable she had been a trader, or a skilled craftswoman, and that the carved ball might have been her own work.
Callum, who had been listening in silence, observed that people on islands had always been sailors, and that even in that primeval landscape the sea was a road, not a wall.
Elspeth insisted on caution.
"For all we know, she was a refugee, or a captive," she said. "We can't rule anything out, and we mustn't let the story we like best become the story we tell."
Any account of her life would be, at best, a conjecture, and the evidence was sparse: a skeleton, an infant, a carved stone and a few chemical signatures.
But one thing, she conceded, was no longer in doubt: the insular community she had described for twenty years had been connected to a much wider world.
Elspeth wrote the paper herself, and it was, colleagues agreed, a model of intellectual honesty.
It presented the new evidence in full, acknowledged unequivocally that it contradicted her own earlier conclusions, and offered several possible explanations without choosing between them.

Some scholars would have buried such a finding in a footnote; Elspeth put it in the title. It was not the vindication she had hoped for at the end of her career, but it was, she decided, something better.
Mateo found himself thinking about the woman more than he expected.

He had grown up in Lima and had travelled eleven thousand kilometres to dig on a windswept island, and he felt a strange kinship with someone who had also crossed a great distance and made her home among strangers.

When the excavation closed at the end of the season, the team placed a small stone for posterity at the spot where she had lain, as the people of Westray had done four and a half thousand years before.
"We don't know her name," Callum said. "But she's not forgotten. That's something." Four and a half thousand years after her death, she had been rescued from oblivion.

The ethics committee of the Bristol Royal Infirmary met on the first Thursday of every month in a room that had once been the hospital chapel, and some of its members joked that the stained-glass windows were the only part of the building that had never been modernized.
Its chair, Dr. Helen Okafor, was a retired kidney specialist who had led the committee for six years.
The committee's remit was broad but its powers were modest: it could not forbid anything, only advise the hospital's board, although in practice the board had never once gone against its advice.
That month there was only one item on the agenda.

The emergency department wanted to adopt an algorithmic triage system called Sentinel, which read each patient's records and vital signs and predicted which of them was most likely to deteriorate over the next few hours.
The impetus had come from Dr. Tomasz Wren, a consultant in emergency medicine with a reputation for impatience and a habit of speaking in statistics.

"Our nurses are assessing sixty patients a shift," he told the committee. "On a bad night, the wait for a doctor is twelve hours. We cannot prioritize properly when we are this overwhelmed, and people are dying in the waiting room while we try."
During a six-month pilot involving eleven thousand patients, Sentinel had identified forty cases of sepsis, on average ninety minutes before the nurses did.
"In sepsis," Dr. Wren said, "ninety minutes is the difference between a course of antibiotics and a funeral."
The committee had asked Asha Rao, a data scientist from the university, to examine the evaluation independently.

She began by praising it: the methodological standards were high, the predictions had been checked against real outcomes, and there was no sign that anyone had tried to optimize the figures for the committee's benefit.
Then she put a second chart on the screen.
Overall, Sentinel performed reliably, but the averages concealed a striking variability.

For patients with long medical histories, it was more accurate than any nurse; for patients whose records were sparse, such as homeless people, recent migrants and people who rarely saw a doctor, it was markedly worse, and it missed nearly one case in three.
The data on which it had been trained was skewed towards the patients the hospital already knew well.
"It isn't that the algorithm is prejudiced," Asha said. "It simply knows least about the people we know least about."
There was a silence, which the patient representative, Mrs. Joan Pilling, was the first to break.
She was a former headmistress in her seventies who had joined the committee after her husband's death, and she had an unnerving ability to reduce a long discussion to a single sentence.
"So the people the system already fails," she said, "are the people this machine will fail again."
Dr. Wren did not dispute the numbers, but he rejected the conclusion.

"Suppose we turn it down," he said. "Then we go back to a system in which exhausted nurses make these judgements with no help at all. Is that unbiased? Nurses have blind spots too. We just don't measure them."
It was, Helen thought, a fair point, and an uncomfortable one: the committee's presumption that the old way was neutral was exactly that, a presumption.
The finance director, Gerald Fenwick, tried to make the problem simpler.
"Let's say the tool saves thirty lives a year and costs us three," he said. "I'm not saying three is nothing. But surely the arithmetic is clear."
"Would you still say that," Helen asked, "if the three were always from the same group? The same streets, the same shelters, the same people who have no one to complain on their behalf?"
Gerald conceded that he would find that harder to defend, and the discussion moved, as ethical discussions often did, from the numbers to the principle behind them.
A purely utilitarian calculation would approve Sentinel at once, since it would save more lives in total.
But most of the committee felt that a tool which systematically disadvantaged one group was antithetical to the whole idea of a public hospital, whatever its average performance.
"Then where do you draw the line?" Dr. Wren asked. "No treatment in this building works equally well for everyone. If the standard is perfection, we'd have to close the hospital."
It was Asha who turned the argument from the hypothetical to the actual.
Among the pilot records, she said, was the case of a fifty-two-year-old man brought in by paramedics on a freezing night in February, confused, feverish and with no fixed address.
Because his record contained almost nothing, Sentinel had rated him low risk.
The triage nurse, a woman with thirty years' experience, had not liked the look of him; she had overridden the rating and called a doctor, and the man turned out to have advanced sepsis.
He survived.
"So the system worked," Gerald said. "The nurse caught it."
"This nurse caught it," Joan replied. "The question is whether the next one will. Will a junior nurse at four in the morning, on her third night shift in a row, really contradict the screen?"
Dr. Wren was silent for a moment, and then, to his credit, he admitted that she probably would not.
People tended to attribute a kind of infallibility to anything that produced a number, and the more tired they were, the more readily they deferred to it.
The danger, Helen suggested, was not that Sentinel would replace clinical judgement but that it would quietly relegate it to a formality.
By the end of the evening, the committee had agreed on a recommendation, though not without dissension.
Sentinel would be approved, but only under strict stipulations.

It would advise and never decide; nurses would be able to override it without filling in any form, since an administrative hindrance would discourage the very judgements the committee wanted to protect; and its performance for each group of patients would be stringently audited every three months.
Any patient with a sparse record would be seen by a senior nurse regardless of the score, and if the gap between groups had not narrowed within a year, the system would be discontinued.
Gerald thought the conditions were expensive, and said so.
Dr. Wren worried that they would detract from the very benefits that had made the proposal worth considering, but he accepted them rather than lose the tool altogether.
"I don't condone the gap," he said as they packed up. "I just don't think refusing to use the tool will close it."
The vote was seven to two, and the board ratified the recommendation the following month.
A year later, the gap had narrowed, though it had not closed.
Partly at the committee's behest, the hospital had begun collecting better information about patients it had rarely seen before, and the tool had been trained again on the new data.

The quarterly audits had also revealed something nobody had predicted: nurses were overriding Sentinel more often than expected, and they were right about half the time, which suggested that the conversation between human and machine was more useful than either of them alone.
When Helen presented the review to the committee, Joan asked whether they had, in the end, found the line Dr. Wren had challenged them to draw.
Helen thought about it for a moment.

"I don't think lines like that are found," she said. "I think they're drawn, by the people who have to live with them, and then moved when the evidence changes. The only unethical thing would be to draw one and never look at it again."
The news reached Daniel Okafor in a rehearsal room in Leeds, where he was directing a production of Hamlet that was three weeks from opening and not yet ready.
Arthur Penhaligon, who had taught him English at a comprehensive school in Penzance thirty years earlier, had died at the age of eighty-six.

Daniel had not seen him for more than a decade, and he was surprised by the force of his own reaction, a grief that seemed almost disproportionate: he sat down on the edge of the stage and found that he could not speak.
Mr. Penhaligon had been, by universal agreement, the most formidable teacher in the school.
He was austere, sardonic and exacting, his methods were idiosyncratic, and his comments on essays were notorious: brief, handwritten in green ink and occasionally devastating.
Daniel, at fifteen, had been a defiant and rather lazy pupil with a talent for clever sentences that meant very little, and their relationship had begun badly.
His first essay for Mr. Penhaligon came back with a single comment, written across the top of the page: "Say what you mean. Then stop."
He took the train from Paddington on the morning of the funeral, a journey of more than five hours to the far western tip of the country.

As the train ran along the coast, where the line hugged the sea so closely that spray sometimes struck the windows, he found himself recalling fragments of his adolescence with an unexpected, almost painful clarity.
He remembered, with a wistful ache, being sent out of the classroom for mocking a poem, and the long silence afterwards in the corridor, where Mr. Penhaligon had come to find him.
"You mock it because it frightens you," the old man had said, with no trace of derision. "It frightens me too. That's how you know it's good."
He also remembered the day, a year later, when Mr. Penhaligon had surreptitiously handed him a key.
It opened the school's tiny theatre, which was locked outside lessons, and the teacher had given it to him without explanation, except to say that he should not tell the headmaster.

Daniel had spent most of his evenings there for the next two years, directing his friends in plays that he wrote himself, and it was in that clandestine theatre, he had often thought since, that he had found his vocation.
The chapel in Penzance was small, cold and melancholy in the winter light, and it was full, which surprised him.

He recognized faces he had not seen in thirty years, grown heavier and greyer, and others he did not know at all: generations of former pupils, it turned out, some of whom had travelled from as far as Scotland. Arthur had published nothing and would leave no mark on posterity, except in the people gathered in that room.
Before the service began, a woman in her fifties approached him and introduced herself as Harriet, Arthur's daughter.
"You're Daniel," she said. "He talked about you. The boy with the key."
Then she explained, apologetically, that the former headmaster, who had been due to speak, had been taken ill that morning, and asked whether Daniel would be willing to say a few words in his place.
"Nothing elaborate," she said. "He hated elaborate things. Just whatever comes to you."
Daniel, who spent his professional life telling actors that nothing on a stage should ever be improvised, heard himself say yes.
When his turn came, he walked to the lectern without notes, and for a moment the silence of the chapel seemed to press on him physically.
"I wasn't planning to say anything today," he began, "so you'll have to forgive me if this is less polished than he would have liked."
A few people laughed, gently, because they knew exactly what he meant.
He told them about the first essay and its green comment, and about the poem he had mocked.
He recounted one of the anecdotes that pupils had passed down for decades: that the old man had once returned an essay with the single word "Why?" written forty times in the margin.
He told them about the key, which he had never returned, and which he took out of his pocket and held up so that they could see it.

He said that Mr. Penhaligon had been the least sentimental man he had ever known, and also, paradoxically, the kindest, because his kindness took the form of refusing to accept anything less than your best.
"He taught us that a sentence is a promise," Daniel said, "and that it's dishonest to make promises you can't keep."
Then, remembering the green ink, he stopped.
The silence afterwards was different from the silence before, and it was the spontaneity of the speech, not its eloquence, that had moved them.
Somewhere near the back, a man who must have been in his sixties was weeping openly, and several others were smiling through their tears.
It was, Daniel thought as he sat down, the only speech he had ever given that he could not have rehearsed, and perhaps the only one that had mattered.
Afterwards, at the house, Harriet found him in the garden, thanked him with a heartfelt embrace and gave him a large brown envelope.
"He left it with his papers," she said. "It has your name on it. I've no idea what's inside."
Inside was Daniel's first essay, thirty years old and faded, the green ink still legible across the top.
Pinned to it was a newspaper review of one of Daniel's productions from the previous year, and a note in the same handwriting, frail and shakier now, that said only: "You did. Well done."
Daniel stood in the garden for a long time, holding the envelope, while the light faded over the sea.

It was a bittersweet solace, but a real one: the old man had been watching all along, from a distance, and had kept his approval, like everything else, until it could be expressed in the fewest possible words.
On the train back to Leeds, Daniel took out the script of Hamlet and began, ruthlessly, to cut it.
The case of Holloway against Veridian Motors had been listed for eight days in the High Court in London, and by the fifth it had become a contest between two stories about a single second.
On a wet night two years earlier, Tom Holloway's car had drifted out of its lane on the M4 and struck a barrier, and he had been killed instantly.
The car was equipped with a system designed to keep it in its lane, and his widow, Rosa, alleged that the system had malfunctioned.
Veridian maintained that the system had functioned exactly as intended, and that the fault lay with a driver who had been distracted.
Rosa's barrister was Sebastian Crane, a lawyer of formidable prowess in cross-examination whose manner in court was so courteous that witnesses often failed to notice they were being dismantled.
Veridian's principal expert was Dr. Philippa Marsh, an eminent engineer who had written a seminal textbook on vehicle safety and whose reputation for integrity was, by common consent, impeccable.
Her written report concluded unequivocally that the system had worked correctly.
Everyone in court understood that if her evidence stood, the case was lost.
Rosa sat in the front row every day, her hands folded in her lap, listening to hours of technical evidence about her husband's death with a stoicism that Sebastian found almost unbearable to watch.
She had refused two offers of settlement, both conditional on her silence, because what she wanted was not money but an acknowledgement that the car had failed.
"If it happened to Tom," she had told Sebastian at their first meeting, "it will happen to someone else, and I won't be the reason nobody knows."
Sebastian had spent three nights reading her report, and he had found no error in it.
Its methodology was rigorous, its reasoning clear, and its conclusions followed logically from its evidence.
What troubled him was not what the report said, but what it did not say.
Nowhere did it describe the raw telemetry from Tom Holloway's car, the second-by-second record of steering, speed and sensor readings stored in the vehicle's computer.
Instead, it relied on a summary prepared by Veridian's own engineers.
It was the kind of omission that an expert might make in good faith, trusting the data she had been given.
But if the summary was selective, the report built on it might be erroneous without anyone having lied.
Sebastian decided that he would not attack her conclusions at all.
He would ask only about the foundations, and he would ask questions to which there could be only one honest answer.
"Dr. Marsh, you have enormous experience in this field, haven't you?" he began, when she had taken the oath.
"I have," she said, a little warily.
"And you would agree that an expert's conclusions can be no more reliable than the data on which they are based?"
"Naturally."
"Isn't it the case that your report relies on a summary of the car's data, prepared by the defendant's own engineers?"
"It relies on the data provided to me, yes."
"Did you examine the raw telemetry yourself? Yes or no, please."
There was a pause, which the judge, Mrs. Justice Adebayo, noted without comment.
"No," Dr. Marsh said. "The raw files are in a proprietary format. I was told the summary contained everything relevant."
"Who told you that?"
"Veridian's legal department."
Sebastian let the answer settle in the silence of the courtroom before he asked his next question.
"Would you agree that a summary, by its nature, omits information?"
"Of course. That is what a summary is."
"And that, as an independent expert, you cannot tell us what the summary left out, because you have never seen what it was summarizing?"
Dr. Marsh looked at him for a long moment, and something in her expression changed.
"That is correct," she said.
"No further questions, my lady," said Sebastian, and sat down.
Veridian's barrister rose to repair the damage, but the judge adjourned the hearing for the afternoon and ordered the company to disclose the raw telemetry to both parties within seven days.
In the corridor outside, Rosa Holloway gripped Sebastian's arm and asked whether they had won.
"Not yet," he said. "But we've stopped losing."
He did not tell her that he felt, beneath his satisfaction, a certain discomfort.
He had not caught the expert in a lie; he had merely demonstrated, with the relentless politeness of his profession, that she had trusted the wrong people.
That evening, to his considerable surprise, Dr. Marsh telephoned his chambers.
She could not, she said, discuss the substance of the case, and she would say nothing that compromised her duty to the court.
But she wanted him to know that she had asked Veridian for the raw files twice during her investigation and had been refused both times, and that she had been uneasy ever since.
"You asked exactly the question I should have insisted on," she said. "I'm not sure whether to thank you or resent you."
When the telemetry was finally disclosed, it took the engineers on both sides less than a day to find what the summary had omitted.

In the four seconds before the crash, one of the camera sensors had repeatedly lost sight of the lane markings in the rain, and the system had switched itself off without giving the driver the audible warning that the manual promised.
The discrepancy was small, a matter of software rather than hardware, but it was precisely the kind of detail that had disappeared from the summary.
Dr. Marsh filed a supplementary report acknowledging that her original conclusion could not be sustained.
Veridian settled the case a week later, on terms that were confidential but that Rosa described to the newspapers as "an admission in everything but words".
The company also quietly updated the software in thousands of cars.
In hindsight, Sebastian thought, the whole case had turned on a single omission, and on an expert honest enough to admit it.
Sebastian kept the transcript of the cross-examination, and he sometimes gave it to young barristers as an example.
"The best question," he would tell them, "isn't the one that proves the witness wrong. It's the one that lets an honest witness tell the truth."
When Zofia Nowak was appointed to lead the water infrastructure team at a large engineering consultancy in Belfast, her first feeling was not pride but dread.

She was thirty-four, and the most senior member of the team was Desmond Carlin, sixty-one, who had led it for twelve years, had hired her straight out of university, and had been widely expected to keep the job until he retired.

The directors, citing a need for fresh thinking, had decided otherwise, and they had informed Des of their decision in a meeting that lasted, by his account, eleven minutes, a brevity that struck many colleagues as callous.
He had congratulated Zofia with impeccable courtesy, and then, she heard from colleagues, gone home early for the first time in a decade.
Zofia owed him a great deal.
He was a formidable engineer, adept at the kind of practical judgement that no software could replicate, and he knew every reservoir and pumping station in Northern Ireland by heart.
He was also, she knew, proud, stubborn and occasionally patronizing, and his resentment, if it festered, could quietly erode the cohesion of a team that was already stretched.
The team had lost two engineers in the past year, an attrition that the directors attributed to low morale, and a third, Kieran Walsh, was so overloaded that he had started sleeping at his desk.
Her first instinct was to do everything herself, to prove that the directors had been right.
Her second, wiser instinct was to resist the first.
A manager who hoarded work, she had learned from watching others, created bottlenecks, exhausted herself and conveyed, however unintentionally, that she did not trust her team.
Trust, she believed, was a prerequisite for delegation, and delegation, on the other hand, was not simply a matter of handing out tasks.
It required her to match each responsibility to the person best equipped for it, to explain why it mattered, and then to step back without either micromanaging or disappearing.
She began with Kieran, because his situation was the most urgent. He had been reluctant to admit that he was struggling, fearing that it would mark him out for redundancy.

Rather than simply taking work away from him, which he might have interpreted as a judgement on his competence, she asked him to list everything he was doing and to mark the tasks that only he could do.
There were four such tasks out of nineteen.
To Kieran's evident gratification, the remaining fifteen were redistributed, and within a month Kieran was going home at six.
The conversation with Des was harder, and she postponed it for a week, which she later regarded as a mistake.

In that week he was scrupulously polite and conspicuously unhelpful: he answered every question she asked and volunteered nothing, and when a client telephoned with a complex problem about a failing dam, he passed the call to her with a faint, sardonic smile.
It was a tacit challenge, and they both knew it; it was not posturing, exactly, but it was close.
She asked him to lunch, away from the office, and began by acknowledging what nobody else had said aloud.
"I know this isn't the outcome you expected," she said, "and I know the way it was handled was poor. I'm not going to pretend otherwise."
Des looked at her for a long moment.
