"Twelve years," he said. "And they told me in eleven minutes."

She let him talk, and his grievance, once spoken aloud, seemed to lose some of its force; he talked for a long time, about the projects he had led, the graduates he had trained and the humiliation of learning about his future from a slide presentation.
When he had finished, she told him plainly that the team could not succeed without him, and that she did not want him to spend his last years merely waiting for retirement.
Then she asked him whether he would be willing to take on two responsibilities that she thought only he could carry out.
The first was the failing dam, a project so technically delicate that a misjudgement could have calamitous consequences for the towns downstream.

She would remain accountable for it, she said, but she wanted him to lead the technical work, with full authority over the engineering decisions, because nobody in the company understood old dams as he did.
The second was the training of the team's graduates, whose development had been neglected during the years of overwork, and whose attrition was costing the firm dearly.
"You're giving me the hardest project and the most junior people," Des said slowly.
"I'm giving you the two things I'm most afraid of getting wrong," Zofia replied. "Would you be willing to take them on?"
He did not answer immediately.

But on the way back to the office he asked her, in an ostensibly casual tone, whether she had read the original survey of the dam from 1962, and when she admitted that she had not, he promised to dig it out for her.
The repair of the dam was completed on time and under budget, and the regulator described the engineering as exemplary. For Des, it was a quiet vindication.
Des presented the project to the directors himself, at Zofia's insistence, in a meeting that lasted considerably longer than eleven minutes.
The graduates he trained became, within a year, the most capable junior engineers in the firm, and none of them left. What had begun in something close to hostility ended in a genuine reconciliation.

At his retirement party, Des made a short speech, dry at first and then unexpectedly heartfelt, in which he thanked the directors, dryly, for their "brisk communication", and then thanked Zofia for something he found harder to name.
"She gave me work instead of sympathy," he said. "It turns out that's what I wanted."
Zofia, who had spent the year learning that leadership consisted less in doing things than in deciding who should do them, found that she could not reply without her voice betraying her.

The miners' institute in Cwmderyn had been built in 1908 with money the miners collected from their own wages, a penny a week, so that the valley would have a library, a reading room and a hall where anyone could come to hear a lecture.
More than a century later, the building was half derelict, its paint peeling and its roof patched with plastic sheeting, but the hall was still in use.
Dr. Ingrid Solberg, a Norwegian climate scientist who worked at the university in Cardiff, had been invited by the town's librarian, Bethan Hughes, to give a talk on the future of the climate.

She had given the same lecture perhaps fifty times, to students, politicians and sympathetic audiences in comfortable cities, and she had almost refused this invitation, because she suspected, correctly, that it would be different.
The opencast coal mine above the town had closed two years earlier, and with it had gone four hundred jobs, the last large employer in the valley.
The high street was moribund, with more empty shops than open ones, and the valley, like many others in Wales, had been blighted by unemployment since the deep pits closed in the 1980s.

The government had promised that the town would share in the new green economy, with training schemes, subsidies for new businesses and a wind farm on the hill, but so far the wind farm had produced more planning disputes than jobs, and the site on the hill stood forlornly empty.
When Ingrid arrived, there were about eighty people in the hall, most of them over fifty, sitting with their coats on because the heating had broken.
She began, as she always did, with the graph of global temperatures, the long flat line of the last thousand years and the sharp rise at the end.
The logic, in her view, was inexorable: the burning of coal, oil and gas had warmed the planet, and it would go on warming it until the burning stopped.
She had reached the part about coal, and was explaining why the remaining mines would have to close, when a man in the third row stood up.
"Easy for you to say," he said indignantly, loudly enough to be heard at the back. "You've got a job for life at the university. Who's paying for your graph?"
He paused, rhetorically, and then answered his own question: "We are."
His name, she learned later, was Gareth Pryce.
He was fifty-eight, and he had driven the huge trucks at the mine for thirty-one years, until the morning he was told, along with everyone else, that his job had been made redundant.
The hall had gone completely silent, and several people were nodding.
The contrast between her tidy graph and the cold hall full of people in coats suddenly seemed jarring.
Ingrid had given this lecture fifty times, but she was unprepared for this; she had never seen firsthand what the closure of a mine did to a town.
She felt the familiar urge to retort with a barrage of statistics, and suppressed it.
"I hear you," she said, "and I don't want to brush that aside. Let me finish this point, if I may, and then I'll come straight back to you. I promise."
Gareth sat down, visibly surprised, and she finished her point in two minutes rather than the usual ten.
Then she did something she had never done before: she stopped the lecture, walked to the edge of the stage and asked him to say what he wanted to say.
He was not, it turned out, a belligerent man, merely an understandably angry one, and he spoke for nearly five minutes without notes.
He described the mine, not as a romantic place, since it had been dirty and dangerous work, but as the bedrock of the town, the thing that had held it together.
He talked about the men he had worked with, three of whom had not found another job, and one of whom had taken his own life.
He talked about the training courses that had been offered in Cardiff, an hour and a half away by a bus that ran twice a day.

"You people come here and lament what's happening to the planet," he said. "Nobody laments what's happened to us. You think we're parochial because we want to stay where we were born. We've been marginalized for forty years, and now we're being told it's for our own good."
When he sat down, the applause was resounding, and Ingrid understood that the room was no longer an audience but a jury.
She was determined not to equate his anger with ignorance, which was the mistake she had watched so many experts make.
She could have defended herself; instead, she began by conceding what was true.

"You're right that the people who make climate policy rarely pay its costs," she said. "You're right that promises were made to this valley and broken, and you're right that I have a secure job and a comfortable house. I'd be misleading you if I pretended otherwise."
She paused.

"But I'd also be misleading you if I said the science was different because the politics has been unfair. The physics doesn't care who pays. What we can argue about, and what we should argue about, is who pays, and how much, and when."
It was not a conciliatory speech, exactly, but nor was it confrontational, and she made no attempt to appease the room with promises she could not keep.
But it was, she hoped, an honest one.

She told them that she thought the wind farm should belong partly to the town, as some villages in Denmark owned theirs, and that the training should come to the valley rather than the other way round.
Someone at the back said that she should tell that to the government, and she replied that she intended to, which got the first laugh of the evening.
After the talk, there was tea in a small kitchen that smelled of damp, and Gareth came over with two cups and handed her one.
"I came here to shout at you," he admitted. "My granddaughter told me not to. Seren's very outspoken. She's doing environmental science at school, and she says you're right about all of it."
"She's right about the physics," Ingrid said. "You're right about the rest. I nearly lost my temper, you know."
"You hid it well," he said, and the disarming honesty of it made her laugh.
They talked for another hour, long after Bethan had begun stacking the chairs.
He told her about the nostalgia that was common in the valley, which he distrusted, because the old days had also meant lungs full of dust and funerals at forty.
What he could not forgive was not that the mine had closed, but that it had closed in such a heartless way, as if the people who worked there did not matter.
Ingrid rewrote her lecture on the train home, with Gareth's words still reverberating in her head.
She no longer began with the graph, which she moved to the middle, but with a photograph of the hall in Cwmderyn and the story of the penny a week that had built it.
The science, she now told her audiences, was settled; the fairness was not, and it would decide whether the rest of the argument could be won.

The following spring, she and Gareth spoke together at a conference in Cardiff on the future of the old coal towns, and the organizers, who had expected a debate, got something closer to a conversation.
When a young man in the audience interrupted her to ask why anyone should listen to a scientist, Gareth leaned towards the microphone before she could answer.
"Let her finish, if you don't mind," he said. "Then you can have your turn. It works, I promise you."
The interview room in Croydon had no windows, a table bolted to the floor and a clock that ran four minutes fast.

Amira Haddad had spent a great part of the past twelve years in rooms like it, interpreting for people who were asking the British state for protection, and she had learned to think of herself as a kind of window: something the words passed through without being altered.
The ideal interpreter, her first trainer had told her, was unobtrusive, a conduit rather than a participant, and the moment she began to judge what she heard, she ceased to be useful to anyone.
Her professional code was strict and unequivocal.
She was to render everything that was said, verbatim where possible, without adding, omitting or softening anything, and she was to remain impartial, neither helping the applicant nor hindering him.

The applicant that morning was Karim Nasser, a twenty-four-year-old from Homs, who had fled Syria after being detained, he said, by a pro-government militia that suspected him of supporting the insurgency.
He had crossed into Lebanon by a clandestine route, spent a year in limbo in Beirut, and eventually reached Britain hidden in a truck.
This was his second interview.

The caseworker, a tired, conscientious man named Philip Dunmore, explained at the start that there were inconsistencies between Karim's first interview, conducted a year earlier with a different interpreter, and the statement he had since submitted in writing.
"If we can't explain them," Mr. Dunmore said, "they'll damage the credibility of the whole claim."
Home Office guidance required him to consider whether an account was internally consistent, and a story that changed each time it was told was, in his experience, very hard to substantiate.
He was not, he added carefully, accusing anyone of fabricating evidence.
For three hours, Amira rendered Karim's account into English, sentence by sentence.
Nothing he said reached Mr. Dunmore unmediated; every word passed first through her.

He described the checkpoint where he had been stopped, the weeks of incarceration in a basement, the interrogator who never gave his name, the intimidation of his family afterwards, and the scars on his back that a doctor had already documented.
He spoke quietly and precisely, and when he reached the most painful parts, he looked at the table rather than at either of them.
He seemed to grasp the tacit rules of the room without being told: he paused after every two or three sentences so that Amira could keep up, and he never once addressed her instead of the caseworker.
Amira kept her own voice level and her face composed, since it was not her place to show emotion, but it was the kind of testimony that she would carry home with her.
Then Mr. Dunmore turned to the inconsistency that troubled him most.
In the first interview, according to the transcript, Karim had said that his brother had been arrested with him at the checkpoint.
In his written statement, however, he said that he had no brothers, only two sisters, and that the man arrested with him was his cousin.
"So which is true?" Mr. Dunmore asked. "Your brother or your cousin? Because you can't have both."
Karim looked at him in consternation.
The ostensible question was a detail about his family, but what was really at stake was whether anything he said could be believed.
Amira rendered the question faithfully, and as Karim answered, she felt a small, cold certainty forming.

In the colloquial Arabic of Homs, as in many dialects, young men often referred to a close male cousin, the son of a father's brother, with a term that could, in context, sound very much like "brother", and families who grew up in the same house frequently used the two words almost interchangeably.
The word's connotation of closeness and loyalty went well beyond its literal denotation, and every family had its own idiosyncrasies when it came to names.
A previous interpreter, perhaps from a different region, or perhaps simply rushing, might easily have translated the one as the other.
The discrepancy on which the caseworker was building his doubts might be semantic rather than factual.
She was struck by the incongruity of it: a young man's safety might depend on the translation of a single word.
The difficulty was that she could not say so as an advocate.
She was an intermediary, not an ally, and she had never felt a qualm about that principle, but in practice the line between clarifying a word and arguing a case was not always easy to see.

Her code prohibited her from offering opinions about the case, and if she seemed to be taking Karim's side, she would compromise both her own impartiality and the credibility of anything he said through her.
But the same code required her to flag any problem of interpretation that might distort communication.
She took a breath, and spoke to Mr. Dunmore directly, as the procedure allowed.
"Before the applicant answers," she said, "I'd like to point out a possible issue of interpretation, if I may."
She explained, briefly and neutrally, the ambiguity of the term, and suggested that the question be put to Karim in a way that avoided it.
Mr. Dunmore considered this for a moment.
"All right," he said. "Put the question in whatever way you think is clearest."
Amira then asked Karim, in Arabic, to name the man who had been arrested with him, to say who his father was, and to explain exactly how they were related.
Karim's answer was precise.
The man was called Samir; his father was the brother of Karim's father; they had grown up in the same house, shared a bedroom until they were fifteen, and called each other brother all their lives.
"If I've understood you correctly," Amira rendered for Mr. Dunmore, "you're saying that he is your cousin by blood, but that in your family you call him your brother."
"Yes," Karim said, in English. "Exactly. He is my brother. He is my cousin. Both."
The interview ended an hour later, after Amira had stolen several surreptitious glances at the clock.
"Thank you, Ms Haddad," Mr. Dunmore said in a neutral voice, as protocol required, and she left the building without knowing what he would decide.
Interpreters rarely learned the outcome of the cases they worked on; their role ended when the talking stopped, and the anonymity was part of what made them trustworthy.
She went home, cooked dinner for her daughter and did not sleep well.
She felt oddly bereft, as she often did after a long case, as if she had lent her voice to a stranger and not quite got it back.

Four months later, a colleague who worked for a refugee charity mentioned, not knowing Amira's involvement, that a young man from Homs had been granted asylum after an appeal hearing at which the judge had criticized an earlier mistranslation.
Amira said nothing, since there was nothing she was permitted to say, but that evening she allowed herself a glass of wine and a long look out of the window.
She had not taken anyone's side, she reflected.
She did not feel triumphant, or even vindicated, since her own opinion had never been the point.
She had simply insisted that a word mean what the person who said it meant, which was, when she thought about it, the whole of her profession.
The hall in Dublin held six hundred people, and on the night of the national university debating final every seat was taken.
Eleanor Whitlock, the incumbent champion, had reached the final three years in a row, and she had a reputation for audacity that she both enjoyed and slightly feared.
She was known for the speed of her thinking and the ferocity of her rebuttals, and younger debaters spoke of her rhetorical prowess with a mixture of admiration and dread.

Her opponent in the final was Kwame Ofori, an engineering student from Cork who spoke slowly, prepared meticulously and had won his semi-final by making the other team's arguments collapse under the weight of their own assumptions.
The motion was announced fifteen minutes before the debate, as the rules required.
"This House would give rivers the rights of legal persons," the chair read, and a murmur ran through the audience.
Kwame and his partner, Aoife Brennan, would propose the motion.
Eleanor and her partner, Cian Doherty, would oppose it.
"Easy," Cian whispered as they hurried to the preparation room. "We just have to make it sound as farcical as it is."
They built their case quickly.
A river could not consent, could not vote and could not appear in court, so the language of rights, applied to it, was at best a metaphor and at worst an absurdity.
Rights, they would argue, were reciprocal: they came with duties, and nobody could hold a river responsible when it burst its banks and drowned a village.
Most damaging of all, someone would have to speak for the river, and whoever did so would wield enormous power without any democratic accountability.
Eleanor wrote her opening line on a card and underlined it twice.
"My opponents want to give the vote to the weather," it read.
It was the kind of line that made audiences laugh, and she knew from experience that an audience which laughed at a proposition rarely voted for it.
Yet as the minutes passed she felt a small, persistent unease that she could not quite name.
Kwame spoke first, and he did not make a single joke.
He spoke without rhetorical flourishes, and the effect was disarming.
He began by reminding the audience that the law already treated many things that were not human beings as persons.
"Every company in this country is a legal person," he said. "It can own property, sign contracts and sue. Nobody thinks a company can vote. We call it a legal fiction, and it is extremely useful."
If a corporation could have rights without a body or a conscience, he asked, why should the idea be any more absurd when applied to a river?
He then described the Whanganui River in New Zealand, which had been recognized as a legal person in 2017 after a long campaign by the Māori communities who regarded it as an ancestor.

The river was represented by two guardians, one appointed by the Māori and one by the Crown, who could take polluters to court on its behalf without having to prove that any individual person had been harmed.
"This is not poetry," Kwame said. "It is plumbing. It gives the river a pipe into the courtroom."
The audience laughed then, but with him, not at him.
Eleanor looked down at her card and realized that her opening line had just become a liability.
She discarded the card and spoke without it.

She argued that the analogy with corporations was spurious, because a company existed to serve the interests of identifiable human beings, whereas the interests of a river were whatever its guardians declared them to be.
Would a river have the right to flood? she asked. Would a farmer who drained a field be violating its rights?
"The proposition offers us the metaphysical language of personhood," she said, "when what they are really describing is a new and unaccountable form of authority."
It was a cogent speech, and she delivered it with her usual fluency, but she could feel that the room had not moved.
Aoife, speaking second for the proposition, dismantled her questions one by one, beginning with the most contentious.

Rivers already flooded without anyone's permission, she pointed out, and the guardians were bound by a statute that defined their duties precisely, which made them more accountable, not less, than many of the corporations that had poisoned the river for a century.
When Aoife sat down, the applause went on for a long time.
Eleanor had four minutes for the final speech of the opposition, and during the two speeches that followed hers she had made a decision that frightened her.
The usual strategy in a summation was to concede nothing, to repeat one's strongest points and to portray the other side's arguments as a collection of errors.
She had done it many times, and she knew it worked; but she also knew that tonight it would be a kind of posturing, and that the audience would see through it.
"I want to begin by granting my opponents two things," she said, and the room went very quiet.

"They are right that a company is no less a fiction than a river would be, and my partner and I were wrong to treat the idea as a joke. They are also right that the Whanganui guardians have done real good."

She paused. "But that is precisely why the question matters. The problem is not whether rivers deserve protection. It is whether we protect them best by inventing a new kind of person, or by writing better laws for the persons we already have."

She argued that the success in New Zealand depended on a particular history and a particular relationship between a people and a river, and that exporting it to places without that history risked creating guardians who spoke for nobody.
It was a narrower argument than the one she had planned, and a more honest one.
Some would later call it magnanimous; to Eleanor it felt simply necessary.
The adjudicators deliberated for twenty minutes.
When they returned, the chief adjudicator announced that the debate had been won by the proposition, and Kwame and Aoife embraced to a standing ovation.
Then he added that the award for the best individual speaker had been decided unanimously, and read out Eleanor's name.
"In twenty years of judging," he said, "I have rarely heard a summation that conceded so much and lost so little."
Afterwards, in a crowded pub near the river, Kwame found her at the bar.
"You could have ridiculed us," he said. "It would probably have worked on half the room."
"Probably," Eleanor admitted. "But it would have been grandstanding. And you were right about the corporations."
"You were right about the history," he said. "I'm going to have to think about that."

They argued amiably until closing time, without a trace of the derision she usually reserved for her opponents, and Eleanor realized, walking home along the dark river, that it was the first debate in years that she had not wanted to win at any cost.

At a quarter past six on a grey October morning, Carl Rennie climbed the ladder of the tower crane on a building site beside the river Clyde, pulled the ladder hatch shut behind him and did not come down.
He had operated the crane for fourteen months, and for the last four of them he had not been paid.

The contractor that employed him had gone into liquidation, its directors had disappeared, and the developer who owned the site insisted that the remuneration of subcontractors was not his responsibility.
Carl's grievance was entirely legitimate; his method of expressing it was extremely dangerous.
By seven o'clock the police had established a cordon around the site, and by eight Inspector Maria Solano had arrived.

She had spent eleven years as a negotiator and had been called to bridges, rooftops and hostage situations, and she had learned that the most important skill in her profession was not persuasion but patience, a quiet stoicism that could outlast almost anyone's anger.
The senior officers wanted the incident resolved quickly, since the crane overlooked a busy road that had been closed, and the resulting congestion was already attracting complaints.
"We have all day," Maria told them firmly. "If we rush him, we may not have him at all."
The site manager lent her a radio that connected to the cab of the crane, and for twenty minutes Carl refused to answer.
When he finally did, his voice was hoarse and furious.
"If you've come to talk me down, you're wasting your breath," he said. "I'm not moving until I'm paid."
Maria did not argue.
"My name's Maria," she said. "I'm not here to arrest you or to trick you. Help me understand what's happened, Carl. From the beginning, in your own words."
He talked for almost an hour.
He described the months of excuses, the unanswered emails and the day he had arrived at the contractor's office to find it empty, with the furniture gone and the phones disconnected.
He was three months behind with his mortgage, his family's finances were precarious, and his daughter Ellie, who was nine, had started asking why he no longer went to work.
Maria listened without interrupting, occasionally repeating a phrase back to him so that he knew she had heard it.
"It sounds as if you've done everything properly," she said at one point, "and nobody has listened."
There was a long silence on the radio, and then, for the first time, his voice cracked.
Maria waited, and her silence, which some colleagues found unnerving, gave him room to continue.
Maria's training had taught her a set of principles that sounded simple and were extraordinarily difficult to follow.
Anger, she knew, was often grief in disguise, and it was futile to meet it with logic.
She was not to lie, because a single discovered lie would destroy the fragile rapport she was building, and she was not to promise anything she could not deliver.

She was not to argue with his feelings, however unreasonable they seemed, and she was to avoid the platitudes that people in crisis find most patronizing, such as telling them that everything would be fine.
Above all, she was to slow everything down, because time, in her experience, was almost always on the side of the negotiator.
By noon, the wind had risen, and the arm of the crane was swaying in the gusts.
Carl had brought no water, and Maria was worried about dehydration and about his judgement, which exhaustion was beginning to make erratic.
She proposed a small exchange: if he would put on the safety harness that hung in the cab, she would arrange for water and food to be sent up by rope.
"That's not a trick," she said. "It's so that I can sleep tonight."
He laughed, reluctantly, and agreed.
It was the first concession of the day, and Maria knew that such incremental steps mattered more than any grand speech.
In the early afternoon, Carl issued what amounted to an ultimatum: he would come down only if the developer, Graham Lyle, came to the site and apologized in person.
The senior officers were reluctant, fearing that a confrontation would escalate the situation, but Maria argued that Carl needed to see that someone with power had heard him.
Lyle arrived at three, irritated, defensive and faintly belligerent, and he began by describing Carl's protest as a stunt.
Maria took him aside and spoke to him quietly for ten minutes; she later refused to say exactly what she had told him, but when he picked up the radio, his tone had changed.

He did not admit liability, which his lawyers had forbidden, but he acknowledged that the subcontractors had been treated callously, and he committed, in writing, to a fund that would pay the wages the vanished contractor owed.
Maria had the document photographed and sent up the rope with a flask of tea, so that Carl could read it with his own eyes.
It was not quite an apology, and it was not quite a victory, but it was a form of vindication, and Carl seemed to understand that it was the most he was likely to get.
He still did not move.
It was only at six, when the light was fading, that Maria played him a voice message his wife had recorded, in which Ellie asked him to come home in time to read her a story.
Negotiators are taught to use such messages cautiously, since they can inflame a situation as easily as calm it, and Maria had kept this one in reserve all day.
For a long time, the radio was silent.
The child's voice seemed to offer him a solace that no written promise could.
Then Carl said, very quietly, "All right. I'm coming down."
He descended slowly, attached to the harness, while the firefighters waiting at the bottom of the ladder held their breath.
When he reached the ground, he was not arrested immediately; Maria had insisted that he first be checked by paramedics and allowed to speak to his wife.

He was later given a caution rather than a prosecution, and the fund that Lyle had promised eventually paid every subcontractor on the site, a gesture he later described, with unexpected magnanimity, as overdue.
When a young officer asked Maria afterwards how she had done it, she shrugged.
"Nobody climbs down for a stranger," she said. "They climb down for a future they can believe in. My job is just to keep them talking until they can see one."

The cottage on the shore of Coniston Water had been Marcus's idea, and it was, like most of Marcus's ideas, slightly too expensive, an extravagant gesture that he justified as an investment in friendship.

Twenty-five years had passed since the four of them had graduated from Durham, and in that time they had met as a group only twice, at a wedding and a funeral, both times too briefly for anything except promises to do this properly. They had become, in the way of old friends, slightly estranged without ever quarrelling.
Now, finally, they were doing it properly: a whole weekend, no children, no partners, and, Rob insisted, no discussion of mortgages.
Their lives had diverged in ways that none of them could have predicted at twenty-one.
Marcus, once the most idealistic of the group, had become a banker in Frankfurt, prosperous, divorced and, by his own self-deprecating admission, faintly ridiculous in his expensive jackets.
Anjali was a GP in Leeds with three teenagers and a formidable reputation among her patients.
Freya had moved to Copenhagen and written four novels, one of which, to the group's delight and slight alarm, contained a character whose eccentricity was unmistakably Rob's.
And Rob taught history at a comprehensive school in Kendal and remained, as he had always been, the source of most of the jokes and the target of the rest.
The banter began before Rob had even got out of his car.
"You haven't changed a bit," Anjali called from the door, "which is not, I should warn you, a compliment."
"And you've aged magnificently," Rob replied. "Like a cheese."

Marcus, who had arrived first and claimed the best bedroom, was accused within minutes of treating the weekend as a hostile takeover, and Freya, who had flown in from Denmark, was greeted with cheerful derision for her new habit of saying "one" instead of "you".
It was an idiosyncratic kind of affection, expressed almost entirely through mockery, and an outsider would have found it baffling.
But the teasing had its own strict etiquette, developed over three years of sharing a crumbling house and a single functioning radiator.

You could ridicule someone's clothes, their career and their taste in music without mercy, but never their real wounds, and the sharper the joke, the warmer the tone had to be. The rules were frivolous in appearance and serious in purpose.
Within an hour, the twenty-five years had collapsed, and they were arguing about the same things they had argued about at twenty, with exactly the same arguments.
That evening, in a spirit of shameless indulgence, they cooked badly, drank too much wine and told stories that each of them remembered differently.
There was the night Marcus had tried to cook a turkey in a kettle, and the exam Rob had sat with a traffic cone on his head, for reasons that had never been satisfactorily explained.
Freya, who had used several of these anecdotes in her novels, insisted that her fictional versions were more accurate than the originals.
"Fiction is just memory with the boring parts removed," she said. "And posterity gets the better version."
"Then my life must be very fictional," said Rob. "I don't remember any of it."
The stories were funny, but the laughter had a bittersweet edge.
Later, when the others had gone quiet by the fire, Anjali looked around the room with a wistful expression.
"Do you ever think we peaked at twenty-one?" she said.
It was a moment of nostalgia so pure that nobody could mock it, and for a while nobody tried.
It was Rob, of course, who spoiled it, although not in the way they expected.
He cleared his throat and said, in the same light tone he used for jokes, that he had something to tell them, and that he would like them to promise not to be boring about it.
Six months earlier, he had been diagnosed with Parkinson's disease.

It was early, the prognosis was reasonable, and he would probably be able to keep teaching for several years, but the disease would progress, slowly but inexorably, and his hands had already begun to shake.
The silence that followed was the first real silence of the weekend.
Anjali, the doctor, asked him the right questions in a calm, professional voice, and he answered them candidly, with a stoicism that somehow made it harder to bear.
Marcus got up and stood at the window, looking out at the dark lake, and Freya, who was usually never without words, found that she had none.
"This is exactly what I asked you not to do," Rob said gently. "I didn't come here to be mourned. I came here to be insulted, as usual."
It was Marcus, unexpectedly, who understood first.

He turned from the window and said, with enormous seriousness, that he had always known Rob would find a way to become the centre of attention, and that the sheer audacity of this method was shameless and frankly excessive.
Rob laughed so much that he had to sit down.

The banter resumed, gentler now, and it carried them through the evening, and it seemed to Freya that the jokes were doing the work that sympathy could not: they were telling him that he was still himself, and that, oddly, was a solace. Marcus, in a rare moment of magnanimity, even gave Rob the best bedroom.
At dawn, the four of them walked down to the jetty in the cold, as they had once walked down to the river in Durham after exams, and, against every sensible instinct, went swimming.
The water was so cold that it hurt, and they shrieked like students in a brief, ridiculous euphoria.
Afterwards, wrapped in towels on the jetty, they made a promise that they had made many times before and broken every time: to do this every year.
The moment was ephemeral, and they all knew it, which is perhaps why Anjali proposed a heartfelt toast with a flask of coffee. This time, for reasons none of them needed to say aloud, they kept it.

The email arrived on a wet Friday afternoon in November, when Professor Alasdair Munro was halfway through a pile of undergraduate essays and wondering, not for the first time, whether he ought to have retired the year before.
In the summer he would become an emeritus professor, which, as far as he could tell, meant keeping his office and losing his salary.
The email came from Professor Kwesi Ampofo, who chaired the committee appointing a new professor of computational biology at an institute in Toronto.
One of the candidates on the shortlist was Dr. Astrid Berglund, who had done her doctorate in Munro's laboratory twelve years earlier, and she had named him as a referee.
Professor Ampofo did not want a letter.

"Written references have become so laudatory as to be almost useless," he wrote. "Every candidate is exceptional, and every weakness is a strength in disguise. I shall be in Durham next week for a conference, and I would be grateful for half an hour of your time and your candid view."
The request was laudable, Munro thought, but it put him in an extremely uncomfortable position.
He read the email twice, closed his laptop and went for a long walk along the river.
Astrid Berglund had arrived in Durham at twenty-two, a Swedish prodigy who had already published two papers and who made no attempt to hide that she found most of her new colleagues slow.

She was, by any measure, the most gifted student he had ever supervised: within a year she had built a model of protein folding that was faster than anything in the published literature, and her thesis remained one of the seminal works in the field.
Her confidence was as precocious as her talent, and she had never been ingratiating, even with people who could help her career.
She was also, by the same measure, the most difficult.
She was abrasive in meetings, contemptuous of work she considered careless, and capable of a derisive silence that was worse than any insult.
It was not that she was haughty; she simply did not see why anyone's feelings should matter more than the truth.
Some colleagues admired her as a maverick, while others simply thought she was rude.

Two research assistants left the group, a process the department euphemistically described as rebalancing, and a technician named Gail once left the laboratory in tears after Astrid described her careful measurements, in front of everyone, as "decorative".
Munro had remonstrated with her more than once.
She had listened, apologized grudgingly, and carried on exactly as before.
The real rift had come in her third year.
While checking some old data, Astrid found an error in the most cited paper of Munro's career, a study that had made his name and that younger researchers still tried to emulate.
The mistake did not destroy the paper's conclusions, but it weakened them considerably.
Rather than tell him privately, she presented her findings, clearly and compellingly, at an international conference in Stockholm, in a session he was chairing, in front of three hundred people.
Munro could still remember the heat in his face as the room turned to look at him.
He had responded badly.
In the questions afterwards, he had been patronizing, suggesting that she had misunderstood the method, and when it became clear that she had not, he had said nothing at all.
He published a correction six months later, but he never thanked her, and she never apologized for the way she had done it.
She finished her thesis in a strained silence, left for a job in industry, and, as far as he knew, had not mentioned his name since.
They met the following Tuesday in a quiet corner of the university library.
Professor Ampofo had a warm, equable voice and the unhurried manner of a man who had conducted a great many of these conversations.
"Let me start with the obvious question," he said. "How good is she?"

"She's the most talented scientist I've ever trained," Munro said. "Her work on protein folding was genuinely revelatory, and I don't use that word lightly. In my experience, her mathematical ability is unsurpassed."
"She sounds formidably gifted," Ampofo said. "And the rest?"
Munro had rehearsed several versions of the next part.
One of them was generous to the point of dishonesty; another, he suspected, was his own resentment dressed up as objectivity.

"She's not without her flaws," he said at last. "She can be abrasive, and at times she's been disparaging about colleagues' work in ways that did real damage. Two people left my group partly because of her. I'd be lying if I told you she was easy to manage."
"Would you hire her again?"
There was a long pause.
"Yes," Munro said. "But there are things I'd do differently, and to be fair to her, most of them are mine."
He had not planned to tell Ampofo about Stockholm, but he found that he could not give an honest account of Astrid without it.
He described the conference, the error and his own reaction, and he did not soften the part that reflected badly on him.

"She was right about the paper," he said. "Her way of telling me was an indiscretion, certainly, and a painful one. But my response was worse. I was an eminent professor being corrected by a student in public, and I behaved as if the problem was her manners rather than my mistake."
Ampofo was quiet for a moment.
"That's unusually candid of you," he said.

"You asked me to be candid," Munro said, and then, because it seemed important to be precise, he added: "Some of what people found difficult about her was simply a refusal to defer to people who hadn't earned it. I was one of those people. I've had twelve years of retrospection to work that out."
Ampofo thanked him, magnanimously declined to ask any further questions about the paper, and said that the committee would decide by the end of the month.
Walking home, Munro felt oddly exposed, as though he had given evidence against himself in a trial nobody had asked him to attend.
In January, Munro read in a university newsletter that Dr. Astrid Berglund had been appointed to the chair in Toronto.
A week later, a card arrived at his office, written in the same small, fierce handwriting he remembered from her laboratory notebooks.

"Kwesi told me what you said," she had written. "Thank you for not making me sound nicer than I am. And thank you for the part about Stockholm. I have waited twelve years for somebody to say it, and I did not expect it to be you."
At the bottom, in smaller letters, she had added: "I should have told you privately. I was twenty-four and furious with everybody. I am sorry about Gail."
Munro, an undemonstrative man, read the card several times.
Then he put it in the top drawer of his desk, where he kept the few things he did not want to lose, and went back to his essays, feeling lighter than he had in years.
The parcel arrived at the offices of Larkspur, a small independent publisher in Bristol, on a wet Monday morning in February.
Margot Delacroix recognized the handwriting on the label before she had even picked it up, and she felt her heart lift and sink at the same time.
The press received hundreds of unsolicited manuscripts a year, but this one was different.
Inside was a manuscript of almost six hundred pages and a short note: "My first novel in ten years. I wanted you to see it before anyone else. With affection, as always, Lionel."
Lionel Achterberg had been, for most of Margot's adult life, the most eminent novelist she knew.

He had won a major literary prize in the 1980s, and his early novels, with their lyrical prose and their melancholy portraits of provincial England, were still taught in universities. In his prime he had been prolific, publishing a novel every two years, and critics had begun to lament his long silence.
More importantly, he had given Margot her first job, as his assistant, when she was twenty-two and had no qualifications except a passion for books.
Everything she had become, she sometimes thought, she owed to him, and she had watched his eminence grow and then, slowly, begin to fade.
She took the manuscript home and read it over three evenings, with mounting dismay.
It was not that the novel was incompetent; Lionel was incapable of writing a clumsy sentence.
It was not mediocrity, exactly; it was something sadder, a book without life in it.

The story of an ageing composer revisiting the scenes of his youth meandered for hundreds of pages without tension, and the prose, once so precise, had become ponderous and self-indulgent, as though the author were listening admiringly to his own voice.
Worse, several passages seemed to be pastiches of his own early work, as if he had forgotten that he had already written them.
Her assistant, Tessa, read the first hundred pages and came into her office looking stricken.
"It's not good, is it?" she said quietly. "I kept hoping it would get better."
"It doesn't," Margot said.
They both knew what publishing it would mean.

Critics who had revered Lionel for forty years would be obliged to review it, and the reviews would be kind in the way that is worse than cruelty, full of phrases about late style and the privileges of a master.
It would not destroy his reputation, but it would diminish it and hasten his slide into obscurity, and it would be the last thing that many readers, and perhaps posterity, remembered.
Margot could have written him a letter, as editors usually did, full of careful praise and regret.
Instead, she drove to Somerset and took him to lunch at the pub near his cottage, because she felt that a refusal from her deserved to be delivered in person.
He looked older than she remembered, thinner and more hesitant, and he ordered his food twice, as if he had forgotten doing it the first time.
"Well?" he said at last, with a smile that did not quite conceal his anxiety. "Don't keep an old man in suspense."

She had rehearsed the conversation many times and had resolved not to hide behind euphemism, and she began, as she had planned, with what was true and good: the beauty of individual sentences, the tenderness of the scenes with the composer's sister.
Then she said, as gently as she could, that she did not think Larkspur should publish it.
"I don't think it's worthy of you," she said. "And I would hate to be the one who put a book into the world that doesn't do you justice."
For a long time he said nothing, and she braced herself for anger, or worse, for tears.
Instead, he laughed softly and looked out of the window at the rain.
"Thank God," he said. "I was afraid you were going to say yes."
His response was more magnanimous than anything she had dared to hope for.
He told her then what he had told nobody else.
Six months earlier, his doctor had diagnosed an incipient dementia, and the prognosis was uncertain: it might be years before the illness became severe, or it might be months.
He had written the novel in a kind of compulsive frenzy, trying to prove to himself that his mind was still his own.

"Somewhere around page three hundred, I knew it wasn't working," he said. "But I couldn't tell whether that was the book or the illness. Perhaps it was an old man's indulgence, but I needed someone I trusted to tell me the truth."
"Other publishers would have taken it," Margot said, "for your name."
"I know," Lionel said. "That's precisely why I sent it to you."
"It would have been patronizing to pretend," Margot said.
He reached across the table and, without a trace of reproach, patted her hand, as he used to do when she was twenty-two and had made a mistake in a letter.
"You were always the only one who would say no to me," he said. "It's the most valuable quality an editor can have, and the rarest."
On the drive back to Bristol, Margot found herself thinking not about the novel but about the anecdotes Lionel had told her over lunch, once the difficult conversation was over.

He had described meeting a famous poet as a nervous young man, a disastrous first reading in a freezing library in the north, and the week in 1983 when he had learned that he had won the prize, with an unguarded, wistful wit that had been absent from every page of the manuscript.
A week later she wrote to him.
She did not want the novel, she said, and she was sorry.

But if he was willing, she would like to publish something else: a memoir, told in his own voice, of fifty years of an illustrious career, and she would come to Somerset every fortnight with a recorder and a notebook to help him shape it, for as long as he wanted to talk.
His reply came by return of post, and it consisted of a single line.
"I accept," he wrote, "with more gratitude than I can decently express."
The paper had made Konrad Weiss famous.

Published in 2019, it reported that a protein discovered in his laboratory in Freiburg could slow the degeneration of nerve cells in mice, and it had been cited more than two thousand times, attracted millions of euros in funding and turned Weiss into one of the most eminent figures in his field.
Colleagues spoke of him, only half joking, as a future laureate.
Lena Hartmann had joined his lab as a postdoctoral researcher two years earlier, and her project was to extend the original findings to human cells.
For eighteen months, nothing worked.
She repeated the key experiment eleven times, adjusting every variable she could think of, and each time the protein had no measurable effect.
At first she assumed the fault was hers; she was meticulous, but even meticulous people make mistakes.
Then, one evening, while comparing her images with those in the original paper, she noticed something that made her go cold.
Two panels in the third figure, supposedly showing cells from different experiments, were the same photograph, rotated and with the contrast subtly adjusted.
She spent the night trying to find an innocent explanation.
It was possible, she told herself, that a student had simply uploaded the wrong file, an erroneous but honest mistake of the kind that journals corrected every week.
But when she searched the lab's archival server for the raw data behind the figure, the files for one of the panels did not exist.
The discrepancy was no longer something she could explain away.
The next morning she showed the images to Tomás Ortega, a doctoral student from Spain whose entire thesis was built on the 2019 paper.
He looked at them for a long time and then closed the laptop.
"Please don't do anything yet," he said quietly. "If that paper goes, my doctorate goes with it. Three years of my life."
Lena understood his fear, and shared it.
She knew what happened to junior researchers who accused powerful men: their contracts were not renewed, their references were lukewarm, and their names became quietly associated with trouble.
Nevertheless, she asked to see Weiss in his office.
She had prepared carefully, printing the two panels side by side and overlaying them so that the correspondence was unmistakable.
"I'm not sure the figure holds up," she said, keeping her voice steady. "With respect, these two images appear to be identical."
Weiss studied the pages for less than a minute.
Then he smiled, with the patient benevolence of a man accustomed to being right.
"A clerical error," he said. "One of my former students prepared that figure, and she was not always careful. We'll send the journal a correction."
When Lena mentioned that the raw data were missing, his smile did not change, but his voice did.
"You have a promising career, Dr. Hartmann," he said. "It would be a pity to waste your energy on archaeology when there is so much real science to do."
It was not quite a threat, but it was not quite anything else, either, and Lena left the office indignant and shaken.
For a week, Lena said nothing to anyone.

She thought about the patients with degenerative diseases who were following the research in the hope of a treatment, and about the other laboratories around the world that might be wasting years, as she had, trying to replicate a spurious result.
She also thought, less nobly, about the insidious pressure of her own precarious contract, which had fourteen months to run.
In the end, it was Tomás who decided it.
He came to her office on a Friday evening with a folder of his own.
He had gone through the lab's other papers, figure by figure, and found similar anomalies in three of them, all involving images that had passed through Weiss's own computer.
"If I build my thesis on this, I'm complicit," he said. "I'd rather lose three years than spend thirty pretending."
The next Monday, they went together to Dr. Anja Pohl, the university's officer for research integrity, and submitted a formal complaint.
The inquiry took seven months and was conducted, as the rules required, in strict confidentiality.
Weiss was adamant from the beginning that he was the victim of an error by others.
He blamed the former student, who was now working in Zurich and who, when contacted, produced emails showing that she had sent him the original, unaltered images.
The metadata embedded in the files revealed the rest: the duplicated images had been edited on Weiss's computer, under his account, late at night, a week before the paper was submitted.
The committee concluded that the evidence of fabrication was conclusive.

The journal retracted the 2019 paper, along with two others, and Weiss resigned before the university could dismiss him, issuing a statement in which he expressed regret for "irregularities" without admitting responsibility for them or offering a single remorseful word to the students whose work he had compromised.
For a man who had cultivated his reputation so carefully, the ending was ignominious.
The lab was dissolved, and its researchers scattered.

Lena expected her career to suffer, and for a while it did: two applications were rejected without explanation, and she heard, indirectly, that she had acquired a reputation for being difficult, a notoriety she had never sought.

But a year later, a laboratory in Zurich that had spent two years failing to replicate the Freiburg result offered her a position, explicitly because of what she had done, and it felt like vindication.
Tomás rebuilt his thesis around the failure itself, a painstaking account of why the protein did not work, and defended it successfully two years late.
At the celebration afterwards, he raised a glass to her.
"To the most expensive negative result in the history of the university," he said, and everyone laughed.

Lena laughed too, but she was thinking of something Anja Pohl had told her at the end of the inquiry: that science corrects itself only when individual people are willing to pay the cost of correcting it.
Imogen Pryce had known Tobias Wren for forty years, since they were students together at an art school in London, and for most of that time she had been his most devoted admirer.
His early abstract paintings, enormous canvases of torn, luminous colour, had seemed to her works of an audacity unmatched in their generation.
She had written about him in her first published review, and she had defended him fiercely when other critics dismissed his work as chaotic.
Her advocacy had helped to rescue him from obscurity, and he had never forgotten it.

Now, at sixty-two, Tobias was being honoured with a retrospective at a major gallery in Liverpool, and Imogen, who had become the chief art critic of a national newspaper, had been asked to review it.
She knew before she went that it would be difficult.
Over the past fifteen years, Tobias's work had changed.
The violence had gone out of it, replaced by a graceful, decorative competence that sold extremely well.
His recent canvases hung in the lobbies of banks and luxury hotels, and a gallery in New York could barely keep up with demand.
Imogen had said nothing about this to him, and he had never asked.
Their friendship had survived two divorces, a bankruptcy and the death of his son, but she was not certain it could survive her candour.
The curator, Dev Mistry, met her at the entrance on the morning of the press view.
He had arranged the exhibition chronologically, so that visitors moved through Tobias's career from the cramped rooms of his youth to the spacious, brightly lit halls of his success.
The first three rooms took Imogen's breath away, as they always had.
The paintings from the 1980s were visceral, almost violent, their pigment scraped and slashed as if the artist had been fighting with the canvas and had only just won.
There was a melancholy series painted after his first marriage ended, dark and translucent, that she still considered among the finest British paintings of the century.
Then came the later rooms.
The paintings were larger, cleaner and more expensive-looking, and they were, she thought, curiously empty.
The colours were harmonious, the brushstrokes elegant, and the compositions balanced with a practised ease; everything that had once been dangerous in his work had been smoothed away.
It was as if the artist had become a connoisseur of his own style, reproducing it with an immaculate, lifeless precision.
"They're beautiful," Dev said, watching her face.
"They are," Imogen agreed. "That's rather the problem."
She wrote the review over two days, rewriting it more times than anything she had written in years.
Her first draft was so cautious that it said nothing; her second was so harsh that it was unfair.
She did not want to disparage a career that she admired, nor did she want to write the kind of hollow praise that readers could recognize instantly as a favour to a friend.
She wanted to explain what had been lost: the idiosyncratic, reckless energy that had once made his paintings unmistakably his own.
In the end, she decided to write exactly what she saw.
The published review praised the early work in terms that were almost lyrical, describing the paintings of the 1980s as "a record of a mind at war with its own talent".
Then it turned, carefully, to the later rooms.

"What strikes me in these paintings is their ease," she wrote. "There is a tension, in all great art, between control and risk, and in the recent work that tension has quietly been resolved in favour of control. The virtuosity is undeniable, but the paintings no longer seem to need us. They are superbly made, and they don't quite come off."
She ended by saying that an artist capable of the first three rooms was capable of anything, and that she hoped the retrospective would prove to be not a summary but a turning point.
Tobias did not call.

For three weeks, Imogen heard nothing from him, and she learned from mutual friends that he was wounded and angry, and that he had described her review, in a phrase that was quoted back to her twice, as "a knife wrapped in a compliment".
Other critics, sensing a quarrel, wrote pieces that were far crueller than hers, and one magazine published a cartoon of Tobias painting a hotel wallpaper that held him up to public derision.

Imogen found the mockery painful, partly because she felt responsible for it and partly because, in her most honest moments, she suspected it was not entirely undeserved. For the first time in forty years, they were estranged.
She considered writing to apologize, and decided against it.
She was not sorry for what she had written; she was only sorry that it had hurt him.
The distinction seemed important, and she did not think an apology could preserve it.
She had meant the review as praise and reproach at once, and she could not take back one without the other.
Eight months later, a flat parcel arrived at her flat, wrapped in brown paper and tied with string.
Inside was a small painting, no larger than a book, and a note.

The painting was nothing like the work in the later rooms: it was rough, dark and unfinished-looking, with a single slash of red across the middle, and it was, Imogen thought at once, the most alive thing he had made in twenty years.
The note said: "I've moved to Cornwall, stopped answering the New York gallery and started again. It's terrible, most of it. But it's mine. You were right, damn you. Come and see."
It felt less like vindication than relief.
Imogen hung the painting above her desk, where she could see it while she worked, and reflected that posterity would judge the paintings, not the reviews.
Critics, she had always believed, were supposed to serve art rather than artists; it had taken her forty years and one terrible month to discover that, occasionally, the two could be the same thing.
The first person to notice was an angler named Megan Hughes, who arrived at her favourite stretch of the river Fenn at six in the morning and found it silver with dead fish.

Trout and young salmon lay in their thousands along the banks, and the water had a faint, acrid smell that caught in the back of her throat. Carcasses drifted in the shallows, and gulls had already begun to gather.
She photographed the devastation, walked upstream for two kilometres until she reached the outflow pipe of the Calder Chemicals plant, and photographed that too.

By nine o'clock, her pictures had been shared thousands of times, and by noon the Environment Agency had confirmed that ammonia from the plant, a toxin lethal to fish even in small concentrations, had killed almost every fish along eight kilometres of river.
Rachel Ambrose, the chief executive of Calder, heard the news in a boardroom in Manchester, where she was presenting the company's annual results to investors.

She had run the company for six years, and its profitability had improved in every one of them, largely because of a programme of cost reductions that she had personally championed and that analysts had lauded.

She drove north that afternoon, and by the time she reached the plant in Northumberland she had learned the cause: a corroded valve had failed during the night, releasing a tank of effluent into the river.
The plant manager, Owen Price, met her at the gate, grey with exhaustion.
In his office, he showed her a maintenance report from eighteen months earlier, which had recommended replacing that valve and several others.
The work had been scheduled, then deferred, then deferred again, as part of the savings that the head office had demanded.
"I signed off the delays," Owen said, visibly remorseful. "But I was told the budget wasn't negotiable."
Rachel recognized the budget; she had approved it herself.
Julian Frost, the company's director of communications, arrived that evening with a draft statement.

It expressed "deep regret for any environmental impact", described the spill as "an unforeseen technical incident", and promised that the company was "cooperating fully with the relevant authorities".
It did not mention the maintenance report.
"Our lawyers are clear," Julian said. "Admitting that the failure was foreseeable would expose us to enormous liability. We express regret; we don't accept fault."
Rachel read the statement twice.
It was a masterpiece of euphemism.
Every sentence was accurate, and together they amounted to a lie, the kind of statement that breeds public distrust.
A public meeting had been called for the following evening in the town hall at Fennbridge, and Julian advised her strongly not to attend.
The mood in the town was hostile, he warned, the outcry had already reached the national newspapers, and anything she said could be used against the company in court.
Rachel went anyway.
The hall was packed with anglers, farmers, parents and local councillors, and the anger in the room was palpable; someone had pinned Megan's photographs to the wall beside the stage.
Many of those present had long-standing grievances against the plant, from night-time noise to lorries on narrow lanes.
When Rachel stood up to speak, there were jeers from the back.
She did not read the statement.
"I'm not going to talk about regret for any impact," she said. "The impact is on that wall. Eight kilometres of your river are dead, and it's our fault."
The room went quiet.
She explained, without euphemism, that the valve had been due for replacement, that the work had been postponed to save money, and that the budget which postponed it had been approved by her.
"So this was not an unforeseen incident," she said. "It was foreseeable, and it was foreseen. I take full responsibility for that, and there is no excuse for it."
She then set out what the company would do, and she was careful to promise nothing she could not deliver.
Calder would pay for the full restoration of the river, however long it took, under the supervision of an independent panel that would include local anglers.
It would publish the results of stringent monitoring at the outflow every month, and it would replace every valve of the same age at all of its plants within a year.
"You have no reason to trust me," she said. "So don't. Watch what we do, and judge us by that. That's what accountability means."
Megan Hughes, standing near the front, asked the question that everyone was thinking.
"Why should we believe this isn't just a more sophisticated kind of posturing?"
Rachel considered the question seriously before answering.
"Because my lawyers told me not to say any of it," she said. "Better public relations would have been much cheaper."
For the first time that evening, a few people laughed, though grimly.
The consequences were immediate and severe.

The company's share price fell by a fifth in two days, the board held an emergency meeting at which two directors demanded her resignation, and the regulatory authorities, armed with her public admission, imposed the largest fine in the history of the region.
Julian resigned, telling colleagues that she had committed an act of corporate suicide.
But the board did not dismiss her, partly because the largest shareholders and other stakeholders, to general surprise, supported her.
They had seen other companies attempt to minimize disasters of this kind and watched the concealment become a second scandal, far more damaging than the first.

Within eighteen months the share price had largely recovered, a partial vindication that she was careful not to celebrate, and the independent panel reported that the river was recovering too, more slowly.
Two years after the spill, Megan Hughes caught a small trout at the stretch where she had found the dead fish, the first sign of the resurgence that the panel had predicted.
She photographed it, released it and, after some hesitation, sent the picture to Rachel.
She added only one line: "Still watching. But this is a start."
Rachel printed the photograph and pinned it to the wall of her office, next to the maintenance report that she had never allowed herself to throw away.

Three times a year, the editorial board of the Ashdown Dictionary of English met in a panelled room above the publisher's offices in Bath, and three times a year its chief editor, Dr. Miriam Castell, wondered how a book about words could produce so many arguments about them.
The dictionary had been in print since 1911, and its ninth edition was due at the printers in six weeks.
Most of the forty thousand revisions had been approved without discussion, but three items remained, and Miriam suspected, correctly, that they would take the whole afternoon.
Around the table sat the usual cast.

Professor Crispin Farrow had served on the board for thirty years; a grammarian of the old school, fluent in the nomenclature of Latin grammar, he had been gently ridiculed in the newspapers for decades and rather enjoyed it.
He saw the dictionary as a keeper of standards, and every new edition as an invitation to surrender.

Opposite him sat Kasia Borowska, the youngest lexicographer on the staff, who spent her days on meticulous analysis of a corpus of four billion words of real English and had little patience with anyone who told the language how to behave; Crispin, in turn, regarded her faith in data as a modern heresy.

Beatrix Wynne, the publishing director, attended for commercial reasons and made no secret of the fact that she would welcome a little notoriety, provided it sold books; Crispin called her, not entirely affectionately, the board's resident philistine.
The first item was the word "literally".

Kasia's corpus showed that in about a third of its appearances it no longer meant "in a literal sense" but served simply as an intensifier, as in "I was literally dying of embarrassment", and she proposed recording this as a second sense.
Crispin was indignant.
"That isn't a second sense," he said. "It's a lazy colloquialism, and it's the opposite of the first one. If we give it our blessing, we're not describing the language; we're helping it degenerate."
"With respect, Crispin, that's exactly the prescriptive attitude this dictionary abandoned a century ago," Kasia replied. "We record how words are used. We don't legislate."

She pointed out that the emphatic use was hardly new: it appeared in Dickens, in Mark Twain and in Fitzgerald, whose Gatsby "literally glowed", and it had been common in the vernacular for two centuries.
The idea that it was simply wrong had long since become a truism, repeated most confidently by people who had never looked at the evidence.
Beatrix, who had been scrolling through her phone, looked up.
"Can I just say that 'Dictionary surrenders to literally' is a headline I would happily pay for?"
Nobody laughed except Beatrix.
The second item, the word "decimate", produced the same argument in a slightly different costume.
Its original sense, from a Roman punishment in which one soldier in ten was killed, had long been archaic, and almost every modern use meant simply "to destroy a large part of something".

Crispin conceded that nobody now used the word in its Latin sense, but he argued that a dictionary which recorded every semantic drift without comment would end up with no standards at all, only a register of popular mistakes.
Kasia retorted that his distinction between meaning and mistake was a kind of snobbery dressed up as scholarship.
"The whole history of English is a history of popular mistakes," she said. "Nice once meant foolish. Silly once meant blessed. Should we have proscribed those too?"
"Perhaps we should," Crispin said, "and perhaps I would have lost that argument too."
Miriam, who had heard versions of this exchange for a decade, let it run for exactly as long as it seemed useful, and then made a note.
The third item was the most delicate, and it did not come from inside the building.
A group of linguists had written to the dictionary pointing out that its example sentences told a story of their own.
The examples for "shrill", "hysterical" and "bossy" all described women, while those for "brilliant" and "authoritative" almost all described men.
Some of the words had carried a gendered connotation since ancient Greek medicine blamed certain illnesses on the womb.

None of the definitions was derogatory, the letter said, and none of the sentences was false, but together they reproduced a quiet misogyny that the dictionary's authority made more insidious, not less.
To Miriam's surprise, the first to respond was Kasia, and not in the way she had expected.
"Those examples came from the corpus," Kasia said. "They're real sentences. If we change them, aren't we doing exactly what I accused Crispin of doing, deciding how the language ought to look?"
It was Crispin, of all people, who disagreed.

"The corpus shows us what people say," he said slowly. "The examples are what we choose to show. Choosing is an editorial act, Kasia. It always has been. I've spent thirty years insisting that we exercise judgement, and I'm not going to stop now just because, for once, it puts me on the side of people who usually revile me."
Beatrix observed that a dictionary accused of sexism would sell extremely well, and was ignored.
By five o'clock the discussion had begun to repeat itself, and Miriam put down her pen.

"If I could pull the threads together," she said, "I think we agree on more than it sounds. Nobody here wants the dictionary to become a rule book, and nobody wants it to become a mirror that simply reflects whatever it's shown."
"Where we all seem to agree is that we describe meaning. The sticking point, in our jargon, is how much we prescribe."
She proposed a synthesis.
"Literally" would gain its second sense, labelled as used colloquially for emphasis, with a short usage note explaining that some readers still object to it.
"Decimate" would have its Roman origin recorded in the etymology and its modern sense given first.
And every example sentence in the dictionary would be reviewed, not to hide how English was used, but to stop the dictionary's own choices from reinforcing a stereotype.
"And the usage note?" Crispin asked. "Who writes it?"
"You and Kasia, together," Miriam said. "If the two of you can agree on three sentences, I suspect the rest of the English-speaking world can live with them."
Kasia laughed; Crispin, after a pause, did too.
The usage note took them eleven drafts and two long lunches.

The final version was forty-one words long, neither euphemistic nor dogmatic, and it said, in effect, that "literally" was widely used figuratively for emphasis, that this use had a long history, and that careful writers often avoided it in formal contexts.

When the ninth edition appeared in the spring, the newspapers did exactly what Beatrix had hoped: one headline declared that the dictionary had "literally lost the plot", and sales in the first month were the best in twenty years.
Few reviewers noticed the revised example sentences, which was, Miriam thought, exactly as it should be.
A dictionary, she had come to believe, could not stand outside the language it described; it could only decide, as honestly as possible, which way it was facing.
Crispin sent her a postcard of the Roman baths with a single line on the back: "Decimated, but not defeated."
For five years, Priya Raman had lived in the company of a book that nobody else seemed to love.

It was a small, battered psalter, its leather binding cracked and its pages stained by centuries of damp, and it had sat almost unnoticed in the special collections of the university library in Edinburgh since the nineteenth century, its provenance lost in obscurity.
The catalogue dated it to the eleventh century, but Priya was convinced that the catalogue was wrong.
Over five years she had meticulously documented every letter form, every correction and every faded stroke of colour.
The script, the pigments and a handful of archaic readings in the Latin text all pointed, she believed, to a monastic workshop of the eighth century, perhaps on the island of Iona.
If she was right, the psalter would be one of the oldest surviving books made in Scotland, her doctorate would make her name, and her scholarly reputation would be secure.
Her supervisor, Dr. Fiona Baird, had been encouraging from the start, although she had occasionally warned Priya against falling in love with her own hypothesis.
"The manuscript doesn't care what we want it to be," she liked to say. "Our job is to listen to it."
The thesis was finished, bound and submitted, and the viva, the oral examination at which Priya would have to defend it, was a week away.

The external examiner was Professor Anders Halvorsen of the University of Oslo, an eminent palaeographer whose reviews were so exacting that younger scholars referred to him, only half in jest, as the executioner.
The email arrived on a Tuesday evening, three days before the viva.
Months earlier, Priya had asked a laboratory to date a tiny sample of the parchment by radiocarbon analysis, and the results, delayed by a backlog, had been almost forgotten.
She opened the attachment expecting confirmation.
Instead, the calibrated range was between 890 and 1020, at least a century later than the date on which her entire argument depended.
She read the figures three times, as though they might rearrange themselves if she stared hard enough.
For a wild moment she wondered whether the result might be erroneous, a contaminated sample or a clerical error.
Her next, shameful thought was that nobody else had seen the figures.
The examiners had their copies of the thesis, but the laboratory report was addressed to her alone.
She could say nothing, defend the thesis as written and deal with the discrepancy later, if at all.
She rang Fiona instead, and her supervisor listened without interrupting.
"You know what we have to do," Fiona said at last. "We send the report to both examiners tonight, with a short covering note."
"It will destroy the third chapter," Priya said. "It may destroy the whole thesis."
"It may," Fiona replied. "But concealing it would destroy something more important."
Priya did not sleep much over the next two nights.
She spread her notes across the floor of her flat and went back through her methodology as if she were reading it for the first time, trying to see what a hostile reader would see.

The carbon dates were not infallible, since the calibration curve for that period was notoriously uneven, but she knew that clutching at such technicalities would convince nobody, least of all herself.
The dates measured when the animal whose skin became the parchment had died, and parchment was rarely stored for long before it was used.
Somewhere after midnight on the second night, she began to see another possibility.
The archaic features she had documented were real; she had not imagined them.
But perhaps they belonged not to the book in front of her but to an older book from which it had been copied.

Medieval scribes often reproduced their exemplars with extraordinary fidelity, copying their errors and idiosyncratic spellings verbatim, so that a tenth-century copy of an eighth-century book might preserve the textual fingerprints of its ancestor.
If so, the psalter was not the oldest book of its kind, but it was the only surviving witness to a lost one, which was, she realized with a surprising lightness, almost as interesting.
It was a conjecture, not a proof, and she could not yet substantiate it fully.
She drafted a short statement for the viva, rewriting every sentence until its claims were no stronger than the evidence could bear.
By dawn it was full of cautious phrases: the evidence would seem to suggest, it would be premature to conclude, one plausible interpretation might be.
The viva took place in a panelled room overlooking the Meadows, with rain streaking the windows.
Professor Halvorsen was a tall, grey man with half-moon glasses, and he placed the thesis on the table in front of him as though it were an exhibit in a trial.
Beside him sat the internal examiner, a historian from Priya's own department, who gave her an encouraging nod.
"Before we begin," Priya said, surprising herself, "I'd like to address the radiocarbon report, which I sent you on Tuesday."
Halvorsen raised an eyebrow, and she spoke for five minutes without looking at her notes.
She acknowledged that the report was incompatible with the date she had proposed, and that her third chapter, as written, overstated the certainty of its conclusions.
She then presented her new hypothesis, with every qualification she had written at dawn.
"It would be premature to claim that the exemplar can be dated precisely," she concluded. "But the evidence would seem to suggest that it was considerably older than the surviving copy."
For a long moment Halvorsen said nothing.

Then he asked her to explain, letter by letter, why she believed a particular abbreviation was archaic rather than merely old-fashioned, and for the next two hours he interrogated every link in her reasoning.
At one point her whole argument seemed precarious, resting on the reading of a single damaged line.
Twice she had to admit that she did not know; once she corrected him, politely, on that very line, and he conceded the point with a slight smile.
By the end she felt as though she had been dismantled and reassembled.
They asked her to wait in the corridor while they deliberated.
